synth_text.title: Key Weighted‑Average Actuarial Assumptions (31 March)
synth_text.text:
The Group’s pension scheme liabilities are valued using the projected unit‑credit method, applying a set of principal actuarial assumptions that represent a weighted average of all individual schemes. As of 31 March, the weighted‑average assumptions are:

- **Rate of inflation:** 3.0 %  
- **Rate of increase in salaries:** 2.6 %  
- **Discount rate:** 2.6 %

These figures are used to project future pension payments and deferred revaluations, with the rate of pension increases directly linked to the inflation rate. The weighted‑average approach ensures that the assumptions reflect the overall characteristics of the Group’s diverse pension arrangements.

synth_text.title: Weighted Average Actuarial Assumptions for the Group’s Pension Schemes (31 March)
synth_text.text:
The Group’s pension scheme liabilities are measured using the projected unit‑credit method, applying the principal actuarial assumptions shown below. As of 31 March, the weighted‑average assumptions across all individual schemes are:

- **Rate of inflation:** 2.9 % (used to determine increases in pensions in payment and deferred revaluation)  
- **Rate of increase in salaries:** 2.7 %  
- **Discount rate:** 2.3 % to 2.5 % (reflecting a slight variation among schemes)

These figures represent a consolidated view of the assumptions applied to each scheme, ensuring a consistent basis for liability valuation. The inflation rate directly influences pension revaluation, while the salary growth rate and discount rate are used to project future benefit obligations and present‑value them appropriately.

text.value: 11 Intangible assets (continued)
(a) Intangible assets
RIGHTS AND LICENCES

Certain licences that NEXTDC possesses have an indefinite useful life and are carried at cost less impairment losses and are subject to impairment review at least annually and whenever there is an indication that it may be impaired.

Other licences that NEXTDC acquires are carried at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses. Amortisation is recognised on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful life. The estimated useful life and amortisation method are reviewed at the end of each annual reporting period.
INTERNALLY GENERATED SOFTWARE

Internally developed software is capitalised at cost less accumulated amortisation. Amortisation is calculated using the straight-line basis over the asset’s useful economic life which is generally two to three years. Their useful lives and potential impairment are reviewed at the end of each financial year.
SOFTWARE UNDER DEVELOPMENT

Costs incurred in developing products or systems and costs incurred in acquiring software and licenses that will contribute to future period financial benefits through revenue generation and/or cost reduction are capitalised to software and systems. Costs capitalised include external direct costs of materials and services and employee costs.

Assets in the course of construction include only those costs directly attributable to the development phase and are only recognised following completion of technical feasibility and where the Group has an intention and ability to use the asset.

synth_text.title: NEXTDC Intangible Asset Movements – Summary for the Year Ended 30 June 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary outlines the movements in NEXTDC’s intangible assets for the financial year ended 30 June 2019, compared with the prior year (30 June 2018). The data are presented in thousands of Australian dollars ($'000) and are aligned with the company’s accounting policies for rights and licences, internally generated software, and software under development.

**1. Rights and Licences (Finite‑life licences)**  
- **Cost:** $104 k (unchanged)  
- **Accumulated amortisation:** $(91 k) (increased from $(48 k) in 2018)  
- **Net book amount (30 June 2019):** $13 k (down from $43 k at 1 July 2017)  

**Key movements**  
- Opening net book amount (1 July 2017): $43 k  
- Additions – externally acquired: $13 k  
- Amortisation charged during the year: $(43 k)  
- No internal transfers, re‑classifications or disposals were recorded.  

The net book value fell to $13 k after the sole addition was fully amortised during the year, reflecting the straight‑line amortisation approach applied to licences with a defined useful life.

**2. Internally Generated Software**  
- **Cost:** $9,555 k (up from $8,? k in 2018 – the table shows the current cost)  
- **Accumulated amortisation:** $(3,170 k) (up from $(1,424 k) in 2018)  
- **Net book amount (30 June 2019):** $7,381 k (up from $6,385 k in 2018)  

**Key movements**  
- Opening net book amount (1 July 2017): $442 k  
- Additions – externally acquired: – (none)  
- Additions – internally developed: – (none recorded this year)  
- Amortisation charged: $(1,746 k)  
- Transfers into this class: $7,563 k  
- Transfer between classes (re‑classification): $744 k  
- Disposals: $(618 k)  
- Closing net book amount (30 June 2019): $6,385 k  

The substantial increase in the net book amount is driven primarily by internal transfers of software assets into the “internally generated software” class, offset partially by disposals and amortisation. The straight‑line amortisation over an estimated useful life of two to three years, as described in the policy, is applied to these assets.

**3. Accounting Policy Highlights**  
- **Indefinite‑life licences** are carried at cost less impairment and are reviewed annually for impairment.  
- **Finite‑life licences** and **internally generated software** are amortised on a straight‑line basis over their estimated useful lives, with the useful life and amortisation method reviewed each reporting period.  
- **Software under development** costs are capitalised once technical feasibility is established and are subsequently amortised over the asset’s economic life.

**Conclusion**  
During the year ended 30 June 2019, NEXTDC’s intangible‑asset portfolio saw modest growth in cost and net book value, largely due to internal transfers of software assets. Amortisation continued to be applied consistently in line with the company’s policy of straight‑line allocation over the assets’ useful lives, while no new external acquisitions were made for the internally generated software category. The overall net book value of intangible assets increased, reflecting the company’s ongoing investment in software development and the re‑classification of existing assets.

synth_text.title: NEXTDC Intangible Asset Movements – Summary for the Year Ended 30 June 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary outlines the movements in NEXTDC’s intangible assets between 30 June 2018 and 30 June 2019, focusing on two distinct categories: (1) licences with indefinite useful lives (“Rights and licences”) and (2) internally generated software (“Software under development” and “Internally generated software”). All amounts are presented in thousands of Australian dollars ($'000).

---

### 1. Rights and licences (indefinite‑life assets)

| Item | 30 June 2018 | 30 June 2019 |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| Opening net book amount (1 July 2017) | 8,053 | – |
| Additions – externally acquired | 5,253 | – |
| Additions – internally developed | 1,256 | – |
| Transfers out of the class | (7,563) | – |
| Disposals | (490) | – |
| **Closing net book amount** | 6,509 | 6,509 |
| **Cost of the class** | – | 6,509 |
| **Accumulated amortisation** | – | – |
| **Net book amount (cost less impairment)** | – | 16,284 |

**Key points**  
- These licences are carried at cost less impairment only; no amortisation is recorded.  
- The net book amount fell from $8,053 k to $6,509 k, mainly because of a large transfer out of the class ($7,563 k) and modest disposals ($490 k).  
- The cost of the class at 30 June 2019 is $6,509 k, giving a net book amount of $16,284 k after accounting for any impairment adjustments.

---

### 2. Internally generated software (finite‑life assets)

| Item | 30 June 2018 | 30 June 2019 |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| Opening net book amount (1 July 2017) | 8,538 | – |
| Additions – externally acquired | 5,266 | – |
| Additions – internally developed | 1,256 | – |
| Amortisation (straight‑line, 2‑3 yr life) | (1,789) | – |
| Transfer between classes (into software) | 744 | – |
| Disposals | (1,108) | – |
| **Closing net book amount** | 12,907 | 12,907 |
| **Cost of the class** | – | 16,168 |
| **Accumulated amortisation** | (3,261) | – |
| **Net book amount (cost less amortisation & impairment)** | – | 23,678 |

**Key points**  
- Software assets are amortised over an estimated economic life of two to three years on a straight‑line basis, as per the accounting policy.  
- The net book amount increased from $8,538 k to $12,907 k, driven by significant additions (external $5,266 k and internal $1,256 k) and a transfer into the class ($744 k).  
- Amortisation of $1,789 k and disposals of $1,108 k partially offset the additions.  
- At year‑end, the total cost of the software class is $16,168 k, with accumulated amortisation of $3,261 k, resulting in a net book amount of $23,678 k.

---

### 3. Interpretation in light of accounting policies  

- **Rights and licences**: Because many licences have an indefinite useful life, they are not amortised. Their carrying amount is reviewed annually for impairment only, which explains the absence of amortisation entries.  
- **Internally generated software**: These assets are capitalised once technical feasibility is established and are amortised over their useful economic life (2‑3 years). The straight‑line amortisation recorded aligns with the policy description.  

Overall, NEXTDC’s intangible asset portfolio shows a modest net increase in total net book value, primarily due to the growth of internally generated software, while the indefinite‑life licences experienced a net reduction because of transfers out of the class.

synth_text.title: Lifeway Net Sales Distribution by Dairy Category (Year Ended December 31)
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, Lifeway recorded total net sales of **$93.7 million**. The sales breakdown by product category is as follows:

| Category (as defined by Lifeway) | Net Sales (in $ thousands) | Share of Total Sales |
|----------------------------------|----------------------------|----------------------|
| **Drinkable Kefir (excluding ProBugs)** | $71,822 | **77 %** |
| **Cheese (European‑style soft cheeses, e.g., farmer cheese)** | $11,459 | **12 %** |
| **Cream and other (primarily cream, a kefir by‑product)** | $4,228 | **4 %** |
| **ProBugs Kefir (children’s kefir line)** | $2,780 | **3 %** |
| **Other Dairy (Cupped Kefir, Icelandic Skyr, etc.)** | $1,756 | **2 %** |
| **Frozen Kefir (soft‑serve and pint‑size containers, includes Kefir Shop sales)** | $1,617 | **2 %** |

**Key insights**

- **Drinkable Kefir dominates the portfolio**, contributing three‑quarters of total revenue. This category includes a wide range of organic and non‑organic kefir products, such as low‑fat, non‑fat, whole‑milk, protein‑enriched, and BioKefir varieties.
- **Cheese is the second‑largest segment**, accounting for roughly one‑tenth of sales and representing Lifeway’s European‑style soft cheese offerings.
- **Cream and other** products, largely derived as a by‑product of kefir production, generate a modest 4 % of sales.
- The **ProBugs line**, targeted at children, and **Frozen Kefir** each represent a small but strategic portion of the business (3 % and 2 % respectively).
- **Other Dairy** products, including Cupped Kefir and Icelandic Skyr, together contribute a minor 2 % of total revenue.

Overall, Lifeway’s sales are heavily concentrated in the core drinkable kefir segment, reflecting the company’s focus on cultured dairy beverages while maintaining a diversified portfolio of complementary dairy products.

synth_text.title: Lifeway Net Sales Breakdown by Dairy Product Category (Fiscal Year Ended December 31)
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, Lifeway recorded total net sales of **$103.35 million**. Sales were distributed across six primary dairy product categories, each reflecting a distinct line of offerings:

- **Drinkable Kefir (excluding the ProBugs line)** generated the largest share, with **$78.5 million** in revenue, representing **76 %** of total sales. This category includes a wide range of organic and non‑organic kefir products—low‑fat, non‑fat, whole‑milk, protein‑enriched, and the BioKefir variant that adds extra probiotic cultures.
- **European‑style soft cheeses** contributed **$11.5 million** (11 %). These are farmer‑style cheeses sold in resealable cups.
- **Cream and other**—primarily the cream by‑product of kefir production—accounted for **$5.3 million** (5 %).
- **ProBugs Kefir**, the child‑focused kefir line, produced **$2.8 million** in sales (3 %).
- **Other dairy** products, which include Cupped Kefir and Icelandic Skyr (strained kefir and yogurt in resealable cups), added **$3.8 million** (4 %).
- **Frozen Kefir** (soft‑serve and pint‑size containers, including Lifeway Kefir Shop sales) contributed the smallest portion, **$1.4 million** (1 %).

All of Lifeway’s consolidated revenues stem from cultured dairy products manufactured using common processes and sold through a unified distribution network across the United States. The company reports a single segment, overseen by its chief operating decision makers (CEO, CFO, COO, and board chair). Sales are heavily concentrated among a few large retail customers—two major accounts together accounted for roughly 22 % of net sales, and the ten largest customers represented about 57 % of total revenue.

This breakdown underscores the pivotal role of drinkable kefir in Lifeway’s portfolio, while also highlighting the diversified yet smaller contributions from cheese, cream, child‑focused, other dairy, and frozen kefir offerings.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Summary: 2018 vs 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the fiscal year ended 31 December 2019, the company’s operating revenues fell modestly by 2.0 % to NT$148,202 million (US$4,955 million) from NT$151,253 million in 2018. The decline was driven by lower other operating revenues, a 2.9 % drop in average selling price for foundry wafers, and a 2.5 % depreciation of the New Taiwan dollar. Despite a slight increase in wafer shipments (1.1 %), revenue pressure persisted.

**Cost Structure**  
Operating costs decreased 1.2 % to NT$126,887 million (US$4,242 million), mainly because of reduced depreciation and other operating expenses, partially offset by higher direct material costs. As a percentage of revenue, operating costs rose from 81.9 % in 2019 to 84.9 % in 2018, indicating tighter cost control in the later year.

**Profitability**  
- **Gross profit** fell from NT$22,840 million in 2018 to NT$21,315 million in 2019, translating to a gross margin decline from 15.1 % to 14.4 %.  
- **Operating expenses** (sales & marketing, G&A, R&D) together accounted for 14.8 % of revenue in 2019, compared with 14.7 % in 2018.  
- **Operating income** improved to 4.4 % of revenue in 2019 (versus 3.8 % in 2018).  
- **Net income** rose to 4.5 % of revenue in 2019, up from 2.1 % in 2018, reflecting lower income tax expense and modest non‑operating gains.

**Comprehensive Income**  
Total comprehensive income dropped to 1.3 % of revenue in 2019 from 2.7 % in 2018, driven by a larger other comprehensive loss (‑3.2 % vs +0.6 %). Net income attributable to the parent company was NT$3.3 billion in 2019, down from NT$5.7 billion in 2018, while non‑controlling interests moved from a 5.7 billion credit to a 3.0 billion debit.

**Key Takeaways**  
- Revenue contraction was modest, but lower selling prices eroded gross margins.  
- Cost discipline helped contain operating expenses, allowing operating income to improve despite weaker top‑line performance.  
- The company delivered higher net income in 2019, though comprehensive income fell due to larger unrealized losses.  

Overall, the 2019 results reflect a transition to tighter cost management and improved profitability at the operating level, offset by pricing pressures and currency effects on revenue and comprehensive earnings.

synth_text.title: 2019 Financial Performance Summary: Revenue Decline and Margin Compression
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In 2019 the company generated operating revenues of NT$148,202 million, a 2.0 % decline from the prior year. When expressed as a percentage of revenue, the income‑statement components are as follows:

- **Operating revenues:** 100.0 % (baseline)  
- **Operating costs:** 85.6 % of revenue, leaving a **gross profit** of 14.4 % (NT$21,315 million). This represents a drop in gross margin from 15.1 % in 2018, driven primarily by a 2.9 % fall in average wafer selling price.  
- **Operating expenses** (total 14.6 % of revenue) consist of:  
  - Sales & marketing: 2.6 %  
  - General & administrative: 3.6 %  
  - Research & development: 8.0 %  
  - Expected credit losses: 0.4 %  

  After accounting for these expenses, **net other operating income and expenses** contributed a positive 3.5 % of revenue, resulting in an **operating income** of 3.3 % of revenue.

- **Non‑operating items** reduced income by 0.1 % of revenue, so **income from continuing operations before tax** stood at 3.2 % of revenue.  
- **Income tax benefit (expense)** was –0.1 % of revenue, leaving **net income** at 3.1 % of revenue (approximately NT$4.6 billion).  

**Comprehensive income** was higher due to other comprehensive items, reaching 5.0 % of revenue. Of this, 7.4 % is attributable to the parent‑company shareholders, while a 2.4 % offset reflects non‑controlling interests.

**Key drivers of the 2019 results**  

1. **Revenue pressure:** A 2.5 % depreciation of the New Taiwan Dollar and a 2.9 % decline in average wafer selling price reduced top‑line growth, despite a modest 1.1 % increase in wafer shipments (7,189 k 8‑inch‑equivalent wafers vs. 7,108 k in 2018).  
2. **Cost management:** Operating costs fell 1.2 % year‑over‑year, mainly because of lower depreciation and other operating expenses, partially offset by higher direct material costs.  
3. **Margin compression:** The combined effect of lower pricing and unchanged expense mix narrowed the gross margin to 14.4 % and limited operating income to just over 3 % of revenue.

**Conclusion**  
The 2019 financial performance reflects a challenging market environment that pressured revenues and margins. While the company succeeded in modestly curbing operating costs, the decline in average selling price and currency effects outweighed these savings, resulting in lower profitability metrics across the board. Continued focus on cost efficiency and pricing strategy will be essential to improve margins in the coming periods.

synth_text.title: Q4 Unaudited Net Revenue Summary by Business Group
synth_text.text:
**Overall Performance**  
For the most recent quarter, the company reported unaudited consolidated net revenues of **$2.648 billion**, representing a **7.9 % sequential increase** and a **4.0 % year‑over‑year rise**.

**Segment Revenues (in millions)**  
| Segment | Q4 Revenue | Sequential Growth |
|---------|------------|-------------------|
| Automotive and Discrete Group (ADG) | $967 | 3.3 % |
| Analog, MEMS and Sensors Group (AMS) | $988 | 12.1 % |
| Microcontrollers and Digital ICs Group (MDG) | $689 | 7.9 % |
| Others | $4 | — |
| **Total** | **$2,648** | **7.9 %** |

**Key Drivers – Sequential Basis**  
- **ADG:** Revenue grew 3.3 % thanks to an **≈8 % volume increase**, partially offset by a **≈5 % drop in average selling price (ASP)** due to a less favorable product mix.  
- **AMS:** Revenue rose 12.1 % driven by **Analog and Imaging products**. Growth stemmed from a **≈5 % ASP increase** (product‑mix effect) and **≈7 % higher volumes**.  
- **MDG:** Revenue climbed 7.9 % primarily from **Microcontrollers**, supported by a **≈6 % ASP uplift** (product‑mix driven) and **≈2 % volume growth**.  

**Key Drivers – Year‑Over‑Year Basis**  
- **ADG:** Q4 revenue fell 4.5 % YoY, reflecting **lower ASPs (≈4 %)** across Automotive and Power Discrete lines, while volumes were essentially flat. The price decline resulted from an unfavorable product mix and reduced selling prices.  
- **AMS:** YoY revenue increased 9.9 %, largely due to **≈18 % higher ASPs** (product‑mix effect) that more than offset a **≈8 % volume decline**.  
- **MDG:** YoY revenue grew 7.6 % driven by **≈9 % higher ASPs** (again from an improved product mix) with volumes remaining stable.

**Takeaway**  
All three core groups delivered sequential revenue growth, with AMS leading the pace thanks to strong pricing and mix benefits. Year‑over‑year, ADG faced pricing pressure, while AMS and MDG continued to improve profitability through favorable product mixes and modest price increases. The company’s total Q4 revenue growth reflects these mixed dynamics across its business segments.

synth_text.title: Q4 Revenue Overview: ADG Decline Amid Strong AMS and MDG Growth
synth_text.text:
In the fourth quarter, the company’s consolidated net revenues rose 4.0 % year‑over‑year. The performance varied markedly across its three primary business groups:

* **Automotive and Discrete Group (ADG)** recorded a 4.5 % YoY decline. The drop was driven entirely by lower average selling prices (≈4 % lower), reflecting an unfavorable product mix, while volumes remained essentially flat. On a sequential basis, ADG still managed a modest 3.3 % increase, supported by an 8 % volume rise that was partially offset by a 5 % reduction in ASP.

* **Analog, MEMS and Sensors Group (AMS)** delivered robust growth, with revenues up 9.9 % YoY. The increase stemmed from a significant ASP uplift of about 18 %—entirely due to a more favorable product mix—despite an 8 % dip in volumes. Quarter‑over‑quarter, AMS outperformed even further, posting a 12.1 % rise driven by a 5 % ASP increase (mix) and a 7 % volume expansion.

* **Microcontrollers and Digital ICs Group (MDG)** posted a 7.6 % YoY revenue gain. This was primarily the result of a 9 % rise in ASP, again attributable to an improved mix, while volumes stayed roughly steady. Sequentially, MDG grew 7.9 %, helped by a 6 % ASP increase (mix) and a modest 2 % volume boost.

The “Others” category had no reported change. Overall, the company’s revenue growth was anchored by strong pricing and mix improvements in AMS and MDG, offsetting the price‑driven weakness in ADG.

synth_text.title: Q4 Net Revenue Performance Overview: Growth Across ADG, AMS, and MDG Segments
synth_text.text:
In the latest quarter the company delivered total consolidated net revenues of **$2.754 billion**, up from **$2.553 billion** in the prior quarter.  The increase was broad‑based across all three core groups:

* **Automotive and Discrete Group (ADG)** – revenue rose to **$924 million** (+3.3 % QoQ).  Growth was driven by an **≈8 % volume increase**, partially offset by a **≈5 % decline in average selling price (ASP)** caused by a less favourable product mix.  Year‑over‑year, ADG fell 4.5 % as ASP dropped about 4 % while volumes were flat.

* **Analog, MEMS and Sensors Group (AMS)** – revenue climbed to **$1.085 billion** (+12.1 % QoQ).  The uplift stemmed from a **≈5 % ASP rise** (product‑mix effect) and a **≈7 % volume increase**.  On a YoY basis AMS grew 9.9 % thanks to an **≈18 % ASP increase** (product‑mix) that more than compensated for an **≈8 % volume decline**.

synth_text.title: Key Assumptions Underpinning the Company’s Actuarial Benefit Obligation
synth_text.text:
The actuarial benefit obligation is measured using a set of core assumptions that reflect expected future costs and discounting. The principal assumptions are:

| Assumption | Value(s) |
|------------|----------|
| **Discount rate** | 3.90 % (base case) – up to 4.00 % in the range scenario |
| **Future salary growth** | 2.50 % (single‑year assumption) – not specified in the range scenario |
| **Health‑care cost trend rate** | Not applicable in the base case; 3.49 % – 5.49 % in the range scenario |
| **Other medical trend rate** | Not applicable in the base case; 4.00 % – 4.56 % in the range scenario |

These assumptions are the “significant assumptions adopted in measuring the Company’s pension and other benefit obligations,” as noted in the accompanying commentary.

For certain Canadian post‑retirement plans, the health‑care and other medical trend rates follow a defined trajectory: the rates applicable from 2019 through 2024 increase linearly, reaching **4.75 % by 2029**. After 2029, the trend rates gradually decline, stabilising at an **ultimate rate of 3.57 % per annum beginning in 2040** and thereafter.

Together, these discount, salary, and medical cost assumptions provide the basis for projecting the present value of future pension and post‑retirement benefit payments.

During the third quarter of fiscal 2018, the Canadian broadband services segment implemented a new customer management system, replacing 22 legacy systems. Variations of each services are also explained as follows:

INTERNET Fiscal 2019 Internet service customers net additions stood at 5,966 compared to 14,173 for the prior year mainly due to: • the ongoing interest in high speed offerings; • the sustained interest in bundle offers; and • the increased demand from Internet resellers; partly offset by • competitive offers in the industry; and • contact center congestion during the stabilization period of the new customer management system.

VIDEO Fiscal 2019 video service customers net losses stood at 39,185 compared to 37,035 for the prior year as a result of: • highly competitive offers in the industry; • a changing video consumption environment; and • contact center congestion during the stabilization period of the new customer management system; partly offset by • customers' ongoing interest in digital advanced video services; and • customers' interest in video services bundled with fast Internet offerings.

synth_text.title: Canadian Broadband Services: 2018 Penetration Snapshot and 2019 Customer Trends
synth_text.text:
**2018 Service Penetration (as % of homes passed)**  
- **Internet:** 44.7 %  
- **Video:** 39.3 %  
- **Telephony:** 22.6 %  

*Note:* These percentages exclude adjustments linked to the migration to a new customer‑management system that began in the third quarter of fiscal 2018.

**Impact of the 2018 System Migration**  
During Q3 FY2018 the Canadian broadband segment replaced 22 legacy systems with a unified customer‑management platform. While the new system was being stabilized, contact‑center congestion reduced service activations throughout the remainder of FY2018 and into Q1 FY2019. Normal operations resumed only after the first quarter of 2019.

**2019 Net Customer Changes**  
- **Internet:** +5,966 customers (vs. +14,173 in FY2018) – driven by continued interest in high‑speed and bundled offers and growth from Internet resellers, partially offset by competitive industry offers and the earlier contact‑center bottleneck.  
- **Video:** –39,185 customers (vs. –37,035 in FY2018) – caused by intense competition, evolving video‑consumption habits, and the same contact‑center constraints, partially mitigated by demand for advanced digital video and bundled video‑Internet packages.  
- **Telephony:** –23,333 customers (vs. –32,987 in FY2018) – primarily due to technical activation issues during the system rollout and a shift toward wireless services, with offsets from business‑sector growth and increased telephony bundling later in FY2019.

**Bundling Adoption**  
By August 31 2019, **69 %** of the segment’s customers were subscribed to “double‑play” (Internet + Video or Internet + Telephony) or “triple‑play” (Internet + Video + Telephony) bundles, underscoring the strong market preference for combined service packages.

**Overall Insight**  
The 2018 penetration figures illustrate a solid base of Internet and Video adoption, with Telephony lagging. The 2019 data reveal that, despite temporary operational disruptions, the segment’s growth is increasingly driven by bundled offerings and a shift away from traditional landline telephony toward wireless alternatives.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Canadian Broadband Services – Customer Count and Net Changes
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 the Canadian broadband services segment served **1,810,366 primary service units**. The customer base was composed of:

* **Internet:** 788,243 customers (net addition of **5,966**)
* **Video:** 649,583 customers (net loss of **39,185**)
* **Telephony:** 372,540 customers (net loss of **23,333**)

**Drivers of the net changes**

* **Internet:** The modest gain of 5,966 customers reflects continued interest in high‑speed and bundled offerings, as well as demand from Internet resellers. Growth was partially offset by competitive industry offers and contact‑center congestion caused by the stabilization of a new customer‑management system introduced in Q3 FY 2018.

* **Video:** The loss of 39,185 video customers was driven by intense competition, a shift in video‑consumption habits, and the same contact‑center bottlenecks. Offsetting factors included sustained interest in advanced digital video services and bundled video‑Internet packages.

* **Telephony:** The decline of 23,333 landline customers stemmed from technical issues with telephony activations during the system migration, and a broader move by consumers toward wireless‑only solutions. Growth in the business sector and increased telephony bundling in the latter half of the year helped mitigate the loss.

**Bundling prevalence**  
As of August 31 2019, **69 %** of the segment’s customers enjoyed “double‑play” or “triple‑play” bundled services, underscoring the importance of combined offerings in retaining and attracting subscribers.

Overall, while Internet subscriptions grew slightly, Video and Telephony experienced notable declines, largely attributable to system‑implementation challenges and evolving market dynamics. The high rate of bundled service adoption remains a key strength for the segment.

synth_text.title: Customer Trends in Canada’s Broadband Services Segment (FY 2018‑FY 2019)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Canadian broadband services segment experienced divergent trends across its three core offerings between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2019. While Internet subscriptions grew, both Video and Telephony services saw substantial declines. A major systems migration during the third quarter of FY 2018 influenced activation rates and contributed to the observed shifts.

**FY 2018 (baseline)**  
- **Internet service customers:** 14,173  
- **Video service customers:** 37,035  
- **Telephony service customers:** 32,987  

These figures exclude adjustments related to the migration to a new customer‑management system (see note (1)).

**FY 2019 (penetration rates)**  
- **Internet:** 44.7 % of homes passed  
- **Video:** 36.8 % of homes passed  
- **Telephony:** 21.1 % of homes passed  

**Net changes in FY 2019**  
- **Internet:** +5,966 customers (net addition) – driven by strong demand for high‑speed plans, bundled offers, and reseller activity, partially offset by competitive pricing and temporary contact‑center congestion.  
- **Video:** –39,185 customers (net loss) – caused by intense competition, evolving video‑consumption habits, and the same congestion issue, partially mitigated by interest in advanced digital video and bundled video‑Internet packages.  
- **Telephony:** –23,333 customers (net loss) – primarily due to technical activation issues during the system rollout and a shift of residential users toward wireless alternatives, with partial offsets from business‑sector growth and promotional bundling later in FY 2019.

**Operational impact**  
The migration replaced 22 legacy systems with a unified customer‑management platform. While the new system stabilized by the end of Q1 FY 2019, earlier contact‑center congestion suppressed service activations throughout Q4 FY 2018 and Q1 FY 2019.

**Bundling prevalence**  
As of August 31 2019, 69 % of the segment’s customers enjoyed “double‑play” (Internet + Video or Telephony) or “triple‑play” (Internet + Video + Telephony) bundles, underscoring the importance of bundled offerings in retaining and attracting subscribers.

**Key take‑aways**  
- Internet remains the growth engine, with nearly half of all homes now subscribed.  
- Video and Telephony are contracting, reflecting competitive pressures and changing consumer preferences.  
- System‑migration challenges temporarily hampered activations but were resolved by early FY 2019.  
- High bundling rates suggest that integrated service packages are a critical lever for future customer acquisition and retention.

synth_text.title: Breakdown of the Group’s Tax Expense and Key Adjustments for the Year
synth_text.text:
The Group reported a profit (loss) before tax of **€2,792 million**. Based on the geographic split of this profit and the applicable local tax rates, the “expected” tax expense would have been **€795 million**. However, the final income tax expense recorded for the year was **€4,764 million**, reflecting a range of adjustments and deferred‑tax movements.

**Major contributors to the €4,764 million tax expense**

| Item | Impact (€/m) |
|------|--------------|
| **Recognition/derecognition of deferred tax assets for losses in Luxembourg and Spain** | **+€1,603** |
| **Effect of current‑year changes in statutory tax rates on deferred tax balances** | **+€2,755** |
| **Deferred tax following revaluation of investments in Luxembourg** | **‑€329** |
| **Disposal of Group investments** | **‑€271** |
| **Adjustments in respect of prior‑year tax liabilities (closing audits in Germany and Romania)** | **‑€107** |
| **Impact of tax credits and irrecoverable taxes** | **+€98** |
| **Financing costs not deductible for tax purposes** | **+€25** |
| **Expenses not deductible (income not taxable) for tax purposes** | **+€72** |
| **Deferred tax on overseas earnings (including €42 m credit from the Vodafone‑India/Idea Cellular combination)** | **+€26** |
| **Other temporary‑difference movements (unused, expected to be used, or revalued assets)** | **+€139** (net) |

**Key observations**

1. **Deferred‑tax effects dominate the variance.** The two largest line‑items—recognition of deferred tax assets in Luxembourg and Spain (+€1,603 m) and the impact of statutory‑rate changes (+€2,755 m)—together account for more than 90 % of the difference between the expected tax (€795 m) and the actual tax expense (€4,764 m).

2. **Geographic and regulatory factors.** The note on Luxembourg and Spain (see pages 140‑141 of the full report) explains that the Group recognised significant deferred tax assets for loss carry‑forwards in these jurisdictions, boosting the tax charge.

3. **Closing tax audits.** Adjustments of €107 m relate to the finalisation of tax audits across the Group, notably in Germany and Romania, which reduced the overall tax liability.

4. **Overseas earnings credit.** A €42 m credit arises from the integration of Vodafone India with Idea Cellular, partially offsetting the tax expense.

5. **Non‑deductible costs and revaluations.** Financing costs, non‑taxable income, and asset revaluations contributed modestly to the total expense.

In summary, while the Group’s “expected” tax based on profit allocation was €795 m, extensive deferred‑tax movements—particularly those linked to Luxembourg, Spain, and statutory‑rate changes—along with audit adjustments and specific credits, resulted in a final income tax expense of **€4,764 million** for the year.

synth_text.title: Analysis of Group Tax Expense Drivers for the Two Reporting Years
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table breaks down the elements that explain the gap between the Group’s expected tax expense (derived from the geographic split of profits multiplied by local tax rates) and the actual tax expense recorded in the consolidated income statement for two consecutive years.

**Year 1 (Loss‑making year)**  
- **Profit before tax:** (€2,613 m) – a loss.  
- **Net tax result:** Tax credit of **€1,496 m**.  
- **Key contributors:**  
  * **Deferred tax assets recognised** for loss carry‑forwards in Luxembourg and Spain: **+€1,186 m**.  
  * **Tax credits/irrecoverable taxes:** **+€79 m**.  
  * **Taxation of associates & JVs:** **+€262 m**.  
  * **Deferred tax from Luxembourg revaluation:** **‑€488 m**.  
  * **Adjustments for prior‑year audit outcomes (Germany, Romania):** **‑€94 m**.  
  * **Non‑deductible financing costs** and **other expenses:** **+€67 m** and **+€97 m** respectively.  
  * **Deferred tax on overseas earnings:** **‑€39 m** (reflecting a €42 m credit from the Vodafone India‑Idea Cellular combination).

**Year 2 (Profit‑making year)**  
- **Profit before tax:** €3,878 m – a strong profit.  
- **Net tax result:** Tax credit of **€879 m** (still a benefit, but smaller than in Year 1).  
- **Key contributors:**  
  * **Deferred tax assets derecognised** for Luxembourg and Spain losses: **‑€1,583 m**.  
  * **Disposal of Group investments:** **+€55 m** (gain).  
  * **Tax credits/irrecoverable taxes:** **+€93 m**.  
  * **Taxation of associates & JVs:** **+€90 m**.  
  * **Deferred tax from Luxembourg revaluation:** **‑€330 m**.  
  * **Adjustments for prior‑year audit outcomes:** **‑€244 m**.  
  * **Utilised previously unrecognised temporary differences:** **‑€29 m**.  
  * **Non‑deductible financing costs** and **other expenses:** **+€23 m** and **+€61 m** respectively.  
  * **Deferred tax on overseas earnings:** **+€24 m** (reflecting the same overseas credit effect).

**Interpretation**  
- The swing from a large deferred‑tax‑asset recognition in Year 1 to a substantial derecognition in Year 2 is the dominant factor behind the reduced tax benefit despite higher operating profit.  
- Audit‑related adjustments (note 2) and the treatment of overseas earnings (note 3) also materially affect the final tax position.  
- Temporary differences that are not expected to be used (€78 m in Year 1, €20 m in Year 2) have a marginal impact.  

**Conclusion**  
The tax expense for each year is shaped by a mix of statutory rates, the Group’s profit mix, and several non‑operational items—most notably deferred tax asset movements in Luxembourg and Spain, audit adjustments, and overseas earnings credits. Understanding these components clarifies why the actual tax result deviates from the simple “geographic profit × local tax rate” expectation.

text.value: Share Options

The Company estimates the fair value of employee share options on the date of grant using the Black-Scholes option-pricing model, which requires the use of highly subjective estimates and assumptions. The Company estimates the expected term of share options for service-based awards utilizing the “Simplified Method,” as it does not have sufficient historical share option exercise information on which to base its estimate. The Simplified Method is based on the average of the vesting tranches and the contractual life of each grant.

The risk-free interest rate is based on a treasury instrument whose term is consistent with the expected life of the share option. Since there was no public market for the Company’s ordinary shares prior to the IPO and as its shares have been publicly traded for a limited time, the Company determined the expected volatility for options granted based on an analysis of reported data for a peer group of companies that issue options with substantially similar terms.

synth_text.title: 2017 Employee Share Option Valuation: Assumptions and Fair‑Value Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the Company granted employee share options that were valued using the Black‑Scholes option‑pricing model. Because the Company lacked sufficient historical exercise data, the expected term of the options was estimated with the “Simplified Method,” which averages the vesting periods and the contractual life of each grant. The key assumptions applied to the 2017 valuation are:

| Assumption | Value |
|------------|-------|
| Expected term (years) | 6.1 |
| Risk‑free interest rate | 2.1 % (based on a Treasury instrument matching the option’s expected life) |
| Expected volatility | 41.0 % (derived from the average historical volatility of a peer group with similar option terms) |
| Expected dividend yield | 0 % (the Company does not anticipate paying dividends) |
| Fair value of ordinary share on grant date | $20.22 (closing market price on the grant date) |

Using these inputs, the Black‑Scholes model produced a weighted‑average fair value of $8.65 per share option for the 2017 grant year. This figure reflects the Company’s best estimate of the economic benefit provided to employees through the share‑option awards, given the subjective nature of the underlying assumptions.

Overall, the 2017 share‑option valuation combines market‑based data (risk‑free rate, peer‑group volatility, share price) with the Company’s internal estimation methods to arrive at a transparent and auditable fair‑value measurement for financial reporting purposes.

Shares subject to anti-dilutive stock options and restricted stock-based awards of 1.9 million and 0.2 million for the fiscal years ended February 28, 2019 and 2018, respectively, were excluded from the calculations of diluted earnings per share for the years then ended.

We have the option to pay cash, issue shares of common stock or any combination thereof for the aggregate amount due upon conversion of the Notes. It is our intent to settle the principal amount of the convertible senior notes with cash, and therefore, we use the treasury stock method for calculating any potential dilutive effect of the conversion option on diluted net income (loss) per share. From the time of the issuance of the Notes, the average market price of our common stock has been less than the initial conversion price of the Notes, and consequently no shares have been included in diluted earnings per share for the conversion value of the Notes.

synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2017, the company reported a net loss of **$7.9 million**. The weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding was **35.9 million**, which was the same for both basic and diluted calculations. Consequently, basic earnings (loss) per share and diluted earnings (loss) per share were each **$(0.22)**.

The EPS figures were derived by dividing the net loss by the weighted‑average share count, as described in Note 14. All outstanding stock options (1.0 million) and restricted‑stock awards (1.2 million) were excluded from the diluted EPS computation because their inclusion would have been **antidilutive**. Likewise, the treasury‑stock method was applied to the convertible senior notes, but since the market price of the common stock remained below the conversion price, no additional shares were counted for dilution.

Thus, the reported EPS reflects the company’s loss on a per‑share basis without any dilutive impact from stock options, restricted‑stock awards, or convertible notes for the 2017 fiscal year.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2018‑2019 Net Income and Earnings‑Per‑Share Summary
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the fiscal years ended February 28, 2018 and February 28, 2019, the company reported growth in net income and earnings per share (EPS), while the weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding declined modestly.

**Net Income**  
- 2018: $16.617 million  
- 2019: $18.398 million  

This represents an increase of approximately 10.7 % year over year.

**Basic Shares and EPS**  
- Basic weighted‑average common shares: 35,250 k (2018) → 34,589 k (2019)  
- Basic EPS: $0.47 (2018) → $0.53 (2019)  

The reduction in basic shares contributed to a higher basic EPS, which rose 12.8 % from 2018 to 2019.

**Diluted Shares and EPS**  
- Diluted weighted‑average common shares: 36,139 k (2018) → 35,294 k (2019)  
- Diluted EPS: $0.46 (2018) → $0.52 (2019)  

Diluted EPS increased by 13.0 % despite the inclusion of potential dilutive securities, because certain stock options and restricted‑stock awards were excluded as they were anti‑dilutive.

**Key Accounting Considerations**  
- **Basic EPS** is calculated by dividing net income by the basic weighted‑average shares.  
- **Diluted EPS** uses the treasury‑stock method to account for the dilutive effect of outstanding stock options, restricted‑stock awards, and convertible senior notes.  
- For 2018 and 2019, shares from anti‑dilutive options (1.9 million in 2019 and 0.2 million in 2018) were excluded from the diluted EPS computation, as their inclusion would have reduced EPS.  
- No shares from the convertible senior notes were included in diluted EPS because the market price of the common stock remained below the notes’ conversion price throughout the periods.

**Conclusion**  
The company’s profitability improved in 2019, reflected by higher net income and both basic and diluted EPS. The modest decline in share counts and the exclusion of anti‑dilutive securities under the treasury‑stock method further enhanced the EPS figures.

synth_text.title: IBM 2019 Cloud & Cognitive Software Segment – Revenue Growth Overview
synth_text.text:
In 2019 IBM’s Cloud & Cognitive Software segment generated **$23.2 billion** in external revenue, marking a **4.5 %** increase year‑over‑year (or **6.2 %** when adjusted for currency). The segment’s growth was driven primarily by the **Cloud & Data Platforms** sub‑segment, which posted **$9.5 billion** in revenue and grew **10.4 %** as reported (**12.3 %** at constant currency). This acceleration reflects the successful integration of Red Hat—particularly Red Hat Enterprise Linux, OpenShift, and Ansible—and strong client adoption of hybrid‑cloud solutions such as Cloud Paks.

**Cognitive Applications** contributed **$5.8 billion** and rose **2.3 %** (reported) and **3.9 %** (currency‑adjusted). Growth was powered by double‑digit gains in security offerings and expanding industry‑specific solutions in the Internet of Things (IoT).

Within the segment, **cloud revenue alone reached $4.2 billion**, expanding **40 %** (reported) and **42 %** (currency‑adjusted) year‑over‑year, underscoring the impact of the Red Hat acquisition and the broader shift toward hybrid cloud services.

Conversely, **Transaction Processing Platforms** saw a slight decline, with revenue of **$7.9 billion** falling **0.5 %** as reported, though it grew **1 %** on a constant‑currency basis, buoyed by strong fourth‑quarter performance and ongoing investments in IBM platforms.

Overall, the 2019 results demonstrate robust momentum in IBM’s cloud and data platform businesses, driven by Red Hat synergies and expanding security and IoT portfolios, while Transaction Processing Platforms experienced modest pressure from client buying cycles.

Employee‑benefit provisions fell slightly to $5.0 billion, while tax loss and credit carryforwards decreased to $3.0 billion. The most notable change was a jump in “other assets” to $5.6 billion. The valuation allowance narrowed to **‑$2.26 billion**, a reduction of **$481 million**, reflecting a lower reserve for state and foreign tax uncertainties.  

**Deferred Tax Liabilities**  
- Deferred tax liabilities increased from **$41.6 billion** at the end of 2018 to **$46.0 billion** at the end of 2019. The rise was driven by higher intangible‑amortization charges (from $21.98 billion to $22.39 billion) and higher depreciation (from $15.66 billion to $16.88 billion), with other liabilities also growing modestly.  

**Net Deferred Tax Liability**  
- The net position moved from **$33.7 billion** in 2018 to **$34.6 billion** in 2019, indicating a slight increase in the overall deferred tax burden.  

**Contextual Factors**  
- Verizon’s foreign subsidiaries held undistributed earnings of approximately **$3.8 billion** at year‑end 2019, which are intended to remain indefinitely reinvested abroad. Consequently, no U.S. deferred tax is recognized on these earnings.  
- Net after‑tax loss and credit carryforwards amounted to roughly **$3.0 billion** (primarily state and foreign taxes). Of this, about **$2.0 billion** will expire between 2020 and 2039, while **$1.0 billion** may be carried forward indefinitely.  
- The reduction in the valuation allowance during 2019 aligns with the company’s statement that the allowance, largely related to state and foreign tax positions, decreased by **$481 million**.  

Overall, Verizon’s deferred tax profile in 2019 reflects stronger asset positions, higher liability balances due to increased amortization and depreciation, and a modest rise in the net deferred tax liability, all underpinned by significant foreign earnings that remain outside the U.S. tax base and sizable loss‑carryforward assets.

synth_text.title: Key Assumptions Underlying BCE Stock Option Valuation
synth_text.text:
BCE’s stock option grants were valued using a customized binomial option‑pricing model that incorporates plan‑specific features such as the vesting period. The model relies on a set of core assumptions, which are summarized below for the two most recent grants:

| Assumption | Grant 1 | Grant 2 |
|------------|---------|---------|
| Weighted average fair value per option granted | **$2.34** | **$2.13** |
| Weighted average share price (underlying) | **$58** | **$57** |
| Weighted average exercise price | **$58** | **$56** |
| Expected dividend growth | **5 %** (aligned with BCE’s dividend growth strategy) | **5 %** |
| Expected volatility | **14 %** (based on historical BCE share‑price volatility) | **12 %** |
| Risk‑free interest rate | **2 %** (yield on Government of Canada bonds matching the option’s life) | **2 %** |
| Expected life of the option | **4 years** | **4 years** |

**Interpretation**

- Both grants assume a 5 % dividend growth rate, reflecting BCE’s ongoing dividend policy, and a 2 % risk‑free rate derived from Canadian government bonds with a term equal to the options’ expected four‑year life.
- The primary differences lie in the fair‑value per option and the expected volatility: Grant 1 carries a slightly higher fair value ($2.34 vs. $2.13) and higher volatility (14 % vs. 12 %), indicating a marginally riskier underlying price environment at the time of grant.
- Exercise prices are close to the current share price for Grant 1 ($58) and modestly below the share price for Grant 2 ($56 vs. $57), suggesting a slightly more in‑the‑money position for the latter.

These assumptions collectively provide the foundation for BCE’s option‑valuation calculations, ensuring consistency with the company’s financial strategy and market conditions at the grant dates.

text.value: The following table summarizes our consolidated cash and cash equivalents provided by (used for) operating, financing and investing activities for the periods presented:
Operating Cash Flows

Our consolidated net cash flow from operating activities fluctuates primarily as a result of changes in vessel utilization and TCE rates, changes in interest rates, fluctuations in working capital balances, the timing and amount of dry-docking expenditures, repairs and maintenance activities, vessel additions and dispositions, and foreign currency rates. Our exposure to the spot tanker market has contributed significantly to fluctuations in operating cash flows historically as a result of highly cyclical spot tanker rates.

In addition, the production performance of certain of our FPSO units that operate under contracts with a production-based compensation component has contributed to fluctuations in operating cash flows. As the charter contracts of some of our FPSO units include incentives based on average annual oil prices, the changes in global oil prices during recent years have also impacted our operating cash flows.

Consolidated net cash flow from operating activities increased to $383.3 million for the year ended December 31, 2019, from $182.1 million for the year ended December 31, 2018. This increase was primarily due to a $127.2 million increase in income from operations mainly from operations (before depreciation, amortization, asset impairments, loss on sale of vessels and the amortization of in-process revenue contracts) of our businesses.

For further discussion of changes in income from vessel operations from our businesses, please read “Item 5 – Operating and Financial Review and Prospects: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations – Recent Developments and Results of Operations.”

In addition, there was a $9.9 million increase in cash flows from changes to non-cash working capital, a $23.6 million increase in dividends received from joint ventures, and a $17.1 million increase in direct financing lease payments received, which are presented as an operating cash inflow instead of an investing cash inflow after the adoption of ASU 2016-02 in 2019.

Furthermore, interest expense, including realized losses on interest rate swaps and cross currency swaps, decreased a net amount of $38.1 million for the year ended December 31, 2019 compared to 2018, primarily due to a decrease in realized losses on cross currency swaps. These increases were partially offset by an increase in cash outflows of $15.9 million in dry-dock expenditures for the year ended December 31, 2019, compared to 2018.
Financing Cash Flows

The Daughter Entities hold all of our liquefied gas carriers (Teekay LNG) and all of our conventional tanker assets (Teekay Tankers). Teekay LNG received $317.8 million of net proceeds from the sale-leaseback financing transactions for the Yamal Spirit and Torben Spirit for the year ended December 31, 2019, compared to $370.1 million from the sale-leaseback financing transactions completed for the Magdala, Myrina and Megara for the same period in 2018.

Teekay Tankers received $63.7 million from the sale-leaseback financing transactions completed on two of its Suezmax tankers for the year ended December 31, 2019, compared to $241.3 million in the same period last year from the sale-leaseback financing transactions completed on eight Aframax tankers, one Suezmax tanker and one LR2 Product tanker.

We use our credit facilities to partially finance capital expenditures. Occasionally, we will use revolving credit facilities to finance these expenditures until longer-term financing is obtained, at which time we typically use all or a portion of the proceeds from the longer-term financings to prepay outstanding amounts under the revolving credit facilities. We actively manage the maturity profile of our outstanding financing arrangements.

During 2019, we had a net cash outflow of $227.3 million relating primarily to prepayments of short-term and long-term debt, issuance costs and payments on maturity of cross currency swaps, net of proceeds from the issuances of short-term and long-term debt, compared to net cash inflow of $553.7 million in 2018. Scheduled repayments decreased by $438.1 million in 2019 compared to 2018.

Historically, the Daughter Entities have distributed operating cash flows to their owners in the form of distributions or dividends. There were no equity financing transactions from the Daughter Entities for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018. Teekay LNG repurchased $25.7 million of common units in the year ended December 31, 2019.

Teekay Parent did not raise capital through equity financing transactions in December 31, 2019, compared to $103.7 million raised in 2018 from issuances of new equity to the public, thirdparty investors and two entities established by our founder (including Resolute, our largest shareholder). Cash dividends paid decreased by $16.6 million in 2019, as a result of the elimination of Teekay Parent's quarterly dividend on Teekay’s common stock commencing with the quarter ended March 31, 2019.
Investing Cash Flows

During 2019, we received $100 million from Brookfield for the sale of our remaining interests in Altera (please read "Item 18 – Financial Statements: Note 4 – Deconsolidation and Sale of Altera"). We incurred capital expenditures for vessels and equipment of $109.5 million primarily for capitalized vessel modifications and shipyard construction installment payments in Teekay LNG.

Teekay LNG received proceeds of $11.5 million from the sale of the Alexander Spirit and contributed $72.4 million to its equity-accounted joint ventures and loans to joint ventures for the year ended December 31, 2019, primarily to fund project expenditures in the Yamal LNG Joint Venture and the Bahrain LNG Joint Venture. During 2019, Teekay Tankers received proceeds of $19.6 million related to the sale of one Suezmax tanker.

During 2018, we incurred capital expenditures for vessels and equipment of $0.7 billion, primarily for capitalized vessel modifications and shipyard construction installment payments. Teekay Parent advanced $25.0 million to Altera in the form of a senior unsecured revolving credit facility.

Teekay LNG received proceeds of $54.4 million from the sale of Teekay LNG's 50% ownership interest in the Excelsior Joint Venture and $28.5 million from the sales of the European Spirit and African Spirit. Teekay LNG contributed $40.5 million to its equityaccounted joint ventures and loans to joint ventures for the year ended December 31, 2018, primarily to fund project expenditures in the Yamal LNG Joint Venture, the Bahrain LNG project, and the Pan Union Joint Venture, and for working capital requirements for the MALT Joint Venture.
Teekay incurred a net $25.3 million cash outflow as a result of the 2017 Brookfield Transaction (please read "Item 18 – Financial Statements: Note 4 – Deconsolidation and Sale of Altera").

synth_text.title: Consolidated Cash‑Flow Summary and Analysis for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The consolidated cash‑flow statement shows a pronounced shift in the company’s financial dynamics between 2018 and 2019.

**Operating cash flows** more than doubled, rising from **$182.1 million** in 2018 to **$383.3 million** in 2019. This increase was driven primarily by a $127.2 million boost in income from operations, higher cash generated from non‑cash working‑capital changes, an additional $23.6 million in dividends received from joint ventures, and $17.1 million of direct financing‑lease payments re‑classified as operating inflows under ASU 2016‑02. Lower interest‑expense losses (a $38.1 million reduction) also contributed, partially offset by higher dry‑dock expenditures ($15.9 million).

**Financing cash flows** reversed direction, moving from a net inflow of **$434.8 million** in 2018 to a net outflow of **$(382.2 million)** in 2019. The 2019 outflow reflects substantial debt pre‑payments, issuance costs, and cross‑currency‑swap settlements, while the 2018 inflow was largely the result of sale‑lease‑back financing and other debt‑related activities. No equity financing occurred in either year, and dividend payments decreased by $16.6 million in 2019 after the parent company eliminated its quarterly dividend.

**Investing cash flows** improved markedly, decreasing the cash outflow from **$(663.5 million)** in 2018 to **$(50.4 million)** in 2019. The reduction stems from lower capital‑expenditure outlays and proceeds from asset sales, including a $100 million receipt from Brookfield for the Altera divestiture and modest proceeds from vessel sales. Capital expenditures in 2019 were focused on vessel modifications and shipyard payments totaling $109.5 million, far less than the $0.7 billion spent in 2018.

Overall, the 2019 cash‑flow profile reflects stronger operating performance, aggressive debt reduction, and a more restrained investment program, resulting in a healthier cash position despite the sizable financing outflow.

The table below presents a summary of our results of operations for fiscal years 2019 and 2018. See Part II, Item 7 of our Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2018, filed with the SEC on May 21, 2018, for Management’s Discussions and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations for the fiscal year ended April 1, 2017.
REVENUE

Our overall revenue increased $116.8 million in fiscal 2019, compared to fiscal 2018, primarily due to higher demand for our mobile products in support of customers based in China as well as higher demand for our base station products, partially offset by a decrease in revenue due to weakness in marquee smartphone demand experienced by our largest end customer.

We provided our products to our largest end customer (Apple) through sales to multiple contract manufacturers, which in the aggregate accounted for 32% and 36% of total revenue in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, respectively. Huawei accounted for approximately 13% and 8% of our total revenue in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, respectively. These customers primarily purchase RF and Wi-Fi solutions for cellular base stations and a variety of mobile devices, including smartphones, wearables, laptops, tablets and cellular-based applications for the IoT. In May 2019, the U.S. government imposed restrictions on the sales of products to Huawei (see Note 2 of the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements set forth in Part II, Item 8 of this report).

International shipments amounted to $2,610.0 million in fiscal 2019 (approximately 84% of revenue) compared to $2,449.1 million in fiscal 2018 (approximately 82% of revenue). Shipments to Asia totaled $2,446.3 million in fiscal 2019 (approximately 79% of revenue) compared to $2,329.3 million in fiscal 2018 (approximately 78% of revenue).
GROSS MARGIN
Gross margin was relatively flat for fiscal 2019 as compared to fiscal 2018, with average selling price erosion offset by favorable changes in product mix.
OPERATING EXPENSES
Research and Development

In fiscal 2019, R&D spending increased $5.4 million, compared to fiscal 2018, primarily due to higher personnel related costs, partially offset by lower product development spend driven by R&D efficiency initiatives.
Selling, General and Administrative

In fiscal 2019, selling, general and administrative expense decreased $51.7 million, or 9.8%, compared to fiscal 2018, primarily due to lower intangible amortization, partially offset by higher personnel related costs.
Other Operating Expense

In fiscal 2019, other operating expense was $52.2 million. In fiscal 2019, we recognized $15.9 million of asset impairment charges (to adjust the carrying value of certain property and equipment to reflect fair value) and $11.6 million of employee termination benefits as a result of restructuring actions (see Note 11 of the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements set forth in Part II, Item 8 of this report for information on restructuring actions). In fiscal 2019, we also recorded $18.0 million of start-up costs related to new processes and operations in existing facilities.

In fiscal 2018, other operating expense was $103.8 million. In fiscal 2018, we initiated restructuring actions to improve operating efficiencies, and, as a result of these actions, we recorded approximately $18.3 million of employee termination benefits and adjusted the carrying value of certain held for sale assets located in China and the U.S. to fair market value (resulting in impairment charges totaling approximately $46.3 million). In fiscal 2018, we also recorded integration costs and restructuring costs of $6.2 million and $2.6 million, respectively, associated with the Business Combination, as well as $24.3 million of start-up costs related to new processes and operations in both existing and new facilities.
OPERATING INCOME

Our overall operating income was $216.5 million for fiscal 2019, compared to $70.3 million for fiscal 2018. This increase was primarily due to lower intangible amortization, higher revenue, and lower impairment charges on property and equipment.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Financial Highlights and Operational Overview
synth_text.text:
**Revenue and Profitability**  
In fiscal 2019 the company generated **$3.09 billion** in revenue, a $116.8 million increase over the prior year. Cost of goods sold amounted to **$1.90 billion**, representing **61.3 %** of revenue, leaving a **gross profit of $1.20 billion (38.7 % of revenue)**. Gross margin remained essentially flat year‑over‑year, with average selling‑price erosion offset by a more favorable product mix.

**Customer and Geographic Mix**  
Apple, sold through multiple contract manufacturers, contributed **32 %** of total revenue in 2019 (down from 36 % in 2018). Huawei’s share grew to **13 %** (up from 8 %). International shipments accounted for **84 %** of revenue ($2.61 billion), with **Asia representing 79 %** ($2.45 billion).

**Operating Expenses**  
- **Research & Development:** $450.5 million (14.6 % of revenue), up $5.4 million from 2018, driven mainly by higher personnel costs.  
- **Selling, General & Administrative:** $476.1 million (15.4 % of revenue), down $51.7 million (‑9.8 %) due to lower intangible amortization, partially offset by higher personnel costs.  
- **Other Operating Expense:** $52.2 million (1.7 % of revenue), a sharp decline from $103.8 million in 2018, reflecting reduced impairment charges, fewer termination benefits, and lower restructuring costs.

**Operating Income**  
Operating income rose to **$216.5 million**, representing **7.0 %** of revenue, a substantial increase from $70.3 million in 2018. The improvement stemmed from higher revenue, lower SG&A, reduced impairment charges, and lower intangible amortization.

**Overall Outlook**  
The fiscal‑2019 results demonstrate solid top‑line growth, stable gross margins, and disciplined cost management, leading to a more than three‑fold increase in operating profitability. The company’s diversified customer base and strong presence in Asian markets underpin its continued revenue momentum.

synth_text.title: Effect of a 1 % Assumption Change on Discount Rates and Medical/Dental Trends in Employee Benefit Plans
synth_text.text:
The sensitivity analysis for the employee benefit plans, as of December 31 2018, examines how a one‑percent shift in key assumptions influences two primary metrics: the discount rate and the medical‑and‑dental trend rates.  

* **1 % Increase Scenario** – The discount rate improves (decreases) by **$2,471**, while the medical and dental trend rates rise by **$1,703**.  
* **1 % Decrease Scenario** – The discount rate worsens (increases) by **$3,224**, and the medical and dental trend rates fall by **$1,280**.  

Future salary growth is not applicable in either case.  

These figures are hypothetical and should be used cautiously. Because the relationship between assumption changes and plan amounts is not necessarily linear, the impact of a 1 % change cannot be simply extrapolated. Moreover, the sensitivities were calculated independently; a change in one variable could affect others, potentially amplifying or mitigating the observed effects.  

In the context of the company’s broader benefit strategy, it plans to contribute **$5.1 million** to its defined benefit plans and **$0.6 million** to the defined contribution plan of Telesat Canada during the next fiscal year. These contributions, together with the sensitivity insights, help stakeholders gauge the financial resilience of the benefit programs under modest assumption variations.  

Overall, the analysis underscores the importance of monitoring assumption changes, given their material impact on discount rates and health‑care cost trends within the employee benefit framework.

The chief operating decision‑makers assess the performance of the company’s operating segments chiefly on two metrics: segment revenue and gross profit. Other costs such as selling, marketing, general and administrative expenses, finance costs, and income tax are treated as corporate‑level items and are not allocated to individual segments. - The performance evaluation framework focuses on the top‑line (revenue) and profitability (gross profit) of each segment, guiding resource allocation decisions.  
- Since there were no inter‑segment sales, the reported revenues stem entirely from external customers, measured consistently with the consolidated income statement.  

This summary provides a concise picture of the financial contribution of each operating segment for the year ended 31 December 2019, aligned with the company’s internal performance‑assessment criteria.

During the year ended December 31, 2019, we had an average of 27.2 ships operating in our owned and bareboat fleet (including ships owned by the Partnership), having 9,518 revenue operating days and an average of 27.2 ships operating under our technical management (including 27.0 of our owned and bareboat ships). Revenues: Revenues increased by 8.1%, or $50.3 million, from $618.3 million during the year ended December 31, 2018 to $668.6 million during the year ended December 31, 2019. The increase in revenues is mainly attributable to an increase of $63.4 million deriving from the full operation of the GasLog Houston, the GasLog Hong Kong and the GasLog Gladstone which were delivered on January 8, 2018, March 20, 2018 and March 29, 2018, respectively and the deliveries of the GasLog Gladstone on March 15, 2019 and the GasLog Warsaw on July 31, 2019. synth_text.title: 2019 Financial Performance Overview: Revenue Growth Overshadowed by Major Impairments and Losses
synth_text.text:
In 2019 the Group recorded a modest improvement in its top line. Revenues rose 8.1 % to $668.6 million, an increase of $50.3 million driven primarily by the full‑time operation of newly delivered vessels (GasLog Houston, Hong Kong, Gladstone, Warsaw) and higher spot‑market activity. The average daily hire rate also climbed to $70,167 from $68,392, and the fleet expanded slightly to an average of 27.2 ships, delivering 9,518 revenue operating days.

Despite the revenue uplift, the year ended with a substantial loss. The most significant negative item was an impairment loss on vessels of $162.1 million, reflecting a reassessment of vessel values. Additional large charges included a $49.4 million loss on derivatives, $23.9 million in financial costs, and $72.9 million in other expenses. Operating expenses—net pool allocation, voyage expenses, vessel operating and supervision costs, depreciation, and G&A—totaled $62.5 million, further eroding profitability.

Overall, profit from operations was a loss of $169.2 million, leading to a total loss for the year of $242.0 million. After accounting for non‑controlling interests of $93.7 million, the loss attributable to the Group’s owners amounted to $148.3 million.

In summary, while 2019 saw higher revenues and a slightly larger, more active fleet, the financial results were dominated by extraordinary non‑operating losses, particularly the vessel impairment, resulting in a deep net loss for the year.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview: 2018 vs 2019
synth_text.text:
**Financial Performance Overview: 2018 vs 2019**

The company’s 2019 results reflect a mixed picture of revenue growth and deteriorating profitability compared with 2018.

**Revenue and Fleet Activity**  
Revenues rose 8.1% year‑over‑year, from **$618.3 million** in 2018 to **$668.6 million** in 2019. The increase was driven primarily by the full‑time operation of newly delivered vessels—*GasLog Houston, GasLog Hong Kong, GasLog Gladstone* (delivered early 2018) and *GasLog Warsaw* (delivered July 2019)—which added revenue‑operating days. Spot‑market activity contributed an additional $11.0 million, while the remaining fleet added $2.7 million. Offsetting this were the expirations of several time charters, which reduced revenue by $26.1 million. Average fleet size grew from **26.0** ships (9,030 operating days) in 2018 to **27.2** ships (9,518 operating days) in 2019, and the average daily hire rate increased from $68,392 to $70,167.

**Operating Profitability**  
Despite higher revenues, profit from operations fell sharply from **$292.5 million** in 2018 to **$123.4 million** in 2019. The decline stemmed from higher vessel operating and supervision costs, a steep rise in depreciation, and a significant **impairment loss on vessels of $162.1 million** recorded in 2019 (none in 2018).

**Net Income**  
The bottom line turned negative. After accounting for higher financial costs ($166.6 million in 2018 vs. $190.5 million in 2019), a large loss on derivatives ($6.1 million vs. $55.4 million), and the impairment loss, the company posted a **net loss attributable to owners of $100.7 million** in 2019, compared with a profit of **$47.7 million** in 2018. Non‑controlling interests also moved from a positive $78.7 million in 2018 to a negative $15.0 million in 2019, further eroding attributable earnings.

**Summary**  
The 2019 year saw revenue expansion supported by a larger, more active fleet, but this was outweighed by higher operating expenses, a substantial vessel impairment, and increased financial charges, resulting in a pronounced swing from profit to loss.

text.value: 8. Debt and Interest Rate Swap
Debt The carrying amount of the Company's long-term debt consists of the following:

On May 12, 2017, the Company entered into a credit agreement with certain lenders and a collateral agent in connection with the acquisition of Exar (Note 3). The credit agreement provides for an initial secured term B loan facility (the “Initial Term Loan”) in an aggregate principal amount of $425.0 million. The credit agreement permits the Company to request incremental loans in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed the sum of $160.0 million (subject to adjustments for any voluntary prepayments), plus an unlimited amount that is subject to pro forma compliance with certain secured leverage ratio and total leverage ratio tests. Incremental loans are subject  to certain additional conditions, including obtaining additional commitments from the lenders then party to the credit agreement or new lenders.

Loans under the credit agreement bear interest, at the Company’s option, at a rate equal to either (i) ab ase rate equal to the highest of (x) the federal funds rate, plus 0.50%, (y) the prime rate then in effect and (z) an adjusted LIBOR rate determined on the basis of a one- three- or six-month interest period, plus 1.0% or (ii) an adjusted LIBOR rate, subject to a floor of 0.75%, in each case, plus an applicable margin of 2.50% in the case of LIBOR rate loans and 1.50% in the case of base rate loans. Commencing on September 30, 2017, the Initial Term Loan will amortize in equal quarterly installments equal to 0.25% of the original principal amount of the Initial Term Loan, with the balance payable on the maturity date. The Initial Term Loan has a term of seven years and will mature on May 12, 2024, at which time all outstanding principal and accrued and unpaid interest on the Initial Term Loan must be repaid. The Company is also required to pay fees customary for a credit facility of this size and type.

The Company is required to make mandatory prepayments of the outstanding principal amount of term loans under the credit agreement with the net cash proceeds from the disposition of certain assets and the receipt of insurance proceeds upon certain casualty and condemnation events, in each case, to the extent not reinvested within a specified time period, from excess cash flow beyond stated threshold amounts, and from the incurrence of certain indebtedness. The Company has the right to prepay its term loans under the credit agreement, in whole or in part, at any time without premium or penalty, subject to certain limitations and a 1.0% soft call premium applicable during the first six months for the loan term. The Company exercised its right to prepay and made aggregate payments of principal of $213.0 million to date through December 31, 2019.

The Company’s obligations under the credit agreement are required to be guaranteed by certain of its domestic subsidiaries meeting materiality thresholds set forth in the credit agreement. Such obligations, including the guaranties, are secured by substantially all of the assets of the Company and the subsidiary guarantors pursuant to a security agreement with the collateral agent.

The credit agreement also contains customary events of default that include, among other things, certain payment defaults, cross defaults to other indebtedness, covenant defaults, change in control defaults, judgment defaults, and bankruptcy and insolvency defaults. If an event of default exists, the lenders may require immediate payment of all obligations under the credit agreement, and may exercise certain other rights and remedies provided for under the credit agreement, the other loan documents and applicable law.
As of December 31, 2019 and 2018, the weighted average effective interest rate on long-term debt was approximately4 .9% and 4.6%, respectively.

The debt is carried at its principal amount, net of unamortized debt discount and issuance costs, and is not adjusted to fair value each period. The issuance date fair value of the liability component of the debt in the amount of $398.5 million was determined using a discounted cash flow analysis, in which the projected interest and principal payments were discounted back to the issuance date of the term loan at a market interest rate for nonconvertible debt of 4.6%, which represents a Level 2 fair value measurement. The debt discount of $2.1 million and debt issuance costs of $6.0 million are being amortized to interest expense using the effective interest method from the issuance date through the contractual maturity date of the term loan of May 12, 2024.
During the year ended December 31, 2017, the Company recognized amortization of debt discount of $0.2 million and debt issuance costs of $0.6 million to interest expense.

The approximate fair value of the term loan as of December 31, 2019 and 2018 was $214.6 million and $268.1 million, respectively, which was estimated on the basis
of inputs that are observable in the market and which is considered a Level 2 measurement method in the fair value hierarchy.

As of December 31, 2019 and 2018, the remaining principal balance on the term loan was $212.0 million and $262.0 million, respectively. The remaining principal
balance is due on May 12, 2024 at the maturity date on the term loan.
