synth_text.title: Insurance Segment Performance: Net Income Decline and Adjusted Operating Income (AOI) Highlights for 2019
synth_text.text:
In 2019 the Insurance segment reported a net loss of **$(105.8) million**, a decrease of $105.8 million from the prior year’s $165.2 million profit. To provide a clearer view of operating performance, management adjusts this figure to calculate two non‑U.S. GAAP metrics:

| Metric | Amount (in $ million) |
|--------|----------------------|
| **Insurance AOI** | **105.8** |
| **Pre‑tax Insurance AOI** | **85.1** |

**Adjustments applied to net income**

| Adjustment | Impact (in $ million) |
|------------|----------------------|
| Effect of investment (gains)¹ | **+3.7** |
| Asset impairment expense | **+47.3** |
| Gain on bargain purchase | **+114.3** |
| Gain on reinsurance recaptures | **+47.0** |
| Acquisition costs | **‑0.7** |
| Income tax expense (benefit) | **‑20.7** |

These adjustments collectively convert the reported loss into a positive **Insurance AOI** of $105.8 million and a **Pre‑tax Insurance AOI** of $85.1 million.  

**Context and interpretation**

- **Insurance AOI** and **Pre‑tax Insurance AOI** are widely used, non‑U.S. GAAP performance measures that exclude certain recurring items (e.g., SG&A, tax effects) to highlight underlying operating trends.  
- Management cautions that these metrics should be read alongside U.S. GAAP results because they do not replace traditional income‑from‑operations figures.  
- The increase in **Pre‑tax Insurance AOI** despite the net loss was driven primarily by:
  * Higher net investment income and premium growth from the KIC block acquisition and the legacy CGI block.  
  * Favorable reserve adjustments, lower policy benefits, and improved claims experience.  
- Offsetting factors included higher selling, general and administrative expenses linked to headcount additions from the KIC acquisition.

Overall, while the segment’s GAAP net income deteriorated in 2019, the adjusted operating measures indicate that core underwriting and investment activities generated positive operating performance, underscoring the importance of evaluating both GAAP and non‑GAAP metrics for a complete financial picture.

synth_text.title: Insurance Segment Financial Performance: 2018‑2019 Comparison
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the Insurance segment, reported net income fell sharply from **$165.2 million in 2018** to **$59.4 million in 2019**, a decline of $105.8 million. Despite the drop in GAAP net income, the segment’s **Pre‑tax Adjusted Operating Income (Pre‑tax Insurance AOI)** rose dramatically from **$0.6 million in 2018** to **$85.7 million in 2019**, reflecting the impact of several non‑GAAP adjustments.

**Key Adjustments Driving Pre‑tax Insurance AOI**  

| Item | 2018 (million $) | 2019 (million $) |
|------|------------------|------------------|
| Effect of investment (gains)¹ | (5.6) | (1.9) |
| Asset impairment expense | — | 47.3 |
| Gain on bargain purchase | (115.4) | (1.1) |
| Gain on reinsurance recaptures | (47.0) | — |
| Acquisition costs | 2.8 | 2.1 |
| **Insurance AOI** | — | 105.8 |
| Income tax expense (benefit) | 0.6 | (20.1) |
| **Pre‑tax Insurance AOI** | **0.6** | **85.7** |

*¹ Investment gains include realized and unrealized net investment income and are adjusted for intra‑group transactions.*

**Drivers of the 2019 Increase**  
- **Higher net investment income** and **policy premiums** stemming from the KIC block acquisition and stronger performance of the legacy CGI block.  
- **Favorable reserve and claim developments**, including lower policy benefits, reduced reserve adjustments, and improved claim outcomes.  
- **Increased contingent non‑forfeiture option activity** linked to in‑force rate actions.  

These positive factors were partially offset by **higher selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses**, mainly due to headcount additions associated with the KIC acquisition.

**Context on Insurance AOI**  
Insurance AOI and Pre‑tax Insurance AOI are non‑U.S. GAAP measures used by the company to evaluate operating performance. They exclude certain recurring items (e.g., tax expense, specific gains/losses) to highlight underlying trends, but they are not substitutes for GAAP earnings and should be read alongside the GAAP results.

**Conclusion**  
While GAAP net income declined sharply in 2019, the substantial rise in Pre‑tax Insurance AOI indicates that the core insurance operations generated stronger operating cash flow, driven by investment income, premium growth, and favorable reserve/claim activity. The increase in SG&A costs underscores the cost of integrating recent acquisitions. Stakeholders should consider both GAAP and adjusted metrics to obtain a complete picture of the segment’s performance.

synth_text.title: Summary of Diluted Weighted‑Average Share Calculations
synth_text.text:
The company’s share‑based calculations for the two most recent reporting periods are shown below.

| Period | Weighted‑average common shares – basic | Dilutive effect of stock options | Dilutive effect of restricted stock | Diluted weighted‑average shares |
|--------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| **Period 1** | 45,542,315 | 32,222 | 505,858 | 46,080,395 |
| **Period 2** | 45,280,161 | 33,134 | 467,659 | 45,780,954 |

In each period, the basic share count represents the average number of common shares outstanding. The dilutive effect of stock options adds a modest number of shares (approximately 32–33 k), while restricted‑stock awards contribute a substantially larger amount (approximately 468–506 k). According to the company’s accounting policy, restricted‑stock shares are included in basic earnings‑per‑share (EPS) calculations as they vest and are also incorporated into diluted EPS when they are dilutive, using the treasury‑stock method. Consequently, the combined dilutive impact of stock options and restricted stock raises the weighted‑average share count to the diluted totals shown above.

Overall, the diluted weighted‑average shares increased from 45.78 million in Period 2 to 46.08 million in Period 1, driven primarily by the higher contribution from restricted‑stock awards. This reflects the company’s ongoing use of equity‑based compensation and its effect on EPS calculations.

synth_text.title: Determination of Diluted Weighted‑Average Shares for EPS Calculation
synth_text.text:
The company’s earnings‑per‑share (EPS) calculations are based on a weighted‑average number of common shares. For the period reported, the basic weighted‑average common shares outstanding were **44,855,263**.  

Dilutive securities increase this figure:
- **Stock options** contributed an additional **31,534** shares.
- **Restricted‑stock awards**, which vest and are treated as dilutive under the treasury‑stock method, added **297,406** shares.

When these dilutive effects are combined with the basic share count, the **diluted weighted‑average number of common shares** totals **45,184,203**. This diluted figure is used in the computation of diluted EPS, reflecting the potential impact of all dilutive instruments.  

The methodology follows the company’s accounting policy that includes vested restricted‑stock shares in basic EPS and incorporates them in diluted EPS to the extent they are dilutive.

Productivity and Business Processes

synth_text.title: Microsoft Fiscal Year 2019 Revenue Growth by Segment
synth_text.text:
Microsoft reported a **21 % increase in total revenue** for fiscal year 2019, driven by strong performance across its three primary reportable segments.

**Productivity and Business Processes – 13 % growth**  
Revenue rose 15 % year‑over‑year, led by Office 365 Commercial (up 33 % from higher seat counts and higher average revenue per user) and continued expansion of LinkedIn (up 28 %). Office Consumer contributed modest growth, while Dynamics 365 added 15 % to the segment.

**Intelligent Cloud – 26 % growth**  
The segment posted a 21 % increase, anchored by Azure’s 72 % surge and a 25 % rise in overall server products and cloud services (including GitHub). Enterprise Services also grew modestly, reflecting higher demand for Premier Support and consulting services.

**More Personal Computing – 20 % growth**  
Revenue grew 8 %, propelled by Windows (commercial and OEM) and a 23 % jump in Surface sales. Gaming revenue rose 10 % on strong Xbox software and services subscriptions, while Search advertising increased 9 % thanks to higher revenue per search.

**Corporate and Other**  
No meaningful revenue was recorded for Corporate and Other activities during the period, so it does not affect the overall growth picture.

Overall, Microsoft’s revenue growth was powered by a shift toward cloud‑based subscriptions, robust enterprise and consumer software adoption, and continued strength in hardware and advertising businesses.

synth_text.title: Microsoft FY 2019 Revenue Overview by Segment and Growth Drivers
synth_text.text:
**Revenue Summary (FY 2019 vs. FY 2018)**  
- **Total revenue** rose to **$42.96 billion**, up **$7.90 billion** (≈ 22.5 %) from $35.06 billion in FY 2018.  
- **Productivity and Business Processes** increased to **$16.22 billion**, a gain of **$3.30 billion** (≈ 27 %).  
- **Intelligent Cloud** grew to **$13.92 billion**, up **$2.40 billion** (≈ 20.8 %).  
- **More Personal Computing** reached **$12.82 billion**, up **$2.21 billion** (≈ 20.9 %).  
- “Corporate and Other” reported **$0** in both years, so it had no impact on revenue.

**Key Growth Drivers**

*Productivity and Business Processes*  
- **Office 365 Commercial** drove a 33 % increase in seats and higher average revenue per user, offsetting lower on‑premises licensing.  
- **Office 365 Consumer** added $286 million, supported by strong subscription uptake, especially in Japan.  
- **LinkedIn** contributed $1.5 billion (28 % growth) across all its lines of business.  
- **Dynamics 365** delivered a 15 % rise, reinforcing the segment’s cloud transition.

*Intelligent Cloud*  
- **Azure** was the primary catalyst, posting a 72 % revenue surge thanks to higher consumption‑based IaaS and PaaS usage.  
- **Server products and GitHub** added $6.5 billion (25 % growth), reflecting demand for premium and hybrid solutions.  
- **Enterprise Services** grew modestly (+5 %) through expanded Premier Support and consulting engagements.

*More Personal Computing*  
- **Windows** revenue rose 4 % ($877 million), boosted by commercial and OEM sales and multi‑year agreements.  
- **Surface** devices surged 23 % ($1.1 billion) across both consumer and commercial lines.  
- **Gaming** (Xbox software and services) grew 10 % ($1.0 billion) on the back of strong third‑party titles and subscription growth, despite a 13 % dip in hardware sales.  
- **Search advertising** increased 9 % ($616 million), driven by higher revenue per search.

**Operating Income**  
Operating income also improved, reflecting higher gross margins and controlled operating expenses across the three segments, while foreign‑currency effects remained modestly unfavorable.

**Conclusion**  
Microsoft’s FY 2019 revenue growth was broad‑based, with each major segment delivering double‑digit percentage gains. The shift toward cloud‑based subscriptions (Office 365, Azure, Dynamics 365) and continued strength in Windows, Surface, and gaming services were the primary engines of the $7.9 billion increase in total revenue.

- **Office 365 Consumer** added 7 % revenue, bolstered by strong subscription uptake in Japan.  
- **LinkedIn** surged 28 % (≈ $1.5 billion) across all lines of business.  
- **Dynamics 365** rose 15 % as cloud‑based ERP and CRM solutions expanded.

- **Server products and cloud services** (including GitHub) grew 25 % as enterprises adopted hybrid and premium licensing.

**Corporate and Other** showed a modest loss of **$306 million**, reflecting the absence of restructuring expenses in FY 2019.

Overall, Microsoft’s FY 2019 performance was powered by continued migration to cloud‑based subscriptions, strong growth in Azure and LinkedIn, and robust demand for Surface devices and gaming services. synth_text.title: Year‑over‑Year EPS Summary Highlighting Shift from Profit to Loss
synth_text.text:
The company’s earnings per share (EPS) performance changed markedly between the two most recent fiscal years.

- **Fiscal Year ending December 31, 2017**: Net income attributable to common stockholders was **$19.8 million**. The weighted‑average number of basic common shares was **27.48 million**, producing a **basic EPS of $0.72**. When potential dilution from unvested Restricted Stock Units (RSUs) and stock options is considered, the diluted share count rises to **28.42 million**, resulting in a **diluted EPS of $0.70**. The diluted EPS reflects the inclusion of **438,712 unvested RSUs** and **477,048 stock options** whose exercise prices were below the average market price during the period.

- **Fiscal Year ending December 31, 2018**: The company recorded a **net loss of $16.5 million** attributable to common stockholders. The weighted‑average common share count (both basic and diluted) was **27.62 million**, leading to a **basic and diluted loss of $0.60 per share**. The diluted EPS calculation incorporates **215,196 unvested RSUs** and **716,661 stock options** that were potentially dilutive, as their exercise prices were also below the average market price.

In both years, basic EPS is derived solely from the weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding, while diluted EPS adjusts for securities that could increase the share count. The shift from a positive basic EPS of $0.72 in 2017 to a negative $0.60 in 2018 underscores a significant decline in profitability, despite the consistent methodology for accounting for dilutive securities.

text.value: (8) Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP financial measure that we define as net (loss) income, adjusted to exclude: depreciation, amortization, disposals and impairment of long-lived assets, acquisition-related gains and expenses, litigation-related expenses, share-based compensation expense, restructuring expense, interest income and interest expense, the provision for income taxes and foreign exchange income (expense). Adjusted EBITDA also includes rent paid in the period related to locations that are accounted for as build-to-suit facilities.

We believe that Adjusted EBITDA provides investors and other users of our financial information consistency and comparability with our past financial performance, facilitates period-to-period comparisons of operations and facilitates comparisons with our peer companies, many of which use a similar non-GAAP financial measure to supplement their GAAP results.

We use Adjusted EBITDA in conjunction with traditional GAAP operating performance measures as part of our overall assessment of our performance, for planning purposes, including the preparation of our annual operating budget, to evaluate the effectiveness of our business strategies, to communicate with our board of directors concerning our financial performance, and for establishing incentive compensation metrics for executives and other senior employees.

We do not place undue reliance on Adjusted EBITDA as a measure of operating performance. This non-GAAP measure should not be considered as a substitute for other measures of financial performance reported in accordance with GAAP. There are limitations to using a non-GAAP financial measure, including that other companies may calculate this measure differently than we do, that it does not reflect our capital expenditures or future requirements for capital expenditures and that it does not reflect changes in, or cash requirements for, our working capital.

**Key adjustments**  
- **Depreciation, amortization and disposals** are added back because they are non‑cash charges.  
- **Interest expense (or income)**, **provision for income taxes**, and **foreign‑exchange expense (or income)** are excluded to focus on operating performance.  
- **Share‑based compensation**, **acquisition‑related expenses**, and **rent for build‑to‑suit facilities** (none reported) are also added back.  
- No amounts were recorded for impairments, restructuring, gains on previously held assets, or litigation‑related expenses in either period.

**Purpose of Adjusted EBITDA**  
Adjusted EBITDA is a non‑GAAP metric that provides a consistent view of operating profitability across periods and against peer companies. It is used internally for budgeting, evaluating business strategies, communicating performance to the board, and setting executive incentive targets.

**Limitations**  
While useful for comparison, Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect capital expenditures, changes in working‑capital cash requirements, or the specific calculation methods employed by other firms. It should be considered alongside GAAP measures rather than as a substitute.

Overall, the reconciliations show that after adding back the listed non‑cash and non‑operating items, the company generated $12.5 million of Adjusted EBITDA in 2019 and $15.8 million in 2017, despite reporting net losses in both years.

synth_text.title: Reconciliation of Net Loss to Adjusted EBITDA for Fiscal Years 2019 and 2017
synth_text.text:
**Adjusted EBITDA – definition and purpose**  
Adjusted EBITDA is a non‑GAAP performance metric that starts with net (loss) income and removes items that are not reflective of core operating performance. Specifically, it excludes depreciation, amortization, disposals and impairments of long‑lived assets, acquisition‑related gains and expenses, litigation‑related costs, share‑based compensation, restructuring charges, interest income and expense, income‑tax provision, and foreign‑exchange gains or losses. Rent paid for build‑to‑suit facilities is added back. The company uses this measure to provide investors with a more comparable view of operating results across periods and against peers, to aid internal budgeting, strategy assessment, board reporting, and executive compensation decisions. While useful, Adjusted EBITDA is not a substitute for GAAP results and has known limitations (e.g., it does not reflect capital‑expenditure needs or working‑capital cash requirements).

**Reconciliation summary**

| Item (adjustments) | FY 2019 (ended Mar 31 2019) | FY 2017 (ended Mar 31 2017) |
|--------------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Net (loss) income | **$(7,001)** | **$(12,386)** |
| + Depreciation, amortization & disposals | 29,960 | 19,141 |
| + Rent expense (build‑to‑suit) | (4,482) | (785) |
| + Interest expense (net) | 3,425 | (712) |
| + Provision for income taxes | 2,001 | 2,705 |
| + Share‑based compensation | 25,954 | 11,734 |
| + Impairments of long‑lived assets | — | 1,712 |
| + Restructuring | (170) | 832 |
| + Foreign‑exchange expense (income) | 1,647 | 3,511 |
| + Acquisition‑related expenses | 2,012* | — |
| + Gain on previously held asset | (338)† | — |
| + Litigation‑related expenses | 1,000‡ | — |
| **Adjusted EBITDA** | **$54,008** | **$25,752** |

\* Acquisition‑related expenses relate to costs incurred for acquisition activity in FY 2019 (see Note 5).  
† The gain on the Solebit acquisition is recorded in FY 2019 (Note 5).  
‡ Litigation expenses accrued for loss contingencies are reported only in FY 2019 (Note 12).

**Key observations**

* Adjusted EBITDA increased markedly from $25.8 million in FY 2017 to $54.0 million in FY 2019, driven primarily by higher share‑based compensation expense, larger depreciation/amortization, and the inclusion of acquisition‑related expenses and a gain on a previously held asset in FY 2019.  
* Net loss narrowed from $(12.4) million to $(7.0) million, reflecting improved underlying profitability.  
* Interest expense turned positive in FY 2019 (net interest expense of $3.4 million) after a net interest income of $712 k in FY 2017.  
* Impairments and restructuring costs were present only in FY 2017, while litigation expenses appeared only in FY 2019.  

Overall, the reconciliation demonstrates how the company adjusts GAAP net loss to arrive at a non‑GAAP Adjusted EBITDA figure that better reflects its operating performance for each fiscal year.

synth_text.title: Charter‑In Vessel Lease Commitments and Liabilities Overview (2020‑2024)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Company’s charter‑in fleet consists of one vessel accounted for as a finance lease (the Overseas Key West) and ten vessels accounted for as operating leases. All vessels are bare‑boat charters; the finance‑lease vessel has a 10‑year term, while the operating‑lease vessels have been extended through a series of option exercises that now run to December 2023 for four vessels and to December 2022 for five vessels, with one vessel extended to June 2025.

**Future Minimum Lease Payments**  
The table below summarises the minimum cash payments required under each lease category:

| Year | Finance‑Lease Vessel | Operating‑Lease Vessels |
|------|----------------------|--------------------------|
| 2020 | $92,404 | $4,172 |
| 2021 | $91,164 | $4,161 |
| 2022 | $107,654 | $4,161 |
| 2023 | $43,015 | $4,161 |
| 2024 | $9,168 | $4,172 |
| Thereafter* | $4,534 | $17,180 |

\* “Thereafter” captures payments due after 2024, reflecting the effect of lease‑term extensions and the deferred payment obligations (DPO) that apply to five of the operating‑lease vessels.

**Aggregate Lease Obligations**  
- **Net minimum lease payments**: $347,939 (finance) + $38,007 (operating) = **$385,946**.  
- **Present‑value discount** applied to these cash flows: $40,891 (finance) + $10,448 (operating) = **$51,339**.  
- **Total lease liabilities** (after discount): **$307,048** for the finance lease and **$27,559** for the operating leases, amounting to **$334,607** in total.

**Key Lease‑Related Activities (2018‑2019)**  
- Lease expense for the ten operating‑lease vessels was $90,359 in 2019 (recorded within charter‑hire expense).  
- Sub‑lease income for 2019 amounted to $188,163.  
- Non‑cash operating activities related to lease renewals added $93,407 in 2019.  
- Finance‑lease expense in 2019 comprised $2,052 of amortisation and $1,462 of interest, with non‑cash financing activities of $28,993 for the finance right‑of‑use asset.  
- In 2018, total charter‑in lease expense was $91,350.

**Implications**  
The bulk of the finance‑lease cash outflow occurs in 2022, after which payments decline sharply, reflecting the scheduled termination of the lease term. Operating‑lease payments remain relatively flat each year, with a modest increase in the “Thereafter” column driven by the DPO schedule and the extended terms of the four vessels now ending in 2023. The present‑value discounts reduce the recorded lease liabilities to $334.6 million, a figure that will be reflected on the consolidated balance sheet under right‑of‑use assets and lease liabilities.

Overall, the Company’s lease commitments are well‑structured, with most obligations already accounted for and a clear view of future cash requirements through 2024 and beyond.

text.value: Consolidated Net Income, Consolidated EBITDA and Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA

Consolidated earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization expenses (Consolidated EBITDA) and Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA, which are presented below, are non-generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) measures that we believe are useful to management, investors and other users of our financial information in evaluating operating profitability on a more variable cost basis as they exclude the depreciation and amortization expense related primarily to capital expenditures and acquisitions that occurred in prior years,

as well as in evaluating operating performance in relation to Verizon’s competitors. Consolidated EBITDA is calculated by adding back interest, taxes, and depreciation and amortization expenses to net income.

Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA is calculated by excluding from Consolidated EBITDA the effect of the following non-operational items: equity in losses of unconsolidated businesses and other income and expense, net, as well as the effect of special items. We believe that this measure is useful to management, investors and other users of our financial information in evaluating the effectiveness of our operations and underlying business trends in a manner that is consistent with management’s evaluation of business performance.

We believe that Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA is widely used by investors to compare a company’s operating performance to its competitors by minimizing impacts caused by differences in capital structure, taxes and depreciation policies. Further, the exclusion of non-operational items and special items enables comparability to prior period performance and trend analysis. See “Special Items” for additional information.

It is management’s intent to provide non-GAAP financial information to enhance the understanding of Verizon’s GAAP financial information, and it should be considered by the reader in addition to, but not instead of, the financial statements prepared in accordance with GAAP. Each non-GAAP financial measure is presented along with the corresponding GAAP measure so as not to imply that more emphasis should be placed on the non-GAAP measure.

We believe that non-GAAP measures provide relevant and useful information, which is used by management, investors and other users of our financial information, as well as by our management in assessing both consolidated and segment performance. The non-GAAP financial information presented may be determined or calculated differently by other companies and may not be directly comparable to that of other companies.

† Includes Pension and benefits mark-to-market adjustments and early debt redemption costs, where applicable. ‡ Includes Product realignment charges and impairment charges, where applicable. § Excludes depreciation and amortization expense.

synth_text.title: Verizon Financial Performance: 2019 vs. 2018 – Net Income, EBITDA, and Adjusted EBITDA Overview
synth_text.text:
**Financial Highlights (2018‑2019)**  

- **Consolidated Net Income** rose from **$16,039 million** in 2018 to **$19,788 million** in 2019, reflecting stronger operating results and lower tax provision (down from $3,584 million to $2,945 million).  
- **Consolidated EBITDA** increased from **$41,859 million** to **$44,145 million**, driven by higher net income, reduced interest expense (down to $4,730 million from $4,833 million), and lower depreciation & amortization ($16,682 million vs. $17,403 million).  
- **Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA**—which excludes non‑operational items such as equity losses, other income/expense, and special charges—slightly **declined** from **$47,410 million** in 2018 to **$47,189 million** in 2019. The dip is mainly due to a rise in “Other (income) expense, net” ($2,900 million in 2019 versus a gain of $(2,364) million in 2018) and modest increases in severance and impairment charges.

**Understanding the Non‑GAAP Measures**  

- **Consolidated EBITDA** is a non‑GAAP metric that adds back interest, taxes, and depreciation & amortization to net income. It provides a view of operating profitability on a variable‑cost basis, removing the impact of capital‑intensive investments and financing decisions.  
- **Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA** further refines EBITDA by stripping out equity losses from unconsolidated businesses, other income/expense, and special items (e.g., severance, acquisition integration, product realignment, and impairment charges). This measure is intended to reflect the underlying performance of Verizon’s core operations and to enable more consistent comparisons with peers, regardless of differences in capital structure, tax regimes, or depreciation policies.  

**Key Takeaways**  

1. **Revenue‑driven growth** boosted net income and EBITDA in 2019.  
2. **Tax and interest efficiencies** contributed to higher GAAP profitability.  
3. **Adjusted EBITDA’s modest decline** underscores the effect of one‑time or non‑operational items, even as core operating cash flow improved.  
4. The non‑GAAP metrics are presented alongside GAAP figures to give investors a clearer picture of operating trends while acknowledging that they are supplemental and may differ from similar measures used by other companies.  

Overall, Verizon’s 2019 financial performance shows solid improvement in earnings and cash‑flow generation, with the adjusted EBITDA metric highlighting the importance of monitoring special items that can temporarily affect reported operating results.

text.value: 10. Operating Leases

The Company charters-in vessels from other vessel owners on time-charter-in and bareboat charter contracts, whereby the vessel owner provides use of the vessel to the Company, and, in the case of time-charter-in contracts, also operates the vessel for the Company. A timecharter- in contract is typically for a fixed period of time, although in certain cases the Company may have the option to extend the charter.

The Company typically pays the owner a daily hire rate that is fixed over the duration of the charter. The Company is generally not required to pay the daily hire rate for time-charters during periods the vessel is not able to operate.

With respect to time-charter- With respect to time-charter-in and bareboat charter contracts with an original term of more than one year, for the year ended December 31, 2019, the Company incurred $99.0 million of time-charter and bareboat hire expense related to these time-charter and bareboat charter contracts, of which $68.2 million was allocable to the lease component, and $30.8 million was allocable to the non-lease component.

The amounts allocable to the lease component approximate the cash paid for the amounts included in lease liabilities and are reflected as a reduction in operating cash flows for the year ended December 31, 2019. Three of Teekay Tankers' time-charter-in contracts each have an option to extend the charter for an additional one-year term.

Since it is not reasonably certain that Teekay Tankers will exercise the options, the lease components of the options are not recognized as part of the right-of-use assets and lease liabilities. As at December 31, 2019, the weighted-average remaining lease term and weighted-average discount rate for these time-charter-in and bareboat charter contracts were 2.6 years and 6.1%, respectively.

During the year ended December 31, 2019, Teekay Tankers chartered in two LR2 vessels and one Aframax vessel for periods of 24 months each, Teekay LNG extended the charter-in contract for one LNG carrier for a period of 21 months, and Teekay Parent extended the charterin contract for one FSO unit for a period of 12 months, which resulted in the Company recognizing right-of-use assets and lease liabilities totaling $47.7 million and $47.7 million, respectively.

synth_text.title: Net Periodic Benefit Cost Overview for 2018‑2019 and Effects of the 2018 Accounting Standard Change
synth_text.text:
The table below breaks down the net periodic benefit cost (NPBC) for the Company’s pension plans in fiscal years 2019 and 2018 (all amounts in thousands of dollars).

| Year | Service Cost | Interest Cost | Expected Long‑Term Return on Plan Assets* | Recognized Actuarial Loss | Amortization of Prior Service Credit* | Net Settlement Loss | Net Periodic Benefit Cost |
|------|--------------|---------------|--------------------------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| 2019 | $1,437 | $3,715 | $(5,291) | $741 | $(44) | $634 | $1,192 |
| 2018 | $1,063 | $3,807 | $(5,954) | $1,127 | $(88) | $116 | $71 |

\*Negative figures are shown in parentheses.

**Key observations**

* **Service cost** rose from $1,063 k in 2018 to $1,437 k in 2019, reflecting higher projected benefit payments.
* **Interest cost** fell slightly, from $3,807 k to $3,715 k.
* The **expected long‑term return on plan assets** improved (less negative) from $(5,954) k to $(5,291) k, indicating better asset performance assumptions.
* **Recognized actuarial loss** decreased markedly, from $1,127 k to $741 k, while **amortization of prior service credit** was halved.
* **Net settlement loss** increased sharply, from $116 k to $634 k, contributing to the higher overall NPBC.
* Consequently, **net periodic benefit cost** jumped from $71 k in 2018 to $1,192 k in 2019.

**Impact of the 2018 accounting standard change**

On September 1 2018 the Company adopted a new accounting standard that alters the presentation of NPBC in the Consolidated Statements of Operations. The standard was applied retrospectively to 2018, resulting in:

* **Service cost** being reclassified from selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expense to cost of revenue.
* All other NPBC components (interest cost, expected return, actuarial loss, amortization, settlement loss) being moved from SG&A expense to other expense.

Prior periods (e.g., 2017) were not restated because the effect was deemed immaterial.

Overall, the data illustrate a substantial increase in the Company’s net periodic benefit cost in 2019, driven primarily by higher service cost and a larger net settlement loss, while the 2018 accounting change reshaped how these costs are reported in the financial statements.

synth_text.title: IBM Systems Segment – FY 2019 Revenue Performance Overview
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, IBM’s Systems segment generated **$7.6 billion in external revenue**, marking a **5.3 % decline** year‑over‑year (4.1 % when adjusted for currency). The decline was driven primarily by the hardware sub‑segment, which fell **7.0 %** (5.9 % currency‑adjusted) to **$5.9 billion**.

**Hardware breakdown**

* **IBM Z** – Reported revenue slipped **1.1 %**, essentially flat after currency adjustment. The dip reflects the tail‑end of the z14 product cycle, with a rebound in Q4 thanks to strong z15 shipments that emphasized data‑privacy, resiliency, and hybrid‑cloud capabilities. IBM also announced OpenShift for IBM Z, extending its container and Kubernetes offerings.

* **Power Systems** – Experienced the steepest drop, down **13.5 %** (12 % currency‑adjusted). The decline follows a robust second half of 2018, during which the POWER9 architecture was introduced across mid‑range and high‑end servers.

* **Storage Systems** – Declined **8.9 %** (8 % currency‑adjusted). Performance improved in Q4 of 2019, buoyed by the launch of the next‑generation DS8900 high‑end storage system in November.

**Software and cloud**

* **Operating Systems Software** revenue grew modestly **0.9 %** as reported and **2.6 %** after currency adjustment, reaching **$1.7 billion**.  

* Within Systems, **cloud revenue** amounted to **$2.9 billion**, down **4 %** (3 % currency‑adjusted) year‑over‑year.

Overall, the Systems segment’s revenue contraction was largely a function of hardware declines, while software and cloud components showed relative resilience. Strategic product introductions—z15 mainframes, POWER9 servers, and the DS8900 storage system—provided a foundation for potential recovery in the coming periods.

synth_text.title: IBM Systems Revenue and Product Performance Overview – FY 2018 vs FY 2019
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2019, IBM’s Systems segment generated **$7.6 billion** in external revenue, a **5.3 % decline** from $8.0 billion in 2018 (4 % when adjusted for currency).  

**Systems Hardware** fell to **$5.9 billion**, down **7.0 %** year‑over‑year (6 % currency‑adjusted). The hardware decline was driven primarily by weaker Power Systems and Storage Systems sales.  

- **IBM Z** revenue slipped 1.1 % (essentially flat after currency adjustment). The dip reflected the end of the z14 product cycle, but the fourth quarter saw strong growth from z15 shipments, underscoring client demand for enhanced data privacy, resiliency, and hybrid‑cloud capabilities. In October, IBM announced **OpenShift for IBM Z**, extending its container and Kubernetes platform to the mainframe.  
- **Power Systems** revenue dropped **13.5 %** (12 % currency‑adjusted), a reversal from the strong second half of 2018 that benefited Linux workloads and the introduction of POWER9‑based architectures.  
- **Storage Systems** revenue declined **8.9 %** (8 % currency‑adjusted). Performance improved in Q4 2019, helped by the launch of the next‑generation DS8900 high‑end storage system in November.  

**Operating Systems Software** revenue rose modestly to **$1.7 billion**, a **0.9 % increase** (3 % currency‑adjusted) over the prior year, indicating steady demand for IBM’s software offerings.  

Within the broader Systems segment, **cloud revenue** amounted to **$2.9 billion**, down **4 %** (3 % currency‑adjusted) compared with 2018, reflecting a slight slowdown in cloud‑related sales across the portfolio.  

Overall, the 2019 results show a contraction in hardware sales offset partially by stable mainframe performance and modest software growth, while IBM continues to invest in next‑generation mainframe and storage technologies to drive future demand.

Historically, our primary source of cash has been provided by operations. Supplemental information pertaining to our historical sources and uses of cash is presented as follows and should be read in conjunction with our Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows and notes thereto (in thousands):

Net cash provided by operating activities decreased by $54.7 million in fiscal 2019 compared to fiscal 2018. We believe that our existing cash, cash equivalents and short term investments combined with cash to be provided by operating activities and amounts available under our Revolving Credit Facility will be adequate to cover our working capital needs and planned capital expenditures for at least the next 12 months to the extent such items are known or are reasonably determinable based on current business and market conditions. However, we may elect to finance certain of our capital expenditure requirements through other sources of capital. text.value: Recently Adopted Accounting Guidance

On May 28, 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) issued Accounting Standards Update (“ASU”) No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, Topic 606, requiring an entity to recognize the amount of revenue to which it expects to be entitled for the transfer of promised goods or services to customers. Topic 606 also includes Subtopic 340-40, Other Assets and Deferred Costs - Contracts with Customers, which requires the capitalization of incremental costs to obtain a contract with a customer. The new revenue standard replaces most existing revenue recognition guidance in GAAP and permits the use of either the full retrospective or modified retrospective transition method.

On December 1, 2018, the beginning of our fiscal year 2019, we adopted the requirements of the new revenue standard utilizing the modified retrospective method of transition. Prior period information has not been restated and continues to be reported under the accounting standard in effect for those periods. We applied the new revenue standard to contracts that were not completed as of the adoption date, consistent with the transition guidance. Further, adoption of the new revenue standard resulted in changes to our accounting policies for revenue recognition and sales commissions as detailed below.
We recognized the following cumulative effects of initially applying the new revenue standard as of December 1, 2018
Below is a summary of the adoption impacts of the new revenue standard:

We capitalized $413.2 million of contract acquisition costs comprised of sales and partner commission costs at adoption date (included in prepaid expenses and other current assets for the current portion and other assets for the long-term portion), with a corresponding adjustment to retained earnings. We are amortizing these costs over their respective expected period of benefit.

Revenue for certain contracts that were previously deferred would have been recognized in periods prior to adoption under the new standard. Upon adoption, we recorded the following adjustments to our beginning balances to reflect the amount of revenue that will no longer be recognized in future periods for such contracts: an increase in unbilled receivables (included in trade receivables, net) of $24.8 million, an increase in contract assets (included in prepaid expenses and other current assets for the current portion and other assets for the long-term portion) of $46.4 million and a decrease in deferred revenue of $52.8 million, with corresponding adjustments to retained earnings.
We recorded an increase to our opening deferred income tax liability of $82.8 million, with a corresponding adjustment to retained earnings, to record the tax effect of the above adjustments.
Further, we had other impacts to various accounts which resulted to an immaterial net reduction to our retained earnings.

synth_text.text:

- **Trade receivables, net of allowances for doubtful accounts:** $1,358,606

- **Deferred income taxes:** $129,536  
- **Retained earnings:** $12,257,916  

**Effect of ASC 606 Adoption (December 1 2018)**  

1. **Capitalization of Contract Acquisition Costs** – $413.2 million of sales and partner commissions were capitalized at adoption. The current‑portion resides in “Prepaid expenses and other current assets,” while the long‑term portion is reflected in “Other assets.” These costs are being amortized over their expected benefit periods.  

2. **Revenue Recognition Adjustments** – To align with ASC 606, the company increased:  
   - **Unbilled receivables** (included in trade receivables) by $24.8 million, and  
   - **Contract assets** (included in prepaid/current and other assets) by $46.4 million.  
   Simultaneously, **deferred revenue** was reduced by $52.8 million, reflecting revenue that will no longer be recognized in future periods.  

3. **Tax Impact** – The adjustments generated an additional **deferred income tax liability** of $82.8 million, recorded under “Deferred income taxes.”  

4. **Retained Earnings** – The cumulative effect of the above changes, together with other immaterial adjustments, resulted in a net reduction to retained earnings, which now stands at $12,257,916.  

Overall, the adoption of ASC 606 reshaped the composition of current assets, long‑term assets, and liabilities, primarily through the capitalization of acquisition costs, re‑classification of revenue, and the associated tax effects. These changes provide a clearer representation of the economic benefits derived from customer contracts under the new revenue‑recognition framework.

synth_text.title: Impact of ASC 606 Adoption on the Company’s Balance Sheet (Fiscal Year 2019)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
On December 1 2018 the company adopted the Financial Accounting Standards Board’s ASC 606 revenue‑recognition standard using the modified‑retrospective method. The transition required several balance‑sheet adjustments that are reflected in the post‑adoption figures shown below.

**Key Balance‑Sheet Changes**

| Item | Pre‑Adoption (Prior Period) | Post‑Adoption (FY 2019) | Transition Effect |
|------|-----------------------------|--------------------------|-------------------|
| Trade receivables, net of allowances | $43,028 | $1,315,578 | +$24.8 M (unbilled receivables) |
| Prepaid expenses & other current assets | $186,220 | $312,499 | +$126.3 M (capitalized contract‑acquisition costs) |
| Other assets (long‑term) | $273,421 | $186,522 | –$86.9 M (re‑classification of acquisition costs) |
| Accrued expenses | $30,358 | $1,163,185 | +$1.13 B (operating accruals) |
| Deferred revenue, current | –$52,842 | $2,915,974 | –$52.8 M (reversal of previously deferred revenue) |
| Deferred income taxes | $82,834 | $46,702 | –$36.1 M (tax effect of transition adjustments) |
| Retained earnings | $442,319 | $11,815,597 | +$11.37 M (cumulative impact of all adjustments) |

**Explanation of Adjustments**

1. **Capitalized Contract‑Acquisition Costs** – $413.2 million of sales and partner commissions were capitalized at the adoption date. These costs appear in “Prepaid expenses and other current assets” for the portion expected to be recovered within one year and in “Other assets” for the long‑term portion. The capitalization increased assets and was offset by a corresponding increase in retained earnings.

2. **Revenue Recognition Adjustments** – The new standard required the company to recognize revenue that had been previously deferred. Consequently, unbilled receivables rose by $24.8 million, contract‑asset balances grew by $46.4 million, and deferred revenue decreased by $52.8 million. These changes also impacted retained earnings.

3. **Deferred Tax Liability** – The tax effect of the above balance‑sheet reclassifications added $82.8 million to the deferred income‑tax liability, with a matching adjustment to retained earnings.

4. **Other Minor Impacts** – Additional, immaterial adjustments further reduced retained earnings slightly, but they do not materially affect the overall picture.

**Conclusion**  
The adoption of ASC 606 substantially reshaped the company’s balance sheet for fiscal year 2019. The most material effects were the capitalization of contract‑acquisition costs, the reclassification of revenue and receivables, and the increase in deferred tax liabilities. These adjustments collectively increased total assets, altered current liabilities, and resulted in a net increase to retained earnings, positioning the company under the new revenue‑recognition framework.

text.value: 5.2 Employee share plans (continued)
FY2019, FY2018 & FY2017 offer under LTI Plan

Each LTI Plan share is offered subject to the achievement of the performance measure, which is tested once at the end of the performance period. The LTI Plans will be measured against one performance measure – relative Total Shareholder Return (TSR). LTI Plan shares that do not vest after testing of the relevant performance measure, lapse without retesting.

The shares will only vest if a certain Total Shareholder Return (TSR) relative to the designated comparator group, being the ASX Small Ordinaries Index excluding mining and energy companies, is achieved during the performance period. In relation to the offer, vesting starts where relative TSR reaches the 50th Percentile.

At the 50th Percentile, 50% of LTI Plan shares will vest. All LTI Plan shares will vest if relative TSR is above the 75th Percentile. Between these points, the percentage of vesting increases on a straight-line basis.

synth_text.title: FY2017 Long‑Term Incentive (LTI) Plan Share Movements and Vesting Summary
synth_text.text:
The FY2017 Long‑Term Incentive (LTI) Plan tracked a total of 3,384,696 shares at the beginning of the reporting period. Throughout the year no additional shares were granted and none were exercised. Because the performance condition—relative Total Shareholder Return (TSR) against the ASX Small Ordinaries Index (excluding mining and energy)—was not achieved for the majority of participants, a substantial forfeiture of 2,615,890 shares occurred. This forfeiture reduced the outstanding balance to 768,806 shares by the end of FY2017.

The LTI Plan’s vesting mechanism is percentile‑based: at the 50th percentile of relative TSR, 50 % of the allocated shares vest; at the 75th percentile, all shares vest; and vesting increases linearly between these points. Shares that fail to meet the required TSR threshold lapse without retesting, which explains the large forfeiture recorded.

In summary, the FY2017 LTI share pool shrank from 3.38 million to 768,806 shares due to performance‑related forfeitures, leaving the remaining shares subject to future vesting based on the TSR criteria outlined above.

4. **Earnings per Share** – Basic EPS improves from $1.70 to $2.17, and diluted EPS from $1.69 to $2.16 under the pro forma scenario, indicating stronger profitability on a per‑share basis when the acquisitions are considered.

**Conclusion**  
The pro forma presentation provides a forward‑looking view of Advanced Energy’s financial performance as if the Artesyn and LumaSense acquisitions had been completed at the start of the fiscal year. It demonstrates a materially larger revenue base and enhanced earnings, underscoring the strategic value of the acquisitions for the company’s growth trajectory.

Overall, the data indicate that while the company added new provisions during 2019, the net effect of usage and reversals kept the total provision level steady, with the majority of obligations classified as non‑current, consistent with the long‑term nature of environmental, legal, and asset‑retirement commitments.

text.value: H. Net Income Per Share

Basic net income per share is computed by dividing net income by the weighted-average number of common stock outstanding during the period. Diluted net income per share is computed by dividing net income by the weighted-average number of common stock outstanding and potentially dilutive securities outstanding during the period, as calculated using the treasury stock method. Potentially dilutive securities primarily include unvested restricted stock units (“RSUs”), including PSU awards, and stock options, including purchase options under VMware’s employee stock purchase plan, which included Pivotal’s employee stock purchase plan through the date of acquisition. Securities are excluded from the computation of diluted net income per share if their effect would be anti-dilutive. VMware uses the two-class method to calculate net income per share as both classes share the same rights in dividends; therefore, basic and diluted earnings per share are the same for both classes.

synth_text.title: VMware Net Income and Earnings‑Per‑Share Summary – February 2 2018
synth_text.text:
On February 2 2018, VMware, Inc. reported net income of **$437 million**. The weighted‑average number of basic shares outstanding for both Class A and Class B stock was **410,315 thousand shares**. After accounting for potentially dilutive securities—primarily unvested restricted stock units and employee stock options—an additional **10,572 thousand shares** were included, bringing the diluted share count to **420,887 thousand shares**.

Using these share figures, VMware’s earnings per share (EPS) were calculated as follows:

* **Basic EPS:** $1.07 per share  
* **Diluted EPS:** $1.04 per share  

The basic EPS is derived by dividing net income by the basic weighted‑average shares, while diluted EPS incorporates the effect of dilutive securities using the treasury‑stock method. VMware applies a two‑class method for EPS calculation, meaning the EPS values are identical for both Class A and Class B shareholders.

These figures provide a snapshot of VMware’s profitability and per‑share earnings for the reporting period ending February 2 2018.

synth_text.title: VMware’s Net Income and Earnings‑Per‑Share Growth: FY 2019 Q4 vs. FY 2020 Q1
synth_text.text:
The table compares VMware’s financial performance for the quarter ended February 1 2019 and the quarter ended January 31 2020.  

- **Net Income:** VMware’s net income rose sharply from **$1.65 billion** in 2019 to **$6.412 billion** in 2020, representing an increase of nearly **288 %**.  
- **Share Counts:** The weighted‑average basic shares (Classes A and B) grew modestly from **413,769 k** to **417,058 k**. After accounting for potentially dilutive securities—primarily unvested RSUs and stock options—the diluted share count increased from **421,131 k** to **425,235 k**.  
- **Earnings Per Share (EPS):**  
  - *Basic EPS* climbed from **$3.99** per share in 2019 to **$15.37** per share in 2020.  
  - *Diluted EPS* rose from **$3.92** to **$15.08** per share over the same period.  

The small difference between basic and diluted EPS reflects VMware’s “two‑class method,” where both Class A and Class B shares share identical dividend rights, resulting in essentially the same EPS for both classes. Diluted EPS incorporates the effect of dilutive securities only when they are not anti‑dilutive, as explained in the additional context.

Overall, VMware’s earnings per share improved dramatically year‑over‑year, driven primarily by a substantial increase in net income rather than significant changes in the share base. This highlights strong profitability growth between FY 2019 Q4 and FY 2020 Q1.

text.value: The valuation allowance activity for the years ended September 30, 2019, 2018, and 2017 is as follows:

The Company completed an Internal Revenue Code Section 382 analysis of the loss carry forwards in 2009 and determined then that all of the Company’s loss carry forwards are utilizable and not restricted under Section 382. The Company has not updated its Section 382 analysis subsequent to 2009 and does not believe there have been any events subsequent to 2009 that would impact the analysis.

The Company is required to recognize the financial statement benefit of a tax position only after determining that the relevant tax authority would more likely than not sustain the position following an audit. For tax positions meeting the more likely than not threshold, the amount recognized in the financial statements is the largest benefit that has a greater than 50 percent likelihood of being realized upon ultimate settlement with the relevant tax authority. The Company applies the interpretation to all tax positions for which the statute of limitations remained open. The Company had no liability for unrecognized tax benefits and did not recognize any interest or penalties during the years ended September 30, 2019, 2018, or 2017.

The Company is subject to income taxes in the U.S. federal jurisdiction, and various state jurisdictions. Tax regulations within each jurisdiction are subject to the interpretation of the related tax laws and regulations and require significant judgment to apply. With few exceptions, the Company is no longer subject to U.S. federal, state and local, income tax examinations by tax authorities for fiscal years ending prior to 2004. We are generally subject to U.S. federal and state tax examinations for all tax years since 2003 due to our net operating loss carryforwards and the utilization of the carryforwards in years still open under statute. During the year ended September 30, 2018, the Company was examined by the U.S. Internal Revenue Service for fiscal year 2016. This examination resulted in no adjustments. - The valuation allowance declined sharply from $322,404 in 2017 to $159,154 in 2018, a reduction of $163,250.  
- In 2018 the allowance increased by $79,377, bringing the balance to $159,154.  
- A further increase of $10,448 in 2019 lowered the balance to $104,858.

**Tax Position Context**

- A 2009 Internal Revenue Code §382 analysis confirmed that all of the company’s net operating loss (NOL) carryforwards are fully utilizable and not restricted. No subsequent events have altered this conclusion.  
- The company recognizes tax benefits only when a tax position is more likely than not to be sustained by the tax authority. All such positions have been recorded at the maximum benefit with a greater than 50 % likelihood of realization.  
- No unrecognized tax benefits, interest, or penalties were recorded for the years ended September 30, 2017‑2019.  
- The company is subject to U.S. federal and various state income taxes. Examinations for tax years prior to 2004 are largely complete; examinations for years from 2003 onward continue due to the NOL carryforwards.  
- During 2018, the IRS examined the 2016 tax year, resulting in no adjustments.  
- The fiscal year was changed in 2007 from March 31 to September 30.

**Overall Assessment**

The valuation allowance has been steadily decreasing, reflecting the company’s confidence in the realizability of its NOL carryforwards. The unchanged Section 382 analysis, absence of unrecognized tax benefits, and clean IRS examination outcomes support the stability of the company’s tax position over the 2017‑2019 period.

text.value: CAPITAL MANAGEMENT

The primary objective of the Company’s capital management is to ensure that it maintains a strong credit rating and healthy capital ratios to support its business and maximize the stockholders’ value. The Company also ensures its ability to operate continuously to provide returns to stockholders and the interests of other related parties, while maintaining the optimal capital structure to reduce costs of capital.
To maintain or adjust the capital structure, the Company may adjust the dividend payment to stockholders, return capital to stockholders, issue new shares or dispose assets to redeem liabilities.

Similar to its peers, the Company monitors its capital based on debt to capital ratio. The ratio is calculated as the Company’s net debt divided by its total capital. The net debt is derived by taking the total liabilities on the consolidated balance sheets minus cash and cash equivalents. The total capital consists of total equity (including capital, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings, other components of equity and non-controlling interests) plus net debt.

The Company’s strategy, which is unchanged for the reporting periods, is to maintain a reasonable ratio in order to raise capital with reasonable cost. The debt to capital ratios as of December 31, 2018 and 2019 were as follows:

synth_text.title: FY19 National Storage Acquisition Activity Across Australia and New Zealand
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2019 National Storage completed a total of **35 acquisitions** (plus four development sites) across Australia and New Zealand, representing an investment of **approximately $163 million**. The acquisitions were geographically diverse, with the highest concentration in **Brisbane (5 deals, $25 million)** and **Central Coast, NSW (6 deals, $20.6 million)**. Other notable markets included **Gold Coast (4 deals, $6.5 million)**, **Auckland (NZ) (3 deals, $27 million)**, **Hamilton (NZ) (4 deals, $21.6 million)**, and **Wollongong (3 deals, $12.7 million)**. Smaller‑scale purchases were made on the Sunshine Coast, Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth, Rotorua, and Tauranga, each contributing between one and three transactions and ranging from $3.2 million to $8.6 million in value.

These acquisitions reinforce National Storage’s core growth strategy: leveraging high‑quality, accretive purchases to expand and scale its operating platform, drive efficiencies, and strengthen market presence across both countries. The ability to integrate new assets quickly remains a key competitive advantage.

A significant component of the group’s portfolio is **Wine Ark**, Australia’s largest wine‑storage provider. As part of National Storage, Wine Ark stores over two million bottles across 15 centres and continues to deepen its ties with the wine industry, supporting organisations such as the Wine Communicators of Australia and the Sommeliers Association of Australia.

Overall, FY19’s acquisition activity demonstrates National Storage’s aggressive expansion agenda, its focus on strategic locations, and the complementary role of Wine Ark in broadening the group’s service offering.

synth_text.title: Assumptions and Valuation Summary for 2018‑2019 Stock Options and the 2020 Employee Grant
synth_text.text:
The company’s stock‑option valuations for the 2018 and 2019 grant years were based on a Black‑Scholes model using a 6.2‑year weighted‑average expected life.  

- **2018 Grant Assumptions** – Volatility was assumed to be between **64 % and 69 %**, the risk‑free interest rate ranged from **1.8 % to 2.7 %**, and the average expected life of the options was **6.1–6.3 years**. No dividend yield was incorporated.  

- **2019 Grant Assumptions** – Volatility was higher, set at **75 % to 81 %**, with a risk‑free rate of **2.2 % to 2.8 %**. The expected life remained at **6.2 years**, and again, dividends were assumed to be zero.  

At year‑end 2019, the intrinsic value of all exercisable options was less than **$0.1 million**. The intrinsic value realized from options exercised was **$0.4 million in 2019** and **$0.1 million in 2018**, reflecting the modest economic benefit derived from those grants.  

In **January 2020**, the company issued a new employee option grant covering up to **591,004 shares** of common stock. Each option carries an exercise price of **$1.23** per share, vests in four equal annual installments through **January 2024**, and was recorded with a grant‑date fair value of **$1.26 per share**.  

These assumptions and recent grant terms together provide a comprehensive view of the company’s approach to valuing and issuing stock‑based compensation during the 2018‑2020 period.

text.value: Segments

We operate through three reportable segments: Transportation Solutions, Industrial Solutions, and Communications Solutions. We believe our segments serve a combined market of approximately $190 billion.
Our net sales by segment as a percentage of our total net sales were as follows:
Below is a description of our reportable segments and the primary products, markets, and competitors of each segment.

Transportation Solutions The Transportation Solutions segment is a leader in connectivity and sensor technologies. The primary products sold by the Transportation Solutions segment include terminals and connector systems and components, sensors, antennas, relays, application tooling, and wire and heat shrink tubing. The Transportation Solutions segment’s products, which must withstand harsh conditions, are used in the following end markets:

• Automotive (73% of segment’s net sales)—We are one of the leading providers of advanced automobile connectivity solutions. The automotive industry uses our products in automotive technologies for body and chassis systems, convenience applications, driver information, infotainment solutions, miniaturization solutions, motor and powertrain applications, and safety and security systems. Hybrid and electronic mobility solutions include in-vehicle technologies, battery technologies, and charging solutions.

• Commercial transportation (15% of segment’s net sales)—We deliver reliable connectivity products designed to withstand harsh environmental conditions for on- and off-highway vehicles and recreational transportation, including heavy trucks, construction, agriculture, buses, and other vehicles.

• Sensors (12% of segment’s net sales)—We offer a portfolio of intelligent, efficient, and high-performing sensor solutions that are used by customers across multiple industries, including automotive, industrial equipment, commercial transportation, medical solutions, aerospace and defense, and consumer applications.
The Transportation Solutions segment’s major competitors include Yazaki, Aptiv, Sumitomo, Sensata, Honeywell, Molex, and Amphenol.

Industrial Solutions The Industrial Solutions segment is a leading supplier of products that connect and distribute power, data, and signals. The primary products sold by the Industrial Solutions segment include terminals and connector systems and components, heat shrink tubing, relays, and wire and cable. The Industrial Solutions segment’s products are used in the following end markets:

• Industrial equipment (49% of segment’s net sales)—Our products are used in factory automation and process control systems such as industrial controls, robotics, human machine interface, industrial communication, and power distribution. Our intelligent building products are used to connect lighting, HVAC, elevators/escalators, and security. Our rail products are used in high-speed trains, metros, light rail vehicles, locomotives, and signaling switching equipment. Our products are also used by the solar industry. The medical industry uses our products in imaging, diagnostic, surgical, and minimally invasive interventional applications.

• Aerospace, defense, oil, and gas (33% of segment’s net sales)—We design, develop, and manufacture a comprehensive portfolio of critical electronic components and systems for the harsh operating conditions of the aerospace, defense, and marine industries. Our products and systems are designed and manufactured to operate effectively in harsh conditions ranging from the depths of the ocean to the far reaches of space.

• Energy (18% of segment’s net sales)—Our products are used by OEMs and utility companies in the electrical power industry and include a wide range of solutions for the electrical power generation, transmission, distribution, and industrial markets.
The Industrial Solutions segment competes primarily against Amphenol, Belden, Hubbell, Carlisle Companies, 3M, Integer Holdings, Esterline, Molex, and Phoenix Contact.

Communications Solutions The Communications Solutions segment is a leading supplier of electronic components for the data and devices and the appliances markets. The primary products sold by the Communications Solutions segment include terminals and connector systems and components, relays, heat shrink tubing, and antennas. The Communications Solutions segment’s products are used in the following end markets:

• Data and devices (59% of segment’s net sales)—We deliver products and solutions that are used in a variety of equipment architectures within the networking equipment, data center equipment, and wireless infrastructure industries. Additionally, we deliver a range of connectivity solutions for the Internet of Things, smartphones, tablet computers, notebooks, and virtual reality applications to help our customers meet their current challenges and future innovations.

• Appliances (41% of segment’s net sales)—We provide solutions to meet the daily demands of home appliances. Our products are used in many household appliances, including washers, dryers, refrigerators, air conditioners, dishwashers, cooking appliances, water heaters, air purifiers, floor care devices, and microwaves. Our expansive range of standard products is supplemented by an array of custom-designed solutions.
The Communications Solutions segment’s major competitors include Amphenol, Molex, JST, and Korea Electric Terminal (KET).

Collectively, the three segments serve an estimated combined market of approximately **$190 billion**, underscoring the strategic importance of each business line within Amphenol’s overall portfolio.

synth_text.title: 2019 Cost of Revenues by Business Segment – Summary and Year‑on‑Year Changes
synth_text.text:
In 2019, the company’s total cost of revenues rose 23 % year‑on‑year to **RMB 209.8 billion**, reflecting higher content, FinTech, and channel expenses. As a share of total revenue, cost of revenues increased to **56 %** for the year ended 31 December 2019, up from 55 % in the prior year.

**Segment breakdown (RMB millions, % of total revenue)**  
- **Value‑Added Services (VAS):** RMB 94,086 million, representing **47 %** of total revenue. Costs grew 27 % YoY, driven by higher content expenses for live broadcasts, online games, video‑streaming subscriptions, and increased channel costs for smartphone games.  
- **FinTech & Business Services:** RMB 73,831 million, **73 %** of total revenue. Costs rose 35 % YoY, mainly due to expanded payment‑related and cloud‑service activities.  
- **Online Advertising:** RMB 34,860 million, **51 %** of total revenue. Costs fell 6 % YoY, owing to lower content costs for advertising‑funded long‑form video (fewer releases) and improved cost efficiency, partially offset by other items.  
- **Others:** RMB 6,979 million, **92 %** of total revenue.  

The increase in overall cost of revenues was primarily the result of higher content and FinTech expenses, while the modest decline in online advertising costs helped moderate the total rise. This segment‑level view highlights where the company’s cost structure intensified and where efficiencies were achieved during 2019.

synth_text.text:

**2019 performance (additional context)**  
- **VAS**: Cost rose to **RMB 94,086 million** (+27 % YoY), driven by higher content costs for live broadcasts, online games, video‑streaming subscriptions, and increased channel costs for smartphone games.  
- **FinTech & Business Services**: Cost increased to **RMB 73,831 million** (+35 % YoY), reflecting greater expenses in payment‑related and cloud services as the scale of these activities expanded.

1. The **total cost of revenues** grew from **RMB 170.6 bn (2018)** to **RMB 209.8 bn (2019)**, a 23 % increase.  
2. **VAS and FinTech** were the primary contributors to cost growth, each posting double‑digit percentage increases, largely from expanded content and service offerings.

synth_text.title: 2018‑2019 Cash‑Flow Overview and Key Drivers
synth_text.text:
**Cash‑Flow Summary**

| Year | Operating Activities | Investing Activities | Financing Activities |
|------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| 2019 | **$137.6 million** (inflow) | **$(830.5) million** (outflow) | **$667.2 million** (inflow) |
| 2018 | **$183.9 million** (inflow) | **$(45.4) million** (outflow) | **$(57.7) million** (outflow) |

**Operating Activities**  
Cash generated from operations fell by $46.3 million in 2019, dropping to $137.6 million from $183.9 million in 2018. The decline reflects timing differences in working‑capital items, although the cash flow still consists mainly of net income adjusted for depreciation, amortization, and stock‑based compensation. The company continues to use operating cash to fund capital expenditures, lease payments, stock repurchases, and acquisitions.

**Investing Activities**  
Investing cash outflows surged to $(830.5) million in 2019, driven primarily by the $753.9 million purchase of Speedpay (net of a $0.1 million cash acquisition). Additional outlays included $18.5 million for a payment‑technology company in India, $7.0 million for technology assets of RevChip and TranSend, and $48.0 million for software, property, and equipment. In contrast, 2018 saw a modest $(45.4) million outflow, mainly for equipment purchases.

**Financing Activities**  
Financing cash flow reversed dramatically. In 2019 the company generated $667.2 million, largely from a $500 million Delayed Draw Term Loan and a $280 million revolving credit facility, which financed the Speedpay acquisition and stock repurchases. Repayments of $28.9 million (Initial Term Loan) and $41.0 million (Revolving Credit Facility) were also recorded, along with $35.6 million of common‑stock repurchases. Conversely, 2018 recorded a net outflow of $(57.7) million, reflecting $400 million proceeds from 2026 Notes used to fully redeem 6.375 % Senior Notes due 2020, $109.3 million repayment of the Initial Term Loan, and $54.5 million of common‑stock repurchases.

**Key Takeaways**  
- Operating cash flow decreased in 2019 due to working‑capital timing, but remains a stable funding source.  
- The massive investing outflow in 2019 is attributable to the strategic acquisition of Speedpay and related technology investments.  
- Financing activities shifted from a net outflow in 2018 to a substantial inflow in 2019, providing the liquidity needed for the Speedpay purchase and supporting ongoing stock repurchase programs.

Overall, the cash‑flow profile from 2018 to 2019 reflects a transition from debt‑repayment and modest investing to aggressive acquisition financing and heightened capital‑return activities.

The income‑tax expense of METRO Group rose sharply from €216 million in the earlier fiscal year to €298 million in the most recent year – an increase of €81 million.  

**Break‑down of the tax components**

| Item | Earlier Year | Recent Year |

| – of which Germany | €39 million | €104 million |

**Key drivers of the increase**

1. **Higher actual taxes** – a €42 million rise, largely driven by a €65 million jump in German tax liabilities.  
2. **Deferred tax impact** – deferred tax balances grew by €40 million, reflecting larger impairments on deferred tax assets.  
3. **International tax position** – the shift to a negative €21 million figure indicates tax credits or lower tax rates in foreign operations.  

**Tax rate context**

* In Germany, METRO is subject to a corporate income tax of 15 %, a 5.5 % solidarity surcharge, and a trade tax of 14.7 % (assessment rate 420 %). Combined, this yields an aggregate German tax rate of **30.53 %**, unchanged from the prior year.  
* For foreign subsidiaries, applicable tax rates follow local legislation and range from **0 % to 34.94 %** (the previous year’s range was 0 % to 44.41 %).  

Overall, the €81 million increase in recognized income‑tax expense reflects both stronger earnings and higher tax burdens, especially in Germany, together with larger deferred‑tax adjustments.

* The number of **current accounts** rose by 174, while **past‑due accounts** increased by 53, indicating a slight shift in the aging profile despite the overall balance reduction.

**Credit‑quality oversight**

Following origination, the portfolio’s delinquency and write‑off experience are continuously tracked as primary credit‑quality indicators. Proprietary, empirically‑derived behavioral‑scoring models evaluate each customer’s origination characteristics, account history, and payment patterns. The resulting scores assign accounts to risk categories, which dictate the collection strategy applied.

An account is classified as delinquent and placed in default status when any charge remains unpaid after the day following the bill’s due date. Collection performance and credit quality are therefore monitored through aging metrics such as the “Current” and “Past‑due” counts shown above.

Overall, the 2019 figures reflect a modest reduction in total receivable exposure while showing a slight increase in the number of accounts that are current or past due, underscoring the importance of the ongoing scoring‑based collection framework to manage credit risk effectively.

synth_text.title: Property and Equipment Summary (2018‑2019) and Impact of San Jose Facility Leasehold Amortization
synth_text.text:
The Company’s property and equipment portfolio was reported in thousands of dollars for 2018 and 2019 as follows:

- **Computer equipment and purchased software** decreased slightly from $3,167 k in 2018 to $3,011 k in 2019.  
- **Machinery and equipment** fell from $821 k to $699 k.  
- **Furniture and fixtures** remained essentially flat ($1,113 k in 2018 vs. $1,115 k in 2019).  
- **Leasehold improvements** were unchanged at $3,897 k for both years.

The **total gross cost** of property and equipment therefore declined from $8,998 k in 2018 to $8,722 k in 2019. Accumulated depreciation and amortization increased markedly, rising from $6,655 k to $7,496 k, which drove the **net carrying amount** of property and equipment down from $2,343 k at the end of 2018 to $1,226 k at the end of 2019.

A significant operational change contributed to this shift. In the fourth quarter of 2019, the Company announced its decision to vacate the San Jose, California facility by 31 March 2020. Consequently, the leasehold improvements associated with that facility were amortized on an accelerated schedule over the remaining estimated life (through March 2020). As of 31 December 2019, the net book value of the San Jose leasehold improvements stood at $0.9 million and is expected to be fully amortized by the end of March 2020.

In summary, while the gross investment in property and equipment remained relatively stable, higher depreciation—particularly the accelerated amortization of the San Jose leasehold improvements—reduced the net net value of the Company’s property and equipment by roughly $1.1 million between 2018 and 2019.

1 Net deferred tax liabilities include net deferred tax assets of $2,195,000 (2018: $1,937,000) from the iMoney Group.
Recognition and measurement

Our income tax expense is the sum of current and deferred income tax expenses. Current income tax expense is calculated on accounting profit after adjusting for non-taxable and non-deductible items based on rules set by the tax authorities. Deferred income tax expense is calculated at the tax rates that are expected to apply to the period in which the deferred tax asset is realised or the deferred tax liability is settled. Both our current and deferred income tax expenses are calculated using tax rates that have been enacted or substantively enacted at reporting date.

Our current and deferred taxes are recognised as an expense in profit or loss, except when they relate to items that are directly recognised in other comprehensive income or equity. In this case, our current and deferred tax expenses are also recognised directly in other comprehensive income or equity.
We generally recognise deferred tax liabilities for all taxable temporary differences, except to the extent that the deferred tax liability arises from:
• the initial recognition of goodwill; and
• the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and affects neither our accounting profit nor our taxable income at the time of the transaction.

For our investments in controlled entities and associated entities, recognition of deferred tax liabilities is required unless we are able to control the timing of our temporary difference reversal and it is probable that the temporary difference will not reverse.

Deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which the deductible temporary differences, and the carried forward unused tax losses and tax credits, can be utilised

Deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities are offset in the statement of financial position where they relate to income taxes levied by the same taxation authority and to the extent that we intend to settle our current tax assets and liabilities on a net basis.
