Grocery & Snacks operating profit for fiscal 2018 was $724.8 million, an increase of $69.4 million, or 11%, compared to fiscal 2017. Gross profits were $21.9 million lower in fiscal 2018 than in fiscal 2017. The lower gross profit was driven by investments with retailers (i.e., trade spending reflected as a reduction of net sales), as well as higher input costs and transportation expenses, partially offset by supply chain realized productivity. The Frontera acquisition, Thanasi acquisition, and the acquisition of Angie's Artisan Treats, LLC, which occurred in September 2016, April 2017, and October 2017, respectively, contributed $47.4 million to Grocery & Snacks gross profit during fiscal 2018 through the one-year anniversaries of the acquisitions (if reached). Advertising and promotion expenses for fiscal 2018 decreased by $19.5 million compared to fiscal 2017. Operating profit of the Grocery & Snacks segment was impacted by charges totaling $4.0 million in fiscal 2018 for the impairment of our HK Anderson® , Red Fork® , and Salpica® brand assets and $68.3 million in fiscal 2017 primarily for the impairment of our Chef Boyardee® brand asset. Grocery & Snacks also incurred $11.4 million of expenses in fiscal 2018 related to acquisitions and divestitures, charges of $31.4 million in fiscal 2017 related to the pending divestiture of the Wesson® oil business, and charges of $14.1 million and $23.6 million in connection with our restructuring plans in fiscal 2018 and 2017, respectively.

Refrigerated & Frozen operating profit for fiscal 2018 was $479.4 million, an increase of $33.6 million, or 8%, compared to fiscal 2017. Gross profits were $3.6 million lower in fiscal 2018 than in fiscal 2017, driven by continuing increases in input costs and transportation inflation as well as investments to drive distribution, enhanced shelf presence, and trial, partially offset by increased sales volumes and supply chain realized productivity. The acquisition of the Sandwich Bros. of Wisconsin® business contributed $4.6 million to gross profit in the segment during fiscal 2018. Advertising and promotion expenses for fiscal 2018 decreased by $23.4 million compared to fiscal 2017. Operating profit of the Refrigerated & Frozen segment was impacted by charges totaling approximately $7.7 million in fiscal 2017 related to a product recall, as well as charges of $0.1 million and $6.2 million in connection with our restructuring plans in fiscal 2018 and 2017, respectively.

International operating profit for fiscal 2018 was $86.5 million, compared to an operating loss of $168.9 million for fiscal 2017. The operating loss in fiscal 2017 includes charges totaling $235.9 million for the impairment of goodwill and an intangible brand asset in our Canadian and Mexican operations. Gross profits were $18.6 million higher in fiscal 2018 than in fiscal 2017, as a result of improved price/mix, the favorable impact of foreign exchange, and the planned discontinuations of certain 33 lower-performing products. Operating profit of the International segment was impacted by charges of $1.5 million and $0.9 million in connection with our restructuring plans, in fiscal 2018 and 2017, respectively

Foodservice operating profit for fiscal 2018 was $121.8 million, an increase of $16.7 million, or 16%, compared to fiscal 2017. Gross profits were $13.9 million higher in fiscal 2018 than in fiscal 2017, primarily reflecting the impact of inflation-driven increases in pricing and supply chain realized productivity, partially offset by lower sales volumes and increased input costs. Operating profit of the Foodservice segment was impacted by charges of $1.8 million in fiscal 2017 in connection with our restructuring plans.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2018 Segment Operating‑Profit Performance and Growth Drivers
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal 2018 the company’s reporting segments delivered solid operating‑profit growth, with percentage increases ranging from 8 % to 16 % year‑over‑year. The Commercial segment, however, ceased operations after the sale of its businesses in early 2017.

**Grocery & Snacks** – Operating profit rose 11 % to **$724.8 million**, driven by higher sales volumes and supply‑chain productivity despite lower gross profit due to trade spending, higher input costs, and transportation expenses. Acquisitions (Frontera, Thanasi, Angie's Artisan Treats) contributed $47.4 million to gross profit. Impairments of brand assets and restructuring costs partially offset the gain, while advertising expenses fell by $19.5 million.

**Refrigerated & Frozen** – Operating profit increased 8 % to **$479.4 million**. The segment faced modest gross‑profit pressure from rising input and transportation costs, but benefited from volume growth, productivity gains, and the Sandwich Bros. of Wisconsin acquisition, which added $4.6 million to gross profit. Advertising spend declined by $23.4 million, and restructuring charges were minimal.

**International** – After a loss of $168.9 million in fiscal 2017 (largely due to a $235.9 million goodwill and brand‑asset impairment), the segment posted a **$86.5 million** operating profit in 2018, effectively a turnaround. Improved price/mix, favorable foreign‑exchange effects, and the discontinuation of low‑performing products lifted gross profit by $18.6 million. Restructuring charges were modest.

**Foodservice** – Operating profit grew 16 % to **$121.8 million**, reflecting inflation‑driven price increases and supply‑chain productivity gains that raised gross profit by $13.9 million. Lower sales volumes and higher input costs tempered the upside, and a $1.8 million restructuring charge was recorded in 2017.

**Commercial** – The segment reported no operating profit for fiscal 2018 because the business was sold in Q1 2017. The divestiture generated pre‑tax gains of **$197.4 million**, and the segment is now considered discontinued.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2018 vs. 2017 Segment Operating Profit Overview
synth_text.text:
**Executive Summary**  
In fiscal 2018 the company improved operating profit in four of its five reporting segments, delivering a total increase of roughly $300 million versus fiscal 2017. The gains were driven by modest volume growth, strategic acquisitions, favorable price‑mix and foreign‑exchange effects, and lower advertising spend. Impairments and restructuring costs continued to affect profitability, while the Commercial segment was discontinued after the sale of its businesses in early 2017.

**Segment‑by‑Segment Highlights**

| Segment | FY 2018 Operating Profit | FY 2017 Operating Profit | Year‑over‑Year Change |
|---------|--------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------|
| Grocery & Snacks | **$724.8 M** | $655.4 M | +$69.4 M (↑11 %) |
| Refrigerated & Frozen | **$479.4 M** | $445.8 M | +$33.6 M (↑8 %) |
| International | **$86.5 M** | **$(168.9) M** (loss) | +$255.4 M (turn‑to‑profit) |
| Foodservice | **$121.8 M** | $105.1 M | +$16.7 M (↑16 %) |
| Commercial | – | $202.6 M | – (segment discontinued) |

**Key Drivers**

* **Grocery & Snacks** – Profit rose 11 % despite a $21.9 M dip in gross profit, which stemmed from higher input and transportation costs and trade‑spending reductions. Acquisitions (Frontera, Thanasi, Angie's Artisan Treats) added $47.4 M to gross profit. Advertising expenses fell by $19.5 M, while impairments of HK Anderson®, Red Fork® and Salpica® (totaling $4.0 M) and restructuring costs ($14.1 M) moderated the upside.

* **Refrigerated & Frozen** – Operating profit increased 8 % with only a $3.6 M decline in gross profit, reflecting continued cost inflation offset by higher volumes and supply‑chain productivity. The Sandwich Bros. of Wisconsin® acquisition contributed $4.6 M to gross profit. Advertising spend was $23.4 M lower than the prior year. A 2017 product‑recall charge of $7.7 M and modest restructuring costs ($6.2 M in 2017, $0.1 M in 2018) were the main negative items.

* **International** – The segment swung from a $168.9 M loss in 2017 to a $86.5 M profit in 2018, a turnaround of $255.4 M. The 2017 loss was heavily impacted by a $235.9 M goodwill and intangible‑asset impairment in Canada and Mexico. In 2018, higher gross profit ($18.6 M) was driven by better price/mix, favorable FX, and the discontinuation of low‑performing products. Restructuring charges were modest ($1.5 M in 2018).

* **Foodservice** – Profit grew 16 % to $121.8 M, supported by a $13.9 M increase in gross profit from inflation‑driven price hikes and supply‑chain efficiencies, partially offset by lower sales volumes and higher input costs. A $1.8 M restructuring charge in 2017 was the only notable expense item.

* **Commercial** – The segment reported $202.6 M profit in FY 2017, but the business was sold in Q1 2017 (Spicetec and JM Swank) for a pre‑tax gain of $197.4 M. After the sale, the Commercial segment ceased to exist, and no FY 2018 profit is reported.

**Conclusion**  
Fiscal 2018 marked a solid performance improvement across the core operating segments, with the International segment delivering the most dramatic reversal. Strategic acquisitions, disciplined advertising spend, and modest restructuring costs helped offset cost‑inflation pressures. The exit from the Commercial segment streamlined the portfolio, allowing the remaining businesses to focus on growth and profitability.

Significant components of property, plant and equipment are as follows (in thousands):

In fiscal 2019, we entered into agreements related to the construction and leasing of two buildings on our existing corporate campus in San Diego, California. Under these agreements, a financial institution will own the buildings, and we will lease the property for a term of five years upon their completion.

In the third quarter of fiscal 2019 we sold the land and buildings comprising our separate CTS campus in San Diego. We have entered into a lease with the buyer of this campus and CTS employees will continue to occupy this separate campus until the new buildings on our corporate campus are ready for occupancy in fiscal 2021. In the third quarter of fiscal 2019 we also sold land and buildings in Orlando, Florida and we are entering a lease for new space in Orlando to accommodate our employees and operations in Orlando. In connection with the sale of these real estate campuses we received total net proceeds of $44.9 million and recognized net gains on the sales totaling $32.5 million.

As a part of our efforts to upgrade our current information systems, early in fiscal 2015 we purchased new enterprise resource planning (ERP) software and began the process of designing and configuring this software and other software applications to manage our operations.

Costs incurred in the development of internal-use software and software applications, including external direct costs of materials and services and applicable compensation costs of employees devoted to specific software development, are capitalized as computer software costs. Costs incurred outside of the application development stage, or that are types of costs that do not meet the capitalization requirements, are expensed as incurred. Amounts capitalized are included in property, plant and equipment and are amortized on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful life of the software, which ranges from three to seven years. No amortization expense is recorded until the software is ready for its intended use.

Through September 30, 2019 we have incurred costs of $138.9 million related to the purchase and development of our ERP system, including $3.1 million, $22.5 million, and $40.6 million of costs incurred during fiscal years 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. We have capitalized $1.6 million, $7.5 million, and $16.7 million of qualifying software development costs as internal-use software development in progress during fiscal years 2019, 2018, and 2017, respectively. We have recognized expense for $1.5 million, $15.0 million, and $23.9 million of these costs in fiscal years 2019, 2018, and 2017, respectively, for costs that did not qualify for capitalization. Amounts that were expensed in connection with the development of these systems are classified within selling, general and administrative expenses in the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

Various components of our ERP system became ready for their intended use and were placed into service at various times from fiscal 2016 through fiscal 2019. As each component became ready for its intended use, the component’s costs were transferred into completed software and we began amortizing these costs over their seven-year estimated useful life using the straight-line method. We continue to capitalize costs associated with the development of other ERP components that are not yet ready for their intended use.

Our provisions for depreciation of plant and equipment and amortization of leasehold improvements and software amounted to $22.6 million, $19.5 million and $17.8 million in 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. Generally, we use straight-line methods for depreciable real property over estimated useful lives ranging from 15 to 39 years or for leasehold improvements, the term of the underlying lease if shorter than the estimated useful lives. We typically use accelerated methods (declining balance) for machinery and equipment and software other than our ERP system over estimated useful lives ranging from 5 to 10 years.

synth_text.text:
**Summary of Property, Plant and Equipment (PP&E)**  
The company’s PP&E, reported in thousands of dollars, increased from **$117,546 k** in fiscal 2018 to **$144,969 k** in fiscal 2019, a growth of roughly 23 %. The detailed composition and the drivers behind the changes are outlined below.

| Component | FY 2018 (k) | FY 2019 (k) | Change |
|-----------|------------|------------|--------|
| **Land and land improvements** | 13,132 | 7,348 | –5,784 (‑44 %) |
| **Buildings and improvements** | 57,959 | 48,191 | –9,768 (‑17 %) |
| **Machinery and other equipment** | 81,727 | 107,297 | +25,570 (+31 %) |
| **Software** | 84,631 | 108,526 | +23,895 (+28 %) |
| **Leasehold improvements** | 11,991 | 17,064 | +5,073 (+42 %) |
| **Construction & internal‑use software development in progress** | 12,888 | 16,814 | +3,926 (+30 %) |
| **Accumulated depreciation & amortization** | (144,782) | (160,271) | (‑15,489) |
| **Total PP&E** | 117,546 | 144,969 | +27,423 |

**Key factors influencing the PP&E movements**

1. **Real‑estate transactions** – In FY 2019 the company sold the CTS campus in San Diego and a campus in Orlando, generating **$44.9 M** in net proceeds and **$32.5 M** in gains. The disposals reduced land, buildings, and related leasehold assets, explaining the declines in those categories.

2. **New building leases** – Agreements were signed to construct two new buildings on the existing San Diego corporate campus. A financial institution will own the structures, and the company will lease them for five years once completed (expected occupancy in FY 2021). Leasehold improvements rose as the company prepared for these new facilities.

3. **ERP system implementation** – Since FY 2015 the company has been acquiring and developing enterprise‑resource‑planning software. Capitalized costs for the ERP system total **$138.9 M** through September 30 2019, with **$3.1 M** added in FY 2019 alone. These costs are reflected in the higher **Software** balance and the increase in **Construction & internal‑use software development in progress**. Once ready for use, software costs are transferred to the “Software” line and amortized over a seven‑year straight‑line period.

4. **Depreciation and amortization** – Depreciation expense rose to **$22.6 M** in FY 2019 (from $19.5 M in FY 2018), driven by the larger machinery base and the straight‑line depreciation of newly placed‑in‑service ERP components. Leasehold improvements and software are amortized using straight‑line methods, while machinery and equipment are depreciated on an accelerated (declining‑balance) basis.

**Conclusion**  
The PP&E increase in FY 2019 reflects strategic investments in machinery, software, and leasehold improvements, offset by the divestiture of older campus properties. Ongoing ERP development and the upcoming lease‑to‑own buildings are expected to continue shaping the composition of PP&E in the coming years, while depreciation and amortization will remain significant non‑cash expenses supporting the company’s operational growth.

synth_text.title: Reconciliation of Theoretical UK Corporation Tax to Reported Tax Expense – Key Drivers and Governance Overview
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table reconciles the corporation‑tax expense that would be calculated using the UK statutory rate of 19 % with the tax charge actually reported by Sophos for two distinct financial outcomes – one with a profit before tax and one with a loss before tax. The differences arise from a range of jurisdictional rate differentials, non‑deductible expenses and other adjustments that affect the taxable base reported in the financial statements.

**Profit‑before‑tax year (£53.6 m)**  
* Theoretical UK tax (19 % of profit): **£10.2 m**.  
* Reported tax expense: **£26.7 m**.  
* Net upward reconciling items: **£16.5 m**, comprising:  
  * **Expenses not deductible for tax purposes:** £11.8 m  
  * **Higher tax rates on overseas earnings:** £7.7 m  
  * **Other movements:** (£2.4 m) (net reduction)  
  * **Adjustments in respect of previous years:** £0.8 m  
  * **Change in tax rate during the year:** £1.4 m  
  * **Research & development tax credits:** (‑£1.9 m) (partial offset)  

The principal drivers of the higher reported charge are non‑deductible expenses and the application of higher overseas tax rates, which together add more than £19 m to the theoretical UK liability.

**Loss‑before‑tax year (‑£41.0 m)**  
* Theoretical UK tax credit (19 % of loss): **‑£7.7 m**.  
* Reported tax expense: **£19.9 m**.  
* Net upward reconciling items: **£27.6 m**, made up of:  
  * **Adjustments in respect of previous years:** £7.1 m  
  * **Change in tax rate during the year:** £3.6 m  
  * **Expenses not deductible for tax purposes:** £9.4 m  
  * **Higher tax rates on overseas earnings:** £3.8 m  
  * **Impact of US tax reform on deferred tax:** £5.4 m  
  * **Other movements:** (‑£1.1 m) (net reduction)  
  * **Research & development tax credits:** (‑£0.6 m) (partial offset)  

Even though the underlying result is a loss, the Group records a tax charge because of prior‑year adjustments, a higher effective tax rate on overseas earnings, non‑deductible costs, and a deferred‑tax impact from the US tax reform.

**Context and Governance**  
These reconciling items reflect the gap between the local tax base and the accounting base, driven by:  
* Rate differentials across jurisdictions,  
* Non‑taxable benefits, and  
* Non‑deductible expenses arising from differing tax rules.

Sophos’ taxation strategy – publicly available on its website – aligns tax planning with the overall business strategy and is overseen by the Audit and Risk Committee. The Chief Financial Officer, supported by a global tax team, is responsible for executing the strategy. The Group maintains an open, transparent relationship with tax authorities, seeks arm‑‑length pricing for cross‑border transactions, and actively engages with policymakers and international bodies. Uncertain tax positions are regularly reviewed and appropriately provisioned.

**Conclusion**  
The reconciliation demonstrates that the reported tax expense is substantially higher than the theoretical UK liability due to a combination of jurisdictional tax‑rate differentials, non‑deductible expenses, and specific adjustments such as the impact of US tax reform. Sophos’ robust tax governance framework underpins its approach to managing these complexities while ensuring compliance and strategic alignment.

synth_text.title: Gross Profit and Margin Trends (2017‑2019)
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the company reported a total cost of revenue of **$864.9 million**, a gross profit of **$632.8 million**, and a gross margin of **42.3 %**.  

For the year ending December 31, 2019, gross profit declined by **1.5 %** compared with 2018, while total cost of revenue increased by **3.2 %**, resulting in a lower gross margin (the exact percentage change was not disclosed).  

The decline in 2019 was driven primarily by:
* Higher hosting migration costs and increased amortization of software development,
* Recognition of previously deferred costs,
* The sale of the OneContent business on April 2, 2018, which had a higher margin than the company’s other operations.

These pressures were partially offset by organic sales growth in the Veradigm platform and the company’s acute‑care solutions.

Conversely, the 2018‑to‑2017 period saw gross profit rise, largely due to acquisitions that expanded the recurring‑revenue base (subscription software, support, maintenance, and client services). However, gross margin fell because of reduced sales of higher‑margin perpetual software licenses and higher amortization of intangible assets acquired in recent transactions.

Overall, the data illustrate a shift from a strong, margin‑rich 2017 baseline toward modest profit compression in 2019, reflecting a mix of strategic acquisitions, portfolio changes, and increased cost pressures.

text.value: Fair Value Disclosures

Under the fair value standards fair value is based on the exit price and defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The fair value measurement should reflect all the assumptions that market participants would use in pricing an asset or liability. A fair value hierarchy is established in the authoritative guidance outlined in three levels ranking from Level 1 to level 3 with Level 1 being the highest priority.
Level 1: observable inputs that reflect quoted prices (unadjusted) for identical assets or liabilities in active markets
Level 2: inputs other than quoted prices included in Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability either directly or indirectly
Level 3: unobservable inputs (e.g., a reporting entity’s or other entity’s own data)

The Company had no assets or liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring (except our pension plan assets, see Note 15) or
non-recurring basis as of September 30, 2019 or September 30, 2018.

To estimate fair value of the financial instruments below quoted market prices are used when available and classified within Level 1. If this data is not available, we use observable market based inputs to estimate fair value, which are classified within Level 2. If the preceding information is unavailable, we use internally generated data to estimate fair value which is classified within Level 3.

According to the company’s fair‑value disclosure policy, fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The fair‑value hierarchy classifies inputs into three levels:

1. **Level 1:** Quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets.  
2. **Level 2:** Other observable inputs, either directly or indirectly.  
3. **Level 3:** Unobservable inputs, such as internally generated data.

The company states that, aside from pension‑plan assets, it had no assets or liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis for the periods presented. Consequently, the fair value of the cash balance, as well as the (non‑existent) receivables and note payable, is approximated by their carrying amounts. Where market quotes are available, they would be classified as Level 1; otherwise, observable market‑based inputs would place the valuation in Level 2. No material difference between fair value and carrying value was identified for these items.

In summary, the company held $25,107 in cash, reported no receivables or note payable, and the fair‑value assessment confirms that the carrying amounts reflect the assets’ and liabilities’ fair values under the applicable hierarchy levels.

text.value: Note 7: Income Taxes

On December 22, 2017, the “Tax Cuts & Jobs Act” was signed into law and was effective for the Company starting in the quarter ended December 24, 2017. U.S. tax reform reduced the U.S. federal statutory tax rate from 35% to 21%, assessed a one-time transition tax on earnings of certain foreign subsidiaries that were previously tax deferred, and created new taxes on certain foreign sourced earnings. The impact on income taxes due to a change in legislation is required under the authoritative guidance of Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) 740, Income Taxes, to be recognized in the period in which the law is enacted. In conjunction, the SEC issued Staff Accounting Bulletin (“SAB”) 118, which allowed for the recording of provisional amounts related to U.S. tax reform and subsequent adjustments related to U.S. tax reform during an up to one-year measurement period that is similar to the measurement period used when accounting for business combinations. The Company recorded what it believed to be reasonable estimates during the SAB 118 measurement period. During the December 2018 quarter, the Company finalized the accounting of the income tax effects of U.S. tax reform. Although the SAB 118 measurement period has ended, there may be some aspects of U.S. tax reform that remain subject to future regulations and/or notices which may further clarify certain provisions of U.S. tax reform. The Company may need to adjust its previously recorded amounts to reflect the recognition and measurement of its tax accounting positions in accordance with ASC 740; such adjustments could be material.

The computation of the one-time transition tax on accumulated unrepatriated foreign earnings was recorded on a provisional basis in the amount of $883.0 million in the fiscal year ended June 24, 2018, as permitted under SAB 118. The Company recorded a subsequent provisional adjustment of $36.6 million, as a result of incorporating new information into the estimate, in the Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements in the three months ended September 23, 2018. The Company finalized the computation of the transition tax liability during the December 2018 quarter. The final adjustment resulted in a tax benefit of $51.2 million, which was recorded in the Company’s Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements in the three months ended December 23, 2018. The final balance of total transition tax is $868.4 million. The one-time transition tax is based on the Company’s total post-1986 earnings and profits (“E&P”) that was previously deferred from U.S. income taxes. The Company had previously accrued deferred taxes on a portion of this E&P. The Company has completed the calculation of total post-1986 E&P and related income tax pools for its foreign subsidiaries. The Company elected to pay the one-time transition tax over a period of eight years.

Beginning in fiscal year 2019, the Company is subject to the impact of the GILTI provision of U.S. tax reform. The GILTI provision imposes taxes on foreign earnings in excess of a deemed return on tangible assets. The Company has calculated the impact of the GILTI provision on current year earnings and has included the impact in the effective tax rate. The Company made an accounting policy election in the September 2018 quarter to record deferred taxes in relation to the GILTI provision, and recorded a provisional tax benefit of $48.0 million in the Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements in the three months ended September 23, 2018, under SAB 118. The Company finalized the computation of the accounting policy election during the December 2018 quarter. The final adjustment resulted in a tax expense of $0.4 million, which was recorded in the Company’s Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements in the three months ended December 23, 2018. The final tax benefit of the election is $47.6 million.

synth_text.title: Pre‑Tax Income Composition and the Effect of Recent U.S. Tax Reform on Foreign Earnings
synth_text.text:
The company’s earnings before income taxes are driven almost entirely by foreign operations. In the first reporting period the total pre‑tax income was **$2.45 million**, composed of a **$2.51 million foreign contribution** and a **$59,876 loss** from U.S. activities. In the subsequent period the total rose to **$3.15 million**, with **$3.02 million** generated abroad and a modest **$128,190** gain in the United States.  

These figures must be interpreted against the backdrop of the 2017 Tax Cuts & Jobs Act (TCJA). The TCJA reduced the U.S. statutory corporate tax rate from 35 % to 21 % and introduced a one‑time transition tax on previously untaxed foreign earnings. The company initially recorded a provisional transition‑tax liability of **$883.0 million** for the fiscal year ended June 24 2018, later adjusting it by **$36.6 million** and ultimately recognizing a **$51.2 million tax benefit** in the December 2018 quarter, leaving a final transition‑tax balance of **$868.4 million**.  

In addition, the TCJA’s Global Intangible Low‑Taxed Income (GILTI) provision, effective beginning fiscal 2019, imposes tax on foreign earnings that exceed a deemed return on tangible assets. The company elected to record deferred taxes for GILTI, initially recognizing a **$48.0 million provisional tax benefit** and later finalizing a **$0.4 million tax expense**, resulting in a net GILTI‑related benefit of **$47.6 million**.  

Overall, while U.S. operations contribute only a small share of pre‑tax earnings, the company’s tax position is heavily influenced by the transition tax and GILTI provisions stemming from recent U.S. tax reform. These legislative changes have generated significant provisional adjustments and ongoing tax liabilities that shape the effective tax rate and future cash‑flow considerations.

synth_text.title: Summary of Income Tax Expense and the Impact of Recent U.S. Tax Reform
synth_text.text:
During the reporting period the company recorded a **total income tax expense of $1,811,673**. This amount is split between **$7,553** attributable to United States tax obligations and **$1,804,120** arising from foreign tax liabilities, indicating that foreign taxes represent more than 99 % of the overall tax charge.

The dominance of foreign taxes is largely a result of the 2017 Tax Cuts & Jobs Act (TCJA). The TCJA reduced the U.S. federal statutory tax rate from 35 % to 21 % and introduced a one‑time transition tax on accumulated, untaxed earnings of foreign subsidiaries. The company initially recorded a provisional transition‑tax liability of **$883.0 million** for the fiscal year ended June 24 2018. Subsequent adjustments of **$36.6 million** (September 2018) and a final benefit of **$51.2 million** (December 2018) brought the net transition‑tax liability to **$868.4 million**, which the company elected to pay over eight years.

In addition, beginning fiscal 2019 the Global Intangible Low‑Taxed Income (GILTI) provision imposed a new tax on foreign earnings exceeding a deemed return on tangible assets. The company made a policy election in September 2018, initially recognizing a provisional GILTI tax benefit of **$48.0 million**. The final adjustment in December 2018 resulted in a modest tax expense of **$0.4 million**, leaving a net GILTI benefit of **$47.6 million**.

These legislative changes, together with the provisional accounting guidance under SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin 118, explain why the company’s foreign tax expense is substantially higher than its U.S. tax expense for the period. The figures in the table reflect the net effect after all provisional and final adjustments related to the transition tax and GILTI have been incorporated.

synth_text.title: Operating Performance and Free‑Cash‑Flow Conversion Overview
synth_text.text:
The financial bridge analysis for the two reporting periods shows a steady improvement in operating profitability and cash generation. Operating margin increased from 4.4 % to 5.0 %, while net financial, tax and other items remained negative but improved from ‑3.8 % to ‑2.5 %. Non‑cash charges—depreciation and amortization—added back 3.9 % and 2.9 % respectively, and depreciation of leased assets contributed an additional 1.1 % in the later period.

Working‑capital management continued to support cash flow, delivering a positive impact of 3.7 % and 1.0 % in the two periods. Capital expenditures, planned at roughly 2 % of net sales, slightly increased from ‑2.4 % to ‑2.8 % as the company invested in a new U.S. factory. Leasing payments, absent in the first period, reduced cash by 1.3 % in the second.

Restructuring costs, a focus of the cost‑reduction programme, fell dramatically from ‑3.8 % to ‑0.4 %, aligning with the target of keeping such charges near 1 % of net sales. Consequently, free cash flow before M&A rose from 2.0 % to 3.4 %, reflecting a higher conversion rate of operating income into cash. M&A outflows remained modest (‑0.6 % → ‑0.7 %), within the anticipated 1–2 % of net sales range.

Overall, the company is successfully enhancing its operating margin while maintaining disciplined working‑capital efficiency and controlling capex, restructuring, and M&A expenses, thereby delivering stronger free‑cash‑flow generation.

synth_text.title: Operating Income to Free Cash Flow Bridge – Key Drivers and Outlook
synth_text.text:
The company’s financial profile shows a robust operating margin of **more than 12 % of net sales**, measured before restructuring charges. After accounting for **financial net, tax and other items** (‑4 % of net sales), the cash‑flow bridge adds back non‑cash expenses: **depreciation and amortisation** (+3 % to +4 %) and **depreciation of leased assets** (+1 %). Working‑capital changes are essentially flat (±0 %), indicating that the firm maintains efficient working‑capital management.

Investments and outflows are modest. **Capital expenditures** are planned at roughly **‑2 % of net sales**, consistent with the assumption of a 2 % capex level to support the new U.S. factory. **Leasing payments** further reduce cash by **‑1 %**, while **restructuring costs** are kept around **‑1 %**, reflecting the ongoing cost‑reduction initiatives highlighted in the context.

These elements combine to generate **free cash flow before M&A of over 8 % of net sales**. The impact of mergers and acquisitions is expected to be **‑1 % to ‑2 %**, leaving a net free cash flow in the range of **6 %–7 % of net sales**.

Overall, the company demonstrates a high conversion rate from operating income to free cash flow, supported by disciplined cost control, stable working‑capital dynamics, and a controlled investment and M&A strategy.

- **Equity** fell by about $522 M, primarily because the surge in debt outpaced the growth in assets, a pattern common after large acquisitions.

**Contextual Factors**  
The company’s 2016‑2017 results were significantly shaped by two major transactions: the Verizon Communications acquisition (the “Verizon Transaction”) and the purchase of a controlling interest in Viom Networks Limited (the “Viom Acquisition”). Both deals, closed in March 2015 and April 2016 respectively, added substantial tower assets and related debt, thereby affecting the comparability of year‑over‑year figures. Additionally, the disclosed restricted cash amounts—$149.3 M in 2016 and $152.8 M in 2017—are pledged as collateral and are not freely available for operations.

Overall, the balance‑sheet data illustrate American Tower’s aggressive expansion strategy, funded largely through increased leverage, while maintaining a solid cash position despite the constraints of restricted funds.

synth_text.title: Annual Cash‑Flow Summary for 2019‑2018 (with 2017 Context)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s cash‑flow statements for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018 show a marked shift from operating cash generation to cash consumption, while investing and financing activities remained outflows in both periods.

**Operating Activities**  
- **2019:** Net cash was **used** in operating activities, amounting to **$(9.9 million)** (‑$9,885 k). The outflow stemmed from a $16.5 million net loss, a $4.5 million increase in deferred income taxes, and a $0.7 million loss on the sale of the JVP investment, partially offset by $1.0 million of stock‑based compensation, $2.0 million of depreciation and amortization, and $7.1 million of changes in operating assets and liabilities.  
- **2018:** Net cash was **provided** by operating activities, totaling **$25.6 million** ($25,601 k). This positive cash flow resulted from $20.7 million of net income, $1.6 million of stock‑based compensation, $1.8 million of depreciation and amortization, a $3.4 million increase in warrant liability, and a $2.5 million change in deferred income taxes, offset by a $4.4 million increase in operating assets and liabilities.  
- **2017 (context):** Operating cash flow was $16.6 million, driven mainly by $22.8 million of net income and modest non‑cash adjustments.

**Investing Activities**  
- **2019:** Cash **used** in investing activities was **$(3.8 million)** (‑$3,822 k). The primary uses were purchases of marketable securities ($24.5 million) and property and equipment ($0.4 million), plus an additional $0.7 million investment in JVP, partially offset by redemptions of marketable securities ($18.3 million) and a $3.5 million sale of the JVP interest.  
- **2018:** Investing outflows totaled **$(13.2 million)** (‑$13,203 k), reflecting $11.3 million of investment purchases, $1.0 million of assets under the May 2018 Patent Assignment Agreement, and a $0.9 million JVP investment.  
- **2017 (context):** Investing cash outflow was $2.0 million, mainly for assets under the first Patent Assignment Agreement, offset by a $0.1 million cash distribution from JVP.

**Financing Activities**  
- **2019:** No financing activity occurred; cash flow from financing was **$0**.  
- **2018:** Net cash **used** in financing activities was **$(21.6 million)** (‑$21,556 k). The outflow was driven by the redemption of Series A‑1 Preferred Stock ($19.9 million) and a $2.0 million share‑repurchase program, partially offset by $0.3 million proceeds from stock‑option exercises.  
- **2017 (context):** Financing cash flow was positive at $12.8 million, primarily from issuing Series A‑1 Preferred Stock ($14.4 million) and a common‑share offering ($12.0 million), offset by $13.8 million of redemptions/retirements.

**Key Takeaways**  
- The company moved from a strong operating cash inflow in 2018 to an operating cash outflow in 2019, reflecting a shift from profitability to a net loss that year.  
- Investing activities consistently consumed cash, with a larger outflow in 2018 due to significant investment purchases.  
- Financing activity was absent in 2019, whereas 2018 saw substantial cash use for preferred‑stock redemptions and share repurchases.  

These trends highlight the company’s reliance on operating performance to generate cash, the variability of its investing commitments, and the impact of financing decisions on overall cash‑flow health.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview: 2018 vs. 2017
synth_text.text:
The company’s 2018 financial results show a substantial improvement over 2017, driven primarily by increased licensing activity.  

- **Revenues** rose to **$82.3 million** in 2018 from **$50.5 million** in 2017, reflecting multiple new license agreements secured through the firm’s patent licensing and enforcement program.  
- **Cost of revenues** increased proportionally to **$15.3 million** (2018) from **$6.0 million** (2017), largely due to higher contingent legal fees tied to the same licensing efforts.  
- **Gross profit** grew to **$67.0 million** with an **81 % gross margin**, compared with **$44.5 million** and an **88 % margin** in 2017; the margin dip reflects the larger cost base accompanying higher sales.  

Operating expenses also rose. **Selling, general and administrative (SG&A)** expenses climbed to **$32.2 million** in 2018 from **$28.6 million** in 2017, driven by $4.2 million of additional litigation costs and $1.8 million of higher employee‑related expenses (primarily incentive bonuses). SG&A is still dominated (≈74 %) by legal fees. **Research and development** expenses increased modestly to **$2.1 million** (up $0.6 million) as the Finjan Mobile security business expanded. Total operating expenses were **$34.3 million** in 2018 versus **$30.1 million** in 2017.  

**Other income (expense)** turned negative in 2018, posting a **$(4.0) million** loss mainly from a $3.4 million increase in the fair‑value liability of outstanding warrants and $0.6 million of interest expense, whereas 2017 recorded a $2.2 million gain.  

Consequently, **income before taxes** reached **$28.7 million** in 2018 (down from $16.6 million in 2017 after adjusting for the other‑income swing). The **income tax provision** was **$8.0 million** in 2018, compared with a tax benefit of **$(6.2) million** in 2017, reflecting the shift from a valuation‑allowance reduction to a regular tax expense.  

After taxes, **net income** amounted to **$20.7 million** in 2018, slightly lower than the **$22.8 million** reported in 2017, despite higher revenues, because of increased operating costs, adverse other‑income movements, and the tax expense.  

Overall, the 2018 results demonstrate successful revenue generation from the company’s licensing strategy, offset by higher legal and administrative costs and a less favorable tax position, leading to a modest decline in net earnings relative to the prior year.

synth_text.title: 2018 Financial Performance Summary and Year‑over‑Year Changes
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the year ended December 31, 2018, the company generated **$31.8 million in revenue**, a **63 % increase** over 2017. The rise was driven primarily by multiple new licensing agreements secured under the company’s patent licensing and enforcement program.

**Cost of revenues** rose to **$9.3 million**, a **155 % jump**, reflecting higher contingent legal fees that scale with the expanded licensing activity.

**Gross profit** reached **$22.5 million** (up **51 %**), maintaining a solid gross margin despite the faster growth in costs.

**Operating expenses**  
- **Selling, general and administrative (SG&A)**: $3.6 million, **+13 %**. SG&A is dominated by legal fees (≈ 74 % of SG&A) and employee‑related costs, which together increased by $4.2 million in litigation expenses and $1.8 million in headcount‑related expenses.  
- **Research and development (R&D)**: $0.6 million, **+40 %**, supporting the Finjan Mobile security business as it prepares for future growth.  
- **Total operating expenses**: $4.2 million, **+14 %**.

**Other income (expense)** was a **$6.2 million loss**, a **‑282 %** change, mainly due to a $3.4 million increase in the fair‑value liability of outstanding warrants and $0.6 million of interest expense.

**Income before taxes** stood at **$12.1 million**, **+73 %** year‑over‑year.

**Income tax provision** amounted to **$14.2 million**, a **‑229 %** swing from a 2017 tax benefit, reflecting an $8.1 million tax expense on the 2018 pre‑tax income of $28.7 million.

**Net income** was a **loss of $2.1 million**, a **‑9 %** decline from the prior year.

**Key take‑aways**  
- Revenue growth was robust, fueled by the company’s licensing strategy.  
- Costs rose proportionally, especially legal fees tied to enforcement activities.  
- SG&A and R&D expenses increased modestly, supporting both litigation and product development.  
- The negative other income and higher tax expense contributed to a net loss despite strong operating performance.

Overall, the 2018 results demonstrate successful expansion of licensing revenue, offset by higher legal and tax costs, leading to a modest operating profit but a net loss for the year.

text.value: GreenSky, Inc. NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS — (Continued) (United States Dollars in thousands, except per share data, unless otherwise stated)
Cash and Cash Equivalents

Cash includes non-interest and interest-bearing demand deposit accounts with various financial institutions. Cash equivalents include money market mutual fund accounts, which are invested in government securities. We consider all highly liquid investments that mature three months or less from the date of purchase to be cash equivalents. The carrying amounts of our cash equivalents approximate their fair values due to their short maturities and highly liquid nature. Refer to Note 3 for additional information.

At times, our cash balances may exceed federally insured amounts and potentially subject the Company to a concentration of credit risk. The Company believes that no significant concentration of credit risk exists with respect to these balances based on its assessment of the creditworthiness and financial viability of these financial institutions. Further, our cash equivalents may expose us to credit risk; however, we believe this risk is limited, as the investments are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government.
Restricted Cash

Restricted cash primarily consists of interest-bearing escrow accounts that are required under the terms of the contracts with our Bank Partners. Restricted cash is typically comprised of three components: (i) amounts we have escrowed with Bank Partners as limited protection to the Bank Partners in the event of excess Bank Partner portfolio credit losses; (ii) additional amounts we maintain for certain Bank Partners based on a contractual percentage of the total interest billed on outstanding deferred interest loans that are within the promotional period less previous finance charge reversal ("FCR") settlements on such outstanding loans; and (iii) certain custodial intransit loan funding and consumer borrower payments that we are restricted from using for our operations. These custodial balances are not considered in our evaluation of restricted cash usage. As it relates to our restricted cash escrowed with Bank Partners, we record a liability for the amount of restricted cash we expect to be payable to our Bank Partners, which is accounted for as a financial guarantee. Refer to Note 14 for additional information.

These assets are highly liquid, maturing within three months, and are carried at amounts that approximate fair value.  

Restricted cash primarily comprises interest‑bearing escrow accounts required by contracts with the Company’s Bank Partners. It includes (i) escrowed amounts that protect Bank Partners against excess credit losses, (ii) additional funds tied to a contractual percentage of interest billed on deferred‑interest loans, and (iii) custodial in‑transit loan funding and borrower payments that cannot be used for operations.

synth_text.title: 2019 Segment Income Before Taxes – Performance Highlights and Drivers
synth_text.text:
In 2019, the company reported total income (loss) before income taxes of **$58.0 million**. The contribution from each operating segment was:

- **Semiconductor Test:** **$19.4 million** – growth driven by higher sales of semiconductor testers for 5G infrastructure and image sensors, partially offset by weaker automotive and analog test sales.  
- **System Test:** **$44.6 million** – increase resulted from stronger demand for 3.5‑inch hard‑disk‑drive testers, defense/aerospace test instrumentation, and production board test equipment, all buoyed by 5G‑related activity.  
- **Wireless Test:** **$6.5 million** – rise due to expanding demand for millimeter‑wave and cellular test products linked to new wireless standards and 5G, despite a dip in connectivity test sales.  
- **Industrial Automation:** **$(13.6) million** – a decline caused primarily by higher sales‑and‑marketing and engineering expenses.  
- **Corporate and Other (1):** **$1.0 million** – this line includes contingent consideration adjustments, investment impairments, actuarial gains/losses on pension and post‑retirement plans, interest income/expense, net foreign‑exchange gains/losses, intercompany eliminations, and acquisition‑related charges.

Overall, the positive performance of Semiconductor Test, System Test, and Wireless Test more than offset the loss in Industrial Automation, leading to a modest net pre‑tax income of $58 million for the year.

synth_text.title: Income Before Taxes by Business Segment – 2018 vs 2019 Overview
synth_text.text:
**Overall Performance**  
- Total income before taxes rose from **$467.8 million in 2018** to **$525.8 million in 2019**, a **$58.0 million (≈12.4 %) increase**.

**Segment‑level Changes**  

| Segment | 2018 | 2019 | Δ (Million $) | Δ (%) |
|---------|------|------|---------------|-------|
| Semiconductor Test | $397.6 M | $417.0 M | +$19.4 M | +4.9 % |
| System Test | $48.9 M | $93.5 M | +$44.6 M | +91.2 % |
| Wireless Test | $29.1 M | $35.6 M | +$6.5 M | +22.3 % |
| Industrial Automation | $7.7 M | $(5.9) M | –$13.6 M | –176.6 % (turning from profit to loss) |
| Corporate & Other* | $(15.4) M | $(14.4) M | +$1.0 M (less negative) | +6.5 % |

\*Corporate and Other includes contingent consideration adjustments, investment impairments, pension and post‑retirement plan actuarial gains/losses, interest, foreign‑exchange effects, intercompany eliminations, and acquisition‑related charges.

**Key Drivers of the 2019 Increase**

- **Semiconductor Test:** Higher sales of semiconductor testers for 5G infrastructure and image sensors offset modest declines in automotive and analog test sales.  
- **System Test:** Strong growth in storage‑test (3.5‑inch HDD testers), defense/aerospace test instrumentation, and production‑board test driven by rising 5G demand.  
- **Wireless Test:** Increased demand for millimeter‑wave and cellular test products linked to new wireless standards and 5G, partially offset by lower connectivity‑test sales.  
- **Industrial Automation:** The segment moved to a loss due to elevated sales‑and‑marketing and engineering expenses, counteracting previous profitability.  
- **Corporate & Other:** Slight improvement as negative items (e.g., investment impairments, pension adjustments) were marginally less adverse in 2019.

**Conclusion**  
The 2019 income‑before‑taxs increase was primarily powered by robust growth in the Semiconductor, System, and Wireless test segments, all benefiting from the rollout of 5G technologies. The only area of weakness was Industrial Automation, where higher operating costs turned a modest profit into a loss. Overall, the company’s diversified test‑equipment portfolio delivered a solid year‑over‑year financial uplift.

text.value: Inventory

Inventory is stated at the lower of cost and net realizable value, using the first-in, first-out (“FIFO”) valuation method. Net realizable value is the estimated selling prices in the ordinary course of business, less reasonably predictable costs of completion, disposal, and transportation. Any adjustments to reduce the cost of inventories to their net realizable value are recognized in earnings in the current period.

Due to the low sell-through of our AirBar products, management has decided to fully reserve work-in-process for AirBar components, as well as AirBar related raw materials. Management has further decided to reserve for a portion of AirBar finished goods, depending on type of AirBar and in which location it is stored. The AirBar inventory reserve was $0.8 million and $1.0 million for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018, respectively.

In order to protect our manufacturing partners from losses in relation to AirBar production, we agreed to secure the value of the inventory with a bank guarantee. Since the sale of AirBars has been lower than expected, a major part of the inventory at the partner remained unused when the due date of the bank guarantee neared and Neonode therefore agreed that the partner should keep inventory for the production of 20,000 AirBars and the rest be purchased by us. The inventory value of these purchases has been fully reserved.

As of December 31, 2019, the Company’s inventory consists primarily of components that will be used in the manufacturing of our sensor modules. We segregate inventory for reporting purposes by raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods.

synth_text.title: Neonode Inventory Composition, Valuation, and AirBar Reserve Summary (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
Neonode’s inventory for the years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019 is reported in three categories—raw materials, work‑in‑process (WIP), and finished goods—and is valued at the lower of cost and net realizable value using a first‑in, first‑out (FIFO) method.

| Year | Raw Materials ( $ 000) | Work‑in‑Process ( $ 000) | Finished Goods ( $ 000) | Total Ending Inventory ( $ 000) |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| 2019 | $396 | $186 | $448 | $1,030 |
| 2018 | $246 | $220 | $753 | $1,219 |

Key observations:

* **Raw materials** increased by $150 k (≈61 %) from 2018 to 2019, reflecting higher component purchases for sensor‑module production.  
* **Work‑in‑process** fell by $34 k (≈15 %) as production cycles accelerated, reducing the amount of partially completed inventory.  
* **Finished goods** declined sharply by $305 k (≈40 %), driven largely by lower sell‑through of AirBar products.  
* **Total ending inventory** dropped $189 k (≈15 %) from $1.219 million in 2018 to $1.030 million in 2019.

Because AirBar sales underperformed, management fully reserved the AirBar‑related inventory. The AirBar reserve amounted to **$1.0 million in 2018** and **$0.8 million in 2019**, covering all AirBar raw materials, WIP, and a portion of finished goods. This reserve is reflected in the ending‑inventory figures and is recognized as an expense in the period in which the reduction in net realizable value is identified.

In addition, Neonode secured a bank guarantee to protect its manufacturing partners from potential losses on AirBar production. When the guarantee’s due date approached, the partner retained inventory sufficient for 20,000 AirBars, and Neonode purchased the remaining inventory, which was also fully reserved.

Overall, the 2019 inventory composition shows a shift toward higher raw‑material holdings and lower finished‑goods balances, while the applied FIFO valuation and the AirBar reserve ensure that the reported amounts represent the lower of cost and net realizable value.

synth_text.title: Income Tax Expense Summary and Effective Tax‑Rate Comparison for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table compares the company’s income‑tax results for 2018 and 2019. Both years were subject to a statutory income‑tax rate of 26.7 %.

**Key figures**

| Year | Income before tax (US$ m) | Computed tax (US$ m) | Total tax expense (US$ m) | Effective tax rate | Cash taxes paid (US$ m) |
|------|---------------------------|----------------------|---------------------------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| 2018 | 2,817 | 752 | 758 | 26.9 % | 370 |
| 2019 | 2,755 | 736 | 712 | 25.8 % | 400 |

**Adjustments affecting tax expense**  
- **2018:** Non‑deductible stock‑based compensation (+5 m), equity‑loss portion (+1 m), non‑taxable capital gains (‑9 m), and other items (+9 m) resulted in a total tax expense slightly above the computed amount.  
- **2019:** The only notable adjustments were a small non‑deductible equity‑loss portion (+7 m), a legislative tax change (‑23 m), non‑taxable capital gains (‑2 m), and other items (‑6 m), bringing total tax expense to $712 m.

**Effective tax‑rate change**  
The effective income‑tax rate fell from 26.9 % in 2018 to 25.8 % in 2019. This reduction is primarily attributable to the phased‑down Alberta corporate income‑tax rate, which lowered the overall tax burden despite the unchanged statutory rate.

**Cash taxes paid**  
Cash taxes paid rose from $370 m in 2018 to $400 m in 2019. The increase reflects the timing of installment payments rather than a higher tax liability.

**Conclusion**  
While pre‑tax earnings were marginally lower in 2019, the company achieved a lower effective tax rate and higher cash tax outflows due to regional tax reductions and payment timing. These factors together explain the observed differences between the computed and actual tax expenses for the two years.

synth_text.title: Summary of Receivables, Payables, and Methane Princess Lease Security‑Deposit Movements with Golar Partners (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The table outlines the year‑end balances between the company and Golar Partners (and its subsidiaries) for 2018 and 2019, covering two key items:

| Year | (iii) Balances due to/from Golar Partners (USD m) | (vii) Methane Princess lease security‑deposit movements (USD m) | Total (USD m) |
|------|---------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------|
| 2019 | **(2.708)** (net payable)                         | **(2.253)** (net outflow)                                          | **(4.961)** (net liability) |
| 2018 | **4.091** (net receivable)                        | **(2.835)** (net outflow)                                          | **1.256** (net receivable)   |

**Interpretation**

* **Balances due to/from Golar Partners (iii)** – These amounts represent primarily unpaid management fees, advisory and administrative expenses, dividends on Hilli Common Units, and other related‑party transactions (including occasional invoice reimbursements). In 2019 the company owed Golar Partners $2.708 million, whereas in 2018 it was owed $4.091 million. The balances are unsecured, interest‑free, and settled quarterly in arrears. A $15 million loan to Golar Partners, bearing LIBOR + 5.0%, was fully repaid with $0.1 million interest in December 2019.

* **Methane Princess lease security‑deposit movements (vii)** – These figures capture net advances from Golar Partners linked to the security deposits for the Methane Princess tax‑lease indemnity under the Omnibus Agreement. The amounts are recorded as outflows because they correspond to the release of funds held as lease security. They will be settled when the Methane Princess lease is eventually terminated.

**Overall picture**

In 2019 the combined effect of the payable to Golar Partners and the lease‑security‑deposit outflow resulted in a net liability of $4.961 million. Conversely, in 2018 the company held a net receivable of $1.256 million after accounting for the same lease‑related outflow. The shift reflects a reversal from a net receivable position in 2018 to a net payable position in 2019, driven mainly by changes in management‑fee settlements and the timing of lease‑related cash movements.

synth_text.title: Summary of Contractual and Debt Obligations for 2021‑2022
synth_text.text:
The company’s minimum annual contractual commitments grew markedly between 2021 and 2022, rising from **$1.45 billion** to **$2.92 billion**. The increase was driven primarily by a sharp rise in long‑term debt, which more than tripled from **$702 million** in 2021 to **$2.40 billion** in 2022. 

Other major components of the obligations are:

| Obligation (in $ millions) | 2021 | 2022 |
|----------------------------|------|------|
| Finance lease obligations (including interest) | 42 | 29 |
| Operating leases | 99 | 75 |
| Other contractual obligations* | 295 | 203 |
| Long‑term debt (incl. current portion) | 702 | 2,399 |
| Interest expense | 315 | 216 |
| Pension fund obligations | — | — |
| **Total** | **1,453** | **2,922** |

\*“Other contractual obligations” encompass finance lease obligations (interest portion), facility leases, equipment leases, data and telecommunications service agreements, and payments of principal and interest on debt and pension fund obligations. These figures represent the minimum annual payments for contracts with non‑cancelable terms longer than one year, as disclosed in the company’s commitments schedule. 

The 2022 total reflects a **101 % increase** over the prior year, underscoring the company’s expanded borrowing activities. Notably, finance lease and operating lease commitments fell modestly, while interest expense decreased, suggesting a shift toward longer‑term financing rather than short‑term lease financing. Pension fund obligations remained nil for both years.

It is also important to note that the table excludes **$189 million** related to uncertain tax positions (including $25 million of interest and penalties) because the timing of any cash settlements with tax authorities could not be reliably estimated. Detailed discussions of the debt and lease arrangements are available in Note 12 (“Long‑Term Debt and Other Financing Arrangements”) and Note 5 (“Leases”) of the consolidated financial statements, while operating lease commitments are described in Note 17 (“Commitments and Contingencies”).

Overall, the data indicate a strategic increase in long‑term financing, offset by modest reductions in lease‑related obligations, resulting in a substantially higher total contractual commitment in 2022.

synth_text.title: Summary of Contractual Obligations for 2019 and 2020
synth_text.text:
The company’s contractual commitments are disclosed in two categories—total obligations for the fiscal year ended December 31 2019 and a separate breakdown for 2020. All amounts are presented in millions of U.S. dollars.

**2019 (Total)**
- **Finance lease obligations:** $162 m  
- **Operating leases:** $574 m  
- **Other contractual obligations** (including facility leases, equipment leases, data and telecom service agreements, debt principal and interest payments, and pension fund obligations): $1,639 m  
- **Long‑term debt (including current portion):** $8,164 m  
- **Interest:** $1,038 m  
- **Pension fund obligations:** $28 m  
- **Overall total contractual obligations:** **$11,605 m**

**2020**
- **Finance lease obligations:** $61 m  
- **Operating leases:** $136 m  
- **Other contractual obligations:** $627 m  
- **Long‑term debt (including current portion):** $854 m  
- **Interest:** $354 m  
- **Pension fund obligations:** $28 m  
- **Overall total contractual obligations:** **$2,060 m**

**Key observations**
1. **Substantial reduction in total obligations:** The aggregate contractual commitments fell from $11.6 billion in 2019 to $2.1 billion in 2020, a decline of roughly 82 %.  
2. **Long‑term debt drives the majority of obligations:** In 2019, long‑term debt accounted for about 70 % of the total ($8.2 billion). By 2020, this component decreased to $854 million, reflecting the primary source of the overall reduction.  
3. **Consistent pension obligations:** Pension fund obligations remained unchanged at $28 million across both years.  
4. **Exclusion of uncertain tax positions:** $189 million related to uncertain tax positions (including $25 million of interest and penalties) are not reflected in the table, as the timing of any cash settlements cannot be reliably estimated.

Overall, the data illustrate that the company’s contractual exposure was heavily weighted toward long‑term debt in 2019, and the sharp decline in debt and related interest obligations in 2020 led to a markedly lower total commitment for that year.

- **Expected volatility:** 28.32%  
- **Risk‑free interest rate:** 1.46%  
- **Expected dividend yield:** 1.43%  
- **Expected life of the options:** 4.51 years  
- **Forfeiture rate (historical):** 5%  
- **Average exercise share price:** $31.75  
- **Derived service period:** 1.79 years  

**Accounting Treatment**  
- No cash was used to settle any of the equity instruments granted under the share‑based compensation arrangements.  
- The company did not capitalize any share‑based compensation costs as part of asset costs.

**Cash and Tax Benefits from Option Exercises (2017)**  
- **Cash received** from the exercise of options: **$20.8 million**.  
- **Tax benefit** realized from the deductible portion of the exercised options: **$2.2 million**.

These figures illustrate the financial impact of the 2017 stock option program, combining the valuation methodology, key assumptions, and the actual cash and tax benefits realized when the options were exercised.

NOTE 10 — Contingencies

Certain processes in the manufacture of our current and past products create by-products classified as hazardous waste. We have been notified by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, state environmental agencies, and in some cases, groups of potentially responsible parties, that we may be potentially liable for environmental contamination at several sites currently and formerly owned or operated by us. Two of those sites, Asheville, North Carolina and Mountain View, California, are designated National Priorities List sites under the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Superfund program. We accrue a liability for probable remediation activities, claims and proceedings against us with respect to environmental matters if the amount can be reasonably estimated, and provide disclosures including the nature of a loss whenever it is probable or reasonably possible that a potentially material loss may have occurred but cannot be estimated. We record contingent loss accruals on an undiscounted basis.
A roll-forward of remediation reserves included in accrued expenses and other liabilities in the Consolidated Balance Sheets is comprised of the following:
(1) Other activity includes currency translation adjustments not recorded through remediation expense
Unrelated to the environmental claims described above, certain other legal claims are pending against us with respect to matters arising out of the ordinary conduct of our business.

We provide product warranties when we sell our products and accrue for estimated liabilities at the time of sale. Warranty estimates are forecasts based on the best available information and historical claims experience. We accrue for specific warranty claims if we believe that the facts of a specific claim make it probable that a liability in excess of our historical experience has been incurred, and provide disclosures for specific claims whenever it is reasonably possible that a material loss may be incurred which cannot be estimated. We have an outstanding warranty claim for which we have not yet determined the root cause of a product performance issue. Testing is ongoing. We are not able to quantify the potential impact on our operations, if any, because we have not yet determined the root cause.

We cannot provide assurance that the ultimate disposition of environmental, legal, and product warranty claims will not materially exceed the amount of our accrued losses and adversely impact our consolidated financial position, results of operations, or cash flows. Our accrued liabilities and disclosures will be adjusted accordingly if additional information becomes available in the future.

synth_text.title: Remediation Reserve Roll‑Forward Summary (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
**Remediation Reserve Roll‑Forward (in thousands of dollars)**  

| Year | Balance at beginning of period | Remediation expense | Remediation payments* | Other activity (currency‑translation adjustment) | Balance at end of period |
|------|-------------------------------|---------------------|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 2018 | $17,067 | $1,182 | $(6,967) | $(8) | $11,274 |
| 2019 | $11,274 | $2,602 | $(2,455) | $23 | $11,444 |

\*Negative figures represent cash outflows for remediation activities.

**Interpretation**

- **2018:** The remediation reserve fell by $5,793 k, driven primarily by substantial payments of $6,967 k to address environmental liabilities. The modest expense of $1,182 k and a small translation loss of $8 k left an ending balance of $11,274 k.  
- **2019:** The reserve increased slightly by $170 k. Higher accrued expenses of $2,602 k outweighed payments of $2,455 k, and a modest translation gain of $23 k contributed to an ending balance of $11,444 k.

**Contextual Background**

The company accrues a liability for probable remediation activities related to hazardous‑waste by‑products generated in the manufacture of its products. Two of the sites involved—Asheville, North Carolina, and Mountain View, California—are listed on the EPA’s National Priorities List under the Superfund program. Accruals are recorded on an undiscounted basis when the amount can be reasonably estimated; otherwise, disclosures are provided when a loss is probable or reasonably possible.

“Other activity” reflects currency‑translation adjustments that are not part of remediation expense. The company also notes that additional environmental, legal, and product‑warranty claims could arise, and the ultimate cost of these liabilities may exceed current estimates, potentially affecting its financial position, results of operations, or cash flows.

**Conclusion**

The roll‑forward demonstrates that the remediation reserve decreased sharply in 2018 due to large remediation payments and modestly increased in 2019 as accrued expenses outpaced payments. Ongoing uncertainty surrounding the final resolution of environmental and related claims means the reserve balances may be adjusted in future periods as more information becomes available.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview: FY2018 vs. FY2017
synth_text.text:
**Summary of Key Financial Results**

| Fiscal Year | Net Sales (incl. surcharge) | Surcharge Revenue | Net Sales (excl. surcharge) | Operating Income | Loss on Divestiture | Adjusted Operating Income* | Operating Margin | Adjusted Operating Margin* |
|-------------|----------------------------|-------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|----------------------------|------------------|----------------------------|
| 2018 | $2,157.7 M | $365.4 M | $1,792.3 M | $189.3 M | — | $189.3 M | 8.8 % | 10.6 % |
| 2017 | $1,797.6 M | $239.2 M | $1,558.4 M | $121.5 M | $3.2 M | $124.7 M | 6.8 % | 8.0 % |

\*Adjusted figures exclude surcharge revenue and any special items (e.g., loss on divestiture), providing a non‑GAAP measure of operating performance.

**Key Observations**

1. **Revenue Growth** – Net sales rose 20 % from $1,797.6 M in 2017 to $2,157.7 M in 2018. The increase was driven partly by higher surcharge revenue, which grew from $239.2 M to $365.4 M.

2. **Operating Income Improvement** – Operating income more than doubled, climbing to $189.3 M in 2018 from $121.5 M in 2017. This represents an 8.8 % operating margin in 2018 versus 6.8 % in 2017.

3. **Adjusted Performance** – When surcharge revenue and special items are removed, the adjusted operating margin rose to 10.6 % in 2018, up from 8.0 % in 2017. Adjusted operating income reflects the same $189.3 M figure for 2018 (no loss on divestiture) and $124.7 M for 2017 after accounting for a $3.2 M divestiture loss.

4. **Drivers of Margin Expansion** – Management attributes the higher margins to stronger demand, an improved product mix, and operating cost efficiencies. These gains were partially offset by increased variable compensation expenses.

5. **Special Items Impact** – The 2017 loss on divestiture ($3.2 M) reduced reported operating income. Excluding such special items provides a more consistent basis for comparing periods, as explained in the company’s non‑GAAP financial measures discussion.

**Conclusion**

Fiscal year 2018 demonstrated robust growth across all major financial metrics, with net sales and operating income increasing substantially and adjusted operating margins improving by 2.6 percentage points. The company’s strategic focus on demand generation, product mix optimization, and cost control contributed to these positive results, while the exclusion of surcharge revenue and special items offers a clearer view of underlying operational performance.

text.value: Share Unit Awards

In accordance with stockholder-approved equity incentive plans, we grant awards of restricted stock units and cash-settled restricted stock units ("share units") to employees and directors. These awards generally have requisite service periods of three years. Under each such award, stock or cash (as applicable) is issued without direct cost to the employee. We estimate the fair value of the share units based upon the market price of our stock at the date of grant. Certain share unit grants do not provide for the payment of dividend equivalents to the participant during the requisite service period (the "vesting period"). For those grants, the value of the grants is reduced by the net present value of the foregone dividend equivalent payments.

We recognize compensation expense for share unit awards on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period, accounting for forfeitures as they occur. All cash-settled restricted stock units are marked-to-market and presented within other current and noncurrent liabilities in our Consolidated Balance Sheets. The compensation expense for our stock-settled share unit awards totaled $23.9 million, $21.8 million, and $18.2 million for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, respectively, including discontinued operations of $1.4 million for fiscal 2017. The tax benefit related to the stock-settled share unit award compensation expense for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017 was $6.0 million, $7.2 million, and $7.0 million, respectively. The compensation expense for our cash-settled share unit awards totaled $17.5 million, $5.8 million, and $20.9 million for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, respectively, including discontinued operations of $2.6 million for fiscal 2017. The tax benefit related to the cash-settled share unit award compensation expense for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017 was $4.4 million, $1.9 million, and $8.0 million, respectively.

During the second quarter of fiscal 2019, in connection with the completion of the Pinnacle acquisition, we granted 2.0 million cash-settled share unit awards at a grant date fair value of $36.37 per share unit to Pinnacle employees in replacement of their unvested restricted share unit awards that were outstanding as of the closing date. Included in the compensation expense described above for fiscal 2019 is expense of $18.9 million for accelerated vesting of awards related to Pinnacle integration restructuring activities, net of the impact of marking-to-market these awards based on a lower market price of shares of Conagra Brands common stock. Approximately $36.3 million of the fair value of the replacement share unit awards granted to Pinnacle employees was attributable to pre-combination service and was included in the purchase price and established as a liability. Included in the expense for cash-settled share unit awards above is income of $6.7 million related to the mark-to-market of this liability. As of May 26, 2019, our liability for the replacement awards was $15.9 million, which includes post-combination service expense, the mark-to-market of the liability, and the impact of payouts since completing the Pinnacle acquisition. Post-combination expense of approximately $3.9 million, based on the market price of shares of Conagra Brands common stock as of May 26, 2019, is expected to be recognized related to the replacement awards over the remaining post-combination service period of approximately two years.

During fiscal 2017, we granted 0.4 million cash-settled share units with a weighted average grant date fair value of $48.07 per share unit. synth_text.text:
At the beginning of fiscal 2019 (May 27 2018), Conagra Brands had **0.71 million non‑vested share units** outstanding, valued at a weighted‑average grant‑date fair value of **$34.58 per unit**.  

During the year the company **granted 1.95 million share units** at an average fair value of **$36.37**. Of these, **1.64 million units vested or were issued** (average fair value $35.55), while **0.05 million units were forfeited** (average fair value $36.07).  

As a result, the balance of non‑vested share units at the fiscal year‑end (May 26 2019) increased to **0.97 million units**, with a slightly higher weighted‑average fair value of **$36.20 per unit**.  

The increase in both the number of outstanding units and their fair value reflects, in part, the **Pinnacle acquisition**. In the second quarter of fiscal 2019, Conagra granted **2.0 million cash‑settled share units** to Pinnacle employees at a grant‑date fair value of **$36.37** to replace their pre‑acquisition unvested awards. Approximately $36.3 million of the fair value of these replacement awards related to pre‑combination service and was recorded as a liability, with a remaining liability of $15.9 million as of May 26 2019.  

Overall, the share‑unit activity for FY 2019 resulted in a net increase of **0.26 million non‑vested units** and a modest rise in average fair value, underscoring the company’s continued use of equity incentives—both stock‑settled and cash‑settled—to retain and motivate employees and directors.  

These figures are consistent with the company’s broader compensation expense trends, which included $23.9 million of stock‑settled share‑unit expense and $17.5 million of cash‑settled share‑unit expense for fiscal 2019, as well as related tax benefits.

synth_text.title: Key Financial Highlights for Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s selected financial data show modest growth in top‑line revenue, rising from **$1.47 billion in 2018** to **$1.55 billion in 2019** (a 5 % increase). Revenue comprises license sales, support and service revenues, and hardware sales, net of returns and allowances.

Despite higher revenue, **net income declined** sharply, falling from **$365 million in 2018** to **$272 million in 2019**. This drop reflects the impact of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which reduced the U.S. corporate tax rate, and the related deferred‑tax re‑measurement adjustment for 2018, as well as acquisition‑related costs in 2019. Consequently, basic and diluted earnings per share fell from **$4.73/$4.70** to **$3.52/$3.52**.

Dividends per share increased modestly, from **$1.36** in 2018 to **$1.54** in 2019, indicating a continued commitment to returning cash to shareholders.

On the balance sheet, total deferred revenue grew from **$369.9 million** to **$394.3 million**, and total assets rose from **$2.03 billion** to **$2.18 billion**, reflecting the expansion in operations and acquisitions. The company reported **no long‑term debt** in either year, and stockholders’ equity increased from **$1.32 billion** to **$1.43 billion**, underscoring a strengthening capital position.

Overall, the 2018‑2019 period was characterized by revenue growth, a lower profitability margin due to tax and acquisition effects, and an improved equity base.
