synth_text.title: 2019 Stock Option Grant Valuation: Assumptions, Fair Value, and Expense Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2019 the Board of Directors amended and restated the 2011 Equity Incentive Plan, reserving an additional **1,000,000** stock options for issuance to management and employees. By year‑end the Company had granted **755,000** options (vesting over two years) and **234,000** options (vesting over three years), each with an exercise price of **$4.70** per share.

To determine the grant‑date fair value of these awards, the Company applied the **Black‑Scholes option‑pricing model** using the following assumptions:

| Assumption | Grant 1 | Grant 2 |
|------------|---------|---------|
| Expected volatility (based on two‑year historical company data) | **57.5 %** | **52.5 %** |
| Dividend yield | **10.0 %** | **10.0 %** |
| Risk‑free interest rate | **1.64 %** | **1.65 %** |
| Weighted‑average grant‑date fair value | **$0.59** | **$0.58** |

These inputs produced a weighted‑average fair value of roughly **$0.58‑$0.59 per option**. Consequently, the compensation expense recognized for the year ended **December 31, 2019** was **$0.1 million**. The remaining unrecognized cost associated with non‑vested options amounted to **$0.5 million**, reflecting an average remaining vesting period of **2.1 years**.

Overall, the amendment expanded the company’s equity incentive capacity, and the Black‑Scholes assumptions—particularly the high volatility and dividend yield—resulted in a modest per‑option fair value, driving a relatively low expense charge for the reporting year while leaving a significant portion of the cost to be recognized over the future vesting periods.

text.value: Consolidated Operating Expenses
Operating expenses for our segments are discussed separately below under the heading “Segment Results of Operations.”

Cost of Services Cost of services includes the following costs directly attributable to a service: salaries and wages, benefits, materials and supplies, content costs, contracted services, network access and transport costs, customer provisioning costs, computer systems support, and costs to support our outsourcing contracts and technical facilities. Aggregate customer care costs, which include billing and service provisioning, are allocated between Cost of services and Selling, general and administrative expense.

Cost of services decreased $413 million, or 1.3%, during 2019 compared to 2018, primarily due to decreases in network access costs, a product realignment charge in 2018 (see “Special Items”), decreases in employee-related costs resulting from the Voluntary Separation Program and decreases in digital content costs.

These decreases were partially offset by increases in rent expense as a result of adding capacity to the networks to support demand and the adoption of the new lease accounting standard in 2019, regulatory fees, and costs related to the device protection package offered to our wireless retail postpaid customers.

Cost of Wireless Equipment Cost of wireless equipment decreased $369 million, or 1.6%, during 2019 compared to 2018, primarily as a result of declines in the number of wireless devices sold as a result of an elongation of the handset upgrade cycle, partially offset by a shift to higher priced devices in the mix of wireless devices sold.

Selling, General and Administrative Expense Selling, general and administrative expense includes salaries and wages and benefits not directly attributable to a service or product, bad debt charges, taxes other than income taxes, advertising and sales commission costs, call center and information technology costs, regulatory fees, professional service fees, and rent and utilities for administrative space. Also included is a portion of the aggregate customer care costs as discussed above in “Cost of Services.”

Selling, general and administrative expense decreased $1.2 billion, or 3.8%, during 2019 compared to 2018, primarily due to decreases in employee-related costs primarily due to the Voluntary Separation Program, a decrease in severance, pension and benefits charges (see “Special Items”),

the acquisition and integration related charges in 2018 primarily related to the acquisition of Yahoo’s operating business (see “Special Items”) and a net gain from dispositions of assets and businesses in 2019 (see “Special Items”), partially offset by increases in advertising expenses, sales commission and bad debt expense. The increase in sales commission expense during 2019 compared to 2018, was primarily due to a lower net deferral of commission costs as a result of the adoption of Topic 606 on January 1, 2018, using a modified retrospective approach.

Depreciation and Amortization Expense Depreciation and amortization expense decreased $721 million, or 4.1%, during 2019 compared to 2018, primarily due to the change in the mix of net depreciable assets. Media Goodwill Impairment The goodwill impairment charges recorded in 2019 and 2018 for Verizon Media were a result of the Company’s annual impairment test performed in the fourth quarter (see “Critical Accounting Estimates”).

synth_text.title: 2019 Consolidated Operating Expense Summary and Key Drivers
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019, Verizon’s Consolidated Operating Expenses fell to **$7.1 billion**, a **6.5 % reduction** versus 2018. The decline reflects lower spending across all major cost components, offset by a substantial media goodwill impairment charge.

| Expense Category | Dollar Change (2020 vs 2018) | Percent Change |
|------------------|-----------------------------|----------------|
| Cost of Services | **‑$413 million** | **‑1.3 %** |
| Cost of Wireless Equipment | **‑$369 million** | **‑1.6 %** |
| Selling, General & Administrative (SG&A) | **‑$1.187 billion** | **‑3.8 %** |
| Depreciation & Amortization | **‑$721 million** | **‑4.1 %** |
| Media Goodwill Impairment | **‑$4.405 billion** | **‑95.9 %** |

**Key drivers of the expense reductions**

* **Cost of Services** – Decreased primarily due to lower network access costs, the absence of a 2018 product‑realignment charge, reduced employee‑related costs from the Voluntary Separation Program, and lower digital content expenses. Offsetting factors included higher rent from network capacity expansion, new lease‑accounting impacts, regulatory fees, and costs tied to the device‑protection package for postpaid wireless customers.

* **Cost of Wireless Equipment** – Fell as the handset upgrade cycle lengthened, resulting in fewer device sales, though this was partially mitigated by a shift toward higher‑priced devices.

* **SG&A** – Declined because of reduced employee‑related expenses (voluntary separations, lower severance, pension, and benefits), the absence of 2018 acquisition‑related charges (Yahoo’s operating business), and gains from asset dispositions. Increases in advertising, sales commissions, and bad‑debt expense partially offset the savings.

* **Depreciation & Amortization** – Lowered due to a change in the mix of depreciable assets, leading to a 4.1 % reduction.

* **Media Goodwill Impairment** – The large impairment reflects Verizon Media’s annual goodwill test, resulting in a near‑total write‑down of the 2018 goodwill balance.

Overall, the 6.5 % drop in operating expenses underscores Verizon’s focus on cost discipline across service delivery, equipment procurement, and administrative functions, while the media goodwill impairment remains a significant, non‑cash charge affecting the consolidated expense line.

synth_text.title: Verizon’s Consolidated Operating Expenses: 2018‑2019 Comparative Summary
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the fiscal years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019, Verizon reported a notable decline in total consolidated operating expenses, falling from **$108.6 billion** in 2018 to **$101.5 billion** in 2019—a reduction of **$7.1 billion** (approximately **6.5 %**).

**Key Expense Categories**

| Expense Category | 2018 (US$ bn) | 2019 (US$ bn) | Absolute Change | % Change |
|------------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|----------|
| Cost of Services | 32.185 | 31.772 | – $0.413 bn | – 1.3 % |
| Cost of Wireless Equipment | 23.323 | 22.954 | – $0.369 bn | – 1.6 % |
| Selling, General & Administrative (SG&A) | 31.083 | 29.896 | – $1.187 bn | – 3.8 % |
| Depreciation & Amortization | 17.403 | 16.682 | – $0.721 bn | – 4.1 % |
| Media Goodwill Impairment | 4.591 | 0.186 | – $4.405 bn | – 96 % |
| **Consolidated Operating Expenses** | **108.585** | **101.490** | **– 7.095** | **– 6.5** |

**Drivers of the Expense Reductions**

* **Cost of Services** – Decreased primarily because of lower network access costs, the absence of a 2018 product‑realignment charge, reduced employee‑related costs from the Voluntary Separation Program, and lower digital content expenses. Offsetting factors included higher rent for added network capacity, new lease‑accounting impacts, regulatory fees, and costs tied to device‑protection packages for postpaid wireless customers.

* **Cost of Wireless Equipment** – Fell as the handset upgrade cycle lengthened, leading to fewer device sales, though this was partially mitigated by a shift toward higher‑priced devices.

* **SG&A** – Declined due to the Voluntary Separation Program, reduced severance, pension and benefits charges, and the absence of the 2018 acquisition‑related expenses tied to Yahoo’s operating business. Gains from asset dispositions in 2019 also contributed, while higher advertising, sales‑commission, and bad‑debt expenses partially offset the savings.

* **Depreciation & Amortization** – Lowered because of a change in the mix of depreciable assets, resulting in a 4.1 % reduction.

* **Media Goodwill Impairment** – Dropped dramatically from $4.591 billion in 2018 to $0.186 billion in 2019, reflecting the outcome of Verizon Media’s annual goodwill impairment testing.

**Conclusion**  
The combined effect of operational efficiencies, workforce reductions, strategic asset mix adjustments, and a substantial decline in media goodwill impairment drove a meaningful contraction in Verizon’s operating expense base between 2018 and 2019. This expense discipline contributed to improved cost structure and positioned the company for continued focus on profitability and investment in network capacity.

text.value: In assessing the ability to realize our deferred tax assets, we considered whether it is more likely than not that some portion or all the deferred tax assets will not be realized. We considered the following: we have historical cumulative book income, as measured by the current and prior two years; we have strong, consistent taxpaying history; we have substantial U.S. federal income tax carryback potential; and we have substantial amounts of scheduled future reversals of taxable temporary differences from our deferred tax liabilities. We have concluded that this positive evidence outweighs the negative evidence and, thus, that the deferred tax assets as of March 29, 2019 are realizable on a ‘‘more likely than not’’ basis.
The aggregate changes in the balance of gross unrecognized tax benefits were as follows:

There was a change of $68 million in gross unrecognized tax benefits during fiscal 2019. This gross liability does not include offsetting tax benefits associated with the correlative effects of potential transfer pricing adjustments, interest deductions, and state income taxes.
Of the total unrecognized tax benefits at March 29, 2019, $361 million, if recognized, would favorably affect our effective tax rate.

We recognize interest and/or penalties related to uncertain tax positions in income tax expense. At March 29, 2019, before any tax benefits, we had $43 million of accrued interest and penalties on unrecognized tax benefits. Interest included in our provision for income taxes was an expense of approximately $17 million for fiscal 2019. If the accrued interest and penalties do not ultimately become payable, amounts accrued will be reduced in the period that such determination is made and reflected as a reduction of the overall income tax provision.

We file income tax returns in the U.S. on a federal basis and in many U.S. state and foreign jurisdictions. Our most significant tax jurisdictions are the U.S., Ireland, and Singapore. Our tax filings remain subject to examination by applicable tax authorities for a certain length of time following the tax year to which those filings relate. Our fiscal years 2014 through 2019 remain subject to examination by the IRS for U.S. federal tax purposes. Our fiscal years prior to 2014 have been settled and closed with the IRS. Our 2015 through 2019 fiscal years remain subject to examination by the appropriate governmental agencies for Irish tax purposes, and our 2014 through 2019 fiscal years remain subject to examination by the appropriate governmental agencies for Singapore tax purposes.

The timing of the resolution of income tax examinations is highly uncertain, and the amounts ultimately paid, if any, upon resolution of the issues raised by the taxing authorities may differ materially from the amounts accrued for each year. Although potential resolution of uncertain tax positions involves multiple tax periods and jurisdictions, it is reasonably possible that the gross unrecognized tax benefits related to these audits could decrease (whether by payment, release, or a combination of both) in the next 12 months by $26 million. Depending on the nature of the settlement or expiration of statutes of limitations, we estimate $26 million could affect our income tax provision and therefore benefit the resulting effective tax rate.
We continue to monitor the progress of ongoing income tax controversies and the impact, if any, of the expected tolling of the statute of limitations in various taxing jurisdictions.

synth_text.title: Summary of Gross Unrecognized Tax Benefits and Deferred Tax Asset Realizability for Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s gross unrecognized tax benefits (GUTBs) increased from **$378 million** at the start of fiscal 2018 to **$446 million** at the end of fiscal 2019, reflecting a **net rise of $68 million** during 2019. The primary drivers of this increase were:

* **Current‑year tax positions:** +$75 million  
* **Acquisition‑related benefit:** +$8 million  
* **Increase related to prior‑period positions:** +$16 million  

These gains were partially offset by:

* **Decrease related to prior‑period positions:** –$11 million  
* **Lapse of statutes of limitations:** –$3 million  
* **Settlements with tax authorities:** –$3 million  

In fiscal 2018, the GUTB balance grew by $130 million, largely due to a $98 million increase in current‑year positions and a $35 million rise from prior‑period positions.

From the accompanying narrative, the company concludes that its **deferred tax assets are more‑likely‑than‑not realizable**. This assessment is based on:

* Consistent historical book income over the current and prior two years,  
* A strong tax‑paying record,  
* Substantial U.S. federal income tax carryback potential, and  
* Scheduled future reversals of taxable temporary differences from existing deferred tax liabilities.

If fully recognized, **$361 million** of the $446 million GUTB balance would favorably impact the effective tax rate. The company has accrued **$43 million** in interest and penalties on these uncertain positions, of which **$17 million** was recorded as expense in fiscal 2019. Should the accrued amounts not become payable, they will be reversed, reducing the overall tax provision.

Tax examinations remain ongoing in the United States, Ireland, and Singapore, covering fiscal years 2014‑2019 (U.S.) and 2015‑2019 (Ireland and Singapore). The timing and outcome of these examinations are uncertain, but the company estimates that **up to $26 million** of the GUTBs could be eliminated within the next 12 months, potentially improving the tax provision and effective tax rate.

Overall, the increase in gross unrecognized tax benefits reflects heightened exposure to uncertain tax positions, yet the company’s analysis and monitoring suggest that a substantial portion remains realizable and may ultimately reduce its effective tax burden.

synth_text.title: Deferred Tax Asset Balance – FY 2017: Key Changes and Realizability Assessment
synth_text.text:
**Overview of FY 2017 Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) Movement**  
- **Opening balance (March 31 2016):** $197 million.  
- **Net increase during the year:** $51 million, resulting in a **closing balance (March 31 2017) of $248 million**.

**Drivers of the $51 million increase**

| Component | Effect (in $ million) | Explanation |
|-----------|----------------------|-------------|
| Settlements with tax authorities | (23) | Payments or settlements reduced the DTA balance. |
| Lapse of statute of limitations | (9) | Expired tax positions eliminated related benefits. |
| Increase related to prior‑period tax positions | 21 | Re‑assessment of earlier years added benefits. |
| Decrease related to prior‑period tax positions | (9) | Adjustments to earlier positions removed benefits. |
| Increase related to current‑year tax positions | 38 | New tax positions generated in FY 2017 added benefits. |
| Increase due to acquisition | 33 | Acquired entities contributed additional deferred tax assets. |
| **Net change** | **51** | Sum of all increases and decreases. |

**Realizability of the Deferred Tax Assets**  
The company evaluates DTA realizability on a “more likely than not” basis, considering:  

1. **Historical cumulative book income** over the current and prior two years.  
2. **Strong, consistent tax‑paying history.**  
3. **Substantial U.S. federal income tax carryback potential.**  
4. **Future scheduled reversals of taxable temporary differences** from existing deferred tax liabilities.  

These positive factors outweigh any negative evidence, leading management to conclude that the $248 million DTA balance as of March 31 2017 is expected to be realizable.

**Relation to Unrecognized Tax Benefits**  
While the DTA balance reflects recognized tax benefits, the company also monitors **gross unrecognized tax benefits**—potential liabilities that could affect the effective tax rate if resolved. Recent disclosures (e.g., a $68 million change in 2019 and $361 million that could favorably impact the tax rate if recognized) illustrate the broader tax risk environment. Settlements, statutory expirations, and ongoing examinations in jurisdictions such as the U.S., Ireland, and Singapore can influence both recognized and unrecognized positions, but the FY 2017 DTA increase demonstrates that, despite these risks, the company’s net tax position improved.

**Conclusion**  
For FY 2017, the company’s deferred tax assets grew by $51 million to $248 million, driven primarily by current‑year tax positions and acquisition‑related benefits, partially offset by settlements and statutory lapses. Management’s assessment, grounded in strong earnings history and future reversal prospects, supports the view that these assets are more likely than not realizable, providing a solid foundation for the company’s effective tax rate outlook.

4. **Subsequent Year Activity** – In 2019, after the major reclassifications, only modest additions of $119 million were recorded, leaving an ending AUD balance of **$20 million**, essentially the re‑classified Gimi value awaiting conversion.

### Summary
The 2018 AUD movements were dominated by two strategic reclassifications linked to the company’s FLNG projects: the completion of the Hilli conversion (a $1.3 billion transfer out) and the initiation of the Gimi conversion (a $20 million transfer in). Together with routine additions and capitalized interest, these actions resulted in a net AUD balance of $434 million at year‑end, setting the stage for the next phase of FLNG development.

synth_text.title: FY2019 Cost of Revenues and Gross Margin Summary
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2019, total cost of revenues rose to **$73.9 million**, representing a **47 % increase** over fiscal year 2018. The increase is split between subscription‑related costs and other‑revenue costs:

* **Subscriptions:** Cost of subscription revenues grew by **$50.9 million (46 %)**. The rise was driven by higher third‑party fees to support solution offerings ($21.5 million), increased infrastructure support—including amortization of acquired intangibles ($19.8 million)—and higher headcount and contractor expenses, which also included share‑based compensation ($9.6 million). These investments were aimed at expanding infrastructure, improving service availability, and accommodating growth in both new and existing customers.

* **Other revenues:** Cost of other revenues climbed by **$23.0 million (48 %)**. The primary contributors were higher services personnel costs, including share‑based compensation ($11.1 million), increased product‑sales costs ($10.6 million), and additional overhead ($1.3 million). Variations in this segment are also influenced by the timing of professional‑services project completions and discounting on phone sales.

The combined effect of these cost increases led to a **decline in overall gross margin** for the year. Management expects subscription gross margin to remain in a similar range going forward, as the company continues to invest in infrastructure and capacity while supporting a growing subscriber base.

synth_text.title: Cost of Revenues and Gross Margin Overview (2017‑2018)
synth_text.text:
**Cost of Revenues**  
- **2017:** $121.3 million

The total cost of revenues grew by approximately $35.9 million (about 30 %) from 2017 to 2018. The cost mix shows a slight shift toward subscription‑related expenses, which accounted for 81 % of the total in 2017 and 82 % in 2018. The “Other” cost category increased more noticeably, rising from 16 % to 22 % of total costs.

**Gross Margin**  
- **2017:** 76 %  
- **2018:** 77 %  

Despite the higher absolute cost base, the company’s gross margin improved marginally, moving from 76 % to 77 % over the same period.

**Contextual Insights**  
The additional narrative explains that the cost increases observed in 2019 were driven primarily by:  
- Higher third‑party fees supporting solution offerings,  
- Expanded infrastructure and related amortization of acquired intangibles,  
- Increased headcount, contractor expenses, and share‑based compensation, and  
- Greater professional‑services personnel costs and product‑sales expenses.  

These same cost drivers—particularly investments in infrastructure, personnel, and third‑party services—likely contributed to the upward trend in both subscription and “Other” cost components between 2017 and 2018. While the higher costs placed pressure on margins, the modest improvement in gross margin suggests that revenue growth kept pace with cost growth during this period.

Overall, the data indicate a growing cost base with a shifting composition toward “Other” expenses, yet the company maintained a strong gross margin, positioning it to sustain profitability as it continues to invest in its subscription and services offerings.

synth_text.title: Fiscal Year 2019 Cost of Revenues and Gross Margin Overview
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2019 the company’s total cost of revenues rose sharply, increasing by $35.9 million (a 30 % jump) compared with fiscal 2018. This increase is the combined result of higher costs in both the subscription and “other” revenue streams.

**Subscription revenues** – Cost of subscriptions grew by $50.9 million, a 46 % rise year‑over‑year. The primary contributors were:
- Third‑party costs to support solution offerings: **$21.5 million**
- Infrastructure support costs, including amortization of acquired intangibles: **$19.8 million**
- Headcount, personnel, contractor expenses, and related share‑based compensation: **$9.6 million**

These higher subscription costs compressed the subscription gross margin, although the company expects future subscription gross margins to remain in a similar range as it continues to invest in infrastructure and capacity.

**Other revenues** – Cost of other revenues increased by $23.0 million, a 48 % increase. The main drivers were:
- Services personnel costs (including share‑based compensation): **$11.1 million**
- Cost of product sales: **$10.6 million**
- Overhead expenses: **$1.3 million**

Gross margin for other revenues is more variable, reflecting the timing of professional‑services project completions and discounting on phone sales.

Overall, the $35.9 million (30 %) rise in total cost of revenues reflects substantial investments across both subscription and other business lines, leading to a reduction in gross margin for the period. The company anticipates that subscription gross margins will stabilize around current levels as the newly‑added infrastructure and headcount support continued growth in the customer base and usage.

synth_text.title: Changes in Redeemable Noncontrolling Interests – American Tower Corporation (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
American Tower Corporation’s redeemable noncontrolling interests (RNCIs) experienced notable fluctuations between 2018 and 2019.  

In 2018, the RNCI balance decreased from $1,126.2 million at the start of the year to $1,004.8 million at year‑end, a decline of $121.4 million. The reduction was driven by a loss attributable to noncontrolling interests of $87.9 million, a merger‑related adjustment of $‑28.1 million, and a substantial foreign‑currency translation loss of $92.1 million. No new additions or purchases of redeemable RNCIs were recorded during the year.  

Conversely, 2019 saw the RNCI balance rise to $1,096.5 million, up $91.7 million from the beginning‑of‑year figure of $1,004.8 million. The primary source of this increase was the $525.7 million addition linked to the acquisition of MTN’s noncontrolling stakes in joint‑venture tower assets in Ghana and Uganda (total consideration ≈ $523 million). Net income attributable to RNCIs contributed $35.8 million, while a matching redemption‑value adjustment offset this amount. The company also repurchased redeemable RNCIs for $425.7 million, and a foreign‑currency translation loss of $8.3 million modestly reduced the balance.  

Additional disclosures highlight that, as part of the 2019 activities, American Tower formed Eure‑et‑Loir Réseaux Mobiles SAS in France, holding a 51 % controlling interest while the remaining 49 % is classified as redeemable noncontrolling interest, valued at $2.7 million at December 31, 2019.  

Overall, the RNCI position shifted from a 2018 decline to a 2019 increase, reflecting strategic acquisitions, repurchase activity, and the impact of currency fluctuations.

synth_text.title: 2017 Net Pension Expense – Component Breakdown and Classification
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2017 the company recorded a total net pension expense of **$48.4 million**. This amount is distributed across three functional expense categories in accordance with the company’s accounting policy:

| Functional Category | Amount (in $ millions) | Key Components |
|---------------------|-----------------------|----------------|
| **Cost of Sales**   | **$20.2**             | Includes the **service cost** of **$3.9 M**, which represents the estimated cost of future pension liabilities earned by active employees whose work is classified under cost of sales. |
| **Selling, General & Administrative (SG&A) Expenses** | **$3.9** | Also reflects the **service cost** of **$3.9 M**, allocated here for employees whose duties fall under SG&A. |
| **Other Expense (net)** | **$24.3** | Consists of **Pension earnings, interest and deferrals (Pension EID)** of **$23.8 M**—the expected return on plan assets, interest on projected benefit obligations, and amortization of actuarial gains/losses and prior service costs—plus a **curtailment charge** of **$0.5 M**. |

Adding the three categories ($20.2 M + $3.9 M + $24.3 M) confirms the total net pension expense of **$48.4 million**.

**Interpretation of Components**  
- **Service Cost ($3.9 M):** The cost of pension benefits earned by active employees during the year. It is recorded in the expense category that matches the employees’ functional area (cost of sales or SG&A).  
- **Pension Earnings, Interest & Deferrals ($23.8 M):** Reflects the net effect of investment returns on plan assets, interest on the projected benefit obligation, and the amortization of actuarial gains/losses and prior service costs.  
- **Curtailment Charge ($0.5 M):** Represents expense arising from reductions in the pension plan’s projected obligations.

This breakdown illustrates how the company’s pension accounting aligns expense recognition with the underlying employee activities, providing transparency into the drivers of the overall $48.4 million net pension expense for 2017.

synth_text.title: Summary of Net Pension Expense Components for Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table outlines the composition of net pension expense for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2018 and June 30, 2019, presented in millions of dollars. Net pension expense is split among service cost, pension earnings, interest and deferrals (Pension EID), and is reflected in cost of sales, selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses, and other expense categories.

**Key Components**  

| Fiscal Year | Service Cost | Total Cost of Sales | Total SG&A Expenses | Pension EID | Total Other Expense | Net Pension Expense |
|-------------|--------------|---------------------|---------------------|------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| 2019 | $1.5 M | $10.0 M | $1.5 M | $0.1 M | $0.1 M | $11.6 M |
| 2018 | $1.6 M | $10.5 M | $1.6 M | $2.1 M | $2.1 M | $14.2 M |

- **Service Cost** – Represents the estimated cost of future pension liabilities earned by active employees. It decreased slightly from $1.6 M in 2018 to $1.5 M in 2019.  
- **Pension Earnings, Interest and Deferrals (Pension EID)** – Includes expected returns on plan assets, interest costs on projected benefit obligations, and amortization of actuarial gains/losses and prior service costs. This component fell sharply from $2.1 M in 2018 to $0.1 M in 2019.  
- **Total Other Expense** mirrors the Pension EID amount for each year.  

**Year‑over‑Year Changes**  
- Net pension expense declined by $2.6 M, from $14.2 M in 2018 to $11.6 M in 2019.  
- The reduction is driven primarily by the significant drop in Pension EID, while service cost and the related cost‑of‑sales/SG&A allocations remained relatively stable.  

**Contextual Notes**  
- Net pension expense is allocated to cost of sales, SG&A, and other expense categories based on the functional role of the employees incurring the expense.  
- As of June 30, 2019 and June 30, 2018, amounts capitalized in gross inventory were $1.7 M each year, a figure separate from the pension expense breakdown.  

**Conclusion**  
The data shows a modest decrease in service cost and a pronounced reduction in pension earnings, interest and deferrals, resulting in a lower overall net pension expense in 2019 compared with 2018. This reflects improved pension plan performance and/or changes in actuarial assumptions affecting the Pension EID component.

synth_text.title: 2020 Incentive Plan Enhancements and Metric Weightings Overview
synth_text.text:
In 2020 the company moved from its “Integrate and Transform” phase into the “Operate” phase, prompting a redesign of both short‑term and long‑term incentive metrics.  

During the 2018‑2019 period, the short‑term incentive (STI) plan was weighted heavily toward Adjusted EBITDA (65 %), with Free Cash Flow (25 %) and Customer Experience (10 %) completing the mix; revenue was not a performance driver. The long‑term incentive (LTI) was tied to a two‑year Adjusted EBITDA run‑rate target set at 100 % of the goal.  

For 2020, the STI composition was adjusted to include Revenue (15 %) alongside Adjusted EBITDA (50 %), Free Cash Flow (25 %) and Customer Experience (10 %). This addition encourages top‑line growth. The LTI metric was also changed: it now tracks a three‑year cumulative Adjusted EBITDA target, with full payout at 100 % achievement. Moreover, a three‑year Relative Total Shareholder Return (TSR) Modifier was introduced, allowing the LTI payout to be increased or decreased by up to ±20 % based on TSR performance.  

These enhancements were adopted after an internal review, extensive shareholder dialogue, and consultation with executive compensation advisors, ensuring that the incentive structure directly supports the company’s strategic priorities for the operation phase.

synth_text.title: Connected Home Segment Financial Performance: 2019 vs. 2018 Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2019 the Connected Home segment recorded net revenue of **$771 million**, accounting for **72.8 %** of the company’s total revenue, and generated a contribution income of **$96 million**, resulting in a **12.5 % contribution margin**. Compared with 2018, net revenue slipped by **0.4 %**, while contribution income fell by a more pronounced **14.9 %**.

The modest revenue decline was driven primarily by:
* A $27.8 million drop in sales to service‑provider customers.
* A contraction in the North American home‑Wi‑Fi market, which reduced sales to non‑service‑provider customers.
* Lower sales of home wireless, mobile, and broadband modem/gateway products, especially AC routers, Wi‑Fi mesh systems, and extenders, partially offset by the launch of Wi‑Fi 6 routers.
* Revenue reductions across all three geographic regions (Americas, EMEA, APAC).

The sharper decline in contribution income and margin resulted from:
* Higher product acquisition costs due to Section 301 tariffs and the start‑up of new manufacturing sites.
* Increased channel promotion activities.
* Foreign‑exchange headwinds from a stronger U.S. dollar.

In contrast, the 2018‑2017 period saw growth in net revenue and contribution income, fueled by strong performance of home‑wireless and broadband modem/gateway products, especially in non‑service‑provider channels, and geographic gains in the Americas and EMEA.

Overall, while 2019’s revenue dip was relatively small, the segment’s profitability was more significantly impacted by cost pressures and market headwinds, highlighting the importance of managing tariffs, manufacturing efficiencies, and promotional spend to sustain contribution margins.

The Connected Home segment recorded net revenue of **$768,261**, representing **73.9 %** of total company revenue for the year ended December 31, 2019. Contribution income stood at **$83,870**, yielding a **contribution margin of 10.9 %**.

Compared with 2018, both net revenue and contribution income declined. The drop in net revenue was driven primarily by a **$27.8 million reduction from service‑provider customers**, a contraction in the North American home Wi‑Fi market, and weaker sales of home wireless, mobile, and broadband modem/gateway products. Within home wireless, sales of AC routers, Wi‑Fi mesh systems, and extenders fell, only partially offset by the launch of Wi‑Fi 6 routers. Geographic performance showed revenue declines across all three regions (Americas, EMEA, APAC).

Contribution income fell as well, reflecting the lower net revenue and reduced gross‑margin attainment. The **contribution margin** slipped due to **higher product acquisition costs** stemming from Section 301 tariffs, inefficiencies from new manufacturing locations, increased channel promotion spend, and foreign‑exchange headwinds caused by a stronger U.S. dollar.

In contrast, the 2018 fiscal year had **grown net revenue** over 2017, fueled by strong demand for home wireless and broadband modem/gateway products, especially in non‑service‑provider channels. Although service‑provider revenue still fell by $33.5 million, overall growth was supported by gains in the Americas and EMEA regions. Contribution income also rose in 2018, benefitting from higher net revenue, a favorable product mix, and lower warranty expenses, despite higher operating costs as a proportion of revenue.

Overall, the 2019 results indicate a reversal of the growth trend seen in 2018, with revenue and margin pressures linked to market contraction, product‑mix shifts, and external cost factors.

synth_text.title: Connected Home Segment Financial Snapshot: 2019 Decline After 2018 Growth
synth_text.text:
**Financial Overview (2019)**  
- **Net revenue:** $711.4 million, representing 71.2 % of the company’s total net revenue.  
- **Contribution income:** $67.8 million, yielding a **contribution margin** of 9.5 %.  

**Year‑over‑Year Changes (2019 vs. 2018)**  
- Net revenue decreased by **7.7 %**.  
- Contribution income fell by **29.7 %**, pulling the margin down to 9.5 %.  

**Key Drivers of the 2019 Decline**  
1. **Service‑provider slowdown:** Revenue from service‑provider customers dropped by $27.8 million, reflecting reduced demand for home‑wireless, mobile, and broadband modem/gateway products.  
2. **Market contraction:** The North American home Wi‑Fi market contracted in fiscal 2019, affecting non‑service‑provider sales.  
3. **Product mix shift:** Declines were seen in AC routers, Wi‑Fi mesh systems, and extenders, only partially offset by the launch of Wi‑Fi 6 routers.  
4. **Higher acquisition costs:** Section 301 tariffs, new manufacturing locations, increased channel promotions, and a stronger U.S. dollar raised product costs, compressing contribution margin.  

**Context from the Prior Year (2018 vs. 2017)**  
- 2018 recorded **growth** in Connected Home net revenue, driven by strong performance of home‑wireless and broadband modem/gateway products, despite a $33.5 million drop in service‑provider revenue.  
- Geographic growth was seen in the Americas and EMEA, while APAC declined.  

**Summary**  
The Connected Home segment experienced a notable revenue and contribution income contraction in 2019, reversing the growth trend observed in 2018. The decline stemmed from weaker service‑provider demand, a shrinking North American Wi‑Fi market, an unfavorable product mix, and increased cost pressures from tariffs and currency effects.

The following are biographical summaries of our executive officers other than Mr. Kirchner, for whom a biographical summary is set forth under “Information about Our Board of Directors.”

Robert Andersen is executive vice president and chief financial officer of Xperi Corporation. He became executive vice president and chief financial officer of Xperi Corporation in January 2014. Prior to joining Xperi Corporation, he served as executive vice president and CFO of G2 Holdings Corp. d/b/a Components Direct. Mr. Andersen previously served as CFO at Phoenix Technologies Ltd. and held senior financial roles at Wind River Systems, Inc. and NextOffice, Inc. His finance career began at Hewlett-Packard Company, where he served in various controller, treasury and technology finance management roles. Mr. Andersen served on the board of directors of publicly traded Quantum Corporation through March 2017. He currently serves on the board of directors of the Alameda County Community Food Bank in the role of vice chair. Mr. Andersen holds a B.A. in economics from the University of California, Davis, and an M.B.A. from the Anderson School of Management at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Paul Davis is general counsel and corporate secretary of Xperi Corporation. He joined Xperi Corporation in August 2011, and became general counsel and corporate secretary in July 2013. Before joining Xperi Corporation, he was an attorney at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP, where his practice focused on mergers and acquisitions, corporate securities matters and corporate governance. Mr. Davis holds a Juris Doctor from the University of California, Hastings College of the Law and B.A. degrees in history and political science from the University of California, San Diego. While at Hastings, he was magna cum laude, an Order of the Coif member and a managing editor on the Hastings Law Journal.

Murali Dharan has served as president of Tessera Intellectual Property Corp. (“Tessera”) since October of 2017 and is responsible for the strategic direction, management and growth of the Tessera intellectual property licensing business. He has extensive leadership experience, most recently as CEO of IPVALUE, guiding the company from a start-up to an industry leader and helping partners to generate more than $1.6 billion in IP revenue. Prior to joining IPVALUE in 2002, Mr. Dharan held executive roles at various technology companies, including executive vice president at Preview Systems, vice president and general manager at Silicon Graphics, and vice president and general manager at NEC. Mr. Dharan holds an electrical engineering degree from Anna University in India, a master’s degree in computer science from Indiana University, and an MBA from Stanford University.

Geir Skaaden has served as our chief products and services officer since December 2016 and leads global sales, business development and product management for our portfolio of imaging and audio solutions. He served as DTS’s Executive Vice President, Products, Platforms and Solutions from October 2015 until its acquisition by the Company in December 2016, having previously served as DTS’s Senior Vice President, Corporate Business Development, Digital Content and Media Solutions since December 2013. Prior to that, Mr. Skaaden served as DTS’s Senior Vice President, Products & Platforms from April 2012 to December 2013. From 2008 to 2012, Mr. Skaaden served in a number of positions overseeing numerous aspects including strategic sales, licensing operations, and business development. Prior to joining DTS in 2008, Mr. Skaaden served as the Chief Executive Officer at Neural Audio Corporation from 2004 to 2008, where he previously served as Vice President, Corporate Development from 2002 to 2004. Mr. Skaaden holds a B.A. in Finance from the University of Oregon, a Business degree from the Norwegian School of Management and an M.B.A. from the University of Washington.

We have adopted a written code of business conduct and ethics that applies to our principal executive officer, principal financial officer, principal accounting officer or controller, or persons serving similar functions. text.value: Reporting Channels and Whistleblower Protection
To ensure that our conduct meets relevant legal requirements and the highest ethical standards under the Ethics Code, TSMC provides multiple channels for reporting business conduct concerns.

First of all, our Audit Committee approved and we have implemented the “Complaint Policy and Procedures for Certain Accounting and Legal Matters” and “Procedures for Ombudsman System” that allow employees or any whistleblowers with relevant evidence to report any financial, legal, or ethical irregularities anonymously through either the Ombudsman or directly to the Audit Committee.

TSMC maintains additional internal reporting channels for our employees. To foster an open culture of ethics compliance, we encourage our employees and the third parties we do business with to report any suspected noncompliance with law or relevant TSMC policy.

TSMC treats any complaint and the investigation thereof in a confidential and sensitive manner, and strictly prohibits any form of retaliation against any individual who in good faith reports or helps with the investigation of any complaint. Due to the open reporting channels, TSMC receives reports on various issues from employees and external parties such as our customers and suppliers from time to time. Below is a summary of the Number of Reported Incidents.

Note 1: Among the 205 cases, 132 were related to employee relationship, 47 cases related to other matters (e.g. employee’s individual interest or private matters), and 26 cases related to ethical matters.

Note 2: One case involved an employee who requested a supplier to reserve a hotel and pay advance accommodation fees during his business trip, actions which violate TSMC policy, and the employee was disciplined. Another case involved an employee who abused his work relationship by requesting a supplier to make a personal loan to the employee, a severe violation of our Ethics Code, and the employee was terminated.
Note 3: After the investigation by TSMC’s Sexual Harassment Investigation Committee, four employees involved in confirmed cases of sexual harassment received severe discipline from the Company.

text.value: Net debt
Net debt is a measure that provides valuable additional information on the summary presentation of the Group’s net financial liabilities and is a measure in common use elsewhere.

Prior to this quarter, all financial asset derivatives were current financial assets and so reduced net debt. Following a recent review we now also have financial asset derivatives that are non-current in nature. As all of these derivatives relate to financial liabilities, we continue to exclude them for the purposes of our net debt calculation and have expanded our definition to reflect this.

Net debt is now defined as the excess of total financial liabilities, excluding trade payables and other current liabilities, over cash, cash equivalents and other current financial assets, excluding trade and other current receivables, and non-current financial asset derivatives that relate to financial liabilities.

| **Net debt** (as defined) | **(22,634)** |

**Definition of Net Debt**  
Net debt is calculated as the excess of **total financial liabilities** (excluding trade payables and other current liabilities) over **cash, cash equivalents and other current financial assets** (excluding trade and other current receivables), **minus non‑current financial‑asset derivatives that relate to financial liabilities**. This measure aligns with common practice and provides a clear view of the Group’s net financial obligations.

**Impact of IFRS 16 Restatement**  
The restated figures show a modest reduction in total financial liabilities (from £28,257 m to £26,738 m) and a corresponding decrease in net debt (from £23,051 m to £22,634 m). The change stems from the re‑classification of lease liabilities under IFRS 16, as detailed in the accompanying notes.

**Conclusion**  
Both the current and restated presentations indicate that the Group’s net debt remains substantial, exceeding £22 bn after accounting for cash, cash equivalents, and other current assets, while excluding non‑current derivatives that offset financial liabilities. The restatement provides a slightly more favourable net‑debt position due to the IFRS 16 adjustments.

text.value: This section provides a summary of the capital management activity of the Group during the period, including the Group’s borrowings. The Group manages its liquidity requirements with a range of short-term money market loans, bank loans, and flexible debt instruments with varying maturities.
The Group manages its capital structure with the objective of enhancing long-term shareholder value through funding its business at an optimised weighted average cost of capital.

The Group returns capital to shareholders when consistent with its long-term capital structure objectives and where it will enhance shareholder value. In May 2019, the Group returned $1.7 billion of capital to shareholders through an off-market share buy-back. This resulted in the purchase of 58.7 million shares which were subsequently cancelled. The share buy-back complements dividends of $1.4 billion paid to shareholders this reporting period through the 2018 final and special dividends, and the 2019 interim dividend, with a total of $3.1 billion returned to shareholders, excluding franking credits.

The Group remains committed to solid investment grade credit ratings and a number of actions can be undertaken to support the credit profile including the sale of non-core assets, further working capital initiatives, and adjusting growth capital expenditure and the property leasing profile. The Group’s credit ratings (1) are BBB (stable outlook) according to S&P and Baa2 (stable outlook) according to Moody’s.

In March 2019, the $500 million domestic Medium Term Notes matured. It was refinanced in April 2019 with $400 million of Medium Term Notes issued to meet the Group’s new Green Bond Framework (Green Bonds). The Green Bonds have been issued for a five-year tenor, maturing in April 2024.
In November 2019, $320 million of undrawn syndicated bank loan facilities are due to mature. The Group intends to refinance this facility at maturity.

(1) These credit ratings have been issued by a credit rating agency which holds an Australian Financial Services Licence with an authorisation to issue credit ratings to wholesale clients only and are for the benefit of the Group’s debt providers.

**Borrowing Position at Year‑End 2019**

- **Current (short‑term) borrowings:** $604 million, comprising:  
  - Short‑term money‑market loans: $16 million (up $2 million).  
  - Bank loans: $540 million (up $36 million).  
  - Securities: $1.668 billion (up $110 million).  
- **Non‑current borrowings:** $2.199 billion, consisting of:  
  - Unamortised borrowing costs: $(9) million (increase of $5 million).  
  - Finance leases: $0 million (new $6 million lease liability).  

**Net Movements During 2019**  
- Total borrowings rose by **$164 million**.  
- The increase was driven primarily by higher bank loan facilities and additional securities issued, partially offset by a modest rise in unamortised borrowing costs and new finance leases.

**Capital Management Context**  
- The Group sustains liquidity through a diversified mix of short‑term money‑market loans, bank loans, and flexible debt instruments of varying maturities.  
- Its capital‑structure strategy aims to enhance long‑term shareholder value by funding operations at an optimised weighted‑average cost of capital.  
- In 2019, the Group returned **$3.1 billion** to shareholders (including a $1.7 billion off‑market share buy‑back and $1.4 billion in dividends).  
- Credit ratings remain investment‑grade: BBB (S&P) and Baa2 (Moody’s), both with stable outlooks.  
- Key refinancing actions: the $500 million domestic Medium‑Term Notes that matured in March 2019 were replaced in April 2019 with $400 million of five‑year Green Bonds (maturing April 2024). A $320 million undrawn syndicated bank loan facility is due to mature in November 2019, with plans to refinance at that time.  

**Outlook**  
The modest increase in total borrowings reflects the Group’s ongoing commitment to maintain a strong credit profile while supporting its growth and sustainability initiatives. Continued focus on refinancing, asset optimisation, and disciplined capital returns underpins the Group’s strategy to deliver long‑term value to shareholders.

header: Net operating loss and credit carry-forwards

text.value: The types of temporary differences that give rise to significant portions of the Company’s deferred tax assets and liabilities are as follows (in thousands):

On December 22, 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (the “Act”) was signed into law making significant changes to the Internal Revenue Code. Changes include, but are not limited to, a corporate tax rate decrease from 35% to 21% effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, the transition of U.S. international taxation from a worldwide tax system to a territorial system, and a one-time transition tax on the mandatory deemed repatriation of cumulative foreign earnings as of December 31, 2017.

In connection with the acquisition of Connect First on January 14, 2019, a net deferred tax liability of $3.2 million was established, the most significant component of which is related to the book/tax basis differences associated with the acquired technology and customer relationships. The net deferred tax liability from this acquisition created an additional source of income to realize deferred tax assets. As the Company continues to maintain a full valuation allowance against its deferred tax assets, this additional source of income resulted in the release of the Company’s previously recorded valuation allowance against deferred assets. Consistent with the applicable guidance the release of the valuation allowance of $3.2 million caused by the acquisition was recorded in the consolidated financial statements outside of acquisition accounting as a tax benefit to the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

As of December 31, 2019, the Company has federal net operating loss carryforwards of approximately $782.7 million, of which approximately $272.9 million expire between 2023 and 2037 and the remainder do not expire. As of December 31, 2019, the Company had state net operating loss carryforwards of approximately $675.6 million which will begin to expire in 2021. The Company also has research credit carryforwards for federal and California tax purposes of approximately $20.2 million and $15.7 million, respectively, available to reduce future income subject to income taxes. The federal research credit carryforwards will begin to expire in 2028 and the California research credits carry forward indefinitely

The Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, imposes restrictions on the utilization of net operating losses in the event of an “ownership change” of a corporation. Accordingly, a company’s ability to use net operating losses may be limited as prescribed under Internal Revenue Code Section 382 (“IRC Section 382”). Events which may cause limitations in the amount of the net operating losses that the Company may use in any one year include, but are not limited to, a cumulative ownership change of more than 50% over a three-year period. Utilization of the federal and state net operating losses may be subject to substantial annual limitation due to the ownership change limitations provided by the IRC Section 382 and similar state provisions

The Company’s management believes that, based on a number of factors, it is more likely than not, that all or some portion of the deferred tax assets will not be realized; and accordingly, for the year ended December 31, 2019, the Company has provided a valuation allowance against the Company’s U.S. net deferred tax assets. The net change in the valuation allowance for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018 was an increase of $86.0 million, $18.2 million, respectively

synth_text.title: Deferred Tax Asset and Liability Summary – 2018 vs 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Company’s deferred tax position changed noticeably between 2018 and 2019.  Gross deferred tax assets grew from **$137.0 million** to **$234.1 million**, driven primarily by larger net operating loss (NOL) and credit carry‑forwards.  After applying a valuation allowance, net deferred tax assets decreased from **$42.9 million** to **$54.0 million**, leaving a modest net deferred tax liability of **$1.9 million** at year‑end 2019.

**Key Components – 2019 vs. 2018**

| Component | 2019 (in $ thousands) | 2018 (in $ thousands) |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------------|
| Net operating loss & credit carry‑forwards | 196,930 | 109,812 |
| Research & development credits | 24,452 | 16,380 |
| Sales tax liability | 157 | 258 |
| Share‑based compensation | 5,937 | 5,435 |
| Accrued liabilities | 6,612 | 5,135 |
| **Gross deferred tax assets** | **234,088** | **137,020** |
| Valuation allowance | (180,090) | (94,118) |
| **Total net deferred tax assets** | **53,998** | **42,902** |
| Convertible debt discount (liability) | (16,701) | (21,035) |
| Deferred sales commissions (liability) | (28,601) | (18,253) |
| Acquired intangibles (liability) | (3,857) | (2,670) |
| Property & equipment (liability) | (6,731) | (3,573) |
| **Net deferred tax (liabilities) assets** | **$(1,892)** | **$(2,629)** |

**Contextual Factors Influencing the Numbers**

1. **Tax Reform Impact** – The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reduced the corporate tax rate to 21 % and shifted U.S. international taxation to a territorial system, affecting the valuation of deferred tax items.

2. **Connect First Acquisition** – The January 14 2019 acquisition generated a **$3.2 million** net deferred tax liability tied to the acquired technology and customer relationships.  This liability created an additional source of future taxable income, prompting a **$3.2 million** release of the valuation allowance outside of acquisition accounting.

3. **NOL and Credit Carry‑forwards** – As of 12/31/2019, the Company held federal NOL carryforwards of roughly **$782.7 million** (with $272.9 million expiring 2023‑2037) and state NOLs of **$675.6 million** (beginning to expire in 2021).  Federal and California research credits total about **$20.2 million** and **$15.7 million**, respectively.

4. **Section 382 Limitations** – Ownership changes could restrict the annual utilization of these NOLs, potentially limiting the realizable benefit of the deferred tax assets.

5. **Valuation Allowance** – Management concluded that it is more likely than not that a portion of the deferred tax assets will not be realized.  Consequently, the valuation allowance increased by **$86 million** in 2019 (and $18.2 million in 2018), reflecting heightened uncertainty around the future use of NOLs and credits.

**Conclusion**  
While gross deferred tax assets rose sharply in 2019, the accompanying increase in the valuation allowance and the modest net liability indicate that much of the potential tax benefit remains uncertain.  The acquisition of Connect First, recent tax law changes, and ownership‑change limitations under IRC Section 382 are key drivers of the current deferred tax landscape.

synth_text.text:

- **Opening balance (January 1):** (54) million – the allowance carried forward from the prior year.

- **Additions:** (84) million – new provisions recorded to cover anticipated credit losses on trade receivables.  
- **Usage (write‑offs):** 91 million – amounts written off against the allowance during the year as receivables were deemed uncollectible.  
- **Closing balance (December 31):** (51) million – the remaining allowance at year‑end.

These figures illustrate the company’s active management of credit risk. The allowance serves as a buffer against potential defaults by counterparties to trade receivables and derivative instruments. The firm’s large and diversified customer base, together with its practice of dealing primarily with investment‑grade institutions, helps to minimize concentration risk. Credit risk is continuously monitored, and the allowance is adjusted accordingly to reflect the latest expectations of credit losses, especially in light of the IFRS 9 adoption.

Overall, the net change resulted in a modest reduction of the allowance from (54) million to (51) million, driven primarily by higher usage (write‑offs) that offset the new additions and the IFRS 9 adjustment.

synth_text.text:
Autodesk’s Employee Qualified Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP), approved by shareholders in 1998, allows eligible employees to purchase Autodesk common stock using up to 15 % of their compensation. Purchases are made at a 15 % discount, i.e., 85 % of the lower of the stock’s closing price on the offering date or the exercise date, and are organized into four six‑month exercise periods within a 24‑month offering cycle. Shares are issued on the first trading day after March 31 and September 30 of each fiscal year, and the plan has no expiration date. As of January 31 2019, Autodesk had 8.1 million shares reserved for future ESPP issuances.

synth_text.title: Warrant Outstanding Summary (2017‑2019) and Related Issuances
synth_text.text:
**Overview of Outstanding Warrants**

- **Shares issuable:** The company consistently had **3,826,658 shares** issuable under warrants at the end of each fiscal year—December 31, 2017; December 31, 2018; and December 31, 2019.  
- **Weighted‑average exercise price:** The exercise price remained steady at **$1.05 per share** throughout the same period.  

**Key Issuance Events**

- At the time of the merger and a private offering, holders of prior Protagenic warrants received new warrants to purchase **3,403,367 shares** of Series B Preferred Stock at an average price of **$1.05** per share.  
- Debt holders (with $665,000 of debt and $35,000 of accrued interest) exchanged their obligations for five‑year warrants covering **295,945 shares** at **$1.25** per share.  
- Placement‑agent warrants for **127,346 shares** at **$1.25** per share were also issued in connection with the private offering.  

All of these warrants—totaling **423,291 shares** of Series B Preferred Stock—were recorded as derivative liabilities and automatically converted into warrants to purchase common stock when the company’s reverse stock split became effective in July 2016 (see Note 5).

**Intrinsic Value Changes**

- **2018:** With the same 3,826,658 shares outstanding at a $1.05 exercise price, the intrinsic value of the warrants was **$3,633,335**.  
- **2019:** The intrinsic value declined to **$1,375,990**, despite the unchanged share count and exercise price, indicating a reduction in the underlying market price of the underlying stock.

**Conclusion**

From 2017 through 2019, the company’s warrant portfolio remained quantitatively stable—both in terms of the number of shares and the exercise price—while the intrinsic value fluctuated, reflecting market conditions. The warrants originated from a combination of prior warrant conversions, debt‑for‑warrant exchanges, and placement‑agent issuances, all of which were ultimately converted to common‑stock warrants following the 2016 reverse split.

synth_text.title: Trend in Outstanding Warrant Liabilities and Intrinsic Value (2017‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The company’s warrant‑related obligations have shown a consistent downward trend over the three‑year period. Outstanding warrant liabilities declined from **$4.69 million** at December 31, 2017, to **$3.69 million** at December 31, 2018, and further to **$2.69 million** at December 31, 2019. No additional warrants were granted during this time, as indicated by the empty “Granted” column.

Despite the reduction in liability, the total number of shares issuable under outstanding warrants remained constant at **3,826,658 shares**, each with a weighted‑average exercise price of **$1.05** per share. This pool of warrants originated from several issuances in 2016, including:

* 3,403,367 shares of Series B Preferred Stock warrants issued to prior Protagenic warrant holders (average exercise price ≈ $1.05).
* Warrants issued to a debt holder in exchange for $665,000 of debt and $35,000 of accrued interest (295,945 shares at $1.25 per share).
* Placement Agent warrants for 127,346 shares at $1.25 per share.

All of these were recorded as derivative liabilities and automatically converted to common‑stock warrants after the July 2016 reverse stock split.

The intrinsic value of the warrant pool mirrored the liability decline, falling from **$3,633,335** at the end of 2018 to **$1,375,990** at the end of 2019. This reduction reflects both the decreasing fair‑value measurement of the warrants and the company’s ongoing effort to manage its derivative obligations.

In summary, while the quantity of warrant‑eligible shares stayed steady, the company successfully reduced the associated financial liability and intrinsic value over the 2017‑2019 period.

synth_text.text:
The Company’s auditor and its associated firms received the fees shown below for the financial years 2019 and 2018 (figures in £ 000):

- **Audit of the Group’s annual financial statements**: £559 k in 2019, down from £382 k in 2018.  
- **Audit of subsidiaries**: £533 k in 2019, up from £441 k in 2018.  
- **Total audit fees (annual statements + subsidiaries)**: £1,092 k in 2019, compared with £823 k in 2018.

- **Other non‑audit assurance services**: £534 k in 2019, a notable increase from £230 k in 2018.  
- **Total fees paid to the auditor and its associates**: £1,690 k in 2019, up from £1,104 k in 2018.

In both years, the audit firm (Deloitte in 2019, PwC in 2018) was selected because the work demanded detailed knowledge of the Group; engaging a different firm would have required substantial additional time to acquire that familiarity, making the chosen arrangement more efficient in terms of cost and speed.

The Audit Committee evaluated the independence of the auditors in performing these non‑audit services and concluded that independence was not compromised in either year.

Joint‑venture entities contributed additional audit‑related fees of £156 k (Group’s share) in 2019 and £121 k in 2018, all of which were for audit and audit‑related services.

Overall, the data show a modest increase in total audit‑related remuneration from 2018 to 2019, driven by higher subsidiary audit fees and a significant expansion of non‑audit assurance work linked to the contemplated equity raise.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table below summarizes GreenSky’s loan receivables held for sale (net at the lower of cost or fair value) for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019. The figures are presented in thousands of U.S. dollars.

| Year | Beginning Balance | Additions | Proceeds from Sales & Borrower Payments* | Loss on Sale | Increase in Valuation Allowance | Transfers** | Write‑offs & Other*** | Ending Balance |
|------|-------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------|--------------|----------------------------------|--------------|-----------------------|----------------|
| 2019 | $2,876 | $157,928 | $(104,858) | — | $(1,289) | $251 | $(2,982) | $51,926 |

\** **Transfers** represent loan receivables temporarily held while eligibility of non‑originating bank partners is confirmed; once approved, the loans are transferred to the partner at cost plus accrued interest. The amount also covers loans placed on non‑accrual status pending consumer inquiry resolution.

- **Ending Balance Growth:** Despite the sharp drop in the opening balance, the ending balance grew to $51.9 million in 2019, reflecting the net effect of additions, transfers, and write‑offs after accounting for sales proceeds.  

Overall, the data illustrate GreenSky’s active management of its loan‑receivable‑for‑sale portfolio, with significant sales activity offsetting new loan originations and resulting in a modestly larger net balance by the end of 2019.

The following details our other consolidated results for the years ended December 31, 2018 and 2017:

Interest income: Interest income increased by $4.2 million to $10.1 million for the year ended December 31, 2018, compared to $5.9 million for the same period in 2017 due to returns on our fixed deposits that had been made in 2018, and income derived from the lending capital of our lessor VIEs, that we are required to consolidate under U.S. GAAP.

This was partially offset by a decrease of:
• $5.9 million in interest expense relating to the Hilli disposal; and
• $5.0 million higher capitalized interest on borrowing costs in relation to our investment in Golar Power.

(Losses)/gains on derivative instruments: Losses on derivative instruments increased by $51.2 million to a loss of $30.5 million for the year ended December 31, 2018 compared to a gain of $20.7 million for the same period in 2017. The movement was primarily due to:

Net unrealized and realized gains on interest rate swap agreements: As of December 31, 2018, we have an interest rate swap portfolio with a notional amount of $950 million, none of which are designated as hedges for accounting purposes. Net unrealized gains on the interest rate swaps decreased to a gain of $0.6 million for the year ended December 31, 2018 compared to a gain of $6.6 million for the same period in 2017, due to an improvement in the long-term swap rates, offset by the decreased notional value of the swap portfolio over the period. Realized gains on our interest rate swaps increased to a gain of $8.1 million for the year ended December 31, 2018, compared to a loss of $3.8 million for the same period in 2017. The increase was primarily due to higher LIBOR rates for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Unrealized (losses) gains on Total Return Swap (or equity swap): In December 2014, we established a three month facility for a Stock Indexed Total Return Swap Programme or Equity Swap Line with DNB Bank ASA in connection with a share buyback scheme. The facility has been extended to June 2019. The equity swap derivatives mark-to-market adjustment resulted in a net loss of $30.7 million recognized in the year ended December 31, 2018 compared to a gain of $16.6 million for the same period in 2017. The loss in 2018 is due to the fall in our share price during 2018.

Unrealized mark-to-market losses on Earn-Out Units: This relates to the mark-to-market movement on the Earn-Out Units issuable in connection with the IDR reset transaction in October 2016, which we recognize as a derivative asset in our consolidated financial statements. The decrease in Golar Partners' quarterly distribution to $0.4042 per common unit on October 24, 2018 resulted in the contingent Earn-Out Units arising out of the IDR reset transaction in October 2016 not crystallizing and, accordingly, we recognized a mark-to-market loss of $7.4 million for the year ended December 31, 2018, effectively reducing the derivative asset to $nil at December 31, 2018, compared to a gain of $0.4 million for the same period in 2017.

Net income attributable to non-controlling interests: The net income attributable to non-controlling interests comprises of (i) $19.7 million and $1.5 million in relation to the non-controlling shareholders who hold interests in Hilli LLC and Hilli Corp (prior to the incorporation of Hilli LLC) for the year ended December 31, 2018 and 2017, respectively, and (ii) $43.5 million and $32.9 million in relation to the equity interests in our lessor VIEs for the year ended December 31, 2018 and 2017, respectively.
