**Drivers of the Movements**

*Interest Income* – Rose by $4.2 million to $10.1 million, primarily from higher returns on fixed‑deposit investments made in 2018 and income generated by the lending capital of consolidated lessor VIEs, as required under U.S. GAAP.

*Interest Expense* – Increased by $42.6 million to $101.9 million, driven by:
- $22.7 million higher expense on loan facilities of VIEs (notably the Hilli post‑delivery sale‑and‑lease‑back arrangement);
- $21.7 million lower capitalized interest on the Hilli FLNG conversion;
- $7.0 million more amortization of deferred financing costs for the Hilli facility;
- $1.4 million additional expense from the $402.5 million convertible bond issued in February 2017.  
These increases were partially offset by a $5.9 million reduction related to the Hilli disposal and a $5.0 million rise in capitalized interest on the Golar Power investment.

*Derivative Instruments* – The net loss on derivatives swung from a $20.7 million gain in 2017 to a $30.5 million loss in 2018 (a $51.2 million adverse change). The loss stemmed from:
- A decline in unrealized gains on interest‑rate swaps (from $6.6 million to $0.6 million) due to improved long‑term swap rates and a smaller notional amount;
- Realized gains on those swaps turned positive ($8.1 million) because of higher LIBOR rates;
- A $30.7 million loss on the equity‑swap line with DNB Bank, reflecting the fall in Golar’s share price;
- A $7.4 million mark‑to‑market loss on Earn‑Out Units linked to the IDR reset transaction, as the underlying distribution fell.

*Other Financial Items, Net* – Although the absolute amount is modest (‑$1.4 million), the percentage change is large (+2,046 %) due to the reversal of a prior year’s balance.

*Income Taxes* – Decreased by $238 thousand, reflecting a 16 % reduction in the effective tax rate.

*Non‑Controlling Interests* – Net income attributable to non‑controlling interests improved by $28.8 million (84 % increase) to a loss of $28.8 million. The improvement is attributable to:
- Higher shares of profit from Hilli LLC and Hilli Corp ($19.7 million in 2018 vs. $1.5 million in 2017);
- Increased earnings from equity interests in the lessor VIEs ($43.5 million in 2018 vs. $32.9 million in 2017).

**Conclusion**  
The 2018 non‑operating results were shaped by higher financing costs and a pronounced deterioration in derivative performance, offset partially by stronger interest income and a notable rise in earnings attributable to non‑controlling shareholders. These dynamics underscore the sensitivity of Golar’s non‑operating line items to changes in LIBOR rates, VIE financing structures, and market movements affecting derivative positions.

synth_text.title: Summary of Other Non‑Operating Results – 2018 vs. 2017
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The consolidated non‑operating results for the years ended December 31, 2018 and 2017 show notable shifts across interest income, interest expense, derivative instrument performance, and the share of earnings attributable to non‑controlling interests.

**Interest Income**  
Interest income rose sharply to **$10.1 million** in 2018 from **$5.9 million** in 2017, an increase of **$4.2 million**. The growth stemmed from higher returns on fixed‑deposit investments made in 2018 and income generated from the lending capital of the company’s lessor variable‑interest entities (VIEs), which are required to be consolidated under U.S. GAAP.

**Interest Expense**  
Interest expense also increased substantially, reaching **$101.9 million** in 2018 versus **$59.3 million** in 2017 (a rise of **$42.6 million**). The primary contributors were:
- A **$22.7 million** rise linked to loan facilities of consolidated lessor VIEs, especially the Hilli post‑delivery sale‑and‑leaseback arrangement initiated in June 2018.  
- A **$21.7 million** reduction in capitalized interest related to the Hilli FLNG conversion before vessel acceptance.  
- A **$7.0 million** increase in amortization of deferred financing costs for the Hilli facility.  
- A **$1.4 million** increase from the $402.5 million convertible bond issued in February 2017, which incurred a full year of interest in 2018.  

These increases were partially offset by a **$5.9 million** decrease in interest expense from the Hilli disposal and a **$5.0 million** higher capitalized interest on borrowing costs for the Golar Power investment.

**Derivative Instruments**  
The net result from derivative instruments swung from a **$20.7 million gain** in 2017 to a **$30.5 million loss** in 2018, a negative swing of **$51.2 million**. The loss was driven by:
- **Interest‑rate swaps:** Unrealized gains fell to **$0.6 million** (down from $6.6 million) due to improved long‑term swap rates and a reduced notional amount, while realized gains turned positive at **$8.1 million** (versus a $3.8 million loss) because of higher LIBOR rates.  
- **Equity swap (Total Return Swap) with DNB Bank:** The mark‑to‑market adjustment recorded a **$30.7 million loss** in 2018, reversing the **$16.6 million gain** of 2017, reflecting the decline in the company’s share price.  
- **Earn‑Out Units:** A **$7.4 million loss** was recognized as the contingent Earn‑Out Units tied to the 2016 IDR reset transaction failed to crystallize, reducing the derivative asset to zero at year‑end.

**Other Non‑Operating Items**  
- “Total other non‑operating expense” was negligible in 2018 (recorded as “—”) compared with a modest **$81 thousand** expense in 2017.  
- “Other financial items, net” showed a small loss of **$1.5 million** in 2018 versus a **$69 thousand** loss in 2017.  
- Income taxes related to these items were **$1.3 million** (2018) and **$1.5 million** (2017), both recorded as expenses.

**Net Income Attributable to Non‑Controlling Interests**  
The share of net income attributable to non‑controlling interests declined from a **$34.4 million loss** in 2017 to a **$63.2 million loss** in 2018. The loss comprises:
- **$19.7 million** (2018) and **$1.5 million** (2017) linked to non‑controlling shareholders of Hilli LLC and Hilli Corp.  
- **$43.5 million** (2018) and **$32.9 million** (2017) arising from equity interests in the company’s lessor VIEs.

**Conclusion**  
Overall, 2018 saw higher interest income but a much larger increase in interest expense, leading to a net deterioration in non‑operating results. Derivative activity shifted from a modest gain to a significant loss, primarily due to adverse movements in interest‑rate swaps, equity swaps, and Earn‑Out Unit valuations. These factors, together with larger losses attributable to non‑controlling interests, contributed to the weaker non‑operating performance relative to 2017.

text.value: 11. Share-Based Compensation

As of March 31, 2019, the Company has four share-based compensation plans and an employee share purchase plan. Prior to the Company’s initial public offering (IPO) in November 2015, the Company granted share-based awards under three share option plans, which were the Mimecast Limited 2007 Key Employee Share Option Plan (the 2007 Plan), the Mimecast Limited 2010 EMI Share Option Scheme (the 2010 Plan), and the Mimecast Limited Approved Share Option Plan (the Approved Plan) (the 2007 Plan, the 2010 Plan and the Approved Plan, collectively, the Historical Plans).

Upon the closing of the IPO, the Mimecast Limited 2015 Share Option and Incentive Plan (the 2015 Plan) and the 2015 Employee Share Purchase Plan (the ESPP) became effective. Subsequent to the IPO, grants of share-based awards have been made under the 2015 Plan and no further grants under the Historical Plans are permitted.

The 2015 Plan allows the compensation committee to make equity-based incentive awards to our officers, employees, non-employee directors and consultants. Initially a total of 5.5 million ordinary shares were reserved for the issuance of awards under the 2015 Plan. This number is subject to adjustment in the event of a share split, share dividend or other change in our capitalization.

The 2015 Plan provides that the number of shares reserved and available for issuance under the plan will automatically increase each January 1st by 5% of the outstanding number of ordinary shares on the immediately preceding December 31 or such lesser number of shares as determined by the board of directors.

Under the 2015 Plan, the share option price may not be less than the fair market value of the ordinary shares on the date of grant and the term of each share option may not exceed 10 years from the date of grant. Share options typically vest over 4 years, but vesting provisions can vary based on the discretion of the board of directors.

The Company settles share option exercises under the 2015 Plan through newly issued shares. The Company’s ordinary shares underlying any awards that are forfeited, canceled, withheld upon exercise of an option, or settlement of an award to cover the exercise price or tax withholding, or otherwise terminated other than by exercise will be added back to the shares available for issuance under the 2015 Plan.

Initially, a total of 1.1 million shares of the Company's ordinary shares were reserved for future issuance under the ESPP. This number is subject to change in the event of a share split, share dividend or other change in capitalization. The ESPP may be terminated or amended by the board of directors at any time.

The ESPP permits eligible employees to purchase shares by authorizing payroll deductions from 1% to 10% of his or her eligible compensation during an offering period, a duration of six months. Unless an employee has previously withdrawn from the offering, his or her accumulated payroll deductions will be used to purchase shares on the last day of the offering period at a price equal to 85% of the fair market value of the shares on the first business day or last business day of the offering period, whichever is lower.

synth_text.title: Operating and Share‑Based Compensation Expense Growth, 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s expense profile expanded considerably between the fiscal years ended March 31, 2018 and March 31, 2019.  

- **Cost of revenue** rose from **$1.053 million** to **$1.684 million**.  
- **Research and development** more than doubled, increasing from **$2.555 million** to **$6.199 million**.  
- **Sales and marketing** climbed from **$4.477 million** to **$7.856 million**.  
- **General and administrative** expenses surged from **$3.649 million** to **$10.215 million**.  

The most pronounced change was in **share‑based compensation expense**, which jumped from **$11.734 million** in 2018 to **$25.954 million** in 2019. This increase aligns with the company’s post‑IPO equity compensation structure. After the November 2015 IPO, the historical share‑option plans were replaced by the **2015 Share Option and Incentive Plan** and the **2015 Employee Share Purchase Plan (ESPP)**. The 2015 Plan reserves an initial 5.5 million ordinary shares (adjusted annually by 5 % of outstanding shares) for awards to officers, employees, directors and consultants, while the ESPP allows eligible employees to purchase shares at a 15 % discount through payroll deductions.

Share‑based compensation recognized in the consolidated statements of operations reflects awards under these two plans, as well as any modifications approved by the board. Modification expenses—additional compensation recognized when vesting schedules or exercise restrictions were altered—totaled **$3.2 million** in 2019, compared with **$0.5 million** in 2018, further contributing to the rise in total share‑based expense.

Overall, the data indicate that the company’s operating costs grew across all functional areas, while the expansion of its post‑IPO equity compensation programs and related modification activity drove a more than two‑fold increase in share‑based compensation expense between 2018 and 2019.

synth_text.title: 2017 Operating Expenses and Share‑Based Compensation Overview for Mimecast
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2017 Mimecast reported the following operating expense figures (in millions of US dollars):

Together, these categories contributed to the company’s overall cost structure for the year.  

A notable line item in the 2017 consolidated statements of operations is **total share‑based compensation expense**, which amounted to **$10.294 million**. This expense reflects the cost of equity awards granted under Mimecast’s share‑based compensation framework, which, as of March 31 2019, consists of:

1. **The 2015 Share Option and Incentive Plan** – the primary plan used for granting equity awards to officers, employees, directors, and consultants after the company’s IPO in November 2015. The plan initially reserved 5.5 million ordinary shares, with an automatic annual increase of 5 % of outstanding shares.  
2. **The 2015 Employee Share Purchase Plan (ESPP)** – allowing eligible employees to buy shares through payroll deductions at a discount of up to 15 % of the fair market value. The ESPP initially reserved 1.1 million shares.  

The 2017 share‑based compensation expense also includes a **modification expense of $3.0 million**, arising from board‑approved changes to employee option agreements (e.g., accelerated vesting or removal of exercise restrictions).  

Thus, the $10.294 million reported for share‑based compensation in 2017 captures the combined cost of equity awards issued under the 2015 Plan and ESPP, as well as the expense related to plan modifications. This figure is a significant component of Mimecast’s overall expense profile for the year.  

Overall, Mimecast’s 2017 financials show a balanced cost structure across product delivery, innovation, market expansion, and administrative functions, with share‑based compensation representing a strategic tool for attracting and retaining talent through equity incentives.

synth_text.text:

- **Net Revenues:** Remained essentially flat, with $333.3 million in Q3 (ended September 30) and $331.0 million in Q4 (ended December 31).  
- **Operating Income:** Improved from $23.5 million in Q3 to $26.7 million in Q4, indicating better cost control or higher margin contributions.  

**Bottom‑Line Performance**  
- **Net Income:** Shifted from a small profit of $0.3 million in Q3 to a loss of $5.99 million in Q4, resulting in basic and diluted earnings of $‑0.08 per share for the quarter.  

**Key One‑Time Items Influencing Q4**  
1. **Pension Settlement Charge:** A non‑cash charge of $6.7 million was recorded after transferring pension obligations to an annuity provider.  
2. **Severance Costs:** Integration of FairPoint and ongoing cost‑saving measures led to $8.7 million in severance expenses.  
3. **Debt Extinguishment Gains:** The company recognized gains from repurchasing senior notes—$0.3 million (Q2), $1.1 million (Q3), and $3.1 million (Q4). The Q4 gain partially offset the large pension and severance outlays.  

**Takeaway**  
While revenue and operating performance remained stable and even improved in Q4, the quarter’s net loss was driven primarily by significant one‑time pension and severance expenses, with modest debt‑extinguishment gains providing limited relief. These items are expected to be non‑recurring, suggesting that underlying operating trends remain positive.

synth_text.title: 2019 First‑Half Quarterly Financial Summary and Notable Year‑End Adjustments
synth_text.text:
**Quarterly Performance (First Half of 2019)**  
- **Q1 (ended March 31, 2019)**: Net revenues were $338.6 million, generating operating income of $16.7 million. The company recorded a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $7.3 million, or a basic and diluted loss of $0.11 per share.  
- **Q2 (ended June 30, 2019)**: Net revenues slipped slightly to $333.5 million, with operating income decreasing to $14.3 million. Net loss widened marginally to $7.4 million, translating to a loss of $0.10 per share.

These figures indicate modest revenue contraction and a reduction in operating profitability during the first half of the year, while the company continued to post a net loss on a per‑share basis.

**Key Year‑End Adjustments and One‑Time Items**  
- **Pension Settlement Charge**: In Q4 2019, the company transferred pension obligations for a select retiree group to an annuity provider, recognizing a non‑cash pension settlement charge of $6.7 million.  
- **Debt Extinguishment Gains**: Gains from the partial repurchase of senior notes were recorded as $0.3 million (Q2), $1.1 million (Q3), and $3.1 million (Q4).  
- **Severance Costs**: As part of the FairPoint integration and ongoing cost‑saving measures, severance expenses totaled $8.7 million in Q4 2019.

Together, these events provide context for the overall 2019 financial results, illustrating that while operating performance declined slightly in the first half, the company also incurred significant one‑time charges and realized modest gains from debt restructuring later in the year.

**Overall Outlook**  
The first‑half data reflect a challenging operating environment, with decreasing revenues and operating income and continued net losses. However, the later‑year adjustments—particularly the debt extinguishment gains—partially offset the impact of large non‑operating expenses such as pension settlement and severance costs. Stakeholders should monitor how integration initiatives and cost‑saving strategies influence profitability in the upcoming quarters.

synth_text.title: Cash Flow Summary and Strategic Allocation for the Years Ended December 31, 2019 and 2020
synth_text.text:
The cash‑flow statement for the two most recent fiscal years shows that the company generated robust operating cash of approximately **$3.75 billion** each year. This strong operating cash base was the primary source of liquidity used to fund the business’s core activities, including tower maintenance, communications‑site construction, and network installations.

**Investing activities** were a net cash outflow in both periods, amounting to **$3,987.5 million** in the first year and **$2,749.5 million** in the second year. **Financing activities** differed between the two years. The first year produced a **positive cash flow of $521.7 million**, driven by activities such as equity repurchases and REIT‑taxable‑income distributions required to maintain REIT status. In the second year, financing cash was **negative $607.7 million**, indicating net repayments of debt and other financing outflows.

Both years experienced modest **foreign‑currency exchange impacts**, reducing cash by **$13.7 million** and **$41.1 million**, respectively.

After accounting for operating, investing, financing, and FX effects, the company’s **net increase in cash and cash equivalents** was **$273.1 million** in the first year and **$350.0 million** in the second year. This increase, together with the company’s existing cash balances (including $1.3 billion held by foreign subsidiaries) and borrowing capacity, is expected to be sufficient to meet ongoing capital‑expenditure needs, debt service obligations, required REIT distributions, and upcoming acquisitions.

Overall, the cash‑flow profile demonstrates that operating cash generation comfortably funds the company’s growth initiatives, debt obligations, and distribution requirements while supporting its international expansion strategy through a mix of cash on hand, intercompany debt, and equity contributions.

**Amortization Policies**  
- **Patents**: amortized over 17 years (or 20 years for newly issued patents). Patents acquired from STI are amortized over their remaining useful lives of 1–11 years (as of 12/31/2019).  
- **Domain name**: amortized over 10 years.  
- **Other intangibles from GVR (client base, trademark, backlog, technology)**: amortized over 3–5 years.  

**Write‑offs and Impairments**  
During 2019 the company wrote off **$145,000** of patents that are no longer being pursued; in 2018 the write‑off amount was **$96,000**. These write‑offs are reflected in research and development expense. No other intangible assets were impaired in either year.

**Key Changes Year‑over‑Year**  
- Total intangible assets increased by **$297,000** (≈ 17 %) from 2018 to 2019, driven primarily by higher patent holdings.  
- Accumulated amortization rose by **$95,000**, reflecting ongoing amortization of the larger asset base.  
- Net intangible assets grew by **$202,000**, indicating a strengthening of the company’s intangible‑asset position despite higher amortization and patent write‑offs.  

**Conclusion**  
The company’s intangible‑asset portfolio expanded in 2019, with patents remaining the dominant component. Amortization practices are aligned with the estimated useful lives of each asset class, and the modest write‑offs of non‑viable patents have been absorbed without affecting the overall net intangible‑asset value. No additional impairments were recorded, underscoring the stability of the remaining intangible assets.

synth_text.text:
The cash‑flow statement for the two most recent fiscal years shows that the company generated strong operating cash inflows, while investing and financing activities resulted in outflows.

- **Operating activities** produced $357.3 million in 2018 and $339.1 million in 2019, reflecting the core cash‑generating capacity of the business.  
- **Investing activities** used $221.5 million in 2018 and $217.8 million in 2019, primarily for capital expenditures and other investments.  
- **Financing activities** required $141.9 million in 2018 and $118.5 million in 2019, mainly for debt repayments and other financing costs.  

The net effect was a **decrease of $6.1 million** in cash and cash equivalents in 2018, turning to a **modest increase of $2.8 million** in 2019.

Consistent with the company’s outlook, operating requirements have historically been funded by cash generated from operations and borrowings under existing credit facilities. Going forward, the firm expects to continue financing its operating needs primarily from operating cash flow and existing cash balances, supplementing with borrowings under its revolving credit facility or other external financing if necessary. A substantial portion of cash flow will be allocated to capital expenditures, scheduled long‑term debt payments, and investments in future business opportunities.

synth_text.text:

Going forward, the firm expects to continue financing its operating needs with cash generated from operations, existing cash balances, and, if required, additional borrowings or external financing. A sizable portion of future cash flow is anticipated to be allocated toward capital expenditures, scheduled long‑term debt repayments, and investments in new business opportunities.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table below summarizes the company’s principal operating expenses for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019 (figures in thousands of dollars). In addition, the accompanying notes describe the nature of the stock‑based compensation expense reported.

| Year | Software delivery, support & maintenance | Client services | **Total cost of revenue** | SG&A expenses | R&D expenses | **Total stock‑based compensation** |
|------|------------------------------------------|----------------|---------------------------|---------------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| 2019 | $2,075 | $4,067 | $6,142 | $27,348 | $9,200 | $42,690 |
| 2018 | $2,184 | $3,997 | $6,181 | $24,213 | $8,937 | $39,331 |

**Key observations**

* **Cost of revenue** remained essentially flat, decreasing marginally from $6.181 billion in 2018 to $6.142 billion in 2019. The slight decline was driven by a $109 million reduction in software delivery, support and maintenance, partially offset by a $70 million increase in client‑services revenue.
* **Selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses** rose sharply, from $24.213 billion in 2018 to $27.348 billion in 2019, reflecting higher personnel and overhead costs.
* **Research and development (R&D) expenses** increased modestly, from $8.937 billion to $9.200 billion, indicating continued investment in product innovation.
* **Stock‑based compensation expense** grew to $42.7 million in 2019 from $39.3 million in 2018, a rise of roughly 8 %.

**Stock‑based compensation details**

* The expense includes both the non‑cash charge for stock‑award grants and the cash cost of employee discounts under the employee stock purchase plan.
* For 2019, the estimated income‑tax benefit associated with this expense was approximately **$5.3 million**.
* No portion of the stock‑based compensation was capitalized in 2019, 2018, or 2017.
* The expense calculation incorporates an estimate for forfeitures at the time of grant; actual forfeitures may cause adjustments in future periods.
* As of December 31, 2019, **$62.4 million** of stock‑based compensation related to non‑vested awards and options remained unrecognized. This amount is expected to be recognized over a weighted‑average period of **2.3 years**.

**Conclusion**  
While the company’s cost of revenue stayed stable between 2018 and 2019, SG&A and R&D expenses increased, and stock‑based compensation rose modestly. The additional context clarifies that the reported stock‑based compensation reflects both cash and non‑cash components, provides a tax benefit, and includes a sizable unrecognized portion that will be expensed over the next few years.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview 2018‑2019 and Market Outlook for the UK & Ireland B2B Business
synth_text.text:
**Financial performance**  
For the year to 31 March 2019 the business reported adjusted revenue of **£6,292 million**, a **5 % decline** from £6,647 million in 2018. The drop reflects the continued erosion of traditional fixed‑voice revenue as customers shift to mobile and IP services. Adjusted operating costs fell **6 %** to £4,302 million, driven by labour‑cost efficiencies from the company’s cost‑transformation programmes. Consequently, adjusted EBITDA decreased **4 %** to £1,990 million and adjusted operating profit slipped to £1,356 million from £1,442 million a year earlier.  

Depreciation and amortisation remained broadly unchanged (£634 million in 2019 vs £635 million in 2018). Capital expenditure rose modestly **2 %** to £501 million, while normalised free cash flow fell **7 %** to £1,483 million, reflecting the lower EBITDA and the slight increase in capex.

**Market context**  
The UK and Ireland B2B market remains challenging. The primary headwind is the decline in traditional fixed‑line calls, a segment where the company historically held a strong market share. The IP‑voice market is highly fragmented, prompting a strategic focus on gaining share in this growing area.  

In the mobile arena, intense competition continues to pressure pricing, while broadband growth is modest. Nevertheless, demand for premium offerings—such as fibre and the 4G Assure service—remains robust. Emerging segments, including the Internet of Things, cloud services, SD‑WAN and security, are identified as longer‑term growth opportunities.  

Order intake also weakened: retail orders fell **15 %** to £2.9 billion, largely because a large Irish contract signed the previous year was not repeated, and wholesale orders dropped **22 %** to £1.0 billion after a strong 2017/18 period.  

Overall, the 2019 results illustrate the impact of a shifting communications landscape—declining legacy voice revenue offset partially by growth in IP, mobile and networking services—while cost‑efficiency measures have helped to moderate the effect on profitability. The company remains focused on expanding its share in high‑margin, high‑growth areas to drive future performance.

synth_text.title: Adjusted Financial Results and Market Outlook for the Year to 31 March
synth_text.text:
**Financial Highlights (Year to 31 March)**  
- Adjusted revenue stood at **£6,292 m**, down **£355 m (‑5 %)** year‑on‑year.  
- Adjusted operating costs fell **£268 m (‑6 %)**, reflecting labour‑cost efficiencies from ongoing transformation programmes.  
- Adjusted EBITDA decreased by **£87 m (‑4 %)**.  
- Adjusted operating profit slipped to **£1,356 m**, a decline of **£86 m (‑6 %)**.  
- Depreciation & amortisation was essentially unchanged.  
- Capital expenditure rose modestly by **£9 m (+2 %)**.  
- Normalised free cash flow fell **£104 m (‑7 %)**, driven by lower EBITDA and the slight increase in capex.

**Drivers of Revenue Decline**  
The primary headwind was the continued erosion of traditional fixed‑voice revenue, as calls per line shift to mobile and IP services. Sales of low‑margin equipment and legacy products such as private circuits also fell. These declines were partially offset by growth in IP, mobile, networking solutions and an encouraging rise in messaging volumes within the Ventures segment.

**Cost Management**  
Operating cost reductions were achieved mainly through labour‑cost efficiencies embedded in the company’s cost‑transformation initiatives, helping to mitigate the impact of the revenue drop.

**Market Context**  
- The UK and Ireland B2B market remains challenging, with a fragmented IP‑voice landscape and intense competition in mobile pricing.  
- Broadband growth is modest, but demand for premium offerings—fibre and 4G Assure—remains strong.  
- Emerging opportunities lie in the Internet of Things, cloud services, SD‑WAN and security, which are expected to drive longer‑term growth.

**Outlook**  
While short‑term revenue pressures persist due to the shift away from legacy fixed‑voice services, the company’s focus on expanding its share in the growing IP‑voice market and capitalising on premium broadband, mobile, and emerging digital services positions it to capture future growth opportunities.

text.value: 31. NET DEFERRED GAIN (Cont’d)

NetLink Trust (“NLT”) is a business trust established as part of the Info-communications Media Development Authority of Singapore’s effective open access requirements under Singapore’s Next Generation Nationwide Broadband Network.

In prior years, Singtel had sold certain infrastructure assets, namely ducts, manholes and exchange buildings (“Assets”) to NLT. At the consolidated level, the gain on disposal of Assets recognised by Singtel is deferred in the Group’s statement of financial position and amortised over the useful lives of the Assets. The unamortised deferred gain is released to the Group’s income statement when NLT is partially or fully sold, based on the proportionate equity interest disposed.

Singtel sold its 100% interest in NLT to NetLink NBN Trust (the “Trust”) in July 2017 for cash as well as a 24.8% interest in the Trust. Net deferred gains of S$1.10 billion were correspondingly released to the Group’s income statement in the previous financial year upon this sale. Following the divestment, Singtel ceased to own units in NLT but continues to have an interest of 24.8% in the Trust which owns all the units in NLT.

- The **current portion remains small** (around S$20 million), while the **non‑current portion dominates**, representing the majority of the gain that will be recognised in future periods.

**Contextual background**

Singtel originally sold the aforementioned assets to NLT, deferring the gain on disposal in its balance sheet and amortising it over the assets’ useful lives. In July 2017, Singtel sold its 100 % stake in NLT to NetLink NBN Trust, receiving cash and a 24.8 % interest in the new Trust. That transaction triggered the release of S$1.10 billion of net deferred gains to the income statement for the prior financial year. Post‑sale, Singtel no longer holds units in NLT but retains a 24.8 % interest in the Trust, which continues to own the assets. The figures above represent the remaining unamortised portion of that original gain.

**Conclusion**

The net deferred gain figures illustrate the lingering financial impact of Singtel’s historic asset sale to NetLink Trust. While the bulk of the gain has already been recognised following the 2017 divestment, a substantial unamortised balance remains, predominantly classified as non‑current and set to be amortised over the assets’ remaining life cycles.

text.value: Value-at-Risk (VaR)

We employ various tools to monitor our derivative risk, including value-at-risk ("VaR") models. We perform simulations using historical data to estimate potential losses in the fair value of current derivative positions. We use price and volatility information for the prior 90 days in the calculation of VaR that is used to monitor our daily risk. The purpose of this measurement 45 is to provide a single view of the potential risk of loss associated with derivative positions at a given point in time based on recent changes in market prices. Our model uses a 95% confidence level. Accordingly, in any given one-day time period, losses greater than the amounts included in the table below are expected to occur only 5% of the time. We include commodity swaps, futures, and options and foreign exchange forwards, swaps, and options in this calculation. text.value: Upon adoption, the Company recorded a cumulative effect adjustment of $139.4 million, net of tax adjustment of $21.0 million, which increased the June 25, 2018 opening retained earnings balance on the Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheet, primarily as a result of changes in the timing of recognition of system sales. Under ASC 606, the Company recognizes revenue from sales of systems when the Company determines that control has passed to the customer which is generally (1) for products that have been demonstrated to meet product specifications prior to shipment upon shipment or delivery; (2) for products that have not been demonstrated to meet product specifications prior to shipment, revenue is recognized upon completion of installation and receipt of customer acceptance; (3) for transactions where legal title does not pass upon shipment or delivery and the Company does not have a right to payment, revenue is recognized when legal title passes to the customer and the Company has a right to payment, which is generally at customer acceptance.
The impact of adoption of ASC 606 on the Company’s Consolidated Statement of Operations and Consolidated Balance Sheet was as follows:
Except as disclosed above, the adoption of ASC 606 did not have a significant impact on the Company’s Consolidated Statement of Operations for the year ended June 30, 2019.

In January 2016, the FASB released ASU 2016-01, “Financial Instruments – Overall – Recognition and Measurement of Financial Assets and Financial Liabilities.” The FASB issued a subsequent amendment to the initial guidance in February 2018 within ASU 2018-03. These amendments change the accounting for and financial statement presentation of equity investments, other than those accounted for under the equity method of accounting or those that result in consolidation of the investee. The amendments provide clarity on the measurement methodology to be used for the required disclosure of fair value of financial instruments measured at amortized cost on the balance sheet and clarifies that an entity should evaluate the need for a valuation allowance on deferred tax assets related to available-for-sale securities in combination with the entity’s other deferred tax assets, among other changes. The Company’s adoption of this standard in the first quarter of fiscal year 2019 did not have a material impact on its Consolidated Financial Statements.

In August 2016, the FASB released ASU 2016-15, “Statement of Cash Flows – Classification of Certain Cash Receipts and Cash Payments.” The amendment provides and clarifies guidance on the classification of certain cash receipts and cash payments in the statement of cash flows to eliminate diversity in practice. The Company adopted the standard update in the first quarter of fiscal year 2019, using a retrospective transition method. The Company’s adoption of this standard did not have a material impact on its Consolidated Financial Statements.

In October 2016, the FASB released ASU 2016-16, “Income Tax – Intra-Entity Transfers of Assets Other than Inventory.” This standard update improves the accounting for the income tax consequences of intra-entity transfers of assets other than inventory. The Company adopted this standard in the first quarter of fiscal year 2019 using a modified-retrospective approach through a cumulative-effect adjustment directly to retained earnings. The Company’s adoption of this standard resulted in a $0.4 million decrease to retained earnings and a corresponding $0.4 million offset to other assets on its Consolidated Financial Statements.

In November 2016, the FASB released ASU 2016-18, “Statement of Cash Flows – Restricted Cash.” This standard update requires that restricted cash and restricted cash equivalents be included in cash and cash equivalents when reconciling the beginning-of-period and end-of-period total amounts shown in the statement of cash flows. The Company adopted this standard in the first quarter of fiscal year 2019, using a retrospective transition method to each period presented. The adoption of this standard did not have a material impact on its Consolidated Financial Statements.

In February 2018, the FASB released ASU 2018-02, “Reclassification of Certain Tax Effects from Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income.” This standard update addresses a specific consequence of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (“U.S. Tax Reform”) and allows a reclassification from accumulated other comprehensive income to retained earnings for the stranded tax effects resulting from U.S. tax reform. Consequently, the update eliminates the stranded tax effects that were created as a result of the historical U.S. federal corporate income tax rate to the newly enacted U.S. federal corporate income tax rate. The Company adopted this standard in the first quarter of fiscal year 2019 using a modified-retrospective approach through a cumulative-effect adjustment directly to retained earnings. The adoption of this standard resulted in a $2.2 million increase to retained earnings, with a corresponding $2.2 million decrease to other comprehensive income.

In August 2018, the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) adopted amendments to eliminate, integrate, update or modify certain of its disclosure requirements. The amendments are part of the SEC’s efforts to improve disclosure effectiveness and were focused on eliminating disclosure requirements that have become redundant, duplicative, overlapping, outdated, or superseded. The Company adopted these amendments in the first quarter of fiscal Year 2019. The adoption of these amendments resulted in minor changes within its Consolidated Financial Statements.

synth_text.title: Revenue and Cost of Goods Sold Overview with ASC 606 Adoption Impact
synth_text.text:
The company reported revenue of **$9,653,559** and cost of goods sold (COGS) of **$5,295,100** for the period presented. For ease of presentation, the same figures are also shown “in thousands,” amounting to **$9,049,790** thousand in revenue and **$5,016,679** thousand in COGS.  

Following the adoption of ASC 606, revenue from system sales is now recognized when control passes to the customer—typically at shipment, upon customer acceptance after installation, or when legal title transfers. This change resulted in a cumulative‑effect adjustment of **$139.4 million** (net of tax **$21.0 million**) that increased opening retained earnings, primarily due to the altered timing of system‑sale revenue recognition.  

Despite this adjustment, the adoption of ASC 606 did **not** have a material impact on the Consolidated Statement of Operations for the year ended June 30, 2019. Other recent accounting updates (ASU 2016‑01, 2016‑15, 2016‑16, 2016‑18, 2018‑02) and SEC disclosure amendments were also adopted in fiscal 2019, each having little or no material effect on the company’s financial statements.  

Overall, the reported revenue and COGS reflect the company’s operational performance, while the ASC 606 transition primarily affected retained earnings rather than the current period’s profit‑or‑loss figures.

synth_text.title: Financial Snapshot After ASC 606 Adoption: Revenue, Cost of Goods Sold, and Gross Profit
synth_text.text:
The company reported total revenue of **$603,769** and cost of goods sold (COGS) of **$278,421**, resulting in a gross profit of **$325,348**. These figures are presented under the newly adopted ASC 606 revenue‑recognition framework, which requires the company to record revenue when control of a system passes to the customer—typically at shipment, upon customer acceptance, or when legal title transfers. 

The transition to ASC 606 generated a cumulative‑effect adjustment of $139.4 million (net of a $21.0 million tax effect) to opening retained earnings, primarily due to changes in the timing of system‑sale revenue recognition. Apart from this adjustment, the adoption did **not** have a material impact on the company’s consolidated statement of operations for the year ended June 30, 2019. 

Other recent accounting updates (including ASU 2016‑01, ASU 2016‑15, ASU 2016‑16, ASU 2016‑18, and ASU 2018‑02) were also adopted in the first quarter of fiscal year 2019, each resulting in either negligible changes or modest adjustments to retained earnings and other comprehensive income. Consequently, the reported revenue and COGS figures represent the company’s financial performance under the current accounting standards without significant distortion from the recent standard adoptions. 

Overall, the company’s gross margin remains strong, with gross profit accounting for roughly **54 %** of total revenue, indicating effective cost management in the post‑ASC 606 environment.

synth_text.title: GasLog Ltd. – Basic and Diluted Earnings‑per‑Share Summary for 2017‑2018
synth_text.text:
The consolidated financial statements of GasLog Ltd. show a marked improvement in earnings per share (EPS) between 2017 and 2018.  

- **Basic EPS** rose from **$0.07** in 2017 to **$0.47** in 2018, reflecting a substantial increase in profit available to common‑share owners after deducting the $10,064 k dividend on preference shares.  
- **Diluted EPS** followed a similar trend, moving from **$0.07** to **$0.46**, indicating that the inclusion of dilutive potential ordinary shares (which increased from 643 k to 844 k) had only a modest effect on per‑share earnings.  

The profit attributable to owners grew from **$15,566 k** (pre‑preference dividend) in 2017 to **$47,746 k** in 2018, resulting in profit available to owners of **$5,442 k** and **$37,620 k**, respectively.  

Weighted‑average common shares outstanding rose slightly, from **80,622,788** shares in 2017 to **80,792,837** shares in 2018. When diluted, the total potential ordinary shares used in the EPS denominator increased to **81,637,022** shares in 2018 (up from 81,266,130 in 2017).  

According to the notes, basic EPS is calculated by dividing profit after preference‑share dividends by the weighted‑average number of common shares, while diluted EPS adjusts profit for the effect of all dilutive potential ordinary shares, unless they are anti‑dilutive. The 2018 figures therefore reflect both the higher earnings and the modest dilution from additional potential shares.  

Overall, GasLog Ltd. demonstrated strong earnings growth and a corresponding rise in both basic and diluted EPS over the two‑year period.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the year ended 31 December 2019, GasLog Ltd. and its subsidiaries reported a net loss attributable to owners of **$100.7 million**, after accounting for a **$10.1 million** dividend on preference shares. The loss available to owners of the Group therefore amounted to **$110.7 million**.

**Basic Earnings per Share (EPS)**  
- **Basic EPS:** **$(1.37)** per share  
- **Weighted‑average number of basic shares outstanding:** **80,849,818**  

The basic EPS figure is derived by dividing the loss available to owners ($110.7 million) by the weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding (80.85 million).

**Diluted Earnings per Share (EPS)**  
- **Diluted EPS:** **$(1.37)** per share (identical to basic EPS)  
- **Weighted‑average number of shares used for diluted EPS:** **80,849,818**  

No dilutive potential ordinary shares were included in the diluted calculation because the Group excluded **2,630,173 Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs)** and **367,162 Restricted Stock Units (RSUs)** for 2019, as they were deemed anti‑dilutive. Consequently, the diluted share count matches the basic share count, resulting in the same EPS figure.

**Key Points**  
- The company incurred a loss of **$1.37 per share** on both a basic and diluted basis.  
- Preference‑share dividends of **$10.1 million** reduced the profit attributable to common shareholders, increasing the per‑share loss.  
- Anti‑dilutive SARs and RSUs were excluded from the diluted EPS computation, confirming that no additional shares would have lowered the loss per share.

These figures provide a concise snapshot of GasLog Ltd.’s 2019 profitability on a per‑share basis, reflecting the impact of both the underlying loss and the treatment of preference‑share dividends and stock‑based compensation.

synth_text.title: IBM Financial Highlights for Fiscal Years 2018 and 2019
synth_text.text:
**Financial Overview (FY 2018‑2019)**  
International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) reported a modest decline in revenue from **$79.6 billion in 2018** to **$77.1 billion in 2019**. Net income, after accounting for one‑time U.S. tax reform charges ($2.0 billion in 2018 and $0.1 billion in 2019), fell from **$8.7 billion** to **$9.4 billion** (both figures marked with an asterisk). Operating earnings on a non‑GAAP basis also decreased, moving from **$12.7 billion** to **$11.4 billion**.

Earnings per share (basic) were **$9.56** in 2018 and **$10.63** in 2019, while diluted non‑GAAP earnings per share were **$13.81** and **$12.81**, respectively. Assuming dilution, the EPS for continuing operations was **$9.51** in 2018 and **$10.57** in 2019.

Cash flow from operations remained strong, delivering **$15.2 billion** in 2018 and **$14.8 billion** in 2019. Capital expenditures fell sharply, from **$3.7 billion** to **$2.4 billion**, reflecting a more restrained investment pace. Share repurchases dropped from **$4.4 billion** to **$1.4 billion**, while cash dividends paid on common stock were relatively flat at **$5.7 billion** each year, equating to **$6.21** per share in 2018 and **$6.43** per share in 2019.

At year‑end, IBM held **$9.0 billion** in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash, and marketable securities (down from $12.2 billion in 2018). Total assets grew to **$152.2 billion** in 2019 from $123.4 billion the prior year. Working capital contracted to **$718 million** from **$10.9 billion**, while total debt rose to **$62.9 billion** (up from $45.8 billion). Total equity increased to **$20.9 billion** versus $16.9 billion in 2018.

The company’s share count fell slightly to **887 million** shares outstanding in 2019 from **892 million** in 2018. Correspondingly, the market price per common share rose from **$113.67** at the end of 2018 to **$134.04** at the end of 2019.

*Notes:* Net‑income figures include tax reform charges of $0.1 billion (2019) and $2.0 billion (2018). A detailed reconciliation of net income to operating earnings is provided on page 46 of the full report.

text.value: Net Income (Loss) Per Share: Basic net income (loss) per share (EPS) is computed by dividing the net income (loss) attributable to Cubic for the period by the weighted average number of common shares outstanding during the period, including vested RSUs.

In periods with a net income from continuing operations attributable to Cubic, diluted EPS is computed by dividing the net income for the period by the weighted average number of common and common equivalent shares outstanding during the period. Common equivalent shares consist of dilutive RSUs. Dilutive RSUs are calculated based on the average share price for each fiscal period using the treasury stock method. For RSUs with performance-based vesting, no common equivalent shares are included in the computation of diluted EPS until the related performance criteria have been met. For RSUs with performance and market-based vesting, no common equivalent shares are included in the computation of diluted EPS until the performance criteria have been met, and once the criteria are met the dilutive restricted stock units are calculated using the treasury stock method, modified by the multiplier that is calculated at the end of the accounting period as if the vesting date was at the end of the accounting period. The multiplier on RSUs with performance and market-based vesting is further described in Note 16.
In periods with a net loss from continuing operations attributable to Cubic, common equivalent shares are not included in the computation of diluted EPS, because to do so would be anti-dilutive.

2. **Interest and Penalties** – Recognized interest and penalties decreased modestly from $71 k in 2018 to $59 k in 2019, while accrued amounts at period end fell from $230 k to $212 k.

3. **Potential Impact on Effective Tax Rate** – Of the $28.8 million UTB balance as of December 28 2019, approximately $13.4 million would affect the effective tax rate if the positions were ultimately recognized.

4. **Audit Environment** – The company’s tax years 2016‑2019 (federal), 2015‑2019 (state), and 2014‑2019 (foreign) remain open for examination. Tax authorities may also review earlier periods where net operating losses or credits were carried forward.

5. **Future Outlook** – Management believes that any adjustments to uncertain tax positions over the next 12 months are unlikely to have a material effect on the company’s financial position or results of operations.

**Conclusion**  
The 2019 year‑end data show a modest increase in unrecognized tax benefits, driven primarily by new current‑year tax positions. While a portion of the UTB balance could influence the effective tax rate, the company’s ongoing audit exposure is being monitored, and no significant impact on future financial performance is anticipated.

synth_text.title: Verizon 2019 vs 2018 Operating Revenue and Connection Summary
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the year ended December 31, 2019, Verizon’s total operating revenues slipped to **$31.44 billion**, a decline of **$91 million (‑0.3 %)** from 2018’s $31.53 billion. The modest drop reflects mixed performance across its business segments.

**Segment performance**  
- **Global Enterprise**: Revenue fell to **$10.82 billion** (‑$383 million, ‑3.4 %) as traditional data and voice services faced competitive pricing pressure, partially offset by higher wireless service revenue.  
- **Small and Medium Business (SMB)**: Revenue rose to **$11.46 billion** (+$712 million, +6.6 %). Growth was driven by an 11.7 % increase in wireless post‑paid service revenue, higher‑priced device sales, expanded device‑protection packages, and a **$110 million (13.7 %)** increase in FiOS revenues, which reached **$915 million**.  
- **Public Sector and Other**: Revenue increased to **$5.92 billion** (+$89 million, +1.5 %) thanks to more networking and wireless post‑paid services, linked to the rise in post‑paid connections.  
- **Wholesale**: Revenue declined sharply to **$3.24 billion** (‑$509 million, ‑13.6 %) due to reduced core data and voice services, technology substitution, and continued market‑rate compression.

**Connection statistics**  
- **Wireless retail post‑paid connections** grew to **25.2 million** in 2019 from **23.5 million** in 2018, a **1.24 %** net addition (vs. 1.19 % in 2018).  
- **FiOS Internet connections** increased modestly to **326 k** (up from 307 k).  
- **FiOS video connections** rose to **77 k** (up from 74 k).  
- **Broadband connections** were **489 k** in 2019, slightly down from 501 k in 2018.  
- **Voice connections** fell to **4.96 million** from **5.40 million**.

The growth in wireless post‑paid connections and higher‑priced device sales underpinned SMB’s revenue surge, while declines in traditional enterprise and wholesale services weighed on overall results. No churn rate was disclosed for the period.

synth_text.title: Verizon Business Segment 2019 Financial and Operational Highlights
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In 2019 Verizon’s Business segment generated $91 million less revenue than in 2018, a modest decline of 0.3% overall. The change reflects a mixed performance across its five primary sub‑segments.

**Revenue Performance by Sub‑segment**  

| Sub‑segment | Revenue Change (USD M) | % Change | Key Drivers |
|-------------|------------------------|----------|-------------|
| Global Enterprise | –383 | –3.4% | Declines in traditional data and voice services due to competitive pricing, partially offset by higher wireless service revenue. |
| Small & Medium Business | +712 | +6.6% | Strong growth in wireless post‑paid services (11.7% increase), higher‑priced device mix, expanded device protection sales, and rising Fios uptake. |
| Public Sector & Other | +89 | +1.5% | Gains in networking and wireless post‑paid services linked to more post‑paid connections. |
| Wholesale | –509 | –13.6% | Reduced core data and voice traffic as customers shift to newer technologies and market rates contract. |
| Total Operating Revenues | –91 | –0.3% | Net effect of the above sub‑segment movements. |

**Connection Metrics**  

- **Wireless retail post‑paid connections** grew 7.3% to 1.7 million, fueling the Small & Medium Business revenue boost.  
- **Fios Internet connections** rose 6.2% (to 19 k) and **Fios video connections** increased 4.1% (to 3 k), contributing to a 13.7% rise in Fios revenue ($915 M).  
- **Broadband connections** fell 2.4% (down 12 k) and **voice connections** declined 8.2% (down 441 k), reflecting the broader industry shift away from legacy DSL and voice services.  

**Interpretation**  
The segment’s modest overall revenue dip masks divergent trends: while enterprise and wholesale lines suffered from price pressure and technology substitution, the Small & Medium Business and Public Sector areas benefited from higher‑value wireless services and growing Fios adoption. The increase in post‑paid wireless connections and the shift toward higher‑priced devices were pivotal in offsetting losses elsewhere.

**Conclusion**  
Verizon’s Business segment demonstrated resilience in 2019, with growth in high‑margin wireless and fiber offerings counterbalancing declines in traditional data, voice, and wholesale services. Continued focus on premium device sales, expanded Fios bundles, and targeted enterprise solutions will be critical to sustaining momentum in a competitive market.

synth_text.title: Operating Expense Breakdown and Year‑over‑Year Drivers for Fiscal Year Ended March 31 2019
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended March 31 2019, total operating expenses amounted to **$51.6 million** (‑$51,570 k). The primary expense categories and their contributions are:

| Category                     | Amount (in $ thousands) | % of Total Operating Expense* |
|------------------------------|--------------------------|------------------------------|
| Research & Development (R&D) | $19,566                  | 51 % |
| Sales & Marketing            | $17,948                  | 15 % |
| General & Administrative (G&A)| $16,770                | 45 % |
| Impairment of long‑lived assets| $(1,712)                | n/m |
| Restructuring                | $(1,002)                 | n/m |
| **Total Operating Expenses** | **$51,570**              | **26 %** (as reported) |

\*The percentages for impairment and restructuring are marked “nm” (not meaningful) in the source table, indicating they were excluded from the proportional analysis.

### Drivers of the Increases

- **Research & Development:** Expenses rose by **$19.6 million** versus FY 2018, driven mainly by higher personnel‑related costs (+$11.8 M), increased share‑based compensation (+$3.6 M), and additional IT and facility costs (+$1.6 M). A modest positive currency effect (≈ $0.5 M) from a stronger U.S. dollar also contributed.

- **Sales & Marketing:** Costs grew by **$17.9 million**, reflecting higher IT and facility expenses (+$5.3 M), added personnel costs (+$4.0 M), greater share‑based compensation (+$3.4 M), professional services (+$2.7 M), travel/other costs (+$1.2 M), and marketing spend (+$1.1 M). Favorable foreign‑currency movements added roughly $1.5 M.

- **General & Administrative:** Expenses increased by **$16.8 million**, primarily due to higher personnel costs (+$6.3 M), share‑based compensation (+$5.8 M), IT and facility costs (+$1.9 M), professional services (+$1.2 M), and litigation‑related costs (+$1.0 M).

- **Restructuring & Impairment:** The year included a $0.2 M restructuring charge related to exiting the Watertown, MA office and a $1.7 M non‑cash impairment of leasehold improvements recorded in FY 2018. These items are not expressed as percentages of total operating expense.

Overall, the increase in operating expenses for FY 2019 was largely attributable to **personnel expansion**, **share‑based compensation**, and **technology/facility investments** across all major functions, with additional contributions from professional services and currency effects. The reported percentages align with the dollar amounts, confirming R&D as the largest single cost driver, followed closely by sales & marketing and G&A.

synth_text.title: Operating Expense Comparison for Fiscal Years Ending March 31 2018 and 2019
synth_text.text:
**Summary**

For the fiscal year ended March 31 2019, total operating expenses rose to **$250.7 million**, up **$51.6 million** (≈ 26 %) from **$199.2 million** in the prior year. The increase was driven primarily by higher spending across the three main expense categories—research and development (R&D), sales and marketing, and general and administrative (G&A)—partially offset by a modest reduction in restructuring costs and the absence of a non‑cash impairment charge that was recorded in FY 2018.

**Category‑level changes**

| Category | FY 2018 | FY 2019 | Year‑over‑year change | Key drivers (per context) |
|----------|---------|---------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Research & development | $38.4 M | $57.9 M | **+$19.6 M** | Personnel‑related costs (+$11.8 M), share‑based compensation (+$3.6 M), IT & facility costs (+$1.6 M); modest positive impact from a stronger U.S. dollar. |
| Sales & marketing | $121.2 M | $139.2 M | **+$17.9 M** | IT & facilities (+$5.3 M), personnel‑related costs (+$4.0 M), share‑based compensation (+$3.4 M), professional services (+$2.7 M), travel & other (+$1.2 M), marketing (+$1.1 M); $1.5 M benefit from a stronger dollar. |
| General & administrative | $37.0 M | $53.8 M | **+$16.8 M** | Personnel‑related costs (+$6.3 M), share‑based compensation (+$5.8 M), IT & facilities (+$1.9 M), professional services (+$1.2 M), litigation expenses (+$1.0 M). |
| Impairment of long‑lived assets | $1.7 M (non‑cash) | — | –$1.7 M | One‑time lease‑hold improvement impairment recorded in FY 2018. |
| Restructuring | $0.8 M (FY 2018) | –$0.2 M (FY 2019) | **–$1.0 M** | FY 2018 charge related to exiting the Watertown, MA office; FY 2019 revision of $0.2 M for the same exit. |

**Overall impact**

- The combined increase in R&D, sales & marketing, and G&A ($54.3 M) more than explains the total expense rise, while the $1.0 M net reduction in restructuring and the elimination of the $1.7 M impairment slightly dampened the upward trend.
- Personnel‑related costs, driven by headcount growth, were the dominant factor across all categories, complemented by higher share‑based compensation and expanded IT/facility footprints.
- Currency effects (a stronger U.S. dollar) provided modest offsets, reducing the effective increase in R&D and sales & marketing.

**Conclusion**

The fiscal year 2019 operating expense profile reflects the company’s strategic investment in product development, market expansion, and administrative capacity, financed largely by increased staffing and related compensation. While restructuring and impairment charges were lower than the prior year, the net effect was a substantial rise in total operating costs, aligning with the company’s growth objectives.

POST-EMPLOYMENT BENEFIT PLANS COST
We provide pension and other benefits for most of our employees. These include DB pension plans, DC pension plans and OPEBs.

We operate our DB and DC pension plans under applicable Canadian and provincial pension legislation, which prescribes minimum and maximum DB funding requirements. Plan assets are held in trust, and the oversight of governance of the plans, including investment decisions, contributions to DB plans and the selection of the DC plans investment options offered to plan participants, lies with the Pension Fund Committee, a committee of our board of directors.
The interest rate risk is managed using a liability matching approach, which reduces the exposure of the DB plans to a mismatch between investment growth and obligation growth.
The longevity risk is managed using a longevity swap, which reduces the exposure of the DB plans to an increase in life expectancy.

synth_text.text:
The company’s post‑employment benefit (PEB) plans—comprising defined benefit (DB) pensions, defined contribution (DC) pensions and other post‑employment benefits (OPEBs)—incurred a total service cost of **$247 million** in the first reporting period and **$270 million** in the subsequent period.

**Cost breakdown**

| Component | Period 1 | Period 2 |
|-----------|----------|----------|
| DB pension | $(193) million | $(213) million |
| DC pension | $(110) million | $(106) million |
| OPEBs | $(3) million | $(3) million |
| Capitalized benefit‑plan cost | $59 million | $56 million |
| Other costs (severance, acquisition, etc.) | – | $(4) million |
| **Total PEB service cost** | $(247) million | $(270) million |

*Numbers in parentheses represent expenses.*

**Key trends**
- **DB pension expenses increased** by $20 million, reflecting higher benefit obligations or funding adjustments.
- **DC pension expenses decreased** slightly by $4 million, indicating lower contribution requirements.
- **OPEB costs remained stable** at $3 million.
- **Capitalized benefit‑plan costs fell** by $3 million, suggesting reduced capitalized portions of the plans.
- **Other recognized costs** of $4 million appeared in the second period, contributing to the overall rise in total PEB cost.

**Governance and risk management**
The DB and DC plans operate under Canadian and provincial pension legislation, with assets held in trust. Oversight—including investment decisions, contributions, and DC investment options—is the responsibility of the Pension Fund Committee, a board‑level body. To mitigate key risks:
- **Interest‑rate risk** is managed through a liability‑matching approach, aligning asset growth with obligation growth.
- **Longevity risk** is addressed via a longevity swap, protecting the plans from increases in life expectancy.

These governance structures and risk‑mitigation strategies provide a solid foundation for the reported service‑cost figures and support the sustainable management of the company’s post‑employment benefit obligations.

text.value: Accounts Receivable and Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

Accounts receivable consists primarily of amounts due to the Company from normal business activities. We maintain an allowance for doubtful accounts for estimated losses that result from the inability of our customers to make required payments.

The allowance for doubtful accounts is maintained based on customer payment levels, historical experience and management’s views on trends in the overall receivable agings. In addition, for larger accounts, we perform analyses of risks on a customer-specific basis. We perform ongoing credit evaluations of our customers’ financial condition and management believes that an adequate allowance for doubtful accounts has been provided.

Uncollectible accounts are removed from accounts receivable and are charged against the allowance for doubtful accounts when internal collection efforts have been unsuccessful. These movements indicate that the company’s credit risk management and provisioning practices effectively responded to changing collection outcomes while maintaining an appropriate reserve for doubtful accounts.

synth_text.title: 2017 Allowance for Doubtful Accounts – Activity Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the company’s Allowance for Doubtful Accounts experienced significant movement. The allowance began the year with a balance of **$2.8 million**. During the year, a **provision of $7.1 million** was charged to expense, reflecting the company’s estimate of future credit losses based on customer payment trends, historical experience, and management’s assessment of receivable aging. 

Uncollectible accounts totaling **$6.5 million** were written off (net of recoveries), reducing the allowance. In addition, the company **acquired an additional $3.3 million** of allowance, primarily through targeted risk analyses of larger customers. These activities resulted in an ending allowance balance of **$6.7 million** as of December 31, 2017.

The allowance is maintained to offset expected losses from accounts receivable, which consist mainly of amounts due from normal business operations. Management continuously evaluates customer creditworthiness and believes the resulting allowance is adequate to cover anticipated uncollectible amounts.

synth_text.text:
The Company’s non‑current assets amounted to €437 million at 31 December 2019, down from €452 million a year earlier. The portfolio is comprised of three main items:

* **Equity securities** increased from €19 million in 2018 to €23 million in 2019.  
* **Long‑term state receivables** fell from €391 million to €358 million. These receivables consist of public‑grant funding from Italian and French governmental agencies for long‑term R&D, industrialisation and capital‑investment projects, as well as tax‑refund claims that are expected to be collected beyond one year.  
* **Deposits and other non‑current assets** rose from €42 million to €56 million. The “other” portion includes the assets listed in the Company’s notes (details not reproduced here).

In both years the Company employed a factoring arrangement to accelerate cash collection on a portion of its non‑current assets. As of 31 December 2019, assets totalling $131 million were sold without recourse, compared with $122 million at the end of 2018, incurring a financial cost of less than $1 million in each period.

Overall, the modest decline in total non‑current assets reflects a reduction in long‑term state receivables, partially offset by higher equity securities and increased deposits/other assets, while the factoring transactions provided additional liquidity with minimal expense.

synth_text.title: Earnings Summary and EPS Reconciliation for the Reporting Year
synth_text.text:
For the year ended December 31, the company reported net income of **$116.5 million**. Both basic and diluted earnings per share (EPS) were **$1.68**.

- **Weighted‑average shares** used in the calculations were:
  - **Basic:** 69,175 thousand shares  
  - **Diluted:** 69,424 thousand shares  

- The **effect of common equivalent shares (CESs)** on the diluted calculation was **249 thousand shares**. This modest increase in the share count results in the diluted EPS being identical to the basic EPS.

**Methodology (per the provided context):**  
- *Basic EPS* is computed by dividing net income by the weighted‑average number of basic common shares outstanding.  
- *Diluted EPS* incorporates the treasury‑stock‑method effect of CESs, dividing net income by the weighted‑average diluted share count (basic shares plus the effect of CESs).  

The note that anti‑dilutive CESs were immaterial confirms that the CESs did not reduce EPS, allowing the basic and diluted figures to remain the same.

Overall, the earnings performance is reflected by a solid net income figure and consistent EPS across both basic and diluted measures.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Profit Performance Overview
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 the corporation posted mixed profit results.  

* **Continuing operations** saw a decline: profit from continuing operations fell **7.2 %**, and profit attributable to owners of the corporation dropped **9.4 %**. The decrease was mainly caused by the absence of last year’s US tax‑reform benefit and higher depreciation and amortization linked to the MetroCast acquisition. These headwinds were partially offset by higher adjusted EBITDA, lower financial expenses, and reduced integration, restructuring and acquisition costs.  

* **Overall profit** improved sharply: total profit for the year rose **20.0 %**, and profit attributable to owners increased **18.4 %**. The primary driver was a **$75.4 million** gain from discontinued operations after the sale of Cogeco Peer 1, reversing a **$24.4 million** loss in the prior year.  

* **Non‑controlling interest** (21 % participation held by CDPQ) benefited from the acquisition of MetroCast, with its share of profit from continuing operations surging **80.9 %**.  

* **Earnings per share** mirrored the profit trends: basic EPS grew **18.1 %**, while basic EPS from continuing operations fell **9.5 %**.  

Overall, the strong growth in total profit was driven by the one‑time gain from the Cogeco Peer 1 sale, whereas the core continuing‑operations business experienced modest pressure from integration costs and higher depreciation.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview for Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Summary of Reported Results**

| Fiscal Year | Profit from Continuing Operations | Total Profit | Attributable to Owners (Continuing) | Attributable to Owners (Total) | Non‑Controlling Interest* | Basic EPS (Continuing) | Basic EPS (Total) |
|-------------|-----------------------------------|--------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|-------------------|
| FY 2018 (restated) | **$356.9 M** | **$432.3 M** | $339.97 M | $415.35 M | $16.94 M | $6.89 | $8.41 |
| FY 2019 | **$384.6 M** | **$360.2 M** | $375.21 M | $350.83 M | $9.36 M | $7.61 | $7.12 |

\*The non‑controlling interest reflects CDPQ’s 21 % participation in Atlantic Broadband’s results, effective after the MetroCast acquisition on 4 January 2018.

**Key Observations**

1. **Continuing‑Operation Profit**  
   - FY 2019 saw a modest increase in profit from continuing operations (+7.8 % vs. FY 2018), reaching $384.6 M and delivering an EPS of $7.61.  
   - The rise was partially offset by higher depreciation and amortisation linked to the MetroCast acquisition and the reversal of a $94 M U.S. tax‑rate benefit received in FY 2018.

2. **Total Profit & EPS**  
   - Total profit fell from $432.3 M in FY 2018 to $360.2 M in FY 2019 (‑16.7 %).  
   - Correspondingly, basic EPS declined from $8.41 to $7.12, reflecting the impact of the discontinued‑operations loss in FY 2018 and the gain from the sale of Cogeco Peer 1 in FY 2019.

3. **Discontinued Operations**  
   - FY 2019 recorded a $75.4 M profit from discontinued operations (sale of Cogeco Peer 1), reversing a $24.4 M loss in FY 2018. This contribution was a primary driver of the overall profit increase despite weaker continuing‑operation results.

4. **Non‑Controlling Interest**  
   - The non‑controlling interest amount decreased from $16.9 M in FY 2018 to $9.4 M in FY 2019, reflecting the integration of MetroCast and the related re‑allocation of earnings.

5. **Restatement Note**  
   - FY 2018 figures were restated to comply with IFRS 15 and to reclassify Cogeco Peer 1 results as discontinued operations. Readers should refer to the “Accounting policies” and “Discontinued operations” sections for full details.

**Conclusion**

The company’s FY 2019 performance was shaped by a blend of acquisition‑related costs, the elimination of a prior tax benefit, and a significant gain from the disposal of Cogeco Peer 1. While continuing‑operation profitability improved modestly, total earnings were tempered by the transition in tax treatment and higher depreciation. The non‑controlling interest, representing CDPQ’s stake, contributed less in FY 2019 as the business’s earnings profile shifted post‑MetroCast acquisition.  

Overall, the financial results illustrate the company’s ability to generate higher earnings from core operations while navigating the financial effects of strategic acquisitions and divestitures.

Under this program, which we may suspend or discontinue at any time, we may purchase shares of our outstanding common stock through solicited or unsolicited transactions in the open market, in privately negotiated transactions, through accelerated share repurchase programs, pursuant to a Rule 10b5-1 plan or in such other manner as deemed appropriate by our management.
The following table summarizes activity related to this program (in millions, except per share amounts):

The aggregate purchase price of our stock repurchases for fiscal 2019 consisted of $2.1 billion of open market purchases of which $1.0 billion and $1.1 billion were allocated to additional paid-in capital and retained earnings (accumulated deficit), respectively.

Since the May 13, 2003 inception of our stock repurchase program through April 26, 2019, we repurchased a total of 313 million shares of our common stock at an average price of $37.46 per share, for an aggregate purchase price of $11.7 billion.

synth_text.title: Recent Stock Repurchase Activity – Highlights for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The Company’s stock repurchase program, authorized by the Board for up to **$13.6 billion** of common stock, continues to be executed through open‑market and other transactions. The table below captures the two most recent repurchase events:

| Date | Shares Repurchased (millions) | Avg. Price per Share | Aggregate Purchase Price (millions) | Remaining Authorization (millions) |
|------|------------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **April 26 2019** | 29 | $72.87 | $2,111 | $1,889 |
| **April 27 2018** | 15 | $51.57 | $794 | $4,000 |

- **April 26 2019**: The Company bought **29 million** shares at an average price of **$72.87**, resulting in an aggregate outlay of **$2.1 billion**. After this purchase, the remaining authorization stood at **$1.889 billion**, reflecting the program’s progress toward its $13.6 billion limit.  
- **April 27 2018**: The Company repurchased **15 million** shares at **$51.57** per share, costing **$794 million**. The remaining authorization after this transaction was **$4.0 billion**.

For fiscal year 2019, the total amount spent on open‑market repurchases was **$2.1 billion**, split equally between additional paid‑in capital and retained earnings. Since the program’s inception on May 13 2003 through April 26 2019, the Company has repurchased **313 million** shares at an average price of **$37.46** per share, for a cumulative purchase price of **$11.7 billion**.

These figures illustrate the Company’s ongoing commitment to returning capital to shareholders while managing the remaining authorization within the broader $13.6 billion program framework.

synth_text.text:

After this transaction, the **remaining authorized repurchase amount** for the period stood at **$794 million**.

This activity is part of the company’s broader stock repurchase program, which the Board has authorized up to **$13.6 billion** in total. Since the program’s inception in May 2003, the company has repurchased **313 million shares** at an average price of **$37.46 per share**, for a cumulative purchase price of **$11.7 billion**. The April 2017 repurchase contributes to these ongoing efforts, which may be conducted through open‑market purchases, privately negotiated transactions, accelerated share repurchase programs, or Rule 10b5‑1 plans, and can be suspended or discontinued at management’s discretion.

text.value: xvii. Transfer of unclaimed/unpaid amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund:

Pursuant to Sections 124 and 125 of the Act read with the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016 (“IEPF Rules”), dividend, if not claimed for a consecutive period of 7 years from the date of transfer to Unpaid Dividend Account of the Company, are liable to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (“IEPF”).

Further, all the shares in respect of which dividend has remained unclaimed for seven consecutive years or
more from the date of transfer to unpaid dividend account shall also be transferred to IEPF Authority. The said
requirement does not apply to shares in respect of which there is a specific order of Court, Tribunal or Statutory
Authority, restraining any transfer of the shares.

In the interest of the shareholders, the Company sends periodical reminders to the shareholders to claim
their dividends in order to avoid transfer of dividends/shares to IEPF Authority. Notices in this regard are also
published in the newspapers and the details of unclaimed dividends and shareholders whose shares are liable
to be transferred to the IEPF Authority, are uploaded on the Company’s website (https://www.tcs.com/detailsunclaimed-
dividend-transfer-IEPF-account-2017).

In light of the aforesaid provisions, the Company has during the year under review, transferred to IEPF the
unclaimed dividends, outstanding for 7 consecutive years, of the Company, erstwhile TCS e-Serve Limited and
CMC Limited (since amalgamated with the Company). Further, shares of the Company, in respect of which
dividend has not been claimed for 7 consecutive years or more from the date of transfer to unpaid dividend
account, have also been transferred to the demat account of IEPF Authority.
The details of unclaimed dividends and shares transferred to IEPF during FY 2019 are as follows:

The members who have a claim on above dividends and shares may claim the same from IEPF Authority by

in and sending a physical copy of the same, duly signed to the Company, along with requisite documents
