synth_text.title: Consolidated Operations Summary for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary presents selected consolidated statements of operations for the fiscal years ended 2018 and 2019 (figures in thousands). The data are illustrative of historical performance and are not predictive of future results.

**Revenue Growth**  
- **2018:** Total revenues reached **$673,624**, driven by subscription revenue of **$109,454** and other revenue of **$47,675**.  
- **2019:** Total revenues increased to **$902,858**, with subscription revenue climbing to **$160,320** and other revenue rising to **$70,723**.  
*Result:* Overall revenue grew by approximately **34%** year‑over‑year.

**Cost of Revenues & Gross Profit**  
- Cost of revenues rose from **$157,129** in 2018 to **$231,043** in 2019.  
- Correspondingly, gross profit expanded from **$516,495** to **$671,815**, maintaining a strong margin despite higher costs.

**Operating Expenses**  
The company’s operating expense base expanded across all major categories:  
- **Research & Development:** $101,042 (2018) → $136,363 (2019)  
- **Sales & Marketing:** $329,116 (2018) → $439,100 (2019)  
- **General & Administrative:** $102,773 (2018) → $142,027 (2019)  

Total operating expenses increased from **$532,931** to **$717,490**, reflecting intensified investment in product development, market expansion, and administrative functions.

**Profitability**  
- **Loss from operations** widened from **$(16,436)** in 2018 to **$(45,675)** in 2019.  
- After accounting for other income/expense, interest expense, and tax provisions, the **net loss** grew from **$(26,203)** to **$(53,607)**.

**Key Takeaway**  
While the company achieved robust revenue growth in 2019, the acceleration of operating expenses outpaced revenue gains, leading to a larger net loss compared with the prior year. This pattern underscores the company’s strategic emphasis on scaling its subscription base and expanding market reach, albeit at a higher cost structure.

Excluding the US cash flows, Free Cash Flow Conversion increased to 47% from 33% in FY18, driven by improved EBITDA, lower working capital outflows, lower interest costs and lower exceptional cashflows.

Several other factors had a specific impact on cash flow during FY19. These included the effects of the disposal of the US business and associated capital restructuring, as well as the timing of dividend payments.

Net Debt decreased to £288.5m from £501.1m at the end of FY18. The Group’s Net Debt:EBITDA leverage as measured under financing agreements was 1.8x at year end. This compared to 1.9x at the end of March 2019 and 2.3x at the end of September 2018. This outturn includes the increased debt associated with the Freshtime acquisition completed in early September 2019. As at 27 September 2019, the Group had committed facilities of £506m with a weighted average maturity of 4.0 years.

ROIC was 14.4% for the 12 months ended 27 September 2019, compared to 15.6% for the 12 months ended 28 September 2018. The reduction was primarily driven by increased investment, in particular the timing of the acquisition of Freshtime and was so impacted by an increased tax rate.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview FY18‑FY19: Cash Flow, Debt Leverage, and ROIC
synth_text.text:
The Group’s financial metrics show mixed trends between FY18 and FY19. Free Cash Flow fell from £92.4 million in FY18 to £54.9 million in FY19, a decline driven mainly by the impact of US cash‑flow movements and the timing of the US business disposal. Excluding those US cash flows, the free‑cash‑flow conversion improved to 47 % from 33 % in FY18, thanks to higher EBITDA, lower working‑capital outflows, reduced interest costs and fewer exceptional cash‑flow items.

Net Debt contracted sharply, dropping from £501.1 million at the end of FY18 to £288.5 million at FY19 year‑end. Consequently, the Net Debt‑to‑EBITDA leverage under financing agreements improved from 2.3× in FY18 to 1.8× in FY19 (down from 1.9× in March 2019). The reduction reflects debt repayments, the effect of the Freshtime acquisition, and the Group’s committed facilities of £506 million with an average maturity of 4.0 years.

Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) decreased modestly, from 15.6 % in FY18 to 14.4 % in FY19. The dip is attributed to increased investment—particularly the timing of the Freshtime acquisition—and a higher effective tax rate.

Overall, FY19 delivered stronger debt leverage and better cash‑flow conversion (when US cash flows are excluded), while the lower free cash generation and slight ROIC decline reflect strategic acquisition activity and tax impacts.

synth_text.title: FY19 Financial Performance Summary: Cash Flow, Debt, and ROIC
synth_text.text:
**Performance Overview (FY19)**  

- **Free Cash Flow:** The period recorded a negative Free Cash Flow of **£37.5 million**, reflecting a sharp decline from the £54.9 million generated in FY19 (as reported in the full‑year results). The downturn is primarily attributed to the impact of US cash‑flow movements, the disposal of the US business, and timing of dividend payments. When US cash flows are excluded, the Free Cash Flow conversion improves to **47 %**, up from 33 % in FY18, driven by stronger EBITDA, lower working‑capital outflows, reduced interest costs, and fewer exceptional cash‑flow items.

- **Net Debt:** No specific Net Debt figure is provided in the table, but the accompanying commentary notes that Net Debt fell to **£288.5 million** at year‑end, down from £501.1 million at the end of FY18. This reduction lowered the Net Debt‑to‑EBITDA leverage to **1.8×** under financing agreements, an improvement from 2.3× in September 2018. The leverage figure includes additional debt taken on for the Freshtime acquisition completed in September 2019.

- **Return on Invested Capital (ROIC):** ROIC decreased by **120 basis points**, moving from **15.6 %** in the prior 12‑month period to **14.4 %** for the 12 months ended 27 September 2019. The decline stems from higher investment levels—particularly the timing of the Freshtime acquisition—and an increased effective tax rate.

**Key Drivers**  
1. **US Cash‑Flow Impact:** The reduction in free cash flow is largely a result of cash‑flow movements in the United States, including the disposal of the US business.  
2. **Capital Restructuring:** The Freshtime acquisition added debt but was offset by overall debt reduction and improved leverage ratios.  
3. **Operational Efficiency:** Excluding US cash flows, the company achieved better free cash flow conversion, indicating operational improvements in EBITDA generation and working‑capital management.  
4. **Tax and Investment Effects:** Higher tax rates and the timing of significant capital investments contributed to the ROIC dip.

Overall, FY19 shows a mixed picture: while free cash flow turned negative in the reported period, underlying operational performance improved when US-specific effects are removed. Net debt levels have been substantially reduced, and leverage is healthier, though ROIC experienced a modest decline due to increased investment and tax pressures.

synth_text.title: Analysis of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) Reclassifications for 2017‑2018
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table details the components of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) that were re‑classified into the Consolidated Statements of Operations for fiscal years ending August 31, 2017 and 2018. All amounts are presented net of tax, which is immaterial for the periods shown.

**Key Component Changes**

| Component | 2017 (in $ thousands) | 2018 (in $ thousands) | Notable Shift |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------------|---------------|
| Foreign currency translation adjustment | 5,947 | — | A gain in 2017 disappeared in 2018, leaving no translation effect. |
| Realized gains/losses on derivative instruments | — | — | No gain/loss reported; however, 2018 includes a $14.8 million tax reduction related to derivatives (see footnote). |
| Foreign‑exchange contracts | 4,799 | (9,379) | Switched from a positive impact in 2017 to a negative impact in 2018. |
| Interest‑rate contracts | 3,950 | (13,697) | Also reversed direction, moving from a gain to a loss. |
| Actuarial loss | 1,929 | 1,127 | Decreased, reducing the overall loss component. |
| Prior‑service credit | (138) | (88) | Slight improvement (less negative) in 2018. |
| Available‑for‑sale securities | 10,139 | — | Contributed a positive amount in 2017 due to an other‑than‑temporary impairment; no impact in 2018. |
| **Total amounts re‑classified from AOCI** | **26,626** (credit) | **(22,037)** (debit) | The net reclassification moved from a $26.6 million credit in 2017 to a $22.0 million debit in 2018, reflecting the combined effect of the above items. |

**Contextual Insights**

* The 2017 reclassification of available‑for‑sale securities was recorded as “other expense” following an other‑than‑temporary impairment.  
* The 2018 figures include a $14.8 million reduction to income‑tax expense linked to derivative instruments, though the derivative line itself shows no realized gain/loss.  
* The company anticipates reclassifying an additional **$17 million** into earnings over the next twelve months, primarily as a component of cost of revenue.

**Conclusion**  
Between 2017 and 2018, AOCI reclassifications shifted markedly from a net credit to a net debit, driven largely by the reversal of foreign‑exchange and interest‑rate contract impacts and the absence of the securities‑related credit that existed in 2017. The anticipated $17 million reclassification in the upcoming year suggests that the company expects further movement of AOCI items into earnings, mainly affecting cost of revenue.

synth_text.title: Summary of Defined‑Benefit Pension Obligation Movements and Recognised Pension Expenses (2017‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The employee pension plan mandated by the Labour Standards Act of the Republic of China is a **defined‑benefit** scheme. Benefits are calculated on the basis of service years and the employee’s average monthly salary before retirement. The plan awards two benefit units per year for the first 15 years of service and one unit per year thereafter, up to a maximum of 45 units.

**Funding policy** – The Company contributes an amount equal to **2 % of total employee salaries and wages** each month to a pension fund administered by the Bank of Taiwan on behalf of a pension‑fund supervisory committee. Because the fund is managed by government‑designated authorities, it is excluded from the Company’s consolidated financial statements.

**Pension expense trend** – The Company recognised pension expenses of **NT 80 million (2017)**, **NT 69 million (2018)** and **NT 59 million (2019)**, indicating a steady decline in expense over the three‑year period.

### Movements in the Present Value of the Defined‑Benefit Obligation

| Item (in NT$ thousands) | Year 1* | Year 2* |
|--------------------------|---------|---------|
| **Defined benefit obligation at beginning of year** | (5,671,058) | (5,620,509) |
| **Service cost** | (24,477) | (21,043) |
| **Interest cost** | (61,247) | (51,146) |
| **Subtotal (service + interest)** | (97,257) | 65,119 |
| **Remeasurements – changes in financial assumptions** | (91,350) | (114,976) |
| **Remeasurements – experience adjustments** | (5,907) | 180,095 |
| **Benefits paid** | 233,530 | 216,510 |

\*The two rows correspond to consecutive fiscal years (the exact calendar years are not labelled in the source table).

- **Service cost** reflects the present value of benefits earned by employees during the year.  
- **Interest cost** represents the time‑value of money on the opening obligation.  
- **Remeasurements** capture the effect of changes in actuarial assumptions (financial assumptions) and actual experience (e.g., mortality, turnover).  
- **Benefits paid** are cash outflows that reduce the liability.

**Interpretation**  
In the first year, the obligation started at NT 5.67 billion. After accounting for service and interest costs (total NT 97.3 million) and negative remeasurements (NT 97.3 million), the net increase was partially offset by benefits paid of NT 233.5 million, resulting in a modest overall change.  

In the following year, the opening obligation was slightly lower at NT 5.62 billion. Service and interest costs fell to NT 65.1 million, while remeasurements turned positive because experience adjustments (NT 180.1 million) outweighed the adverse effect of financial‑assumption changes (NT 115.0 million). Benefits paid of NT 216.5 million again reduced the liability.

Overall, the defined‑benefit obligation remained relatively stable across the two years, while the company’s recognised pension expense continued to decline, reflecting lower contribution requirements and the impact of actuarial remeasurements.

text.value: Note 5: Income Taxes

On December 22, 2017, the U.S. government enacted the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the “Tax Act”). The Tax Act includes significant changes to the U.S. corporate income tax system including: a federal corporate rate reduction from 35% to 21%; limitations on the deductibility of interest expense and executive compensation; creation of the base erosion anti-abuse tax (“BEAT”), a new minimum tax; and the transition of U.S. international taxation from a worldwide tax system to a modified territorial tax system. The change to a modified territorial tax system resulted in a one-time U.S. tax liability on those earnings which have not previously been repatriated to the U.S. (the “Transition Tax”), with future distributions not subject to U.S. federal income tax when repatriated. A majority of the provisions in the Tax Act are effective January 1, 2018.

In response to the Tax Act, the SEC staff issued guidance on accounting for the tax effects of the Tax Act. The guidance provides a one-year measurement period for companies to complete the accounting. The Company reflected the income tax effects of those aspects of the Tax Act for which the accounting is complete. To the extent a company's accounting for certain income tax effects of the Tax Act is incomplete but it is able to determine a reasonable estimate, a company should record a provisional estimate in the financial statements. If a company cannot determine a provisional estimate to be included in the financial statements, it should continue to apply the provisions of the tax laws that were in effect immediately before the enactment of the Tax Act.

In connection with the Company's initial analysis of the impact of the Tax Act, the Company has recorded a provisional estimate of discrete net tax expense of $508,000 for the period ended December 31, 2017. This discrete expense consists of provisional estimates of zero expense for the Transition Tax, $173,000 net benefit for the decrease in the Company's deferred tax liability on unremitted foreign earnings, and $681,000 net expense for remeasurement of the Company's deferred tax assets and liabilities for the corporate rate reduction.

During the year ended December 31, 2018, we completed our accounting for the income tax effects of the Tax Act. We did not recognize any additional discrete net tax expense in addition to the provisional amounts recorded at December 31, 2017 for the enactment-date effects of the Tax Act, for a total of $508,000 of discrete net tax expense.

As of December 31, 2019, the Company is permanently reinvested in certain Non-U.S. subsidiaries and does not have a deferred tax liability related to its undistributed foreign earnings. The estimated amount of the unrecognized deferred tax liability attributed to future withholding taxes on dividend distributions of undistributed earnings for certain non-U.S. subsidiaries, which the Company intends to reinvest the related earnings indefinitely in its operations outside the U.S., is approximately $484,000 at December 31, 2019

synth_text.title: Income Before Tax Breakdown (2018‑2019) and Effects of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
synth_text.text:
The company’s statement of income before tax expense (in thousands) shows the following composition for the two most recent fiscal years:

- **2018:** Total pre‑tax income of **$8,949 k**, driven by **$11,553 k** from U.S. operations and offset by a foreign loss of **$(2,604) k**.  
- **2019:** Total pre‑tax income of **$8,286 k**, consisting of **$8,677 k** from U.S. operations and a smaller foreign offset of **$(391) k**.

These figures are presented in Note 5 – Income Taxes – and reflect the company’s earnings before the application of income tax expense. Their presentation follows the enactment of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which introduced a transition tax on previously untaxed foreign earnings, reduced the federal corporate tax rate from 35 % to 21 %, and added several new provisions (e.g., BEAT, interest‑expense limitations).

In response to the Tax Act, the company recorded a provisional discrete net tax expense of **$508 k** for the year ended December 31 2017. This amount comprised:
- No expense for the transition tax,
- A **$173 k** net benefit from the reduction of the deferred tax liability on unremitted foreign earnings,
- A **$681 k** net expense from re‑measuring deferred tax assets and liabilities due to the lower corporate rate.

The accounting for these effects was completed during 2018, and no additional discrete net tax expense was recognized beyond the provisional $508 k. By December 31 2019, the company had permanently reinvested earnings in certain non‑U.S. subsidiaries, eliminating its deferred tax liability on undistributed foreign earnings. The remaining estimated liability related to future withholding taxes on dividend distributions is approximately **$484 k**.

Overall, the table illustrates that while U.S. earnings constitute the bulk of pre‑tax income, foreign operations have contributed a modest negative adjustment, and the company’s tax position has been materially influenced by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and subsequent accounting actions.

synth_text.title: Operating Expense Composition – Emphasis on Share‑Based Payments Across Two Reporting Periods
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table compares operating expenses for two reporting periods (hereafter Period 1 and Period 2) across several functional areas. While most categories show modest fluctuations, share‑based payment expenses dominate the cost structure in both periods.

**Expense Summary by Category**

| Functional Area                     | Period 1 (€ m) | Period 2 (€ m) |
|-------------------------------------|----------------|----------------|
| Cloud and software                  | 138            | 78             |
| Services                            | 246            | 142            |
| Research and development            | 429            | 210            |
| Sales and marketing                 | 562            | 312            |
| General and administration          | 461            | 88             |

**Key Observations**

1. **Share‑based payments are the largest single expense line**, accounting for roughly 39 % of total operating costs in Period 1 and 33 % in Period 2.  
2. **Cash‑settled share‑based payments constitute the overwhelming majority** of this category (≈ 91 % of share‑based expenses in both periods).  
3. The other functional areas—particularly sales & marketing and general & administration—show notable reductions from Period 1 to Period 2, while research & development and services also decline but remain significant cost drivers.  

**Contextual Insight**  
The company’s disclosures note that in 2019 it incurred €79 million in share‑based payments that became fully vested due to terminations linked to a restructuring plan. These termination‑related payments, together with expense portions initially allocated to future services, were classified under share‑based payments rather than as restructuring expenses. This accounting treatment helps explain the elevated share‑based payment figures, especially the cash‑settled component, observed in the periods presented.

**Conclusion**  
Across the two periods, the expense profile is heavily weighted toward share‑based payments, driven largely by cash‑settled awards and, in part, by termination‑related vesting events. Understanding this composition is essential for analysts assessing the company’s cost structure and the impact of its compensation policies on operating profitability.

text.value: Deferred Taxes The components of the net deferred tax liability are as follows:

Deferred income taxes are provided for the temporary differences between assets and liabilities recognized for financial reporting purposes and assets and liabilities recognized for tax purposes. The ultimate realization of deferred tax assets depends upon taxable income during the future periods in which those temporary differences become deductible.

To determine whether deferred tax assets can be realized, management assesses whether it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized, taking into consideration the scheduled reversal of deferred tax liabilities, projected future taxable income and tax-planning strategies.

Consolidated and its wholly owned subsidiaries, which file a consolidated federal income tax return, estimates it has available federal NOL carryforwards as of December 31, 2019 of $349.5 million and related deferred tax assets of $73.4 million.

The federal NOL carryforwards for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017 of $60.7 million and related deferred tax assets of $12.8 million can be carried forward indefinitely. The federal NOL carryforwards for the tax years prior to December 31, 2017 of $288.8 million and related deferred tax assets of $60.6 million expire in 2026 to 2035.

ETFL, a nonconsolidated subsidiary for federal income tax return purposes, estimates it has available NOL carryforwards as of December 31, 2019 of $1.0 million and related deferred tax assets of $0.2 million. ETFL’s federal NOL carryforwards are for the tax years prior to December 31, 2017 and expire in 2021 to 2024.

We estimate that we have available state NOL carryforwards as of December 31, 2019 of $758.5 million and related deferred tax assets of $16.7 million. The state NOL carryforwards expire from 2020 to 2039. Management believes that it is more likely than not that we will not be able to realize state NOL carryforwards of $80.3 million and related deferred tax asset of $5.2 million and has placed a valuation allowance on this amount.

The related NOL carryforwards expire from 2020 to 2037. If or when recognized, the tax benefits related to any reversal of the valuation allowance will be accounted for as a reduction of income tax expense.

The enacted Tax Act repeals the federal alternative minimum tax (“AMT”) regime for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017. We have available AMT credit carryforwards as of December 31, 2019 of $1.5 million, which will be fully refundable with the filing of the 2019 federal income tax return in 2020.

We estimate that we have available state tax credit carryforwards as of December 31, 2019 of $7.7 million and related deferred tax assets of $6.1 million. The state tax credit carryforwards are limited annually and expire from 2020 to 2029.

Management believes that it is more likely than not that we will not be able to realize state tax carryforwards of $1.8 million and related deferred tax asset of $1.5 million and has placed a valuation allowance on this amount. The related state tax credit carryforwards expire from 2020 to 2024. If or when recognized, the tax benefits related to any reversal of the valuation allowance will be accounted for as a reduction of income tax expense.

synth_text.title: Non‑Current Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities: 2019 vs. 2018 – Key Changes and Realizability Assessment
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The consolidated balance sheet shows a detailed composition of non‑current deferred tax assets and liabilities for the years ended 31 December 2019 and 2018 (amounts in thousands). The most significant shift between the two years is the movement from a net deferred tax liability in 2018 to a modest net deferred tax asset position in 2019.

**1. Net Deferred Tax Assets**  
| Component | 2019 | 2018 |
|-----------|------|------|
| Reserve for uncollectible accounts | $1,194 | $1,164 |
| Accrued vacation pay (deducted when paid) | $4,152 | $4,371 |
| Accrued expenses & deferred revenue | $9,839 | $12,848 |
| **Net operating loss (NOL) carryforwards** | **$86,535** | **$76,659** |
| Pension & post‑retirement obligations | $80,245 | $84,786 |
| Share‑based compensation | $693 | $9 |
| Derivative instruments | $5,868 | $(825) |
| Financing costs | $176 | $189 |
| Tax‑credit carryforwards | $6,077 | $6,411 |
| **Subtotal (before allowance)** | **$361,126** | **$364,583** |
| Valuation allowance | $(6,680) | $(9,158) |
| **Net non‑current deferred tax assets** | **$188,099** | **$176,454** |

*The NOL carryforwards are the largest single asset driver, increasing by $9.9 million year‑over‑year. The valuation allowance fell by $2.5 million, reflecting management’s improved view that a greater portion of these assets will be realized.*

**2. Net Deferred Tax Liabilities**  
| Component | 2019 | 2018 |
|-----------|------|------|
| Goodwill and other intangibles | $(66,271) | $(82,992) |
| Basis in investment | $(5) | $(12) |
| Partnership investments | $(16,138) | $(14,425) |
| Property, plant & equipment | $(278,712) | $(267,154) |
| **Net non‑current deferred tax liabilities** | **$(173,027)** | **$(188,129)** |

*Liabilities decreased by $15.1 million, mainly due to a reduction in the goodwill/intangible component.*

**3. Net Deferred Tax Position**  
- **2019:** $188,099 m (assets) – $173,027 m (liabilities) = **$15.1 m net deferred tax asset**  
- **2018:** $176,454 m (assets) – $188,129 m (liabilities) = **$11.7 m net deferred tax liability**

Thus, the company moved from a net liability to a modest net asset over the year.

**4. Realizability & Valuation Allowances**  
Deferred tax assets are contingent on future taxable income. Management applies a “more likely than not” test, considering:

* Scheduled reversals of deferred tax liabilities  
* Projected taxable income and tax‑planning strategies  
* Federal and state NOL carryforwards and tax‑credit carryforwards  

The additional context notes that:

* Federal NOL carryforwards total $349.5 m (with $73.4 m related deferred tax assets) as of 31 Dec 2019; a portion expires between 2026‑2035, while $60.7 m can be carried forward indefinitely.  
* State NOL carryforwards amount to $758.5 m (deferred tax assets $16.7 m), with an $80.3 m portion deemed unrealizable and placed under a valuation allowance.  
* AMT credit carryforwards of $1.5 m are fully refundable after the 2019 return.  
* State tax credit carryforwards of $7.7 m (deferred tax assets $6.1 m) have a $1.8 m portion subject to a valuation allowance.

These disclosures explain the reduction in the valuation allowance from 2018 to 2019, as some previously doubtful state NOL and tax‑credit assets are now expected to be realizable.

**5. Conclusions**  

* The company’s non‑current deferred tax asset base grew modestly, driven by higher NOL carryforwards and a lower valuation allowance.  
* Liability reductions, especially in goodwill and intangible balances, further improved the net position.  
* Management’s assessment of realizability, reflected in the decreased valuation allowance, suggests confidence in future taxable earnings and effective tax‑planning.  
* Ongoing monitoring of expiration schedules for federal and state NOL and tax‑credit carryforwards will be critical to maintaining the net deferred tax asset position.

Overall, the 2019 figures indicate a healthier deferred tax outlook compared with 2018, with a shift from a net liability to a net asset and a more favorable valuation‑allowance profile.

synth_text.title: Key Debt and Liquidity Metrics – Year‑End 2019 Summary
synth_text.text:
At 31 December 2019 the company’s debt profile showed a debt‑to‑assets ratio of **67.8 %**, reflecting the impact of the property revaluation deficit for the year. When the expected proceeds from the disposals of intu Puerto Venecia and intu Asturias are taken into account, the ratio improves to **65.3 %**.  

The **interest cover** stood at **1.67 ×**, comfortably above the company’s minimum target of **1.60 ×**, although it fell slightly due to reduced net rental income.  

The **weighted average debt maturity** was **5.0 years**, and the **weighted average cost of gross debt (excluding RCF)** was **4.3 %**. A high proportion of the debt – **88 %** – is protected against interest‑rate fluctuations.  

Immediately available cash and facilities decreased by **£5.3 million** over the year, ending the period at **£241.5 million**. This figure excludes rents collected at the end of December 2019, which are earmarked for the first quarter of 2020 and remain within the debt structure until interest payments are due. By **10 March 2020**, cash and facilities had fallen to **£200.3 million**, but are expected to be bolstered by the anticipated proceeds from the intu Puerto Venecia sale in early April.  

Overall, the metrics indicate a solid liquidity position with manageable leverage, supported by strong interest‑rate protection and forthcoming cash inflows.

synth_text.title: Key Debt and Liquidity Metrics – Year‑End Summary and Recent Changes
synth_text.text:
**Debt‑to‑Assets Ratio**  
- Current: 53.1 % of assets are financed by debt.  
- Change: The ratio fell by 38.4 percentage points year‑on‑year, reflecting the impact of recent asset disposals and a reduction in overall debt.  
- Context: In 2019 the ratio had risen to 67.8 % (adjusted to 65.3 % after accounting for expected proceeds from the intu Puerto Venecia and intu Asturias sales).

**Interest Cover**  
- Current: 1.91 ×, indicating that earnings before interest and tax cover interest obligations by almost two times.  
- Change: Interest cover decreased by 2.15 × year‑on‑year, moving from a comfortable level above the 1.60 × target to a lower, but still positive, position.  
- Context: The 2019 interest cover of 1.67 × remained above the company’s minimum threshold despite a dip caused by reduced net rental income.

**Weighted‑Average Debt Maturity**  
- Current: 5.8 years, showing a medium‑term debt profile.  
- Change: Maturity shortened by 6.6 years, reflecting the repayment of shorter‑term facilities and a shift toward longer‑dated borrowing.

**Weighted‑Average Cost of Gross Debt (ex‑RCF)**  
- Current: 4.2 % annualised cost.  
- Change: Cost fell marginally by 4.3 percentage points, indicating a modest improvement in borrowing terms.

**Interest‑Rate Protection**  
- Current: 84 % of gross debt is hedged against interest‑rate movements.  
- Change: The protected portion dropped by 80 percentage points, suggesting a re‑balancing of the hedging programme.

**Immediately Available Cash and Facilities**  
- Current: £246.8 million of cash and undrawn facilities are on hand.  
- Change: Cash fell by £5.3 million, leaving £241.5 million at 31 December 2019 and £200.3 million as of 10 March 2020. The shortfall is expected to be offset by the imminent sale proceeds from intu Puerto Venecia, due in early April.  

**Overall Assessment**  
The company’s debt profile has improved markedly, with a lower debt‑to‑assets ratio and a stronger cash position despite a modest decline in interest cover. The reduction in short‑term debt and the high proportion of interest‑rate protected borrowing provide additional resilience. Upcoming disposal proceeds are expected to further enhance liquidity and reduce leverage, supporting the firm’s financial targets.

synth_text.title: Overview of Plan Asset Movements, Returns, and Expected Contributions
synth_text.text:
The fair value of the company’s plan assets increased from €905 million at the start of the first reporting period to €1,066 million at the end of the second period.  

**Key drivers of the increase**

* **Interest income** contributed €21 million in the first period and €23 million in the second.  
* **Gains/losses on plan assets (excluding interest)** added €24 million and €102 million respectively, reflected in other comprehensive income under the re‑measurement of defined‑benefit plans.  
* **Employer contributions** amounted to €35 million in the first period and €18 million in the second, while **contributions from plan participants** were €11 million and €9 million.  

**Main outflows**

* **Benefit payments (including tax)** reduced the asset base by €34 million and €27 million.  
* **Settlement payments** were €6 million in the first period and nil in the second.  
* A **reclassification under IFRS 5** of €16 million was recorded in the first period, with no such effect in the second.  

**Other effects**

* A negative “other effects” entry of €10 million appeared only in the first period, while currency effects were neutral in the first period and a modest €1 million gain in the second.

**Actual return and future expectations**

The actual return on plan assets for the reporting period was €125 million, a substantial increase from €45 million in 2017/18. Looking ahead to FY 2019/20, the company anticipates employer payments to external pension providers of approximately €18 million and employee contributions of €9 million, primarily from the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. Contributions arising from payment‑commitment obligations in Germany are excluded from this forecast.

**Special note on over‑funding**

At one Dutch subsidiary, plan assets exceeded the value of the related pension commitments at the reporting date. Because the company cannot realise economic benefits from this over‑funding, the balance‑sheet amount was reduced to €0 in accordance with IAS 19.64(b).

Overall, the growth in plan‑asset fair value reflects strong investment performance, continued employer and employee funding, and the impact of accounting adjustments, while benefit and settlement outflows partially offset these gains.

synth_text.text:

synth_text.title: Reconciliation of American Tower Corporation’s Unrecognized Tax Benefits for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
American Tower Corporation (including its subsidiaries) reports its unrecognized tax benefits—liabilities for uncertain tax positions—on a yearly basis. The reconciliation for the two most recent fiscal years is summarized below:

| Year | Balance at Jan 1 | Additions (current‑year tax positions) | Adjustments (prior‑year positions) | Foreign‑currency effect | Reduction – statute of limitations | Reduction – effective settlements | Balance at Dec 31 |
|------|------------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|-------------------|
| 2019 | $107.7 million | $33.3 million | $37.5 million | $(1.6) million | $(1.3) million | — | $175.6 million |

* The liability grew by $67.9 million in 2019, driven primarily by sizable additions for both current‑year ($33.3 M) and prior‑year ($37.5 M) tax positions.

* Reductions from statutes of limitations lapsed amounted to $1.3 M in 2019 and $2.6 M in 2018; effective settlements eliminated the $6.7 M reduction seen in 2018, while no settlement reduction occurred in 2019.  
* Overall, the ending balance rose from $107.7 million at 12/31/2018 to $175.6 million at 12/31/2019.

**Contextual insights**

text.value: A.4.1 Orders and revenue by region

Positive currency translation effects added one percentage point each to order and revenue growth; portfolio transactions had only minimal effects on volume growth year-over-year. The resulting ratio of orders to revenue (book-to-bill) for Siemens in fiscal 2019 was a strong 1.13, again well above 1. The order backlog was € 146 billion as of September 30, 2019, a new high.
1 As defined by the International Monetary Fund.

Orders related to external customers were clearly up year-overyear on growth in nearly all industrial businesses, led by Mobility. Gas and Power, Siemens Healthineers, Smart Infrastructure and SGRE all posted clear growth, while orders declined slightly in Digital Industries. Volume from large orders for Industrial Businesses overall was up substantially due to a sharp increase at Mobility, but also due to a significant increase in SGRE and Gas and Power. Growth in emerging markets was driven by orders from China, and from Russia where Mobility won a € 1.2 billion contract for high-speed trains including maintenance.

Order development was mixed in the Europe, C. I. S., Africa, Middle East region. The majority of industrial businesses posted order growth, led by double-digit growth in Mobility, which won several large contracts in the year under review. This increase was more than offset by a substantial decline in SGRE due mainly to a lower volume from large orders and a decrease in Digital Industries. In contrast to the region overall, orders were up clearly in Germany, driven by sharp growth in Gas and Power which recorded, among others, a large high voltage direct current (HVDC) order. Mobility recorded a significant increase in order intake in Germany, while the other industrial businesses posted declines.

Orders in the Americas region were up significantly year-over-year, benefiting from positive currency translation effects. Double-digit growth in nearly all industrial businesses was led by SGRE and Mobility with particularly sharp increases. The pattern of order development in the U. S. was largely the same as in the Americas region.

In the Asia, Australia region, orders also rose significantly due to growth in nearly all industrial businesses. The primary growth driver was SGRE, which recorded a sharply higher volume from large orders, including two large orders for offshore wind-farms
including service in Taiwan totaling € 2.3 billion. Orders for Mobility dropped substantially compared to the prior year. Clear growth in China included a majority of industrial businesses.

synth_text.title: Siemens Revenue Growth by Region in FY 2019: Strong Gains in the Americas, Asia‑Australia and Germany
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 Siemens generated €97.999 billion in revenue, a 7 % increase over the €91.296 billion recorded in 2018. The rise was driven by robust performance across most regions, reinforced by positive currency translation effects and a healthy order pipeline (book‑to‑bill ratio = 1.13, order backlog €146 billion).

**Regional revenue performance**

| Region (2019) | 2019 (€ m) | 2018 (€ m) | Δ (%) |
|---------------|-----------|-----------|------|
| Europe, CIS, Africa, Middle East | 46 086 | 46 495 | –0.9 % |
| – Germany (key sub‑region) | 12 021 | 11 254 | +6.8 % |
| Americas | 29 812 | 25 060 | +19.0 % |
| – United States | 21 166 | 18 106 | +16.9 % |
| Asia, Australia | 22 101 | 19 742 | +11.9 % |
| – China | 8 989 | 8 459 | +6.3 % |
| Emerging markets* | 31 720 | 30 564 | +3.8 % |
| **Total Siemens** | **97 999** | **91 296** | **+7.3 %** |

*Emerging markets are defined by the International Monetary Fund.

**Key insights**

* **Americas** delivered the strongest revenue lift (+19 %), reflecting double‑digit order growth in most industrial businesses, especially SGRE and Mobility. The United States mirrored this trend.
* **Asia‑Australia** also posted solid growth (+12 %), led by SGRE’s offshore‑wind orders, although Mobility’s revenue fell sharply in the region.
* **Germany** outperformed the broader Europe‑CIS‑Africa‑Middle‑East area, with a 7 % increase driven by Gas & Power (notably a large HVDC order) and Mobility.
* The wider **Europe, CIS, Africa, Middle East** region saw a marginal decline (‑1 %) as SGRE’s volume fell and Digital Industries contracted, offsetting Mobility’s double‑digit gains.
* **Emerging markets** continued to expand, buoyed by strong Chinese orders and a €1.2 billion high‑speed‑train contract in Russia.

Overall, the revenue picture aligns with the reported order dynamics: robust growth in Mobility, SGRE, and Gas & Power, modest setbacks in Digital Industries, and a diversified geographic mix that lifted Siemens’ total turnover while maintaining a strong order backlog.

synth_text.title: Siemens FY 2019 Order and Revenue Distribution by Region – Key Highlights
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 Siemens recorded a diversified order and revenue mix across its global markets. According to the actual figures, the Americas accounted for the largest share at **19 %**, with the United States alone contributing **17 %**. The comparable (previous‑year) share for the Americas was **14 %**, and the U.S. **10 %**, indicating a notable increase year‑over‑year.

The **Asia‑Australia** region followed with **12 %** of total orders (up from **11 %** comparable). Growth in this market was driven primarily by the wind‑energy business (SGRE), which secured large offshore‑wind contracts, while Mobility saw a decline.

In **Europe, CIS, Africa and the Middle East** the share remained modest at **(1)%** (both actual and comparable). Within Europe, **Germany** consistently contributed **7 %** of orders, reflecting strong performance in Gas & Power and Mobility, despite an overall mixed regional trend caused by a downturn in SGRE and Digital Industries.

**China** maintained a steady **6 %** share across both periods, and **emerging markets** (as defined by the IMF) contributed **4 %**. Siemens‑wide, the company’s own share rose from **6 %** (comparable) to **7 %** (actual), underscoring a slight overall improvement.

The regional dynamics were reinforced by several macro‑ and business‑specific factors highlighted in the accompanying report:
- Positive currency translation added roughly one percentage point to order and revenue growth.
- The book‑to‑bill ratio reached a robust **1.13**, and the order backlog hit a record **€146 billion** as of 30 September 2019.
- Mobility, SGRE, and Gas & Power were the primary growth engines, with notable contracts such as a €1.2 billion high‑speed‑train deal in Russia and a €2.3 billion offshore‑wind order in Taiwan.
- Europe’s mixed performance stemmed from double‑digit growth in Mobility offset by a decline in SGRE and Digital Industries, whereas the Americas and Asia‑Australia regions experienced broad‑based growth across most industrial businesses.

Overall, Siemens’ FY 2019 order and revenue profile reflects a balanced global footprint, with the Americas and Asia‑Australia driving the strongest growth, Germany delivering consistent performance within Europe, and emerging markets contributing steadily to the company’s expanding international presence.

synth_text.title: Summary of Service Costs, Past Service Costs, and Actuarial Losses Recognised in the SOCI
synth_text.text:
The table outlines two distinct sets of pension‑related charges that have been recorded in the consolidated income statement and the consolidated statement of comprehensive income (SOCI).

| Item | First Set | Second Set |
|------|-----------|------------|
| Current service cost | €31 million | €34 million |
| Past service costs¹ | €16 million | €2 million |
| Net interest charge | €10 million | €8 million |
| Total included within staff costs | €57 million | €44 million |
| Actuarial losses recognised in the SOCI | €33 million | €94 million |

**Key observations**

1. **Past service costs** – The first set records a past service cost of €16 million, which directly reflects the pre‑tax amount disclosed in the additional context. This amount stems from a High Court judgment (21 October 2018) that required the Group to equalise guaranteed minimum pension (GMP) benefits for men and women, leading to the €16 million (≈ £14 million) charge for the year ended 31 March 2019. The second set shows a much lower past service cost of €2 million, indicating a different set of assumptions or a later reporting period.

2. **Current service cost** – The second set has a slightly higher current service cost (€34 million) compared with the first set (€31 million), suggesting an increase in the cost of benefits accrued during the reporting period.

3. **Net interest charge** – Both sets record modest net interest charges, with the first set at €10 million and the second set at €8 million.

4. **Staff‑cost inclusion** – The total amount allocated to staff costs is higher in the first set (€57 million) than in the second set (€44 million), driven primarily by the larger past service cost and actuarial loss in the first set.

5. **Actuarial losses** – A notable disparity exists in actuarial losses recognised in the SOCI: €33 million in the first set versus €94 million in the second set. The higher loss in the second set indicates a more adverse actuarial assumption or a larger deviation between expected and actual scheme experience.

Overall, the data illustrate how the High Court‑driven past service cost of €16 million significantly influences the first set of figures, raising both the total staff‑cost inclusion and the overall charge to the SOCI. The second set, with lower past service costs but substantially higher actuarial losses, reflects a different risk profile and assumption set for the pension scheme.

text.value: B. Liquidity and Capital Resources

As of June 30, 2019, we had cash and cash equivalents totaling $1.3 billion, short-term investments totaling $445.0 million and trade receivables totaling $82.5 million. Since our inception, we have primarily financed our operations through cash flows generated by operations.
Our cash flows from operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities for the fiscal years ended 2019, 2018 and 2017 were as follows:

We believe that our existing cash and cash equivalents, together with cash generated from operations, will be sufficient to meet our anticipated cash needs for at least the next 12 months. Our future capital requirements will depend on many factors including our growth rate, the timing and extent of spend on research and development efforts, employee headcount, marketing and sales activities, acquisitions of additional businesses and technologies, the timing and extent of exchange of the Notes for payments of cash, the introduction of new software and services offerings, enhancements to our existing software and services offerings and the continued market acceptance of our products.

Cash provided by operating activities has historically been affected by the amount of net income (loss) adjusted for non-cash expense items such as non-coupon impact related to the Notes and capped calls, depreciation and amortization and expense associated with share-based awards, the timing of employee-related costs such as bonus payments, collections from our customers, which is our largest source of operating cash flows, and changes in other working capital accounts.

Accounts impacting working capital consist of trade receivables, prepaid expenses and other current assets, current derivative assets, trade and other payables, provisions, current derivative liabilities, current portion of our Notes and other current liabilities. Our working capital may be impacted by various factors in future periods, such as billings to customers for subscriptions, licenses and maintenance services and the subsequent collection of those billings or the amount and timing of certain expenditures.

Net cash provided by operating activities was $466.3 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019, as a result of $605.6 million in loss before income tax expense adjusted by non-cash charges including the loss of marking to fair value of the embedded exchange feature of the Notes and related capped call transactions of $533.9 million, depreciation and amortization of $70.2 million, share-based payment expense of $257.8 million and debt discount and issuance cost amortization of $33.9 million. The net increase of $169.0 million from our operating assets and liabilities was primarily attributable to a $122.5 million increase in our deferred revenue as a result of increased sales of subscriptions and renewals of maintenance contracts and a $75.6 million increase in trade and other payables, provisions and other non-current liabilities, offset by a $30.2 million increase in trade receivables. Net cash provided by operating activities was also impacted by tax refunds received, net of income tax paid of $7.0 million.

Net cash provided by operating activities was $311.5 million for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2018, as a result of $58.1 million in loss before income tax expense adjusted by non-cash charges including the loss of marking to fair value of the embedded exchange feature of the Notes and related capped call transactions of $12.4 million, depreciation and amortization of $79.4 million, share-based payment expense of $162.9 million and debt discount and issuance cost amortization of $7.5 million. The net increase of $113.1 million from our operating assets and liabilities was primarily attributable to a $97.7 million increase in our deferred revenue as a result of increased sales of subscriptions and renewals of maintenance contracts, a $43.5 million increase in trade and other payables, provisions and other noncurrent liabilities, offset by a $19.6 million increase in trade receivables and a $8.4 million increase in prepaid expenses and other current and non-current assets. Net cash provided by operating activities was also impacted by income taxes paid, net of refunds, of $4.2 million.

Net cash used in investing activities during the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019 was $604.2 million. This was primarily related to cash paid for business combinations, net of cash acquired, totaling $418.6 million, purchases of investments totaling $648.0 million and purchases of property and equipment totaling $44.2 million to support the growth of our business, including hardware, equipment and leasehold improvements, offset by cash received from the maturing of investments which totaled $485.0 million and proceeds from sales of investments of $20.5 million.

Net cash used in investing activities during the fiscal year ended June 30, 2018 was $51.7 million. This was primarily related to purchases of investments totaling $347.8 million and purchases of property and equipment totaling $30.2 million to support the growth of our business, including hardware, equipment and leasehold improvements, offset by cash received from the maturing of investments which totaled $206.1 million and proceeds from sales of investments of $123.9 million.

Net cash used in financing activities for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019 was $3.2 million and was primarily related to coupon interest payments on the Notes of $6.3 million, offset by proceeds from exercises of employee share options of $3.5 million.

Net cash provided by financing activities for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2018 was $906.8 million and was primarily related to proceeds from the issuance of our Notes of $990.5 million offset by the purchase of the capped calls for $87.7 million.

synth_text.title: Cash‑Flow Summary and Liquidity Outlook for Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Cash‑flow performance (in U.S. $ thousands)**  

| Fiscal year (ended June 30) | Operating activities | Investing activities | Financing activities | Net change in cash & equivalents |
|-----------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **2019**                     | **$466,342** (cash provided) | **$(604,198)** (cash used) | **$(3,187)** (net cash used) | **$(141,898)** (decrease) |
| **2018**                     | **$311,456** (cash provided) | **$(51,696)** (cash used)  | **$906,789** (cash provided) | **$1,165,919** (increase) |

**Key observations**

1. **Operating cash generation**  
   * 2019: $466.3 M was generated, driven by a $605.6 M loss before tax offset by large non‑cash charges (e.g., $533.9 M fair‑value loss on embedded exchange features, $70.2 M depreciation, $257.8 M share‑based compensation). Increases in deferred revenue ($122.5 M) and payables ($75.6 M) also contributed.  
   * 2018: $311.5 M was generated, reflecting a $58.1 M loss before tax plus non‑cash adjustments (e.g., $12.4 M fair‑value loss, $79.4 M depreciation, $162.9 M share‑based compensation). Deferred revenue rose $97.7 M and payables $43.5 M.

2. **Investing cash outflows**  
   * 2019: $604.2 M was used, mainly for business‑combination payments ($418.6 M), investment purchases ($648.0 M) and property/equipment ($44.2 M). These were partially offset by $485.0 M of maturing investments and $20.5 M sales of investments.  
   * 2018: $51.7 M was used, primarily for investment purchases ($347.8 M) and property/equipment ($30.2 M), offset by $206.1 M maturing investments and $123.9 M proceeds from investment sales.

3. **Financing cash flows**  
   * 2019: A modest net outflow of $3.2 M, mainly coupon interest payments on notes ($6.3 M) offset by $3.5 M from employee share‑option exercises.  
   * 2018: A large inflow of $906.8 M, primarily from the issuance of notes ($990.5 M) less the purchase of capped calls ($87.7 M).

4. **Liquidity position**  
   * As of June 30 2019 the company held $1.3 B in cash and cash equivalents plus $445 M in short‑term investments.  
   * The firm emphasizes that operating cash generation, together with existing cash resources, is expected to satisfy cash needs for at least the next 12 months. Future capital requirements will depend on growth, R&D spending, acquisitions, and other strategic initiatives.

**Conclusion**  
The cash‑flow statement shows that while operating activities consistently provide substantial cash, the dramatic swing in financing cash between 2018 and 2019 reflects a one‑time financing event (note issuance) in 2018. Investing activities are heavily weighted toward acquisitions and investment purchases, explaining the sizable cash outflows. Overall, the company’s strong operating cash generation and sizable cash balances underpin a solid liquidity outlook for the near term.

synth_text.title: Principal Accounting Assumptions for Premier and RHM Pension Schemes (Balance‑Sheet Date)
synth_text.text:
At the balance‑sheet date, the principal accounting assumptions for the two UK‑based pension arrangements – Premier schemes and RHM schemes – are identical:

- **Discount rate:** 2.45 %  
- **Inflation assumptions:** 3.25 % (Retail Price Index) and 2.15 % (Consumer Price Index)  
- **Expected salary increases:** not applicable (n/a)  
- **Future pension increases:** 2.10 %

These assumptions are applied uniformly across both schemes.

For comparison, the smaller overseas schemes use more conservative figures: a discount rate of 1.50 % (down from 1.80 % in 2017/18) and future pension increases of 1.30 % (down from 1.45 % in 2017/18).  

The discount rate for all schemes is derived from a bond‑yield curve that has been expanded to incorporate bonds rated AA by one credit agency (which may be rated A or AAA by other agencies). This approach ensures that the discount rate reflects a broad range of high‑quality government and corporate bond yields.

Overall, the Premier and RHM schemes rely on a higher discount rate and a higher projected pension increase than the overseas schemes, reflecting differences in market conditions and actuarial assumptions across jurisdictions.

synth_text.title: Principal Accounting Assumptions for Premier and RHM Pension Schemes (2019)
synth_text.text:
At the balance‑sheet date, the principal accounting assumptions for the Premier and RHM pension schemes were identical. Both schemes used a discount rate of **2.70 %**, inflation assumptions of **3.15 % (RPI)** and **2.05 % (CPI)**, and projected **future pension increases of 2.10 %**. No expected salary increases were applied to either scheme.

These assumptions differ from those applied to the smaller overseas schemes, which employed a lower discount rate of **1.50 %** (down from 1.80 % in 2017/18) and a reduced future pension increase of **1.30 %** (down from 1.45 % in 2017/18).

The 2.70 % discount rate for the Premier and RHM schemes was derived from a bond‑yield curve that was expanded to include bonds rated AA by one credit agency (these bonds might be rated A or AAA by other agencies). This approach ensures that the discount rate reflects a broader range of high‑quality bond yields.  

Overall, the consistent assumptions across the two main schemes provide a clear basis for valuation, while the distinct treatment of overseas schemes reflects their different risk and inflation profiles.

synth_text.title: Income Tax Provision Reconciliation Summary for the Two Most Recent Fiscal Years
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table reconciles the reported income‑tax benefit (or provision) to the amount that would result from applying the U.S. statutory corporate tax rate. The reconciliation covers two fiscal years ending September 30 (the later year shows a $3.3 million benefit, while the prior year records a $3.1 million expense).

**Key Adjustments – Later Fiscal Year**  
- **Statutory‑rate amount:** $841 k  
- **Major positive adjustments:**  
  - Research & development credits: +$1,694 k  
  - Stock‑compensation expense (net): +$1,539 k  
- **Major negative adjustments:**  
  - Net change in valuation allowance for deferred tax assets: –$459 k  
  - State income tax: –$370 k  
  - Foreign income tax: –$494 k  
  - Non‑deductible items: –$151 k  
- **Resulting provision:** $3,264 k (tax benefit)

**Key Adjustments – Prior Fiscal Year**  
- **Statutory‑rate amount:** $2,122 k  
- **Major negative adjustments:**  
  - Impact of the 2017 tax reform on deferred taxes: –$4,901 k (the single largest driver)  
  - Net change in valuation allowance for deferred tax assets: –$367 k  
  - AMT and other: –$191 k  
  - Non‑deductible items: –$276 k  
- **Minor positive adjustments:**  
  - State income tax: +$50 k  
  - Research & development credits: +$475 k  
- **Resulting provision:** –$3,066 k (tax expense)

**Interpretation**  
- The later year’s provision is driven primarily by sizable R&D credits and stock‑compensation deductions, which more than offset valuation‑allowance reductions and state/foreign tax liabilities.  
- In the prior year, the reform‑related deferred‑tax impact overwhelmingly turned the provision into an expense, outweighing all other adjustments.  

**Conclusion**  
The reconciliation demonstrates how various permanent and temporary tax items—particularly R&D credits, stock‑compensation, valuation‑allowance changes, and the 2017 tax‑reform effects—cause the reported income‑tax benefit (or expense) to diverge significantly from a simple statutory‑rate calculation.

synth_text.title: Income Tax Provision Reconciliation Summary – Year Ended September 30 2019
synth_text.text:
The income‑tax provision for the fiscal year ended September 30 2019 amounts to **$10,921 thousand**. This figure results from a detailed reconciliation of the statutory tax computation and several adjustment items:

* **Statutory rate computation:** $(1,078) k – the tax that would have been due using the U.S. federal statutory rate.  
* **Net change in valuation allowance for net deferred tax assets:** $10,058 k – the primary positive driver, reflecting a significant reduction in the allowance for future tax benefits.  
* **Research and development credits:** $2,494 k – additional tax savings generated from qualifying R&D activities.  
* **AMT and other:** $20 k – a modest positive adjustment.  
* **Foreign rate differential:** $(169) k – a negative adjustment related to differences between foreign and U.S. tax rates.  
* **Non‑deductible items:** $(370) k – items that cannot be deducted for tax purposes.

synth_text.title: Summary of Net Other Gains (2019 vs 2020) – Key Drivers and Component Breakdown
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The “Other Gains, Net” line item reflects a mixture of investment‑related earnings, government incentives, and other miscellaneous items. Two consecutive reporting periods are shown:

| Component | 2019 (RMB mn) | 2020 (RMB mn) |
|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| Net gains on disposals and deemed disposals of investee companies (Note a) | 8,492 | 2,932 |
| Net fair‑value gains on FVPL (Note b) | 9,511 | 28,738 |
| Subsidies and tax rebates | 4,263 | 3,456 |
| Impairment provision / reversal for investee companies and intangible assets (Note c) | (4,006) | (17,577) |
| Net fair‑value gains on other financial instruments (Notes 27 & 38) | 1,647 | 1,019 |
| Dividend income | 1,014 | 686 |
| Donations to Tencent Charity Funds | (850) | (730) |
| Others | (382) | (1,810) |
| **Total Other Gains, Net** | **19,689** | **16,714** |

**Key drivers in 2019**  
- **Disposal gains (RMB 8.5 bn)** were primarily the result of:  
  1. Dilution of the Group’s equity stakes in internet‑related associates following new share issuances (≈ RMB 4.9 bn).  
  2. Direct or partial disposals of various investments (≈ RMB 3.6 bn).  
- **FVPL fair‑value gains (RMB 9.5 bn)** came from:  
  1. Re‑classification of several internet‑focused investments from FVPL to associate status after conversion of redeemable instruments (≈ RMB 1.9 bn).  
  2. Pure fair‑value movements of FVPL holdings (≈ RMB 7.6 bn).  
- Government subsidies and tax rebates added RMB 4.3 bn, while an impairment reversal of RMB 4.0 bn partially offset the total.

**Key drivers in 2020**  
- **FVPL fair‑value gains surged to RMB 28.7 bn**, reflecting stronger market appreciation of the Group’s FVPL portfolio.  
- **Disposal gains fell to RMB 2.9 bn**, indicating fewer divestments or dilution events compared with the prior year.  
- **Impairment provision rose sharply to RMB 17.6 bn**, largely erasing the net gain advantage from higher FVPL performance.  
- Subsidies, dividend income, and charitable donations remained broadly stable, while “Others” turned more negative, contributing to a lower overall net figure.

**Conclusion**  
While 2019’s net other gains were driven by a balanced mix of disposal proceeds, fair‑value appreciation, and modest impairments, 2020 saw a pronounced increase in FVPL gains that was more than offset by a substantial impairment charge. The result was a modest decline in the total net other gains from RMB 19.7 bn to RMB 16.7 bn. Government subsidies and charitable contributions continued to play a relatively small but consistent role in the composition of this line item.

synth_text.title: 2017 Reconciliation of GAAP Net Income to Adjusted EBITDA (Non‑GAAP)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table reconciles the company’s fiscal‑year‑2017 (ended March 31, 2018) U.S. GAAP net income to a non‑GAAP Adjusted EBITDA figure, illustrating the adjustments applied to arrive at a performance metric that excludes certain accounting items.

**Key Figures**  

| Item | Amount (in $ thousands) |
|------|------------------------|
| GAAP Net Income | **$47,157** |
| Income Tax Expense (added back) | $4,294 |
| Interest Expense, Net (added back) | $39,731 |
| Depreciation & Amortization (added back) | $38,151 |
| **GAAP EBITDA (non‑GAAP)** | **$129,333** |
| Equity loss from equity‑method investments | $(41,643) |
| Change in value of TOKIN options | $(10,700) |
| Gain on disposal of long‑lived assets | $10,671 |
| ERP integration / IT transition costs | $7,045 |
| Stock‑based compensation | $4,720 |
| Restructuring charges | $5,404 |
| Legal expenses/fines (antitrust) | $2,640 |
| Net foreign exchange loss | $(3,758) |
| TOKIN investment‑related expenses | $1,101 |
| Plant start‑up costs | $427 |
| **Adjusted EBITDA (non‑GAAP)** | **$105,240** |

**Interpretation**  
Starting from GAAP net income, the company adds back major cash‑flow‑related expenses—taxes, interest, and depreciation—to compute a GAAP EBITDA of $129.3 million. It then subtracts several non‑GAAP items, most notably a $41.6 million equity loss and a $10.7 million reduction in the value of TOKIN options, while adding back modest gains and other costs. After these adjustments, the Adjusted EBITDA stands at $105.2 million, which the company uses as a key indicator of operating performance.

**Additional Context**  
- The fiscal years ending March 31, 2018 and 2017 were restated to reflect the adoption of ASC 606.  
- A note in later years reclassified $0.9 million of plant start‑up costs to restructuring charges; this reclassification does not affect the 2017 reconciliation.

**Conclusion**  
The reconciliation demonstrates how the company transforms GAAP net income into a non‑GAAP Adjusted EBITDA metric by excluding items that are non‑recurring, non‑cash, or not reflective of core operating performance, resulting in an Adjusted EBITDA of $105.2 million for fiscal year 2017.

synth_text.title: Reconciliation of GAAP Net Income to Adjusted EBITDA for Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table below reconciles U.S. GAAP Net income to non‑GAAP Adjusted EBITDA for the fiscal years ending March 31, 2018 and 2019 (amounts in thousands). Adjusted EBITDA adds back a set of non‑recurring items to provide a clearer view of operating performance.

**Key Financial Highlights**

| Item | FY 2019 | FY 2018 |
|------|---------|---------|
| Net income (U.S. GAAP) | **$206,587** | **$254,127** |
| Income tax expense (benefit) | **(39,460)** | **9,132** |
| Interest expense, net | **19,204** | **32,073** |
| Depreciation & amortization | **52,628** | **50,661** |
| EBITDA (non‑GAAP) | **$238,959** | **$345,993** |
| Adjusted EBITDA (non‑GAAP) | **$289,507** | **$191,705** |

**Adjustment Details**

* **Equity‑method income/loss** – A modest gain of $3,304 in 2019 replaces a $76,192 loss in 2018.  
* **Acquisition gain/loss** – No acquisition‑related impact in 2019, whereas 2018 recorded a $130,880 loss.  
* **ERP/IT integration costs** – Increased to $8,813 in 2019 from $80 in 2018.  
* **Stock‑based compensation** – Rose to $12,866 in 2019 from $7,657 in 2018.  
* **Restructuring charges** – Decreased to $8,779 in 2019 (after re‑classifying $0.9 million of plant start‑up costs) from $14,843 in 2018.  
* **R&D grant reimbursements** – A negative $4,559 in 2019; none reported in 2018.  
* **Legal expenses (antitrust class actions)** – $11,896 in 2019 versus $16,636 in 2018.  
* **Net foreign‑exchange gain/loss** – A loss of $7,230 in 2019 compared with a gain of $13,145 in 2018.  
* **Loss on early extinguishment of debt** – $15,946 in 2019, a modest $486 in 2018.  

**Interpretation**

* Net income declined by roughly $47.5 million year‑over‑year, primarily due to a shift from a small tax benefit in 2018 to a $39.5 million tax expense in 2019 and higher interest costs.  
* EBITDA fell by $107 million, reflecting the lower net income and increased interest expense.  
* Adjusted EBITDA, however, rose by $97.8 million because the large negative equity‑method and acquisition adjustments recorded in 2018 were absent in 2019, and the 2019 loss on debt extinguishment was partially offset by other adjustments.  
* The re‑classification of $0.9 million of plant start‑up costs to restructuring charges (footnote 2) explains the higher restructuring figure in 2019.

**Footnotes**

1. Fiscal years ending March 31, 2018 and 2017 were restated to reflect ASC 606 adoption.  
2. $0.9 million of costs related to relocating the tantalum‑powder facility from Carson City, Nevada to Matamoros, Mexico were moved from “Plant start‑up costs” to “Restructuring charges” in FY 2019.

These reconciliations illustrate how non‑GAAP adjustments can materially affect the perception of operating performance, turning a lower GAAP net income into a higher Adjusted EBITDA in FY 2019.

text.value: Goodwill

Goodwill arises from the acquisition method of accounting for business combinations and represents the excess of the purchase price over the fair value of the net assets and other identifiable intangible assets acquired. The fair values of net tangible assets and intangible assets acquired are based upon preliminary valuations and the Company's estimates and assumptions are subject to change within the measurement period (potentially up to one year from the acquisition date).
The following table presents the changes in the carrying amount of goodwill for the periods indicated:

The Company performs an annual goodwill impairment assessment on October 31st each year, using a two-step quantitative assessment. Step one is the identification of potential impairment. This involves comparing the fair value of each reporting unit, which the Company has determined to be the entity itself, with its carrying amount, including goodwill.

If the fair value of a reporting unit exceeds the carrying amount, the goodwill of the reporting unit is considered not impaired and the second step of the impairment test is unnecessary. If the carrying amount of a reporting unit exceeds its fair value, the second step of the impairment test is performed to measure the amount of impairment loss, if any.

The Company determined there were no indications of impairment associated with goodwill. As a result,n o goodwill impairment was recognized as of October 31, 2019. In addition to its annual review, the Company performs a test of impairment when indicators of impairment are present. As of December 31, 2019, there were no indications of impairment of the Company’s goodwill balances.

The Group recognised £41.5m of estimated costs in the year associated with the equalisation of GMP for pension benefits accrued between 1990 and 1997. This follows a judgement case of Lloyds Banking Group on 26 October 2018 which referred to the equal treatment of men and women who contracted out of the State Earnings Related Pension Scheme between these dates.

It should be noted that the final cost will differ to the estimated cost when the actual method of equalisation is agreed between the scheme Trustees in due course. All UK companies who operated defined benefit pension schemes during these dates will be affected by this ruling.

Of this £41.5m non-cash charge, approximately two-thirds relates to the
RHM pension scheme and the balance relates to the Premier Foods pension schemes. Restructuring costs were £16.8m in the year; an £8.3m increase on the prior year and included circa £14m associated with the consolidation of the Group’s logistics operations to one central location in the year due to higher than anticipated implementation costs.

This programme has now completed and the Group does not expect to incur any further restructuring costs associated with this programme. Advisory fees associated with strategic reviews and corporate activity were also included in restructuring costs in the year. Other non-trading items of £1.9m refer to a past service pension credit of £3.9m due to inflation increases no longer required in a smaller Irish pension scheme, partly offset by costs related to the departure of previous CEO Gavin Darby.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance 2018/19: Operating Profit Collapse Driven by GMP Equalisation, Impairments and Restructuring Costs
synth_text.text:
The Group’s financial results for the year ended 2018/19 show a dramatic contraction in operating profit, falling from **£69.3 million** in the prior year to **£4.5 million**. This decline occurred even though **trading profit** rose modestly by **£5.5 million** to **£128.5 million**.

The increase in trading profit was largely offset by three non‑trading items:

1. **GMP equalisation charge – £41.5 million**  
   The Group recognised an estimated cost to equalise Guaranteed Minimum Pension (GMP) benefits accrued between 1990 and 1997, following a Lloyds Banking Group judgment. Approximately two‑thirds of this non‑cash charge relates to the RHM pension scheme, with the remainder linked to Premier Foods schemes. The final amount may vary once the trustees agree on the exact equalisation method.

2. **Impairment of goodwill and intangible assets – £30.6 million**  
   This impairment reflects the write‑down of acquired goodwill and intangible assets, contributing significantly to the profit shortfall.

3. **Restructuring costs – £16.8 million** (up £8.3 million YoY)  
   The higher cost includes about £14 million for consolidating logistics operations into a single location and advisory fees for strategic reviews. The restructuring programme is now complete, and no further costs of this nature are expected.

Other notable movements include:

* **Amortisation of intangible assets** fell by **£1.9 million** to **£34.4 million**, as several SAP software modules became fully amortised.  
* **Fair‑value movements on foreign exchange and derivatives** recorded a **£1.3 million** charge, compared with a modest £0.1 million credit in the prior year.  
* **Net interest on pensions and administrative expenses** was a **£1.3 million** charge, slightly lower than the **£2.5 million** expense recorded previously.  
* **Other non‑trading items** contributed **£1.9 million**, mainly a past‑service pension credit of £3.9 million offset by costs linked to the departure of the former CEO.

In summary, the 2018/19 operating profit collapse is primarily attributable to the one‑off GMP equalisation expense, a large goodwill and intangible‑asset impairment, and elevated restructuring costs, which together outweighed the modest improvement in core trading performance.

synth_text.title: 2018/19 Financial Performance Summary: Effects of GMP Equalisation, Impairments and Restructuring
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the year ended 2018/19 the Group generated a modest trading profit of **£5.5 million** and an Adjusted EBITDA of **£5.9 million**. After accounting for depreciation, amortisation, fair‑value adjustments and a series of significant non‑operating items, the operating result recorded in the raw statement was a loss of **£64.8 million**. Subsequent adjustments and credits reduced the headline operating profit to a small positive **£4.5 million**, as reported in the Group’s consolidated accounts.

**Key Profit Drivers**

| Item | Amount (£m) | Comment |
|------|-------------|---------|
| Trading profit | 5.5 | Core operating earnings before non‑trading items |
| Adjusted EBITDA | 5.9 | EBITDA after minor adjustments |
| Depreciation | (0.4) | Small charge |
| Amortisation of intangibles | 1.9 | Lower than the prior year because SAP software modules were fully amortised |
| Fair‑value movements (FX & derivatives) | (1.4) | Charge aligns with the £1.3 m fair‑value loss described in the narrative |
| Net interest on pensions & admin | 1.2 | Net of a £9.0 m interest credit from pension surplus |
| GMP equalisation | (41.5) | Estimated cost arising from a UK court ruling on gender‑pay equality for pension benefits accrued between 1990‑1997; two‑thirds relates to the RHM scheme, the remainder to Premier Foods |
| Restructuring costs | (8.3) | Includes £14 m logistics‑consolidation expense and advisory fees; the restructuring programme is now complete |
| Impairment of goodwill & intangibles | (24.1) | Reflects a write‑down of acquired assets; the narrative cites a total goodwill impairment of £30.6 m |
| Other non‑trading items | 1.9 | Primarily a past‑service pension credit of £3.9 m offset by costs linked to the former CEO’s departure |

**Explanation of the Operating Loss**  
The large **GMP equalisation charge (£41.5 m)** and the **goodwill/intangible impairment (£24.1 m)** are the principal reasons the operating profit appears negative in the line‑item table. Both are non‑cash, accounting adjustments triggered by external legal judgments and the reassessment of acquired asset values.  

Restructuring costs, although lower in the table (£8.3 m) than the total reported (£16.8 m), still contributed materially to the loss, mainly due to the consolidation of logistics operations and associated advisory fees.  

Fair‑value movements on foreign exchange and derivatives added a modest charge, while net interest on pensions slightly offset other expenses thanks of a surplus in the Group’s defined‑benefit schemes.

**Net Result**  
After all adjustments, the Group reported an **operating profit of £4.5 million**, a sharp decline from the **£69.3 million** recorded in the prior year. The decline is almost entirely explained by the one‑off GMP equalisation estimate, the goodwill impairment, and the higher restructuring outlay. The underlying trading performance remains modestly positive, indicating that the core business continues to generate earnings before the impact of these extraordinary items.
