text.value: The following table summarizes the change in fair value of the Level 3 liabilities with significant unobservable inputs (in thousands):
The money market accounts are included in our cash and cash equivalents in our consolidated balance sheets. Our money market assets are valued using quoted prices in active markets.

The liability for the subsidiary unit awards relates to agreements established with employees of our subsidiaries for cash awards contingent upon the subsidiary companies meeting certain financial milestones such as revenue, working capital, EBITDA and EBITDA margin. We account for these subsidiary awards using fair value and establish liabilities for the future payment for the repurchase of subsidiary units under the terms of the agreements based on estimating revenue, working capital, EBITDA and EBITDA margin of the subsidiary units over the periods of the awards through the anticipated repurchase dates. We estimated the fair value of each liability by using a Monte Carlo simulation model for determining each of the projected measures by using an expected distribution of potential outcomes. The fair value of each liability is calculated with thousands of projected outcomes, the results of which are averaged and then discounted to estimate the present value. At each reporting date until the respective payment dates, we will remeasure these liabilities, using the same valuation approach based on the applicable subsidiary's revenue and future collection of financed customer receivables, the unobservable inputs, and we will record any changes in the employee's compensation expense. Some of the awards are subject to the employees' continued employment and therefore, recorded on a straight-line basis over the remaining service period. During the year ended December 31, 2019, we settled $0.2 million of the liability related to the subsidiary unit awards. The remaining liability balances are included in either accounts payable, accrued expenses and other current liabilities or other liabilities in our consolidated balance sheets (see Note 13).

The contingent consideration liability consists of the potential earn-out payment related to our acquisition of 85% of the issued and outstanding capital stock of OpenEye on October 21, 2019. The earn-out payment is contingent on the satisfaction of certain calendar 2020 revenue targets and has a maximum potential payment of up to $11.0 million. We account for the contingent consideration using fair value and establish a liability for the future earn-out payment based on an estimation of revenue attributable to perpetual licenses and subscription licenses over the 2020 calendar year. We estimated the fair value of the liability by using a Monte Carlo simulation model for determining each of the projected measures by using an expected distribution of potential outcomes. The contingent consideration liability was valued with Level 3 unobservable inputs, including the revenue volatility and the discount rate. At October 21, 2019, the fair value of the liability was $2.8 million. At each reporting date until the payment date in 2021, we will remeasure the liability, using the same valuation approach. Changes in the fair value resulting from information that existed subsequent to the acquisition date are recorded in the consolidated statements of operations. During the year ended December 31, 2019, the contingent consideration liability decreased $0.2 million to $2.6 million as compared to the initial liability recorded at the acquisition date, primarily due to a change to OpenEye's 2020 projected revenue. The unobservable inputs used in the valuation as of December 31, 2019 included a revenue volatility of 45% and a discount rate of 3%. Selecting another revenue volatility or discount rate within an acceptable range would not result in a significant change to the fair value of the contingent consideration liability.
The contingent consideration liability is included in other liabilities in our consolidated balance sheet as of December 31, 2019 (see Note 13).

We monitor the availability of observable market data to assess the appropriate classification of financial instruments within the fair value hierarchy. Changes in economic conditions or model-based valuation techniques may require the transfer of financial instruments from one fair value level to another. In such instances, the transfer is reported at the beginning of the reporting period. There were no transfers between Levels 1, 2 or 3 during the years ended December 31, 2019, 2018 and 2017. We also monitor the value of the investments for other-than-temporary impairment on a quarterly basis. synth_text.title: Subsidiary Unit Awards Liability – 2019 Summary
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
During the fiscal year ended December 31, 2019 the liability for subsidiary unit awards decreased markedly from $3.16 million at the beginning of the period to $0.385 million at period end.

**Key movements**  

| Description | Amount (in $ thousands) |
|-------------|--------------------------|
| Beginning of period balance | 3,160 |
| Acquired liabilities | — |
| Changes in fair value (recorded in earnings) | +27 |
| Settlements (cash payments) | –2,802 |
| **End of period balance** | **385** |

**Nature of the liability**  
The subsidiary unit awards represent cash compensation promised to employees of our subsidiaries, contingent on the subsidiaries achieving specific financial milestones (revenue, working capital, EBITDA, EBITDA margin). The liability reflects the estimated present‑value cost of repurchasing subsidiary units under the award agreements.

**Valuation methodology**  
- Fair value is estimated using a Monte Carlo simulation that projects the underlying performance metrics across thousands of possible outcomes.  
- Projected outcomes are averaged and discounted to present value.  
- The liability is re‑measured at each reporting date; any change in fair value is recognized in compensation expense.  
- Some awards are amortized on a straight‑line basis over the remaining service period, while others depend on continued employment.

**Settlements**  
Cash settlements of $2.8 million were made during the year, reflecting payments to employees for the repurchase of subsidiary units. These settlements reduced the liability to the $385 thousand balance reported at year‑end.

**Financial statement impact**  
- The $27 thousand increase from fair‑value adjustments was recorded in earnings as compensation expense.  
- The $2.802 million settlement was recorded as a cash outflow and reduced the liability shown in the consolidated balance sheet (included in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities).

Overall, the substantial decline in the subsidiary unit awards liability was driven primarily by cash settlements, with a minor offset from fair‑value adjustments. The remaining balance of $385 thousand continues to be presented in the consolidated balance sheet under current liabilities.

synth_text.title: 2019 Summary of Level 3 Liabilities: Subsidiary Unit Awards and Contingent Consideration
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
During 2019 the company reported changes to two Level 3 liabilities that depend on significant unobservable inputs: (1) subsidiary unit awards and (2) the contingent consideration liability arising from the acquisition of OpenEye. Both liabilities are measured at fair value using Monte Carlo simulation models that project key financial metrics (revenue, working capital, EBITDA, EBITDA margin) and discount the results to present value. The fair‑value adjustments are recorded in earnings each reporting period.

**Subsidiary Unit Awards**  
- **Beginning balance (1 Jan 2019):** $385 k  
- **Acquired liabilities:** none were added during the year.  
- **Change in fair value (recorded in earnings):** –$14 k, reflecting a modest decline in the estimated present value of the awards.  
- **Settlements:** $200 k were paid in 2019, reducing the liability.  
- **Ending balance (31 Dec 2019):** $171 k, now classified within accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current or non‑current liabilities.

These awards are contingent on subsidiary performance milestones. The company re‑measures the liability at each reporting date using updated projections of the subsidiary’s financial measures; any change is reflected in compensation expense.

**Contingent Consideration Liability from Acquisitions**  
- **Beginning balance (1 Jan 2019):** $0 (the liability was first recognized at acquisition).  
- **Acquired liability (at acquisition, 21 Oct 2019):** $2,793 k, representing the fair‑value of the earn‑out tied to OpenEye’s 2020 revenue targets (maximum potential $11 m).  
- **Change in fair value (recorded in earnings):** –$198 k, primarily due to a downward revision of OpenEye’s projected 2020 revenue.  
- **Settlements:** none during 2019.  
- **Ending balance (31 Dec 2019):** $2,595 k, presented in other liabilities.

The contingent consideration is valued with Level 3 inputs, notably a revenue volatility of 45 % and a discount rate of 3 %. The liability will be re‑measured each period until the earn‑out payment date in 2021, with any fair‑value changes recognized in the consolidated statements of operations.

**Key Takeaways**  
- The subsidiary unit awards liability decreased by $214 k (settlements of $200 k plus a $14 k fair‑value decline).  
- The contingent consideration liability fell by $198 k, driven by revised revenue expectations, with no cash outflow in 2019.  
- Both liabilities remain classified as Level 3 and are subject to ongoing re‑measurement using the same Monte Carlo‑based valuation approach.  

These movements reflect the company’s active management of performance‑based obligations and acquisition‑related earn‑out commitments, ensuring that the reported balances represent the best estimate of future cash outflows as of year‑end.

synth_text.title: Breakdown of Effective Tax Rate Components and Influencing Factors for 2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s tax provision for the reporting period shows a statutory federal income tax rate of **35.0%**, while the **effective tax rate**—the tax expense expressed as a percentage of income before taxes—reached **52.8%**. This divergence results from a combination of items that either increase or decrease the overall tax burden:

| Component | Impact on Rate |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Tax Reform** | **+26.8** |
| **ISecG divestiture** | **+3.3** |
| **Other adjustments** | **+1.1** |
| **Non‑U.S. income taxed at different rates** | **‑7.6** |
| **Research & Development tax credits** | **‑2.3** |
| **Domestic manufacturing deduction** | **‑1.3** |
| **Foreign‑derived intangible income benefit** | — (no effect) |

**Key observations from the additional context**

1. **One‑time benefits drive the 2019 increase** – The rise in the effective tax rate for 2019, compared with 2018, is largely attributable to one‑time benefits that were present in 2018 but not in 2019. These benefits effectively lowered the 2018 effective rate, making the 2019 figure appear higher.

2. **Tax Reform and ISecG divestiture influence 2018** – The decline in the effective tax rate from 2017 to 2018 stemmed mainly from the initial tax expense associated with the Tax Reform legislation and the tax impact of the ISecG divestiture, both of which occurred in 2017. Their absence in 2018 contributed to a lower effective rate that year.

3. **Non‑U.S. income benefit** – The reduction of **‑7.6** points reflects lower tax rates on earnings from China, Hong Kong, Ireland, and Israel, where statutory rates range from **12.5% to 25.0%**. In China and Israel, additional conditional reduced rates apply when eligible activities and capital investments are made; these rates are set to expire through 2026, with renewal applications expected.

Overall, the effective tax rate of **52.8%** is the net result of statutory obligations (35.0%) plus the cumulative effect of the listed adjustments. Understanding each component clarifies why the effective rate deviates from the statutory baseline and highlights the impact of both permanent tax provisions and temporary, one‑off items.

synth_text.title: Effective Federal Tax Rate Analysis: Drivers of Change Across Two Fiscal Periods
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
Both fiscal periods were subject to the same statutory U.S. federal income tax rate of **21.0 %**. However, the **effective tax rates** differed markedly—**12.5 %** in the first period and **9.7 %** in the second—because of a series of statutory reductions and a few offsetting items.

**Key Adjustments Reducing the Statutory Rate**

| Adjustment | First Period | Second Period |
|------------|--------------|---------------|
| Non‑U.S. income taxed at lower rates* | **(3.7 %)** | **(3.6 %)** |
| Research & Development tax credits | **(2.3 %)** | **(2.7 %)** |
| Foreign‑Derived Intangible Income (FDII) deduction | **(3.2 %)** | **(3.7 %)** |
| Tax Reform effects | — | **(1.3 %)** |
| Other (net increase) | **+0.7 %** | **(0.1 %)** |
| Domestic manufacturing deduction | — | — |
| ISecG divestiture | — | — |

\*The non‑U.S. benefit mainly stems from operations in **China, Hong Kong, Ireland, and Israel**, where statutory rates range from **12.5 % to 25 %**. Conditional reduced rates in China and Israel are tied to eligible activities and capital investments and are set to expire through 2026, with renewals expected.

**Resulting Effective Tax Rates**  
- **First period:** 21.0 % – (3.7 % + 2.3 % + 3.2 %) + 0.7 % ≈ **12.5 %**  
- **Second period:** 21.0 % – (3.6 % + 2.7 % + 3.7 % + 1.3 %) – 0.1 % ≈ **9.7 %**

**Contextual Drivers of the Changes**  
- The **increase** in the effective rate for the first period (relative to the prior year) was largely due to **one‑time benefits that occurred in the earlier year**, which reduced the net tax benefit in the current period.  
- The **decrease** in the second period’s effective rate (compared with the year before) resulted from the **initial tax expense of the Tax Reform** and the **absence of the ISecG divestiture impact** that had been present in the earlier year. The overall reduction was further amplified by the combined effect of the statutory rate cut and the net impact of enacted or repealed tax provisions under Tax Reform.

**Conclusion**  
The effective federal tax rate fell from **12.5 % to 9.7 %** primarily because of larger tax benefits from **Tax Reform**, a slightly higher FDII deduction, and modestly increased R&D credits, while the non‑U.S. income benefit remained relatively stable. Understanding these components clarifies how statutory changes, one‑time events, and international operations together shape the company’s overall tax burden.

text.value: 6. Financial Instruments
The composition of financial instruments is as follows:

The fair values of the Company’s financial instrument is the amount that would be received in an asset sale or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between unaffiliated market participants and is recorded using a hierarchical disclosure framework based upon the level of subjectivity of the inputs used in measuring assets and liabilities. The levels are described below:

Level 1: Quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets that are accessible at the measurement date for assets or liabilities. Level 2: Observable prices that are based on inputs not quoted on active markets, but corroborated by market data. Level 3: Unobservable inputs are used when little or no market data is available.

The Company classifies its financial instrument within Level 2 of the fair value hierarchy on the basis of models utilizing market observable inputs. The interest rate swap has been valued on the basis of valuations provided by third-party pricing services, as derived from standard valuation or pricing models. Market-based observable inputs for the interest rate swap include one month LIBOR-based yield curves over the term of the swap. The Company reviews third-party pricing provider models, key inputs and assumptions and understands the pricing processes at its third-party providers in determining the overall reasonableness of the fair value of its Level 2 financial instruments. The Company also considers the risk of nonperformance by assessing the swap counterparty's credit risk in the estimate of fair value of the interest rate swap. As of December 31, 2019 and 2018, the Company has not made any adjustments to the valuations obtained from its third party pricing providers.

The company records warranty reserves to cover estimated costs of product returns and repairs under its standard 15‑ to 18‑month warranty period. Reserves are calculated using historical warranty expense data for each product line, and adjustments are made if actual return rates or repair costs diverge from these estimates.

**2017 Reserve Movements (in thousands of dollars)**  

- **Beginning balance:** $15,949  
- **Additions from current‑period sales:** $41,365  
- **Warranty costs incurred:** –$31,825 (deduction)  
- **Accruals from acquisitions:** $14,314  
- **Adjustments for foreign‑exchange and other factors:** –$3,654  

These items resulted in an **ending balance of $36,149** for the warranty reserve at the close of 2017.

The increase from the opening to the closing balance reflects strong sales‑related additions and acquisition accruals, partially offset by warranty claims and foreign‑exchange adjustments. Future periods may see further adjustments to cost of sales if actual warranty experience differs significantly from the estimates used to establish the reserve.

text.value: 10. Segment Information
The Company reports financial performance based on its segments, ACI On Premise and ACI On Demand, and analyzes Segment Adjusted EBITDA as a measure of segment profitability.

The Company’s interim Chief Executive Officer is also the chief operating decision maker ("CODM"). The CODM, together with other senior management personnel, focus their review on consolidated financial information and the allocation of resources based on operating results, including revenues and Segment Adjusted EBITDA, for each segment, separate from Corporate operations.

ACI On Premise serves customers who manage their software on site or through a third-party cloud service provider. These onpremise customers use the Company’s software to develop sophisticated solutions, which are often part of a larger system located and managed at the customer specified site. These customers require a level of control and flexibility that ACI On Premise solutions can offer, and they have the resources and expertise to take a lead role in managing these solutions.

ACI On Demand serves the needs of banks, merchants, and billers who use payments to facilitate their core business. These ondemand solutions are maintained and delivered through the cloud via our global data centers and are available in either a singletenant environment for SaaS offerings, or in a multi-tenant environment for PaaS offerings.

Revenue is attributed to the reportable segments based upon the product sold and mechanism for delivery to the customer. Expenses are attributed to the reportable segments in one of three methods, (1) direct costs of the segment, (2) labor costs that can be attributed based upon time tracking for individual products, or (3) costs that are allocated. Allocated costs are generally marketing and sales related activities as well as information technology and facilities related expense for which multiple segments benefit. The Company also allocates certain depreciation costs to the segments.

Segment Adjusted EBITDA is the measure reported to the CODM for purposes of making decisions on allocating resources and assessing the performance of the Company’s segments and, therefore, Segment Adjusted EBITDA is presented in conformity with ASC 280, Segment Reporting. Segment Adjusted EBITDA is defined as earnings (loss) from operations before interest, income tax expense (benefit), depreciation and amortization (“EBITDA”) adjusted to exclude stock-based compensation, and net other income (expense).

Corporate and unallocated expenses consist of the corporate overhead costs that are not allocated to reportable segments. These overhead costs relate to human resources, finance, legal, accounting, merger and acquisition activity, and other costs that are not considered when management evaluates segment performance. For the year ended December 31, 2017, corporate and unallocated expenses included $46.7 million of general and administrative expense for the legal judgment discussed in Note 15, Commitments and Contingencies.

synth_text.title: 2017 Financial Overview and Segment Performance Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the Company generated total revenue of **$1.024 billion**. Revenue was split between its two reportable segments:

* **ACI On Premise** – $2.234 million  
* **ACI On Demand** – $2.230 million  

These segments serve distinct customer bases: ACI On Premise delivers software that customers host on‑site or via a third‑party cloud, while ACI On Demand provides cloud‑based payment solutions to banks, merchants and billers.

Key expense and profit figures for the year were:

* **Corporate and unallocated expenses:** $(144.7 million)  
* **Interest, net:** $(38.4 million)  
* **Other, net:** $(2.6 million)  
* **Depreciation and amortization (total):** $102.2 million  
* **Stock‑based compensation expense (total):** $13.7 million  
* **Corporate expense:** $9.2 million  

After accounting for these items, the Company reported **income before income taxes of $43.6 million**.

The interim Chief Executive Officer, acting as the chief operating decision maker (CODM), evaluates segment performance primarily through **Segment Adjusted EBITDA**—earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, stock‑based compensation, and other net items. Although the exact Segment Adjusted EBITDA figure is not disclosed in the table, it remains the central metric for allocating resources and assessing profitability across ACI On Premise and ACI On Demand.

Expenses are allocated to segments via direct costs, labor tracking, and shared (allocated) costs such as marketing, IT, and facilities. Corporate and unallocated expenses cover overhead functions like HR, finance, legal, and M&A activities, and are excluded from segment performance evaluation.

Overall, the 2017 results reflect strong top‑line growth, significant investment in depreciation and stock‑based compensation, and a focus on segment profitability as guided by Segment Adjusted EBITDA.

synth_text.title: Financial Highlights and Segment Performance for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Company reports its results through two operating segments: **ACI On Premise**, which serves customers that host the software on‑site or via a third‑party cloud, and **ACI On Demand**, which delivers cloud‑based payment solutions to banks, merchants and billers. Management evaluates segment profitability using **Segment Adjusted EBITDA**, a measure that excludes interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, stock‑based compensation and other net income.

**Revenue Growth**  
- **Total revenue** rose from **$1,009.8 million** in 2018 to **$1,258.3 million** in 2019, a **≈24.6 % increase**.  
- **ACI On Premise** revenue more than doubled, climbing from **$4.3 million** to **$7.7 million**.  
- **ACI On Demand** revenue also more than doubled, increasing from **$4.3 million** to **$8.0 million**.  

Both segments experienced strong top‑line growth, reflecting higher adoption of on‑premise solutions and expanding demand for cloud‑based payment services.

**Expense and Profitability Trends**  
- **Corporate and unallocated expenses** grew from **$(92.3 million)** to **$(104.7 million)**, driven by higher overhead and allocation of shared costs.  
- **Interest expense** rose sharply, from **$(30.4 million)** to **$(52.1 million)**, reflecting increased financing costs.  
- **Other (net)** moved from a **$(3.7 million)** outflow in 2018 to a **$0.5 million** inflow in 2019.  
- **Depreciation & amortization** increased from **$97.4 million** to **$122.6 million**.  
- **Stock‑based compensation expense** more than doubled, from **$20.4 million** to **$36.8 million**.  
- **Corporate expense** rose from **$11.7 million** to **$21.1 million**.

Despite the revenue surge, **income before income taxes** fell from **$91.8 million** in 2018 to **$72.2 million** in 2019, primarily because the growth in operating expenses, interest, depreciation, and stock‑based compensation outpaced revenue growth.

**Segment Adjusted EBITDA**  
The Company uses Segment Adjusted EBITDA as the primary metric for evaluating segment performance and allocating resources. While the table does not disclose the specific EBITDA figures, the increase in expenses and interest suggests that the adjusted EBITDA likely grew at a slower pace than revenue, prompting management to focus on cost efficiency across both segments.

**Key Takeaway**  
The 2018‑2019 period was marked by robust segment revenue expansion, especially in both on‑premise and on‑demand offerings. However, higher corporate overhead, financing costs, and non‑cash expenses reduced pre‑tax profitability. Management’s focus on Segment Adjusted EBITDA will be critical for guiding future resource allocation and sustaining the growth momentum of ACI On Premise and ACI On Demand.

synth_text.title: Income Tax and Deferred Tax Summary (Amounts in $ Million)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table compares two reporting periods, presenting the composition of current income tax, deferred tax, and the resulting total income tax charge. All figures are expressed in millions of US dollars ($ M).

**Current Income Tax**  
- **UK corporation tax**: $1.3 M in the first period and $1.2 M in the second. This aligns with the UK corporation tax rate of 19 % applied to the estimated assessable loss for the year ended 31 March 2019.  
- **Adjustments for previous‑year UK tax**: Both periods show a modest addition of $0.3 M.  
- **Overseas tax (before exceptional items)**: The dominant component, amounting to $22.2 M and $23.0 M respectively.  
- **Adjustment for previous years**: A reduction of $(12.7) M in the first period and $(3.5) M in the second, reflecting the reversal of prior‑year tax adjustments.

*Total current tax charge*: $36.9 M (Period 1) vs. $34.7 M (Period 2).

**Deferred Tax**  
- **Origination and reversal of temporary differences**: A credit of $2.5 M in the first period turns into a debit of $(16.7) M in the second, indicating a significant reversal of temporary differences.  
- **Impact of changes in US tax rate**: No effect in the first period; a positive impact of $5.4 M in the second period.  
- **Total deferred tax credit**: $(10.2) M in Period 1 improves to $(14.8) M in Period 2, driven by the above movements.

**Total Income Tax Charge**  
- Period 1: $26.7 M  
- Period 2: $19.9 M  

**Key Drivers of Change**  
1. **Reduced adjustments for prior years** in the second period lowered the current tax charge.  
2. **Reversal of temporary differences** and the **US tax rate impact** increased the deferred tax credit, further decreasing the overall tax expense.  

Overall, the total income tax charge declined by $6.8 M from the first to the second period, primarily due to the combined effect of smaller prior‑year adjustments and more favorable deferred tax movements.

text.value: 2016 Collective Bargaining Negotiations

During 2016, we adopted changes to our defined benefit pension plans and other postretirement benefit plans to reflect the agreed upon terms and conditions of the collective bargaining agreements ratified in June 2016. synth_text.title: Pension Plan Funding Status and Earnings Impact Following 2016 Collective‑Bargaining Adjustments (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The company’s defined‑benefit pension plans continued to show an underfunded position at the close of 2018 and 2019.  

- **Projected Benefit Obligation (PBO)** rose from **$19,510 million** in 2018 to **$21,190 million** in 2019.  
- **Accumulated Benefit Obligation (ABO)** increased from **$19,461 million** to **$21,134 million** over the same period.  
- **Fair value of plan assets** grew from **$17,757 million** to **$19,388 million**.  

Despite the growth in assets, the obligations remain higher than the assets, confirming that the plans have an accumulated benefit obligation that exceeds plan assets.

These figures reflect the effects of the **2016 collective‑bargaining negotiations**, which introduced changes to the pension and other post‑retirement benefit plans. The adjustments generated a **net increase of $2.9 billion (after‑tax $1.8 billion) in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI)**. Under the agreed accounting treatment, this amount is being reclassified to net periodic benefit cost on a straight‑line basis over the weighted‑average remaining service periods—**12.2 years for defined‑benefit pension plans** and **7.8 years for other post‑retirement benefit plans**.

The amortization of the AOCI increase has **reduced net periodic benefit cost and increased pre‑tax income by approximately $658 million in each of the years 2017, 2018, and 2019**. Consequently, while the pension obligations have risen, the earnings impact of the 2016 agreement adjustments has been favorable to the company’s reported profitability during this period.

Overall, the data illustrate a modest improvement in plan assets relative to obligations, but the pension plans remain underfunded, and the financial statements continue to reflect the ongoing amortization of the 2016 collective‑bargaining adjustments.

text.value: 18. Trade and other receivables
Following the application of IFRS 16, trade and other receivables have been restated (note 2).

Trade receivables are amounts due from customers for services performed in the ordinary course of business. They are generally due for settlement within 30 days and therefore are all classified as current. Trade receivables are recognised initially at the amount of consideration that is unconditional and has been invoiced at the reporting date. The Group holds the trade receivables with the objective to collect the contractual cash flows and therefore measures them subsequently at amortised cost using the effective interest method.

Accrued income relates to the Group’s rights to consideration for services provided but not invoiced at the reporting date. Accrued income is transferred to receivables when invoiced. Other receivables include £0.1m due from Auto Trader Auto Stock Limited, a related party (note 34).
Exposure credit risk and expected credit losses relating to trade and other receivables are disclosed in note 31.

synth_text.text:
The Group’s trade and other receivables are presented in millions of pounds for two consecutive reporting periods. All trade receivables are classified as current, measured at amortised cost, and are recognised when invoiced. A provision for impairment is recognised to reflect expected credit losses.

| Item                              | Period 1 (£m) | Period 2 (£m) |
|-----------------------------------|---------------|---------------|
| Trade receivables                 | 27.0          | 28.8          |
| Less: provision for impairment    | (2.1)         | (3.4)         |
| **Net trade receivables**         | **24.9**      | **25.4**      |
| Accrued income*                   | 28.0          | 26.7          |
| Prepayments                       | 2.9           | 2.7           |
| Other receivables**               | 0.3           | 0.1           |
| **Total receivables**             | **56.1**      | **54.9**      |

\*Accrued income represents the Group’s right to consideration for services already provided but not yet invoiced; it is transferred to receivables once invoiced.  
\**Other receivables consist mainly of a £0.1 m amount due from the related party Auto Trader Auto Stock Limited.

**Key observations**

* Trade receivables grew modestly from £27.0 m to £28.8 m, while the impairment provision increased from £2.1 m to £3.4 m, resulting in a slight rise in net trade receivables (from £24.9 m to £25.4 m).  
* Accrued income fell by £1.3 m, reflecting a reduction in services rendered but not yet invoiced.  
* Prepayments and other receivables remained low and relatively stable.  
* Overall, total receivables decreased from £56.1 m to £54.9 m, mainly due to the decline in accrued income offsetting the increase in trade receivables.

The figures have been restated in accordance with IFRS 16 (see note 2). Exposure to credit risk and the expected credit losses associated with these receivables are disclosed in note 31.

Domestic operations are responsible for the design, development and wafer fabrication of products, as well as the coordination of production planning and shipping to meet worldwide customer commitments. * **Overall growth:** Total long‑lived assets rose from $767.9 M in 2018 to $996.7 M in 2019, a 29 % increase.  
* **U.S. assets:** The United States segment saw the largest absolute and relative gain, climbing $127.8 M (≈ 32 %). This reflects continued investment in domestic design, development, wafer fabrication, and production‑planning capabilities.  
* **Thailand assets:** Assets at the Thailand assembly and test facility slipped slightly, decreasing by $6.2 M (≈ 3 %). The facility is reimbursed for the value added through assembly, testing, and related functions, which may explain the modest change.  
* **Other countries:** Assets in “Various other countries” grew markedly, up $107.2 M (≈ 67 %). These locations include foreign sales, support, and design centers that receive compensation for sales within their territories.  

**Operational context**

The company sells primarily to distributors and OEMs worldwide, with about 80 % of net sales in fiscal 2019 generated outside the United States—roughly half from Asia and a quarter from Europe. Because foreign sales offices and the Thailand assembly/test site are compensated on a value‑added basis, the firm does not separate sales or operating profit for those operations in its financial statements. This asset distribution aligns with the global nature of its customer base: no single distributor (aside from Arrow Electronics, which accounts for 10 % of net sales) or end‑customer exceeds a 10 % share of total sales.

In summary, the company’s asset base expanded significantly between 2018 and 2019, driven primarily by growth in U.S. facilities and a substantial increase in assets located in other foreign regions, while the Thailand operation remained relatively stable. This pattern supports the firm’s strategy of maintaining a strong domestic R&D and manufacturing core while expanding its international sales and support footprint.

Revenues

Our Products and Licensing segment included revenues from sales of test and measurement systems, primarily representing sales of our Optical Backscatter Reflectometer, ODiSI, and Optical Vector Analyzer platforms, optical components and sub-assemblies and sales of our Hyperion and Terahertz sensing platforms. Our Products and Licensing segment revenues increased $22.5 million to $44.5 million for the year ended December 31, 2019 compared to $21.9 million for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Continued growth in sales of our fiber-optic sensing products, including our ODiSI products directed toward the expanding use of composite materials and the need for improved means of testing their structural integrity, and our communications test instruments also contributed to this increase.

Our Technology Development segment revenues increased $5.1 million to $26.0 million for the year ended December 31, 2019 compared to $21.0 million for the year ended December 31, 2018. Revenues within this segment increased due to additional contract awards, including higher value Phase 2 SBIR contracts. The increase continues a growth trend experienced over the past two years largely driven by successes in Phase 2 SBIR awards. The increase was realized primarily in our intelligent systems, advanced materials, optical systems and terahertz research groups. As Phase 2 SBIR contracts generally have a performance period of a year or more, we currently expect Technology Development segment revenues to remain at a similar level for the near term.

synth_text.title: Comprehensive Income (Loss) Overview for the Fiscal Year Ended June 30 2019
synth_text.text:
During the fiscal year ending June 30 2019, the company’s accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) grew from a negative $57.449 million on June 24 2018 to a negative $64.030 million on June 30 2019, reflecting a net comprehensive loss of $6.581 million for the period.

The change in AOCI can be broken down as follows:

* **Other comprehensive (loss) income before reclassifications:** A net loss of $4.228 million was generated within OCI during the year.  
* **Reclassifications to net income:** A modest net loss of $0.126 million was transferred out of OCI. Detailed reclassifications included a $9.6 million after‑tax gain moved from OCI to net income under revenue, offset by after‑tax losses of $5.0 million (cost of goods sold), $1.7 million (selling, general & administrative), and $0.1 million (other income & expense).  
* **Effects of ASU 2018‑02 adoption:** The adoption of Accounting Standards Update 2018‑02 reduced OCI by $2.227 million.  

When these components are combined, they produce the reported “Net current‑period other comprehensive income (loss)” of $(6.581) million, which aligns with the increase in the year‑end AOCI balance.

Tax impacts related to OCI and its components for the years ended June 30 2019, June 24 2018, and June 25 2017 were deemed immaterial, and therefore do not materially affect the presented figures.

Overall, the company’s comprehensive loss for the year was driven primarily by the generation of OCI losses, the reclassification of gains and losses into net income, and the accounting impact of ASU 2018‑02.

synth_text.title: Fiscal‑Year 2019 Comprehensive Income Summary for Two Entities
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table compares the accumulated other comprehensive income (OCI) positions of two entities at the beginning (June 24 2018) and end (June 30 2019) of the fiscal year, together with the components that drove the changes.

**Entity 1**  
- **Opening balance (June 24 2018):** $(1,190) k (negative).  
- **OCI activity:** $3,535 k of other comprehensive (loss) income before any reclassifications, offset by a $(199) k reclassification to net income. No effect from the adoption of ASU 2018‑02 is reported.  
- **Net OCI for the period:** $3,336 k, turning the balance positive.  
- **Closing balance (June 30 2019):** $2,146 k.

**Entity 2**  
- **Opening balance (June 24 2018):** $(19,495) k (negative).  
- **OCI activity:** $(1,153) k of other comprehensive (loss) income before reclassifications and a $(1,828) k impact from the adoption of ASU 2018‑02. No reclassifications to net income are shown.  
- **Net OCI for the period:** $(2,981) k, deepening the loss position.  
- **Closing balance (June 30 2019):** $(22,476) k.

**Key Drivers and Context**  
- **Reclassifications:** As detailed in Note 18, after‑tax gains and losses are routinely moved from accumulated OCI into net income. For the fiscal year, gains were recognized in other expense (≈ $9.6 M) while losses appeared in cost of goods sold (≈ $5.0 M), selling, general & administrative expenses (≈ $1.7 M), and other income/expense (≈ $0.1 M). These movements affect the “Losses (gains) reclassified” line in the table.  
- **ASU 2018‑02 Adoption:** The second entity recorded a $(1,828) k effect from this accounting update, contributing to its larger OCI loss. The first entity reported no impact.  
- **Tax Impact:** Tax effects related to OCI and its components were immaterial for the periods shown.

**Conclusion**  
During the 2019 fiscal year, Entity 1 transformed a modest OCI deficit into a surplus, primarily through substantial positive OCI before reclassifications. In contrast, Entity 2 experienced a further deterioration in OCI, driven by negative OCI activity and the accounting impact of ASU 2018‑02. The note on reclassifications underscores that such adjustments are a normal part of OCI reporting and that tax considerations did not materially affect the presented figures.

synth_text.title: Summary of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss and Reclassifications for Fiscal Years Ending June 2018 and June 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary details the movement in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) for two reporting groups between the balance dates of June 24 2018 and June 30 2019. It outlines the primary components that affected AOCI during fiscal year 2019, including reclassifications to net income, the impact of Accounting Standards Update (ASU) 2018‑02, and the net current‑period OCI (loss).

**Group 1**  
- **Balance as of June 24 2018:** $(32,722)  
- **Other comprehensive (loss) income before reclassifications (FY 2019):** $(9,470)  
- **Reclassifications to net income:** $2,822 (gain) – primarily driven by after‑tax gains moved from AOCI into net income, such as a $9.6 million gain recognized in revenue.  
- **Effect of ASU 2018‑02:** — (no impact)  
- **Net current‑period OCI (loss):** $(6,648)  
- **Balance as of June 30 2019:** $(39,370)  

*Result:* AOCI deteriorated by $6,648, reflecting a net loss after accounting for the $2,822 gain from reclassifications.

**Group 2**  
- **Balance as of June 24 2018:** $(4,042)  
- **Other comprehensive (loss) income before reclassifications (FY 2019):** $2,860 (gain)  
- **Reclassifications to net income:** $(2,749) (loss) – includes after‑tax losses from cost of goods sold ($5.0 million), selling, general & administrative expenses ($1.7 million), and other income/expense ($0.1 million).  
- **Effect of ASU 2018‑02:** $(399) (loss)  
- **Net current‑period OCI (loss):** $(288)  
- **Balance as of June 30 2019:** $(4,330)  

*Result:* AOCI increased (more negative) by $288, driven mainly by the reclassification losses and the ASU 2018‑02 impact.

**Key Takeaways**  
1. **Reclassifications were a major driver** of AOCI changes. Group 1 recorded a net gain from reclassifications, while Group 2 experienced a net loss, largely due to losses originating from cost of goods sold and SG&A.  
2. **ASU 2018‑02 had no effect on Group 1** but contributed a $399 loss to Group 2’s AOCI.  
3. **Net current‑period OCI was negative for both groups**, indicating that the underlying comprehensive loss items outweighed the gains.  
4. **Tax effects on OCI were immaterial**, as noted in the accompanying footnote.

text.value: VMware and Pivotal Employee Stock Purchase Plans

In June 2007, VMware adopted its 2007 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (the “ESPP”), which is intended to be qualified under Section 423 of the Internal Revenue Code. On June 25, 2019, VMware amended its ESPP to increase the number of shares available for issuance by 9.0 million shares of Class A common stock. As of January 31, 2020, the number of authorized shares under the ESPP was a total of 32.3 million shares. Under the ESPP, eligible VMware employees are granted options to purchase shares at the lower of 85% of the fair market value of the stock at the time of grant or 85% of the fair market value at the time of exercise. The option period is generally twelve months and includes two embedded six-month option periods. Options are exercised at the end of each embedded option period. If the fair market value of the stock is lower on the first day of the second embedded option period than it was at the time of grant, then the twelve-month option period expires and each enrolled participant is granted a new twelve-month option. As of January 31, 2020, 14.3 million shares of VMware Class A common stock were available for issuance under the ESPP.

synth_text.text:

*Key points*  
- Payments decline steadily each year, reflecting the weighted‑average remaining term of **4.5 years** for charter‑in contracts.  
- The total undiscounted obligation over the forecast horizon is **$367.4 million**, of which **$304.6 million** is recorded as operating‑lease liability.  
- Applying the incremental borrowing rate reduces the present‑value liability by **$62.8 million**.

**2. Office and Land Leases (Secondary Lease Portfolio)**

*Key points*  
- Annual payments are modest ($556) through 2024, rising to $23,002 from 2025 onward, consistent with the long‑term nature of land leases (average remaining term **46.3 years**).  
- The total undiscounted commitment for this portfolio is **$25.8 million**, with a recorded liability of **$7.7 million** after discounting.

- The weighted‑average remaining lease terms differ markedly across lease types: charter‑in contracts (4.5 years), office leases (1.9 years), and land leases (46.3 years), which explains the divergent payment patterns and liability structures shown above.

Navios Maritime’s lease commitments are front‑loaded for its charter‑in contracts, with payments tapering as the contracts near expiry, while office and especially land leases exhibit a long‑term, low‑frequency payment profile. synth_text.title: GMSL Financial Overview for 2018‑2019 with Context on Fugro Transactions and Management Fees
synth_text.text:
**Financial Summary (2018‑2019)**  
GMSL’s reported figures for the two most recent fiscal years show a pronounced contraction in both revenue generation and cash distribution to shareholders.

| Year | Net Revenue | Operating Expenses | Interest Expense | Accounts Receivable | Long‑Term Obligations | Accounts Payable | Dividends |
|------|-------------|--------------------|------------------|---------------------|-----------------------|------------------|-----------|
| 2019 | $6.4 M | $1.0 M | $1.0 M | $1.2 M | $22.5 M | $0.1 M | $4.5 M |
| 2018 | $21.8 M | $4.8 M | $1.3 M | $5.0 M | $28.5 M | $2.2 M | $25.8 M |

* **Revenue:** Net revenue fell by roughly 71 % from $21.8 M in 2018 to $6.4 M in 2019.  
* **Operating & Interest Costs:** Operating expenses dropped by 79 % and interest expense decreased slightly, reflecting a leaner cost structure.  
* **Working‑Capital Items:** Accounts receivable declined from $5.0 M to $1.2 M, while accounts payable fell sharply from $2.2 M to $0.1 M, indicating tighter cash flow management.  
* **Long‑Term Obligations:** Obligations were reduced by $6.0 M, but still represent the bulk of the balance sheet.  
* **Dividends:** Payouts contracted from $25.8 M to $4.5 M, mirroring the revenue decline.

**Contextual Factors**  
- In November 2017, GMSL acquired Fugro N.V.’s trenching and cable‑laying services business. As part of that deal, Fugro obtained a 23.6 % stake in GMSL’s parent, Global Marine Holdings, LLC (GMH).  
- Ongoing transactions with Fugro contributed $0.8 M of revenue and $11.3 M of expenses in 2019, and $9.3 M of expenses in 2018. These figures are embedded within the operating expense totals shown above.  
- GMH charged GMSL management fees of $0.6 M in each year, also reflected within the operating expenses.  
- GMSL maintains additional dealings with several equity‑method investees; while specific amounts are not broken out in the table, they form part of the broader financial landscape.

**Interpretation**  
The steep revenue decline, coupled with reduced dividends, suggests that the post‑acquisition integration with Fugro has not yet translated into sustained earnings growth. However, the company has successfully lowered its cost base, trimmed long‑term obligations, and improved its working‑capital position. Continued monitoring of the Fugro‑related revenue and expense streams, as well as the performance of equity‑method investees, will be critical to assessing GMSL’s path to profitability.

REVENUE Fiscal 2019 revenue increased by 22.4% (17.9% in constant currency). In local currency, revenue amounted to US$782.3 million compared to US$662.3 million for fiscal 2018. The increase resulted mainly from: • the impact of the MetroCast acquisition completed on January 4, 2018 which was included in revenue for only an eight-month period in the prior year; • rate increases; • continued growth in Internet service customers; and • the FiberLight acquisition completed in the first quarter of fiscal 2019; partly offset by • a decrease in video service customers. Excluding the MetroCast and FiberLight acquisitions, revenue in constant currency increased by 5.2% for fiscal 2019.

OPERATING EXPENSES Fiscal 2019 operating expenses increased by 19.5% (15.2% in constant currency) mainly as a result of: • the impact of the MetroCast acquisition which was included in operating expenses for only an eight-month period in the prior year; • programming rate increases; • the FiberLight acquisition completed in the first quarter of fiscal 2019; • higher compensation expenses due to higher headcount to support growth; and • higher marketing initiatives to drive primary service units growth; partly offset by • the prior year's non-recurring costs of $3.1 million (US$2.5 million) related to hurricane Irma.

ADJUSTED EBITDA Fiscal 2019 adjusted EBITDA increased by 26.1% (21.5% in constant currency). In local currency, adjusted EBITDA amounted to US$351.3 million compared to US$288.4 million for fiscal 2018. The increase was mainly due to the impact of the MetroCast and FiberLight acquisitions combined with strong organic growth. Excluding the MetroCast and FiberLight acquisitions and the prior year's non-recurring costs of $3.1 million ($US2.5 million) related to hurricane Irma, adjusted EBITDA in constant currency increased by 5.7% for fiscal 2019.

CAPITAL INTENSITY AND ACQUISITIONS OF PROPERTY, PLANT AND EQUIPMENT Fiscal 2019 acquisitions of property, plant and equipment decreased by 9.4% (12.4% in constant currency) mainly due to: • the acquisition of several dark fibres throughout south Florida from FiberLight, LLC for a consideration of $21.2 million (US$16.8 million) during the second quarter of fiscal 2018; partly offset by • additional capital expenditures related to the impact of the MetroCast acquisition; and • additional capital expenditures related to the expansion in Florida. synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Financial Highlights: Revenue Growth, EBITDA Expansion, and Lower Capital Intensity
synth_text.text: Fiscal 2019 delivered strong top‑line and profitability growth. Reported revenue rose 22.4 % (17.9 % in constant currency), reaching US $782.3 million, driven primarily by the inclusion of the MetroCast acquisition (which contributed only eight months of revenue in the prior year), rate increases, continued growth in Internet service customers, and the first‑quarter acquisition of FiberLight. Operating expenses increased 19.5 % (15.2 % constant currency), reflecting the same acquisitions, higher programming rates, added compensation for a larger headcount, and expanded marketing initiatives, partially offset by the absence of the prior‑year non‑recurring hurricane Irma costs. Adjusted EBITDA grew 26.1 % (21.5 % constant currency) to US $351.3 million, benefitting from the combined impact of MetroCast and FiberLight together with robust organic performance; excluding those acquisitions and the prior‑year hurricane costs, EBITDA still rose 5.7 % in constant currency. Capital expenditures fell 9.4 % (12.4 % constant currency), as spending on new dark‑fiber assets from FiberLight and other expansion projects was lower than the previous year. Consequently, capital intensity improved markedly, dropping to 18.6 % from 25.1 % in fiscal 2018. Overall, the fiscal‑year results underscore the company’s ability to grow revenue and earnings while becoming more capital‑efficient, supported by strategic acquisitions and organic service growth.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Financial Performance Overview – Comparison with Fiscal 2018
synth_text.text:
**Summary of Key Financial Metrics**

| Metric | FY 2018 (thousands $) | FY 2019 (thousands $) | YoY Change |
|--------|----------------------|----------------------|------------|
| Revenue | 847,372 | 1,036,853 | +22.4 % (≈ +18 % in constant currency) |
| Operating expenses | 478,172 | 571,208 | +19.5 % (≈ +15 % in constant currency) |
| Adjusted EBITDA | 369,200 | 465,645 | +26.1 % (≈ +22 % in constant currency) |
| Adjusted EBITDA margin | 43.6 % | 44.9 % | ↑ 1.3 pp |
| Acquisitions of property, plant & equipment | 212,580 | 192,605 | –9.4 % |
| Capital intensity | 25.1 % | 18.6 % | ↓ 6.5 pp |

**Drivers of Revenue Growth**

- **Acquisitions:** The MetroCast acquisition (effective Jan 4 2018) and the FiberLight acquisition (Q1 FY 2019) added significant new customers and infrastructure, contributing to most of the top‑line increase.  
- **Rate increases** and **continued growth in Internet service customers** further boosted revenue.  
- **Offsetting factor:** A modest decline in video‑service customers partially offset the gains.  
- Excluding the two acquisitions, revenue still rose 5.2 % in constant currency, indicating solid organic growth.

**Operating Expense Dynamics**

- Expenses rose mainly due to the same acquisitions (higher operating costs for the newly integrated assets), **programming rate hikes**, **higher headcount** to support growth, and **increased marketing spend**.  
- The increase was partially mitigated by the absence of the prior‑year non‑recurring hurricane‑Irma costs of $3.1 M.

**Adjusted EBITDA Improvement**

- Adjusted EBITDA grew 26.1 % (21.5 % in constant currency), driven by the combined effect of the MetroCast and FiberLight acquisitions and strong organic performance.  
- When the acquisitions and the prior‑year non‑recurring hurricane costs are excluded, constant‑currency EBITDA still rose 5.7 %, underscoring underlying profitability gains.  
- The EBITDA margin improved modestly to 44.9 % from 43.6 %.

**Capital Expenditure and Capital Intensity**

- Capital spending fell 9.4 % (12.4 % in constant currency) despite the FiberLight dark‑fiber purchase ($21.2 M) and MetroCast‑related outlays, reflecting a more disciplined capex program.  
- Revenue growth outpaced the decline in capex, driving **capital intensity down to 18.6 %** from 25.1 %, indicating a more efficient allocation of capital.

**Conclusion**

Fiscal 2019 delivered robust top‑line and profitability growth, primarily fueled by strategic acquisitions (MetroCast and FiberLight) and favorable pricing actions. Operating expenses rose in line with the expanded business, but margin expansion and a marked reduction in capital intensity highlight improved operational efficiency. The company’s financial trajectory suggests continued strength, provided it sustains organic growth while managing integration costs of recent acquisitions.

Research and development expenses in 2019 decreased by $4.6 million, or 21%, as compared to 2018. synth_text.title: Decline in Research and Development Expenditures from 2018 to 2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s research and development (R&D) expenses fell sharply between 2018 and 2019. In 2018, R&D costs were $22.45 million, representing 38 % of net revenues. By 2019, these expenses had decreased to $17.85 million, or 36 % of net revenues—a 21 % reduction amounting to approximately $4.6 million.

The company also eliminated the $0.1 million restructuring cost incurred in 2018 and reduced professional fees by $0.6 million through a smaller pool of R&D contractors.

Overall, the lower staffing levels, decreased contractor usage, and the absence of restructuring charges collectively contributed to the notable drop in both the absolute R&D spend and its proportion of total revenue.

The cumulative tax effect of significant items comprising our net deferred tax amount at the expected rate of 21% is as follows as of December 31, 2019 and 2018:

The ultimate realization of deferred tax assets is dependent upon the Company’s ability to generate sufficient taxable income during the periods in which the net operating losses expire and the temporary differences become deductible. The Company has determined that there is significant uncertainty that the results of future operations and the reversals of existing taxable temporary differences will generate sufficient taxable income to realize the deferred tax assets; therefore, a valuation allowance has been recorded. In making this determination, the Company considered historical levels of income as well as projections for future periods.

The tax years 2016 to 2019 remain open for potential audit by the Internal Revenue Service. There are no uncertain tax positions as of December 31, 2018 or December 31, 2019, and none are expected in the next 12 months. The Company’s foreign subsidiaries are cost centers that are reimbursed for expenses, so generate no income or loss. Pretax book income (loss) is all from domestic operations. Up to four years of returns remain open for potential audit in foreign jurisdictions, however any audits for periods prior to ownership by the Company are the responsibility of the previous owners.

Under certain circumstances issuance of common shares can result in an ownership change under Internal Revenue Code Section 382, which limits the Company’s ability to utilize carry-forwards from prior to the ownership change. Any such ownership change resulting from stock issuances and redemptions could limit the Company’s ability to utilize any net operating loss carry-forwards or credits generated before this change in ownership. These limitations can limit both the timing of usage of these laws, as well as the loss of the ability to use these net operating losses. It is likely that fundraising activities have resulted in such an ownership change.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s balance sheet includes detailed deferred tax assets (DTAs) and deferred tax liabilities (DTLs) for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2019 and December 31, 2018. Although the gross DTA balances are sizable, a full valuation allowance eliminates any net deferred tax benefit in both periods.

**2019 (as of December 31, 2019)**

**2018 (as of December 31, 2018)**  
- **Deferred Tax Assets**  
  - Net operating loss carryover: **$2,290,000**  
  - Stock‑based compensation: **$535,000**  
  - Intangible assets: **$124,000**

  - **Total DTL (gross): $(2,952,000)**  

- **Net deferred tax asset:** **$0** (valuation allowance fully offsets the gross DTA).

**Key Contextual Factors**  

1. **Uncertainty of Realization** – The company has determined that future taxable income may be insufficient to utilize the NOL carryforwards and other temporary differences. Consequently, a full valuation allowance has been recorded, reflecting the significant uncertainty about realizing the DTAs.  

2. **Audit Exposure** – Tax years 2016‑2019 remain open for potential IRS audit. No uncertain tax positions exist as of the reporting dates, and none are expected in the next 12 months. Foreign subsidiaries are cost‑center entities that do not generate taxable income; all pretax book income (or loss) originates from domestic operations.  

3. **Ownership‑Change Limitations (IRC § 382)** – Issuance of common shares may trigger an ownership change that restricts the use of pre‑change NOL carryforwards. Recent fundraising activities are likely to have caused such a change, further limiting the ability to realize the deferred tax assets.

**Conclusion**  
While the company holds substantial gross deferred tax assets derived mainly from net operating loss carryovers and stock‑based compensation, a full valuation allowance eliminates any net benefit for both 2019 and 2018. This reflects management’s assessment of future taxable income uncertainty, ongoing audit risk, and potential limitations imposed by ownership‑change rules under IRC § 382.

synth_text.text:
The company’s cash equivalents, current‑asset investments and derivative‑related financial assets are concentrated with counterparties of high credit quality. Using the lower rating where Moody’s and S&P differ, the exposure is broken down as follows:

- **Aa2/AA and above:** £2.5 billion in each reporting period, representing the largest share of the portfolio.  
- **Aa3/AA‑:** £1.4 billion (first period) and £0.3 billion (second period).  
- **A‑grade (A1/A+, A2/Aa, A3/A‑a):** Combined £1.8 billion in the first period and £1.5 billion in the second period.  
- **BBB‑grade (Baa1/BBB+, Baa2/BBB‑ and below):** £0.2 billion in the first period and £0.3 billion in the second period.  

The total amount of assets covered by these ratings was **£5,977 million** in the first period and **£4,613 million** in the second period.

To further mitigate credit risk, the firm holds **£638 million of cash collateral** against derivative positions (up from £492 million in 2017/18 and down from £702 million in 2016/17). Netting arrangements under standard ISDA documentation are used where multiple transactions involve the same counter‑party or related groups, reducing the net exposure.

In addition, credit support agreements are in place for long‑dated cross‑currency and interest‑rate swaps with a notional value of **£3,289 million**. Collateral on these swaps generated a **net cash inflow of £129 million** during the year (compared with an outflow of £220 million in 2017/18 and an inflow of £100 million in 2016/17). The collateral received and paid is reflected respectively in current‑asset investments and loans/other borrowings.

Overall, the portfolio is dominated by high‑rated counterparties, and the combination of cash collateral, netting arrangements, and credit support agreements provides robust protection against credit concentration risk.

synth_text.title: Q4 2019 Net Revenue Performance: Sequential and Year‑Over‑Year Highlights
synth_text.text:
In the fourth quarter of 2019, the company reported unaudited net revenues of **$2,754 million**, up from **$2,553 million** in the prior quarter—a **7.9 % sequential increase** that exceeded the midpoint of guidance by 290 basis points. Net sales rose to **$2,750 million**, while other revenues contributed **$4 million**.

The sequential growth was driven by:
* **Higher volumes** of approximately **7 %**, reflecting stronger demand across all product groups.  
* A modest **~1 % rise in average selling prices**, stemming entirely from a more favorable product mix; selling prices otherwise remained stable.

On a **year‑over‑year basis**, net revenues increased by **4.0 %**. This annual uplift was primarily the result of a **~6 % increase in average selling prices**, which was largely due to an improved product mix (about **9 %**). The price benefit was partially offset by a **~2 % decline in volumes** and a **~3 % reduction in selling prices** for certain items.

Overall, the Q4 2019 results demonstrate solid sequential momentum driven by volume growth and strategic product‑mix enhancements, while the year‑over‑year performance underscores the importance of pricing strategy in offsetting modest volume headwinds.

synth_text.title: Q4 2019 Financial Highlights: Net Revenues Rise 7.9 % Sequentially
synth_text.text:
In the fourth quarter of 2019 the company reported net revenues of **$2.754 billion**, representing a **7.9 % sequential increase**—the same growth rate shown in the table (Net revenues + 7.9 %). Net sales contributed $2.633 billion, while other revenues added $15 million, bringing total net revenues to $2.648 billion in the tabular snapshot.

The sequential growth was driven by two main factors:

1. **Higher volumes** – sales volumes rose approximately **7 %** year‑over‑year, providing a solid base for revenue expansion.  
2. **Improved product mix** – average selling prices increased by about **1 %**, entirely due to a more favorable mix of higher‑margin products; overall selling prices remained largely stable.

On a **year‑over‑year basis**, net revenues grew **4.0 %**. This increase was fully attributable to a **~6 % rise in average selling prices**, which stemmed from an improved product mix (≈ 9 % positive impact) that was partially offset by a modest **~3 % decline in selling prices** for certain items. Volume changes contributed a **~2 % decrease**, partially offset by the price‑mix effect.

In summary, the quarter’s performance reflects strong volume growth and strategic product‑mix improvements that together lifted net revenues by nearly 8 % sequentially and delivered modest year‑over‑year growth.

synth_text.title: Q4 2019 Revenue Performance Summary
synth_text.text:
In the fourth quarter of 2019 the company delivered solid revenue growth across its core segments. Net sales rose by **4.5%**, while Other revenues fell sharply, decreasing by **$77.4 million**. Net revenues increased by **4.0%** year‑over‑year, reaching **$2,754 million**, which represents a **7.9% sequential gain**—290 basis points above the midpoint of our guidance.

The sequential improvement was driven by:
* **Volume growth of approximately 7%**, reflecting higher unit shipments across all product groups.  
* A modest **average selling‑price increase of about 1%**, entirely attributable to a more favorable product mix; overall selling prices remained largely stable.

On a year‑over‑year basis, the 4.0% net‑revenue rise was fully explained by an **average selling‑price increase of roughly 6%**. This price uplift was largely the result of an improved product mix (+9%), partially offset by lower selling prices on certain items (‑3%). The price benefit was partially neutralized by a **2% decline in volumes**.

In summary, while Net sales showed modest growth and Other revenues contracted sharply, the company’s net‑revenue performance was bolstered by strong volume expansion and strategic product‑mix enhancements that lifted average selling prices.

synth_text.title: 2018 Consolidated Statement of Operations – Key Financial Highlights
synth_text.text:
**Revenue Overview**  
For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2018, the company generated **$7.5 billion** in total net revenues. Revenue was split between **product sales of $2.255 billion (30 % of net revenues)** and **subscription, licensing, and other revenues of $5.245 billion (70 %).**

**Cost Structure**  
Costs were reported both in absolute terms and as percentages of the related revenue stream:

- **Product‑related costs** amounted to **$719 million**, representing **32 % of product‑sale revenue**.  
- **Software royalties, amortization, and IP licences** were **$399 million (8 % of product‑sale revenue)**.  
- **Game operations and distribution** cost **$1.028 billion (20 % of subscription revenue)**.  
- **Product development** expense was **$1.101 billion (15 % of subscription revenue)**.  
- **Sales and marketing** costs totaled **$1.062 billion (14 % of subscription revenue)**.  
- **General and administrative** expenses were **$822 million (11 % of subscription revenue)**.  
- **Restructuring and related costs** were minimal at **$10 million**.

Overall, **total costs and expenses** summed to **$5.512 billion**, leaving an **operating income of $1.988 billion**, which is **27 % of net revenues**.

**Profitability**  
After accounting for interest and other net expenses of **$71 million** and a **loss on extinguishment of debt of $40 million**, the company reported **income before tax of $1.877 billion**. Income‑tax expense was **$29 million**, resulting in **net income of $1.848 billion**—equivalent to **25 % of total net revenues**.

**Key Adjustments**  
- A post‑year‑end review identified a $35 million overstatement of income‑tax expense, which has been corrected in the presented figures.  
- The $40 million loss on extinguishment of debt consists of a $25 million premium payment and a $15 million write‑off of unamortized discount and deferred financing costs.

**Bottom Line**  
The 2018 results demonstrate a strong revenue mix heavily weighted toward subscription services, disciplined cost management, and robust profitability, with operating margins of 27 % and net margins of 25 % after the noted tax and debt‑extinguishment adjustments.

synth_text.title: 2019 EPS Decline and Share‑Count Reduction for Continuing Operations
synth_text.text:
In 2019, earnings per share (EPS) from continuing operations showed modest declines across all reported measures.  

* **Basic EPS** fell **2.7 %** year‑over‑year.  
* **Assuming dilution** (which incorporates the effect of dilutive securities such as stock options and awards using the treasury‑stock method) decreased by **2.6 %**.  
* **Diluted operating EPS (non‑GAAP)** dropped more sharply, down **7.2 %**.  

These percentages reflect the change from 2018, a year that included a one‑time $2.0 billion charge (or $2.23 per share) related to U.S. tax reform. That charge boosted 2018 EPS figures, making the 2019 declines appear larger in comparison.

Share‑count dynamics also contributed to the EPS movement. The weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding fell from **892.5 million in 2018** to **887.1 million in 2019**, a reduction primarily driven by the company’s ongoing common‑stock repurchase program. When dilution is assumed, the average share count was **23.5 million lower** in 2019 than in the prior year, further influencing the diluted EPS calculations.

In summary, 2019 saw a modest contraction in both basic and diluted EPS, a more pronounced decline in non‑GAAP diluted operating EPS, and a lower share base due to active share repurchases, all set against the backdrop of a significant tax‑reform charge that had inflated the 2018 EPS baseline.

synth_text.title: Summary of Continuing Operations EPS and Share Metrics for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Earnings per Share (EPS) Overview**  
The company reported EPS from continuing operations for two fiscal years. Basic EPS increased from **$8.87** (2018) to **$9.12** (2019), reflecting higher profitability on a per‑share basis. Diluted (non‑GAAP) EPS rose from **$12.81** to **$13.81** over the same period, indicating that even after accounting for potentially dilutive securities, earnings per share improved.

**Share Count Details**  
- **Basic weighted‑average shares outstanding** were 892.5 million at the end of 2018 and 887.1 million at the end of 2019.  
- Assuming dilution, the average share count was **23.5 million lower in 2019** than in 2018, consistent with the company’s ongoing common‑stock repurchase program.  

**Impact of Tax Reform**  
A one‑time charge of **$2.0 billion** (or $2.23 per share) related to U.S. tax reform was included in the 2018 EPS figures, lowering both basic and diluted EPS for that year. The absence of a comparable charge in 2019 contributed to the observed EPS increase.

**Key Takeaways**  
- Both basic and diluted EPS showed year‑over‑year growth, driven by higher earnings and a reduced share base.  
- The share repurchase program effectively decreased the number of shares outstanding, enhancing EPS.  
- The 2018 EPS figures were partially offset by a significant tax‑reform charge, which was not present in 2019.

Overall, the company’s financial performance improved from 2018 to 2019, with stronger EPS metrics supported by operational gains and strategic share‑repurchase actions.

These liabilities primarily relate to federal and state research and development credits and intercompany profit on the transfer of certain intellectual‑property rights to a foreign subsidiary, a consequence of the Company’s 2015 tax reorganization. Management continuously monitors these positions, applying judgment based on evolving tax regulations, court outcomes, and other relevant information. Interest and penalties associated with uncertain tax positions are recorded as a component of income‑tax expense; as of December 31, 2019, accrued interest and penalties amounted to **$25,000**. The total unrecognized tax benefits that could affect the effective tax rate, if recognized, were **$97,000** at that date.

Because the Company retains net operating loss and credit carryforwards, the statutes of limitations for federal, state, and foreign tax authorities remain open for all tax years from 2000 onward, allowing continued review of the Company’s tax filings.

Overall, the 2017 reconciliation demonstrates a material reduction in the Company’s unrecognized tax benefit liability, driven mainly by the favorable effect of the federal tax‑rate change on prior‑year positions.

text.value: 18. Business Segments

We primarily derive our revenues from sales of our proprietary software (either as a direct license sale or under a subscription delivery model), which also serves as the basis for our recurring service contracts for software support and maintenance and certain transaction-related services. In addition, we provide various other client services, including installation, and managed services such as outsourcing, private cloud hosting and revenue cycle management.

During the first quarter of 2019, we realigned our reporting structure as a result of the divestiture of our investment in Netsmart on December 31, 2018, the evolution of the healthcare IT industry and our increased focus on the payer and life sciences market. As a result, we changed the presentation of our reportable segments to Provider and Veradigm. The new Provider segment is comprised of our core integrated clinical software applications, financial management and patient engagement solutions targeted at clients across the entire continuum of care. The new Veradigm segment primarily focuses on the payer and life sciences market. These changes to our reportable segments had no impact on operating segments. The segment disclosures below for the years ended December 31, 2018 and 2017 have been revised to our current presentation.

We sold all of our investment in Netsmart on December 31, 2018. Prior to the sale, Netsmart comprised a separate reportable segment, which due to its significance to our historical consolidated financial statements and results of operations, is reported as a discontinued operation as a result of the sale. In addition, the results of operations related to two of the product offerings acquired with the EIS Business (Horizon Clinicals and Series2000) are also presented throughout these financial statements as discontinued operations and are included within the Provider reportable segment, except for acquisition-related deferred revenue adjustments, which are included in “Unallocated Amounts”. Refer to Note 17, “Discontinued Operations.”

As a result of the above changes, as of December 31, 2019, we had eight operating segments, which are aggregated into two reportable segments. The Provider reportable segment includes the Hospitals and Health Systems, Ambulatory, CarePort, FollowMyHealth®, EPSiTM, EIS-Classics and 2bPrecise strategic business units, each of which represents a separate operating segment. This reportable segment derives its revenue from the sale of integrated clinical software applications, financial management and patient engagement solutions, which primarily include EHR-related software, connectivity and coordinated care solutions, financial and practice management software, related installation, support and maintenance, outsourcing, private cloud hosting, revenue cycle management, training and electronic claims administration services. The Veradigm reportable segment is comprised of the Veradigm business unit, which represents a separate operating segment. This reportable segment provides data-driven clinical insights with actionable tools for clinical workflow, research, analytics and media. Its solutions, targeted at key healthcare stakeholders, help improve the quality, efficiency and value of healthcare delivery.

Our Chief Operating Decision Maker (“CODM”) uses segment revenues, gross profit and income from operations as measures of performance and to make decisions about the allocation of resources. In determining these performance measures, we do not include in revenue the amortization of acquisition- related deferred revenue adjustments, which reflect the fair value adjustments to deferred revenue acquired in a business combination. We also exclude the amortization of intangible assets, stock-based compensation expense, non-recurring expenses and transaction-related costs, and non-cash asset impairment charges from the operating segment data provided to our CODM. Non-recurring expenses relate to certain severance, product consolidation, legal, consulting and other charges incurred in connection with activities that are considered one-time. Accordingly, these amounts are not included in our reportable segment results and are included in an “Unallocated Amounts” category within our segment disclosure. The “Unallocated Amounts” category also includes (i) corporate general and administrative expenses (including marketing expenses) and certain research and development expenses related to common solutions and resources that benefit all of our business units (refer to discussion above), all of which are centrally managed and (ii) revenue and the associated cost from the resale of certain ancillary products, primarily hardware. We do not track our assets by segment.
