text.value: A. Selected Financial Data The table set forth below presents our selected historical consolidated financial data for the periods and at the dates indicated. The selected historical consolidated statements of income data for each of the three years ended March 31, 2019, 2018, and 2017 and the selected statements of financial position data as of March 31, 2019 and 2018 have been derived from and should be read in conjunction with “Part I — Item 5.

Operating and Financial Review and Prospects” and our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 20-F. The selected historical consolidated statements of income data for each of the two years ended March 31, 2016 and 2015 and the selected historical statements of financial position data as of March 31, 2017, 2016, and 2015 have been derived from audited consolidated financial statements not included in this Annual Report on Form 20-F.

(1) References to “net income” in this document correspond to “profit/(loss) for the period” or “profit/(loss) for the year” line items in our consolidated financial statement appearing elsewhere in this document. (2) Gross Revenue is defined as reported revenue adjusted in respect of significant financing component that arises on account of normal credit terms provided to catalogue customers.

(3) We use EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA and Gross Adjusted EBITDA as supplemental financial measures. EBITDA is defined by us as net income before interest expense, income tax expense and depreciation and amortization (excluding amortization of capitalized film content and debt issuance costs).

Adjusted EBITDA is defined as EBITDA adjusted for (gain)/impairment of available-for-sale financial assets, profit/loss on held for trading liabilities (including profit/loss on derivative financial instruments), transactions costs relating to equity transactions, share based payments, Loss / (Gain) on sale of property and equipment, Loss on de-recognition of financial assets measured at amortized cost, net,

Credit impairment loss, net, Loss on financial liability (convertible notes) measured at fair value through profit and loss, Loss on deconsolidation of a subsidiary and exceptional items such as impairment of goodwill, trademark, film & content rights and content advances.

Gross Adjusted EBITDA is defined as Adjusted EBITDA adjusted for amortization of intangible films and content rights. EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA and Gross Adjusted EBITDA as used and defined by us, may not be comparable to similarly-titled measures employed by other companies and is not a measure of performance calculated in accordance with GAAP.

EBITDA Adjusted EBITDA and Gross Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for operating income, net income, cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities, or other income or cash flow statement data prepared in accordance with GAAP. EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA and Gross Adjusted EBITDA provide no information regarding a Company’s capital structure, borrowings, interest costs, capital expenditures and working capital movement or tax position.

synth_text.title: Financial Highlights for the Year Ended 31 March 2019
synth_text.text:
**Revenue and Profitability**  
For the fiscal year ended 31 March 2019, the company generated **gross revenue of $284.2 million**. After deducting cost of sales of $155.8 million, gross profit stood at **$128.4 million**. Administrative expenses of $49.5 million were incurred, leaving an **operating profit (before any exceptional items) of $78.9 million**. No impairment loss was recorded, so operating profit remained $78.9 million.

**Net Finance and Other Items**  
Net finance costs amounted to **$(5.9) million**, while other gains/(losses), net were **$(10.5) million**. After these items, profit before tax was **$62.5 million**. Income tax expense of **$(13.2) million** resulted in a **profit for the year of $49.3 million**.

**Earnings per Share**  
The profit translates to **basic earnings per share of 74.3 cents** and **diluted earnings per share of 72.4 cents**.

**Supplemental Non‑GAAP Measures**  
- **EBITDA** (net income before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, excluding amortisation of capitalised film content and debt‑issuance costs) was **$70.1 million**.  
- **Adjusted EBITDA**, which further excludes gains/losses on financial assets, equity‑transaction costs, share‑based payments, and other exceptional items, was **$101.2 million**.  
- **Gross Adjusted EBITDA**, adding back amortisation of intangible film and content rights to Adjusted EBITDA, reached **$218.4 million**.

These non‑GAAP metrics are provided for supplemental insight and are not a substitute for GAAP‑based operating income, net income, or cash‑flow figures. They should be considered alongside the full set of financial statements for a comprehensive view of performance.

synth_text.title: Comparative Summary of Selected Income‑Statement Metrics for FY 2019 vs. FY 2018
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table contrasts key income‑statement figures for two consecutive fiscal years ending 31 March. While revenue showed a modest increase, profitability deteriorated sharply in the later year due to a substantial impairment charge.

**Revenue & Gross Profit**  
- Revenue rose from **$261.3 million** to **$270.1 million**.  
- Cost of sales increased from **$134.7 million** to **$155.4 million**, reducing gross profit from **$126.5 million** to **$114.7 million**.

**Operating Expenses & Impairment**  
- Administrative costs climbed from **$68.0 million** to **$87.1 million**.  
- A one‑time **impairment loss of $423.3 million** was recorded in the later year, turning operating profit of $27.6 million into an operating loss of **$(395.7 million)**. No impairment loss was reported in the earlier year, which posted an operating profit of **$58.5 million**.

**Net Loss & Earnings per Share**  
- Profit (loss) before tax swung from a small loss of **$0.6 million** to a large loss of **$(403.1 million)**.  
- After tax, the loss expanded from **$(9.7 million)** to **$(410.5 million)**.  
- Correspondingly, basic and diluted earnings per share fell from a loss of **36.3 cents** to **599.5 cents** per share.

**Non‑GAAP Performance Measures**  
- **EBITDA** moved from a positive **$20.2 million** to a negative **$(393.2 million)**, reflecting the impact of the impairment.  
- **Adjusted EBITDA** remained positive, improving from **$82.96 million** to **$103.85 million**.  
- **Gross Adjusted EBITDA** increased from **$198.2 million** to **$234.0 million**, indicating better underlying cash‑flow generation when intangible amortization is excluded.

**Key Takeaways**  
1. Revenue growth was insufficient to offset higher cost of sales and administrative expenses.  
2. The impairment loss was the primary driver of the sharp decline in operating and net profitability.  
3. Adjusted EBITDA and Gross Adjusted EBITDA suggest the core business retained profitability despite the GAAP loss.  

These insights should be read in conjunction with the detailed definitions of “Gross Revenue”, “EBITDA”, “Adjusted EBITDA”, and “Gross Adjusted EBITDA” provided in the accompanying annual‑report notes.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table presents selected consolidated income‑statement data for the two most recent fiscal years, expressed in thousands of dollars (except earnings‑per‑share).  The figures are derived from the company’s audited financial statements and are discussed in the “Operating and Financial Review and Prospects” section of the Annual Report on Form 20‑F.

**Key Results**

| Metric (in $ thousands) | FY 2019 (ended 31 Mar 2019) | FY 2018 (ended 31 Mar 2018) |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Revenue (Gross Revenue)** | 252,994 | 274,428 |
| **Cost of sales** | (164,240) | (172,764) |
| **Gross profit** | 88,754 | 101,664 |
| **Administrative costs** | (63,309) | (64,019) |
| **Operating profit (pre‑exceptional)** | 25,445 | 37,645 |
| **Net finance costs** | (17,156) | (8,010) |
| **Other gains/(losses), net** | 14,205 | (3,636) |
| **Profit before tax** | 22,494 | 25,999 |
| **Income tax** | (11,039) | (12,711) |
| **Profit for the year** | 11,455 | 13,288 |
| **Basic EPS (cents)** | 6.4 | 6.6 |
| **Diluted EPS (cents)** | 5.1 | 5.2 |
| **EBITDA** | 42,548 | 36,294 |
| **Adjusted EBITDA** | 55,664 | 70,852 |
| **Gross Adjusted EBITDA** | 190,980 | 199,155 |

**Interpretation**

* **Revenue** fell by roughly 7.8 % year‑over‑year, reflecting a decline in catalogue‑customer sales after adjusting for financing components (as defined in the additional context).  
* **Gross profit** decreased proportionally, while **administrative costs** remained stable, leading to a lower **operating profit** of $25.4 million in FY 2019 versus $37.6 million in FY 2018.  
* **Net finance costs** rose sharply in FY 2019, offset partially by a sizable **other gain** of $14.2 million, which helped limit the drop in profit before tax.  
* **Profit after tax** declined by $1.8 million (≈ 13 %) and basic EPS fell from 6.6 cents to 6.4 cents.  
* **EBITDA** improved to $42.5 million in FY 2019, driven mainly by the other gain, but **Adjusted EBITDA** and **Gross Adjusted EBITDA** fell, indicating that the underlying operating performance (excluding non‑recurring items, financing effects, and intangible amortisation) weakened.

**Non‑GAAP Measures (Contextual Definitions)**  
- **EBITDA**: profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (excluding amortisation of capitalised film content and debt‑issuance costs).  
- **Adjusted EBITDA**: EBITDA further adjusted for gains/losses on financial assets, derivative instruments, equity‑transaction costs, share‑based payments, asset sales, credit‑impairment losses, convertible‑note losses, de‑consolidation impacts and other exceptional items.  
- **Gross Adjusted EBITDA**: Adjusted EBITDA less amortisation of intangible film and content rights.

These supplemental metrics are provided for additional insight but are not substitutes for GAAP‑based operating income, net income, or cash‑flow figures.

**Conclusion**  
While FY 2019 showed a modest decline in core revenue and profitability compared with FY 2018, the company’s EBITDA increased due to non‑recurring gains.  Adjusted and Gross Adjusted EBITDA, which strip out such items, indicate a contraction in underlying operating performance.  Stakeholders should consider both GAAP results and the non‑GAAP measures, together with the definitions provided, to assess the company’s financial health.

text.value: Deferred tax (liabilities) assets are comprised of the following at:

The Company has Federal tax credit carryforwards of $5.4 million that expire in various tax years from 2028 to 2038. The Company has a Federal operating loss carryforward of $24.5 million expiring from 2029 through 2037 and a Federal operating loss carryforward of $17.9 million with an unlimited carryforward period. The Company also has state tax credit carryforwards of $0.3 million and state operating loss carryforwards of $43.3 million, which vary by jurisdiction and expire in various tax years through 2039.

In assessing the ability to realize deferred tax assets, management considers whether it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. The ultimate realization of deferred tax assets is dependent upon the generation of future taxable income during the periods in which the temporary differences become deductible. Management considers the scheduled reversal of deferred tax liabilities, projected future taxable income, and tax planning strategies in making this assessment.

As a result of this analysis and based on the current year’s taxable income, and utilization of certain carryforwards management determined an increase in the valuation allowance in the current year to be appropriate.

In calculating the valuation allowance, the Company was not permitted to use its existing deferred tax liabilities related to its indefinite-lived intangible assets (i.e. “naked credit deferred tax liabilities”) as a source of taxable income to support the realization of its existing finite-lived deferred tax assets.

Due to the Tax Act, U.S. net operating losses ("NOLs") arising in tax years ending after December 31, 2017 will no longer be subject to the limited 20-year carryforward period. Under the new law, these NOLs carry forward indefinitely, resulting in the creation of indefinite-lived deferred tax assets. Consequently, as the Company schedules its deferred taxes and considers the ability to realize its deferred tax assets in future periods, it needs to consider how existing deferred tax assets, other than historical NOLs, will reverse.

If the reversal is expected to generate an indefinite carryforward NOL under the new law, this may impact the valuation allowance assessment. The indefinite carryforward period for NOLs also means that its deferred tax liabilities related to indefinite-lived intangibles, commonly referred to as “naked credits,” can be considered as support for realization. The adjustment for the 2019 “naked credit” resulted in a $0.01 million deferred tax liability.

In 2019, it was determined that the foreign tax credit carryforward of the Company would not be realizable. The reduction of the foreign tax credit carryforward resulted in a decrease in the valuation allowance for those credits. Therefore, there is no net income tax provision in 2019 related to the reduction in the foreign tax credit carryforward. A valuation allowance is required to the extent it is more likely than not that the future benefit associated with certain Federal and state tax loss carryforwards will not be realized.

The current year income tax provision includes a reduction of the Company’s valuation allowance due to the establishment of a deferred tax liability in connection with the issuance of convertible debt. The establishment of that deferred tax liability created “future taxable income” for the utilization of existing deferred tax assets of the Company, resulting in the $4 million reduction of the Company’s valuation allowance.

The Company records the benefits relating to uncertain tax positions only when it is more likely than not (likelihood of greater than 50%), based on technical merits, that the position would be sustained upon examination by taxing authorities. Tax positions that meet the more likely than not threshold are measured using a probability-weighted approach as the largest amount of tax benefit that is greater than 50% likely of being realized upon settlement.

At December 31, 2019, the Company’s reserve for uncertain tax positions is not material and we believe we have adequately provided for its tax-related liabilities. The Company is no longer subject to United States federal income tax examinations for years before 2014.

synth_text.title: Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities – Comparative Summary for 2018 and 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**

The Company’s deferred tax schedule shows a substantial increase in gross deferred tax assets from **$20,958 k in 2018** to **$25,287 k in 2019**, while gross deferred tax liabilities rose modestly from **$(2,630) k** to **$(6,496) k**. After applying a valuation allowance, the net deferred tax position shifted from a neutral $0 in 2018 to a small net liability of **$(64) k** in 2019.

**Key Drivers of Change**

| Item | 2018 | 2019 | Notable Change |
|------|------|------|----------------|
| **Software development costs** | $(1,954) k | $(1,219) k | Decrease in the deductible temporary difference. |
| **Acquired intangible assets** | $(676) k | $(446) k | Smaller reversal of intangible‑related liabilities. |
| **Depreciation on property, plant & equipment** | $373 k (asset) | — (no asset) | Reversal of a previous deferred tax asset. |
| **Subordinated debt** | $— | $(3,659) k (liability) | New deferred tax liability from convertible debt issuance. |
| **Lease liabilities** | $— | $772 k (liability) | Recognition of right‑of‑use asset liabilities under ASC 842. |
| **Federal NOL carryforward** | $6,512 k | $8,563 k | Additional NOLs generated, now indefinite under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. |
| **State NOL carryforward** | $2,112 k | $2,317 k | Slight increase. |
| **Tax credit carryforwards** | $6,176 k | $5,777 k | Minor reduction, partly offset by the expiration of some credits. |
| **Other** | $722 k | $912 k | Miscellaneous temporary differences. |

**Valuation Allowance**

- **Gross deferred tax assets** grew by **$4,329 k** (≈ 21 %).  
- The **valuation allowance** increased from **$(18,328) k** to **$(18,855) k**, reflecting management’s assessment that a portion of the newly added assets may not be realizable.  
- The increase is driven by:
  * The need to offset the new deferred tax liability from subordinated debt, which creates future taxable income that can be used to realize existing assets (resulting in a $4 M reduction of the allowance).  
  * The determination that foreign tax credit carryforwards are no longer realizable, which lowered the allowance for those credits.  
  * Ongoing uncertainty around the utilization of certain Federal and state loss carryforwards, especially where “naked credit” deferred tax liabilities cannot be used as taxable income under current guidance.

**Impact of Recent Tax Legislation**

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act eliminated the 20‑year limitation on NOLs arising after 2017, converting many of the Company’s NOL carryforwards into **indefinite‑life deferred tax assets**. This change introduces “naked credit” deferred tax liabilities related to indefinite‑life intangibles, which, under the new law, can support the realization of other deferred tax assets. The 2019 adjustment for such a “naked credit” added a modest **$0.01 M** liability.

**Conclusion**

Between 2018 and 2019 the Company expanded its pool of deferred tax assets, primarily through larger Federal and State NOL carryforwards and modest growth in other temporary differences. However, the simultaneous emergence of new deferred tax liabilities (subordinated debt, lease liabilities) and a more conservative valuation allowance resulted in a net deferred tax liability of **$(64) k** at year‑end 2019. Management continues to evaluate realizability based on projected taxable income, the scheduled reversal of liabilities, and tax planning strategies, while maintaining a modest reserve for uncertain tax positions.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
Teradyne’s deferred revenue and customer advances, reported in thousands of dollars, consist of three primary service categories: maintenance, service and training; extended warranties; and customer advances for undelivered elements and other items. These amounts are recorded as short‑ and long‑term deferred revenue on the balance sheet and are recognized in accordance with the company’s revenue‑recognition policies for each service type.

**Fiscal Year 2019 (ended December 31, 2019)**  
- **Maintenance, service and training:** $63,815 k  
- **Extended warranty:** $30,677 k  
- **Customer advances, undelivered elements and other:** $56,358 k

- **Maintenance, service and training:** $58,362 k

- **Customer advances, undelivered elements and other:** $24,677 k

**Key Insights**  
- The total deferred revenue grew by **$40,389 k** (approximately **36 %**) from 2018 to 2019, driven by increases across all three components.  
- Maintenance, service and training saw the largest absolute rise, reflecting higher demand for ongoing support, training, and application services.  
- Extended warranty balances also increased, consistent with the company’s practice of recognizing warranty revenue over the service period.  
- The “customer advances, undelivered elements and other” category more than doubled, indicating a higher volume of prepaid contracts or orders for future delivery.

**Contextual Note**  
Teradyne’s services—including extended warranties, training, application support, service agreements, post‑contract customer support (PCS), and replacement parts—are recognized based on their relative standalone selling prices. Extended warranties, training, support, service agreements, and PCS are recognized over time, while replacement parts are recognized at the point of transfer. The company does not allow product or service returns or refunds, and its standard 12‑month product warranty is not treated as a separate performance obligation.

These figures illustrate the growing reliance of Teradyne’s customers on its service portfolio and the resulting increase in deferred revenue obligations.

text.value: Results of Operations
Revenue (in thousands, except for percentages)
Comparison of Years Ended December 31, 2018 and 2017
Total net revenue for the year ended December 31, 2018, increased by $1,083.9 million, or 49%, compared to the year ended December 31, 2017.

Transaction-based revenue for the year ended December 31, 2018, increased by $551.3 million, or 29%, compared to the year ended December 31, 2017. This increase was attributable to the growth in GPV processed of $19.3 billion, or 30%, to $84.7 billion from $65.3 billion. We continued to benefit from growth in processed volumes from our existing sellers, in addition to meaningful contributions from new sellers. Additionally, GPV from larger sellers, which we define as all sellers that generate more than $125,000 in annualized GPV, represented 51% of our GPV in the fourth quarter of 2018, an increase from 47% in the fourth quarter of 2017. We continued to see ongoing success with attracting and enabling large seller growth, which we believe will help drive strong GPV growth as we scale.

Subscription and services-based revenue for the year ended December 31, 2018 increased by $339.0 million, or 134%, compared to the year ended December 31, 2017. Growth was driven primarily by Instant Deposit, Caviar, Cash Card, and Square Capital, as well as acquisitions completed in the second quarter. Subscription and services-based revenue grew to 18% of total net revenue in the year ended December 31, 2018, up from 11% in the year ended December 31, 2017.

Hardware revenue for the year ended December 31, 2018, increased by $27.1 million, or 65%, compared to the year ended December 31, 2017. The increase primarily reflects growth in shipments of Square Register following its launch in the fourth quarter of 2017 and, to a lesser extent, the launch of Square Terminal during the fourth quarter of 2018. The increase was also driven by continued growth in sales of our contactless and chip readers, as well as growth in sales of our Square Stand and third-party peripherals driven primarily by new features and product offerings. Additionally, the adoption of ASC 606 resulted in an increase of $5.9 million in hardware revenue for the year ended December 31, 2018 primarily related to the earlier revenue recognition of hardware sold through retail distribution channels and hardware installment sales, which were previously recorded upon sell through to the end user customer.

Bitcoin revenue for the year ended December 31, 2018, increased by $166.5 million compared to the year ended December 31, 2017. During the fourth quarter of 2017, we started offering our Cash App customers the ability to purchase bitcoin from us. Bitcoin revenue comprises the total sale amount we receive from bitcoin sales to customers and is recorded upon transfer of bitcoin to the customer’s account. The sale amount generally includes a small margin added to the price we pay to purchase bitcoin and accordingly, the amount of bitcoin revenue will fluctuate depending on the volatility of market bitcoin prices and customer demand.

synth_text.title: Square Inc. Revenue Growth Summary: FY 2017 vs. FY 2018
synth_text.text:
Square reported strong financial momentum in 2018, with total net revenue rising to **$3.30 billion**, a **49 % increase** (up $1.08 billion) over the $2.21 billion recorded in 2017.

**Transaction‑based revenue** grew to **$2.47 billion**, up $551 million (29 %) year over year. The boost stemmed from a 30 % rise in gross payment volume (GPV) processed—from $65.3 billion to $84.7 billion—driven by higher volumes from existing sellers, new seller acquisition, and a larger share of GPV (51 %) coming from “large” sellers (>$125 k annualized GPV) versus 47 % in 2017.

**Subscription and services‑based revenue** jumped to **$592 million**, an increase of $339 million (134 %). Growth was powered by Instant Deposit, Caviar, Cash Card, Square Capital, and acquisitions made in the second quarter. This segment’s share of total revenue rose to 18 % from 11 % in the prior year.

**Hardware revenue** rose to **$68.5 million**, up $27 million (65 %). The increase reflected higher shipments of Square Register (launched Q4 2017), the introduction of Square Terminal (Q4 2018), continued sales of contactless/chip readers, Square Stand, and third‑party peripherals. Adoption of ASC 606 added $5.9 million by accelerating revenue recognition for hardware sold through retail channels and installment sales.

**Bitcoin revenue** appeared for the first time in 2018 at **$166.5 million**, up from zero in 2017 after Cash App began offering bitcoin purchases in Q4 2017. Bitcoin revenue fluctuates with market price volatility and customer demand, as it includes a modest margin on each sale.

Overall, the 2018 results demonstrate diversified growth across transaction processing, subscription services, hardware, and emerging Bitcoin offerings, positioning Square for continued scaling of its payment ecosystem.

synth_text.text:

Credit risk

Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty will fail to discharge its obligations and cause a financial loss and arises from cash and cash equivalents, short-term investments, favorable derivative financial instruments and deposits with banks and financial institutions, as well as credit exposures to customers, including trade and other receivables, dividends receivable and other amounts due from related parties. The Group is exposed to credit risk in the event of non-performance by any of its counterparties. To limit this risk, the Group currently deals primarily with financial institutions and customers with high credit ratings.

For the year ended December 31, 2019, 70.0% of the Group’s revenue was earned from Shell (December 31, 2018 and December 31, 2017, 74.2% and 92.6%, respectively) and accounts receivable were not collateralized; however, management believes that the credit risk is partially offset by the creditworthiness of the Group’s counterparties. BG Group was acquired by Shell on February 15, 2016. This acquisition does not impact the contractual obligations under the existing charter party agreements. The Group did not experience significant credit losses on its accounts receivable portfolio during the three years ended December 31, 2019. The carrying amount of financial assets recorded in the consolidated financial statements represents the Group’s maximum exposure to credit risk. Management monitors exposure to credit risk, and they believe that there is no substantial credit risk arising from the Group’s counterparties.
The credit risk on liquid funds and derivative financial instruments is limited because the counterparties are banks with high credit ratings assigned by international credit-rating agencies.

**Key observations**

* **Liquidity decline** – Cash and cash equivalents fell by about **23 %** (from $342.6 m to $263.7 m).  
* **Short‑term investments** dropped sharply, decreasing by **82 %** to $4.5 m, reflecting a shift away from marketable securities.  
* **Trade receivables** grew modestly (+23 %) to $24.9 m, indicating higher sales on credit, primarily to Shell, which accounted for 70 % of revenue in 2019.  
* **Dividends receivable** collapsed from $33.4 m to $0.6 m, suggesting that dividend‑related claims were largely settled or written off.  
* **Derivative instruments** were reduced by **74 %**, lowering exposure to potential credit losses from these contracts.

**Credit‑risk context**

These asset categories represent the Group’s credit‑risk exposure. The risk arises if counterparties—banks, financial institutions, or customers—fail to meet their obligations. GasLog mitigates this risk by dealing mainly with high‑rated banks and financially strong customers. In 2019, despite 70 % of revenue being earned from Shell (an un‑collateralised counter‑party), management considered the credit risk manageable due to Shell’s creditworthiness. No significant credit losses were recorded over the three‑year period, and the carrying amounts shown above reflect the maximum exposure.

Overall, the data illustrate a contraction in liquid assets and derivatives, a modest rise in trade receivables, and a near‑elimination of dividend receivables, all within a credit‑risk framework that the Group deems well‑controlled.

*Key observations*  
- Total inventories fell by **£25.3 m** (≈ 13.6 %) from Period 1 to Period 2.

**Write‑down Activity**  
During the latest year, the expense recognised for inventory write‑downs was **£0.7 m**, a substantial reduction from **£3.5 m** in the prior year. **Long‑term Recoverable Inventory**  
Inventories expected to be recovered after more than 12 months amount to **£13.4 m**, up from **£11.2 m** in the previous year, indicating a modest increase in longer‑term stock.

**Valuation Assurance**  
There is no material difference between the carrying amounts of inventories on the Statement of Financial Position and their replacement cost. Moreover, none of the inventory has been pledged as security, confirming that the assets remain unencumbered.

**Conclusion**  
The data show a clear contraction in overall inventory levels, driven primarily by a reduction in raw material holdings, while the company has successfully limited write‑down expenses through reversals linked to improved demand. The inventory valuation remains robust, with replacement costs aligning closely with book values and no security interests attached to the stock.

text.value: Capital and financial risk management
13 Capital risk management

The Group's objectives when managing capital are to safeguard its ability to continue as a going concern, so that it can continue to provide returns to its shareholders and benefits to its stakeholders and to maintain an optimal capital structure to reduce the cost of capital.

In the future, the Directors may pursue funding options such as debt, sale and leaseback of assets, additional equity and various other funding mechanisms as appropriate in order to undertake its projects and deliver optimum shareholders’ return.
The Group intends to maintain a gearing ratio appropriate for a company of its size and growth.

The Group manages its capital structure by regularly reviewing its gearing ratio to ensure it maintains an appropriate level of gearing within facility covenants. This ratio is calculated as net debt divided by total capital. Net debt is calculated as total interest bearing financial liabilities, less cash and cash equivalents. Total capital is calculated as equity, as shown in the Consolidated Balance Sheet, plus net debt.

synth_text.title: Capital Structure and Gearing Summary
synth_text.text:
The Group’s latest capital‑risk metrics illustrate a strong shift in its balance‑sheet profile.  

- **Total borrowings** fell from $867.2 million to $303.0 million, while **cash and cash equivalents** rose slightly from $399.0 million to $418.0 million.  
- Consequently, **net debt** moved from a positive $468.2 million to a **net cash surplus** of $115.0 million.  
- **Equity** remained robust, increasing modestly from $875.3 million to $894.0 million.  
- **Total capital** (equity + net debt) decreased from $1.34 billion to $779.0 million, reflecting the lower borrowing level.  
- The **gearing ratio** (net debt ÷ total capital) dropped from 35.0 % to a non‑applicable figure, as the Group now holds more cash than debt.

These figures align with the Group’s capital‑risk management objectives: safeguarding solvency, delivering shareholder returns, and maintaining an “optimal” capital structure. The Group regularly reviews its gearing ratio to stay within facility covenants and may employ a mix of funding options—including additional debt, sale‑and‑lease‑back arrangements, or equity issuances—to support future projects while keeping gearing at a level appropriate for its size and growth trajectory.  

Overall, the transition from net debt to net cash indicates a more conservative financing stance, positioning the Group to pursue strategic investments with reduced financial risk.

synth_text.title: 2017 Equity Investment Activity and Financial Impact Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the company reported the following results from its equity‑investment portfolio (all amounts in millions of dollars):

- **Mark‑to‑market adjustments** on marketable equity securities were negligible, and there were no observable price adjustments on non‑marketable equity securities.
- **Impairment charges** totaled **$833 million**, driven primarily by write‑downs of the Cloudera investment ($278 million) and the Unisoc investment ($308 million). These impairments reflect a decline in the fair value of those holdings.
- **Sale of equity investments and other assets** generated **$3,484 million** in cash. The bulk of this inflow came from a realized gain of approximately **$3.4 billion** on the sale of a portion of the company’s interest in ASML Holding N.V.
- **Net gains on equity investments** amounted to **$2,651 million**, indicating that, after accounting for the impairments and the proceeds from the ASML sale, the equity portfolio contributed a substantial positive return.
- **Interest and other, net** recorded a **loss of $349 million**. The loss was attributed to higher losses on debt conversions, lower assets under construction (which reduced capitalized interest), and comparatively modest divestiture gains for the year.

Overall, 2017 was characterized by strong cash generation from the sale of the ASML stake and robust net gains on equity investments, offset by significant impairment charges and a net loss in interest‑related activities.

synth_text.title: Equity Investment Performance Overview: 2018‑2019 Highlights and Drivers
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In 2019 the company recorded a markedly stronger equity‑investment performance compared with 2018. Net gains on equity investments rose from a $125 million loss to a $1.54 billion gain, while net interest and other income more than tripled, moving from $126 million to $484 million.

**Mark‑to‑Market Adjustments**  
- *2019*: Positive mark‑to‑market adjustments on marketable equity securities amounted to **$277 million**, driven primarily by gains on ASML Holding N.V. and Cloudera Inc.  
- *2018*: The same line reflected a **$129 million loss**, reflecting adverse price movements in those holdings.

**Observable Price Adjustments (Non‑Marketable Securities)**  
- *2019*: The company recognized **$293 million** in observable price adjustments, largely from a single investment.  
- *2018*: Adjustments were **$202 million**, indicating a smaller impact from non‑marketable positions.

**Impairment Charges**  
- *2019*: Impairments were limited to **$122 million**, a reduction from the prior year.  
- *2018*: The firm recorded a larger **$424 million** impairment, primarily from a $290 million charge on its equity‑method investment in IMFT.

**Sales of Equity Investments and Other**  
- *2019*: Proceeds surged to **$1.09 billion**, fueled by **$632 million** in dividends from McAfee and a **$107 million** gain from the sale of a non‑controlling interest in IMFT.  
- *2018*: Sales generated **$226 million**, reflecting a more modest level of divestitures and dividend income.

**Net Gains (Losses) on Equity Investments**  
- *2019*: The company posted a **$1.54 billion** net gain, reflecting the sale of its ASML stake and strong performance of remaining holdings.  
- *2018*: A **$125 million loss** was recorded, driven by the earlier impairment of IMFT and weaker market movements.

**Interest and Other, Net**  
- *2019*: Net interest and other income rose to **$484 million**, attributed to lower losses on debt conversions and larger divestiture gains.  
- *2018*: Net income in this category was **$126 million**, already an improvement over 2017 due to similar factors (reduced debt‑conversion losses, higher assets under construction, and greater divestiture gains).

**Key Takeaways**  
- The turnaround from 2018 to 2019 was anchored by the sale of the ASML investment, robust dividend receipts from McAfee, and reduced impairment exposure.  
- Positive mark‑to‑market and observable price adjustments further bolstered 2019 results.  
- Enhanced interest and other income complemented the equity‑investment gains, delivering a substantially stronger overall financial outcome for the year.

synth_text.title: Impact of Foreign Currency Translation on Consolidated Financial Results
synth_text.text:
The company’s foreign‑currency translation has produced both favorable and unfavorable effects on its consolidated financial results. For the first reporting period, translation reduced net sales by **$137.2 million** and net earnings by **$15.7 million**, while it boosted cost of sales by **$98.4 million**, SG&A expenses by **$16.3 million**, and lowered Non‑U.S. GAAP Adjusted EBITDA by **$25.3 million**. In the second period, the impact was smaller but followed a similar pattern: net sales fell by **$43.4 million** and net earnings by **$8.2 million**, whereas cost of sales improved by **$31.7 million**, SG&A expenses by **$1.0 million**, and Adjusted EBITDA decreased by **$11.1 million**.  

These translation effects arise from fluctuations in the major foreign currencies that the company regularly encounters—including the euro, Australian dollar, Mexican peso, British pound, Canadian dollar, Brazilian real, and Chinese renminbi—when converting foreign‑currency‑denominated results into U.S. dollars.

synth_text.title: Net Interest Income Summary – $30 M Income vs. $52 M Expense Resulting in a $22 M Net Loss
synth_text.text:
For the reporting period, the company generated **$30 million** in interest income while incurring **$52 million** in interest expense, producing a **net interest loss of $22 million**.

**Interest income** originates from cash and cash equivalents held by the company and from government bonds and floating‑rate notes classified as available‑for‑sale marketable securities (approximately $6 million each year).

**Interest expense** comprises:
- Cash charges on senior unsecured convertible bonds issued in July 2014 and July 2017 (charges of $39 million, $38 million and $37 million in 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively).
- A non‑cash component resulting from the accretion of the discount on the liability portion of those bonds ($37 million, $36 million and $33 million for the same years).
- Additional costs such as banking fees and expenses related to the sale of trade and other receivables.

No borrowing costs were capitalized in 2019, 2018, or 2017. The combination of modest interest earnings and substantial expense—largely driven by bond‑related charges—explains the negative net interest figure reported.

synth_text.title: Net Interest Income and Expense Summary
synth_text.text:
The recent interest‑related data show a narrow swing in net results. In the first reporting line, interest income of $55 million was almost offset by expenses of $54 million, leaving a net positive total of $1 million. In the second line, income fell to $47 million while expenses remained at $54 million, producing a net loss of $7 million.

These figures reflect the composition described in the accompanying notes. Interest income is generated primarily from cash and cash equivalents held by the Company, supplemented by $6 million of earnings from government bonds and floating‑rate notes classified as available‑for‑sale securities each year.  

Interest expense consists of cash interest on senior unsecured convertible bonds issued in 2014 and 2017—charges of $39 million, $38 million and $37 million for 2019, 2018 and 2017 respectively—and a non‑cash accretion component of $33 million to $37 million arising from the discount on the liability component of those bonds. Additional expense items include banking fees and the financial impact of selling trade and other receivables. No borrowing costs were capitalized during the periods under review.

Overall, the net interest position is highly sensitive to modest changes in income, given the relatively stable expense base driven by bond interest and related non‑cash charges. The shift from a $1 million net gain to a $7 million net loss underscores this volatility.

The company’s short‑term debt composition for the two most recent fiscal years shows a notable improvement in liquidity.  

- **Notes payable (including commercial paper)** fell from **$3.2 billion** in 2018 to **$2.0 billion** in 2019, a reduction of roughly **$1.2 billion**. This category comprises commercial paper issued under the U.S. program, which is hedged against foreign‑currency fluctuations through forward contracts.  

- **Loans secured by trade receivables** increased slightly, from **$919 million** in 2018 to **$1.05 billion** in 2019, reflecting a modest rise of about **$130 million**.  

- **Long‑term debt due within one year** (the current portion of long‑term obligations) declined from **$525 million** in 2018 to **$837 million** in 2019. The figure includes the current portion of lease liabilities—$775 million in 2019 and $466 million in 2018—highlighting a shift in lease‑related financing.  

- Consequently, **total debt due within one year** dropped from **$4.65 billion** in 2018 to **$3.88 billion** in 2019, a decrease of **$770 million** (approximately 17%).  

Overall, the reduction in notes payable and the lower current portion of long‑term debt contributed to a stronger short‑term financial position, while the slight increase in receivable‑backed loans was offset by the broader decline in total near‑term obligations.

text.value: The following table presents the percentage relationship of our Consolidated Statement of Operations line items to our consolidated net revenues for the periods presented:

Net revenue. Total revenue decreased $0.3 million, or 0.2% in fiscal 2018 compared to fiscal 2017. Products revenue decreased $4.6 million or 12.1% while support, maintenance and subscription services revenue increased 5.8 million, or 9.1%, as a result of continued focus on selling hosted perpetual and subscription services which increased 35% year over year. Hosted perpetual and subscription services revenue comprised 16% of total consolidated revenues in 2018 compared to 12% in 2017. Professional services revenue decreased $1.4 million, or 5.5%, primarily as a result of a decrease in proprietary services of $1.5 million offset by an increase in remarketed services of $0.1 million.

Gross profit and gross profit margin. Our total gross profit increased $0.6 million, or 1.0%, in fiscal 2018 and total gross profit margin increased 0.6% to 50.6%. Products gross profit decreased $2.8 million and gross profit margin decreased 4.6% to 21.7% primarily as a result of lower product revenue coupled with higher amortization of developed technology by $2.0 million related to the previously announced general availability of the latest version of our rGuest Buy and rGuest Stay software that were placed into service in the first and second quarters of fiscal 2017, and the second quarter of fiscal 2018.

Support, maintenance and subscription services gross profit increased $6.0 million and gross profit margin increased 260 basis points to 75.8% due to the scalable nature of our infrastructure supporting and hosting customers. Professional services gross profit decreased $2.6 million and gross profit margin decreased 9.0% to 19.2% due to lower professional services revenues on higher cost structure following a recent alignment toward enabling the Company to provide more customer-centric services going forward.

Operating expenses Operating expenses, excluding legal settlements and restructuring, severance and other charges, increased $1.0 million, or 1.4%, in fiscal 2018 compared with fiscal 2017. As a percent of total revenue, operating expenses have increased 0.9% in fiscal 2018 compared with fiscal 2017

Product development. Product development includes all expenses associated with research and development. Product development decreased $1.1 million, or 3.8%, during fiscal 2018 as compared to fiscal 2017. This decrease is primarily driven by our shift from contract labor to internal resources resulting in a decrease in contract labor of $5.9 million and an increase in payroll related expenses of $4.7 million.

Sales and marketing. Sales and marketing decreased $2.7 million, or 13.2%, in fiscal 2018 compared with fiscal 2017. The change is due primarily to a decrease of $2.2 million in incentive commissions related to revision of our commission plan from total contract value to annual contract value coupled with lower sales in fiscal 2018.
Depreciation of fixed assets. Depreciation of fixed assets increased $0.2 million or 9.2% in fiscal 2018 as compared to fiscal 2017.

Amortization of intangibles. Amortization of intangibles increased $0.5 million, or 35.0%, in fiscal 2018 as compared to fiscal 2017 due to our latest version of rGuest Pay being placed into service on March 31, 2017.

Restructuring, severance and other charges. Restructuring, severance, and other charges increased $0.2 million during fiscal 2018 compared to fiscal 2017 related to our ongoing efforts to create more efficient teams across the business, which included certain executive changes during the year.
Our restructuring actions are discussed further in Note 4, Restructuring Charges.
Legal settlements. During fiscal 2018 and 2017, we recorded $0.2 million and $0.1 million, respectively, in legal settlements for employment and other business-related matters.

synth_text.title: Consolidated Statement of Operations – Fiscal 2017 vs. Fiscal 2018 Summary
synth_text.text:
**Revenue Composition**  
In fiscal 2018 total net revenue was essentially flat, decreasing only $0.3 million (‑0.2 %) versus 2017. The revenue mix shifted noticeably: product revenue fell to 26.5 % of net revenue (down from 30.0 %), while support, maintenance and subscription services grew to 13.1 % (up from 13.3 %) and accounted for 16 % of total revenue—up from 12 % in 2017. Professional services contributed 15.6 % of revenue, a slight decline from 14.6 % the prior year. The decline in product revenue ($4.6 million, ‑12.1 %) was partially offset by a $5.8 million (‑9.1 %) increase in hosted perpetual and subscription services, reflecting the company’s strategic focus on recurring‑service offerings.

**Gross Profit and Margins**  
Overall gross profit rose modestly by $0.6 million (‑1.0 %) to a margin of 50.6 % in 2018. Product gross profit fell $2.8 million, dragging the product margin down 4.6 percentage points to 21.7 % because of lower product sales and higher amortization of newly released rGuest Buy and rGuest Stay software. Conversely, support, maintenance and subscription services generated a strong gross profit increase of $6.0 million, lifting its margin 260 basis points to 75.8 % thanks to the scalable nature of the hosted infrastructure. Professional services gross profit declined $2.6 million, with its margin slipping 9.0 percentage points to 19.2 % due to reduced revenue and a higher cost structure.

**Operating Expenses**  
Excluding legal settlements and restructuring charges, operating expenses grew $1.0 million (‑1.4 %) in 2018, representing a 0.9 percentage‑point increase as a share of revenue.  
- *Product Development*: Expenses fell $1.1 million (‑3.8 %) as the company moved from contract labor to internal staff, cutting contract‑labor costs by $5.9 million while payroll rose $4.7 million.  
- *Sales & Marketing*: Costs dropped $2.7 million (‑13.2 %) driven by a $2.2 million reduction in incentive commissions after shifting the compensation model from total contract value to annual contract value, alongside lower sales volumes.  
- *General & Administrative*: Increased modestly to 18.9 % of revenue in 2018 from 15.6 % in 2017.  
- *Depreciation*: Rose $0.2 million (‑9.2 %).  
- *Amortization of Intangibles*: Jumped $0.5 million (‑35 %) due to the rollout of the latest rGuest Pay version in March 2017.  

**Restructuring, Severance, and Legal Settlements**  
Restructuring and related charges grew $0.2 million in 2018, reflecting ongoing efficiency initiatives and executive changes. Legal settlements amounted to $0.2 million in 2018 (up from $0.1 million in 2017) for employment and other business matters.

**Operating Result**  
The combined effect of these dynamics produced an operating loss of 9.5 % of net revenue in fiscal 2018, slightly deeper than the 8.9 % loss recorded in fiscal 2017.

Overall, the company’s shift toward higher‑margin subscription services improved gross profitability, while disciplined cost reductions in product development and sales & marketing partially offset the pressure from declining product revenues, resulting in a modestly larger operating loss percentage year‑over‑year.

text.value: The Group made an operating profit of $60.9 million in the year and adjusted operating profit increased by $50.7 million to $109.0 million, primarily as a result of strong revenue growth. This year's result benefited from a foreign exchange gain of $1.5 million, compared to a foreign exchange loss of $6.9 million in the prior-year.

The Group’s profit before taxation increased by $94.6 million to $53.6 million, from a loss of $41.0 million in the prior-year, primarily as a consequence of the $80.6 million improvement in operating profit supported by a $13.4 million reduction in finance expenses. Finance expenses benefited from foreign exchange gains in the current year resulting from the strengthening of both sterling and the euro against the US dollar, compared to foreign exchange losses in the prior-year.

The Group’s profit for the year increased by $87.8 million to $26.9 million in the year-ended 31 March 2019, which given only a small increase in the year-on-year income tax charge was primarily attributable to the improvement in the profit before taxation.

Cash flow from operating activities remained strong at $142.9 million, reduced by $4.8 million from $147.7 million in the prior-year. The small overall decrease was due to an increase in overheads, partially offset by a reduction in the cashflow outflow on exceptional items and an improved use of working capital. synth_text.title: Financial Highlights Summary – Year Ended 31 March 2019
synth_text.text:
The Group delivered a robust set of financial results for the year ended 31 March 2019, underpinned by strong revenue growth and favourable foreign‑exchange movements.

- **Revenue** increased by **11.2 %**, reflecting the primary driver behind the rise in operating profit.
- **Adjusted operating profit** surged **87.0 %** to **$109.0 million**, a boost of $50.7 million versus the prior year, largely due to the revenue expansion.
- **Operating profit** reached **$60.9 million**, while **profit before taxation** improved dramatically, rising **$94.6 million** to **$53.6 million** after a prior‑year loss of $41.0 million. This turnaround was supported by an $80.6 million increase in operating profit and a $13.4 million reduction in finance expenses, aided by a $1.5 million foreign‑exchange gain (versus a $6.9 million loss the year before).
- **Net cash flow from operating activities** fell modestly **3.2 %** to **$142.9 million**, a slight decline of $4.8 million driven by higher overheads, partially offset by lower cash outflows on exceptional items and better working‑capital utilisation.
- **Billings** decreased **1.1 %**, and **Cash EBITDA** contracted **15.7 %**, indicating tighter cash generation from core operations.
- **Unlevered free cash flow** dropped **11.3 %** to **$123.8 million**, reflecting the reduction in net operating cash flow after adjusting for exceptional items.

Overall, the Group’s performance was markedly stronger than the prior year, with profit for the year rising **$87.8 million** to **$26.9 million**, driven mainly by the substantial improvement in profit before tax and modest changes in the income‑tax charge.

synth_text.text:

**Key observations**

* **Revenue growth:** The Group’s revenue rose by $71.6 million (≈11 %) to $710.6 million, underpinning the improvement in profitability.
* **Turnaround in profit before tax:** A loss of $41.0 million in the prior year turned into a profit of $53.6 million, a swing of $94.6 million. This was driven mainly by an $80.6 million increase in operating profit and a $13.4 million reduction in finance expenses, helped by foreign‑exchange gains from a stronger sterling and euro.
* **Adjusted operating profit:** Increased by $50.7 million to $109.0 million, reflecting the strong revenue performance.
* **Operating cash flow:** Remained robust at $142.9 million, only $4.8 million lower than the prior year, despite higher overheads. The slight decline was partially offset by lower cash outflows on exceptional items and better working‑capital utilisation.
* **Unlevered free cash flow:** Fell by $15.8 million to $123.8 million, mirroring the modest reduction in net operating cash flow after adjusting for exceptional items.
* **Other non‑GAAP measures:** Billings were slightly lower, and Cash EBITDA decreased to $167.9 million from $199.2 million, consistent with the overall cash‑flow dynamics.

Overall, the Group delivered a markedly stronger financial performance year‑on‑year, driven by solid revenue growth, a reversal of the pre‑tax loss, and improved operating efficiency, while maintaining healthy cash‑flow generation.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Quarterly Financial Highlights: Q1 vs. Q4
synth_text.text:
The unaudited quarterly results for fiscal 2019 show modest growth and improved profitability from the first to the fourth quarter.

- **Net sales** rose from **$765.5 million** in Q1 to **$789.1 million** in Q4, an increase of roughly **$23.5 million** (≈3 %).
- **Gross profit** slipped slightly, moving from **$72.4 million** to **$70.6 million**, reflecting a marginal decline in margin despite higher sales.
- **Net income** improved, climbing from **$22.2 million** to **$24.8 million**, a gain of about **$2.5 million** (≈11 %).
- **Earnings per share (EPS)** followed the same upward trend. Basic EPS increased from **$0.71** to **$0.81**, while diluted EPS rose from **$0.69** to **$0.79**.

The quarter‑over‑quarter changes were influenced by several one‑time items noted in the footnotes:

1. **Q1 tax expense** – $0.23 per share was incurred due to the 2018 U.S. Tax Reform, reducing Q1 EPS.
2. **Q4 restructuring costs** – $1.7 million (net of taxes) lowered Q4 earnings, but this was partially offset by a **$0.05 per‑share restructuring expense**.
3. **Permanent reinvestment assertion** – Q4 included a tax benefit of $0.35 per share from undistributed earnings of two foreign subsidiaries, boosting Q4 EPS.

Overall, fiscal 2019 demonstrated solid top‑line growth and higher profitability in the fourth quarter, with EPS improvements driven both by operational performance and favorable tax adjustments.

synth_text.title: Unaudited First‑Quarter Fiscal 2019 Financial Highlights
synth_text.text:
The unaudited first‑quarter results for fiscal 2019 show robust operating performance. Net sales reached **$3.16 billion**, generating a **gross profit of $291.8 million**. After accounting for tax and other adjustments, the company reported **net income of $108.6 million**. This translates to **basic earnings per share of $3.59** and **diluted earnings per share of $3.50**.

Key adjustments influencing these figures include:

- A **$7.0 million tax expense** arising from new U.S. tax reform regulations, which contributed $0.23 per share to the basic EPS.
- **Restructuring costs** of $1.7 million (net of taxes) in the fourth quarter, reflected as a $0.05 per‑share expense.
- A **permanent reinvestment assertion** involving $10.5 million of undistributed earnings from two foreign subsidiaries, providing a $0.35 per‑share tax benefit.

These items are disclosed in footnotes (2, 3, 4, 7) and affect the net income and EPS calculations for the quarter. Overall, the company delivered solid revenue growth and profitability despite the one‑time tax and restructuring impacts.

Other assets consist of the following (in thousands):

We have a non-qualified deferred compensation plan in which certain members of management and all nonemployee
directors are eligible to participate. Participants may defer a portion of their compensation until retirement
or another date specified by them in accordance with the plan. We are funding the plan obligations through cash
deposits to a Rabbi Trust that are invested in various equity, bond and money market mutual funds in generally the
same proportion as investment elections made by the participants. The deferred compensation plan liability is included
in Other Non-Current Liabilities in the accompanying consolidated balance sheets.

Our investment in international licensees at February 28, 2019 consists principally of a 12.5% equity interest in
a Mexican licensee of $1.7 million, which became a wholly-owned subsidiary as of March 19, 2019 (see Note 2), as
well as other smaller interests in Benelux and French licensees. Generally, the investments in international licensees
are accounted for using the cost method of accounting and carried at cost as we do not exercise significant influence
over these investees. We have received dividends from our investment in the Mexican licensee in the amount of $0.3
million, $0.3 million and $0.2 million for fiscal years ended February 28, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively.

In September 2015, we invested £1,400,000 or approximately $2.2 million for a 49% minority ownership
interest in Smart Driver Club Limited (“Smart Driver Club”), a technology and insurance startup company located in
the United Kingdom. This investment has been accounted for under the equity method since we have significant
influence over the investee. As of February 28, 2019, we had made loans aggregating £5,700,000 or approximately
$7.6 million to Smart Driver Club bearing interest at an annual interest rate of 8%, with all principal and all unpaid
interest due in 2021. Our equity in the net loss of Smart Driver Club amounted to $1.8 million, $1.4 million and $1.3
million in fiscal years ended February 28, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. As of February 28, 2019, we determined
that this equity method investment was subject to other than temporary impairment. This decision was dictated by the
continuing operating losses and deteriorating liquidity position of Smart Driver Club. Accordingly, we recorded an
impairment charge of $5.0 million in the impairment loss and equity in net loss within our consolidated statement of
comprehensive income (loss). Smart Driver Club drew an additional £400,000 of debt on March 26, 2019 under a
fourth amendment to the original agreement dated March 14, 2019

Effective August 24, 2017, we acquired an ownership interest valued at $1.4 million in ThinxNet GmbH, a
company headquartered in Munich, Germany (“ThinxNet”). ThinxNet is an early stage company focused on
commercializing cloud-based mobile device and applications in the automotive sector throughout Europe. This
represents a cost basis investment as we cannot exercise significant influence over the investee. Contemporaneously,
we executed an unsecured convertible note receivable for $1.27 million with an interest rate of 6%, which has a fixed
term of 12 months, after which the loan can be converted into equity in ThinxNet or a loan due on demand at our
option. The equity investment and note receivable were consideration we received in exchange for our outstanding
accounts receivable from ThinxNet. No gain or loss was recorded on this exchange. The assets received in this
exchange are included in Other Assets in the consolidated balance sheet as of February 28, 2019 and 2018.

In August 2018, ThinxNet commenced a subsequent financing transaction to raise additional funds for working capital purposes. In connection with this transaction, we converted approximately $300,000 of outstanding accounts receivable due from ThinxNet into additional ownership interest in an in-kind exchange of assets. Based on the fair value of ThinxNet at the time of conversion, we revalued the initial ownership interest and recorded an impairment charge of $326,000, which is netted within Investment Income in our consolidated statement of comprehensive income (loss). Effective March 2019, we notified ThinxNet that we expect the outstanding loan to be repaid in June 2019.

synth_text.title: Composition and Year‑over‑Year Changes in Other Assets (Fiscal Years Ended February 28 2019 and 2018)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s “Other assets” category, reported in thousands of dollars, totaled **$22,510 k** for the fiscal year ended February 28 2019 and **$18,829 k** for the prior year. The increase of $3,681 k reflects shifts in several underlying components, each explained below.

| Component | FY 2019 | FY 2018 | Description |
|-----------|---------|---------|-------------|
| **Deferred compensation plan assets** | $6,413 k | $5,641 k | Cash deposited in a Rabbi Trust to fund a non‑qualified deferred compensation plan for eligible managers and non‑employee directors. The plan liability is shown elsewhere on the balance sheet. |
| **Investment in international licensees** | $2,263 k | $2,349 k | Primarily a 12.5 % equity interest in a Mexican licensee (originally $1.7 M, later a wholly‑owned subsidiary) plus smaller stakes in Benelux and French licensees. These are carried at cost under the cost method. |
| **Equity investment and loan to ThinxNet GmbH** | $2,650 k | $2,674 k | Cost‑basis equity purchase of $1.4 M in the German mobile‑device firm plus a $1.27 M convertible note (6 % interest, 12‑month term). The assets are recorded in “Other assets” because the company does not have significant influence. |
| **Equity investment and loan to Smart Driver Club** | – | $3,814 k | A 49 % equity stake in the UK‑based technology/insurance startup and associated loans (≈$7.6 M). The investment was deemed impaired in 2019 and removed from “Other assets,” resulting in a $5.0 M impairment charge. |
| **Deferred product cost** | $10,094 k | $3,523 k | Costs deferred for products that have not yet been recognized as expense. The sizable increase in 2019 reflects additional product development activities. |
| **Other** | $1,090 k | $828 k | Miscellaneous items not captured elsewhere. |

**Key Drivers of Change**  
1. **Deferred compensation** grew by $772 k as additional contributions were made to the Rabbi Trust.  
2. **International licensee investments** fell slightly (‑$86 k) due to the conversion of the Mexican licensee to a subsidiary, which moved the related amount out of “Other assets.”  
3. **ThinxNet investment** remained essentially flat, with a marginal $24 k decrease.  
4. **Smart Driver Club** was removed from the 2019 column after an impairment assessment, eliminating the $3,814 k previously recorded.  
5. **Deferred product cost** surged by $6,571 k, the primary source of the overall increase in “Other assets.”  
6. **Other** items rose modestly by $262 k.

**Conclusion**  
The rise in total “Other assets” from 2018 to 2019 is driven mainly by higher deferred product costs and modest growth in deferred compensation plan assets, offset by the removal of the impaired Smart Driver Club investment and a slight decline in international licensee holdings. The detailed breakdown aligns with the company’s disclosed transactions, including the acquisition of the Mexican licensee, ongoing ThinxNet financing, and the impairment of the Smart Driver Club stake.

text.value: FINANCIAL CONDITION, LIQUIDITY AND CAPITAL RESOURCES
All currency amounts are in millions unless specified
Selected cash flows for the years ended December 31, 2019, 2018 and 2017 are as follows:

Operating activities—The growth in cash provided by operating activities in 2019 and in 2018 was primarily due to increased earnings net of non-cash expenses, partially offset by higher cash taxes paid in 2019, most notably cash taxes paid on the gain on sale of the Imaging businesses.

Investing activities—Cash used in investing activities during 2019 was primarily for business acquisitions, most notably iPipeline and Foundry, partially offset by proceeds from the disposal of the Gatan business and the Imaging businesses. Cash used in investing activities during 2018 was primarily for business acquisitions, most notably PowerPlan.

Financing activities—Cash provided by/(used in) financing activities in all periods presented was primarily debt repayments/ borrowings as well as dividends paid to stockholders. Cash provided by financing activities during 2019 was primarily from the issuance of $1.2 billion of senior notes partially offset by $865.0 of revolving debt repayments and to a lesser extent dividend payments. Cash used in financing activities during 2018 was primarily from the pay-down of revolving debt borrowings of $405.0, partially offset by the net issuance of senior notes of $200.0 and dividends paid to shareholders.

Net working capital (current assets, excluding cash, less total current liabilities, excluding debt) was negative $505.4 at December 31, 2019 compared to negative $200.4 at December 31, 2018, due primarily to increased income taxes payable, deferred revenue, and the adoption of ASC 842, partially offset by increased accounts receivable. The increase in income taxes payable is due primarily to the approximately $200.0 of taxes incurred on the gain associated with the divestiture of Gatan. We expect to pay these taxes in the second quarter of 2020. The deferred revenue increase is due to a higher percentage of revenue from software and subscription-based services.

Total debt excluding unamortized debt issuance costs was $5.3 billion at December 31, 2019 (35.9% of total capital) compared to $5.0 billion at December 31, 2018 (39.1% of total capital). Our increased total debt at December 31, 2019 compared to December 31, 2018 was due primarily to the issuance of $500.0 of 2.35% senior unsecured notes and $700.0 of 2.95% senior unsecured notes, partially offset by the pay-down of revolving debt borrowings of $865.0.

On September 23, 2016, we entered into a five-year unsecured credit facility, as amended as of December 2, 2016 (the “2016 Facility”) with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., as administrative agent, and a syndicate of lenders, which replaced our previous unse- cured credit facility, dated as of July 27, 2012, as amended as of October 28, 2015 (the “2012 Facility”). The 2016 Facility comprises a five year $2.5 billion revolving credit facility, which includes availability of up to $150.0 for letters of credit. We may also, subject to compliance with specified conditions, request term loans or additional revolving credit commitments in an aggregate amount not to exceed $500.0.

The 2016 Facility contains various affirmative and negative covenants which, among other things, limit our ability to incur new debt, enter into certain mergers and acquisitions, sell assets and grant liens, make restricted payments (including the payment of dividends on our common stock) and capital expenditures, or change our line of business. We also are subject to financial cove- nants which require us to limit our consolidated total leverage ratio and to maintain a consolidated interest coverage ratio. The most restrictive covenant is the consolidated total leverage ratio which is limited to 3.5 to 1.

The 2016 Facility provides that the consolidated total leverage ratio may be increased, no more than twice during the term of the 2016 Facility, to 4.00 to 1 for a consecutive four quarter fiscal period per increase (or, for any portion of such four quarter fiscal period in which the maximum would be 4.25 to 1). In conjunction with the Deltek acquisition in December of 2016, we increased the maximum consolidated total leverage ratio covenant to 4.25 to 1 through June 30, 2017 and 4.00 to 1 through December 31, 2017.

At December 31, 2019, we had $5.3 billion of senior unsecured notes and $0.0 of outstanding revolver borrowings. In addition, we had $7.7 of other debt in the form of finance leases and several smaller facilities that allow for borrowings or the issuance of letters of credit in foreign locations to support our non-U.S. businesses. We had $74.0 of outstanding letters of credit at December 31, 2019, of which $35.8 was covered by our lending group, thereby reducing our revolving credit capacity commensurately.
We may redeem some or all of our senior secured notes at any time or from time to time, at 100% of their principal amount, plus a make-whole premium based on a spread to U.S. Treasury securities.
We were in compliance with all debt covenants related to our credit facility throughout the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018.
See Note 8 of the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements included in this Annual Report for additional information regarding our credit facility and senior notes.

Cash and cash equivalents at our foreign subsidiaries at December 31, 2019 totaled $291.8 as compared to $339.0 at December 31, 2018, a decrease of 13.9%. The decrease was due primarily to the repatriation of $290.6 during the year and cash used in the acquisition of Foundry, partially offset by cash generated from foreign operations. We intend to repatriate substantially all historical and future earnings subject to the deemed repatriation tax.

Capital expenditures of $52.7, $49.1 and $48.8 were incurred during 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. Capitalized software expenditures of $10.2, $9.5 and $10.8 were incurred during 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. Capital expenditures and capitalized software expenditures were relatively consistent in 2019 as compared to 2018 and 2017. In the future, we expect the aggregate of capital expenditures and capitalized software expenditures as a percentage of annual net revenues to be between 1.0% and 1.5%.

**Key take‑aways**

1. **Operating cash generation**  
   The company generated $1.23 billion of cash from operations in 2019. This increase was driven primarily by higher earnings after non‑cash expenses. The benefit was partially offset by higher cash taxes, notably taxes on the gain from the sale of the Imaging businesses.

2. **Investing cash use**  
   Investing activities consumed $209.6 million. The outflow was mainly for acquisitions, most prominently the purchases of iPipeline and Foundry. Proceeds from the disposal of the Gatan and Imaging businesses partially offset the spending.

   Financing activities resulted in a net outflow of $1.17 billion. The dominant components were debt repayments and dividend payments. Although the issuance of $1.2 billion of senior notes provided cash, it was largely consumed by $865 million of revolving‑debt repayments and dividend distributions.

4. **Net cash position**  
   Combining the three categories, the company experienced a net cash outflow of approximately $145 million for the year.

5. **Liquidity and capital resources context**  
   - Total debt (excluding issuance costs) stood at $5.3 billion, representing 35.9 % of total capital, up from $5.0 billion in 2018 due to new senior‑note issuances.

   - Cash and cash equivalents at foreign subsidiaries fell to $291.8 million, reflecting repatriation of earnings and cash used for the Foundry acquisition.  

Overall, 2019’s cash‑flow profile reflects robust operating performance that was largely neutralized by strategic investing in acquisitions and significant financing activities focused on debt management and shareholder returns.

text.value: NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (in thousands, except for share and per share data)
NOTE 13 — Derivatives

Our earnings and cash flows are subject to fluctuations due to changes in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates. We selectively use derivative financial instruments including foreign currency forward contracts and interest rate swaps to manage our exposure to these risks.

The use of derivative financial instruments exposes the Company to credit risk, which relates to the risk of nonperformance by a counterparty to the derivative contracts. We manage our credit risk by entering into derivative contracts with only highly rated financial institutions and by using netting agreements.

The effective portion of derivative gains and losses are recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss until the hedged transaction affects earnings upon settlement, at which time they are reclassified to cost of goods sold or net sales. If it is probable that an anticipated hedged transaction will not occur by the end of the originally specified time period, we reclassify the gains or losses related to that hedge from accumulated other comprehensive loss to other income (expense).

We assess hedge effectiveness qualitatively by verifying that the critical terms of the hedging instrument and the forecasted transaction continue to match, and that there have been no adverse developments that have increased the risk that the counterparty will default. No recognition of ineffectiveness was recorded in our Consolidated Statement of Earnings for the twelve months ended December 31, 2019.
Foreign Currency Hedges

We use forward contracts to mitigate currency risk related to a portion of our forecasted foreign currency revenues and costs. The currency forward contracts are designed as cash flow hedges and are recorded in the Consolidated Balance Sheets at fair value.

We continue to monitor the Company’s overall currency exposure and may elect to add cash flow hedges in the future. At December 31, 2019, we had a net unrealized gain of $655 in accumulated other comprehensive loss, of which $595 is expected to be reclassified to income within the next 12 months. The notional amount of foreign currency forward contracts outstanding was $8,011 at December 31, 2019.
Interest Rate Swaps

We use interest rate swaps to convert a portion of our revolving credit facility's outstanding balance from a variable rate of interest to a fixed rate. As of December 31, 2019, we have agreements to fix interest rates on $50,000 of long-term debt through February 2024. The difference to be paid or received under the terms of the swap agreements will be recognized as an adjustment to interest expense when settled.

These swaps are treated as cash flow hedges and consequently, the changes in fair value are recorded in other comprehensive loss. The estimated net amount of the existing gains or losses that are reported in accumulated other comprehensive loss that are expected to be reclassified into earnings within the next twelve months is approximately $82.
The location and fair values of derivative instruments designated as hedging instruments in the Consolidated Balance Sheets as of December 31, 2019, are shown in the following table:

The Company has elected to net its foreign currency derivative assets and liabilities in the balance sheet in accordance with ASC 210-20 (Balance Sheet, Offsetting). On a gross basis, there were foreign currency derivative assets of $648 and foreign currency derivative liabilities of $68 at December 31, 2019.

synth_text.title: Derivatives Hedge Positions – Balance‑Sheet Summary for 2018 and 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Company uses derivative financial instruments—primarily foreign‑currency forward contracts and interest‑rate swaps—to hedge exposure to currency and interest‑rate fluctuations. These hedges are recorded at fair value on the balance sheet and, as cash‑flow hedges, their unrealized gains and losses flow through accumulated other comprehensive loss until the underlying transaction settles.

**Balance‑sheet presentation (in thousands of dollars)**  

| Year | Interest‑Rate Swaps – Other Current Assets | Interest‑Rate Swaps – Other Assets | Interest‑Rate Swaps – Other Long‑Term Obligations | Foreign‑Currency Hedges – Other Current Assets |
|------|--------------------------------------------|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| 2019 | $ 82 | $ — | $(78) | $ 580 |
| 2018 | $ 576 | $ 369 | $ — | $ 393 |

**Key observations**

1. **Interest‑rate swaps**  
   * The fair‑value of swaps moved from a larger amount in “Other current assets” ($576 k) and “Other assets” ($369 k) in 2018 to a much smaller balance ($82 k) in 2019.  
   * A negative balance of $(78 k) appears under “Other long‑term obligations” in 2019, reflecting a liability‑side fair‑value adjustment for swaps linked to the Company’s long‑term debt.  
   * The shift aligns with the Company’s strategy (as noted in the 2019 footnotes) to fix interest on $50 million of long‑term debt through February 2024, with the expected reclassification of approximately $82 k of gains into earnings over the next twelve months.

2. **Foreign‑currency hedges**  
   * The fair‑value of forward contracts recorded in “Other current assets” increased from $393 k in 2018 to $580 k in 2019, indicating a larger notional exposure (the notional amount of contracts was $8,011 k at year‑end 2019).  
   * The Company reported a net unrealized gain of $655 k in accumulated other comprehensive loss at December 31, 2019, of which $595 k is expected to be reclassified to income within the next year—consistent with the growth in the hedge balance.

**Contextual notes**  
* All derivative contracts are with highly rated financial institutions, and netting agreements are used to mitigate credit risk.  
* Hedge effectiveness is assessed qualitatively; no ineffectiveness was recorded for 2019.  
* On a gross basis, foreign‑currency derivative assets totaled $648 k against liabilities of $68 k at the end of 2019, reflecting the net position shown in the table.

**Conclusion**  
The table illustrates the Company’s active management of interest‑rate and foreign‑currency risk through derivatives. Between 2018 and 2019, the portfolio shifted toward a higher concentration of foreign‑currency forward contracts and a reduced, re‑balanced interest‑rate swap exposure, with the associated fair‑value adjustments captured in the balance‑sheet categories described above.
