- The net figure appears on Autodesk’s consolidated balance sheet as “Developed technologies, net” and as part of “Other assets.”

text.value: Base Salary

Base salary for our named executive officers is the fixed component of our executive compensation program. We use base salary to compensate our named executive officers for services rendered during the year and to recognize the experience, skills, knowledge and responsibilities required of each named executive officer. We apply no specific formula to determine adjustments to base salary. Adjustments to base salary have been made to reflect our economic condition and future expected performance. We continue to provide base salaries that are conservative relative to competitive market pay levels.

In April 2018, our compensation committee reviewed the base salaries of Mses. Friar, Henry, Reses and Whiteley, taking into consideration a competitive market analysis performed by Compensia, the recommendations of our CEO and our then-current People Lead, the desire to retain our highly qualified executive team and the other factors described above. Following this review, our compensation committee approved an increase in the annual base salary levels for Mses. Friar, Henry, Reses and Whiteley to $400,000, in each case effective as of April 1, 2018, in order to improve competitive alignment with our peers. In addition, our compensation committee determined that it was appropriate to leave our CEO’s 2018 base salary level at $2.75 per year, at the request of our CEO and with compensation committee approval.
The annualized base salaries of our named executive officers as of December 31, 2018 compared to December 31, 2017 were:
(1) Ms. Friar resigned from her position as Chief Financial Officer, effective as of November 16, 2018, at which time her annual base salary was $400,000.
(2) Ms. Whiteley was appointed to General Counsel and Corporate Secretary effective March 18, 2018, and her salary was adjusted to reflect her promotion to this role.

(3) The base salaries of Messrs. Daswani and Murphy were not adjusted in conjunction with their service as interim co-CFOs. Salary adjustments for Messrs. Daswani and Murphy made in April 2018, prior to their becoming named executive officers, were made as part of the company-wide compensation review program. Their salary adjustments were recommended by their direct manager and approved by the then-current People Lead. Messrs. Daswani and Murphy’s annualized base salaries at the time of their appointment as interim co-CFOs were $300,000 and $295,000, respectively.

synth_text.title: Portfolio Companies Financial Performance Overview 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 the Portfolio Companies recorded modest but broad‑based growth compared with 2018. Orders rose to €5,806 million from €5,569 million, and revenue increased to €5,526 million from €4,930 million. Adjusted EBITA improved markedly, narrowing the loss to €71 million from €305 million, which lifted the adjusted EBITA margin from –6.2 % to –1.3 %.

The upside was underpinned by a recovery in commodity‑related markets and the strongest gains in the mechanical‑drives segment. All fully consolidated units reported better adjusted EBITA, and the large‑drives‑applications business was a key contributor to the overall turnaround.

Other notable developments include a reduction in severance charges to €14 million (down from €86 million in 2018) and a slight improvement in the result from equity investments, although these remained negative. The order backlog stood at €5 billion at year‑end, with €3 billion expected to convert into revenue in fiscal 2020.

Looking ahead, the portfolio faces moderate growth expectations amid geopolitical and economic uncertainties. From fiscal 2020, equity stakes in Ethos Energy Group Limited, Voith Hydro Holding, the subsea business and most of the process‑solutions business will be transferred to the Gas and Power operating company, which would have reduced the 2019 figures to €4,746 million in orders, €4,558 million in revenue and an adjusted EBITA loss of €115 million. Additionally, Mitsubishi‑Hitachi Metals Machinery and Siemens agreed in September 2019 for MHMM to acquire Siemens’ stake in Primetals Technologies, with closing expected early in 2020.

Overall, the 2019 results demonstrate a positive shift in profitability and operational performance, setting a foundation for continued, albeit moderate, growth in the coming years.

synth_text.title: Portfolio Companies FY 2020 Financial Highlights: Orders, Revenue, and Adjusted EBITA Growth
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2020 the Portfolio Companies delivered solid year‑over‑year growth across their core financial metrics. Actual orders increased by **4 %**, outpacing the comparable (Comp.) growth of **3 %**, while revenue rose **12 %** versus a **11 %** rise on a comparable basis. The most notable improvement was seen in Adjusted EBITA, which jumped **77 %** in the actual results, turning the consolidated figure positive for the first time.

This performance was underpinned by a recovery in commodity‑related markets and especially strong growth in the mechanical drives business. Adjusted EBITA improved in every fully consolidated unit, driven largely by the large‑drives applications segment.

Other highlights include:
- **Order backlog** of **€5 billion** at year‑end, with **€3 billion** expected to convert into revenue in FY 2020.
- **Severance charges** fell sharply to **€14 million**, down from **€86 million** in fiscal 2018.
- Results from equity investments improved slightly, though they remained negative; volatile outcomes are anticipated in the coming quarters.
- Market outlook remains cautious due to geopolitical and economic uncertainties, but moderate growth is expected in the main markets served.
- From FY 2020 onward, equity investments in Ethos Energy Group Limited, Voith Hydro Holding, the subsea business, and most of the process‑solutions business will be transferred to the Gas and Power operating company. Had this structure been in place in FY 2019, the Portfolio Companies would have reported **€4.746 billion** in orders, **€4.558 billion** in revenue, and an Adjusted EBITA of **‑€115 million**.
- A strategic transaction is pending: Mitsubishi‑Hitachi Metals Machinery (MHMM) will acquire Siemens’ stake in Primetals Technologies, with closing expected early in calendar 2020.

Overall, the Portfolio Companies achieved broad‑based growth, improved profitability, and positioned themselves for continued moderate expansion despite a challenging macro‑economic environment.

text.value: Customer Contract - Related Balance Sheet Amounts

The Company generally invoices customers in annual installments payable in advance. The difference between the timing of revenue recognition and the timing of billings results in the recognition of unbilled accounts receivable or deferred revenue in the consolidated balance sheets. Amounts related to customer contract-related arrangements are included on the consolidated balance sheets as of August 1, 2018 and July 31, 2019 as follows (in thousands):
(1) The short- and long-term portions of this balance are reported in ‘Prepaid expenses and other current assets’ and ‘Other assets,’ respectively, on the consolidated balance sheets.
Unbilled accounts receivable

Unbilled accounts receivable includes those amounts that are unbilled due to agreed-upon contractual terms in which billing occurs subsequent to revenue recognition. This situation typically occurs when the Company transfers control of time-based software licenses to customers up-front, but invoices customers annually over the term of the license, which is typically two years.

During the fiscal year ended July 31, 2019, the Company transferred control of a ten year timebased license that resulted in $9.7 million of unbilled accounts receivable as of July 31, 2019, representing future billings in years two through ten of the license term.

Unbilled accounts receivable is classified as either current or non-current based on the duration of remaining time between the date of the consolidated balance sheets and the anticipated due date of the underlying receivables.
Contract costs

Contract costs consist of customer acquisition costs and costs to fulfill a contract, which includes commissions and their related payroll taxes, royalties, and referral fees. Contract costs are classified as either current or non-current based on the duration of time remaining between the date of the consolidated balance sheets and the anticipated amortization date of the associated costs.

The current portion of contract costs as of July 31, 2019 in the amount of $7.0 million is included in prepaid and other current assets on the Company’s consolidated balance sheets. The non-current portion of contract costs as of July 31, 2019 in the amount of $23.4 million is included in other assets on the Company’s consolidated balance sheets. The Company amortized $5.5 million of contract costs during the fiscal year ended July 31, 2019.
Deferred revenue

Deferred revenue consists of amounts that have been invoiced and for which the Company has the right to bill, but that have not been recognized as revenue because the related goods or services have not been transferred. Deferred revenue that will be realized during the 12-month period following the date of the consolidated balance sheets is recorded as current, and the remaining deferred revenue is recorded as non-current.
During the fiscal year ended July 31, 2019, the Company recognized revenue of $112.2 million related to the Company’s deferred revenue balance as of August 1, 2018.

This growth reflects revenue that has been recognized for time‑based software licenses delivered up‑front, while billing is deferred to annual installments. Notably, a ten‑year license transferred during FY 2019 generated $9.7 million of unbilled receivables, representing future billings for years two through ten.

* **Contract costs, net** rose sharply from **$12.9 million** to **$30.4 million**. These costs comprise customer‑acquisition expenses and contract‑fulfillment costs such as commissions, payroll taxes, royalties, and referral fees. As of July 31 2019, $7.0 million of the costs were classified as current (recorded in prepaid and other current assets) and $23.4 million as non‑current (recorded in other assets). The Company amortized $5.5 million of these costs during the fiscal year.

* **Deferred revenue, net** improved from **$(141.7 million)** to **$(131.8 million)**. Deferred revenue represents invoiced amounts for which the related goods or services have not yet been transferred. During FY 2019, the Company recognized $112.2 million of revenue from the August 1 2018 deferred balance, reducing the liability.

In summary, the fiscal‑year transition shows higher unbilled receivables and contract costs as the Company continues to recognize revenue ahead of billing, while deferred revenue declines as previously invoiced amounts are earned. These trends are consistent with the Company’s practice of invoicing customers annually in advance of revenue recognition for time‑based software licenses.

On April 1, 2018, the Company adopted ASU 2014-09-Revenue from Contracts with Customers (ASC 606) and all related amendments (“New Revenue Standard”) using the modified retrospective method. The Company has applied the new revenue standard to all contracts that were entered into after adoption and to all contracts that were open as of the initial date of adoption. The comparative information has not been restated and continues to be reported under the accounting standards in effect for those periods. The adoption of the new standard impacts the Company's net sales on an ongoing basis depending on the relative amount of revenue sold through its distributors, the change in inventory held by its distributors, and the changes in price concessions granted to its distributors. Previously, the Company deferred revenue and cost of sales on shipments to distributors until the distributor sold the product to their end customer. As required by the new revenue standard, the Company no longer defers revenue and cost of sales, but rather, estimates the effects of returns and allowances provided to distributors and records revenue at the time of sale to the distributor. Sales to non-distributor customers, under both the previous and new revenue standards, are generally recognized upon the Company’s shipment of the product. The cumulative effect of the changes made to the consolidated April 1, 2018 balance sheet for the adoption of the new revenue standard is summarized in the table of opening balance sheet adjustments below. Prior to the acquisition of Microsemi, Microsemi already recognized revenue on a sell-in basis, so the impact of the adoption of the New Revenue Standard was primarily driven by Microchip's historical business excluding Microsemi.

synth_text.title: Effect of ASC 606 Adoption on Microchip Technology’s Balance Sheet (April 1 2018)
synth_text.text:
On April 1 2018 Microchip Technology adopted ASC 606 – the new revenue‑recognition standard – using a modified retrospective approach. The transition from a sell‑through to a sell‑in model required several balance‑sheet adjustments, which are summarized below (values in $ millions):

**Assets**  
- **Accounts receivable, net:** + $324.5 – higher because revenue is now recorded at the point of sale to distributors, reducing the need for a large receivable balance.  
- **Inventories:** ‑ $12.5 – lower as the company no longer holds inventory on behalf of distributors under the old model.  
- **Other current assets:** + $36.9 – increase reflects adjustments related to the new revenue‑recognition calculations.  
- **Other assets:** + $5.5 – modest rise from re‑classification of certain deferred tax items.  
- **Long‑term deferred tax assets:** ‑ $23.5 – decrease due to the reversal of tax benefits previously associated with deferred revenue.

**Liabilities**  
- **Accrued liabilities:** + $367.0 – higher because costs previously deferred with distributors are now recognized earlier.  
- **Deferred income on shipments to distributors:** ‑ $288.2 – the most significant reduction, as ASC 606 eliminates the practice of deferring revenue and cost of sales until distributors sell to end‑customers.  
- **Long‑term deferred tax liability:** + $16.8 – slight increase reflecting the tax effect of the new revenue timing.

**Stockholders’ Equity**  
- **Retained earnings:** + $235.3 – the cumulative effect of the adoption, primarily driven by the removal of deferred income and the earlier recognition of revenue and expenses.

The dominant drivers of these changes are the elimination of the “deferred income on shipments to distributors” balance and the shift to recognizing revenue at the point of sale to distributors. This transition markedly reduced accounts receivable, increased accrued liabilities, and boosted retained earnings. The impact is consistent with the company’s disclosure that the adoption of ASC 606 fundamentally altered its revenue‑recognition mechanics, especially for distributor sales, while non‑distributor sales continued to be recognized upon shipment.

synth_text.title: Impact of ASC 606 Adoption on Microchip’s Balance Sheet
synth_text.text:
The adoption of ASC 606 (the New Revenue Standard) on April 1 2018 produced noticeable shifts in Microchip’s balance‑sheet composition. When the company applied the standard using a modified retrospective approach, the cumulative effect was recorded as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings, raising that balance from $2,975.3 million (without adoption) to $3,210.6 million (as reported).

Key balance‑sheet changes include:

* **Accounts receivable, net** – increased to $880.6 million after adoption from $556.1 million without adoption, reflecting the new timing of revenue recognition.
* **Inventories** – remained relatively stable, moving slightly from $724.2 million to $711.7 million.
* **Other current assets** – rose modestly to $191.6 million from $154.7 million.
* **Deferred income on shipments to distributors** – was eliminated under ASC 606, dropping from $288.2 million (pre‑adoption) to $0.
* **Accrued liabilities** – grew to $787.3 million after adoption, up from $420.3 million, largely due to the re‑classification of distributor‑related obligations.
* **Long‑term deferred tax assets** and **liabilities** shifted only slightly, reflecting the tax effects of the accounting change.

Overall, the transition from sell‑through to sell‑in revenue recognition removed the deferred‑income balance, reduced the accounts receivable tied to distributor shipments, and substantially boosted retained earnings. These adjustments illustrate how ASC 606 reshaped Microchip’s financial position, aligning revenue recognition with the point of sale to distributors while preserving the comparability of prior‑period figures.

text.value: ACCOUNTING POLICY

Accounts receivable represent amounts owing to us that are currently due and collectible. We initially recognize accounts receivable on the date they originate. We measure accounts receivable initially at fair value, and subsequently at amortized cost, with changes recognized in net income. We measure an impairment loss for accounts receivable as the excess of the carrying amount over the present value of future cash flows we expect to derive from it, if any. The excess is allocated to an allowance for doubtful accounts and recognized as a loss in net income.
EXPLANATORY INFORMATION

We have retrospectively reclassified $23 million as at December 31, 2018 and January 1, 2019 related to our wireless financing programs from “accounts receivable” to “other current assets” as the collection time frame of the amounts differs from accounts receivable.

synth_text.title: 2018 Accounts Receivable Summary and Related Accounting Adjustments
synth_text.text:
In 2018 the company reported total accounts receivable of **$2.236 billion**. This amount consists of:

* **Customer accounts receivable:** $1.529 billion  
* **Other accounts receivable:** $762 million  

From the gross receivable balance, an **allowance for doubtful accounts of $55 million** was recorded, reflecting the estimated portion of receivables that may not be collectible. After this allowance, the net receivable balance remains $2.236 billion.

**Accounting policy:** Receivables are recognized on the date they originate, initially measured at fair value and subsequently carried at amortized cost. Any impairment loss is recognized when the carrying amount exceeds the present value of expected future cash flows, with the excess transferred to the allowance for doubtful accounts and recorded as a loss in net income.

**Reclassification adjustment:** As disclosed, $23 million of amounts related to the company’s wireless financing programs were retrospectively reclassified from “accounts receivable” to “other current assets” at year‑end. This reclassification reflects the longer collection time frame of those amounts compared with standard receivables.

Overall, the 2018 figures illustrate the composition of the company’s receivable portfolio, the impact of credit risk allowances, and the effect of a targeted reclassification that aligns asset presentation with collection expectations.

synth_text.title: 2019 Accounts Receivable Summary and Related Accounting Policies
synth_text.text:
**Overview of 2019 Receivables**  
In 2019 the company reported total accounts receivable of **$2.304 billion**. This amount consists of:

- **Customer accounts receivable:** $1.579 billion  
- **Other accounts receivable:** $785 million  

From this gross total, an **allowance for doubtful accounts of $60 million** was recorded, reducing the net realizable value of receivables to **$2.244 billion**. The allowance represents the company’s estimate of amounts that may ultimately be uncollectible, in line with its impairment policy.

**Allowance Trend**  
The prior‑period note shows an allowance of $15 million, indicating that the provision for doubtful accounts increased by $45 million in 2019, reflecting a more conservative view of collectibility.

**Accounting Policy Highlights**  
- Receivables are recognized on the date they originate and initially measured at fair value; thereafter they are carried at amortized cost.  
- Impairment losses are recognized when the carrying amount exceeds the present value of expected future cash flows. The excess is transferred to the allowance for doubtful accounts and recorded as a loss in net income.  
- Changes in the allowance affect net income in the period they are recognized.

**Retrospective Reclassification**  
The company retrospectively reclassified **$23 million** (as of December 31 2018 and January 1 2019) from “accounts receivable” to “other current assets.” This adjustment relates to wireless financing programs whose collection periods differ from standard receivable terms, ensuring that the receivable balance more accurately reflects amounts due within the normal credit cycle.

**Key Takeaway**  
The 2019 accounts receivable figures, adjusted for the allowance and the $23 million reclassification, provide a transparent view of the company’s credit exposure and the prudential measures applied under its accounting policies to manage potential credit risk.

synth_text.title: Assumptions Underlying Fair‑Value Valuation of Stock Options for Fiscal Years 2017‑2018
synth_text.text:
The fair value of the company’s stock options granted in fiscal years 2017 and 2018 is estimated using the Black‑Scholes option‑pricing model, in accordance with ASC 718. The model relies on weighted‑average assumptions that reflect market conditions and the company’s historical experience:

| Fiscal Year | Expected Life (years) | Risk‑Free Interest Rate | Expected Volatility | Expected Dividend Yield |
|-------------|-----------------------|------------------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| 2018        | 5.6                   | 2.7 %                  | 26.4 %              | 0 % (no dividends)       |
| 2017        | 5.6                   | 1.9 %                  | 29.4 %              | 0 % (no dividends)       |

**Key points from the additional context**

* **Expected life** – Both years assume a 5.6‑year option life, derived from historical employee exercise behavior, indicating the period the options are expected to remain outstanding.  
* **Risk‑free rate** – Based on the yield of U.S. Treasury zero‑coupon bonds whose term matches the 5.6‑year expected life at the grant date (1.9 % in 2017, 2.7 % in 2018).  
* **Expected volatility** – Calculated from the company’s historical common‑stock price volatility over periods comparable to the option’s expected life (higher in 2017 at 29.4 % than in 2018 at 26.4 %).  
* **Dividend yield** – Set to zero because the company has never paid dividends and does not anticipate doing so in the future.

These assumptions provide the inputs required for the Black‑Scholes model to determine the fair value of the options granted in each fiscal year.

Selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses fell $0.5 million (‑2 %), driven by lower employee‑related costs (down $2.0 million to $3.6 million) despite a $3.0 million increase in litigation expenses, which rose to $19.4 million because of the timing of several pending actions. * **Operating expenses** – SG&A stayed near $32 M, with legal fees representing roughly 60 % of SG&A. Litigation expenses rose by $3 M to $19.4 M in 2019, reflecting the timing of ongoing lawsuits, while employee‑related SG&A fell by $2 M due to lower incentive bonuses.  
* **R&D** expense was essentially unchanged at about $2 M each year.  
* **Other expense** decreased because the company eliminated exposure from a warrant liability and recorded a $0.7 M gain from the sale of its investment in JVP, offset by a modest $0.3 M net interest income.  
* **Tax provision** shifted from an $8.0 M expense in 2018 to a $6.2 M benefit in 2019, driven by the 2019 loss and a foreign intangible tax benefit related to 2018 earnings.

**Resulting performance**

The combination of a steep revenue contraction and steady operating costs turned operating income from a $28.7 M profit in 2018 to a $22.7 M loss in 2019. After accounting for the tax benefit, the company posted a net loss of $16.5 M in 2019, compared with a net profit of $20.7 M the previous year.

Overall, while the company maintained strong gross margins and controlled expense growth, the timing of licensing revenues and increased litigation costs were the primary factors behind the 2019 financial downturn.

synth_text.title: Jabil Inc. – Unaudited Quarterly Financial Summary for May 31 and August 31 2018
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary presents Jabil Inc.’s unaudited quarterly financial results for the periods ending May 31, 2018 and August 31, 2018. All figures are expressed in thousands of dollars unless otherwise noted. Management has adjusted the numbers to align with the audited consolidated statements, incorporating normal recurring accruals. As disclosed, quarterly performance is not necessarily indicative of future results.

**Key Metrics**

| Metric (in $ thousands) | May 31 2018 | August 31 2018 |
|--------------------------|------------|----------------|
| Net revenue              | 5,436,952  | 5,771,831 |
| Gross profit             | 398,227    | 442,147 |
| Operating income         | 112,971    | 153,896 |
| Net (loss) income        | 42,702     | (56,608) |
| Net income attributable to Jabil Inc. | 42,541 | (57,314) |
| Basic EPS (per share)    | $0.25      | $(0.34) |
| Diluted EPS (per share)  | $0.25      | $(0.34) |

**Quarter‑to‑Quarter Comparison**  
- **Revenue & Gross Profit:** Both increased modestly in the August quarter (+$334 M in revenue and +$44 M in gross profit).  
- **Operating Income:** Rose by $40.9 M, reflecting higher gross margins despite higher costs.  
- **Net Income:** Switched from a profit of $42.7 M in May to a loss of $56.6 M in August, resulting in a negative EPS of $0.34.  

**Contextual Factors Influencing August 2018 Results**  
- **Acquisition & Integration Charges:** The August 31, 2018 quarter includes $8.1 M of acquisition‑related expenses tied to Jabil’s strategic collaboration with JJMD.  
- **Distressed‑Customer Charge:** A $18.0 M charge was recorded for the same period, reducing profitability.  
- **Tax Adjustments:** A tax benefit of $111.4 M related to the Tax Act was recognized, partially offsetting other expenses but not enough to prevent a net loss.  

**Conclusion**  
While top‑line revenue and operating performance improved in the August 2018 quarter, the combination of acquisition costs, distressed‑customer charges, and tax adjustments led to a net loss and negative earnings per share. Stakeholders should view these unaudited figures as a snapshot of the period and not as a forecast of future performance.

synth_text.title: 2017 Net Income per Share and Dilution Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the Company reported net income from continuing operations of **$170.6 million**. The basic weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding during the year was **217.2 million**, which produced a **basic net income per common share of $0.79**.

Dilutive securities increased the share count for diluted earnings calculations. The dilutive effect of employee equity incentives (stock options and RSUs) added **4.4 million** shares, while convertible debt contributed additional shares: **12.7 million** from the 2007 Junior Convertible Debt and **0.5 million** from the 2015 Senior Convertible Debt. No dilutive effect was recorded for the 2017 Senior or Junior Convertible Debt. After accounting for all dilutive instruments, the diluted weighted‑average common shares outstanding rose to **234.8 million**.

Using this diluted share count, diluted net income per common share from continuing operations was **$0.73**.

The calculations follow the methodology described in Note 20: basic EPS is derived from net income divided by the basic weighted‑average shares, while diluted EPS incorporates the potentially dilutive shares from stock options, RSUs (via the treasury‑stock method), and convertible debt. No anti‑dilutive option shares were present for 2017, so all identified dilutive securities were included in the diluted share count.

synth_text.title: Summary of Basic and Diluted Net Income per Share – Fiscal Years 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary presents the company’s net income from continuing operations and the corresponding basic and diluted earnings per share (EPS) for the fiscal years ended March 31, 2018 and March 31, 2019. Basic EPS is calculated using the weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding, while diluted EPS incorporates potentially dilutive securities—stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), and convertible debt—using the treasury‑stock method. No anti‑dilutive option shares were identified in either year.

**Key Financial Metrics**

| Fiscal Year | Net Income (continuing) | Basic Shares (M) | Dilutive Effect of Stock Options & RSUs (M) | Dilutive Effect of Convertible Debt (M) | Diluted Shares (M) | Basic EPS | Diluted EPS |
|-------------|------------------------|------------------|---------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------|-----------|------------|
| 2019 | $355.9 M | 236.2 | 3.8 | 9.9 (2015 Senior Convertible Debt) | 249.9 | $1.51 | $1.42 |
| 2018 | $255.4 M | 232.9 | 4.4 | 1.3 (2007 Junior Convertible Debt) + 10.3 (2015 Senior Convertible Debt) | 248.9 | $1.10 | $1.03 |

**Observations**

1. **Net Income Growth** – Net income from continuing operations rose by $100.5 million (≈ 39 %) from 2018 to 2019.
2. **Share Count** – The basic weighted‑average common shares increased modestly (by 3.3 M shares). Diluted shares also grew slightly, reflecting the net effect of dilutive securities.
3. **Dilutive Securities** –  
   * The dilutive impact of stock options and RSUs decreased from 4.4 M shares in 2018 to 3.8 M shares in 2019.  
   * Convertible debt contributed 10.3 M dilutive shares in 2018 (2015 Senior) and 1.3 M from the 2007 Junior issue; in 2019 only the 2015 Senior debt remained, contributing 9.9 M shares.
4. **Earnings per Share** – Both basic and diluted EPS improved markedly: basic EPS increased from $1.10 to $1.51, and diluted EPS from $1.03 to $1.42, reflecting higher profitability and relatively stable share dilution.

**Conclusion**  
The company’s financial performance improved significantly in 2019, with higher net income and EPS despite modest increases in share dilution. The absence of anti‑dilutive option shares underscores that all potential dilutive securities were indeed dilutive during the periods examined.

synth_text.title: Equity Incentive Securities and Repurchase Shares – 2018 vs 2019 Summary
synth_text.text:
The company’s equity‑incentive program showed a modest contraction in 2019 compared with 2018. Stock options declined from **229,294** to **223,259**, while restricted stock units fell from **148,175** to **136,600**. No restricted stock awards were granted in either year. Notably, the amount of common stock subject to repurchase dropped sharply, from **957** shares in 2018 to **250** shares in 2019.

These securities are excluded from the diluted weighted‑average common‑share count because their inclusion would be anti‑dilutive. They are classified as “participating securities” – primarily stock options from the 2015 Plan (and earlier 2009 Equity Incentive Plan) that can be exercised before vesting. Unvested shares carry a non‑forfeitable dividend right, and any shares issued through early exercise are subject to repurchase at the original exercise price if the employee’s service terminates. Once the repurchase right lapses and the awards vest, the shares revert to ordinary common stock and are no longer considered participating securities.

Additionally, the company reports a redeemable non‑controlling interest related to its 85 % ownership of OpenEye. This interest is treated as temporary equity and is presented between liabilities and stockholders’ equity on the consolidated balance sheet; its impact on net income is reflected in the consolidated statements of operations. The put and call options governing this interest become exercisable in the first quarter of 2023.

Overall, the 2019 figures reflect a reduction in both outstanding options and RSUs, as well as a significant decline in shares subject to repurchase, consistent with the company’s ongoing management of its equity‑based compensation and related anti‑dilutive securities.

- **Common stock subject to repurchase:** 13,281  

These securities are excluded from the calculation of diluted weighted‑average common shares outstanding because their inclusion would have an anti‑dilutive effect. They are classified as **participating securities**, which include certain stock options granted under the 2015 Plan and earlier 2009 Equity Incentive Plan. Such options may be exercised before they vest; unvested shares carry a non‑forfeitable right to dividends. If early‑exercised, the resulting unvested shares are subject to repurchase at the original exercise price upon termination of employment or services. Once the awards vest and the repurchase right lapses, the shares revert to ordinary common stock and are no longer considered participating securities.

Additionally, the company holds a **redeemable noncontrolling interest** representing its 85 % equity stake in OpenEye. Under the OpenEye stockholder agreement, minority shareholders have a put option to sell their shares to the company, and the company holds a call option to purchase the remaining shares. Both options become exercisable in the first quarter of 2023. This interest is treated as temporary equity and is presented between liabilities and stockholders’ equity on the consolidated balance sheet, with its attributable portion of net income or loss reflected in the consolidated statements of operations.

Together, these items illustrate the composition of the company’s equity incentive program in 2017 and the accounting treatment applied to ensure that anti‑dilutive securities do not distort diluted earnings per share calculations.

On December 22, 2017, the U.S. government enacted comprehensive tax legislation commonly referred to as the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the “Tax Act”). The Tax Act makes broad and complex changes to the U.S. tax code, including, but not limited to, the following that impact the Company: (1) reducing the U.S. federal corporate income tax rate from 35 percent to 21 percent; (2) eliminating the corporate alternative minimum tax; (3) creating a new limitation on deductible interest expense; (4) limiting the deductibility of certain executive compensation; and (5) limiting certain other deductions.

The Company follows ASC 740-10 “Income Taxes” which requires the recognition of deferred tax liabilities and assets for the expected future tax consequences of events that have been included in the financial statement or tax returns. Under this method, deferred tax liabilities and assets are determined based on the difference between financial statements and tax bases of assets and liabilities using enacted tax rates in effect for the year in which the differences are expected to reverse.

synth_text.title: Reconciliation of Statutory Tax Benefit to Actual Income‑Tax Expense Under ASC 740‑10
synth_text.text:
The Company’s income‑tax reconciliation, prepared in accordance with ASC 740‑10, translates the tax benefit calculated at the statutory federal rate into the actual income‑tax expense (or benefit) reported in the financial statements. The reconciliation reflects the impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act) of 2017, which lowered the U.S. federal corporate income‑tax rate from 35 % to 21 % and introduced several other tax‑code changes.

**Key components of the reconciliation (two periods):**

| Component | Period 1 | Period 2 |
|-----------|----------|----------|
| Tax benefit computed at the statutory rate | $(427,244) | $(631,497) |
| State taxes | 6,525 | 6,874 |
| Book expenses not deductible for tax purposes | 2,980 | 2,882 |
| Rate change (effect of the Tax Act) | 45,656 | – |
| Other adjustments | 2,517 | (27,286) |
| **Subtotal** (sum of above) | (369,566) | (649,027) |
| Change in valuation allowance for deferred tax assets | 269,203 | 658,650 |
| **Income‑tax (benefit) expense** | $(100,363) | $9,623 |

- **Statutory tax benefit:** The base benefit before any adjustments, negative because the Company recorded a loss from operations before taxes.  
- **State taxes & nondeductible expenses:** Small positive adjustments that increase the tax expense.  
- **Rate change:** In Period 1, the Tax Act’s reduced federal rate generated a $45,656 benefit; no comparable rate‑change effect appears in Period 2.  
- **Other adjustments:** Miscellaneous items that either increase (Period 1) or decrease (Period 2) the tax expense.  
- **Valuation allowance change:** A significant increase in the allowance for deferred tax assets, reflecting the Company’s reassessment of future tax recoverability; this adjustment contributed the bulk of the net benefit in both periods.  

**Resulting net tax position:** After incorporating all adjustments, the Company reported a net tax benefit of $100,363 in Period 1 and a modest tax expense of $9,623 in Period 2.

This reconciliation demonstrates how the statutory tax computation is modified by state obligations, nondeductible items, the Tax Act’s rate reduction, other adjustments, and changes to deferred tax asset allowances, ultimately producing the final income‑tax expense (or benefit) shown in the financial statements.

For our internal budgeting and resource allocation process and as a means to provide consistency in period-to-period comparisons, we use non-GAAP measures to supplement our consolidated financial statements presented on a GAAP basis. These non-GAAP measures do not include certain items that may have a material impact upon our reported financial results. synth_text.title: Comparison of GAAP and Non‑GAAP Financial Results for the Recent Fiscal Year and Prior Unaudited Period
synth_text.text:
**Overview**

The company reports its financial performance using both U.S. GAAP and adjusted non‑GAAP measures. Non‑GAAP figures exclude certain items that management believes do not reflect the core operating results, providing additional insight for investors and internal decision‑making. Below is a side‑by‑side summary of the key metrics for the most recent audited fiscal year and the preceding unaudited period.

| Metric | Recent Fiscal Year (GAAP) | Recent Fiscal Year (Non‑GAAP) | Prior Period (Unaudited, GAAP) | Prior Period (Unaudited, Non‑GAAP) |
|--------|---------------------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Gross profit** | $2,283.9 M | $2,317.0 M | $1,753.2 M | $1,785.5 M |
| **Gross margin** | 89 % | 90 % | 85 % | 87 % |
| **Loss from operations** | $(25.0) M | $316.0 M (income) | $(509.1) M | $(112.0) M (loss) |
| **Operating margin** | (1) % | 12 % | (25) % | (5) % |
| **Net loss / income** | $(80.8) M | $223.3 M (income) | $(566.9) M | $(106.3) M (loss) |
| **Diluted loss per share** | $(0.37) | $1.01 (income) | $(2.58) | $(0.48) |
| **Weighted‑average diluted shares** | 218.9 M | 222.0 M | 219.5 M | 219.5 M |

**Key Takeaways**

1. **Profitability improves when adjusted:**  
   - Under GAAP, the company posted a modest operating loss of $25 M and a net loss of $80.8 M for the recent year.  
   - After adjusting to non‑GAAP, operating income turned positive at $316 M and net income rose to $223.3 M, reflecting a 12 % operating margin and a diluted earnings per share of $1.01.

2. **Margin expansion:**  
   - Gross margin increased from 89 % (GAAP) to 90 % (non‑GAAP) in the recent year, and from 85 % to 87 % in the prior period, indicating that the adjustments primarily affect operating and net results rather than core cost of goods sold.

3. **Significant reduction in losses for the prior period:**  
   - The unaudited prior period showed a GAAP net loss of $566.9 M, while the non‑GAAP net loss was $106.3 M, a reduction of roughly 81 % after excluding certain items.

4. **Share count stability:**  
   - Diluted weighted‑average shares used in per‑share calculations remained stable around 219 M across both periods, ensuring comparability of per‑share figures.

**Why Non‑GAAP Measures Matter**

The company uses non‑GAAP metrics to:
- Provide a clearer view of core operating performance by excluding items such as certain credits, expenses, and one‑time charges.
- Support internal budgeting, resource allocation, and incentive compensation decisions.
- Offer investors and analysts supplemental data that aligns with management’s perspective on earnings potential.

**Limitations**

Non‑GAAP figures are not prepared under GAAP, may differ from those used by other firms, and involve management judgment about which items to exclude. Consequently, they should be considered alongside GAAP results, not as a substitute.

**Conclusion**

The adjusted (non‑GAAP) results portray a stronger operating profile and profitability than the GAAP numbers, especially when comparing the recent fiscal year to the prior unaudited period. While these measures enhance transparency into the company’s core business, investors should evaluate both GAAP and non‑GAAP data to obtain a comprehensive understanding of financial health.

synth_text.text:
In 2019 the company recorded a **19 % increase in total revenue** compared with 2018, reflecting robust growth across all of its subscription‑based product lines.

**Key drivers of growth**

* **Hosting & Presence** – Up 20 %, growth was fueled by stronger sales of website‑building and security products and the full‑year impact of the MSH acquisition.  
* **Domains** – Up 15 %, driven by a rise in domains under management (from 77.6 million to 79.6 million), greater aftermarket sales, and continued international expansion.  

Overall, the revenue uplift was powered by a larger customer base, higher ARPU, and the inclusion of a full year of revenue from the MSH acquisition, partially offset by foreign‑currency movements. The company’s subscription model—collecting fees up front while recognizing revenue over the contract term—ensures a steady, recurring revenue stream across all segments.  

These results underscore the effectiveness of the company’s diversified subscription portfolio and its ability to generate consistent, year‑over‑year growth.

The fair value of the Company’s Level 1 financial instruments is based on quoted market prices in active markets for identical instruments. The fair value of the Company’s Level 2 financial instruments is based on observable inputs other than quoted prices in active markets for identical assets and liabilities, quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in inactive markets, or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by observable market data.

In addition, Level 2 assets and liabilities include derivative financial instruments associated with hedging activity, which are further discussed in Note 4. synth_text.title: Year‑to‑Year Changes in Non‑Operating Income, Expense, and Adjustments for 2019
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2019 the company reported notable shifts in its non‑operating line items, expressed as year‑to‑year percent changes:

- **Foreign currency transaction losses/(gains)** fell 34.6 %.  
- **Gains/(losses) on derivative instruments** declined sharply by 96.6 %.  
- **Interest income** increased 32.2 %.  
- **Net gains/(losses) from securities and investment assets** dropped 67.9 %.  
- **Retirement‑related costs/(income)** decreased 60.9 %.  
- **Amortization of acquired intangible assets** rose 50.0 %.  
- **Operating (non‑GAAP) other (income) and expense** surged 239.4 %.  

Categories marked “NM” (Not Meaningful) – such as “Other” and “Total consolidated other (income) and expense” – reflect situations where the net change cannot be expressed meaningfully because the underlying components offset each other.

**Contextual dollar impact**  
The “Other (income) and expense” line moved from a $1,152 million expense in 2018 to a $968 million income in 2019. This swing was primarily driven by:
1. **Lower non‑operating retirement‑related costs** (down $957 million).  
2. **Higher gains from divestitures**, recorded in the “Other” category (up $833 million).  
3. **Higher net exchange gains**, including gains on derivative instruments (up $272 million).  

The company’s hedging programs helped mitigate currency volatility, contributing to the net exchange gains.

**Operating (non‑GAAP) other income** rose to $1,431 million in 2019, an increase of $1,010 million over the prior year. The same three factors—reduced retirement costs, stronger divestiture gains, and improved exchange‑rate outcomes—were the primary drivers, with the retirement‑cost reduction excluded from the non‑GAAP calculation.

Overall, the data illustrate a transition from a net expense to net income in the “Other” non‑operating category, driven by cost reductions and favorable one‑time gains, while several other non‑operating items experienced significant declines. The substantial rise in operating (non‑GAAP) other income underscores the impact of these same drivers on the company’s adjusted earnings.

synth_text.title: Consolidated Other Income/Expense and Non‑GAAP Operating Results – 2018 vs 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2019 the company reported a net **income of $968 million** from consolidated other (income) and expense, a reversal from the **$1,152 million expense** recorded in 2018.  The non‑GAAP operating other (income) and expense also improved markedly, delivering **$1,431 million of income** in 2019 versus **$422 million in 2018**.

**Key Drivers of the 2019 Improvement**  

| Driver | 2019 Impact | 2018 Impact | Net Change |
|--------|------------|------------|------------|
| **Non‑operating retirement‑related costs** | $615 million (expense) | $1,572 million (expense) | ↓ $957 million |
| **Gains from divestitures (recorded in “Other”)** | $833 million (income) | – | ↑ $833 million |
| **Net foreign‑currency and derivative gains** | $272 million (gain) | – | ↑ $272 million |
| **Interest income / securities gains‑losses** | Small net losses (‑$349 M interest, ‑$32 M securities) | Small net losses (‑$264 M interest, ‑$101 M securities) | Minor effect |

* The reduction in retirement‑related costs was the largest single contributor, cutting expense by nearly $1 billion.  
* Divestiture proceeds added $833 million of other income, reflected in the “Other” line item.  
* The company’s hedging program generated a net foreign‑currency gain of $272 million, offsetting the modest losses from interest and securities.

**Non‑GAAP Operating Other (Income) and Expense**  
Operating (non‑GAAP) other (income) and expense swung to **$1,431 million of income** in 2019, an increase of **$1,010 million** over 2018.  The same factors that drove the consolidated other income (divestiture gains, currency/derivative gains, and lower retirement costs) were responsible, with the exception that the retirement‑related cost reduction is excluded from the non‑GAAP measure.

**Conclusion**  
The 2019 financial period saw a significant turnaround in both consolidated and non‑GAAP other income categories, primarily due to lower retirement‑related expenses, strong divestiture performance, and effective currency hedging.  These improvements contributed to a healthier bottom line relative to the prior year.

text.value: Contract Assets and Liabilities
The following table provides information about receivables, contract assets and contract liabilities from our revenue contracts with customers:

Contract assets include costs that are incremental to the acquisition of a contract. Incremental costs are those that result directly from obtaining a contract or costs that would not have been incurred if the contract had not been obtained, which primarily relate to sales commissions. These costs are deferred and amortized over the expected customer life.

We determined that the expected customer life is the expected period of benefit as the commission on the renewal contract is not commensurate with the commission on the initial contract. During the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018, the Company recognized expense of $6.3 million and $2.9 million, respectively, related to deferred contract acquisition costs.

Contract liabilities include deferred revenues related to advanced payments for services and nonrefundable, upfront service activation and set-up fees, which under the new standard are generally deferred and amortized over the expected customer life as the option to renew without paying an upfront fee provides the customer with a material right. During the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018, the Company deferred and recognized revenues of $397.5 million and $354.2 million, respectively.

A receivable is recognized in the period the Company provides goods or services when the Company’s right to consideration is unconditional. Payment terms on invoiced amounts are generally 30 to 60 days.

synth_text.text:
**Summary of Key Balance‑Sheet Items**

| Fiscal Year | Net Accounts Receivable | Contract Assets | Contract Liabilities |
|-------------|------------------------|----------------|----------------------|
| 2019 (in $ millions) | $120.0 | $18.8 | $51.0 |
| 2018 (in $ millions) | $133.1 | $12.1 | $53.0 |

- **Accounts Receivable, net** declined by roughly **$13 million** (≈ 10 %) from 2018 to 2019, reflecting a reduction in amounts billed to customers that remain unpaid. The company records a receivable when it has an unconditional right to consideration, with typical payment terms of 30‑60 days.

- **Contract assets** grew by about **$6.7 million** (≈ 55 %) over the same period. Contract assets represent costs that are incremental to obtaining a contract—primarily sales commissions—that are deferred and amortized over the expected customer life. The company recognized $6.3 million of expense related to these deferred acquisition costs in 2019, up from $2.9 million in 2018, indicating higher upfront investment in new contracts.

- **Contract liabilities** fell slightly by roughly **$2 million** (≈ 4 %). These liabilities consist of deferred revenue from advanced payments, non‑refundable activation fees, and set‑up fees. Under the new accounting standard, such amounts are amortized over the expected customer life because the renewal option without an upfront fee provides the customer a material right. Correspondingly, the company deferred and recognized $397.5 million of revenue in 2019, compared with $354.2 million in 2018.

**Interpretation**

The decrease in receivables suggests faster collection or lower sales volume, while the rise in contract assets indicates increased investment in acquiring new contracts, reflected in higher deferred acquisition‑cost expense. The modest reduction in contract liabilities, despite higher deferred revenue, points to a shift in the timing of cash receipts versus revenue recognition, consistent with the company’s practice of amortizing upfront fees over the expected customer life.

Overall, the 2019 figures show a company that is investing more in contract acquisition, improving the amortization of deferred costs, and managing its revenue deferral and collection processes within the framework of the new revenue‑recognition standard.

header: Fair value changes recognized in cost of revenue(3)

text.value: GreenSky, Inc. NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS — (Continued) (United States Dollars in thousands, except per share data, unless otherwise stated)
Finance charge reversal liability

Our Bank Partners offer certain loan products that have a feature whereby the account holder is provided a promotional period to repay the loan principal balance in full without incurring a finance charge. For these loan products, we bill interest each month throughout the promotional period and, under the terms of the contracts with our Bank Partners, we are obligated to pay this billed interest to the Bank Partners if an account holder repays the loan balance in full within the promotional period. Therefore, the monthly process of billing interest on deferred loan products triggers a potential future finance charge reversal ("FCR") liability for the Company. The FCR component of our Bank Partner contracts qualifies as an embedded derivative. The FCR liability is not designated as a hedge for accounting purposes and, as such, changes in its fair value are recorded within cost of revenue in the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

The FCR liability is carried at fair value on a recurring basis in the Consolidated Balance Sheets and is estimated based on historical experience and management’s expectation of future FCR. The FCR liability is classified within Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy, as the primary component of the fair value is obtained from unobservable inputs based on the Company’s data, reasonably adjusted for assumptions that would be used by market participants. The following table reconciles the beginning and ending fair value measurements of our FCR liability during the periods indicated.

(1) Includes: (i) incentive payments from Bank Partners, which is the surplus of finance charges billed to borrowers over an agreedupon portfolio yield, a fixed servicing fee and realized net credit losses, (ii) cash received from recoveries on previously charged-off Bank Partner loans, and (iii) the proceeds received from transferring our rights to Charged-Off Receivables attributable to previously charged-off Bank Partner loans. We consider all monthly incentive payments from Bank Partners during the period to be related to billed finance charges on deferred interest products until monthly incentive payments exceed total billed finance charges on deferred products, which did not occur during any of the periods presented.
(2) Represents the reversal of previously billed finance charges associated with deferred payment loan principal balances that were repaid within the promotional period.

(3) A fair value adjustment is made based on the expected reversal percentage of billed finance charges (expected settlements), which is estimated at each reporting date. The fair value adjustment is recognized in cost of revenue in the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

synth_text.title: 2017 Reconciliation of GreenSky’s Finance Charge Reversal Liability Fair Value
synth_text.text:
The 2017 reconciliation details the fair‑value movements of GreenSky, Inc.’s Finance Charge Reversal (FCR) liability—a Level 3 embedded derivative that is not designated as a hedge and is therefore measured at fair value on the balance sheet.  

- **Beginning balance:** At the start of 2017 the FCR liability was recorded at **$68.1 million**.  
- **Receipts (1):** Throughout the year the company received **$109.8 million** in cash. These receipts consist of incentive payments from bank partners (the surplus of billed finance charges over the agreed‑upon portfolio yield, plus a fixed servicing fee and net credit losses), recoveries on previously charged‑off loans, and proceeds from transferring rights to charged‑off receivables.  
- **Settlements (2):** The liability was reduced by **$127.0 million** as previously billed finance charges were reversed when loan principals were repaid in full during their promotional periods.  
- **Fair‑value changes recognized in cost of revenue (3):** Management estimated the expected reversal percentage of billed finance charges and recorded a **$43.3 million** fair‑value adjustment in cost of revenue. This adjustment reflects the change in the liability’s fair value based on historical experience and management expectations.  
- **Ending balance:** After accounting for receipts, settlements, and the fair‑value adjustment, the FCR liability stood at **$94.1 million** at year‑end.

In summary, the 2017 reconciliation shows that while substantial cash inflows and charge reversals occurred, the fair‑value adjustment increased the liability, resulting in a net increase of roughly $26 million over the year. This movement is captured in the consolidated statements of operations as part of cost of revenue, consistent with GreenSky’s accounting policy for the FCR liability.

synth_text.title: Reconciliation of GreenSky’s Finance Charge Reversal Liability Fair‑Value Measurements (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
GreenSky’s Finance Charge Reversal (FCR) liability represents the company’s obligation to repay interest that was billed to borrowers during promotional periods when the principal is repaid in full. Because the FCR component of its Bank‑Partner contracts is an embedded derivative, it is measured at fair value on a recurring basis and classified in Level 3 of the fair‑value hierarchy. The liability is not designated as a hedge; therefore, changes in its fair value are recorded in cost of revenue.

The table below reconciles the fair‑value measurement of the FCR liability for the fiscal years ended 2018 and 2019 (amounts in thousands of U.S. dollars):

- **2018**  
  - Beginning balance: **$94,148**  
  - Receipts (incentive payments, recoveries, and proceeds from charged‑off receivables): **$129,153**  
  - Settlements (reversal of previously billed finance charges for loans repaid within the promotional period): **$(181,590)**  
  - Fair‑value changes recognized in cost of revenue (adjustments for expected reversal percentages): **$96,878**  
  - **Ending balance:** **$138,589**

- **2019**  
  - Beginning balance: **$138,589**  
  - Receipts: **$159,527**  
  - Settlements: **$(262,449)**  
  - Fair‑value changes recognized in cost of revenue: **$170,368**  
  - **Ending balance:** **$206,035**

Key observations:

1. **Growth in Receipts:** The company’s cash inflows related to the FCR liability increased from $129.2 million in 2018 to $159.5 million in 2019, reflecting higher incentive payments and recoveries from Bank Partners.  
2. **Larger Settlements:** Settlements rose sharply, from $181.6 million to $262.4 million, indicating more loan principals were repaid within the promotional period, triggering reversals of previously billed finance charges.  
3. **Significant Fair‑Value Adjustments:** Fair‑value changes recorded in cost of revenue more than doubled, from $96.9 million to $170.4 million, as management’s expectations of future reversals were updated at each reporting date.  
4. **Resulting Balance Increase:** The combined effect of higher receipts, larger settlements, and greater fair‑value adjustments expanded the FCR liability’s fair‑value balance from $138.6 million at the end of 2018 to $206.0 million at the end of 2019.

These figures illustrate how GreenSky’s FCR liability evolves with borrower behavior, incentive structures, and management’s fair‑value estimates, and how the associated adjustments impact the company’s cost of revenue.

text.value: 14. INCOME TAXES

Our effective tax rates for each of the periods presented are the result of the mix of income earned in various tax jurisdictions that apply a broad range of income tax rates. The more significant provisions of the Tax Act as applicable to us are described in Note 1 above under “Impacts of the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.” During fiscal 2019, we recorded a net benefit of $389 million in accordance with SAB 118 related to adjustments in our estimates of the one-time transition tax on certain foreign subsidiary earnings, and the remeasurement of our net deferred tax assets and liabilities affected by the Tax Act. Our provision for income taxes for fiscal 2019 varied from the 21% U.S. statutory rate imposed by the Tax Act primarily due to earnings in foreign operations, state taxes, the U.S. research and development tax credit, settlements with tax authorities, the tax effects of stock-based compensation, the Foreign Derived Intangible Income deduction, the tax effect of GILTI, and a reduction to our transition tax recorded consistent with the provision of SAB 118. Our provision for income taxes for fiscal 2018 varied from the 21% U.S. statutory rate imposed by the Tax Act primarily due to the impacts of the Tax Act upon adoption, state taxes, the U.S. research and development tax credit, settlements with tax authorities, the tax effects of stock-based compensation and the U.S. domestic production activity deduction. Prior to the January 1, 2018 effective date of the Tax Act, our provision for income taxes historically differed from the tax computed at the previous U.S. federal statutory income tax rate due primarily to certain earnings considered as indefinitely reinvested in foreign operations, state taxes, the U.S. research and development tax cr edit, settlements with tax authorities, the tax effects of stock-based compensation and the U.S. domestic production activity deduction.

Consequently, the company’s tax expense reflects a blend of domestic and international tax rules rather than a single statutory rate.  

This geographical breakdown underscores the importance of foreign operations in the company’s earnings profile and provides context for the variability in its income‑tax provision.

text.value: 2017 ESPP

synth_text.text:
The Company’s defined‑benefit pension arrangements for French and German employees are unfunded plans acquired through the Atmel and Microsemi transactions. Benefits are paid in accordance with local statutory rules and are based on years of service and employee compensation. The French plan provides termination benefits of roughly one to five months of salary at retirement, while the German plan offers standard defined‑benefit payouts after retirement. Pension liabilities and the related expense are calculated using annually updated assumptions such as discount rates, salary growth, turnover and mortality.

**Net pension expense (in millions of dollars)**  

| Year | Service costs | Interest costs | Amortization of actuarial loss | Settlements | Net pension period cost |

* **Service costs** – the cost of benefits earned by employees during the year – fell from $2.2 M in 2018 to $1.5 M in 2019, reflecting lower accruals, possibly due to reduced payroll or staffing levels.  
* **Interest costs** – the increase from 1.0 M to 1.1 M is driven by the discount‑rate assumptions applied to the existing liability.  
* **Amortization of actuarial loss** – decreased from 0.8 M to 0.4 M, indicating an improvement in actuarial assumptions or a reduction in the accumulated loss.  
* **Settlements** – no cash settlements occurred in either year.  

The aggregate net pension expense therefore declined by $1.0 M, from $4.0 M in 2018 to $3.0 M in 2019. Interest costs and the amortization of actuarial losses are presented in the “other (loss) income, net” line of the income statement, as noted in the accompanying disclosures.

synth_text.title: Post‑Retirement Benefit Plan Funding Summary and Obligation Status
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Company’s post‑retirement benefit plans—comprising a contributory health‑care plan for shore‑based employees and Deck Officers, and a non‑contributory life‑insurance plan for all employees—are not pre‑funded. Benefits are provided to qualifying retirees and their dependents, with the Company retaining the right to amend or terminate the arrangements. Prescription‑drug coverage ceases at age 65.

**Financial Position – Year‑End Comparison**  

| Item | Earlier Year* | Later Year* |
|------|---------------|------------|
| Benefit Obligation (beginning) | $44,015 k | $48,500 k |
| Interest Cost on Obligation | $1,673 k | $1,802 k |
| Actuarial Losses/(Gains) | (3,456) k (gain) | $3,805 k (loss) |
| Benefits Paid | (2,702) k | (2,686) k |
| Benefit Obligation (year‑end) | $44,015 k | $46,936 k |
| Plan Assets (beginning) | $35,591 k | $31,929 k |
| Actual Return on Assets | (1,882) k | $6,790 k |
| Employer Contributions | $922 k | $721 k |
| Plan Assets (year‑end) | $31,929 k | $36,754 k |
| Unfunded Status (deficit) | $(12,086) k | $(10,182) k |

\*Exact fiscal years are not labeled in the source data; the rows represent two consecutive reporting periods.

**Key Observations**

1. **Benefit Obligation Growth** – The projected obligation rose from $44,015 k to $46,936 k, driven primarily by interest cost and a shift from actuarial gains to actuarial losses.
2. **Plan‑Asset Performance** – Asset values improved markedly in the later year, thanks to a strong actual return of $6.79 million, offsetting a modest employer contribution of $721 k.
3. **Unfunded Deficit Reduction** – The gap between obligations and assets narrowed by $1.9 million, decreasing the unfunded status from $(12,086) k to $(10,182) k. Although the plans remain unfunded, this trend reflects a healthier balance between liabilities and the assets generated by the plans.
4. **Benefit Payments** – Cash outflows for retiree benefits were relatively stable across the two periods, hovering around $2.7 million.

**Implications**  
Given that the Company does not set aside dedicated funding for these post‑retirement arrangements, the unfunded status represents a contingent liability. The improvement in the deficit suggests that recent asset performance and controlled benefit payments have mitigated the shortfall, but the Company must continue to monitor actuarial assumptions and investment returns to manage the liability effectively.

**Conclusion**  
The post‑retirement benefit plans exhibit a modest improvement in funding position despite an increase in projected obligations. Ongoing stewardship of plan assets and careful management of actuarial assumptions will be essential to further reduce the unfunded deficit while honoring the health‑care and life‑insurance benefits promised to retirees and their dependents.

synth_text.title: Post‑Retirement Benefit Obligation and Unfunded Status Summary
synth_text.text:
The Company’s post‑retirement benefit plans – which provide health‑care coverage for eligible shore‑based employees and retired deck officers, and non‑contributory life‑insurance coverage for all retirees – are measured as of December 31 and are currently unfunded.

**Year‑end obligation and funding details**

| Year‑end | Opening PBO | Service cost | Interest cost | Actuarial gain/loss | Benefits paid | Closing PBO | Employer contributions | Unfunded status |
|----------|-------------|--------------|---------------|---------------------|---------------|-------------|------------------------|-----------------|
| **Year 1** (Dec 31) | $3,401 | $105 | $140 | $84 loss | $(158) | $3,572 | $158 | $(3,572) |
| **Year 2** (Dec 31) | $4,548 | $119 | $142 | $(1,206) gain | $(202) | $3,401 | $202 | $(3,401) |

* **Benefit obligation:** The projected benefit obligation (PBO) increased from $3,401 million to $3,572 million in the first year, driven primarily by service and interest costs that outweighed the actuarial loss and benefits paid. In the following year the PBO fell to $3,401 million, reflecting a substantial actuarial gain of $1,206 million that more than offset service, interest costs, and benefits paid.

* **Plan assets:** The plans hold no invested assets; the only inflow each year is the employer’s cash contribution ($158 million in Year 1 and $202 million in Year 2). Consequently, the fair value of plan assets remains zero at both the beginning and end of each period.

* **Unfunded status:** Because assets are essentially nil, the plans are fully unfunded, with a deficit equal to the closing PBO ($3,572 million in Year 1 and $3,401 million in Year 2).

**Contextual notes**

- The health‑care plan is contributory at retirement for eligible shore‑based employees and deck officers, while the life‑insurance plan is non‑contributory.
- Coverage is limited to retirees hired before 1 January 2005 (for shore‑based staff) and to deck officers meeting age‑and‑service criteria; prescription‑drug benefits cease at age 65.
- The Company retains the right to amend or terminate these post‑retirement benefits at any time and does not currently fund the arrangements.

In summary, the Company’s post‑retirement health‑care and life‑insurance obligations have fluctuated due to service costs, interest, and actuarial experience, while the plans remain unfunded, relying solely on periodic employer contributions.

text.value: The components of net deferred income tax assets for income tax purposes are as follows (in thousands):

The net deferred tax assets as of February 28, 2018 in the above table include the deferred tax assets of our Italian and Canadian subsidiaries amounting to $7.4 million and $7.6 million, respectively, which were disclosed narratively in the fiscal 2018 Form 10-K. The deferred tax assets primarily relate to net operating losses (NOL’s) and research and development expenditure pool carryforwards. We had provided a 100% valuation allowance against these deferred tax assets at February 28, 2018, as it was more likely than not that the deferred tax assets would not be realized.

As of February 28, 2019 and 2018, we maintained a valuation allowance with respect to certain of our deferred tax assets relating primarily to NOL’s in certain non-U.S. jurisdictions and certain state tax credits that we believe are not likely to be realized. During fiscal 2019, we decreased the valuation allowance against our deferred tax assets by approximately $5.9 million, as it is more likely than not that these deferred tax assets would be realized based upon the assessment of positive and negative evidence. This reduction in our valuation allowance is primarily attributable to a release of valuation allowance against foreign deferred tax assets, partially offset by an increase in valuation allowances for state tax credits.

At February 28, 2019, we had net operating loss carryforwards of approximately $30.1 million, $60.8 million and $44.7 million for federal, state and foreign purposes, respectively, expiring at various dates through fiscal 2039. Approximately $18.3 million of foreign net operating loss carryforwards do not expire. The federal net operating loss carryforwards are subject to various limitations under Section 382 of the Internal Revenue Code. If substantial changes in our ownership were to occur, there may be certain annual limitations on the amount of the NOL carryforwards that can be utilized

As of February 28, 2019, we had R&D tax credit carryforwards of $9.1 million and $8.9 million for federal and state income tax purposes, respectively. The federal R&D tax credits expire at various dates through 2039. A substantial portion of the state R&D tax credits have no expiration date.

We adopted the updated guidance on stock based compensation and we have tax deductions on exercised stock options and vested restricted stock awards that exceed stock compensation expense amounts recognized for financial reporting purposes. The gross excess tax deductions were $2.9 million, $2.6 and $0 in fiscal years 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. Under the new guidance, all excess tax benefits and tax deficiencies are recognized in the income statement as they occur.

We follow ASC Topic 740, “Income Taxes,” which clarifies the accounting for income taxes by prescribing a minimum recognition threshold that a tax position is required to meet before being recognized in the financial statements. Management determined based on our evaluation of our income tax positions that we have uncertain tax benefit of $3.2 million, $1.0 million and $1.0 million on at February 28, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively, for which we have not yet recognized an income tax benefit for financial reporting purposes.

At February 28, 2019, we increased the uncertain tax benefits related to certain foreign net operating loss carryforwards. Such deferred tax assets were previously offset by a valuation allowance so that the increase in the unrecognized tax benefit coupled with the reduction of the valuation allowance on such net operating losses did not result in an income tax expense during the current fiscal year. If total uncertain tax benefits were realized in a future period, it would result in a tax benefit of $3.2 million. As of February 28, 2019, our liabilities for uncertain tax benefits were netted against our deferred tax assets on our consolidated balance sheet. It is reasonably possible the amount of unrecognized tax benefits could be reduced within the next 12 months by at least $0.6 million.
We recognize interest and/or penalties related to uncertain tax positions in income tax expense. No amounts of interest and/or penalties have been accrued as of February 28, 2019.

synth_text.title: Deferred Tax Asset Composition and Valuation Allowance Summary – FY 2018 & 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s deferred tax position for fiscal years 2018 and 2019 is presented in two detailed schedules. Both years show a substantial gross deferred tax asset balance that is partially offset by a valuation allowance, resulting in net deferred tax assets of $31.6 million in 2018 and $21.7 million in 2019. Deferred tax liabilities are minimal ($0.96 million in 2019) and were nil in 2018.

**Key Components – 2019**  
- **Net operating loss (NOL) carryforwards:** $19.3 million  
- **Depreciation, amortization & impairments:** –$11.9 million (deduction)  
- **Research & development (R&D) credits:** $19.2 million  
- **Stock‑based compensation (excess tax deductions):** $2.8 million  
- **Other tax credits:** $1.0 million  
- **Reserves & accruals:** inventory $0.6 million, warranty $0.3 million, payroll & benefits $2.2 million, doubtful accounts $0.45 million, other accrued liabilities $6.2 million  
- **Convertible debt (net):** –$10.8 million (liability)  
- **Other, net:** $3.3 million  

These items combine to a **gross deferred tax asset** of $32.6 million. After applying a **valuation allowance** of $10.9 million, the **net deferred tax asset** stands at $21.7 million, reported as $22.6 million of deferred tax assets and $0.96 million of deferred tax liabilities.

**Key Components – 2018**  
- **NOL carryforwards:** $22.0 million  
- **Depreciation, amortization & impairments:** –$11.1 million  
- **R&D credits:** $17.4 million  
- **Stock‑based compensation:** $2.4 million  
- **Other tax credits:** $2.0 million  
- **Reserves & accruals:** inventory $0.29 million, warranty $0.43 million, payroll & benefits $1.94 million, doubtful accounts $0.35 million, other accrued liabilities $9.0 million  
- **Convertible debt (net):** –$0.19 million  
- **Other, net:** $3.9 million  

The **gross deferred tax asset** was $48.4 million. A larger **valuation allowance** of $16.8 million reduced the **net deferred tax asset** to $31.6 million, reported entirely as deferred tax assets with no corresponding liability.

**Valuation Allowance Changes**  
- Both years a valuation allowance was maintained for deferred tax assets tied to NOLs in non‑U.S. jurisdictions and certain state tax credits deemed unlikely to be realized.  
- In FY 2019 the allowance was reduced by approximately $5.9 million, reflecting a more favorable assessment of foreign NOL assets, partially offset by an increase for state tax credits.

**Additional Tax Positions**  
- **NOL Carryforwards (as of 2/28/2019):** Federal $30.1 million, State $60.8 million, Foreign $44.7 million (with $18.3 million non‑expiring).  
- **R&D Credit Carryforwards (as of 2/28/2019):** Federal $9.1 million, State $8.9 million.  
- **Stock‑Based Compensation:** Excess tax deductions of $2.9 million (2019) and $2.6 million (2018) under the updated ASC 740 guidance.  
- **Uncertain Tax Benefits:** $3.2 million at 2/28/2019 (up from $1.0 million in 2018), netted against deferred tax assets. No interest or penalties have been accrued.

**Conclusion**  
The company’s deferred tax assets are primarily driven by sizable NOL and R&D credit carryforwards, offset by valuation allowances that reflect the uncertainty of realizing these benefits, especially in foreign jurisdictions. The reduction in the valuation allowance during 2019 indicates improved confidence in the recoverability of foreign deferred tax assets, while ongoing uncertain tax positions remain modest.

synth_text.title: Fiscal Year 2018‑2019 Financial Highlights and Key Adjustments
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019 the company reported $125.8 billion in revenue, up 14 % from $110.4 billion in 2018. Gross margin increased to $82.9 billion (66 % of revenue) from $72.0 billion (65 % of revenue), and operating income rose to $43.0 billion versus $35.1 billion a year earlier.

**Net Income and EPS**  
Net income jumped to $39.2 billion in 2019, more than double the $16.6 billion reported in 2018. Diluted earnings per share (EPS) followed the same trend, climbing to $5.06 from $2.13. The 2019 results were boosted by a $2.6 billion net income tax benefit related to intangible‑property transfers and a $157 million tax charge from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), which together added $2.4 billion to net income and $0.31 to EPS (see Note b). Conversely, 2018 net income was depressed by a $13.7 billion TCJA‑related tax charge, reducing net income and EPS by $13.7 billion and $1.75, respectively (Note c).

**Dividends**  
The board declared cash dividends of $1.84 per share in 2019, up from $1.68 per share in 2018.

**Balance‑Sheet Highlights**  
Total assets grew to $286.6 billion in 2019 from $258.8 billion in 2018, driven largely by cash, cash equivalents and short‑term investments of $133.8 billion in both years. Long‑term obligations fell slightly to $114.8 billion from $117.6 billion, while stockholders’ equity increased to $102.3 billion from $82.7 billion.

**Key Adjustments**  
- **GitHub acquisition**: Beginning October 25, 2018, GitHub’s results have been consolidated (Note a).  
- **Tax impacts**: The TCJA produced both a sizable benefit in 2019 and a large charge in 2018, materially affecting net income and EPS (Notes b and c).  

Overall, the company demonstrated strong top‑line growth, improved profitability, and a healthier balance sheet in 2019, despite the one‑time tax benefit that inflated earnings. The fiscal 2018 figures were negatively impacted by the TCJA tax charge, which explains the lower net income and EPS for that year.
