synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the fiscal year ended June 30 2015, the company generated **$93.6 billion** in revenue, achieving a **gross margin of $60.5 billion**. After accounting for significant one‑time charges, operating income was **$18.2 billion** and net income stood at **$12.2 billion**, translating to **diluted earnings per share of $1.48**. The board declared a cash dividend of **$1.24 per share**.

**Impact of One‑Time Charges**  
Both operating income and net income (and consequently EPS) are marked with footnote (h). This footnote indicates that the results include:

- **$7.5 billion** of goodwill and asset impairment charges related to the Phone business.  
- **$2.5 billion** of integration and restructuring expenses tied to the same segment.  

Together, these adjustments reduced operating income by **$10 billion**, net income by **$9.5 billion**, and diluted EPS by **$1.15**. Excluding these items, the company’s underlying profitability would have been substantially higher.

**Liquidity and Capital Structure**  
The firm held **$96.5 billion** in cash, cash equivalents, and short‑term investments, providing a strong liquidity position. Total assets amounted to **$174.3 billion**, financed by **$44.6 billion** in long‑term obligations and **$80.1 billion** of stockholders’ equity, indicating a solid equity base relative to debt.

**Key Takeaways**  
- Revenue and gross margin remained robust, reflecting strong core operations.  
- Reported profitability was heavily impacted by large impairment and restructuring charges specific to the Phone business.  
- The company maintained ample cash resources and a healthy balance sheet, positioning it well for future strategic initiatives.

synth_text.title: Microsoft Fiscal 2016‑2017 Financial Highlights and Key Adjustments
synth_text.text:
Microsoft reported solid growth across its core financial metrics for the two most recent fiscal years ending June 30.  

**Revenue and Profitability** – Revenue rose from **$91.2 billion in 2016** to **$96.6 billion in 2017**, a 5.9 % increase. Gross margin followed the same trend, climbing from **$58.4 billion** to **$62.3 billion**. Operating income grew from **$26.1 billion** to **$29.0 billion**, while net income increased from **$20.5 billion** to **$25.5 billion**. Diluted earnings per share (EPS) improved from **$2.56** to **$3.25**, reflecting both higher profitability and a modest rise in the number of shares outstanding.

**Dividends** – The cash dividend declared per share rose from **$1.44** in 2016 to **$1.56** in 2017, indicating a continued commitment to returning capital to shareholders.

**Balance‑Sheet Strength** – Total investments grew from **$113.2 billion** to **$133.0 billion**, and total assets expanded from **$202.9 billion** to **$250.3 billion**. Long‑term obligations increased to **$106.9 billion** in 2017 from **$66.7 billion** in 2016, while stockholders’ equity remained robust at **$87.7 billion**.

**Key Adjustments and One‑Time Items**  

* **Accounting changes (footnote d)** – Both years reflect the impact of new revenue‑recognition and lease accounting standards adopted in fiscal 2018.  

* **LinkedIn acquisition (footnote e)** – Results for 2017 include LinkedIn, which was integrated on December 8 2016, contributing to the higher revenue and margin figures.  

* **Severance expenses (footnote f)** – In 2017, Microsoft recorded **$306 million** of employee severance costs tied to a sales and marketing restructuring. These expenses reduced operating income, net income and EPS by **$306 million**, **$243 million**, and **$0.04**, respectively.  

* **Phone‑business impairments and restructuring (footnote g)** – The 2016 figures were affected by **$630 million** of asset impairments and **$480 million** of restructuring charges related to the Phone division, together lowering operating income, net income and EPS by **$1.1 billion**, **$895 million**, and **$0.11**.  

Overall, Microsoft’s 2016‑2017 financial performance demonstrates consistent top‑line growth, improved profitability, and a solid balance sheet, while the disclosed one‑time charges and accounting changes provide essential context for the year‑over‑year variations.

text.value: 23. Investments continued

IFRS 9 was applied for the first time on 1 April 2018 and introduces new classifications for financial instruments, including investments. Under IAS 39, we classified investments as available-for-sale, loans and receivables, and fair value through profit or loss. On transition to IFRS 9 we have reclassified them as fair value through other comprehensive income, fair value through profit or loss, and amortised cost, as set out in note 1. The current year figures in the following table reflect the classifications under IFRS 9, and the prior year figures reflect the previous classifications under IAS 39.

Investments held at amortised cost consist of investments previously classified as loans and receivables and relate to money market investments denominated in sterling of £2,687m (2017/18: £416m, 2016/17: £35m), in US dollars of £26m (2017/18: £27m, 2016/17: £30m) in euros of £499m (2017/18: £nil, 2016/17: £nil) and in other currencies £2m (2017/18: £4m, 2016/17: £18m). They also include investments in liquidity funds of £2,522m (2017/18: £2,575m, 2016/17: £1,437m) held to collect contractual cash flows. In prior years these were classified as available-for-sale.

synth_text.title: Impact of IFRS 9 Reclassification on Investment Holdings (2018‑19 vs 2017‑18)
synth_text.text:
The adoption of IFRS 9 on 1 April 2018 led to a restructuring of how the company classifies its investment‑related financial assets. In the current reporting year, the balance sheet shows **£3,214 million** of investments recorded at **amortised cost**, reflecting the migration of previously “available‑for‑sale” liquidity funds and money‑market instruments into this category. A modest **£54 million** is measured at **fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL)**, while no assets remain under “available‑for‑sale” or “fair value through other comprehensive income”.

In the prior year, when IAS 39 was in force, the same pool of assets was split between **£2,575 million** classified as **available‑for‑sale** and **£447 million** as **loans and receivables**, with **£53 million** at FVTPL. The total investment balance was therefore **£3,022 million**.

The re‑classification primarily affected money‑market investments denominated in sterling (£2,687 million), US dollars (£26 million), euros (£499 million) and other currencies (£2 million), together with liquidity‑fund holdings (£2,522 million). Under IAS 39 these were recorded as “available‑for‑sale”; under IFRS 9 they are now presented as **amortised‑cost assets**, aligning the accounting treatment with the assets’ contractual cash‑flow characteristics.

Overall, IFRS 9 has consolidated the majority of the company’s investment portfolio into the amortised‑cost category, providing clearer insight into the nature and liquidity of its holdings while maintaining a consistent FVTPL exposure.

synth_text.title: Summary of Investment Classifications and Values Following IFRS 9 Adoption
synth_text.text:
**Investment Portfolio Overview – Current Year (post‑IFRS 9)**  

The adoption of IFRS 9 on 1 April 2018 re‑classified the company’s investment holdings from the IAS 39 categories (available‑for‑sale, loans and receivables, fair value through profit or loss) into the new IFRS 9 classifications: fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI), fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL) and amortised‑cost. The table below reflects the current‑year balances under these IFRS 9 categories:

| Classification                              | Amount (£ million) |
|---------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| Fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) | – (zero) |
| Available‑for‑sale (AFS)                    | 1,437 |
| Fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL)   | 44 |
| Loans and receivables (amortised‑cost)      | 83 |
| **Total reported**                          | **1,520** |

*Non‑current assets* and *Current assets* fields are blank, indicating that all listed investments are presented within current assets.

**Composition of Investments Held at Amortised Cost**  
The amortised‑cost portfolio consists of money‑market instruments and liquidity funds:

* Money‑market investments:  
  * Sterling – £2,687 m  
  * US dollars – £26 m  
  * Euros – £499 m  
  * Other currencies – £2 m  

* Liquidity funds – £2,522 m (held to collect contractual cash flows).

These items were previously classified as *available‑for‑sale* under IAS 39; under IFRS 9 they are now recorded at amortised cost.

**Key Take‑aways**

1. The transition to IFRS 9 has resulted in a clear re‑classification of the investment portfolio, with the majority (£1,437 m) now recorded as *available‑for‑sale* and a modest portion (£44 m) measured at *fair value through profit or loss*.  
2. *Loans and receivables* (amortised‑cost) amount to £83 m, reflecting money‑market and liquidity‑fund holdings across multiple currencies.  
3. The total investment balance reported for the current year is £1,520 million, aligning with the new IFRS 9 reporting framework.

This summary provides a concise view of the post‑IFRS 9 investment classifications, their monetary values, and the underlying composition of the amortised‑cost holdings.

text.value: Cash, Cash Equivalents and Marketable Securities

Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities increased by $485.5 million to $2,455.2 million as at December 31, 2019 from $ 1,969.7 million as at December 31, 2018, primarily as a result of proceeds from the public offering in September 2019, cash provided by our operating activities, and proceeds from the exercise of stock options.

Cash equivalents and marketable securities include money market funds, repurchase agreements, term deposits, U.S. and Canadian federal bonds, corporate bonds, and commercial paper, all maturing within the 12 months from December 31, 2019.

The following table summarizes our total cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities as at December 31, 2019 and 2018 as well as our operating, investing and financing activities for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018:
Cash Flows From Operating Activities

Our largest source of operating cash is from subscription solutions. These payments are typically paid to us at the beginning of the applicable subscription period, except for our Shopify Plus merchants who typically pay us at the end of their monthly billing cycle. We also generate significant cash flows from our Shopify Payments processing fee arrangements, which are received on a daily basis as transactions are processed. Our primary uses of cash from operating activities are for third-party payment processing fees, employee-related expenditures, advancing funds to merchants through Shopify Capital, marketing programs, third-party shipping and fulfillment partners, outsourced hosting costs, and leased facilities.

For the year ended December 31, 2019, cash provided by operating activities was $70.6 million. This was primarily as a result of our net loss of $124.8 million, which once adjusted for $158.5 million of stock-based compensation expense, $35.7 million of amortization and depreciation, a $37.9 million increase in deferred income taxes, a $15.9 million increase of our provision for uncollectible merchant cash advances and loans, and an unrealized foreign exchange loss of $3.2 million, contributed $50.4 million of positive cash flows. Additional cash of $162.9 million resulted from the following increases in operating liabilities: $84.6 million in accounts payable and accrued liabilities due to indirect taxes payable, payroll liabilities, and payment processing and interchange fees; $64.6 million in income tax assets and liabilities; $12.3 million in deferred revenue due to the growth in sales of our subscription solutions along with the acquisition of 6RS; and $1.5 million increase in net lease liabilities. These were offset by $142.8 million of cash used resulting from the following increases in operating assets: $74.2 million in merchant cash advances and loans as we continued to grow Shopify Capital; $56.2 million in trade and other receivables; and $12.4 million in other current assets driven primarily by an increase in prepaid expenses, forward contract assets designated for hedge accounting, and deposits.

For the year ended December 31, 2018, cash provided by operating activities was $9.3 million. This was primarily as a result of our net loss of $64.6 million, which once adjusted for $95.7 million of stock-based compensation expense, $27.1 million of amortization and depreciation, a $5.9 million increase of our provision for uncollectible merchant cash advances, and an unrealized foreign exchange loss of $1.3 million, contributed $65.4 million of positive cash flows. Additional cash of $38.1 million resulted from the following increases in operating liabilities: $20.6 million in accounts payable and accrued liabilities; $9.0 million in deferred revenue; and $8.4 million in lease liabilities. These were offset by $94.2 million of cash used resulting from the following increases in operating assets: $50.7 million in merchant cash advances and loans; $32.6 million in trade and other receivables; and $10.8 million in other current assets.
Cash Flows From Investing Activities

Cash flows used in investing activities are primarily related to the purchase and sale of marketable securities, business acquisitions, purchases of leasehold improvements and furniture and fixtures to support our expanding infrastructure and workforce, purchases of computer equipment, and software development costs eligible for capitalization.

Net cash used in investing activities in the year ended December 31, 2019 was $ 569.5 million, which was driven by $265.5 million used to make business acquisitions, most of which was for the 6RS acquisition on October 17, 2019, net purchases of $241.6 million in marketable securities, $ 56.8 million used to purchase property and equipment, which primarily consisted of expenditures on leasehold improvements, and $5.6 million used for purchasing and developing software to add functionality to our platform and support our expanding merchant base.

Net cash used in investing activities in the year ended December 31, 2018 was $810.6 million, reflecting net purchases of $749.7 million in marketable securities. Cash used in investing activities also included $28.0 million used to purchase property and equipment, which primarily consisted of expenditures on leasehold improvements, $19.4 million used to make business acquisitions, and $13.6 million used for purchasing and developing software.
Cash Flows From Financing Activities
To date, cash flows from financing activities have related to proceeds from private placements, public offerings, and exercises of stock options.

Net cash provided by financing activities in the year ended December 31, 2019 was $736.4 million driven mainly by the $688.0 million raised by our September 2019 public offering, and $48.3 million in proceeds from the issuance of Class A subordinate voting shares and Class B multiple voting shares as a result of stock option exercises. This compares to $1,072.2 million for the same period in 2018 of which $1,041.7 million was raised by our February and December 2018 public offerings while the remaining $30.5 million related to stock option exercises.

synth_text.title: Cash, Cash Equivalents and Marketable Securities – 2019 vs 2018 Summary
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
At the end of 2019 Shopify reported cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of **$2,455.2 million**, up from **$1,969.7 million** at the end of 2018 – a net increase of **$485.5 million**.

**Cash‑flow drivers**

| Category | 2019 (in $ million) | 2018 (in $ million) |
|----------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Operating activities | **+70.6** (driven by subscription revenue, Shopify Payments fees and working‑capital changes) | **+9.3** |
| Investing activities | **‑569.5** (business acquisitions – notably the 6RS purchase, marketable‑securities purchases, property & equipment) | **‑810.6** |
| Financing activities | **+736.4** (September 2019 public offering of $688 million and $48 million from stock‑option exercises) | **+1,072.2** (public offerings in February & December 2018 and $30 million from stock‑option exercises) |
| Effect of foreign exchange | **+1.7** | **‑1.9** |
| **Net cash increase** | **+239.2** | **+269.0** |
| Change in marketable securities | **+246.3** | **+762.6** |
| **Total net increase in cash, cash equivalents & marketable securities** | **+485.5** | **+1,031.6** |

**Key insights**

* The **$485.5 million** rise in 2019 was primarily the result of:
  * **Financing inflows** of $736.4 million, largely from the September 2019 public offering.
  * **Operating cash generation** of $70.6 million, reflecting higher subscription sales and payment‑processing fees.
  * **Modest investing outflows** of $569.5 million, mainly for the 6RS acquisition and marketable‑securities purchases.

* In 2018, the cash position grew by **$1,031.6 million**, driven by:
  * **Large financing proceeds** of $1,072.2 million from two public offerings.
  * **Higher change in marketable securities** of $762.6 million, offset by a larger investing cash outflow of $810.6 million.

* Across both years, **cash equivalents and marketable securities** consist of short‑term, highly liquid instruments such as money‑market funds, repurchase agreements, term deposits, and short‑dated government and corporate bonds.

**Conclusion**  
Shopify’s cash balance strengthened in 2019 thanks to a successful public offering, steady operating cash flow, and controlled investing activity. The 2018 period showed a similar pattern but with larger financing proceeds and a greater shift into marketable securities. These cash‑flow dynamics underpin the company’s ability to fund growth initiatives, acquisitions, and ongoing operational needs.

synth_text.text:
**Summary of 2015 Financial Reconciliation**

For the year ended 2015, the company reported a net loss of **$405,460**.  The reconciliation from operating performance metrics to this net loss is detailed below:

| Item | Amount (USD) |
|------|--------------|
| **Net (loss) income** | **$405,460** |
| Income tax expense (recovery) | (16,767) |
| Depreciation and amortization | 509,500 |
| Interest expense, net of interest income | 236,481 |
| **EBITDA** | **1,134,674** |
| Foreign exchange loss (gain) (a) | 2,195 |
| Other loss (income) (b) (c) | (1,566) |
| Write‑down and loss on sale of vessels | 70,175 |
| Direct finance lease payments received in excess of revenue recognized | 24,429 |
| Amortization of in‑process revenue contracts and other | (33,226) |
| Realized and unrealized losses on non‑designated derivative instruments | 102,200 |
| Realized gains (losses) from settlements of non‑designated derivative instruments | (20,008) |
| Loss on deconsolidation of Altera | — |
| Adjustments related to equity (loss) income (d) | 136,921 |
| **Adjusted EBITDA** | **1,415,794** |

### Key Adjustments Explained

* **(a) Foreign exchange loss (gain):** This line captures the effect of currency‑forward contracts. In 2015 the company recorded a modest loss of **$2.2 million**, contrasting with prior years that showed gains.

* **(b) & (c) Other loss (income):** These items aggregate several non‑recurring events, such as the write‑down of a cost‑accounted investment and related tax indemnification guarantees. The net effect for 2015 was a small loss of **$1.6 million**.

* **Write‑down and loss on sale of vessels:** Reflects the depreciation and disposal of vessel assets, amounting to **$70.2 million**.

* **Direct finance lease payments received in excess of revenue recognized:** Represents cash received from lease arrangements that exceeds the revenue recognized under accounting rules, contributing **$24.4 million**.

* **Amortization of in‑process revenue contracts and other:** A non‑cash charge of **$33.2 million** related to contracts still under development.

* **Derivative instrument gains/losses:** The company experienced a net **$82.2 million** loss from unrealized and realized positions in non‑designated derivatives.

* **Adjustments related to equity (loss) income (d):** This non‑GAAP adjustment aggregates items such as depreciation, net interest, tax recovery, lease‑payment excess, vessel write‑downs, derivative results, and other equity‑accounted entity effects. For 2015, these adjustments added **$136.9 million** to the reconciliation.

### Interpretation

- **EBITDA** of **$1.13 billion** reflects earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, but does not include the numerous non‑operating items listed above.
- **Adjusted EBITDA** of **$1.42 billion** adds back the equity‑related adjustments, providing a broader view of cash‑flow‑generating capacity as defined by the company’s non‑GAAP metric.
- After accounting for all taxes, interest, depreciation, foreign‑exchange effects, asset write‑downs, lease‑payment timing differences, and derivative activity, the company’s bottom‑line result is a modest net loss of **$405 thousand**.

**Note:** Adjusted EBITDA is a non‑GAAP financial measure and should not be considered a substitute for GAAP‑based earnings or liquidity metrics. Its composition may differ from similarly titled measures used by other companies.

**Drivers of the 2017 Net Loss**

- **Loss on deconsolidation of Altera:** $104.8 million, reflecting the removal of Altera’s results after its new‑building contracts were cancelled.  
- **Adjustments related to equity (loss) income:** $217.9 million, a non‑GAAP adjustment that adds back items such as depreciation, interest, tax, lease‑related payments, vessel write‑downs, and derivative gains/losses (see note d).  
- **Other loss (income):** $53.98 million, which includes the $23.4 million provision for Altera’s contract cancellations (note b) and a $19.0 million write‑down of a cost‑accounted investment (note c).  
- **Foreign exchange loss (gain):** $26.46 million, a swing from the 2016 gain of $6.55 million (note a).

**Comparative Highlights**  
- EBITDA fell by **$730 million** year‑over‑year, primarily due to the vessel write‑down and Altera loss.  
- Adjusted EBITDA, which excludes many non‑recurring items, remained robust at **$951 million** in 2017, indicating that core operating performance was still strong despite the headline loss.  
- The “Other loss” line in 2016 reflected a $23.4 million provision for Altera’s cancelled contracts and a $19.0 million investment write‑down (notes b and c). In 2017, the same line grew to $53.98 million, driven by additional lease‑related liabilities and derivative activity.

**Contextual Notes**  
- **(a) Foreign currency exchange:** Includes unrealized gains/losses on cross‑currency swaps; 2017 saw a $26.5 million loss versus a $6.5 million gain in 2016.  
- **(b) Altera contract cancellations:** Resulted in accrued damages and reversal of contingent liabilities, contributing to the “Other loss” item.  
- **(c) Investment write‑down and lease liability:** A $19.0 million write‑down in 2016 and a $50 million tax indemnification guarantee liability in 2017 affected the “Other loss” and “Write‑down and loss on sale of vessels” lines.  
- **(d) Adjustments related to equity (loss) income:** A non‑GAAP measure that adds back several items (depreciation, interest, tax, lease payments, vessel write‑downs, derivative gains/losses, etc.) to provide a view of earnings attributable to equity‑accounted entities.

**Conclusion**  
The reconciliation demonstrates that while 2017’s headline net loss was driven by significant non‑recurring charges—particularly vessel write‑downs, the Altera deconsolidation, and equity‑related adjustments—the underlying Adjusted EBITDA remained healthy. This suggests that the core operating business retained strong cash‑generating capacity, with the loss primarily reflecting one‑time events and accounting adjustments rather than a deterioration in ongoing operations.

synth_text.title: 2018‑2019 Consolidated EBITDA Reconciliation and Net Loss Overview
synth_text.text:
**Summary of 2018‑2019 Financial Performance**

The table reconciles the company’s consolidated EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA to net (loss) income for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019.

| Item | 2018 (US$ m) | 2019 (US$ m) |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| Net (loss) income | (57.7) | (149.0) |
| Income tax expense (recovery) | 19.7 | 25.5 |
| Depreciation & amortization | 276.3 | 290.7 |
| Interest expense, net of interest income | 245.6 | 271.3 |
| **EBITDA** | 483.9 | 438.4 |
| Foreign exchange loss (gain) | (6.1) gain | 13.6 loss |
| Other loss (income) | 2.0 | 14.5 |
| Write‑down & loss on sale of vessels | 53.7 | 170.3 |
| Direct finance lease payments received in excess of revenue recognized | 11.1 | 21.6 |
| Amortization of in‑process revenue contracts and other | (10.2) | (4.1) |
| Realized & unrealized losses on non‑designated derivative instruments | 14.9 | 13.7 |
| Realized gains (losses) from settlements of non‑designated derivative instruments | — | 1.5 |
| Loss on deconsolidation of Altera | 7.1 | — |
| **Adjustments related to equity (loss) income** | 219.4 | 282.4 |
| **Adjusted EBITDA** | 775.6 | 951.9 |

### Key Drivers of the 2019 Results

1. **Widening Net Loss** – The consolidated loss more than doubled, primarily due to a $170.3 million write‑down and loss on the sale of vessels, compared with $53.7 million in 2018.  
2. **Foreign‑Currency Impact** – A $13.6 million foreign‑exchange loss replaced a $6.1 million gain. The loss includes an unrealized $13.2 million loss on cross‑currency swaps, as highlighted in the footnotes.  
3. **Higher Interest Expense** – Net interest expense rose by $25.7 million, reflecting increased borrowing costs.  
4. **Improved Adjusted EBITDA** – Despite lower EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA increased by $176.3 million, driven by larger “adjustments related to equity (loss) income.” This non‑GAAP measure aggregates depreciation, interest, tax recovery, lease‑payment excesses, vessel write‑downs, derivative gains/losses, and other equity‑accounted items.  

### Contextual Notes

- **Foreign‑exchange losses** are part of the company’s swap program; 2019’s loss contrasts with gains in prior years (e.g., $21.2 million gain in 2018).  
- **Adjustments related to equity (loss) income** are non‑GAAP and should not be viewed as a substitute for GAAP equity income. They reflect the company’s share of results from equity‑accounted entities, including depreciation, interest, tax, lease‑related excesses, vessel disposals, and derivative activity.  
- The **loss on deconsolidation of Altera** appears only in 2018, indicating that Altera’s financial impact was removed from the consolidated statements in 2019.  

### Overall Assessment

The company’s core operating profitability, as measured by EBITDA, declined in 2019, largely because of significant vessel write‑downs and adverse currency movements. However, the Adjusted EBITDA metric shows a robust improvement, underscoring the material effect of equity‑related adjustments. Stakeholders should consider both GAAP and non‑GAAP measures to obtain a complete picture of financial performance.

text.value: Stock Ownership Requirements

We believe that in order to align the interests of our executive officers with those of our stockholders, our executive officers should have a financial stake in our Company. We have maintained stock ownership requirements for our executive officers since October 2005. For FY19, our executive officers were required to hold the following minimum number of shares:
• CEO: 6x base salary; • CFO, COO and President: 3x base salary; and • Executive Vice Presidents: 2x base salary.

text.value: Allowances for Receivables and Sales Returns
The allowances for receivables were as follows (in millions, except percentages):
(1) Calculated as allowance for credit loss on lease receivables as a percentage of gross lease receivables and residual value before unearned income.

The allowance for doubtful accounts is based on our assessment of the collectibility of customer accounts. We regularly review the adequacy of these allowances by considering internal factors such as historical experience, credit quality and age of the receivable balances as well as external factors such as economic conditions that may affect a customer’s ability to pay as well as historical and expected default frequency rates, which are published by major third-party credit-rating agencies and are updated on a quarterly basis. We also consider the concentration of receivables outstanding with a particular customer in assessing the adequacy of our allowances for doubtful accounts. If a major customer’s creditworthiness deteriorates, if actual defaults are higher than our historical experience, or if other circumstances arise, our estimates of the recoverability of amounts due to us could be overstated, and additional allowances could be required, which could have an adverse impact on our operating results.

The allowance for credit loss on financing receivables is also based on the assessment of collectibility of customer accounts. We regularly review the adequacy of the credit allowances determined either on an individual or a collective basis. When evaluating the financing receivables on an individual basis, we consider historical experience, credit quality and age of receivable balances, and economic conditions that may affect a customer’s ability to pay. When evaluating financing receivables on a collective basis, we use expected default frequency rates published by a major third-party credit-rating agency as well as our own historical loss rate in the event of default, while also systematically giving effect to economic conditions, concentration of risk and correlation. Determining expected default frequency rates and loss factors associated with internal credit risk ratings, as well as assessing factors such as economic conditions, concentration of risk, and correlation, are complex and subjective. Our ongoing consideration of all these factors could result in an increase in our allowance for credit loss in the future, which could adversely affect our operating results. Both accounts receivable and financing receivables are charged off at the point when they are considered uncollectible.

A reserve for future sales returns is established based on historical trends in product return rates. The reserve for future sales returns as of July 27, 2019 and July 28, 2018 was $84 million and $123 million, respectively, and was recorded as a reduction of our accounts receivable and revenue. If the actual future returns were to deviate from the historical data on which the reserve had been established, our revenue could be adversely affected.

synth_text.title: Receivables Allowance Summary – Comparative Overview (Latest vs. Prior Period)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company reports allowances for doubtful accounts and credit losses on financing receivables in two consecutive periods. These allowances are expressed both in absolute dollar terms (millions) and as a percentage of the related gross receivable balances.

**Key Figures**

| Category | Latest Period | % of Gross (Latest) | Prior Period | % of Gross (Prior) |
|----------|---------------|----------------------|--------------|--------------------|
| Allowance for doubtful accounts (accounts receivable) | $136 M | 2.4 % | $129 M | 2.3 % |
| Allowance for credit loss – lease receivables | $46 M | 1.8 % | $135 M | 4.7 % |
| Allowance for credit loss – loan receivables | $71 M | 1.3 % | $60 M | 1.2 % |

**Interpretation**

* **Accounts receivable** – The allowance rose modestly by $7 M (0.1 % of gross), reflecting a slight increase in the estimated collectibility risk.
* **Lease receivables** – The allowance fell sharply from $135 M to $46 M, decreasing the percentage of gross lease receivables from 4.7 % to 1.8 %. This suggests an improvement in lease‑related credit quality or a change in the composition of lease assets.
* **Loan receivables** – The allowance increased by $11 M, with the percentage moving from 1.2 % to 1.3 %, indicating a marginally higher perceived risk on loan portfolios.

**Methodological Context**  
Both the allowance for doubtful accounts and the credit‑loss allowances on financing receivables are derived from a comprehensive assessment that includes:

* Historical loss experience, credit quality, and age of receivable balances.  
* External economic conditions and third‑party default‑frequency rates, updated quarterly.  
* Concentration risk—particularly exposure to major customers whose creditworthiness may deteriorate.  

The company reviews these allowances regularly, applying either an individual‑account approach or a collective‑portfolio approach, and adjusts them when actual defaults diverge from expectations. Any future increase in these allowances could negatively impact operating results, as the allowances are recorded as reductions to receivables and revenue.

**Conclusion**  
The comparative data show a generally stable allowance for accounts receivable, a notable reduction in lease‑receivable allowances, and a slight uptick in loan‑receivable allowances. These movements are consistent with the company’s ongoing, factor‑driven evaluation of credit risk, which remains subject to change based on evolving economic conditions and customer credit profiles.

synth_text.title: Key Financial Highlights for 2019 and 2018
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary presents the company’s selected consolidated financial data for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018. These figures are extracted from the audited Form 10‑K statements and reflect the adoption of ASC 606 (Contracts with Customers) on a modified retrospective basis as of January 1, 2018.

**Income Statement Highlights**  
- **Revenue** fell to **$212.6 million** in 2019 from **$232.2 million** in 2018, a decrease of roughly 8.5 %.  
- **Cost of revenue** declined to **$48.9 million** (down from $51.9 million), keeping the **gross profit** at **$163.7 million** in 2019 versus **$180.3 million** in 2018.  
- **Loss from operations** narrowed to **$(17.1 million)** in 2019, improving from **$(27.7 million)** in 2018.  
- **Net loss** followed the same trend, reaching **$(17.8 million)** in 2019 compared with **$(27.6 million)** in 2018.  
- **Net loss per share (basic and diluted)** was **$(0.23)** in 2019, better than **$(0.38)** in the prior year, based on a weighted‑average share count of **76,080 k** (2019) and **72,882 k** (2018).

**Balance Sheet Highlights**  
- **Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities** remained strong at **$129.9 million** in 2019, a slight increase from **$128.4 million** in 2018.  
- **Working capital** improved to **$123.4 million** (up from $117.6 million).  
- **Total assets** grew to **$274.1 million**, reflecting the increase in cash and other current assets.  
- **Deferred revenue (current and non‑current)** rose to **$101.2 million**, up from **$98.0 million**.  
- **Total stockholders’ equity** increased to **$108.8 million**, compared with **$103.9 million** in 2018.

**Contextual Notes**  
- The presented data are “selected” figures; they should be read in conjunction with the full audited financial statements, the accompanying notes, and the Management’s Discussion and Analysis sections of the Form 10‑K.  
- The adoption of ASC 606 in 2018 altered the revenue recognition methodology; the impact of this change was recorded as of January 1, 2018. All prior‑year amounts were prepared under the previous revenue‑recognition guidance.

**Conclusion**  
While revenue declined in 2019, the company achieved a markedly narrower operating and net loss, improved per‑share loss metrics, and strengthened its liquidity and equity positions. The financial trends reflect both operational performance and the accounting impact of ASC 606 adoption.

synth_text.text:
The table below reconciles the company’s Adjusted Gross Profit to the Gross Profit reported under U.S. GAAP.

- **Depreciation & amortization expense (a):** $2,566 – this amount is included in cost of goods sold under GAAP but is added back for the adjusted measure.  
- **Plant start‑up expense (b):** — – no start‑up costs were incurred for the Freshpet Kitchens expansion in the reported period.  
- **Non‑cash share‑based compensation (c):** $201 – a non‑cash expense recorded in cost of goods sold, also added back.

text.value: Jack in the Box restaurants offer a broad selection of distinctive products including classic burgers like our Jumbo Jack® and innovative product lines such as Buttery Jack® burgers. We also offer quality products such as breakfast sandwiches with freshly cracked eggs, and craveable favorites such as tacos and curly fries, along with specialty sandwiches, salads, and real ice cream shakes, among other items. We allow our guests to customize their meals to their tastes and order any product when they want it, including breakfast items any time of day (or night). We are known for variety and innovation, which has led to the development of four strong dayparts: breakfast, lunch, dinner, and late-night.

The Jack in the Box restaurant chain was the first major hamburger chain to develop and expand the concept of drive-thru restaurants. In addition to drive-thru windows, most of our restaurants have seating capacities ranging from 20 to 100 people and are open 18-24 hours a day. Drive-thru sales currently account for approximately 70% of sales at company-operated restaurants. The average check in fiscal year2019 was $8.34 for company-operated restaurants.
With a presence in only 21 states and one territory, we believe Jack in the Box is a brand with significant growth opportunities. In fiscal 2019, franchisees continued to expand in existing markets.
The following table summarizes the changes in the number of company-operated and franchise restaurants over the past five years:

Site selections for all new company-operated restaurants are made after an economic analysis and a review of demographic data and other information relating to population density, traffic, competition, restaurant visibility and access, available parking, surrounding businesses, and opportunities for market penetration. Restaurants developed by franchisees are built to brand specifications on sites we have approved.

Our company-operated restaurants have multiple restaurant models with different seating capacities to improve our flexibility in selecting locations. Management believes that this flexibility enables the Company to match the restaurant configuration with the specific economic, demographic, geographic, or physical characteristics of a particular site.

Typical costs to develop a traditional restaurant, excluding the land value, range from approximately$1.4 million to $2.0 million. The majority of our corporate restaurants are constructed on leased land or on land that we purchase and subsequently sell, along with the improvements, in sale and leaseback transactions. Upon completion of a sale and leaseback transaction, the Company’s initial cash investment is reduced to the cost of equipment, which ranges from approximately $0.4 million to $0.5 million.

synth_text.title: Jack in the Box System Growth Summary: 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview of Restaurant Count Changes**

- **Company‑operated restaurants**
  - *2018*: Began the year with 1,975 locations, added 11 new units, refranchised 135, and closed 21, ending the year with **2,100** restaurants – a net increase of 125 units.
  - *2019*: Started with 2,100 locations, opened 19 new units and closed 13, finishing the year with **2,106** restaurants – a modest net gain of 6 units.
  - Company‑operated sites represent **94 %** of the total system in both years.

- **Franchise restaurants**
  - The franchise segment remained stable, with the overall system (company‑operated + franchise) growing from **2,237** locations in 2018 to **2,243** in 2019, an increase of 6 franchise sites.

**Operational Highlights**

- Drive‑thru service drives roughly **70 %** of sales at company‑operated restaurants, reinforcing the brand’s focus on quick, convenient service.
- The average check for a company‑operated restaurant in FY 2019 was **$8.34**, reflecting the value‑oriented menu that includes items such as the Jumbo Jack®, Buttery Jack® burgers, breakfast sandwiches, tacos, curly fries, and specialty shakes.
- Jack in the Box operates in **21 states and one U.S. territory**, offering four distinct dayparts—breakfast, lunch, dinner, and late‑night—providing ample growth opportunities in existing markets.

**Strategic Implications**

- The modest net increase in company‑operated locations in 2019, combined with a stable franchise base, suggests a deliberate, data‑driven expansion strategy that prioritizes site selection based on demographic and traffic analyses.
- Flexibility in restaurant models (seating capacities from 20 to 100) and the ability to develop sites on leased or sale‑and‑leaseback land help manage capital outlays, with typical development costs ranging from **$1.4 M to $2.0 M** (excluding land) and equipment costs of **$0.4 M to $0.5 M**.

Overall, Jack in the Box’s restaurant system grew slightly from 2,237 locations in 2018 to 2,243 in 2019, driven primarily by continued franchise expansion and a steady, though modest, increase in company‑operated units. The brand’s strong drive‑thru presence, diverse menu, and flexible site strategy position it well for further growth within its current geographic footprint.

synth_text.title: Jack in the Box 2015 Restaurant Portfolio Overview
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2015 Jack in the Box operated a total of **1,836 company‑owned restaurants**, up from **1,819** at the start of the year—a net gain of **17 locations**. The growth stemmed from 16 newly opened sites, 21 restaurants that were refranchised back to the company, and the acquisition of 7 former franchisee locations, offset by the closure of 13 under‑performing units. Company‑operated restaurants accounted for **82 % of the entire system**.

Franchise locations saw a modest decline, with **7 franchised restaurants sold to the company**, leaving a **system‑wide total of 2,249 restaurants** at year‑end. This composition underscores Jack in the Box’s strategic emphasis on expanding its company‑operated footprint while maintaining a robust franchised network.

The brand’s operational model supports this growth. Most restaurants feature drive‑thru lanes—responsible for roughly **70 % of sales**—and operate 18–24 hours a day, offering flexible seating for 20 to 100 guests. With a presence in only 21 states and one U.S. territory, Jack in the Box identifies significant expansion opportunities, especially as franchisees continue to develop new sites in existing markets. Site selection is driven by detailed economic and demographic analyses, ensuring new locations align with market demand and visibility criteria.

Overall, the 2015 data reflect a steady increase in company‑controlled assets, reinforcing Jack in the Box’s focus on operational control, drive‑thru dominance, and long‑term growth potential across its limited geographic footprint.

synth_text.title: Jack in the Box Restaurant Portfolio: 2016‑2017 Growth Overview
synth_text.text:
**Overview of Restaurant Footprint (2016‑2017)**  

- **Company‑operated locations** grew from **1,838** at the start of 2016 to **1,975** by the end of 2017, a net increase of **137 restaurants (≈7.5 %)**.  
  - New openings: **18** (2017) vs. **12** (2016)  
  - Refranchised units: **178** (2017) vs. **1** (2016)  
  - Acquisitions from franchisees: **50** (2017) vs. **1** (2016)  
  - Closures were minimal, with only **9** restaurants closed in 2017 (10 in 2016).  

- **Franchise‑owned locations** slipped slightly from **2,255** to **2,251**. The modest decline reflects the transfer of **50** franchised sites to the company in 2017 (only one in 2016).  

- **Total system size** expanded from **4,093** restaurants in 2016 to **4,226** in 2017, an overall growth of **133 locations**.  

- **System composition** shifted markedly: company‑operated restaurants rose from **82 %** of the total system in 2016 to **88 %** in 2017, indicating a strategic move toward greater corporate control.

**Strategic Context**

Jack in the Box’s growth is supported by several brand strengths:

1. **Drive‑Thru Dominance** – Approximately 70 % of sales at company‑operated sites come from drive‑thru lanes, a model the chain pioneered and continues to leverage.  
2. **24‑Hour Flexibility** – Most locations operate 18‑24 hours daily, catering to all four dayparts (breakfast, lunch, dinner, late‑night).  
3. **Menu Innovation** – A broad, customizable menu—including signature items like the Jumbo Jack® and Buttery Jack® burgers—drives repeat traffic across dayparts.  
4. **Rigorous Site Selection** – New company‑operated restaurants are placed after detailed economic, demographic and traffic analyses, ensuring optimal market penetration.  
5. **Scalable Restaurant Models** – Varying seating capacities (20‑100 seats) allow the company to match site characteristics, while typical development costs range from $1.4 M to $2.0 M (excluding land).  

With a footprint in only 21 states and one U.S. territory, Jack in the Box identifies significant growth opportunities. The 2017 increase in company‑operated locations, combined with the brand’s strong drive‑thru sales and flexible restaurant designs, positions the chain well for continued expansion in existing and new markets.

synth_text.title: American Tower Corporation – ROIC Reconciliation (2018 vs 2019)
synth_text.text:
The 2019 Annual Report of American Tower Corporation includes a detailed reconciliation of Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) for the two most recent fiscal years. The key figures are presented in millions of dollars, with totals subject to rounding.

| Metric | 2018 | 2019 |
|--------|------|------|
| Adjusted EBITDA | $3,206 | $3,743 |
| Cash Taxes | $(107) | $(98) |
| Maintenance Capex | $(124) | $(159) |
| Corporate Capex | $(26) | $(27) |
| Numerator (NOPAT‑adjusted) | $2,948 | $3,459 |
| Gross PPE | $14,397 | $15,652 |
| Gross Intangibles | $12,671 | $14,795 |
| Gross Goodwill* | $4,240 | $4,510 |
| Denominator (Invested Capital) | $31,308 | $34,957 |
| ROIC | 9.4 % | 9.9 % |

**Key observations**

1. **Operating performance** – Adjusted EBITDA grew by roughly 17 % year‑over‑year, indicating stronger core earnings.  
2. **Tax and capex impact** – Cash taxes fell modestly, while both maintenance and corporate capital expenditures increased, reflecting continued investment in network infrastructure.  
3. **Invested capital** – The numerator (NOPAT‑adjusted) rose by 17 %, driven by higher earnings, whereas the denominator expanded by about 12 % due to growth in property, plant, equipment, intangibles and goodwill.  
4. **ROIC improvement** – The combined effect of higher earnings and a proportionally smaller increase in invested capital lifted ROIC from 9.4 % to 9.9 %.  
5. **Footnote considerations** – Goodwill figures exclude deferred‑tax adjustments related to valuation (footnote 6). Historical denominator balances incorporate purchase‑accounting adjustments (footnote 1). The numbers also reflect annualized impacts of acquisitions closed during the year (footnote 4).

Overall, the reconciliation demonstrates that American Tower’s capital allocation and operational efficiency have enhanced its return on invested capital, moving the metric closer to the high‑single‑digit range in 2019.

text.value: Accounts Receivable

Accounts receivable are uncollateralized customer obligations due under normal trade terms. The Company records allowances for doubtful accounts based on customer-specific analysis and general matters such as current assessment of past due balances and economic conditions. The Company writes off accounts receivable when they become uncollectible. The allowance for doubtful accounts was $55,039 and $65,542 at December 31, 2019 and 2018, respectively. Management identifies a delinquent customer based upon the delinquent payment status of an outstanding invoice, generally greater than 30 days past due date. The delinquent account designation does not trigger an accounting transaction until such time the account is deemed uncollectible. The allowance for doubtful accounts is determined by examining the reserve history and any outstanding invoices that are over 30 days past due as of the end of the reporting period. Accounts are deemed uncollectible on a case-by-case basis, at management’s discretion based upon an examination of the communication with the delinquent customer and payment history. Typically, accounts are only escalated to “uncollectible” status after multiple attempts at collection have proven unsuccessful.

- The ESPP is structured to qualify under **Section 423 of the Internal Revenue Code**.

synth_text.title: Key Valuation Assumptions for the 2011 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The 2011 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) permits eligible employees—those with at least 90 days of service—to purchase Company common stock through payroll deductions of up to 10 % of compensation. Shares are bought at a discount of 15 % off the lower of the fair market value at the beginning or end of the offering period, and the plan is structured to qualify under Section 423 of the Internal Revenue Code. As of August 31 2019, 3,397,019 of the 12 million authorized shares remained available for issuance.

For financial reporting, the fair value of ESPP shares was estimated at the start of each offering period using the Black‑Scholes option‑pricing model. The model relied on the following weighted‑average assumptions:

| Offering Year | Expected Dividend Yield | Risk‑Free Interest Rate | Expected Volatility* | Expected Life |
|---------------|------------------------|------------------------|----------------------|---------------|
| 2019          | 0.6 %                  | 2.3 %                  | 28.6 %               | 0.5 years     |
| 2018          | 0.6 %                  | 1.4 %                  | 23.0 %               | 0.5 years     |

\*Volatility was derived from the historical volatility of the Company’s common stock.

These inputs reflect the market environment and the Company’s stock behavior during each period. The higher risk‑free rate and increased volatility in 2019 indicate a more uncertain interest‑rate environment and greater stock price fluctuation compared with 2018. The consistent dividend yield and option life (half a year) align with the plan’s design and the typical offering duration.

Together, the ESPP’s eligibility rules, purchase discount, and the Black‑Scholes assumptions provide a transparent framework for valuing the employee purchase rights and for reporting the associated expense in the Company’s financial statements.

| Executive | Termination Type | Cash Severance | COBRA Reimbursement | Stock/RSU Acceleration | Total Cash & COBRA |

* **Cash Severance** – Calculated on the basis of months of base salary and a percentage of the executive’s annual target bonus, as detailed in the footnotes.  
* **COBRA Reimbursement** – Provided for the same number of months of health‑coverage continuation as the cash severance period, except for Mr. Walcott, who chose not to receive COBRA benefits.

synth_text.title: Director Remuneration Summary (Non‑Executive & Executive) – FY 2018‑19 & FY 2019‑20
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table below captures the cash remuneration paid to the company’s directors for two consecutive financial years. Figures are expressed in ₹ crore. Symbols accompanying certain names clarify the nature of the payment or the director’s status during the year.

| Director (Role) | FY 2018‑19 | FY 2019‑20 | Notes |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| **Non‑Executive Directors** | | | |
| Aman Mehta | 51.55 | 5.00 | Full‑year remuneration in 2018‑19; reduced payment in 2019‑20. |
| V Thyagarajan* | ^ | ^ | Relinquished independent‑director position on 10 July 2018; remuneration only for part of the year (not comparable). |
| Prof Clayton M Christensen** | ^ | ^ | Relinquished independent‑director position on 28 Sept 2018; part‑year remuneration (not comparable). |
| Dr Ron Sommer | 36.00 | 4.76 | Full‑year remuneration in 2018‑19; part‑year payment in 2019‑20 (not comparable). |
| O P Bhatt | 35.18 | 7.50 | Full‑year remuneration in 2018‑19; part‑year remuneration in 2019‑20 (not comparable). |
| Aarthi Subramanian@@ | – | – | No commission paid as she is a full‑time employee of another Tata company (policy). |
| Dr Pradeep Kumar Khosla | 24.55 | ^^ | 2019‑20 figure not comparable with 2018‑19. |
| Hanne Sorensen*** | ^ | ^ | Appointed additional independent director on 18 Dec 2018; part‑year remuneration (not comparable). |
| Keki Mistry*** | ^ | ^ | Appointed additional independent director on 18 Dec 2018; part‑year remuneration (not comparable). |
| Don Callahan**** | ^ | ^ | Appointed additional independent director on 10 Jan 2019; part‑year remuneration (not comparable). |
| **Executive Directors** | | | |
| Rajesh Gopinathan | 262.30 | 28.31 | CEO – remuneration fell sharply in FY 2019‑20 due to a change in compensation structure. |
| N Ganapathy Subramaniam | 190.01 | 24.88 | CFO – similar reduction in FY 2019‑20. |
| **Chief Financial Officer** | – | 22.58 | Ramakrishnan V – remuneration for FY 2019‑20 (new appointment). |
| **Company Secretary** | – | 18.23 | Rajendra Moholkar – remuneration for FY 2019‑20 (new appointment). |

**Key Interpretations**

1. **Policy‑Driven Non‑Payment** – Chairman N Chandrasekaran abstains from any commission, and directors who are full‑time employees of other Tata entities (e.g., Aarthi Subramanian) receive no remuneration, as per company policy.  
2. **Part‑Year Appointments/Relinquishments** – Directors marked with “^” served only part of the fiscal year (either appointed or relinquished their independent‑director status). Consequently, their remuneration ratios to median employee pay and percentage changes are not disclosed.  
3. **Non‑Comparable Figures** – The “^^” symbol for Dr Pradeep Khosla indicates that the FY 2019‑20 amount cannot be directly compared with the prior year’s figure.  

**Contextual Comparison with Overall Employee Compensation**

- The company employed **424,285** permanent staff, with a **median remuneration increase of 3.70 %** for the year.  
- Average salary growth across the workforce was **approximately 7.2 %** (6 % base increase plus promotion‑related adjustments).  
- Managerial remuneration (including directors) rose by **14.66 %**, substantially higher than the median employee increase, reflecting market‑aligned compensation for senior leadership.  

**Conclusion**  
The remuneration data illustrate a significant reduction in cash payments to executive directors in FY 2019‑20, while several non‑executive directors either received no payment or only part‑year compensation due to appointments, resignations, or policy restrictions. Overall, managerial remuneration growth outpaced the median increase for the broader employee base, consistent with the company’s remuneration policy and prevailing market trends.

synth_text.title: Jabil Inc. 2017 Financial Highlights and Non‑GAAP Core Measures Overview
synth_text.text:
**Jabil Inc. – FY 2017 Financial Summary**

For the fiscal year ended August 31 2017, Jabil reported the following key U.S. GAAP results (figures in thousands of dollars unless noted otherwise):

- **Operating income (U.S. GAAP):** $410,230  
- **Net income attributable to Jabil Inc.:** $129,090  
- **Diluted earnings per share (U.S. GAAP):** $0.69  
- **Diluted weighted‑average shares outstanding:** 185,838  

**Non‑GAAP “Core” Adjustments**

Jabil adjusts its GAAP operating income by excluding several non‑recurring or non‑cash items to derive a “core” operating income that reflects the performance of its ongoing manufacturing operations. The adjustments for 2017 total $256,773 and consist of:

| Excluded Item (in $ thousands) | Amount |
|--------------------------------|--------|
| Amortization of intangibles | 35,524 |
| Stock‑based compensation expense and related charges | 48,544 |
| Restructuring and related charges | 160,395 |
| Distressed customer charges (energy‑sector disengagement) | 10,198 |
| Loss on disposal of subsidiaries | 2,112 |
| Other adjustments (e.g., settlement of receivables) | 0* |

\*No other listed charges (business interruption, acquisition, etc.) were recorded for 2017.

**Resulting Non‑GAAP Core Metrics**

- **Core operating income (Non‑GAAP):** $667,003  
- **Core earnings (Non‑GAAP):** $392,676  
- **Diluted core earnings per share (Non‑GAAP):** $2.11  

**Context for Non‑GAAP Measures**

Jabil’s non‑GAAP “core” financial measures are disclosed to provide investors with a view of the company’s underlying manufacturing performance, stripped of items that are either non‑cash (e.g., stock‑based compensation) or not expected to recur (e.g., restructuring, distressed‑customer charges). Management emphasizes that:

1. These measures are **not a substitute** for GAAP results and may differ from other companies’ definitions of “core” metrics.  
2. The tax effect of each excluded item is calculated based on the statutory tax rate of the jurisdiction where the pre‑tax expense occurred; where no tax benefit is expected, a reduced or 0 % rate is applied.  
3. Core metrics are used internally for operating decisions, performance assessment, and as a factor in employee incentive compensation.  

By presenting both GAAP and non‑GAAP figures, Jabil aims to give a clearer picture of its ongoing profitability while acknowledging the impact of significant, non‑operational charges that affect cash flow and balance‑sheet assets.

**Takeaway**

In 2017, Jabil’s GAAP operating income of $410 million translates to a substantially higher non‑GAAP core operating income of $667 million after removing $256 million of adjustments. This yields core earnings of $393 million and a diluted core EPS of $2.11, compared with GAAP EPS of $0.69. The non‑GAAP presentation underscores the company’s focus on its core manufacturing business and provides a benchmark for evaluating future performance.

synth_text.title: Jabil Inc. Fiscal 2019 vs 2018 Financial Performance: GAAP Results and Non‑GAAP Core Measures
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
Jabil Inc. reported substantial growth in its manufacturing operations between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2019. The company presents both U.S. GAAP results and non‑GAAP “core” financial measures, the latter excluding a range of non‑recurring or non‑cash items to better reflect ongoing operating performance.

**GAAP Highlights**  

| Metric (in thousands) | FY 2019 | FY 2018 |
|------------------------|---------|---------|
| Operating income (U.S. GAAP) | $701,356 | $542,153 |
| Net income attributable to Jabil (U.S. GAAP) | $287,111 | $86,330 |
| Diluted earnings per share (U.S. GAAP) | $1.81 | $0.49 |
| Diluted weighted‑average shares outstanding | 158,647 | 175,044 |

Operating income rose 29% year‑over‑year, driven by higher contract manufacturing volumes and improved pricing. Net income more than tripled, reflecting both the operating gain and a $13.3 million tax benefit recorded in 2019.

**Non‑GAAP “Core” Measures**  
Jabil’s core operating income and core earnings exclude items such as amortization of intangibles, stock‑based compensation, restructuring charges, distressed‑customer write‑downs, acquisition and integration costs, and other one‑time adjustments. These measures are intended to provide a clearer view of the underlying manufacturing business.

| Metric (in thousands) | FY 2019 | FY 2018 |
|------------------------|---------|---------|
| Core operating income (Non‑GAAP) | $876,611 | $768,147 |
| Core earnings (Non‑GAAP) | $473,365 | $458,530 |
| Diluted core earnings per share (Non‑GAAP) | $2.98 | $2.62 |
| Adjustments to operating income | $175,255 | $225,994 |

Core operating income increased 14% despite larger adjustments in 2019 (e.g., $31.9 M amortization, $61.3 M stock‑based compensation, $25.9 M restructuring). The reduction in total adjustments from 2018 to 2019 (‑$50.6 M) reflects lower distressed‑customer charges and acquisition costs, partially offset by a $52.7 M acquisition‑integration charge related to the strategic collaboration with Johnson & Johnson Medical Devices.

**Key One‑Time Items**  

- **Distressed customer charges:** $6.2 M in 2019 vs. $32.7 M in 2018, mainly inventory write‑downs in networking and consumer wearables.  
- **Business interruption & impairment (Hurricane Maria):** A net charge of $(2.9 M) in 2019 after insurance recoveries; $11.3 M net charge in 2018.  
- **Acquisition & integration charges:** $52.7 M in 2019 (JJMD collaboration) vs. $8.1 M in 2018.  
- **Restructuring of securities loss:** $29.6 M recorded in 2019; none in 2018.  
- **Tax adjustments:** A $13.3 M tax benefit in 2019 versus a $142.3 M provisional tax estimate in 2018.

**Interpretation**  
Management uses the non‑GAAP core metrics to evaluate the performance of its ongoing manufacturing operations on a comparable basis across periods. By stripping out non‑cash expenses (e.g., stock‑based compensation) and irregular charges, the core figures highlight operational profitability and cash‑flow generation. However, investors should consider that excluded items can affect cash requirements (e.g., future restructuring payments) and share dilution (stock‑based compensation).

**Conclusion**  
Jabil’s fiscal 2019 results demonstrate robust growth in both GAAP and core operating profitability. The increase in core earnings per share to $2.98 (from $2.62) underscores the strength of its manufacturing platform, while the GAAP earnings per share of $1.81 reflects the net impact of one‑time charges and tax effects. The non‑GAAP core measures provide a useful complement to GAAP results for assessing the sustainability of Jabil’s operating performance.

synth_text.text:
**Overall Performance**  
Consolidated net revenues fell from **$7,500 million in 2018** to **$6,489 million in 2019**, a decline of **$1,011 million (≈13.5 %)**.

**Regional Breakdown**

- **Americas** – Revenue dropped from **$3,880 million** to **$3,341 million** (‑$539 million). The primary cause was lower recognition from the *Destiny* franchise after Activision sold the publishing rights to Bungie in December 2018.

- **EMEA (Europe, Middle East, Africa)** – Revenue decreased from **$2,618 million** to **$2,239 million** (‑$379 million). The decline stemmed from reduced earnings from both the *Destiny* franchise and *Call of Duty: Black Ops 4* (released Oct 2018), compared with the stronger performance of *Call of Duty: WWII* (Nov 2017).

- **Asia Pacific** – Revenue fell from **$1,002 million** to **$909 million** (‑$93 million). This was mainly due to lower *Hearthstone* earnings—2028 had included additional digital‑content revenue linked to a contract renewal with NetEase, Inc., which did not recur in 2019—and reduced *Destiny* revenues. Offsetting this decline were new or higher‑earning titles: *Crash Team Racing Nitro‑Fueled* (June 2019), *Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice* (March 2019), and increased sales of *Call of Duty: Modern Warfare* (Oct 2019) versus *Black Ops 4*.

**Conclusion**  
All three regions experienced revenue reductions in 2019, driven largely by the loss of *Destiny* licensing income and the natural sales cycle of major franchise releases. New game launches in Asia Pacific partially mitigated the regional decline, but the overall effect was a notable drop in Activision’s consolidated net revenue for the year.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Summary 2018‑2019: Revenue Mix Shift and Resulting Net Loss
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In 2019 the company’s total revenues fell to **$36.0 million**, a **68 % decline** from 2018. The drop was driven primarily by a **$70.9 million reduction in fixed‑fee license revenue** and a **$4.0 million decrease in per‑unit royalty revenue**. Part of this change reflects the adoption of ASC 606 (effective 1 Jan 2018) which altered the accounting treatment of license arrangements.

**Revenue composition**  
- **Fixed‑fee license revenue** shrank dramatically from **75.3 % of total revenue in 2018** to **35.1 % in 2019**.  
- **Per‑unit royalty revenue** rose in relative importance, moving from **24.3 %** to **64.0 %** of revenue.  
- Together, royalty and license streams still accounted for **≈99 %** of total revenues in both years.

**Cost and expense profile**  
- Total costs and expenses were **52.2 % of revenue in 2018** but surged to **159.6 % in 2019**.  
- The most pronounced increase was in **General & Administrative expenses**, which jumped from **37.7 %** of revenue in 2018 to **119.4 %** in 2019.  
- Other cost categories (cost of revenues, sales & marketing, R&D) also rose as a share of the much smaller revenue base.

**Operating and net results**  
- **Operating income** swung from a **47.8 % gain** in 2018 to a **(59.6 %) loss** in 2019.  
- After accounting for interest, other income, and a modest tax provision, **net income** turned from a **48.9 % profit** in 2018 to a **(55.7 %) loss** in 2019, equating to a **$20.0 million net loss** versus a **$54.3 million net profit** the prior year.

**Key take‑aways**  
The 2019 financial picture reflects a severe contraction in revenue, a shift away from high‑margin fixed‑fee licenses toward lower‑margin royalty streams, and a cost structure that now exceeds revenue. The adoption of ASC 606 contributed to the reported revenue change, but the underlying business dynamics—particularly the loss of fixed‑fee contracts—were the primary drivers of the net‑loss outcome.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Snapshot: Revenue Mix and Cost Structure (Percent of Revenue) with 2019 Trend Insights
synth_text.text:
The consolidated statement of income presented as a percentage of total revenues reveals the composition of earnings and expenses for the fiscal year shown (labelled “2017”).  

**Revenue composition**  
- Fixed‑fee license revenue contributed **36 %** of total revenue.  
- Per‑unit royalty revenue accounted for **61.4 %**, together representing **97.4 %** of all revenue.  
- Development, services, and other activities supplied the remaining **2.6 %**.  

**Expense profile**  
- Cost of revenues was minimal at **0.6 %** of revenue.  
- Sales and marketing expenses consumed **38.6 %**.  
- Research and development costs were **33.6 %**.  
- General and administrative expenses were the most significant line item, at **152.4 %** of revenue.  

Because total costs and expenses summed to **229.8 %** of revenue, the company recorded an **operating loss of 129.8 %** of revenue. After accounting for interest, other income/expense, and taxes, the **net loss equated to 129.3 %** of revenue.  

**Contextual trend (2019)**  
The additional narrative explains that in 2019 total revenues fell dramatically—down **68 %** from the prior year—driven primarily by a **$70.9 million** reduction in fixed‑fee license revenue and a **$4.0 million** drop in per‑unit royalties. This revenue contraction turned a previous net income of **$54.3 million** (2018) into a **$20.0 million net loss** in 2019, despite a modest decline in operating expenses.  

The 2017 percentage‑based income statement therefore illustrates a business model heavily reliant on royalty income, with a cost structure that can quickly outpace revenue. When revenue declines, as observed in 2019, the imbalance between high fixed and administrative costs and shrinking top‑line earnings leads to substantial net losses.  

**Key takeaway** – Maintaining profitability will require either a sustained increase in royalty‑derived revenue, a reduction in the disproportionately high general and administrative expenses, or a combination of both to keep total costs below the revenue base.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table presents IBM Global Financing’s key balance‑sheet metrics for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019. All figures are expressed in millions of U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted.

**Liquidity**  
- **Cash and cash equivalents** fell slightly from **$1,833 M** in 2018 to **$1,697 M** in 2019, indicating a modest reduction in liquid resources.

**Financing Assets**  
- **Net investment in sales‑type and direct financing leases** decreased from **$6,924 M** to **$6,224 M**, reflecting a reduction in new lease commitments.  
- **Equipment under operating leases – external clients** dropped sharply from **$444 M** to **$238 M**, suggesting fewer assets placed under operating leases for third‑party use.  
- **Client loans** remained relatively stable, moving from **$12,802 M** to **$12,884 M**.  
- Consequently, **total client financing assets** declined from **$20,170 M** to **$19,346 M**.  
- **Commercial financing receivables** fell markedly, from **$11,838 M** to **$3,820 M**, indicating a shift away from commercial financing activities.  
- **Intercompany financing receivables** (eliminated in IBM’s consolidated statements) were **$4,873 M** in 2018 and **$3,870 M** in 2019.

**Overall Balance Sheet**  
- **Total assets** contracted from **$41,320 M** to **$29,568 M**, driven primarily by the reduction in commercial financing receivables and operating‑lease equipment.  
- **Debt** also decreased, from **$31,227 M** to **$24,727 M**, improving the leverage profile.  
- **Total equity** fell from **$3,470 M** to **$2,749 M**, reflecting the net effect of asset and liability changes.

**Portfolio Composition & Credit Quality**  
- At year‑end 2019, virtually all financing assets were **IT‑related**, aligning with IBM’s core business.  
- Approximately **62 %** of the external financing portfolio was held by **investment‑grade clients**, a **7‑point** increase over 2018. This rating‑based metric excludes direct consumer exposure.  
- When accounting for risk‑mitigation actions (e.g., credit insurance, guarantees, non‑recourse borrowings, true‑sale receivable transfers, and equipment lease sales), the investment‑grade share would rise to **67 %**, representing a **3‑point** decline year‑over‑year after adjustment.

**Key Takeaways**  
- The firm’s balance sheet contracted in 2019, primarily due to a strategic reduction in commercial financing and operating‑lease assets.  
- Debt levels fell, modestly improving leverage, while equity also decreased in line with the asset contraction.  
- The financing portfolio’s credit quality improved, with a higher proportion of investment‑grade exposure, especially after considering mitigation measures.  
- Overall, IBM Global Financing continued to focus on IT‑centric financing solutions, maintaining a strong credit profile despite the downsizing of certain asset categories.

Up to one third of the performance stock units may vest following year three, depending upon the achievement of the performance criteria for year three as well as 3-year Relative TSR (covering years one, two and three).

Performance stock units are not considered outstanding stock at the time of grant, as the holders of these units are not entitled to any of the rights of a stockholder, including voting rights. Autodesk has determined the grant-date fair value for these awards using the stock price on the date of grant or if the awards are subject to a market condition, a Monte Carlo simulation model. The fair value of the performance stock units is expensed using the accelerated attribution over the vesting period. Autodesk recorded stock-based compensation expense related to performance stock units of $28.6 million, $33.7 million, and $22.9 million during fiscal years ended January 31, 2019, 2018, and 2017 respectively. As of January 31, 2019, total compensation cost not yet recognized of $5.6 million related to unvested performance stock units, is expected to be recognized over a weighted average period of 0.81 years. synth_text.title: Key Black‑Scholes Inputs and Fair‑Value Summary for Equity‑Settled Share Options (FY 2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The fair value of equity‑settled share options granted by the company is calculated at the grant date using a Black‑Scholes model. The model incorporates weighted‑average inputs that reflect the market and contractual conditions of the options. The table below summarises these inputs for the two most recent reporting dates:

| Reporting date | Weighted average share price (cents) | Weighted average exercise price (cents) | Expected volatility | Expected life of options (years) | Risk‑free rate | Dividend yield |
|----------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|----------------------|-----------------------------------|----------------|----------------|
| 31 Mar 2019    | 676.10                               | 558.54                                   | 54.91 %              | 1.69                              | 1.56 %         | 0.81 %         |
| 31 Mar 2018    | 628.23                               | 516.70                                   | 38.20 %              | 2.08                              | 1.49 %         | 0.70 %         |

**Fair‑value outcomes**  
- 2019: Weighted‑average fair value of options granted = **$220.53 cents**.  
- 2018: Weighted‑average fair value of options granted = **$185.33 cents**.

**Interpretation of key assumptions**

*Expected volatility* – The model assumes that historical share‑price volatility is indicative of future movements. The higher volatility assumed for 2019 (54.91 % vs 38.20 % in 2018) increases the estimated fair value of the options.

*Expected life* – Based on historical exercise patterns and adjusted for restrictions, behavioural factors and non‑transferability, the expected life was shortened to 1.69 years in 2019 from 2.08 years in 2018. A longer expected life would raise the fair value; the reduction partially offsets the effect of higher volatility.

*Other inputs* – The risk‑free rate and dividend yield rose modestly year‑over‑year, while both the share price and the exercise price increased, reflecting the company’s market performance.

Overall, the combination of a higher share price, substantially higher expected volatility, and a slightly lower expected life resulted in a higher estimated fair value for the options granted in 2019 compared with 2018.

synth_text.title: MSA Segment FY2019 Financial Performance Overview
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2019, the Electro‑Magnetic, Sensors, and Actuators (MSA) segment reported net sales of **$240.7 million** and segment operating income of **$22.5 million**, representing an operating‑income margin of **9.4 %** of net sales.

Compared with FY 2018, net sales rose 6.1 % (up $13.8 million) from $227.0 million. The increase was driven primarily by:
- A $15.0 million boost in OEM sales in the JPKO region,
- A $4.3 million rise in EMS sales across all regions,
- A $3.7 million gain in distributor sales in the Americas and EMEA regions.

These gains were partially offset by:
- A $5.5 million decline in distributor sales in APAC and JPKO,
- A $3.8 million drop in OEM sales across the Americas, APAC, and JPKO.

Operating income improved to $22.5 million, up $6.9 million from $15.7 million in FY 2018. The main contributors to this increase were:
- A $6.6 million reduction in SG&A expenses, mainly from lower payroll due to head‑count reductions,
- A $2.9 million decrease in restructuring charges,
- A $1.3 million lower net loss on write‑downs and disposals of long‑lived assets,
- A $0.2 million cut in R&D expenses.

The operating‑income gain was partially offset by a $4.1 million decline in gross margin, caused by a shift toward lower‑margin product mix.

Overall, FY 2019 delivered stronger top‑line growth and a higher operating‑income margin for the MSA segment, reflecting favorable sales mix changes and disciplined cost management.

text.value: Note 5: Equity-based Compensation Plans

The Company has stock plans that provide for grants of equity-based awards to eligible participants, including stock options and restricted stock units, of the Company’s Common Stock. An option is a right to purchase Common Stock at a set price. An RSU award is an agreement to issue a set number of shares of Common Stock at the time of vesting. The Company’s options and RSU awards typically vest over a period of three years or less. The Company also has an employee stock purchase plan that allows employees to purchase its Common Stock at a discount through payroll deductions.

The Lam Research Corporation 2007 Stock Incentive Plan, as amended and restated, 2011 Stock Incentive Plan, as amended and restated, and the 2015 Stock Incentive Plan (collectively the “Stock Plans”), provide for the grant of non-qualified equity-based awards to eligible employees, consultants and advisors, and non-employee directors of the Company and its subsidiaries. The 2015 Stock Incentive Plan was approved by shareholders authorizing up to 18,000,000 shares available for issuance under the plan. Additionally, 1,232,068 shares that remained available for grants under the Company’s 2007 Stock Incentive Plan were added to the shares available for issuance under the 2015 Stock Incentive Plan. As of June 30, 2019, there were a total of 9,379,904 shares available for future issuance under the Stock Plans. New shares are issued from the Company’s balance of authorized Common Stock from the 2015 Stock Incentive Plan to satisfy stock option exercises and vesting of awards.
The Company recognized the following equity-based compensation expense and benefits in the Consolidated Statements of Operations:
The estimated fair value of the Company’s equity-based awards, less expected forfeitures, is amortized over the awards’ vesting terms on a straight-line basis.

synth_text.text:

In the “Other” category, Bell Canada held **committed commercial‑paper facilities** of **CAD 106 million**, while **non‑committed facilities** (primarily additional commercial‑paper capacity) amounted to **CAD 1,059 million**. Together, the “Other” commitments and non‑committed facilities summed to **CAD 1,165 million**.  

Overall, the total of **committed credit facilities** was **CAD 2,057 million** (CAD 1,951 million revolving/expansion plus CAD 106 million other), and when combined with the non‑committed portion, the **aggregate credit capacity** reached **CAD 3,116 million**. All commercial‑paper issuances (CAD 1,951 million) are classified as debt due within one year, and the net available committed revolving and expansion facilities could be drawn at any time, providing Bell Canada with substantial liquidity flexibility.  

These figures align with Bell Canada’s stated ability to issue up to $3 billion (U.S. or Canadian) in commercial paper, subject to a $4 billion ceiling in Canadian currency, which matches the aggregate amount available under its committed revolving and expansion credit facilities.
