synth_text.title: Openreach Financial Performance Summary 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the year to 31 March 2019, Openreach reported adjusted revenue of £5,075 million, a 4 % decline from £5,278 million in 2018. The drop was driven by regulated price reductions on FTTC and Ethernet services, non‑regulated price cuts linked to volume‑discount agreements with major communications providers, a modest reduction in the physical line base, and a re‑classification of certain costs to revenue.  

**Operating Results**  
Adjusted operating costs remained broadly flat (£2,652 m in 2019 vs £2,663 m in 2018). Higher spending on recruiting and training engineers for the “Fibre First” programme, pay inflation, and increased business rates was largely offset by efficiency savings and the cost‑to‑revenue re‑classification. Adjusted EBITDA fell 7 % to £2,423 million, and adjusted operating profit decreased to £955 million from £1,214 million the previous year.  

**Capital Investment and Cash Flow**  
Capital expenditure rose sharply to £2,081 million in 2019, up 22 % year‑on‑year, reflecting accelerated investment in FTTP and Gfast network build‑out and higher BDUK net grant funding deferrals. Normalised free cash flow fell 38 % to £685 million, a result of the EBITDA decline, higher underlying capital spending, and the timing of customer receipts.  

**Strategic Context**  
Openreach continues to expand its fibre‑to‑the‑premises network, delivering the next‑generation service suite. A volume‑discount deal with the majority of major communications providers generated a record quarter for fibre sales, while demand for Ethernet circuits remained strong for the second consecutive quarter. Competition is increasing as alternative network providers extend their fibre footprints, overlapping Openreach’s UK‑wide presence in roughly half of the country.  

**Key Take‑aways**  
- Revenue fell 4 % due to price reductions and cost re‑classifications.  
- Operating costs were stable; however, EBITDA and operating profit declined.  
- Capital spending increased by 22 % to support FTTP/Gfast roll‑out.  
- Free cash flow contracted significantly, reflecting lower EBITDA and higher capex.  
- Strong fibre sales and Ethernet demand underpin future growth, despite rising competition.  

These figures illustrate the financial impact of Openreach’s strategic shift toward a fibre‑first network and the associated cost pressures, while highlighting the continued demand for high‑speed connectivity services.

synth_text.title: Openreach FY 2024 Financial Performance Summary
synth_text.text:
**Financial Highlights (Year to 31 March)**  
- **Adjusted revenue:** £5,075 million, **‑4 %** year‑on‑year.  
- **Adjusted operating profit:** £955 million, **‑21 %** YoY.  
- **Adjusted EBITDA:** down **7 %** YoY.  
- **Depreciation & amortisation:** £67 million, **+5 %**.  
- **Capital expenditure:** £2.1 billion, **+22 %** YoY.  
- **Normalised free cash flow:** (£415) million, **‑38 %** YoY.  

**Key drivers of performance**  
The revenue decline was primarily caused by regulated price reductions on FTTC and Ethernet services, alongside non‑regulated price cuts stemming from volume‑discount agreements with major communications providers. A modest reduction in the physical line base and a re‑classification of certain costs to revenue also contributed. These headwinds were partially offset by a **25 % increase in the fibre‑rental base** and a **9 % rise in Ethernet rental**, reflecting strong demand for Openreach’s fibre‑to‑the‑premises and Ethernet offerings.

Operating costs remained broadly flat. Higher expenses for recruiting and training engineers to support the “Fibre First” programme, pay inflation, and business rates were balanced by efficiency savings and the same cost‑to‑revenue re‑classification that affected revenue.

Capital spending rose sharply as Openreach accelerated its FTTP and Gfast network build‑out, reaching **£2.1 bn**, a **22 %** increase, while also absorbing higher BDUK net‑grant‑funding deferrals.  

The **38 %** drop in normalised free cash flow reflects the lower EBITDA, the higher underlying capex (excluding BDUK grant deferrals), and the timing of customer receipts.

Overall, despite a challenging pricing environment, Openreach delivered record fibre sales, expanded its fibre‑to‑the‑premises network, and saw continued strong demand for Ethernet circuits, positioning the business for future growth as alternative network providers expand their fibre footprints.

Equity in net losses of affiliates: Pursuant to the formation of OneLNG in July 2016, we equity account for our share of net losses in OneLNG. Given the difficulties in finalizing an attractive debt financing package along with other capital and resource priorities, in April 2018, Golar and Schlumberger decided to wind down OneLNG and work on FLNG projects as required on a case-by-case basis. As a result, activity levels have been substantially reduced for the year ended December 31, 2018 and the carrying value of the investment was written down to $nil.

synth_text.title: 2018 Financial Highlights for the FLNG Segment – Hilli Vessel
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In 2018 the FLNG segment recorded its first full year of operations after the Hilli was accepted by the customer on 31 May 2018. The vessel generated **$127.6 million** in total operating revenues from liquefaction services.

**Key Income Statement Items (in thousands of $)**  

| Item | Amount | % Change vs. prior period |
|------|--------|---------------------------|
| Total operating revenues | **127,625** | 100 % |
| Vessel operating expenses | **(26,315)** | 1,315,750 % |
| Voyage expenses | **(1,242)** | 1,026 % |
| Administrative expenses | **1,911** | (110 %) |
| Project development expenses | **(14,020)** | 559 % |
| Depreciation & amortization | **(28,193)** | 100 % |
| Other operating gains* | **(12,351)** | (82 %) |
| **Operating income** | **47,415** | 442 % |
| Equity in net losses of affiliates | **6,106** | (75 %) |

\*Other operating gains comprise a realized gain of **$26.7 million** on the LTA oil‑derivative instrument, offset by an unrealized fair‑value loss of **$10.0 million** and a write‑off of **$1.3 million** related to capitalized conversion costs for the Gandria project. A further **$12.7 million** write‑off reflects the wind‑down of OneLNG.

**Interpretation of Major Drivers**

* **Revenues:** The $127.6 million reflects the Hilli’s liquefaction services after commencing operations in May 2018.  
* **Vessel operating expenses:** The massive percentage increase stems from the fact that the vessel had negligible expenses in the prior year; the $26.3 million incurred covers fuel, crew, and routine maintenance now that the Hilli is active.  
* **Project development expenses:** Up $14.0 million, driven by higher engineering consultancy fees and front‑end engineering & design costs for the Gimi GTA project.  
* **Depreciation:** Recognized from Q2 2018 onward, amounting to $28.2 million, reflecting the Hilli’s capitalized cost being allocated over its useful life.  
* **Other operating gains:** Net negative $12.4 million after accounting for the realized derivative gain, unrealized loss, and write‑offs.  
* **Equity in net losses of affiliates:** A positive $6.1 million, as the OneLNG investment was written down to nil and the associated losses were removed from the books.

**Bottom‑line**  
Despite sizable operating expenses and non‑recurring write‑offs, the Hilli’s inaugural year delivered a solid **operating income of $47.4 million**, underscoring the commercial viability of the FLNG business once the vessel is in service. The wind‑down of OneLNG eliminated prior affiliate losses, further improving the segment’s profitability.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance of the FLNG Segment – 2017 vs 2018
synth_text.text:
The FLNG segment’s results show a dramatic shift between 2017 and 2018, driven primarily by the commissioning of the liquefaction vessel **Hilli**.

**2018** – After Hilli was accepted by the customer on 31 May 2018, the vessel generated **$127.6 million** in total operating revenues from liquefaction services. Operating income rose to **$58.2 million**, reflecting the new revenue stream despite higher costs. Vessel operating expenses amounted to **$26.3 million**, and project‑development expenses increased to **$16.5 million** due to engineering and design work on the Gimi GTA project. Depreciation and amortization, which began in Q2 2018, were **$28.2 million**. Other operating gains were modest (**$2.7 million**) after a realized gain of $26.7 million on an oil‑derivative instrument was partially offset by a $10.0 million unrealized loss and write‑offs of $1.3 million (Gandria conversion costs) and $12.7 million (OneLNG trading balance). The segment recorded an equity loss from affiliates of **$2.0 million**, reflecting the wind‑down of OneLNG and the write‑down of its carrying value to zero.

**2017** – Prior to Hilli’s entry into service, the segment reported negligible operating revenues (not disclosed). Operating income was **$10.7 million**, supported mainly by other operating gains of **$15.1 million** (unrealized fair‑value gain on the oil‑derivative instrument). Expenses were low: vessel operating expenses of **$0.0 million**, voyage expenses of **$0.1 million**, administrative expenses of **$1.7 million**, and project‑development expenses of **$2.5 million**. However, the segment bore a larger equity loss from affiliates of **$8.2 million**, linked to OneLNG’s ongoing financial difficulties.

**Key take‑aways**
- Hilli’s acceptance generated a new, sizable revenue base in 2018, lifting operating income from $10.7 million to $58.2 million.
- Expenses rose proportionally, with notable increases in vessel operating costs, project‑development spend, and the start of depreciation.
- Other operating gains fell sharply after a large unrealized gain in 2017 was replaced by a modest net gain in 2018.
- The wind‑down of OneLNG eliminated the affiliate loss in 2018, improving the segment’s bottom line.

Overall, 2018 marks the transition of the FLNG segment from a pre‑revenue phase to an operational phase with significant earnings potential, albeit with higher cost structures and one‑off write‑offs.

synth_text.title: Group Operating Performance – Reported vs. Underlying Figures
synth_text.text:
The Group recorded a turnover of **€53,715 million** for the period. Reported operating profit amounted to **€8,957 million**, which translates into an **operating margin of 16.7 %** (operating profit ÷ turnover).

A component of **€543 million** is classified as a non‑underlying item within operating profit (see Note 3, p. 96). When this amount is added back, the **underlying operating profit**—the measure used for resource allocation and performance assessment—rises to **€9,500 million**. Consequently, the **underlying operating margin** improves to **17.7 %** (underlying operating profit ÷ turnover).

Underlying figures exclude the impact of non‑underlying items and therefore provide a clearer view of the Group’s core operating performance. Detailed reconciliations of operating profit to underlying operating profit are presented in Note 3, while division‑level breakdowns and margin calculations can be found in Note 2 (p. 94).

synth_text.title: Operating Profit and Underlying Performance: Current vs. Restated Figures
synth_text.text:
The Group’s latest financial results show an operating profit of **€8,708 million**, which includes **€1,239 million** of non‑underlying items (see note 3). After removing these items, the **underlying operating profit**—the measure used for resource allocation and performance assessment—is **€9,947 million**. With a turnover of **€51,980 million**, this yields an **operating margin of 16.8 %** and an **underlying operating margin of 19.1 %**.

For comparison, the restated figures (labelled “(Restated)(a)”) report a higher operating profit of **€12,639 million**, but this includes a negative adjustment of **€3,176 million** for non‑underlying items. The resulting **underlying operating profit** is **€9,463 million**, based on a turnover of **€50,982 million**. Consequently, the restated data show an **operating margin of 24.8 %** and an **underlying operating margin of 18.6 %**.

Key take‑aways:
- **Underlying operating profit** excludes non‑underlying items and provides a consistent basis for evaluating segment performance.
- The current period’s underlying operating margin (19.1 %) is slightly higher than the restated period’s (18.6 %), indicating a modest improvement in profitability after adjusting for non‑underlying effects.
- The restated operating margin appears higher (24.8 % vs. 16.8 %) because the non‑underlying items in that set are negative, inflating the headline margin.

Further details on the non‑underlying items can be found in note 3 of the consolidated financial statements, and the full reconciliation of operating profit to underlying operating profit by Division is provided in note 2.

synth_text.text:

synth_text.title: Key SaaS Renewal Rates and Adjusted EBITDA for 2016‑2017
synth_text.text:
The company’s selected financial data show that the SaaS and license revenue renewal rate—a measure of how much recurring subscription revenue is retained over a trailing twelve‑month period—was **94 % in 2016** and **93 % in 2017**. Together, they illustrate that while subscription retention remained high (above 90 %), the company improved its profitability and cash‑flow generation between 2016 and 2017.

synth_text.title: Financial Overview of Discontinued Operations (Compute & Automotive) – FY 2017 vs FY 2018
synth_text.text:
**Summary**

The company’s discontinued operations, primarily the Compute business sold in October 2017, showed a marked contraction from fiscal year 2017 to fiscal year 2018. The financial results, presented in thousands of dollars, reflect the effects of the divestiture, transition‑services reimbursements, and ancillary consulting arrangements.

**FY 2017 (Compute Business – Pre‑Divestiture)**  
- **Revenue & Gross Margin:** $660 k of revenue versus $2,252 k of cost of revenue produced a gross loss of $1,592 k.  
- **Operating Expenses:** R&D expenses of $29,167 k and SG&A of $13,840 k drove total operating expenses to $43,007 k.  
- **Discontinued‑Operations Loss:** $44,599 k, largely attributable to the Compute segment.  
- **Offsetting Items:**  
  * Other income of $7,500 k from a consulting agreement (non‑design advisory services).  
  * Gain on sale of $18,022 k from the earlier disposal of the Automotive business (sold in FY 2015).  
- **Net Result:** Loss before income taxes of $19,077 k.  
- **Cash Flow:** Operating activities used $42,776 k; investing activities generated $25,522 k.

**FY 2018 (Post‑Divestiture)**  
- **Revenue & Gross Margin:** No revenue was recorded; cost of revenue was $596 k, yielding a modest gross profit of $596 k.  
- **Operating Expenses:** R&D fell to $5,251 k and SG&A to $1,560 k (after a $3.6 M reimbursement under the Compute Transition Services Agreement, recorded as a reduction to SG&A), for total operating expenses of $6,811 k.  
- **Discontinued‑Operations Loss:** $6,215 k, reflecting the remaining wind‑down costs of the Compute business.  
- **Other Income / Gains:** None reported for 2018 (the consulting agreement generated no income after FY 2017, and the indemnification escrow of $18 M was received in FY 2017).  
- **Net Result:** Loss before income taxes of $6,215 k.  
- **Cash Flow:** Operating activities used $10,734 k; there were no investing cash flows.

**Key Contextual Factors**

1. **Compute Business Sale (Oct 27 2017):** The transaction provided an equity interest valued at approximately $36.5 M (less than 20 % of the buyer’s equity). The business was accounted for as discontinued through the divestiture date.  
2. **Transition Services Agreement (TSA):** The company performed limited general‑administrative functions for the buyer, receiving reimbursements of $3.6 M in FY 2018 (recorded as a reduction to SG&A) and $0.1 M in FY 2019.  
3. **Automotive Business Sale (FY 2015):** The $18,022 k gain in FY 2017 stems from this earlier disposal and is unrelated to the Compute segment.  
4. **Consulting Agreement:** Up to $15 M of advisory services were contracted; $7.5 M was recognized as other income in FY 2017 (and FY 2016). No consulting income was recognized in FY 2018 or FY 2019.  
5. **Indemnification Escrow:** The full $18 M escrow was received in FY 2017, contributing to the “Other income” line.

**Conclusion**

The discontinued‑operations results illustrate a transition from a loss‑heavy, high‑expense Compute business in FY 2017 to a largely wound‑down operation in FY 2018, with significantly lower expenses and a smaller net loss. The financial impact of the Compute divestiture, TSA reimbursements, and the cessation of consulting income are clearly reflected in the year‑over‑year changes.

text.value: Note 5. Fair Value of Financial Instruments

The Company measures and reports certain cash equivalents, including money market funds and certificates of deposit, in addition to its long-term investments at fair value in accordance with the provisions of the authoritative accounting guidance that addresses fair value measurements. This guidance establishes a hierarchy for inputs used in measuring fair value that maximizes the use of observable inputs and minimizes the use of unobservable inputs by requiring that the most observable inputs be used when available
The hierarchy is broken down into three levels based on the reliability of the inputs as follows:
Level 1: Observable inputs that reflect unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities

Level 2: Other inputs, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities, quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in inactive markets, or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by observable market data for substantially the full term of the asset or liability

Level 3: Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are based on management’s assumptions, including fair value measurements determined by using pricing models, discounted cash flow methodologies or similar techniques

The Company’s other financial instruments, including accounts receivable, accounts payable, and other current liabilities, are carried at cost, which approximates fair-value due to the relatively short maturity of those instruments.

synth_text.title: Summary of Selected Financial Data for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s selected financial data for the years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019 are presented below (figures in thousands unless noted otherwise).

| Year | Total Revenues | Net Income | Basic EPS | Diluted EPS |
|------|----------------|------------|-----------|------------|
| 2019 | $1,258,294 | $67,062 | $116,175 | $118,571 |

**Key observations**

* **Revenue growth:** Total revenues rose by approximately 24.6 % from $1.01 billion in 2018 to $1.26 billion in 2019. The increase reflects, in part, the acquisition of Speedpay, which was incorporated into the consolidated statements for 2019 (see footnote 1).

* **Net income:** Net income declined slightly in 2019, falling $1,859 million (about 2.7 %) to $67,062 from $68,921 in 2018. * **Earnings per share:** Both basic and diluted earnings per share increased marginally in 2019. Basic EPS rose from $116,057 to $116,175, while diluted EPS grew from $117,632 to $118,571, reflecting the slight net‑income dip offset by a stable share count.

**Contextual notes**

1. The 2019 figures include the impact of the Speedpay acquisition (Note 3, Item 15 of the Form 10‑K) and the application of ASC 842 (lease accounting) (Note 14).  
2. The 2018 results incorporate the adoption of ASC 606 (revenue from contracts with customers), which produced a cumulative adjustment of $244 million to retained earnings (Note 2).  

Overall, the company demonstrated solid top‑line growth in 2019, while profitability measured by net income and earnings per share remained relatively stable, reflecting the financial effects of strategic acquisitions and new accounting standards.

text.value: D) SHARE-BASED PAYMENT PLANS

The Corporation offers an Employee Stock Purchase Plan for the benefit of its employees and those of its subsidiaries and a Stock Option Plan to its executive officers and designated employees. No more than 10% of the outstanding subordinate voting shares are available for issuance under these plans. Furthermore, the Corporation offers an Incentive Share Unit Plan ("ISU Plan") and a Performance Share Unit Plan ("PSU Plan") for executive officers and designated employees, and a Deferred Share Unit Plan ("DSU Plan") for members of the Board of Directors ("Board").

Stock purchase plan The Corporation offers, for the benefit of its employees and those of its subsidiaries, an Employee Stock Purchase Plan, which is accessible to all employees up to a maximum of 7% of their base annual salary and the Corporation contributes 25% of the employee contributions. The subscriptions are made monthly and employee subordinate voting shares are purchased on the stock market.

Stock option plan A total of 3,432,500 subordinate voting shares are reserved for the purpose of the Stock Option Plan. The minimum exercise price at which options are granted is equal to the market value of such shares at the time the option is granted. Options vest equally over a period of five years beginning one year after the day such options are granted and are exercisable over ten years.
Under the Stock Option Plan, the following options were granted by the Corporation and are outstanding at August 31:

synth_text.title: Year‑End Summary of Cogeco’s Share‑Based Payment Plans and Stock Option Activity (FY 2019)
synth_text.text:
During the fiscal year ended August 31 2019, Cogeco’s share‑based payment programmes saw notable activity across its Stock Option Plan and related unit plans. At the beginning of the year, 652,385 options were outstanding, representing an average value of $56.61 per share. Throughout the year the corporation granted an additional 281,350 options (valued at $85.08 per share on average) while 60,337 options were exercised and 54,005 were cancelled. These transactions increased the total outstanding options to 819,393 by year‑end, with the average value per outstanding option rising to $65.27. Of the year‑end balance, 277,108 options remain exercisable, carrying an average exercisable price of $49.76 per share.

The weighted‑average exercise price for options actually exercised during 2019 was $92.43, reflecting market‑based pricing consistent with the plan’s requirement that the minimum exercise price equal the market value at grant. The Stock Option Plan, which reserves 3,432,500 subordinate voting shares (no more than 10 % of total outstanding shares), granted 97,725 options to executive officers in 2019, up from 126,425 in the prior year.

These figures sit alongside Cogeco’s broader share‑based compensation framework, which includes an Employee Stock Purchase Plan (allowing employees to purchase up to 7 % of their base salary with a 25 % corporate contribution), an Incentive Share Unit Plan, a Performance Share Unit Plan, and a Deferred Share Unit Plan for board members. Collectively, the data illustrate a growing pool of outstanding options and a healthy level of exercisable rights, underscoring the company’s continued use of equity‑based incentives to align employee and executive interests with shareholder value.

synth_text.title: Revenue Distribution by Region for SAP Group – Comparison of Two Reporting Periods
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The SAP Group’s revenue, measured by the location of its customers, is presented for two consecutive reporting periods. In the first period the group generated **€27.6 billion**, which fell to **€24.7 billion** in the second period – a decline of **€2.85 billion (≈10 %)**.

**Regional Performance**  

| Region | Period 1 | Period 2 | Change (€ bn) | % Change |
|--------|----------|----------|---------------|----------|
| **EMEA** (Europe, Middle East, Africa) | €12.1 bn | €11.1 bn | –€1.0 bn | –8.3 % |
| **Americas** (North & Latin America) | €11.2 bn | €9.7 bn | –€1.5 bn | –13.2 % |
| **APJ** (Asia‑Pacific Japan) | €4.3 bn | €3.9 bn | –€0.4 bn | –8.5 % |
| **SAP Group Total** | €27.6 bn | €24.7 bn | –€2.85 bn | –10.3 % |

**Key Sub‑regional Insights**  

- **Germany** contributed €3.95 bn in Period 1 and €3.66 bn in Period 2 (down €0.29 bn, –7 %).  
- **Rest of EMEA** fell from €8.16 bn to €7.45 bn (down €0.71 bn, –8.7 %).  
- **United States** saw the largest absolute drop, from €9.09 bn to €7.88 bn (down €1.21 bn, –13.3 %).  
- **Rest of Americas** decreased from €2.11 bn to €1.83 bn (down €0.28 bn, –13.2 %).  
- **Japan** slipped from €1.18 bn to €0.96 bn (down €0.22 bn, –18.6 %).  
- **Rest of APJ** declined modestly from €3.07 bn to €2.93 bn (down €0.14 bn, –4.7 %).

**Interpretation**  
The revenue contraction is evident across all three major geographic clusters, with the **Americas** experiencing the steepest percentage decline, driven primarily by a reduction in U.S. sales. The **EMEA** region also showed a notable decrease, while the **APJ** market remained relatively more stable. These trends reflect shifting customer demand across the SAP Group’s global footprint.

**Conclusion**  
Across the two periods, the SAP Group’s revenue distribution highlights a broad-based slowdown, with the most pronounced weakness in the United States and the broader Americas region. Monitoring these geographic dynamics will be essential for future growth strategies.

text.value: Debt

Our funding requirements are continually monitored and we execute our strategies to manage the overall asset and liability profile. Additionally, we maintain sufficient flexibility to access global funding sources as needed.

Total debt of $62,899 million increased $17,087 million from December 31, 2018, driven by issuances of $32,415 million; partially offset by debt maturities of $12,673 million and a decrease in commercial paper of $2,691 million.
Non-Global Financing debt of $38,173 million increased $23,587 million from prior year-end levels primarily driven by issuances to fund the Red Hat acquisition.
Global Financing debt of $24,727 million decreased $6,500 million from December 31, 2018, primarily due to the wind down of OEM IT commercial financing operations.

Global Financing provides financing predominantly for IBM’s external client assets, as well as for assets under contract by other IBM units. These assets, primarily for GTS, generate long-term, stable revenue streams similar to the Global Financing asset portfolio. Based on their attributes, these GTS assets are leveraged with the balance of the Global Financing asset base.

The debt used to fund Global Financing assets is composed of intercompany loans and external debt. Total debt changes generally correspond with the level of client and commercial financing receivables, the level of cash and cash equivalents, the change in intercompany and external payables and the change in intercompany investment from IBM. The terms of the intercompany loans are set by the company to substantially match the term, currency and interest rate variability underlying the financing receivable and are based on arm’s-length pricing. The Global Financing debt-to-equity ratio remained at 9 to 1 at December 31, 2019.

As previously stated, we measure Global Financing as a stand-alone entity, and accordingly, interest expense relating to debt supporting Global Financing’s external client and internal business is included in the “Global Financing Results of Operations” and in note D, “Segments.” In the Consolidated Income Statement, the external debt-related interest expense supporting Global Financing’s internal financing to IBM is reclassified from cost of financing to interest expense.

synth_text.title: IBM Debt Profile and Year‑Over‑Year Changes (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
At the close of fiscal 2019, IBM’s total company debt rose to **$62.9 billion**, an increase of **$17.1 billion** from the $45.8 billion reported at the end of 2018. The growth was driven primarily by new debt issuances of $32.4 billion, partially offset by maturities of $12.7 billion and a $2.7 billion reduction in commercial paper.

**Segment‑level shifts**

* **Global Financing debt** fell to **$24.7 billion**, down $6.5 billion from the prior year. The decline reflects the wind‑down of IBM’s OEM IT commercial financing operations. Global Financing continues to fund external client assets and internal contracts, with its debt‑to‑equity ratio remaining steady at **9 to 1**.

* **Non‑Global Financing debt** surged to **$38.2 billion**, up $23.6 billion year‑over‑year. The bulk of this increase was used to finance the **Red Hat acquisition**, expanding IBM’s non‑Financing debt base.

**Debt supporting clients**

* Debt allocated to **external clients** amounted to **$21.5 billion** in 2019, compared with $27.5 billion in 2018, indicating a reallocation of financing resources.
* Debt for **internal clients** was **$3.2 billion** in 2019, slightly lower than $3.7 billion in 2018.

**Strategic funding outlook**

IBM continuously monitors its funding needs, balancing its asset‑liability profile while preserving flexibility to tap global capital markets as required. The debt supporting Global Financing consists of a mix of intercompany loans—structured to match the term, currency, and interest characteristics of the underlying receivables—and external borrowings. Interest expense related to Global Financing’s external client and internal business is reported within the segment’s results, with internal financing interest re‑classified in the consolidated statement.

Overall, IBM’s debt composition in 2019 reflects strategic investments (notably Red Hat), a deliberate reduction in financing‑related operations, and a disciplined approach to maintaining a robust, flexible capital structure.

synth_text.title: 2018 Q4 Canadian Broadband Service Customer Net Changes and Operational Impact
synth_text.text:
In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2018, the Canadian broadband services segment reported a total of **35,818 primary service units**. After excluding adjustments linked to the migration to a new customer‑management system (footnote (1)), the segment experienced net declines across all service categories:

- **Internet services:** ‑2,965 customers  
- **Video services:** ‑15,953 customers  
- **Telephony services:** ‑16,900 customers  

The migration, which replaced 22 legacy systems, entered a stabilization phase during Q3 FY 2018. Ongoing issues in the contact centre led to congestion and reduced service activations throughout most of Q4 FY 2018. Normal operations in the contact centre and marketing functions were not restored until the end of Q1 2019.

Comparative data for the same quarter in fiscal 2019 show a reversal of this trend, with net additions of **2,540 Internet customers** and **2,778 Telephony customers**, and a smaller net loss of **8,164 Video customers**. The improvement is attributed to renewed interest in high‑speed Internet bundles, increased demand from resellers, promotional bundling for telephony, and a shift in video consumption patterns.

Overall, the 2018 Q4 figures reflect the temporary impact of the system migration on customer acquisition, while the 2019 data indicate a recovery as operational stability returned.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Service Portfolio Overview and Quarterly Performance Drivers
synth_text.text:
As of August 31 2019, the company’s primary service units totaled **1,810,366**, serving **788,243 Internet**, **649,583 Video**, and **372,540 Telephony** customers.  

During fiscal 2019, the net changes in each service category were:

- **Internet**: **+2,540** customers  
- **Video**: **‑8,164** customers (net loss)  
- **Telephony**: **+2,778** customers  

These variations reflect the fourth‑quarter dynamics after the company completed a major migration to a new customer‑management system in Q3 FY 2018. The migration, which replaced 22 legacy systems, caused contact‑center congestion and reduced activations in Q4 FY 2018, but operations returned to normal by the end of Q1 2019.

**Internet** growth was driven by sustained interest in high‑speed broadband, attractive bundle offers, and increased demand from Internet resellers, partially offset by competitive industry pricing.  

**Video** experienced a net loss due to highly competitive offers and a shift in consumer video‑consumption habits, though interest in advanced digital video services and bundled packages with fast Internet provided some mitigation.  

**Telephony** added customers thanks to expanded bundle promotions in the second half of FY 2019 and growth in the business sector, while the rise of wireless‑only plans and unlimited wireless offers led some landline customers to switch away, tempering the gains.  

Overall, the service portfolio shows a solid base of Internet and Telephony customers, with Video facing the most pressure from market competition and changing viewing preferences.

The $113.8 million change was primarily driven by $99.6 million increase in net income (loss), from $45.3 million net loss for 2017 to $54.3 million net income for 2018 and $27.0 million increase in deferred revenue, partially offset by $7.0 million increase in other assets, $4.2 million increase in prepaid expenses and other current assets, and $3.7 million decrease in accounts payable. The increases in deferred revenue and other non-current assets primarily reflected the effect of the adoption of ASC 606 on January 1, 2018. Cash provided by operating activities was also affected by an increase in non-cash charges of $2.6 million primarily related to higher stock-based compensation expense incurred for 2018 compared to 2017.

Cash provided by (used in) investing activities - Net cash provided by investing activities during 2018 was $8.2 million, a decrease of $2.8 million compared to $11.1 million cash provided by investing activities during 2017. Net cash provided by investing activities during 2018 consisted of maturities of short-term investments of $26.0 million partially offset by purchases of short-term investments of $17.7 million and purchases of property, plant and equipment of $0.1 million. Net cash provided by investing activities during 2017 consisted of maturities of short-term investments of $35.0 million partially offset by purchases of short-term investments of $23.8 million and purchases of property, plant, and equipment of $0.1 million.

Cash provided by (used in) financing activities - Net cash provided by financing activities during 2018 was $8.2 million an increase of $7.7 million compared to $0.5 million net cash provided by financing activities during 2017. Net cash provided by financing activities during 2018 consisted primarily of $8.2 million in proceeds from stock option exercises and stock purchases under our employee stock purchase plan. Net cash provided by financing activities during 2017 consisted primarily of $0.8 million proceeds from stock option exercises and stock purchases under our employee stock purchase plan partially offset by repurchases of treasury stock of $0.3 million.

We believe that our cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments will be sufficient to meet our working capital needs for at least the next twelve months. Of our total cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments of $89.5 million as of December 31, 2019, 5% was held by our foreign subsidiaries and subject to repatriation tax effects. Our intent is to permanently reinvest all of our earnings from foreign operations, and current plans do not anticipate that we will need funds generated from foreign operations to fund our domestic operations. We will continue to invest in, protect, and defend our extensive IP portfolio, which is expected to result in the continued use of cash. At December 31, 2019 there was $30.6 million remaining under our previously-approved share repurchase program. We anticipate that capital expenditures for property and equipment for the year ending December 31, 2020 will be less than $1.0 million. Cash from operations could also be affected by various risks and uncertainties, including, but not limited to the risks detailed in Part I, Item 1A, Risk Factors of this Annual Report on Form 10-K.

synth_text.text:
**Cash‑flow performance in 2017**

| Category | Cash flow (in $ thousands) |
|----------|----------------------------|
| Net cash used in operating activities | **$(43,829)** |
| Net cash provided by investing activities | **$11,068** |
| Net cash provided by financing activities | **$518** |

In 2017 the company generated a **net cash outflow of $43.8 million from operating activities**. The primary drivers were a **$45.3 million net loss**, a **$27.0 million decrease in deferred revenue**, and modest increases in other assets and receivables. These operating cash demands were partially offset by:

* **Investing activities**, which supplied **$11.1 million** mainly from the maturity of short‑term investments.
* **Financing activities**, which contributed a modest **$0.5 million**, largely from stock‑option exercises and employee stock‑purchase plan proceeds.

**Broader perspective (2017‑2019)**  

* **2018** marked a turnaround: operating cash shifted to a **$69.9 million inflow**, driven by a $99.6 million swing from a net loss to net income and a $27.0 million increase in deferred revenue.  
* **2019** saw operating cash turn negative again (**$34.1 million used**) due to a $74.4 million drop in net income and changes in working‑capital items, though investing cash remained positive.

**Liquidity position**  

Cash, cash equivalents and short‑term investments were primarily held in money‑market funds and U.S. Treasury bills, classified as available‑for‑sale. As of December 31 2019, total cash‑related assets were **$89.5 million**, down from $124.9 million in 2018, reflecting the cumulative effect of the cash‑flow trends described above. The company believes this liquidity is sufficient to meet working‑capital needs for at least the next twelve months.

**Key take‑aways**

* 2017’s operating cash outflow underscores the impact of a sizable net loss and reduced deferred revenue.  
* Investing cash flows consistently provided a modest cushion, while financing cash flows were relatively small.  
* The subsequent years illustrate how operational profitability and cash‑flow management can dramatically alter the cash‑generation profile, reinforcing the importance of monitoring both earnings and working‑capital dynamics.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**

The cash‑flow statement for the two most recent fiscal years shows a marked shift in the company’s sources and uses of cash. In 2018 the company generated cash across all three activities, whereas in 2019 it experienced a cash outflow from operations and financing, offset by a modest inflow from investing.

**Operating Activities**

| Year | Net cash (used in) / provided by operating activities |
|------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| 2019 | **$(34,099) k** (cash used) |
| 2018 | **$69,924 k** (cash provided) |

The 2019 operating cash outflow of $34.1 million contrasts sharply with the $69.9 million inflow in 2018. The decline is primarily attributable to:

* A $74.4 million reduction in net income.
* A $25.6 million decrease in deferred revenue linked to the adoption of ASC 606.
* Increases in other assets ($4.2 million), accounts and other receivables ($2.1 million), and a $0.9 million drop in accrued compensation.
* Lower non‑cash charges, including a $3.2 million decrease in stock‑based compensation and a $0.5 million reduction in other non‑cash items, partially offset by a $0.9 million impairment charge and higher depreciation/amortization ($1.3 million).

**Investing Activities**

| Year | Net cash provided by investing activities |
|------|--------------------------------------------|
| 2019 | **$10,920 k** |
| 2018 | **$8,237 k** |

Investing cash remained positive in both years, driven mainly by maturities of short‑term investments. In 2019, $20.0 million of maturities were offset by $8.9 million of new short‑term investments and $0.2 million of PP&E purchases. In 2018, maturities of $26.0 million were offset by $17.7 million of purchases and $0.1 million of PP&E.

**Financing Activities**

| Year | Net cash (used in) / provided by financing activities |
|------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| 2019 | **$(1,331) k** (cash used) |
| 2018 | **$8,205 k** (cash provided) |

Financing cash swung from a $8.2 million inflow in 2018—largely from stock‑option exercises and employee‑stock‑purchase‑plan (ESPP) proceeds—to a $1.3 million outflow in 2019, driven by $2.7 million of treasury‑stock repurchases that exceeded the $1.4 million of ESPP proceeds.

**Liquidity Position**

Cash, cash equivalents, and short‑term investments fell from $124.9 million at 31 Dec 2018 to $89.5 million at 31 Dec 2019, a decline of $35.4 million. The portfolio consists mainly of money‑market funds and U.S. Treasury bills, classified as available‑for‑sale and reported at market value. Despite the reduction, management believes the remaining resources are sufficient to meet working‑capital needs for at least the next twelve months. Approximately 5 % of the cash is held by foreign subsidiaries and subject to repatriation tax, but the company intends to reinvest foreign earnings permanently.

**Outlook**

The company expects capital expenditures for 2020 to be under $1.0 million and retains $30.6 million under an approved share‑repurchase program. Ongoing investment in its intellectual‑property portfolio will continue to generate cash outflows, but the firm remains confident in its ability to fund operations and strategic initiatives from existing liquidity.

synth_text.text:
The organization’s cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities portfolio experienced a substantial contraction from fiscal year 2018 to fiscal year 2019. Total investments fell from **$52.4 billion** in 2018 to **$27.9 billion** in 2019, a decline of roughly **47 %**.

* Within marketable securities, the share maturing within one year rose to **33 %** in 2019 (up from 26 % in 2018), while the remainder (≈ 67 %) now matures in one to four years.

text.value: Major components of the Company’s deferred tax assets (liabilities) are as follows (in thousands):

At December 31, 2019, the Company had federal, state, and foreign net operating losses of approximately $256.8 million, $275.5 million, and $89.7 million, respectively. The federal net operating loss carryforward will begin expiring in 2022, the state net operating loss carryforward will begin expiring in 2020, and the foreign net operating loss has an unlimited carryforward period. The Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, imposes substantial restrictions on the utilization of net operating losses in the event of an “ownership change” of a corporation. Accordingly, a company’s ability to use net operating losses may be limited as prescribed under Internal Revenue Code Section 382 (“IRC Section 382”). Events which may cause limitations in the amount of the net operating losses that the Company may use in any one year include, but are not limited to, a cumulative ownership change of more than 50% over a three-year period. Due to the effects of historical equity issuances, the Company has determined that the future utilization of a portion of its net operating losses is limited annually pursuant to IRC Section 382. The Company has determined that none of its net operating losses will expire because of the annual limitation.

The Company has recorded a full valuation allowance against its otherwise recognizable US, UK, New Zealand, Hong Kong, and Brazil deferred income tax assets as of December 31, 2019. Management has determined, after evaluating all positive and negative historical and prospective evidence, that it is more likely than not that these assets will not be realized. The net (decrease) increase to the valuation allowance of $(0.1) million, $(1.5) million, and $6.8 million for the years ended December 31, 2019, 2018, and 2017, respectively, was primarily due to additional net operating losses generated by the Company.

Deferred income taxes have not been provided on the undistributed earnings of the Company’s foreign subsidiaries because the Company’s practice and intent is to permanently reinvest these earnings. The cumulative amount of such undistributed earnings was $5.3 million and $3.1 million at December 31, 2019 and December 31, 2018, respectively. Any future distribution of these non-US earnings may subject the Company to state income taxes, as adjusted for tax credits, and foreign withholding taxes that the Company estimates would be $0.1 million and $0.1 million at December 31, 2019 and 2018, respectively.

\*The Company holds federal, state, and foreign NOLs of approximately $256.8 million, $275.5 million, and $89.7 million, respectively, as of 12/31/2019. Federal NOLs begin to expire in 2022, state NOLs in 2020, while foreign NOLs have an unlimited carryforward period. IRC Section 382 limits the annual usable portion of these NOLs due to historic equity issuances, but management has concluded that none of the NOLs will expire because of the Section 382 limitation.

**Valuation Allowance**  
A full valuation allowance of $(117,058) thousand was recorded against U.S., UK, New Zealand, Hong Kong, and Brazil DTAs in 2019 (the same amount in 2018). Management determined, based on historical and prospective evidence, that it is more likely than not that these assets will not be realized. The net change to the allowance was negligible in 2019 (‑$0.1 million) compared with a $1.5 million increase in 2018 and a $6.8 million increase in 2017, primarily reflecting additional NOLs generated in each year.

**Deferred Tax Liabilities**  

| Component | 2018 | 2019 |
|-----------|------|------|
| Prepaid expenses & deferred commissions | $(10,831) | $(14,502) |
| Operating right‑of‑use assets | — | $(16,960) |
| **Total DTLs** | $(11,807) | $(32,257) |

**Net Deferred Tax Position**  
After applying the valuation allowance, net DTAs were $12.8 million in 2018 and $33.3 million in 2019. Offsetting DTLs left a net deferred tax asset of $1,042 thousand in 2018 and $1,045 thousand in 2019.

**Foreign Undistributed Earnings**  
Deferred taxes on undistributed earnings of foreign subsidiaries are not recorded because the Company intends to permanently reinvest these earnings. Undistributed earnings amounted to $5.3 million at 12/31/2019 and $3.1 million at 12/31/2018. Future distributions could trigger state income taxes and foreign withholding taxes estimated at $0.1 million for each year.

**Conclusion**  
The Company’s deferred tax balances are dominated by sizable NOL carryforwards, offset by a full valuation allowance that reflects uncertainty about their realizability. While total DTAs grew in 2019, the net deferred tax asset remained essentially unchanged due to a proportional increase in DTLs, primarily from prepaid expenses, deferred commissions, and the newly recognized operating right‑of‑use assets under the new lease accounting standard. The ongoing limitation under IRC Section 382 and the intent to retain foreign earnings further shape the Company’s deferred tax outlook.

Management uses Adjusted EBITDA as one of many measures to assess the performance of the business. Additionally, Adjusted EBITDA is the performance metric used by the Company's chief operating decision maker to evaluate performance of our reportable segments. Adjusted EBITDA is also a metric used to determine performance in the Company's Annual Incentive Plan. We do not believe there are estimates underlying the calculation of Adjusted EBITDA, other than those inherent in our U.S. GAAP results of operations, which would render the use and presentation of Adjusted EBITDA misleading. While the nature and amount of individual Special Items vary from period to period, we believe our calculation of Adjusted EBITDA is applied consistently to all periods and, in conjunction with other U.S. GAAP and non- U.S. GAAP measures, provides a useful and consistent comparison of our Company's performance to other periods. In our evaluation of Adjusted EBITDA, management assumes that gain/losses related to Special Items may not be reflective of our core operating results.

synth_text.title: Adjusted EBITDA and Core Operating Performance: 2018‑2019 Financial Summary
synth_text.text:
**Financial Overview (2018‑2019)**  
The company’s reconciliation from U.S. GAAP Net Earnings to non‑U.S. GAAP Adjusted EBITDA shows a solid improvement in core operating performance over the two‑year period.

| Item | 2018 (in $ M) | 2019 (in $ M) |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| Net earnings from continuing operations | 150.3 | **293.7** |
| Interest expense, net | 177.9 | 184.1 |
| Income tax provision | **307.5** | **76.6** |
| Depreciation & amortization (net of adjustments) | 159.0* | 184.5* |
| Pre‑tax impact of Special Items | 94.8 | **225.9** |
| **Adjusted EBITDA (Non‑U.S. GAAP)** | **889.5** | **964.8** |

\* Adjustments of $(0.8) M (2019) and $(2.4) M (2018) are reflected in the footnote.

**Key Drivers**

1. **Higher Net Earnings** – Earnings more than doubled, driven by stronger operating results and a sharp decline in the income tax provision (down $230.9 M).  
2. **Stable Financing Costs** – Interest expense remained flat, indicating unchanged debt service levels.  
3. **Increased Special Items** – The pre‑tax impact of Special Items rose by $131.1 M, primarily due to:  
   - A $59.0 M charge for the Novipax settlement (absent in 2018).  
   - Higher restructuring‑related costs and professional‑service fees (Other Special Items $29.1 M vs. $7.5 M).  
   - No gain from class‑action litigation in 2019, whereas 2018 recorded a $(14.9) M gain.  

Despite the larger Special Items, **Adjusted EBITDA grew 8.5 %** (from $889.5 M to $964.8 M). This metric excludes the impact of Special Items, providing a consistent view of the company’s core operating profitability.

**Context on Adjusted EBITDA**

Adjusted EBITDA is defined as earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, **adjusted to remove the effect of Special Items**. Management uses this measure to:

- Evaluate the performance of reportable segments.  
- Determine Adjusted EBITDA Margin (Adjusted EBITDA ÷ Net Trade Sales) as an indicator of sales profitability and operational efficiency.  
- Benchmark performance in the Annual Incentive Plan.

The calculation is applied consistently across periods, and the company believes it offers a reliable, non‑misleading comparison of core results, independent of one‑time or infrequent events.

**Conclusion**

The 2019 financial results reflect stronger underlying operations, as evidenced by higher Adjusted EBITDA and net earnings, even though Special Items were more pronounced. The consistent use of Adjusted EBITDA allows stakeholders to assess the company’s core profitability and operational efficiency across years.

text.value: Markets and Pricing

The three largest customer markets in the fresh and frozen chicken industry are food service customers that purchase fresh, bulk-packed products produced from a relatively big bird, retail grocery store customers that purchase fresh, tray- packed products produced from a medium-sized bird, and quick-serve food service customers that purchase products produced from relatively small birds.

The following table sets forth, for each of the Company’s poultry processing plants, the general customer market to which the plant is devoted, the weekly capacity of each plant at full capacity expressed in number of head processed, and the industry's average size of birds processed in the relevant market.

Our big bird plants process a relatively large bird. The chicken products produced at these plants is generally sold as fresh, bulk-packed chicken cut into a variety of products, including boneless breast meat, chicken tenders, whole and cut wings and boneless thigh meat, and is sold primarily to restaurants, food service customers and further processors at negotiated spreads from quoted commodity market prices for those products. We have long-term contracts with many of our customers for these products produced at our big bird plants, but prices for products sold pursuant to those contracts fluctuate based on quoted commodity market prices. The contracts do not require the customers to purchase, or the Company to sell, any specific quantity of product. The dark meat from these birds that is not deboned is sold primarily as frozen leg quarters in the export market or as fresh whole legs to further processors. While we have long-standing relationships with many of our export partners, virtually all of our export sales are at negotiated or spot commodity prices, which prices exhibit fluctuations typical of commodity markets. We have few long-term contracts for this product.

As of October 31, 2019, the Company had the capacity to process 7.1 million head per week in its big bird plants, and its results are materially affected by fluctuations in the commodity market prices for boneless breast meat, chicken tenders, wings, leg quarters and boneless thigh meat as quoted by Urner Barry.

Urner Barry is an independent company specializing in the timely, accurate and independent reporting on market news and market price quotations to its customers in various food and protein industries, including poultry. The Urner Barry spot market prices for boneless breast meat, chicken tenders, leg quarters, whole wings and boneless thighs for the past five calendar years are set forth below and are published with Urner Barry's permission. Realized prices will not necessarily equal quoted market prices since most contracts offer negotiated discounts to quoted market prices, which discounts are negotiated on a customer by customer basis and are influenced by many factors. Selection of a particular market price benchmark is largely customer driven:

Our chill-pack plants process medium sized birds and cut and package the product in various sized individual trays to customers’ specifications. The trays are weighed and pre-priced primarily for customers to resell through retail grocery outlets. While the Company sells some of its chill-pack product under store brand names, most of its chill-pack production is sold under the Company’s Sanderson Farms® brand name. The Company has long-term contracts with most of its chill-pack customers. These agreements typically provide for the pricing of product based on agreed upon, flat prices or on negotiated formulas that use an agreed upon, regularly quoted market price as the base, as well as various other guidelines for the relationship between the parties. All of our contracts with retail grocery store customers also provide for the sale of negotiated quantities of product at periodically negotiated prices, rather than the flat and formula-driven prices discussed above. None of our contracts with retail grocery store customers require the customers to purchase, or the Company to sell, any specific quantity of product. As of October 31, 2019, the Company had the capacity to process 6.5 million head per week at its chill-pack plants, and its results are materially affected by fluctuations in Urner Barry prices and other market benchmarks.

As with products produced at our big bird plants, selection of the desired methodology for pricing chill-pack products is largely customer driven. Prior to the discontinuation in November 2016 of the Georgia Dock index, which had been published by the Georgia Department of Agriculture, many of our chill-pack customers used that index as the base for pricing formulas. As new and renewing contracts have been negotiated, many of our chill-pack customers chose to negotiate flat prices for the life of the contracts, while some of our customers have chosen to use an index published by Express Markets, Inc. ("EMI").

Almost all of our products sold by our prepared chicken plant are sold under long-term contracts at fixed prices related to the spot commodity price of chicken at the time the contract is negotiated, plus a premium for additional processing.

Upon adoption of IFRS 16 on January 1, 2019, we recognized right-of-use assets of $2,257 million within property, plant and equipment, and lease liabilities of $2,304 million within debt, with an increase to our deficit of $19 million. These amounts were recognized in addition to assets under finance leases of $1,947 million and the corresponding finance lease liabilities of $2,097 million at December 31, 2018 under IAS 17. The table below shows the impacts of adopting IFRS 16 on our January 1, 2019 consolidated statement of financial position.

BCE’s operating lease commitments at December 31, 2018 were $1,612 million. The difference between operating lease commitments at December 31, 2018 and lease liabilities of $2,304 million upon adoption of IFRS 16 at January 1, 2019, is due mainly to an increase of $1,122 million related to renewal options reasonably certain to be exercised, an increase of $112 million mainly related to non-monetary transactions and a decrease of ($542) million as a result of discounting applied to future lease payments, which was determined using a weighted average incremental borrowing rate of 3.49% at January 1, 2019.

synth_text.title: Impact of IFRS 16 Adoption on BCE’s Consolidated Statement of Financial Position (January 1 2019)
synth_text.text:
The adoption of IFRS 16 on 1 January 2019 introduced significant changes to BCE’s balance sheet. A new right‑of‑use asset of **$2,257 million** was added to Property, Plant and Equipment, while corresponding lease liabilities of **$4,401 million** were recorded within debt—$293 million as current debt (due within one year) and $2,011 million as long‑term debt, in addition to the existing finance‑lease liability of $2,097 million.

These lease‑related entries increased the company’s deficit by **$19 million**, moving it from a pre‑adoption deficit of **$(4,937) million** to **$(4,956) million** after the transition. The larger lease liability relative to the prior operating‑lease commitments of $1,612 million is explained by:

* $1,122 million for renewal options that are reasonably certain to be exercised,  
* $112 million arising from non‑monetary transactions, and  
* a discounting reduction of $542 million, calculated using a weighted‑average incremental borrowing rate of 3.49 % at the transition date.

Other balance‑sheet items—prepaid expenses, other current and non‑current assets, trade payables, deferred tax liabilities, other non‑current liabilities, and non‑controlling interest—show only marginal adjustments as a result of the IFRS 16 conversion.

Overall, the IFRS 16 adoption substantially increased both assets and liabilities on BCE’s consolidated statement of financial position, reflecting the new accounting treatment of operating leases as assets and corresponding lease obligations.

**Equity**

**Impact of IFRS 16 Adoption**  
On January 1 2019 BCE adopted IFRS 16, which required the recognition of right‑of‑use (ROU) assets of **$2,257 million** within property, plant and equipment and corresponding lease liabilities of **$2,304 million** within debt. These entries increased the deficit by **$19 million**.  

Prior to adoption, operating lease commitments at December 31 2018 were **$1,612 million**. The higher lease‑liability figure of $2,304 million reflects:
- **$1,122 million** for renewal options that are reasonably certain to be exercised,  
- **$112 million** arising from non‑monetary transactions, and  
- A discounting adjustment of **$(542) million**, calculated using a weighted‑average incremental borrowing rate of **3.49 %** at the adoption date.  

Thus, the IFRS 16 transition added significant lease‑related assets and liabilities, reshaping BCE’s balance sheet while modestly widening the reported deficit.

synth_text.title: GreenSky, Inc. – Selected Consolidated Balance Sheet Summary (2016 vs 2017)
synth_text.text:
The selected consolidated balance‑sheet data for GreenSky, Inc. show a marked expansion of the company’s financial position between 2016 and 2017.

- **Cash and cash equivalents** increased from **$185,243 k** in 2016 to **$224,614 k** in 2017, reflecting stronger liquidity.  
- **Restricted cash** rose sharply, from **$42,871 k** to **$129,224 k**, indicating a larger portion of cash set aside for specific obligations.  
- **Loan receivables held for sale, net** more than doubled, climbing from **$41,268 k** to **$73,606 k**, suggesting growth in the loan‑sale pipeline.  
- **Total assets** grew from **$302,205 k** to **$462,889 k**, driven primarily by the increases in cash, restricted cash, and loan receivables.

On the liability side:

- **Finance‑charge reversal liability** increased from **$68,064 k** to **$94,148 k**.  
- A **term loan** of **$338,263 k** appears on the 2017 balance sheet (none was reported in 2016), adding a significant long‑term financing component.  
- **Total liabilities** rose from **$89,995 k** to **$488,928 k**, largely due to the new term loan and higher reversal liability.

Equity positions:

- **Total temporary equity** expanded from **$335,720 k** in 2016 to **$430,348 k** in 2017, reflecting the company’s financing activities.  
- **Total permanent equity (deficit)** widened from a deficit of **$(123,510 k)** to **$(456,387 k)**, indicating that cumulative losses continued to outweigh permanent capital.  

Overall, the sum of liabilities, temporary equity, and permanent equity matches total assets for each year (**$302,205 k** in 2016 and **$462,889 k** in 2017), confirming the balance‑sheet integrity.

The FY 2019 figures demonstrate a solid expansion in sales and profitability compared with the third quarter, with operating income more than doubling and EPS increasing by 35 cents. As noted in the supplemental quarterly data, the volatility of the industries served means these results may not predict future quarters, but the year‑end performance indicates a strong financial position for Advanced Energy Industries.

5. **Unaudited Data Disclaimer:** As highlighted in the supplemental quarterly financial note, these results are unaudited and subject to volatility inherent in the industries served by AEI; therefore, they may not be indicative of future performance.

text.value: Adoption of ASC 606

On January 1, 2018, the Company adopted ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, applying the modified retrospective method to all contracts not completed as of January 1, 2018. Results for reporting periods beginning after January 1, 2018 are presented under ASC 606, while prior period amounts are not adjusted and continue to be reported under the accounting standards in effect for the prior period.

The impact of adopting the standard primarily related to a change in the timing of revenue recognition for voyage charter contracts. In the past, the Company recognized revenue from voyage charters ratably over the estimated length of each voyage, calculated on a discharge-to-discharge basis.

Under the new standard, the Company recognizes revenue from voyage charters ratably over the estimated length of each voyage, calculated on a load-to-discharge basis. In addition, the adoption of ASC 606 resulted in a corresponding change in the timing of recognition of voyage expenses for voyage charter contracts.

synth_text.title: Balance‑Sheet Impact of ASC 606 Adoption on Voyage Receivables, Deferred Taxes, and Accumulated Deficit
synth_text.text:
The Company’s transition to ASC 606 on January 1 2018 introduced a new method for recognizing revenue and related expenses on voyage charter contracts. This change produced a noticeable shift in several balance‑sheet items, as illustrated in the table below.

| Item                     | Pre‑ASC 606 (Prior to 2018) | Post‑ASC 606 (After Adoption) |
|--------------------------|----------------------------|------------------------------|
| Voyage receivables       | $1,336                     | $24,209                      |
| Deferred income taxes    | $(108) ( liability)        | $83,671 ( asset)             |
| Accumulated deficit      | $(1,228)                   | $(265,758)                   |

**Key observations**

1. **Voyage receivables** increased dramatically from $1,336 to $24,209. Under ASC 606, revenue is now recognized on a load‑to‑discharge basis, which accelerates the timing of revenue recognition and consequently raises the amount of receivables recorded at period end.

2. **Deferred income taxes** shifted from a modest liability of $108 to a substantial tax asset of $83,671. The new revenue timing created temporary differences that generated a larger deferred tax asset on the balance sheet.

3. **Accumulated deficit** expanded from $(1,228) to $(265,758). The cumulative effect of the accounting change, together with the company’s operating results, contributed to a deeper deficit.

These changes reflect the cumulative effect of adopting ASC 606, as the Company reported that revenues for 2018 increased by $1,418 and net income rose by $1,101 due to the new standard. The balance‑sheet adjustments captured in the table are a direct manifestation of those accounting impacts.

text.value: Valuation of Goodwill
Goodwill balances by reporting unit are as follows:

Goodwill represents the purchase price paid in excess of the fair value of net tangible and intangible assets acquired. Goodwill is not amortized but is subject to an impairment test at a reporting unit level on an annual basis and when circumstances indicate that an impairment is more-likely-than-not. Such circumstances that might indicate an impairment is more-likely-than-not include a significant adverse change in the business climate for one of our reporting units or a decision to dispose of a reporting unit or a significant portion of a reporting unit. The test for goodwill impairment is a two-step process. The first step of the test is performed by comparing the fair value of each reporting unit to its carrying amount, including recorded goodwill. If the carrying amount of a reporting unit exceeds its fair value, the second step is performed to measure the amount of the impairment, if any, by comparing the implied fair value of goodwill to its carrying amount. Any resulting impairment would be recorded in the current period.

Determining the fair value of a reporting unit for purposes of the goodwill impairment test or for changes in our operating structure is judgmental in nature and involves the use of estimates and assumptions. These estimates and assumptions could have a significant impact on whether or not an impairment charge is recognized and also the magnitude of any such charge. Estimates of fair value are primarily determined using discounted cash flows and market multiples from publicly traded comparable companies. These approaches use significant estimates and assumptions including projected future cash flows, discount rate reflecting the inherent risk in future cash flows, perpetual growth rate and determination of appropriate market comparables.

We evaluate our reporting units when changes in our operating structure occur, and if necessary, reassign goodwill using a relative fair value allocation approach. As described in Note 18 to our Consolidated Financial Statements in Item 8 of this Form 10-K, beginning on October 1, 2017, we concluded that CMS became a separate operating segment. In conjunction with the changes to reporting units, we reassigned goodwill between CGD and CMS based on their relative fair values as of October 1, 2017. We estimated the fair value of CGD and CMS at October 1, 2017 based upon market multiples from publicly traded comparable companies in addition to discounted cash flows models for CMS and for a combination of CGD and CMS based on discrete financial forecasts developed by management for planning purposes. Cash flows beyond the discrete forecasts were estimated based on projected growth rates and financial ratios, influenced by an analysis of historical ratios and by calculating a terminal value at the end of the discrete financial forecasts. For the October 1, 2017 valuations, future cash flows were discounted to present value using a discount rate of 13% for our CMS reporting unit and 11% for the combination of our CGD and CMS reporting units.

For the first step of our fiscal 2019 annual impairment test, we estimated the fair value of CTS based upon market multiples from publicly traded comparable companies and for CGD and CMS, we estimated the fair value based upon a combination of market multiples from publicly traded comparable companies and discounted cash flow models. The discounted cash flows were based on discrete three-year financial forecasts developed by management for planning purposes. Cash flows beyond the discrete forecasts were estimated based on projected growth rates and financial ratios, influenced by an analysis of historical ratios and by calculating a terminal value at the end of the three-year forecasts. The future cash flows were discounted to present value using a discount rate of 15% for CGD and 12.5% for CMS. The results of our 2019 annual impairment test indicated that the estimated fair value for our CTS and CGD reporting units exceeded their carrying amounts by over 100%, while the estimated fair value of our CMS reporting unit exceeded its carrying amount by over 60%.

Unforeseen negative changes in future business or other market conditions for any of our reporting units including margin compression or loss of business, could cause recorded goodwill to be impaired in the future. Also, changes in estimates and assumptions we make in conducting our goodwill assessment could affect the estimated fair value of our reporting units and could result in a goodwill impairment charge in a future period.

Goodwill reflects the premium paid over the fair value of net tangible and intangible assets acquired. It is not amortized; instead, it is subject to an annual impairment test (or more frequently if adverse conditions arise). The test involves:

1. **Step 1:** Comparing each reporting unit’s fair value—determined using discounted cash‑flow analyses and market multiples—to its carrying amount, which includes goodwill.  
2. **Step 2:** If the carrying amount exceeds fair value, measuring the impairment by comparing the implied fair value of goodwill to its recorded amount.

Recent impairment assessments (fiscal 2019) indicated that the fair values of CTS, CGD, and CMS all exceeded their respective carrying amounts by substantial margins (over 100% for CTS and CGD, and over 60% for CMS), resulting in **no goodwill impairment** for the period.

Management continues to monitor market conditions, business performance, and underlying assumptions used in the fair‑value calculations. Significant adverse changes—such as margin compression, loss of business, or revised cash‑flow forecasts—could trigger future goodwill impairments.

In summary, Cubic’s goodwill is concentrated in CTS and CGD, with a total of $321.6 million, and current impairment testing shows the recorded goodwill remains fully supported by the estimated fair values of the reporting units.

synth_text.text:
**Goodwill Balances (in millions of dollars)**  

| Reporting Unit | Goodwill Balance |
|----------------|-----------------|
| Cubic Transportation Systems (CTS) | $254.6 |
| Cubic Mission Solutions (CMS)      | $181.4 |
| Cubic Global Defense (CGD)         | $142.1 |
| **Total Goodwill**                 | **$578.1** |

*All amounts are presented in millions of dollars.*

**Key Points on Goodwill**

- **Definition:** Goodwill reflects the excess of the purchase price over the fair value of the net tangible and intangible assets acquired in a business combination.  
- **Accounting Treatment:** Goodwill is not amortized. Instead, it is tested for impairment at the reporting‑unit level at least annually, and more frequently if events suggest that an impairment is more likely than not (e.g., adverse business climate changes, disposals, or significant operational shifts).  

**Impairment Testing Process**

1. **First Step – Fair‑Value Comparison:** The fair value of each reporting unit is estimated (using discounted cash‑flow models and market multiples) and compared to its carrying amount, which includes recorded goodwill.  
2. **Second Step – Impairment Measurement:** If the carrying amount exceeds fair value, the implied fair value of goodwill is calculated and compared to its carrying amount to determine any impairment loss.  

**Assumptions & Estimates**

- Fair‑value estimates rely on management’s projections of future cash flows, discount rates that reflect risk, perpetual growth rates, and selection of comparable public companies.  
- For example, the 2019 impairment test used discount rates of 15 % for CGD and 12.5 % for CMS, and the fair values of CTS and CGD were found to exceed their carrying amounts by more than 100 %, while CMS exceeded its carrying amount by over 60 %.  

**Implications**

- The current goodwill balances of $578.1 million across CTS, CMS, and CGD are fully supported by recent impairment testing, which indicated no need for a charge.  
- Ongoing monitoring of market conditions and internal forecasts is essential, as adverse changes could trigger future impairments.  

Overall, Cubic’s goodwill reflects the premium paid for strategic acquisitions across its three core units, and the company’s rigorous, judgment‑based impairment framework ensures that this intangible asset remains appropriately valued on the balance sheet.

text.value: Orders and revenue for Smart Infrastructure rose in all three businesses – solutions and services, systems and software, and the products business – and in all three reporting regions. Order growth was strongest in the solutions and services business on a sharply higher volume from large orders in the Americas and Europe, C. I. S., Africa, Middle East. Revenue rose most strongly in the systems and software and the solutions and services businesses, particularly in the Americas. Revenue growth in the product business was due to low voltage products, while revenue in the other products businesses came in close to prior-year levels due partly to less favorable conditions in short-cycle markets.

Adjusted EBITA declined due mainly to the systems and software business including negative effects related to grid control projects early in the year. Adjusted EBITA also included higher expenses year-over-year related to expansion of smart building offerings and for grid edge activities. Severance charges were € 48 million in fiscal 2019 compared to € 34 million a year earlier. Smart Infrastructure’s order backlog was € 10 billion at the end of the fiscal year, of which € 7 billion are expected to be converted into revenue in fiscal 2020.

Smart Infrastructure achieved its results in overall moderately growing markets in fiscal 2019. The grid markets benefited from the need for intelligent and flexible energy networks and for automation, particularly in Asia, Australia and the Americas. Heavy industries and the infrastructure industry also developed favorably during fiscal 2019, driven by investments in oil and gas markets, in data centers and in transportation infrastructure, such as for e-mobility. Discrete industries, which started strong
in fiscal 2019, experienced a downturn in the second half of the fiscal year.

Construction markets continued their stable growth during the fiscal year, particularly in the U. S. and China and in the non-residential construction market overall. Growth in the important building electrification and automation market was driven by demand for building performance and sustainability offerings, including strong demand for energy efficiency and digital services. In fiscal 2020, market growth overall is expected to
be lower than in fiscal 2019, due to an expected continuation of the downturn in the short-cycle markets, economic uncertainty in a number of countries due to trade conflicts, and other factors.

Beginning with fiscal 2020, the distribution transformer business will be transferred to the Operating Company Gas and Power. If this organizational structure had already existed in fiscal 2019, Smart Infrastructure would have posted orders of € 15.590 billion, revenue of € 14.597 billion, Adjusted EBITA of € 1.465 billion and an Adjusted EBITA margin of 10.0 %.
