synth_text.title: Operating Expense Breakdown and Key Drivers of Cost Reductions
synth_text.text:
The company’s operating expenses for the reported fiscal year total $452 million, representing 12 % of revenue. The expense categories and their contributions are:

- **Sales and Marketing:** $100 million (6 % of total)  
- **Research and Development:** $43 million (4 %)  
- **General and Administrative:** $127 million (22 %)  
- **Amortization of Intangible Assets:** $13 million (6 %)  
- **Restructuring, Transition, and Other Costs:** $169 million (41 %)

The reductions across these categories are driven by several specific factors:

1. **Sales and Marketing** expenses fell mainly due to a $51 million decline in stock‑based compensation and a $41 million reduction linked to the divestiture of the WSS and PKI solutions.  
2. **Research and Development** costs decreased primarily because stock‑based compensation was $66 million lower than the prior period.  
3. **General and Administrative** expenses were reduced by $130 million, again reflecting a lower stock‑based compensation component.  
4. **Amortization of Intangible Assets** declined as a result of the sale of intangible assets associated with the WSS and PKI divestitures.  
5. **Restructuring, Transition, and Other Costs** dropped by $70 million in severance and related restructuring outlays. Additionally, transition costs fell sharply from $88 million in fiscal 2018 (related to the WSS and PKI divestiture) to just $3 million in fiscal 2019.

Overall, the expense profile shows a significant shift away from high‑cost restructuring and transition activities, alongside lower compensation‑related outlays, contributing to a more streamlined cost structure.

text.value: 2) Cloud Services and Subscriptions:

Cloud services and subscriptions revenues are from hosting arrangements where in connection with the licensing of software, the end user doesn’t take possession of the software, as well as from end-to-end fully outsourced business-to-business (B2B) integration solutions to our customers (collectively referred to as cloud arrangements). The software application resides on our hardware or that of a third party, and the customer accesses and uses the software on an as-needed basis via an identified line. Our cloud arrangements can be broadly categorized as "platform as a service" (PaaS), "software as a service" (SaaS), cloud subscriptions and managed services.

Cost of Cloud services and subscriptions revenues is comprised primarily of third party network usage fees, maintenance of in-house data hardware centers, technical support personnel-related costs, and some third party royalty costs.

Cloud services and subscriptions revenues increased by $78.8 million or 9.5% during the year ended June 30, 2019 as compared to the prior fiscal year; up 10.8% after factoring the impact of $10.8 million of foreign exchange rate changes. Geographically, the overall change was attributable to an increase in Americas of $61.6 million, an increase in EMEA of $14.7 million, and an increase in Asia Pacific of $2.6 million.
The number of Cloud services deals greater than $1.0 million that closed during Fiscal 2019 was 46 deals, consistent with that in Fiscal 2018.

Cost of Cloud services and subscriptions revenues increased by $19.8 million during the year ended June 30, 2019 as compared to the prior fiscal year, due to an increase in labour-related costs of approximately $19.1 million and an increase in third party network usage fees of $1.3 million. These were partially offset by a decrease in other miscellaneous costs of $0.6 million. The increase in labour-related costs was primarily due to increased headcount from recent acquisitions.
Overall, the gross margin percentage on Cloud services and subscriptions revenues increased to approximately 58% from approximately 56%.

For illustrative purposes only, had we accounted for revenues under proforma Topic 605, Cloud services and subscriptions revenues would have been $901.5 million for the year ended June 30, 2019, which would have been higher by approximately $72.5 million or 8.7% as compared to the prior fiscal year; and would have been up 10.1% after factoring the impact of $11.0 million of foreign exchange rate changes. Geographically, the overall change would have been attributable to an increase in Americas of $56.4 million, and an increase in EMEA of $12.4 million and an increase in Asia Pacific of $3.7 million.

The $6.4 million difference between cloud service and subscription revenues recognized under Topic 606 and those proforma Topic 605 cloud services and subscriptions revenues described above is primarily the result of timing differences on professional services related to cloud contracts, where under Topic 605, revenues would have been deferred over the estimated life of the contract, but under Topic 606 these revenues are recognized as services are performed. For more details, see note 3 "Revenues" to our Consolidated Financial Statements.

synth_text.title: Fiscal 2019 Cloud Services & Subscriptions – Revenue, Cost, and Margin Highlights
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2019 the company generated **$907.8 million** in Cloud Services and Subscriptions revenue, representing a **9.5 % increase** (10.8 % when adjusted for foreign‑exchange effects) over the prior year. The revenue mix by region was heavily weighted toward the **Americas (67.9 %)**, with **EMEA contributing 22.7 %** and **Asia Pacific 9.4 %**.

The $78.8 million revenue uplift broke down as follows:
- **Americas:** +$61.6 million  
- **EMEA:** +$14.7 million  
- **Asia Pacific:** +$2.6 million  

Cost of Cloud Services and Subscriptions rose to **$384.0 million**, an increase of **$19.8 million**. The cost growth was driven primarily by higher labour expenses ($19.1 million) and increased third‑party network usage fees ($1.3 million), partially offset by a $0.6 million reduction in miscellaneous costs.  

GAAP gross profit reached **$523.8 million**, up $59.0 million year‑over‑year, and the **gross margin improved to approximately 58 %**, up from about 56 % in the previous fiscal period.

The number of cloud deals exceeding $1 million remained steady at **46** during FY 2019, indicating consistent large‑deal activity despite the overall growth.

Overall, FY 2019 demonstrated solid expansion across all geographies, disciplined cost management, and an enhanced profitability profile for the Cloud Services and Subscriptions segment.

synth_text.title: 2017 Cloud Services and Subscriptions – Revenue, Cost, Margin, and Geographic Breakdown
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal year 2017, the company generated **$705.5 million** in Cloud Services and Subscriptions revenue. The cost of delivering these services was **$299.9 million**, resulting in a **gross profit of $405.6 million** and a **GAAP gross margin of 57.5 %**.

**What the figures represent**  
Cloud Services and Subscriptions encompass hosting arrangements where software is accessed on‑demand (PaaS, SaaS, cloud subscriptions, and managed services). Revenue is recognized when the customer uses the software, while costs primarily consist of third‑party network fees, data‑center maintenance, technical‑support personnel expenses, and occasional royalty payments.

**Geographic distribution**  
Revenue was heavily weighted toward the Americas, which contributed **68.7 %** of total cloud revenue. EMEA accounted for **21.4 %**, and the Asia‑Pacific region contributed **9.9 %**.

**Contextual insight**  
Later fiscal periods (e.g., FY‑2019) showed a modest increase in both revenue and margin, with the gross margin rising to roughly **58 %**. The 2017 margin of **57.5 %** therefore reflects the early stage of this upward trend.

**Key take‑aways**  
- Strong profitability with a margin near 58 % in 2017.  
- Dominant revenue generation in the Americas, with growing contributions from EMEA and Asia‑Pacific.  
- Cost structure driven by network usage, data‑center operations, and labor—areas that have historically influenced margin performance.

These figures illustrate a solid foundation for the company’s cloud business, positioning it for continued growth and margin improvement in subsequent years.

synth_text.title: 2017 Income Tax Provision Reconciliation Summary
synth_text.text:
In 2017 the Company recorded a statutory federal income‑tax expense of **$6.66 million**. After applying a series of adjustments, the overall tax provision turned into a modest **net benefit of $47 thousand**. The key components of the reconciliation are:

- **State income‑tax expense (net of the federal effect):** $(421) k  
- **Nondeductible permanent items:** $1.506 million  
- **Foreign rate differential:** $599 k  
- **Tax‑rate change:** $7.226 million (reflecting the shift from the statutory to the effective rate)  
- **Adjustment to deferred taxes:** $37 k  
- **Change in valuation allowance:** $(2.291) million  
- **Uncertain tax positions:** $76 k  
- **Other items:** $(26) k  
- **Non‑qualified stock‑option and performance‑award windfall:** none reported  

These adjustments collectively offset the statutory expense. The Company uses a **notional 26 % tax rate** for reconciling the statutory rate to the effective rate, as described in the supplemental notes. The primary reasons for the divergence between the statutory federal rate and the effective tax rate include the impact of state taxes, differences between U.S. and foreign tax rates, deferred‑tax state‑rate adjustments, share‑based compensation effects, true‑ups of deferred taxes, other nondeductible permanent items, and changes to the valuation allowance. Additionally, the Company’s foreign subsidiaries are subject to varied statutory rates, further influencing the overall provision.

Overall, the 2017 tax reconciliation demonstrates how multiple tax‑benefit items reduced the statutory liability, resulting in a near‑break‑even net tax position for the year.

synth_text.title: Income Tax Provision Reconciliation Summary – 2018 & 2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s income‑tax provision for 2018 and 2019 is reconciled from the statutory federal tax expense to the effective tax provision by applying a notional 26 % tax rate.  

**2019**  
- Statutory federal tax expense: **$(10.9 million)**  
- State income‑tax expense (net of federal effect): **$(3.7 million)**  
- Nondeductible permanent items added back: **$3.5 million**  
- Foreign‑rate differential: **$(0.4 million)**  
- Adjustment to deferred taxes: **$(1.9 million)**  
- Change in valuation allowance: **$22.5 million** (primary positive driver)  
- Uncertain tax positions: **$0.1 million**  
- Share‑based compensation (stock‑option windfall): **$(9.1 million)**  
- Other items: **$0.2 million**  

After all adjustments, the net provision for 2019 resulted in a **$0.425 million benefit**.

**2018**  
- Statutory federal tax expense: **$(9.8 million)**  
- State income‑tax expense (net of federal effect): **$(2.7 million)**  
- Nondeductible permanent items: **$(1.5 million)** (deduction)  
- Foreign‑rate differential: **$0.6 million**  
- Tax‑rate change: **$0.1 million**  
- Adjustment to deferred taxes: **$0.3 million**

The combined effect produced a **$0.796 million benefit** for 2018.

**Key drivers of the difference between statutory and effective rates**  
The reconciliation highlights that state taxes, foreign‑rate differentials, adjustments to deferred taxes, share‑based compensation, nondeductible permanent items, and especially the changes in valuation allowance are the main contributors to the lower effective tax rate in both years. The company’s foreign subsidiaries are subject to varying statutory rates, further influencing the overall provision.

Overall, despite sizable statutory tax expenses, the combination of the above adjustments yields modest net tax benefits in both 2018 and 2019.

The selected consolidated statements of operations for GreenSky, Inc. show a clear upward trend from 2016 to 2017.  

- **Total revenue** increased from **$263.9 million** in 2016 to **$325.9 million** in 2017, reflecting a **23 % growth** year‑over‑year.  
- **Cost of revenue** (excluding depreciation and amortization) rose from **$79.1 million** to **$89.7 million**, maintaining a roughly consistent margin relative to revenue.  
- **Total costs and expenses** grew from **$144.1 million** to **$180.3 million**, driven primarily by the higher cost of revenue and operating expenses.  
- **Operating profit** improved from **$119.8 million** to **$145.6 million**, indicating stronger operational efficiency.  
- **Total other income (expense), net** shifted from a modest **$4.7 million gain** in 2016 to a **$6.9 million loss** in 2017, slightly offsetting operating gains.  
- **Income before income tax** rose from **$124.5 million** to **$138.7 million**, and **net income** mirrored this increase, moving from **$124.5 million** to **$138.7 million**.  

No income‑tax expense is reported for either year, and earnings per share (basic or diluted) are not applicable because the company had not yet completed its reorganization and IPO; EPS data are only available for periods after May 24 2018.  

These figures are drawn from Item 6 of GreenSky’s Form 10‑K filing, presented in thousands of dollars, and should be read in conjunction with the Management’s Discussion and Analysis and the full consolidated financial statements for a complete understanding of the company’s performance.

synth_text.title: GreenSky, Inc. – Selected Financial Highlights for 2018 & 2019
synth_text.text:
**Financial Overview (2018‑2019)**  
GreenSky, Inc. reported substantial growth in total revenue, rising from **$414.7 million** in 2018 to **$529.6 million** in 2019, a year‑over‑year increase of roughly 28 %.  The cost of revenue also grew, from **$160.4 million** to **$248.6 million**, reflecting the higher volume of business.

Despite the revenue expansion, operating profit declined from **$152.8 million** in 2018 to **$121.0 million** in 2019, driven by the larger cost base and higher other expenses (total other income/expense moved from a net gain of $19.3 million to a net loss of $32.1 million). Consequently, income before tax fell from **$133.5 million** to **$88.8 million**, and the company recorded an income‑tax benefit of **$7.1 million** in 2019 versus a tax expense of **$5.5 million** in 2018.

Net income decreased from **$128.0 million** in 2018 to **$96.0 million** in 2019. The portion attributable to GreenSky, Inc. dropped from **$24.3 million** to **$32.0 million**, while net income attributable to non‑controlling interests fell from **$103.7 million** to **$64.0 million**.

Earnings per share (EPS) improved after the reorganization and IPO. Basic EPS rose from **$0.43** to **$0.52**, and diluted EPS increased from **$0.41** to **$0.49**. These EPS figures are applicable only for the period from May 24 2018 through December 31 2019, as noted in the company’s Form 10‑K.

**Contextual Notes**  
- The presented data are extracted from GreenSky’s Form 10‑K (Item 6) and represent selected consolidated statements of operations for the years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019.  
- Figures are expressed in thousands of dollars, except per‑share data.  
- GreenSky’s historical results prior to the 2018 reorganization (when the company operated as GS Holdings or GSLLC) are not included in this summary.  
- The financial trends should be read in conjunction with the Management’s Discussion and Analysis (Item 7) and the full consolidated financial statements (Item 8) for a comprehensive view.

Overall, GreenSky demonstrated strong top‑line growth in 2019, while profitability metrics contracted, resulting in lower net income but higher earnings per share due to the post‑IPO capital structure.

synth_text.title: 2017 Effective Tax Rate Reconciliation and Key Drivers
synth_text.text:
The Company’s 2017 effective tax rate was 42.4 %, notably above the U.S. statutory federal rate of 35.0 %. The reconciliation of the effective rate to the statutory rate is broken down as follows:

- **State taxes, net of federal effect:** –5.4 %
- **Foreign rate differential:** –9.3 %
- **Tax credits:** +4.1 %
- **Domestic production activities deduction:** –3.5 %
- **Stock‑based compensation:** –5.3 %
- **Change in prior‑year reserves:** –2.0 %
- **Change in valuation allowance:** –35.2 %
- **Effect of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (change in tax rate):** –23.4 %
- **Other (1):** +2.6 %

These adjustments collectively raise the effective tax rate to 42.4 %. The most significant upward pressures stem from the large increase in the valuation allowance (–35.2 %) and the impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (–23.4 %). Stock‑based compensation and foreign rate differentials also contributed to a higher rate, while tax credits and the domestic production activities deduction provided modest offsets.

The additional context clarifies that such reconciliations are standard practice: the effective tax rate diverges from the statutory rate due to items like stock‑based compensation (as highlighted in the Altera Corp v. Commissioner decision), full valuation allowances on U.S. deferred tax assets, the mix of income and losses across foreign jurisdictions, and non‑recognizable pretax losses. Similar factors influenced the Company’s effective tax rate in subsequent years (e.g., 2019), underscoring the recurring nature of these adjustments.

In summary, the 2017 effective tax rate of 42.4 % reflects a combination of state and foreign tax effects, significant valuation allowance changes, and statutory tax reforms, offset partially by tax credits and other deductions.

synth_text.title: Company Effective Tax Rate Reconciliation for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s statutory U.S. federal tax rate remained constant at 21 % for both 2018 and 2019. However, the reported effective tax rates were substantially lower—(0.9)% in 2018 and (3.8)% in 2019—due to a series of adjustments detailed in the reconciliation table and explained in the accompanying notes.

**Key Adjustments (2019 vs. 2018)**  

| Adjustment | 2019 (percentage points) | 2018 (percentage points) |
|------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| State taxes, net of federal effect | (0.3) | (0.1) |
| Foreign rate differential | (6.0) | (3.9) |
| Tax credits | 1.6 | 6.3 |
| Stock‑based compensation | (1.0) | (4.9) |
| Change in prior‑year reserves | (1.5) | (0.1) |
| Change in valuation allowance | (13.4) | (15.2) |
| Other (incl. uncertain tax positions) | (4.2) | (4.0) |
| **Net effective tax rate** | **(3.8)%** | **(0.9)%** |

*Notes on major drivers*  

- **Stock‑Based Compensation:** The 2019 rate reflects a modest (1.0)‑point reduction, while 2018 saw a larger (4.9)‑point impact, stemming from the Altera Corp v. Commissioner decision.  
- **Valuation Allowance:** A full valuation allowance on U.S. deferred tax assets contributed (13.4) and (15.2) percentage‑point reductions in 2019 and 2018, respectively.  
- **Foreign Differential:** Losses and lower taxable income in foreign jurisdictions lowered the rate by (6.0) points in 2019 and (3.9) points in 2018.  
- **Uncertain Tax Positions:** The footnote indicates that changes in uncertain tax positions added (3.8)% (2019) and (3.4)% (2018) to the effective‑rate gap.  

**Financial Impact**  
For the year ended December 31, 2019, the company recorded an income‑tax expense of $11.6 million, resulting in the (3.8)% effective tax rate. The disparity between the statutory 21 % rate and the effective rate is primarily driven by the items listed above, especially the valuation allowance, stock‑based compensation adjustments, and the mix of foreign results.

**Conclusion**  
The reconciliation demonstrates that the company’s effective tax rates for 2018 and 2019 are markedly lower than the statutory federal rate due to a combination of state and foreign tax effects, tax credits, stock‑based compensation adjustments, substantial valuation allowances, and changes in uncertain tax positions. These factors collectively produced a net tax benefit, reflected in the negative effective tax rates reported for both years.

header: Total revenue from contracts with customers

text.value: Telecommunications Segment

ICS operates an extensive network of direct routes and offers premium voice communication services for carrying a mix of business, residential and carrier long-distance traffic, data and transit traffic. Customers may have a bilateral relationship with ICS, meaning they have both a customer and vendor relationship with ICS. In these cases, ICS sells the customer access to the ICS supplier routes but also purchases access to the customer’s supplier routes.

Net revenue is derived from the long-distance data and transit traffic. Net revenue is earned based on the number of minutes during a call multiplied by the price per minute, and is recorded upon completion of a call. Completed calls are billable activity while incomplete calls are non-billable. Incomplete calls may occur as a result of technical issues or because the customer’s credit limit was exceeded and thus the customer routing of traffic was prevented.

Revenue for a period is calculated from information received through ICS’s billing software, such as minutes and market rates. Customized billing software has been implemented to track the information from the switch and analyze the call detail records against stored detailed information about revenue rates. This software provides ICS with the ability to perform a timely and accurate analysis of revenue earned in a period.

ICS evaluates gross versus net revenue recognition for each of its contractual arrangements by assessing indicators of control and significant influence to determine whether the ICS acts as a principal (i.e. gross recognition) or an agent (i.e. net recognition). ICS has determined that it acts as a principal for all of its performance obligations in connection with all revenue earned. Net revenue represents gross revenue, net of allowance for doubtful accounts receivable, service credits and service adjustments. Cost of revenue includes network costs that consist of access, transport and termination costs. The majority of ICS’s cost of revenue is variable, primarily based upon minutes of use, with transmission and termination costs being the most significant expense.

It is recognized on a gross basis—ICS acts as the principal in its contracts—so the reported figures reflect gross revenue net of allowances for doubtful accounts, service credits, and adjustments. Revenue is calculated from the number of completed call minutes multiplied by the applicable market rate, with billing data captured in a customized system that tracks switch‑generated call detail records. The majority of the segment’s cost of revenue is variable, driven primarily by minutes of use, with transmission and termination costs being the most significant expense.

Overall, the data illustrate a notable contraction in long‑distance minute revenue between 2018 and 2019, while the segment’s cost structure remains closely tied to usage volume.

The consolidated financial statements of GasLog Ltd. disclose the composition of voyage‑related costs for 2017 and 2018. synth_text.title: Cubic Corporation Backlog Decline from FY 2018 to FY 2019: Segment Breakdown and Key Drivers
synth_text.text:
Cubic Corporation’s total backlog fell by **$663.5 million** between September 30 2018 and September 30 2019, dropping from **$4,064.5 million** to **$3,401.0 million**. The segment‑level figures for the two dates are:

| Segment                     | September 30 2018 | September 30 2019 | Change |
|-----------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|--------|
| Cubic Transportation Systems (CTS) | $3,544.9 M | $2,953.3 M | **‑$591.6 M** |
| Cubic Mission Solutions (CMS)      | $77.0 M   | $103.7 M | **+ $26.7 M** |
| Cubic Global Defense (CGD)          | $442.6 M  | $344.0 M | **‑$98.6 M** |
| **Total**                           | **$4,064.5 M** | **$3,401.0 M** | **‑$663.5 M** |

The reduction in backlog is primarily attributed to three factors:

1. **Progress on Large Contracts** – Work completed in 2019 on four major CTS contracts awarded in fiscal 2018 removed a substantial amount of pending revenue from the backlog.
2. **ASC 606 Adoption** – The transition to the new revenue‑recognition standard resulted in a net backlog decrease of **$104.5 million** as revenue was recognized earlier.
3. **Foreign‑Exchange Impact** – Changes in exchange rates between the U.S. dollar and the currencies of Cubic’s foreign operations reduced the backlog by **$79.7 million**.

Overall, while the Mission Solutions segment saw modest growth, the Transportation Systems and Global Defense segments experienced notable declines, driving the aggregate backlog reduction for the year.

text.value: Annual Recurring Revenue

Beginning with the fourth quarter of 2018, we began monitoring a new operating metric, total annual recurring revenue (“Total ARR”), which is defined as the annualized value of all recurring revenue contracts active at the end of a reporting period. Total ARR includes the annualized value of subscriptions (“Subscription ARR”) and the annualized value of software support contracts related to perpetual licenses (“Perpetual license support ARR”) active at the end of a reporting period and does not include revenue reported as perpetual license or professional services in our consolidated statement of operations. We are monitoring these metrics because they align with how our customers are increasingly purchasing our solutions and how we are managing our business. These ARR measures should be viewed independently of revenue, unearned revenue, and customer arrangements with termination rights as ARR is an operating metric and is not intended to be combined with or replace those items. ARR is not an indicator of future revenue and can be impacted by contract start and end dates and renewal rates.

synth_text.title: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) Summary for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
Beginning in Q4 2018, the company started reporting Total Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR), an operating metric that annualizes the value of all active recurring‑revenue contracts at the end of a reporting period. Total ARR comprises two components:

* **Subscription ARR** – the annualized value of subscription contracts.  
* **Perpetual‑license‑support ARR** – the annualized value of software support contracts tied to perpetual licenses.

These figures exclude revenue from perpetual‑license sales and professional services and are presented solely as a measure of recurring‑revenue performance; they are not intended to replace or be combined with traditional revenue metrics.

**ARR Results (unaudited) – December 31**

| Fiscal Year | Total ARR | YoY % Change | Subscription ARR | Perpetual‑License‑Support ARR | YoY % Change (Support) |
|-------------|-----------|--------------|------------------|------------------------------|------------------------|
| 2019 | **$179.5 M** | **+19 %** | **$113.9 M** | **$65.6 M** | **‑2 %** |
| 2018 | **$162.6 M** | **+32 %** (vs. 2017) | **$95.9 M** | **$66.7 M** | **+6 %** |

**Key Takeaways**

1. **Total ARR grew 19 % year‑over‑year**, reaching $179.5 million in 2019, reflecting the increasing adoption of recurring‑revenue contracts by customers.  
2. **Subscription ARR showed the strongest growth**, rising from $95.9 million to $113.9 million (≈19 % increase), underscoring a shift toward subscription‑based purchasing.  
3. **Perpetual‑license‑support ARR declined slightly**, falling from $66.7 million to $65.6 million, a 2 % decrease, indicating modest contraction in support contracts for perpetual licenses.  
4. The 32 % YoY increase reported for 2018 pertains to the change from 2017 to 2018 and is provided for historical context.

**Interpretation**  
These ARR metrics align with the company’s strategic focus on recurring‑revenue models. While Total ARR continues to expand, the growth is driven primarily by subscriptions, with support for perpetual licenses remaining relatively stable. As an operating metric, ARR should be viewed independently of traditional revenue figures and does not predict future revenue on its own.

text.value: Cubic Global Defense

Sales: CGD sales decreased 10% to $325.2 million in 2018 compared to $360.2 million in 2017. The year-over-year comparative sales and operating income were significantly impacted by an $8.0 million gain recognized on an equitable contract adjustment in fiscal 2017 for our littoral combat ship virtual training contract with the U.S. Navy. Sales were lower in fiscal 2018 on virtual training sales, air combat training system sales, and ground combat training system sales, while sales of international training support services increased between fiscal 2017 and 2018. The average exchange rates between the prevailing currency in our foreign operations and the U.S. dollar had no significant impact on CGD sales between 2017 and 2018.
Amortization of Purchased Intangibles: Amortization of purchased intangibles included in the CGD results amounted to $1.1 million in 2018 and $0.9 million in 2017.

Operating Income: CGD had operating income of $16.6 million in 2018 compared to $28.1 million in 2017. The decrease in operating income was primarily caused by the gain of $8.0 million recognized in fiscal 2017 due to the approval of a contract adjustment with the U.S. Navy described above. In fiscal 2018 an arbitrator awarded $1.7 million to a former reseller of our air combat training systems in the Far East, which was recorded as SG&A expense by CGD in 2018. In addition, CGD’s R&D expenditures increased approximately $1.8 million year-over-year. The increase in R&D expenditures is indicative of the acceleration of our development of next generation live, virtual, constructive, and game-based training systems. These decreases in operating income in fiscal 2018 were partially offset by increased operating income from ground combat training systems, which was higher primarily due to improvements in expected total costs for the development of two ground combat training system contracts in the Far East. The average exchange rates between the prevailing currency in our foreign operations and the U.S. dollar had no significant impact on CGD operating income between 2017 and 2018.

Adjusted EBITDA: CGD Adjusted EBITDA was $26.3 million in 2018 compared to $39.4 million in 2017. The decrease in Adjusted EBITDA was primarily driven by the same factors that drove the decrease in operating income described above excluding the increase in amortization which is excluded from Adjusted EBITDA.

synth_text.title: Cubic Global Defense Financial Performance: FY 2018 vs. FY 2017
synth_text.text:
Cubic Global Defense (CGD) reported a modest contraction in its financial results for fiscal year 2018 compared with fiscal year 2017.  

**Sales** fell 10 % to **$325.2 million** in 2018 from **$360.2 million** in 2017. The decline was driven primarily by lower virtual‑training sales, reduced air‑combat training system sales, and weaker ground‑combat training system sales. International training support services, however, grew year‑over‑year. Currency fluctuations had no material effect on sales in either year.

**Operating income** dropped to **$16.6 million** in 2018 from **$28.1 million** in 2017. The 2017 figure was boosted by an $8.0 million gain from a contract adjustment with the U.S. Navy for a littoral combat ship virtual‑training program. In 2018, operating income was pressured by a $1.7 million arbitration award recorded as SG&A expense, higher R&D spending (up $1.8 million as CGD accelerated development of next‑generation training systems), and increased amortization of purchased intangibles ($1.1 million versus $0.9 million in 2017). Offsetting these pressures, ground‑combat training system income rose due to improved cost expectations on two Far‑East contracts. Exchange rates again had no significant impact.

**Adjusted EBITDA** declined to **$26.3 million** in 2018 from **$39.4 million** in 2017. The reduction mirrors the operating‑income decline, excluding the effect of higher amortization, which is not part of Adjusted EBITDA.

In summary, CGD’s FY 2018 performance was characterized by lower sales and profitability, largely reflecting the absence of a one‑time contract‑adjustment gain recorded in 2017, a shift in product‑mix sales, increased R&D investment, and a modest arbitration expense, while foreign‑exchange effects remained neutral.

synth_text.title: Cubic Global Defense FY2018 Financial Performance Overview
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2018, Cubic Global Defense (CGD) experienced a notable contraction across its core financial metrics. Net sales fell 10 % year‑over‑year, decreasing to **$325.2 million** from $360.2 million in 2017. The decline was driven by lower virtual‑training sales, reduced air‑combat training system sales, and weaker ground‑combat training system sales, although international training support services saw modest growth. 

Operating income dropped sharply by **41 %**, falling to **$16.6 million** from $28.1 million. The primary reasons were the absence of an $8.0 million contract‑adjustment gain recorded in 2017, a $1.7 million arbitration expense related to a former reseller, and a $1.8 million increase in R&D expenditures as CGD accelerated development of next‑generation training systems. Offsetting these pressures, higher operating income from ground‑combat training contracts partially mitigated the decline. Exchange‑rate fluctuations had no material impact.

Adjusted EBITDA also declined, down **33 %** to **$26.3 million** from $39.4 million in the prior year. This reduction mirrors the operating‑income decline, excluding the increase in amortization of purchased intangibles (which rose to $1.1 million in 2018). 

Overall, CGD’s FY2018 results reflect a challenging market environment for its training‑system portfolio, offset by strategic investments in R&D and stable foreign‑currency conditions.

**Overview**  
At 31 March the company reported total trade and other payables of **£7,437 million**. The breakdown is as follows:

| Item | Amount (£ million) |

| **Total** | **7,437** |

\*Other payables include operating lease liabilities and deferred gains from a 2001 sale‑and‑finance‑leaseback transaction (see note b).

**Key points from the accounting notes**

1. **Recognition and measurement** – Trade and other payables are initially recorded at fair value (generally the invoiced amount) and subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective‑interest method.  
2. **Deferred income** – Previously recognised deferred income has largely been re‑classified to contract liabilities under IFRS 15. The remaining balance comprises **£51 million** of current and **£586 million** of non‑current liabilities linked to the Broadband Delivery UK programme; these may be subject to repayment or reinvestment depending on programme take‑up.  
3. **Other payables** – Apart from the amounts shown, this category also reflects obligations arising from operating leases and the residual effects of a historic lease‑back arrangement.

Together, these figures provide a clear picture of the company’s short‑ and medium‑term payable obligations as of the reporting date.

text.value: A.6.1 Capital structure

The increase in short-term debt and current maturities of long-term debt was due mainly to reclassifications of long-term euro and U. S. dollar instruments totaling € 3.9 billion from longterm debt. This was partly offset by € 3.3 billion resulting from the repayment of U. S. dollar instruments.

The decrease in current income tax liabilities was driven mainly by the reversal of income tax provisions outside Germany and tax payments in the context of the carve-out activities related to Siemens Healthineers.

Long-term debt increased due primarily to the issuance of euro instruments totaling € 6.5 billion and currency translation effects for bonds issued in the U. S. dollar. This was partly offset by the above-mentioned reclassifications of euro and U. S. dollar instruments.
The increase in provisions for pensions and similar obligations was due mainly to a lower discount rate. This effect was partly offset by a positive return on plan assets, among other factors.

The main factors for the increase in total equity attributable to shareholders of Siemens AG were € 5.2 billion in net income attributable to shareholders of Siemens AG; the re-issuance of treasury shares of € 1.6 billion; and positive other comprehensive income, net of income taxes of € 0.4 billion, resulting mainly from positive currency translation effects of € 1.8 billion, partly offset by negative effects from remeasurements of defined benefit plans of € 1.1 billion. This increase was partly offset by dividend payments of € 3.1 billion (for fiscal 2018) and the repurchase of 13,532,557 treasury shares at an average cost per share of € 99.78, totaling € 1.4 billion (including incidental transaction charges).

synth_text.title: Key Changes in Siemens AG’s Capital Structure (FY 2018)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal 2018 Siemens AG’s balance sheet showed modest overall movement, with total liabilities rising by 9 % and total equity increasing by 6 %. The most notable shifts occurred within specific liability categories and equity, driven by financing activities, tax adjustments, and pension accounting.

**Current Liabilities**  
- **Short‑term debt and current maturities of long‑term debt** rose sharply by **19 %**, mainly because € 3.9 bn of long‑term euro and U.S.‑dollar bonds were re‑classified to the short‑term bucket, partially offset by € 3.3 bn of repayments.  
- **Trade payables** increased modestly (**+6 %**).  
- **Other current financial liabilities** grew by **17 %**.  
- **Contract liabilities** were up **14 %**.  
- **Current provisions** fell (**‑6 %**).  
- **Current income tax liabilities** dropped significantly (**‑23 %**) due to the reversal of tax provisions outside Germany and tax payments linked to the Siemens Healthineers carve‑out.  
- **Liabilities associated with assets held for disposal** surged (**+54 %**).  
- Overall, **total current liabilities** rose by **6 %**.

**Non‑Current Liabilities**  
- **Long‑term debt** increased by **12 %**, reflecting the issuance of € 6.5 bn of new euro bonds and currency‑translation gains on U.S.‑dollar bonds, offset by the re‑classification mentioned above.  
- **Provisions for pensions and similar obligations** jumped **29 %**, driven primarily by a lower discount rate, partially mitigated by a positive return on plan assets.  
- **Deferred tax liabilities** rose **19 %**.  
- **Other financial liabilities** saw a strong increase (**+44 %**).  
- **Total non‑current liabilities** grew by **13 %**.

**Equity**  
- **Total equity attributable to shareholders** rose **6 %**, supported by:
  * € 5.2 bn of net income attributable to shareholders,
  * € 1.6 bn from the re‑issuance of treasury shares,
  * € 0.4 bn of other comprehensive income, mainly positive currency‑translation effects (€ 1.8 bn) offset by pension plan remeasurements (€ 1.1 bn).  
  This equity increase was partially offset by dividend payments of € 3.1 bn and the repurchase of 13.5 million treasury shares for € 1.4 bn.  
- **Non‑controlling interests** grew **11 %**.  
- **Total liabilities and equity** rose by **8 %**, reflecting the combined effect of the above changes.

**Key Takeaways**  
- The most significant drivers of balance‑sheet movement were financing actions (new bond issuances and re‑classifications), tax adjustments linked to the Healthineers carve‑out, and pension‑plan accounting.  
- Despite higher debt levels, equity also strengthened, keeping the overall capital structure balanced.  
- The increase in current tax liabilities and the reduction in provisions helped improve the net working‑capital position.

synth_text.title: Siemens AG Capital Structure Overview: 2018‑2019 Comparative Summary
synth_text.text:
**Balance‑sheet highlights (in € millions)**  

| Item | 2018 | 2019 | Δ (2019‑2018) |
|------|------|------|--------------|
| Short‑term debt & current maturities of long‑term debt | 5,057 | 6,034 | +977 |
| Trade payables | 10,716 | 11,409 | +693 |
| Contract liabilities | 14,464 | 16,452 | +1,988 |
| Current provisions | 3,931 | 3,682 | –249 |
| Current income‑tax liabilities | 3,102 | 2,378 | –724 |
| **Total current liabilities** | 47,874 | 50,723 | +2,849 |
| Long‑term debt | 27,120 | 30,414 | +3,294 |
| Provisions for pensions & similar obligations | 7,684 | 9,896 | +2,212 |
| **Total non‑current liabilities** | 42,995 | 48,541 | +5,546 |
| **Total liabilities** | 90,869 | 99,265 | +8,396 |
| Debt ratio | 65 % | 66 % | – |
| Total equity attributable to shareholders | 45,474 | 48,125 | +2,651 |
| Equity ratio | 35 % | 34 % | – |
| **Total liabilities & equity** | 138,915 | 150,248 | +11,333 |

**Key drivers of the changes**

* **Short‑term debt:** Rose mainly because €3.9 bn of long‑term euro and U.S.‑dollar bonds were re‑classified as current liabilities, partially offset by €3.3 bn of repayments.  
* **Long‑term debt:** Increased by €6.5 bn through the issuance of new euro‑denominated instruments and currency‑translation effects on U.S.‑dollar bonds; the re‑classifications described above reduced the net increase.  
* **Current income‑tax liabilities:** Fell by €724 m due to the reversal of tax provisions outside Germany and tax payments linked to the Siemens Healthineers carve‑out.  
* **Pension provisions:** Grew by €2.2 bn, driven primarily by a lower discount rate, with the impact partially mitigated by a positive return on plan assets.  
* **Equity growth:** Total equity rose by €2.7 bn, underpinned by €5.2 bn of net income, €1.6 bn from the re‑issuance of treasury shares, and €0.4 bn of other comprehensive income (mainly €1.8 bn of favorable currency‑translation effects offset by €1.1 bn of defined‑benefit plan remeasurements).  
* **Offsets to equity:** Dividend payments of €3.1 bn (FY 2018) and the repurchase of 13.5 m treasury shares for €1.4 bn reduced the equity increase.

**Overall picture**

Between 2018 and 2019 Siemens AG’s balance sheet expanded by roughly €11 bn, with liabilities growing faster than equity. The debt ratio edged up to 66 %, reflecting higher borrowing (both short‑ and long‑term) and larger pension obligations. Nevertheless, robust earnings and share‑related transactions boosted equity, keeping the capital structure relatively balanced despite the modest decline in the equity ratio.  

These movements illustrate Siemens AG’s strategic financing decisions—new euro‑bond issuances, re‑classification of existing debt, and active treasury‑share management—while also highlighting the impact of tax restructuring and pension accounting on its liabilities.

Advanced Energy Industries maintains defined‑benefit pension plans for non‑U.S. employees in the United Kingdom, Germany, and the Philippines. text.value: The significant components of the Company’s deferred income tax assets and liabilities as of December 31, 2019 and 2018 are as follows:

As a result of these actions, the Company transferred regional relationship and territory rights from its Canadian entity to enable each regional headquarters to develop and maintain merchant and commercial operations within its respective region, while keeping the ownership of all of the Company's current developed technology within Canada. These transfers reflect the growing proportion of the Company's business occurring internationally and resulted in a one-time capital gain. As a result of the capital gain, ongoing operations, the recognition of deferred tax assets and liabilities, and the utilization of all applicable credits and other tax attributes, including loss carryforwards, the Company has a provision for income taxes of $29,027 in the year ended December 31, 2019.

During the year ended December 31, 2019, the Company released some of its valuation allowance against its deferred tax assets in Canada, the United States, and Sweden. The Company has provided for deferred income taxes for the estimated tax cost of distributable earnings of its subsidiaries of $292.

text.value: Revenues, Cost of Revenues and Gross Margin by Product Type

1) License: Our license revenue can be broadly categorized as perpetual licenses, term licenses and subscription licenses, all of which are deployed on the customer’s premises (on-premise). Our license revenues are impacted by the strength of general economic and industry conditions, the competitive strength of our software products, and our acquisitions. Cost of license revenues consists primarily of royalties payable to third parties.

License revenues decreased by $9.4 million or 2.2% during the year ended June 30, 2019 as compared to the prior fiscal year; up 0.4% after factoring the impact of $11.2 million of foreign exchange rate changes. Geographically, the overall change was attributable to an increase in Americas of $8.2 million, offset by a decrease in Asia Pacific of $10.6 million and a decrease in EMEA of $7.0 million.

During Fiscal 2019, we closed 153 license deals greater than $0.5 million, of which 49 deals were greater than $1.0 million, contributing approximately $144.1 million of license revenues. This was compared to 140 deals greater than $0.5 million during Fiscal 2018, of which 58 deals were greater than $1.0 million, contributing $152.2 million of license revenues.

Cost of license revenues increased by $0.7 million during the year ended June 30, 2019 as compared to the prior fiscal year. The gross margin percentage on license revenues remained at approximately 97%.

For illustrative purposes only, had we accounted for revenues under proforma Topic 605, license revenues would have been $390.4 million for the year ended June 30, 2019, which would have been lower by approximately $47.1 million or 10.8% as compared to the prior fiscal year; and would have been lower by 8.4% after factoring the impact of $10.4 million of foreign exchange rate changes. Geographically, the overall change would have been attributable to a decrease in Americas of $17.7 million, a decrease in EMEA of $15.7 million and a decrease in Asia Pacific of $13.7 million.

The $37.7 million difference between license revenues recognized under Topic 606 and those proforma Topic 605 license revenues described above is the result of timing differences, where under Topic 605, revenues would have been deferred and recognized over time, but under Topic 606 these revenues are recognized up front. For more details, see note 3 "Revenues" to our Consolidated Financial Statements.

synth_text.title: License Revenue Performance and Geographic Distribution – FY 2017
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal year 2017 the company generated **$369.1 million** in license revenues, representing the core earnings from its on‑premise software offerings (perpetual, term and subscription licenses). The cost associated with these revenues was modest—**$13.6 million**—primarily reflecting royalties paid to third parties. After deducting these costs, the GAAP‑based gross profit stood at **$355.5 million**, delivering an impressive **gross margin of 96.3 %** (consistent with the historical ~97 % margin cited in the company’s disclosures).

Thus, nearly half of the total license revenue originated from the Americas, with EMEA contributing roughly two‑fifths and Asia Pacific accounting for just under one‑tenth.

**Business Context**  
- **Product mix:** License revenue comprises perpetual, term, and subscription licenses deployed on customers’ premises.  
- **Cost drivers:** The primary expense is royalties to third‑party technology owners.  
- **Margin stability:** Gross margins have remained stable around the high‑90 % range, underscoring the low‑cost nature of the license model.  
- **Influencing factors:** Revenue levels are sensitive to overall economic conditions, competitive positioning of the software portfolio, and the impact of acquisitions. Historical data shows that modest year‑over‑year fluctuations (e.g., a 2.2 % decline in 2019) can be offset by foreign‑exchange effects and regional performance shifts.

**Implications**  
The 2017 figures demonstrate a robust, high‑margin license business with a strong foothold in the Americas and a solid presence in EMEA. Maintaining the current product mix and managing royalty costs will be critical to preserving the high gross margin, while strategic initiatives aimed at expanding the Asia Pacific footprint could diversify the revenue base and mitigate regional concentration risk.

text.value: Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
Our foreign exchange forward contracts outstanding at fiscal year-end are summarized in U.S. dollar equivalents as follows (in millions):
At July 27, 2019 and July 28, 2018, we had no option contracts outstanding.

We conduct business globally in numerous currencies. The direct effect of foreign currency fluctuations on revenue has not been material because our revenue is primarily denominated in U.S. dollars. However, if the U.S. dollar strengthens relative to other currencies, such strengthening could have an indirect effect on our revenue to the extent it raises the cost of our products to non-U.S. customers and thereby reduces demand. A weaker U.S. dollar could have the opposite effect. However, the precise indirect effect of currency fluctuations is difficult to measure or predict because our revenue is influenced by many factors in addition to the impact of such currency fluctuations

Approximately 70% of our operating expenses are U.S.-dollar denominated. In fiscal 2019, foreign currency fluctuations, net of hedging, decreased our combined R&D, sales and marketing, and G&A expenses by approximately $233 million, or 1.3%, as compared with fiscal 2018. In fiscal 2018, foreign currency fluctuations, net of hedging, increased our combined R&D, sales and marketing, and G&A expenses by approximately $93 million, or 0.5%, as compared with fiscal 2017. To reduce variability in operating expenses and service cost of sales caused by non-U.S.-dollar denominated operating expenses and costs, we may hedge certain forecasted foreign currency transactions with currency options and forward contracts. These hedging programs are not designed to provide foreign currency protection over long time horizons. In designing a specific hedging approach, we consider several factors, including offsetting exposures, significance of exposures, costs associated with entering into a particular hedge instrument, and potential effectiveness of the hedge. The gains and losses on foreign exchange contracts mitigate the effect of currency movements on our operating expenses and service cost of sales.

We also enter into foreign exchange forward and option contracts to reduce the short-term effects of foreign currency fluctuations on receivables and payables that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currencies of the entities. The market risks associated with these foreign currency receivables, investments, and payables relate primarily to variances from our forecasted foreign currency transactions and balances. We do not enter into foreign exchange forward or option contracts for speculative purposes

synth_text.title: Impact of ASC 606 Adoption on 2018 Revenue, Cost of Goods Sold, and Gross Profit
synth_text.text:
The Company’s 2018 condensed consolidated statement of operations shows a clear effect of adopting ASC 606, the revenue‑recognition standard for contracts with customers. When ASC 606 is applied (“As Reported”), the Company recognized:

- **Revenue:** $70,965 k  
- **Cost of goods sold (COGS):** $58,701 k  
- **Gross profit:** $12,264 k  

In a hypothetical scenario without ASC 606 (“Without Adoption of ASC 606”), the figures would have been:

- **Revenue:** $68,845 k  
- **COGS:** $57,471 k  
- **Gross profit:** $11,374 k  

Thus, adopting ASC 606 increased reported revenue by **$2,120 k** (approximately 3.1 %) and gross profit by **$890 k** (about 7.8 %). The higher gross profit results from the standard’s requirement to recognize revenue—and the associated profit—only as the customer obtains control of the promised goods and services. Costs related to uninstalled materials or equipment are generally excluded from profit measurement unless they are specifically produced for a project, which further aligns expense recognition with the progress of performance obligations.

Overall, the adoption of ASC 606 led to a modest uplift in both revenue and profitability for the year ended December 31, 2018, reflecting the timing differences in revenue and cost recognition mandated by the new standard.

synth_text.text: The adoption of ASC 606 for revenue from contracts with customers altered the timing of revenue and profit recognition on the company’s construction contracts. Under ASC 606, revenue and associated profit are recognized only when the customer obtains control of the goods and services, and costs related to uninstalled materials or equipment are generally excluded from profit calculations unless they are specifically produced for a project. These adjustments reflect the new accounting treatment of performance obligations and illustrate the financial impact of transitioning to ASC 606.

synth_text.title: Fiscal Year 2019 vs. 2018 Revenue Summary and Growth Drivers
synth_text.text:
**Revenue Overview**  
For the fiscal year ended June 30 2019, total revenues reached **$1.21 billion**, a **37 % increase** (up $329.1 million) from the adjusted $880.98 million reported for the fiscal year ended June 30 2018. The increase reflects strong demand from both new and existing customers, with over 90 % of 2019 revenue generated from accounts that existed at the end of 2018.

**Segment Performance**  

| Segment | FY 2019 | FY 2018 (Adjusted) | Absolute Change | % Change |
|---------|---------|--------------------|----------------|----------|
| Subscription | $633.95 M | $410.69 M | +$223.3 M | **+54 %** |
| Maintenance | $394.53 M | $326.51 M | +$68.0 M | **+21 %** |
| Perpetual license | $93.59 M | $83.17 M | +$10.4 M | **+13 %** |
| Other | $88.06 M | $60.60 M | +$27.5 M | **+45 %** |

- **Subscription revenues** grew the most, driven primarily by additional subscriptions sold to the existing customer base as more organizations shift to cloud‑based, term‑based licenses for Data Center products.  
- **Maintenance revenues** rose due to higher renewal rates of software maintenance contracts linked to perpetual‑license offerings.  
- **Perpetual license revenues** increased modestly, with the bulk of the growth coming from extra licenses sold to current customers.  
- **Other revenues**—largely from third‑party applications sold through the Atlassian Marketplace—expanded by 45 %, reflecting the marketplace’s growing ecosystem.

**Customer Base Expansion**  
The number of customers grew to **152,727** at June 30 2019, up from **125,796** at the prior year‑end, underscoring the broadening market reach that underpins the revenue growth.

**Accounting Note**  
All 2018 figures are presented on an *as‑adjusted* basis to incorporate the full retrospective adoption of IFRS 15, as detailed in Note 2 of the consolidated financial statements.

**Outlook**  
Given the continued migration toward subscription‑based cloud services and the expanding marketplace, the company expects subscription revenues to outpace perpetual‑license growth in future periods.

synth_text.title: Fiscal Year 2019 Revenue Growth Overview
synth_text.text:
In the fiscal year ended June 30 2019, total revenues rose to **$329.1 million**, representing a **37 % increase** over FY 2018. The growth was driven by strong performance across all revenue streams:

- **Subscription revenues** reached **$223.3 million**, up **54 %** year‑over‑year, primarily from additional subscriptions sold to the existing customer base as more clients moved to cloud‑based, term‑based licenses.  
- **Maintenance revenues** grew to **$68.0 million**, a **21 %** increase, reflecting higher renewal rates of software maintenance contracts tied to perpetual‑license products.  
- **Perpetual license revenues** climbed to **$10.4 million**, a **13 %** rise, largely due to extra licenses sold to existing customers.  
- **Other revenues**—mainly sales of third‑party apps via the Atlassian Marketplace—expanded to **$27.5 million**, up **45 %**.

Over 90 % of the FY 2019 revenue was generated from customer accounts that existed on or before June 30 2018, underscoring the importance of the established client base. The total number of customers grew to **152,727**, up from **125,796** the prior year, further supporting the revenue expansion.

These results indicate that the company’s shift toward subscription and cloud services is delivering higher growth rates than traditional perpetual‑license sales, and that continued adoption of Marketplace offerings is adding a significant new revenue source.

synth_text.text:
**Selected Consolidated Financial Data (in millions, except per‑share items)**  

| Item | 2019 | 2018 |
|------|------|------|

**Narrative Summary**

For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2019, the company generated net revenues of **$6.5 billion**, a decline of roughly **13 %** from the **$7.5 billion** reported in 2018. Correspondingly, net income fell to **$1.5 billion** (down 19 %) and earnings per share decreased to **$1.96** basic and **$1.95** diluted, compared with **$2.43** and **$2.40** respectively in the prior year. Despite lower profitability, the board increased the cash dividend to **$0.37 per share**, up from **$0.34** in 2018.

Operating cash flow remained robust, rising modestly to **$1.83 billion** from **$1.79 billion** a year earlier. The company’s liquidity improved markedly, with cash and investments climbing to **$5.86 billion**—an increase of **$1.48 billion**—driven by higher cash balances and a larger investment portfolio. Total assets grew to **$19.85 billion**, reflecting the stronger balance‑sheet position.

Long‑term debt stayed essentially flat, with gross debt of **$2.70 billion** and net debt (gross debt less cash and investments) effectively **zero** in both years, underscoring a conservative capital structure.

**Contextual Notes**

* All amounts are presented in millions, except per‑share data.  
* Beginning in 2018 the company adopted a new revenue accounting standard (modified retrospective method); prior periods were not restated.  
* Net income figures for both years include significant tax‑related impacts from the U.S. Tax Reform Act.  
* The 2018 numbers were adjusted to reflect a $35 million reduction in income tax expense identified in early 2019.  
* Cash and investments comprise cash, cash equivalents, and short‑term/long‑term investments (total investments were $69 million in 2019 and $155 million in 2018).  

Overall, the 2019 results show a contraction in revenue and earnings but an improvement in cash generation and balance‑sheet strength, positioning the company for continued operational flexibility.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table below summarizes key consolidated financial metrics for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2016 and December 31, 2017. All monetary amounts are presented in millions of dollars, except per‑share figures, which are expressed in U.S. dollars. The data reflect the company’s operations, including the acquisition of King (effective February 23, 2016).  

**Key Financial Metrics**

| Metric (in millions unless noted) | 2017 | 2016 |
|-----------------------------------|------|------|
| **Net revenues** | $7,017 | $6,608 |
| **Net income** | $273 | $966 |
| **Basic net income per share** | $0.36 | $1.30 |
| **Diluted net income per share** | $0.36 | $1.28 |
| **Cash dividends declared per share** | $0.30 | $0.26 |
| **Operating cash flows** | $2,213 | $2,155 |
| **Cash and investments** | $4,775 | $3,271 |
| **Total assets** | $18,668 | $17,452 |
| **Long‑term debt, net** | $4,390 | $4,887 |
| **Long‑term debt, gross** | $4,440 | $4,940 |
| **Net debt* (gross debt less cash & investments)** | – (net cash position) | $1,669 |

\*Net debt is defined as long‑term debt, gross less cash and investments (see footnote 5 in the filing).

**Year‑over‑Year Highlights**

* **Revenue Growth:** Net revenues rose 6.2 % from $6,608 million in 2016 to $7,017 million in 2017, reflecting continued market demand and integration of King’s operations.  
* **Profitability Decline:** Net income fell sharply by 71.7 % to $273 million in 2017, driven largely by tax‑related impacts from the U.S. Tax Reform Act (footnote 2). Consequently, earnings per share dropped from $1.30 (basic) and $1.28 (diluted) in 2016 to $0.36 in 2017.  
* **Dividend Increase:** The company raised its cash dividend to $0.30 per share in 2017, up from $0.26 per share the prior year, indicating a commitment to returning cash to shareholders despite lower earnings.  
* **Stronger Cash Position:** Cash and investments grew by $1,504 million, reaching $4,775 million, while operating cash flow remained robust at over $2.1 billion each year.  
* **Asset Expansion:** Total assets increased by $1,216 million, supporting the company’s growth initiatives.  
* **Debt Reduction:** Net‑long‑term debt fell by $497 million, and the net‑debt figure turned negative in 2017, meaning cash and investments exceeded gross debt.  

**Additional Context**

* The figures for 2016 and 2017 are reported under the accounting standards that were in effect at the time; a new revenue accounting standard was adopted on January 1, 2018 (footnote 1) and does not affect these years.  
* Net income for 2017 includes the impact of the U.S. Tax Reform Act (footnote 2).  
* Detailed discussions of debt obligations and other financial statement notes can be found in Item 8 of the Form 10‑K filing (footnotes 4 and 5).  

**Conclusion**  
While the company achieved modest revenue growth and significantly improved its liquidity and debt profile in 2017, profitability was adversely affected by tax‑related items, resulting in a steep decline in net income and earnings per share. The increased dividend demonstrates confidence in cash generation despite the earnings dip.

We record a liability for firm, noncancelable, and unconditional purchase commitments for quantities in excess of our future demand forecasts consistent with the valuation of our excess and obsolete inventory. synth_text.title: Year‑to‑Year Performance Summary of Global Business Services Segments
synth_text.text:
For the most recent fiscal year, Accenture’s Global Business Services (GBS) reported modest overall growth, with segment‑level performance reflecting the company’s strategic focus on digital and cloud solutions.

- **GBS external revenue** increased by **3.2 %** year‑over‑year (adjusted for currency: **2.3 %**).  
- **Consulting** was the primary growth engine, rising **6.1 %** (currency‑adjusted **5.1 %**), driven by key digital and cloud offerings that help clients on their digital transformation journeys.  
- **Application Management** showed only a **0.4 %** increase on a reported basis and a slight decline of **‑0.5 %** after currency adjustment, indicating flat performance and continued pressure on traditional application‑management engagements.  
- **Global Process Services (GPS)** grew **4.8 %** (currency‑adjusted **4.7 %**), reinforcing the segment’s steady expansion.

Within GBS, cloud‑related revenue reached **$4.7 billion**, expanding **20 %** (reported) and **19 %** (currency‑adjusted) versus the prior year, underscoring the success of initiatives such as the Cloud Migration Factory and cloud application development.

Overall, the GBS portfolio demonstrated solid growth, anchored by consulting and cloud services, while Application Management remained flat and slightly negative when currency effects are considered.

synth_text.title: Growth of Global Business Services in 2018: Consulting Fuels Revenue Increase
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2018, Global Business Services (GBS) generated **$16.6 billion** in external revenue, up from **$16.1 billion** in 2017 (figures recast to reflect segment changes). The increase was driven primarily by Consulting, which rose to **$7.7 billion** in 2018 from **$7.3 billion** in 2017, reflecting strong demand for digital and cloud‑based solutions. Application Management revenue remained essentially flat at **$7.9 billion** (slightly lower on a currency‑adjusted basis), while Global Process Services (GPS) grew modestly to **$1.0 billion** in 2018 from **$990 million** in 2017.

The surge in Consulting aligns with GBS’s focus on helping clients on their digital transformation journeys, including offerings such as Cloud Migration Factory and cloud application development. Cloud‑related revenue alone reached **$4.7 billion**, expanding 20 % year‑over‑year (19 % when adjusted for currency). In contrast, traditional Application Management engagements continued to decline, offsetting some of the overall growth.

Overall, the 2018 results demonstrate that GBS’s strategic emphasis on digital and cloud services successfully boosted top‑line revenue, while legacy application management services showed limited growth.

synth_text.title: Intu Properties plc – 2019 Financial Position: IFRS Net Assets and EPRA NAV Overview
synth_text.text:
**Key 31 December 2019 figures (in £ million unless stated otherwise)**  

- **Investment and development property:** 6,721.6  
- **Joint ventures and other assets classified as held for sale:** 163.7  
- **Investment in associates:** 53.7  
- **Net external debt:** (4,498.4) – representing the group’s borrowing after netting cash and cash equivalents.  
- **Derivative financial instruments:** (286.9) – fair‑value liability.  
- **Other assets and liabilities:** (307.7) – includes PPE, receivables, payables, tax items, etc.  
- **Net assets:** 1,846.0  
- **Non‑controlling interest:** 58.2 (primarily the 40 % stake in intu Metrocentre).  
- **IFRS net assets attributable to owners:** 1,904.2  
- **Other adjustments:** 73.1 (fair‑value of derivatives, convertible bonds, deferred tax, joint‑venture items, recoverable NCI).  
- **EPRA NAV:** 1,977.3  
- **EPRA NAV per share:** 147 pence  

**What drove these numbers?**  

1. **Revaluation deficit:** Investment and development property fell by £2,534.1 million, largely due to a £1,979.7 million property revaluation loss. This is the principal reason for the decline in both IFRS net assets and EPRA NAV.  

2. **Joint‑venture activity:** The group’s total joint‑venture investment dropped to £163.7 million after disposing of intu Puerto Venecia and intu Asturias (both now classified as assets held for sale). The disposals generated an expected net cash inflow of roughly £95.4 million after debt repayment and fees. Joint‑venture losses of £158.9 million (including a £182.9 million revaluation deficit) also reduced the balance.  

3. **Capital expenditure:** Despite the overall decline, £129.2 million was spent on enhancing centre value – notably the Barton Square extension at intu Trafford Centre (£44.5 million), redevelopment of intu Broadmarsh (£14.5 million), and the leisure extension at intu Lakeside (£11.2 million).  

4. **Debt and derivatives:** Net external debt stands at £4.5 billion, reflecting the group’s borrowing position after accounting for cash. Derivative liabilities of £286.9 million arise from fair‑value accounting of financial instruments.  

5. **Foreign‑exchange exposure:** At year‑end, foreign‑exchange risk equated to 24 % of net assets attributable to shareholders, up from 15 % the prior year due to the UK revaluation deficit. Adjusted for the Puerto Venecia and Asturias disposals, exposure would revert to 15 %.  

6. **Non‑controlling interest and adjustments:** The NCI of £58.2 million is linked to the partner’s stake in intu Metrocentre and is considered recoverable. Additional adjustments of £73.1 million reconcile EPRA NAV to IFRS net assets.  

**Resulting performance metrics**  
- **IFRS net assets attributable to owners:** £1.90 billion.  
- **EPRA NAV:** £1.98 billion, representing a modest premium over IFRS assets after the adjustments.  
- **EPRA NAV per share:** 147 pence, reflecting the market‑relevant valuation per ordinary share.  

Overall, the 2019 financial position shows a substantial contraction in property values and joint‑venture assets, offset partially by strategic disposals and targeted capital investment. The balance sheet remains heavily leveraged, with a notable foreign‑exchange exposure that is expected to normalise once the pending joint‑venture sales are completed.

synth_text.title: Intu Properties plc – 2019 Financial Position: Major Decline in Net Assets and EPRA NAV
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
At 31 December 2019 intu properties plc reported a sharp deterioration in its balance‑sheet strength. EPRA Net Asset Value (NAV) fell to **‑£1.97 bn**, and EPRA NAV per share turned negative to **‑146 p**, compared with a positive EPRA NAV of **£3.95 bn** (293 p per share) in the prior period. IFRS‑measured net assets attributable to shareholders dropped by **£1.91 bn** to **‑£1.91 bn**.

**Key Balance‑Sheet Movements**

| Item | 2018 (pre‑adjustment) | 2019 (post‑adjustment) | Change |
|------|----------------------|-----------------------|--------|
| Investment & development property | £9,255.7 m | **‑£2,534.1 m** | ↓ £11,789.8 m |
| Joint ventures & assets held for sale | – | £163.7 m | ↑ £163.7 m |
| Investment in associates | £65.6 m | **‑£11.9 m** | ↓ £77.5 m |
| Net external debt | **‑£4,867.2 m** (net cash) | £368.8 m (net borrowing) | ↑ £5,236.0 m |
| Derivative financial instruments | **‑£284.0 m** | **‑£2.9 m** | ↓ £281.1 m |
| Other assets & liabilities | **‑£342.0 m** | £34.3 m | ↑ £376.3 m |
| Net assets | £3,828.1 m | **‑£1,982.1 m** | ↓ £5,810.2 m |
| Non‑controlling interest | **‑£16.4 m** | £74.6 m | ↑ £91.0 m |
| IFRS net assets attributable to owners | £3,811.7 m | **‑£1,907.5 m** | ↓ £5,719.2 m |
| Other adjustments | £135.4 m | **‑£62.3 m** | ↓ £197.7 m |
| EPRA NAV | £3,947.1 m | **‑£1,969.8 m** | ↓ £5,916.9 m |
| EPRA NAV per share | 293 p | **‑146 p** | ↓ 439 p |

**Drivers of the Decline**

1. **Property revaluation deficit** – A £1.98 bn write‑down on investment and development property was the single largest negative impact.  
2. **Asset disposals** – The transfer of intu Puerto Venecia and intu Asturias to “held for sale” (valued at £163.7 m) and the partial disposal of intu Derby reduced the property portfolio.  
3. **Joint‑venture performance** – The group recorded a £158.9 m share of loss from joint ventures, including a £182.9 m revaluation deficit and £27.9 m underlying earnings.  
4. **Foreign‑exchange exposure** – Exposure rose to 24 % of net assets (from 15 % in 2018) because of the UK revaluation deficit, amplifying the impact on net assets.  
5. **Changes in debt** – Net external debt swung from a cash‑position of £4.87 bn to a borrowing of £368.8 m, reflecting the financing of disposals and the settlement of asset‑level debt.

**Additional Context**

- Total joint‑venture investment fell to £524.1 m at year‑end, down £299.8 m from the previous year, driven mainly by the loss share and the disposal of intu Puerto Venecia (sale proceeds expected to net ~£95.4 m after costs).  
- “Other assets and liabilities” comprise PPE, receivables, payables, tax liabilities and other provisions.  
- Non‑controlling interest relates chiefly to a 40 % stake in intu Metrocentre, with a recoverable balance of £195.4 m included in group borrowings.  
- Adjustments to EPRA NAV include fair‑value changes in derivatives, convertible bonds, deferred tax on development property, and recoverable non‑controlling interest balances.

**Conclusion**  
The 2019 financial results illustrate a period of significant stress for intu properties plc, characterised by a large property revaluation loss, heightened debt, and reduced equity. The combined effect of disposals, joint‑venture losses, and foreign‑exchange exposure led to a negative EPRA NAV and a per‑share value of –146 p, underscoring the need for strategic asset management and potential capital restructuring.

text.value: 5. Income taxes:

On December 22, 2017, the President of the United States signed into law the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the "TCJA"). The TCJA amended the Internal Revenue Code and reduced the corporate tax rate from a maximum of 35% to a flat 21% rate. The rate reduction was effective on January 1, 2018. The Company's net deferred tax assets represent a decrease in corporate taxes expected to be paid in the future. Under generally accepted accounting principles deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognized for the future tax consequences attributable to differences between the financial statement carrying amounts of existing assets and liabilities and their respective tax basis. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply to taxable income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be recovered or settled. The Company's net deferred tax asset was determined based on the current enacted federal tax rate of 35% prior to the passage of the Act. As a result of the reduction in the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21% and other provisions under the TCJA, the Company made reasonable estimates of the effects of the TCJA and revalued its net deferred tax asset at December 31, 2017 resulting in a reduction in the value of its net deferred tax asset of approximately $9.0 million and recorded a transition tax of $2.3 million related to its foreign operations for a total of $11.3 million, which was recorded as additional noncash income tax expense in the year ended December 31, 2017. As of December 31, 2018, the Company had collected all of the necessary data to complete its analysis of the effect of the TCJA on its underlying deferred income taxes and recorded a $0.1 million reduction in the value to its net deferred tax asset. The TCJA subjects a U.S. shareholder to current tax on global intangible low-taxed income earned by certain foreign subsidiaries. FASB Staff Q&A, Topic 740, No. 5, "Accounting for Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income", states that the Company is permitted to make an accounting policy election to either recognize deferred income taxes for temporary basis differences expected to reverse as global intangible low-taxed income in future years or provide for the income tax expense related to such income in the year the income tax is incurred. The Company has made an accounting policy to record these income taxes as a period cost in the year the income tax in incurred.

The following year, domestic earnings rose to **$72.8 million** and foreign losses narrowed to **$20.1 million**, lifting total pre‑tax income to **$52.7 million**.

These figures are presented in thousands of dollars, as indicated in the accompanying notes. The upward trend reflects stronger domestic performance and a modest improvement in foreign results.

The fiscal years covered also coincide with the implementation of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), which took effect on January 1, 2018 and lowered the U.S. corporate tax rate from 35 % to a flat 21 %. The company re‑valued its net deferred tax assets in response to the rate change, recording a transition tax of $2.3 million for foreign operations and a total adjustment of $11.3 million in 2017. By the end of 2018, a further $0.1 million reduction to the deferred tax asset was recognized after completing the TCJA analysis. These tax adjustments are reflected as non‑cash income tax expense and do not alter the reported pre‑tax income numbers shown above.

Overall, the data demonstrate a solid increase in pre‑tax earnings between 2018 and 2019, set against a backdrop of significant U.S. corporate tax reform that impacted the company’s deferred tax accounting.
