text.value: Note 15. Stock-Based Compensation
The following table summarizes the components of non-cash stock-based compensation expense (in thousands):
2015 Equity Incentive Plan

We issue stock options pursuant to our 2015 Plan. The 2015 Plan allows for the grant of stock options to employees and for the grant of nonqualified stock options, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock awards, restricted stock unit awards, or RSUs, performance-based stock awards, and other forms of equity compensation to our employees, directors and non-employee directors and consultants.

In June 2015, our board of directors adopted and our stockholders approved our 2015 Plan pursuant to which we initially reserved a total of 4,700,000 shares of common stock for issuance under the 2015 Plan, which included shares of our common stock previously reserved for issuance under our Amended and Restated 2009 Stock Incentive Plan, or the 2009 Plan. The number of shares of common stock reserved for issuance under the 2015 Plan will automatically increase on January 1 each year, for a period of not more than ten years, commencing on January 1, 2016 through January 1, 2024, by 5% of the total number of shares of common stock outstanding on December 31 of the preceding calendar year, or a lesser number of shares as may be determined by the board of directors. As a result of the adoption of the 2015 Plan, no further grants may be made under the 2009 Plan. As of December 31, 2019, 6,527,550 shares remained available for future grant under the 2015 Plan.
Stock Options

Stock options under the 2015 Plan have been granted at exercise prices based on the closing price of our common stock on the date of grant. Stock options under the 2009 Plan were granted at exercise prices as determined by the board of directors to be the fair market value of our common stock. Our stock options generally vest over a five-year period and each option, if not exercised or forfeited, expires on the tenth anniversary of the grant date.

Certain stock options granted under the 2015 Plan and previously granted under the 2009 Plan may be exercised before the options have vested. Unvested shares issued as a result of early exercise are subject to repurchase by us upon termination of employment or services at the original exercise price. The proceeds from the early exercise of stock options are initially recorded as a current liability and are reclassified to common stock and additional paid-in capital as the awards vest and our repurchase right lapses. There were 250 and 957 unvested shares of common stock outstanding subject to our right of repurchase as of December 31, 2019 and 2018, respectively. We repurchased 27 and 107 of these unvested shares of common stock related to early exercised stock options in connection with employee terminations during the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018, respectively. We recorded less than $0.1 million in accounts payable, accrued expenses and other current liabilities on our consolidated balance sheets for the proceeds from the early exercise of the unvested stock options as of December 31, 2019 and 2018.

We account for stock-based compensation options based on the fair value of the award as of the grant date. We recognize stock-based compensation expense using the accelerated attribution method, net of actual forfeitures, in which compensation cost for each vesting tranche in an award is recognized ratably from the service inception date to the vesting date for that tranche.

We value our stock options using the Black-Scholes option pricing model, which requires the input of subjective assumptions, including the risk-free interest rate, expected term, expected stock price volatility and dividend yield. The risk-free interest rate assumption is based upon observed interest rates for constant maturity U.S. Treasury securities consistent with the expected term of our stock options. The expected term represents the period of time the stock options are expected to be outstanding and is based on the "simplified method." Under the "simplified method," the expected term of an option is presumed to be the mid-point between the vesting date and the end of the contractual term. We use the "simplified method" due to the lack of sufficient historical exercise data to provide a reasonable basis upon which to otherwise estimate the expected term of the stock options. Beginning in November 2019, the expected volatility for options granted is based on historical volatilities of our stock over the estimated expected term of the stock options. The expected volatility for options granted prior to November 2019 was based on historical volatilities of our stock and publicly traded stock of comparable companies over the estimated expected term of the stock options.

There were 186,500, 219,450 and 252,100 stock options granted during the years ended December 31, 2019, 2018 and 2017, respectively. We declared and paid dividends in June 2015 in anticipation of our IPO, which we closed on July 1, 2015. Subsequent to the IPO, we do not expect to declare or pay dividends on a recurring basis. As such, we assume that the dividend rate is 0%.

synth_text.title: Key Drivers of the Company’s Effective Tax Rate in Fiscal Year 2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s effective tax rate of **14.8 %** is markedly lower than the U.S. federal statutory rate of **35.0 %** due to several reconciling items:

* **Foreign earnings taxed at lower rates (‑11.6 %)** – The bulk of foreign pre‑tax income is generated through regional operating centers in Ireland, Singapore and Puerto Rico, which are subject to tax rates well below the U.S. rate. These centers accounted for **82 %** of foreign income in FY 2019, delivering the largest single reduction to the effective rate.  

* **Phone‑business losses (‑5.7 %)** – Losses from the phone segment offset taxable income, further decreasing the overall rate.  

* **Research & development credit (‑0.9 %)** – Federal R&D incentives provide a modest additional reduction.  

* **Excess tax benefits related to stock‑based compensation (‑2.1 %)** – Favorable treatment of stock‑based compensation contributes to a lower effective rate.  

* **Other reconciling items, net (‑1.3 %)** – Primarily consists of tax credits, GILTI adjustments, and state income taxes.  

* **Interest, net (+1.4 %)** – Net interest expense adds a small upward adjustment.  

The **Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA)** had a **0 % impact** in the table, but the narrative clarifies that a TCJA‑related charge in the second quarter of FY 2018 increased the effective rate for that year, while a **$2.6 billion net income‑tax benefit** from intangible‑property transfers in the fourth quarter of FY 2019 helped lower the rate.  

Overall, the combination of low‑tax foreign operations, segment losses, targeted tax credits, and specific tax‑benefit events compresses the effective tax rate to **14.8 %**, well below the statutory 35 % rate.

synth_text.title: Effective Tax Rate Evolution: Key Drivers Behind FY 2018‑FY 2019 Changes
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s effective tax rate diverged sharply from the U.S. federal statutory rate over the two most recent fiscal years. In FY 2018 the effective rate was **54.6 %**, well above the statutory **28.1 %**. By FY 2019 the effective rate had fallen to **10.2 %**, despite a lower statutory rate of **21.0 %**.  

**Reconciliation of Statutory to Effective Rate**  

| Reconciliation Item | FY 2019 (pp) | FY 2018 (pp) |
|----------------------|--------------|--------------|
| Foreign earnings taxed at lower rates | **‑4.1** | **‑7.8** |
| Impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) | **+0.4** | **+37.7** |
| Phone‑business losses | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| Intangible‑property transfers | **‑5.9** | 0.0 |
| Foreign‑derived intangible income deduction | **‑1.4** | 0.0 |
| Research & development credit | **‑1.1** | **‑1.3** |
| Excess stock‑based compensation benefits | **‑2.2** | **‑2.5** |
| Net interest | **+1.0** | **+1.2** |
| Other reconciling items (tax credits, GILTI, state taxes) | **+2.5** | **‑0.8** |
| **Net Effect** | **‑12.8** | **+26.5** |

*(Positive numbers increase the effective rate; negative numbers decrease it.)*

**Key Drivers Explained**

1. **Foreign Low‑Rate Jurisdictions** – The company’s foreign regional operating centers in Ireland, Singapore and Puerto Rico generated the majority of foreign pre‑tax income (82 % in FY 2019, 87 % in FY 2018, 76 % in FY 2017). Because these jurisdictions tax income at rates below the U.S. statutory rate, they consistently reduced the effective rate, contributing –4.1 pp in FY 2019 and –7.8 pp in FY 2018.

2. **Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA)** – A one‑time net charge related to the TCJA in Q2 FY 2018 added **+37.7 pp** to the effective rate, making FY 2018 the outlier year. A residual effect of **+0.4 pp** persisted into FY 2019.

3. **Intangible‑Property Transfers** – A $2.6 billion net income‑tax benefit from intangible‑property transfers in Q4 FY 2019 lowered the effective rate by **‑5.9 pp**.

4. **Other Credits and Adjustments** – The research‑and‑development credit, excess stock‑based compensation benefits, and a modest net interest expense each provided small reductions (or modest increases) to the effective rate in both years. “Other reconciling items” mainly reflect tax credits, GILTI, and state taxes, adding **+2.5 pp** in FY 2019 and **‑0.8 pp** in FY 2018.

**Resulting Trend**  
The combination of a lower statutory rate, continued foreign low‑rate earnings, the TCJA residual, and a sizable intangible‑property tax benefit drove the effective tax rate down from **54.6 %** in FY 2018 to **10.2 %** in FY 2019. The FY 2018 spike was primarily a TCJA‑related charge, while the FY 2019 decline reflects both the reversal of that charge and the $2.6 billion intangible‑property benefit.

**Conclusion**  
Understanding the composition of reconciling items clarifies why the company’s effective tax rate can deviate dramatically from the statutory rate. Foreign jurisdiction tax differentials and specific one‑time tax events (TCJA and intangible‑property transfers) were the dominant forces shaping the tax‑rate trajectory between FY 2018 and FY 2019.

Accounts Receivable and Deferred Rent Asset—The Company derives the largest portion of its revenues and corresponding accounts receivable and the related deferred rent asset from a relatively small number of tenants in the telecommunications industry, and 54% of its current-year revenues are derived from four tenants.

The Company’s deferred rent asset is associated with non-cancellable tenant leases that contain fixed escalation clauses over the terms of the applicable lease in which revenue is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

The Company mitigates its concentrations of credit risk with respect to notes and trade receivables and the related deferred rent assets by actively monitoring the creditworthiness of its borrowers and tenants. In recognizing tenant revenue, the Company assesses the collectibility of both the amounts billed and the portion recognized in advance of billing on a straight-line basis. This assessment takes tenant credit risk and business and industry conditions into consideration to ultimately determine the collectibility of the amounts billed. To the extent the amounts, based on management’s estimates, may not be collectible, revenue recognition is deferred until such point as collectibility is determined to be reasonably assured. Any amounts that were previously recognized as revenue and subsequently determined to be uncollectible are charged to bad debt expense included in Selling, general, administrative and development expense in the accompanying consolidated statements of operations.

Accounts receivable is reported net of allowances for doubtful accounts related to estimated losses resulting from a tenant’s inability to make required payments and allowances for amounts invoiced whose collectibility is not reasonably assured. These allowances are generally estimated based on payment patterns, days past due and collection history, and incorporate changes in economic conditions that may not be reflected in historical trends, such as tenants in bankruptcy, liquidation or reorganization. Receivables are written-off against the allowances when they are determined to be uncollectible. Such determination includes analysis and consideration of the particular conditions of the account. Changes in the allowances were as follows:

Net write‑offs, recoveries and other adjustments amounted to **($2.1 million)**. According to the accompanying notes, the 2017 figure is driven primarily by recoveries—recognition of revenue that had previously been reserved—indicating that the company was able to collect amounts that were once considered doubtful.  

American Tower’s receivables are concentrated among a small group of telecom tenants, with 54 % of current‑year revenue derived from four tenants. To mitigate credit risk, the company continuously monitors tenant creditworthiness, maintains allowances for doubtful accounts based on payment history and economic conditions, and defers revenue recognition when collectibility is uncertain. These practices help ensure that the reported balances accurately reflect amounts the company expects to collect.  

Overall, the 2017 data demonstrate a substantial net growth in receivables and deferred rent assets, supported by effective credit‑risk management and the recovery of previously reserved amounts.

synth_text.title: American Tower Corporation – Accounts Receivable & Deferred Rent Asset Overview (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The consolidated financial statements show that American Tower’s accounts receivable and related deferred rent asset grew markedly in 2018, rising from a January 1 balance of **$131.0 million** to a December 31 balance of **$282.4 million**. This increase was driven by **$157.8 million** of current‑year additions, partially offset by modest write‑offs and recoveries of **$(6.4) million**.

In 2019 the balance contracted to **$163.3 million** at year‑end. While the company added **$104.3 million** during the year, write‑offs, recoveries and other adjustments amounted to **$(223.4) million**, a sharp reversal largely attributable to uncollectible amounts in India (as disclosed in the notes). Consequently, the year‑end balance fell by **$119.1 million** from the prior year.

The company’s receivables are concentrated: **54 % of current‑year revenue** is derived from just four telecom tenants, and the deferred rent asset reflects non‑cancellable leases with fixed escalation clauses, recognized on a straight‑line basis. American Tower mitigates credit risk by continuously monitoring tenant creditworthiness and by maintaining allowances for doubtful accounts based on payment history, days past due, and broader economic conditions. When amounts become uncollectible, they are written off against these allowances, and any previously recognized revenue that later proves uncollectible is re‑classified to bad‑debt expense.

Overall, the 2018‑2019 data illustrate a period of rapid receivable growth followed by a significant contraction driven by targeted write‑offs, underscoring the importance of the company’s credit‑risk management practices and the impact of tenant concentration on its financial position.

We believe our ability to generate cash flows from operating activities is one of our fundamental financial strengths. synth_text.title: American Tower Corporation – Q3 and Q4 2019 Financial Highlights
synth_text.text:
**Quarterly Overview (2019)**  
American Tower Corporation reported the following unaudited financial results for the third and fourth quarters of 2019:

| Metric | Q3 (ended Sept 30, 2019) | Q4 (ended Dec 31, 2019) |
|--------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| Operating revenues | **$1,953.6 million** | **$1,923.7 million** |
| Costs of operations* | **$559.9 million** | **$550.2 million** |
| Operating income | **$728.3 million** | **$661.3 million** |
| Net income | **$505.3 million** | **$569.4 million** |
| Net income attributable to stockholders (common) | **$498.6 million** | **$562.7 million** |
| Basic EPS (common) | **$1.13** | **$1.27** |
| Diluted EPS (common) | **$1.12** | **$1.26** |

\* *Costs of operations* represent operating expenses **excluding** depreciation, amortization, accretion, selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses, development costs, and other operating expenses, as defined in the notes to the consolidated financial statements.

**Key take‑aways**

1. **Revenue stability:** Operating revenues were relatively flat, decreasing slightly from $1,953.6 million in Q3 to $1,923.7 million in Q4.  
2. **Improved cost efficiency:** Costs of operations fell modestly by $9.7 million, contributing to a lower operating income in Q4 despite the revenue dip.  
3. **Net income rebound:** Net income rose sharply in Q4 to $569.4 million, up $64.1 million from Q3, driven by favorable cost management and other income items.  
4. **Earnings per share growth:** Both basic and diluted EPS increased, with basic EPS moving from $1.13 to $1.27 and diluted EPS from $1.12 to $1.26, reflecting the higher net income and stable share count.

Overall, the fourth quarter of 2019 showed stronger profitability on a per‑share basis, even though operating revenues were marginally lower than in the third quarter. This performance underscores American Tower’s ability to control operating costs and deliver consistent earnings growth.

Performance-Based Restricted Stock Units

Performance-based restricted stock units are eligible to vest at the end of each fiscal year in a three-year performance period based on the Company’s annual growth rate in net sales and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share (subject to certain adjustments) over a multiple of four times the related results for the fourth quarter of 2018 relative to the growth rates for a peer group of companies for the same metrics and periods.

For the performance-based restricted stock units granted in 2019, 60% of each performance-based award is subject to the net sales metric for the performance period and 40% is subject to the non-GAAP diluted earnings per share metric for the performance period. The maximum percentage for a particular metric is2 50% of the target number of units subject to the award related to that metric, however, vesting of the performance stock units is capped at 30% and 100%, respectively, of the target number of units subject to the award in years one and two, respectively, of the three-year performance period.

As of December 31, 2019, the Company believes that it is probable that the Company will achieve performance metrics specified in the award agreement based on its expected revenue and non-GAAP diluted EPS results over the performance period and calculated growth rates relative to its peers’ expected results based on data available, as defined in the award agreement.

text.value: A segment-level summary of the goodwill allocation is presented below.

The recoverable amount of the group’s intangible assets has been assessed based on value-in-use calculations. The value in use is calculated using a discounted cash flow methodology covering a four year period plus terminal value.

Cash flow forecasts 

Cash flow forecasts are post-tax and based on the most recent financial projections covering a maximum of five years. Financial projections are based on assumptions that represent management’s best estimates.

Revenue growth rates 

Revenue growth rates used are based on management’s latest four-year plan. Four-year growth rates averaged between 8.8% to 12.1% for these CGUs (Board & Systems - Americas 8.8%, Board & Systems - EMEA 12.1% and Parts Analytics and Search 11.8%). Sensitivity testing was performed on these CGUs and a reasonably possible decline in these rates would not cause the carrying value of any of these CGUs to exceed its recoverable amount.

Terminal value 

The terminal value calculated after year four is determined using the perpetual growth model, having regard to the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) and terminal growth factor appropriate to each CGU. Terminal growth rates used in the financial projections was 2.0%.

Discount rates 

Discount rates used are WACC and include a premium for market risks appropriate to each country in which the CGU operates. WACCs averaged 8.9% (Board & Systems - Americas 9.1%, Board & Systems - EMEA 8.6% and Parts Analytics and Search 9.1%).
Sensitivity  Any reasonable change to the above key assumptions would not cause the carrying value of any of the remaining CGU’s to materially exceed its recoverable amount.
Accounting policy for intangible assets

Goodwill 

Goodwill arises on the acquisition of a business. Goodwill is not amortised. Instead, goodwill is tested annually for impairment, or more frequently if events or changes in circumstances indicate that it might be impaired, and is carried at cost less accumulated impairment losses. Impairment losses on goodwill are taken to profit or loss and are not subsequently reversed.

Intellectual property 

Significant costs associated with intellectual property are deferred and amortised on a straight-line basis over the period of their expected benefit, being their finite life of 5 to 10 years.

Customer relationships 

Customer relationships acquired in a business combination are amortised on a straight-line basis over the period of their expected benefit, being their finite life of 10 to 15 years.

Software intangibles 

Software intangibles arise from costs associated with the direct development and implementation on an internal project on new and existing software utilised by the group which demonstrates the technical feasibility of providing future economic benefits and amortised on a straight-line basis over the period of their expected benefit, being their finite life of 2 to 5 years.

synth_text.title: Goodwill Allocation Across Business Segments and Underlying Valuation Assumptions
synth_text.text:
The group’s goodwill has been allocated to three cash‑generating units (CGUs) as shown below (values in US$ 000):

| CGU                              | Allocation (Period 1) | Allocation (Period 2) |
|----------------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Board & Systems – Americas       | 10,672               | 8,324                |
| Board & Systems – EMEA           | 5,383                | 5,383                |
| Parts Analytics and Search       | 13,444               | 13,444               |
| **Total Goodwill**               | **29,499**           | **27,151**           |

Key observations  

* The Americas unit accounts for the largest share of goodwill, but its allocation falls by US$ 2,348 k between the two periods.  
* The EMEA allocation remains unchanged at US$ 5,383 k.  
* The Parts Analytics and Search unit retains a steady allocation of US$ 13,444 k.  
* Overall goodwill allocation declines by US$ 2,348 k, from US$ 29.5 m to US$ 27.2 m.

**Accounting treatment**  
Goodwill arises from business acquisitions and is not amortised. It is tested annually for impairment (or more frequently if indicators arise) and is carried at cost less any accumulated impairment losses. Impairment losses are recognised in profit or loss and are not reversed.

**Valuation assumptions underpinning the goodwill assessment**  

* **Revenue growth** – Management’s four‑year plan forecasts growth of 8.8 % (Americas), 12.1 % (EMEA) and 11.8 % (Parts Analytics). Sensitivity testing shows that reasonable declines would not cause the CGU carrying values to exceed their recoverable amounts.  
* **Discount rates (WACC)** – Averaged 8.9 % overall (Americas 9.1 %, EMEA 8.6 %, Parts Analytics 9.1 %). These rates include country‑specific market risk premiums.  
* **Terminal value** – Calculated using a perpetual growth model with a 2.0 % terminal growth rate, applied after the fourth forecast year.  
* **Cash‑flow forecasts** – Post‑tax cash flows are projected for up to five years, based on management’s best estimates.  
* **Sensitivity** – Reasonable changes to any of the above assumptions would not materially increase the CGU carrying values above their recoverable amounts.

In summary, the goodwill allocation reflects the relative economic contributions of the three CGUs, with the Americas unit experiencing a notable reduction. The allocation is supported by robust valuation assumptions, and the group’s accounting policy ensures that goodwill is regularly tested for impairment rather than amortised.

The consolidated operating expenses for the two most recent fiscal years are presented by segment in millions of dollars:

- **Data and Analytics**: $115.0 M in 2018 rose to $123.4 M in 2019, up $8.4 M. This growth reflects higher net personnel costs and greater data‑related costs associated with revenue expansion.

synth_text.title: Depreciation and Amortization Overview: 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
The company’s depreciation and amortization figures show a modest rise from 2018 to 2019.  

- **2018**: Depreciation was $2,174 k, amortization $37 k, resulting in a total depreciation and amortization of **$2,211 k**. No right‑of‑use asset depreciation was recorded.  
- **2019**: Depreciation increased to $2,297 k, amortization fell to $16 k, and depreciation of right‑of‑use assets added $175 k. Consequently, total depreciation and amortization rose to **$2,488 k**.

The **$277 k** increase in total depreciation and amortization (≈12.5 %) is primarily attributable to:

1. **Depreciation of right‑of‑use assets** – introduced after the company adopted IFRS 16 on 1 January 2019, which requires lease assets to be capitalised and depreciated.  
2. **Higher capital expenditures** in the preceding years, which expanded the base of depreciable assets.

Share based payments
Details of share options outstanding under each of the Group’s schemes is set out below:
1 Shares ordinarily exercised immediately on vested date.
2 Relates to non-vested SIP free shares, partnership shares and matching shares granted.

The weighted average exercise prices of the outstanding options and outstanding options exercisable at 31 December 2019 for the Share Option Schemes were 304 pence and 309 pence respectively (2018: 302 pence and 309 pence respectively) and for the Save As You Earn Scheme were 77 pence and 278 respectively (2018: 224 pence and nil respectively).
A Share Option Schemes
Options to subscribe for ordinary shares may be awarded under the intu properties plc Company Share Option Plan and the intu properties plc Non-approved Executive Share Option Scheme.

Such options may not be exercised within three years of grant or before the satisfaction or waiver of any applicable performance conditions and will be forfeited if the employee leaves the Group before their options become capable of exercise, except in certain circumstances. The options will lapse if not exercised within 10 years of the date of grant.
B Performance Share Plan (PSP)
The Company operates a PSP for eligible employees at the discretion of the Remuneration Committee

Awards may be made in the form of nil cost options, a conditional share award or prior to April 2019, a joint share ownership award and fixed-value zero-cost option, and eligible employees may be granted any combination of such awards subject to any individual limits.

The 2020 PSP awards will vest based on (i) 50 per cent of each award – relative Total Shareholder Return vs a bespoke real estate sector peer group (this group being expanded from the very small groups used previously) and (ii) 50 per cent of each award – intu’s Total Property Return vs the MSCI UK Shopping Centre benchmark. This mix of metrics represents a change from the 2019 awards which were based 50 per cent each on relative and absolute TSR targets subject to a Remuneration Committee-operated discretionary assessment of underlying financial performance. It is intended that awards will vest three years following grant (with an additional two year post vesting holding period applying to the net number of shares that vest if the Remuneration Committee considers it appropriate to apply such additional condition).
C Bonus Share Scheme (Bonus Scheme)
Under the Company’s Bonus Scheme, shares may be awarded on a deferred basis as part of a bonus award (Deferred Share Awards).

Deferred Share Awards comprise Restricted Shares and Additional Shares (prior to July 2019). Restricted Shares will vest two or three years after the date of their award and Additional Shares will vest four or five years after the date of award. Vesting is subject, under normal circumstances, to continued employment during the vesting or ‘restricted’ period. There are no further performance conditions applicable to either Restricted Shares or Additional Shares.

Where awarded, the number of Additional Shares would be equal to 50 per cent of the combined total of shares awarded as Restricted Shares and under the Share Incentive Plan (see section D). No Additional Shares were outstanding at 1 January 2014 and no awards of Additional Shares have been made since this time. intu properties
D Share Incentive Plan (SIP)
The Company operates a SIP for all eligible employees, who may receive up to £3,600 worth of shares (Free Shares) as part of their annual bonus. The SIP is an HMRC tax-advantaged scheme.

Any Free Shares awarded under the SIP will be held in trust on behalf of each employee for at least three years following grant, after which time they may be withdrawn, provided the individual employee has remained in employment with the Company. If the Free Shares are held in trust for a further two years, they will qualify for HMRC-approved tax advantages.

As part of the SIP arrangements, the Company also offers eligible employees the opportunity to participate in a Partnership share scheme, under which employees can invest up to £1,800 of pre-tax salary (or, if less, 10 per cent of salary) in any tax year, which will be used to purchase ordinary shares in the Company (Partnership Shares) at the end of a 12-month period. The Group will give each employee one ordinary share (a Matching Share) for every two Partnership Shares purchased by the employee. Matching Shares will be forfeited if the employee leaves the Group within three years of the date of award and will qualify for HMRC-approved tax advantages if they are held in the SIP for five years.
E Save As You Earn Scheme (SAYE)

The Group operates a SAYE under which all eligible UK employees may save up to a maximum of £500 per month for a period of three or five years and use the proceeds at the end of their saving period to purchase shares in the Company. At the start of the saving period, each SAYE participant will be granted an option to purchase such shares at a price usually determined as the average mid-market closing share price of an ordinary share in the Company over the three consecutive dealing days preceding the SAYE invitation date, discounted by up to 20 per cent. Options may normally be exercised within six months following the end of the savings period.
F Joint Share Ownership Plan (JSOP)

Eligible employees were invited to participate in the JSOP which formed part of the intu properties plc Unapproved Share Option Scheme (which was replaced by the Non-approved Executive Share Option Scheme upon its expiry in April 2018) and the PSP. Under the JSOP, shares are held jointly by the employee and the employee share ownership plan trustee with any increases in the share price and dividends paid on those shares being allocated between the joint owners in accordance with the terms of the scheme.
Conditions under which JSOP interests may be exercised (including applicable performance conditions) are the same as those for the Non-approved Executive Share Option Scheme as outlined in section A.

synth_text.title: Summary of Intu Properties plc Share‑Based Payments as of 31 December 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
Intu Properties plc operates a range of share‑based payment arrangements for its employees. At 31 December 2019 the outstanding and exercised share figures for each scheme were as follows:

| Scheme | Shares Outstanding (31 Dec 2019) | Shares Exercised / Removed in 2019* |
|--------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Performance Share Plan (PSP) | 3,734,410 | – |
| Bonus Share Scheme | 556,840 | (996,503) |
| Share Incentive Plan (SIP) | 88,027 | (41,116) |
| Save‑As‑You‑Earn (SAYE) | 448,368 | – |
| Share Option Schemes | – | – |
| Joint Share Ownership Plan (JSOP) | – | – |

\*Negative figures denote shares that were exercised (or otherwise cancelled) during the year; footnote 1 indicates these shares are normally exercised immediately on the vesting date.

**Key points by scheme**

1. **Share Option Schemes** – Options granted under the Company Share Option Plan and the Non‑approved Executive Share Option Scheme. Options cannot be exercised within three years of grant, lapse after ten years, and are forfeited if the employee leaves before they become exercisable.

2. **Performance Share Plan (PSP)** – Discretionary awards for eligible employees, comprising nil‑cost options, conditional share awards, and (pre‑April 2019) joint share ownership awards. The 2020 PSP vests 50 % on relative total shareholder return versus a real‑estate peer group and 50 % on intu’s total property return versus the MSCI UK Shopping Centre benchmark, with a three‑year vesting period plus a possible two‑year post‑vesting hold.

3. **Bonus Share Scheme** – Shares may be awarded on a deferred basis as part of a bonus (Deferred Share Awards). Restricted Shares vest after two‑or three years; Additional Shares (equal to 50 % of the combined Restricted Shares and SIP shares) vest after four‑or five years. No Additional Shares were outstanding at the start of 2014 and none have been awarded since.

4. **Share Incentive Plan (SIP)** – An HMRC‑tax‑advantaged scheme allowing eligible employees to receive up to £3,600 of free shares annually, held in trust for at least three years. Employees may also purchase Partnership Shares (up to £1,800 pre‑tax salary) and receive one Matching Share for every two Partnership Shares bought; Matching Shares are subject to a three‑year stay‑with‑company condition.

5. **Save‑As‑You‑Earn (SAYE)** – Eligible UK employees can save up to £500 per month for three or five years and then purchase shares at a discounted option price (average market price minus up to 20 %). Options are exercisable within six months after the saving period ends.

6. **Joint Share Ownership Plan (JSOP)** – Previously part of the unapproved share option scheme (replaced in 2018) and linked to the PSP. Shares are held jointly by the employee and a trustee; exercise conditions mirror those of the Non‑approved Executive Share Option Scheme.

**Interpretation**  
The PSP remains the largest source of outstanding share‑based awards (over 3.7 million shares). The Bonus Share Scheme shows a net reduction, reflecting the exercise of nearly one million shares during the year. The SIP also saw a modest net decrease. The SAYE scheme retained a substantial balance of 448,368 shares, indicating ongoing employee participation. No outstanding shares were reported for the Share Option Schemes or the JSOP at year‑end.

These figures, together with the scheme descriptions, provide a concise snapshot of Intu Properties plc’s share‑based remuneration landscape for 2019.

text.value: Recently Adopted Accounting Pronouncements

On April 1, 2018, the Company adopted ASU 2014-09-Revenue from Contracts with Customers (ASC 606) and all related amendments (“New Revenue Standard”) using the modified retrospective method. The Company has applied the new revenue standard to all contracts that were entered into after adoption and to all contracts that were open as of the initial date of adoption. The Company recognized the cumulative effect of initially applying the new revenue standard as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings. The comparative information has not been restated and continues to be reported under the accounting standards in effect for those periods. The adoption of the new standard impacts the Company's net sales on an ongoing basis depending on the relative amount of revenue sold through its distributors, the change in inventory held by its distributors, and the changes in price concessions granted to its distributors. Previously, the Company deferred revenue and cost of sales on shipments to distributors until the distributor sold the product to their end customer. As required by the new revenue standard, the Company no longer defers revenue and cost of sales, but rather, estimates the effects of returns and allowances provided to distributors and records revenue at the time of sale to the distributor. Sales to non-distributor customers, under both the previous and new revenue standards, are generally recognized upon the Company’s shipment of the product. The cumulative effect of the changes made to the consolidated April 1, 2018 balance sheet for the adoption of the new revenue standard is summarized in the table of opening balance sheet adjustments below. In accordance with the new revenue standard requirements, the disclosure of the impact of adoption on the consolidated income statement and balance sheet for the period ended March 31, 2019 was as follows (in millions):

The significant changes in the financial statements noted in the table above are primarily due to the transition from sellthrough revenue recognition to sell-in revenue recognition as required by the New Revenue Standard, which eliminated the balance of deferred income on shipments to distributors, significantly reduced accounts receivable, and significantly increased retained earnings. Prior to the acquisition of Microsemi, Microsemi already recognized revenue on a sell-in basis, so the impact of the adoption of the New Revenue Standard was primarily driven by Microchip's historical business excluding Microsemi.

synth_text.title: Impact of ASC 606 Adoption on the Company’s Income Statement for FY 2019
synth_text.text:
The adoption of ASC 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) on April 1 2018 fundamentally changed the way the Company recognizes revenue from its distributor channel. Under the previous sell‑through model, revenue and cost of sales were deferred until distributors sold the product to end customers. ASC 606 requires revenue to be recorded at the point of sale to the distributor, with estimates for returns and allowances, eliminating the deferred revenue balance.

As a result, the company’s income statement for the fiscal year ended March 31 2019 reflects the following adjustments (in millions of dollars):

- **Net sales** decreased by **$30.6 M**.  
- **Cost of sales** fell by **$15.8 M**, reflecting the removal of deferred cost recognition.  
- **Gross profit** declined by **$14.8 M**.  
- **Income before income taxes** was lower by **$14.8 M**.  
- **Income tax (benefit) provision** decreased by **$2.4 M**.  
- **Net income from continuing operations** dropped by **$12.4 M**.

These changes are primarily driven by the transition from a sell‑through to a sell‑in revenue recognition approach, which eliminated the balance of deferred income on shipments to distributors, reduced accounts receivable, and increased retained earnings. The impact is largely attributable to the Company’s historical business model; Microsemi, acquired later, already recognized revenue on a sell‑in basis and therefore contributed minimally to the observed effect.

In summary, the shift to ASC 606 resulted in a material reduction in reported sales and profitability for FY 2019, illustrating the significant influence of accounting policy changes on financial performance metrics.

synth_text.title: Impact of ASC 606 Adoption on the Company’s Income Statement
synth_text.text:
The company’s income‑statement figures for the year ended March 31, 2019 are presented in two ways: (1) “As reported,” which incorporates the adoption of ASC 606 (the New Revenue Standard) on April 1, 2018, and (2) “Balances without adoption of New Revenue Standard,” which show what the results would have been under the previous accounting method.

| Line item | As reported (ASC 606) | Without ASC 606 adoption |
|-----------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Net sales | $5,349.5 million | $5,380.1 million |
| Cost of sales | $2,418.2 million | $2,434.0 million |
| Gross profit | $2,931.3 million | $2,946.1 million |
| Income before income taxes | $204.5 million | $219.3 million |
| Income tax (benefit) provision | $(151.4) million | $(149.0) million |
| Net income from continuing operations | $355.9 million | $368.3 million |

**Key observations**

* Net sales are $30.6 million lower under ASC 606, reflecting the shift from a sell‑through to a sell‑in revenue‑recognition model.  
* Cost of sales is $15.8 million lower, producing a gross profit that is $14.8 million less after adoption.  
* Income before taxes declines by $14.8 million, while the tax benefit is slightly larger under ASC 606, resulting in a net‑income reduction of $12.4 million.

**Why the numbers differ**

On April 1, 2018 the company adopted ASU 2014‑09 (ASC 606) using the modified retrospective method. The new standard requires revenue to be recognized at the point of sale to distributors (sell‑in) rather than when distributors subsequently sell to end customers (sell‑through). Consequently:

* Deferred revenue and cost of sales on shipments to distributors were eliminated.  
* Revenue and cost of sales are now recorded at the time of the distributor sale, with estimates for returns and allowances.  
* The transition reduced accounts receivable, removed the balance of deferred income, and increased retained earnings, as reflected in the comparative figures.

The adoption’s impact is most pronounced for the company’s historical business (excluding Microsemi, which already used sell‑in recognition). Overall, the shift to ASC 606 modestly lowered reported sales and profitability for the period, while aligning revenue recognition with the new accounting framework.

synth_text.title: Revenue Performance Summary of ADG, AMS, and MDG Groups (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
**2018 vs 2017 (double‑digit growth)**  
- **Automotive and Discrete Group (ADG):** Revenue rose **16.2 %**, driven primarily by a 21 % increase in average selling prices (ASP) from an improved product mix, while volumes fell about 5 %.  
- **Analog MEMS and Sensors Group (AMS):** Revenue grew **19.9 %**, thanks to higher volumes (+12 %) and an 8 % ASP uplift from a better product mix (mix effect ≈ 13 %, offset by a 5 % price decline).  
- **Microcontrollers and Digital ICs Group (MDG):** Revenue increased **11.1 %**, mainly from an 11 % rise in ASP due to a stronger product mix (≈ 13 % mix effect) despite a small negative price effect (≈ ‑2 %).  
- **Total consolidated net revenues:** Up **15.8 %** for the year.

**2019 vs 2018 (mixed results)**  
- **ADG:** Revenue edged up **1.4 %**. The modest gain stemmed from a 9 % ASP increase—entirely attributable to a more favorable product mix—while volumes declined roughly 8 %.  
- **AMS:** Revenue rose **4.6 %**. Growth was supported by a 12 % ASP uplift from an improved mix, partially offset by a 7 % drop in volumes.  
- **MDG:** Revenue fell **10.3 %**, primarily because volumes were down about 10 % and ASP remained essentially flat.

**Key take‑aways**  
- 2018 was a strong year for all three groups, with double‑digit growth driven by a combination of higher ASPs (largely from better product mixes) and, for AMS, higher volumes.  
- In 2019, ADG and AMS managed modest growth despite volume declines, relying on price‑mix improvements, whereas MDG experienced a significant downturn due to volume weakness and stagnant pricing.  
- The overall revenue trajectory shows that while the company maintained growth in 2018, the momentum slowed in 2019, highlighting the importance of sustaining product‑mix advantages and addressing volume challenges, especially in the MDG segment.

**2018 vs. 2017 Performance (Contextual Insight)**  
All three groups posted double‑digit growth in 2018:

- **ADG** grew **16.2 %**, driven by a 21 % ASP increase (entirely from improved mix) while volumes fell ~5 %. Growth came from both Power Discrete and Automotive segments.  
- **AMS** rose **19.9 %**, powered by a double‑digit surge in Imaging. ASPs increased ~8 % (13 % mix effect) despite a 5 % price decline, and volumes grew ~12 %.  
- **MDG** increased **11.1 %**, with Digital and Microcontrollers & Memories contributing equally. ASPs rose ~11 % (13 % mix benefit) while volumes were flat; a modest 2 % negative price effect was offset by the mix improvement.

**Key Takeaways**  

1. **ADG** shifted from strong growth in 2018 (driven by mix‑related ASP gains) to modest growth in 2019, with price improvements again offset by lower volumes.  
2. **AMS** maintained an upward trajectory, though the growth rate slowed in 2019; mix‑driven ASP gains continued to be the primary catalyst.  
3. **MDG** experienced a reversal, moving from an 11 % increase in 2018 to a 10 % decline in 2019, reflecting volume weakness and flat pricing.  
4. The overall modest decline in 2019 total revenue (‑1.1 %) reflects the combined effect of MDG’s downturn outweighing the modest gains in ADG and AMS.

These trends illustrate how product‑mix optimization and average selling price dynamics have been pivotal in shaping revenue performance across Analog Devices’ core groups, while volume fluctuations have played a decisive role, especially for MDG in 2019.

synth_text.title: Annual Revenue Performance of Key Product Groups (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 the company generated **$9.56 billion** in total consolidated net revenues, a modest decline of about **1 %** from the **$9.66 billion** recorded in 2018. The performance of the three core product groups explains this slight dip:

* **Automotive and Discrete Group (ADG)** posted **$3.61 billion** in 2019, up **1.4 %** from 2018. The increase was driven primarily by a **9 % rise in average selling prices**, reflecting a more favorable product mix, which partially offset an **8 % drop in volumes**.

* **Analog MEMS and Sensors Group (AMS)** grew to **$3.30 billion** in 2019, a **4.6 %** increase year‑over‑year. Revenue growth stemmed from a **12 % uplift in average selling prices** (again due to a better mix of higher‑value products), while volumes fell roughly **7 %**.

* **Microcontrollers and Digital ICs Group (MDG)** declined to **$2.64 billion** in 2019, down **10.3 %**. The contraction was caused by a **10 % reduction in volumes**, with average selling prices remaining essentially flat.

The “Others” category contributed a negligible **$13‑$14 million** in both years.

Looking back to 2018, all three groups recorded **double‑digit growth** versus 2017:

* ADG rose **16.2 %**, powered by a **21 % increase in average selling prices** (product‑mix effect) despite a **5 % volume decline**.  
* AMS surged **19.9 %**, driven by **12 % higher volumes** and an **8 % price increase** (product‑mix contribution of about **13 %**, partially offset by a **5 % price decline**).  
* MDG grew **11.1 %**, mainly from an **11 % lift in average selling prices** (product‑mix effect of **13 %**) while volumes were largely unchanged.

Overall, the 2019 results reflect a shift from the strong volume‑and‑mix‑driven growth of 2018 to a year where price improvements in ADG and AMS were insufficient to fully counterbalance volume softness, especially in the MDG segment. This nuanced performance led to a slight contraction in total revenue while maintaining growth in two of the three primary groups.

synth_text.text:

**Interpretation**

1. **Profitability** – Both entities display robust profitability. Adjusted EBITDA exceeds raw EBITDA in each case, reflecting the inclusion of equity‑settled share‑based compensation. Entity 2’s adjusted EBITDA margin of 39 % is slightly higher than Entity 1’s 35 %, indicating a more efficient conversion of revenue into profit.

2. **Leverage** – Net debt is negative for both entities, meaning they each hold a net cash position. Entity 2 carries a larger net cash balance (€15.6 m) than Entity 1 (€12.2 m), underscoring strong liquidity.

3. **Financing Costs** – Interest expenses are modest relative to earnings, especially for Entity 1 where interest represents less than 5 % of Adjusted EBITDA. Entity 2’s interest cost, while larger in absolute terms, remains a small fraction of its earnings.

4. **Capital Investment** – Capital expenditures are markedly higher for Entity 2 (€32.4 m) than for Entity 1 (€4.6 m), reflecting the larger scale of its operations and growth initiatives. Capital spending includes additions to property, plant and equipment, construction in progress, investment properties, land‑use rights, and intangible assets (excluding content‑related assets).

**Definitions (as per the provided context)**  
- **EBITDA**: Operating profit less interest income and other net gains/losses, plus depreciation of property, plant and equipment, investment properties, right‑of‑use assets, and amortisation of intangible assets.  
- **Adjusted EBITDA**: EBITDA plus equity‑settled share‑based compensation expenses.  
- **Adjusted EBITDA margin**: Adjusted EBITDA divided by revenue.  
- **Net debt**: Cash and cash equivalents, term deposits, and other cash‑like items minus borrowings and notes payable.  
- **Capital expenditures**: Additions (excluding business combinations) to property, plant and equipment, construction in progress, investment properties, land‑use rights, and intangible assets (excluding video, music, game licences, and other content).

**Conclusion**

Both entities demonstrate solid earnings performance, low financing costs, and healthy liquidity. Entity 2, while larger and more capital‑intensive, achieves a slightly higher profitability margin, suggesting effective scale‑driven operations. The negative net debt positions further reinforce the financial strength of both entities.

synth_text.text:

Despite the cash outflow, the company entered year‑end with strong liquidity. Cash, cash equivalents and short‑term investments totaled **$173.5 million** (up from $137.2 million the prior year). Key contextual points include:

* **Historical financing** – the 2015 IPO raised net proceeds of $68.3 million after underwriting costs.  
* **Operating performance** – the company recorded operating losses of $1.2 million in 2019, $7.0 million in 2018, and $10.4 million in 2017, and expects a loss in FY 2020 while maintaining positive operating cash flow.  
* **Capital expenditures** – FY 2019 capital spending was $28.8 million, largely for expanding the grid architecture ($25.8 million). FY 2020 capital outlays are projected to rise significantly due to one‑time facility build‑outs in the U.K. and additional data‑center expansion in the U.S.

synth_text.text:

synth_text.text:

synth_text.title: Conagra Brands Net Income and Earnings‑Per‑Share Summary (Fiscal 2019 vs. 2018)
synth_text.text:
**Financial Overview**

| Fiscal Year | Net Income Available to Common Stockholders | Basic Shares (M) | Diluted Shares (M) | Basic EPS* | Diluted EPS* |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------|------------------|--------------------|------------|--------------|
| 2019 | **$678.3 million** (continuing operations $680.2 M; discontinued loss $(1.9) M) | 444.0 | 445.6 | **$1.53** | **$1.52** |
| 2018 | **$808.4 million** (continuing operations $794.1 M; discontinued gain $14.3 M) | 403.9 | 407.4 | **$2.00** | **$1.99** |

\*EPS is calculated as net income divided by the respective share count.

**Key Points**

1. **Net Income Trend** – Net income available to common shareholders declined from $808.4 M in fiscal 2018 to $678.3 M in fiscal 2019, reflecting a modest drop in continuing‑operation earnings and a shift from a $14.3 M gain to a $1.9 M loss in discontinued operations.

2. **Earnings‑Per‑Share Impact** – Correspondingly, basic EPS fell from roughly $2.00 per share in 2018 to $1.53 per share in 2019. Diluted EPS showed a similar decline, moving from $1.99 to $1.52 per share.

3. **Share Count Changes** – Basic weighted‑average shares increased from 403.9 M to 444.0 M, and diluted shares rose from 407.4 M to 445.6 M. The increase stems largely from the issuance of 77.5 M shares to former Pinnacle shareholders and a 16.3 M‑share public offering related to the Pinnacle acquisition (see Note 10 of the consolidated financial statements).

4. **Dilution Factors** – Diluted share counts incorporate the dilutive effect of stock options, restricted stock units, and other securities. For fiscal 2019, 2.0 M stock options were excluded because their effect was antidilutive, consistent with the company’s policy of omitting antidilutive options from diluted EPS calculations.

**Conclusion**

While Conagra Brands maintained strong profitability, the combination of higher share counts from the Pinnacle acquisition and a reduction in discontinued‑operation gains led to lower earnings per share in fiscal 2019 compared with fiscal 2018. The figures above provide a concise snapshot of the company’s net income and EPS performance across the two most recent fiscal years.

text.value: ADJUSTED NET EARNINGS AND ADJUSTED EPS
The terms adjusted net earnings and adjusted EPS do not have any standardized meaning under IFRS. Therefore, they are unlikely to be comparable to similar measures presented by other issuers.

We define adjusted net earnings as net earnings attributable to common shareholders before severance, acquisition and other costs, net mark-to-market losses (gains) on derivatives used to economically hedge equity settled share-based compensation plans, net losses (gains) on investments, early debt redemption costs and impairment charges, net of tax and NCI. We define adjusted EPS as adjusted net earnings per BCE common share.

We use adjusted net earnings and adjusted EPS, and we believe that certain investors and analysts use these measures, among other ones, to assess the performance of our businesses without the effects of severance, acquisition and other costs, net mark-to-market losses (gains) on derivatives used to economically hedge equity settled share-based compensation plans, net losses (gains) on investments, early debt redemption costs and impairment charges, net of tax and NCI. We exclude these items because they affect the comparability of our financial results and could potentially distort the analysis of trends in business performance. Excluding these items does not imply they are non-recurring
The most comparable IFRS financial measures are net earnings attributable to common shareholders and EPS.

synth_text.title: Fair‑Value Assessment of the LumaSense Acquisition (2019)
synth_text.text:
In 2019 Advanced Energy Industries completed its fair‑value assessment of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the LumaSense acquisition. The initial fair‑value measurement (first table row) showed total assets of **$105,166 k** and total assumed liabilities of **$20,482 k**, resulting in a net fair‑value of **$84,684 k**. 

During the measurement period, Advanced Energy made several adjustments based on the final valuation report. These adjustments (second table row) reduced goodwill by **$11,774 k**, increased intangible assets to **$17,240 k**, and altered deferred tax assets and other liabilities. After the adjustments, the net assets acquired were recorded at **$0** (the total assets and liabilities both equal $4,559 k), reflecting a bargain‑purchase situation where the fair value of the identifiable net assets exceeded the purchase price.

The adjustments included:
- Elimination of goodwill, turning it into a negative amount (bargain purchase).
- Re‑allocation of excess purchase price to intangible assets.
- Updates to deferred tax assets (now a negative balance) and the addition of other liabilities.

These changes illustrate how Advanced Energy refined its valuation to accurately reflect the fair value of the LumaSense assets and liabilities as of the acquisition date.

**Key observations**

* The majority of both borrowing types are scheduled for repayment in the 2‑to‑5‑year horizon, accounting for roughly 45 % of fixed‑rate debt and 55 % of floating‑rate debt.
* Short‑term obligations (≤1 year) represent a modest share, amounting to just over £110 million in total.
* Long‑term debt (>5 years) remains significant, especially for floating‑rate borrowings (£2.16 billion).

**Additional context**

* Fixed‑rate borrowings and CMBS are measured at Level 1 fair value (quoted market prices), whereas unlisted floating‑rate borrowings are measured at Level 2 (carrying value).
* Certain borrowing agreements contain financial covenants; breaches could alter the repayment schedule.
* As of 31 December 2019, the Group had undrawn borrowing facilities of £238.5 million (down from £274.2 million in 2018), maturing in 2021‑2022, including £42.1 million earmarked for development finance.

Overall, the Group’s debt profile is weighted toward medium‑term maturities, with a balanced mix of fixed‑ and floating‑rate obligations and additional capacity available through undrawn facilities.

synth_text.text:
On 2 October 2017 the Company completed the acquisition of Fagerdala Singapore Pte Ltd., a Singapore‑based polyethylene‑foam manufacturer, for an estimated consideration of **$106.6 million** (equivalent to S$144.7 million). The purchase‑price allocation, expressed in millions of U.S. dollars, is summarised below:

**Initial allocation (as of 2 Oct 2017)**

**Liabilities assumed**  
- **Short‑term borrowings:** $14.0 m

- **Other current liabilities:** $15.1 m  
- **Long‑term debt (net of current portion):** $3.8 m  
- **Non‑current deferred taxes:** $11.7 m  
- **Total liabilities:** **$51.5 m**

**Adjustments (post‑closing)**  
Subsequent purchase‑price adjustments reduced the consideration by **$0.4 m** and slightly altered the asset and liability balances: inventories increased by $0.1 m, identifiable intangibles rose by $0.7 m, goodwill decreased by $1.5 m, other current liabilities fell by $0.1 m, and non‑current deferred taxes were reduced by $0.2 m. **Resulting net assets** after adjustments amount to **$106.3 m** (total assets $157.4 m less total liabilities $51.2 m), closely matching the consideration transferred. The acquisition adds significant manufacturing capacity in Asia, expands the Company’s foam‑fabrication expertise, and strengthens its Product Care division across multiple industries.

synth_text.text:

Expected interest payments on this debt total $127.8 million (due within one year), $166.6 million (1‑3 years), $3.8 million (3‑5 years) and none beyond five years.  

- **Operating lease obligations for vessels in operation** total **$142.7 million** (primary) and **$81.6 million** (secondary). Approximately 41 % of these charter payments are estimated to cover the vessels’ operational costs.  

- **Operating lease obligations for vessels to be delivered** are **$13.6 million** and **$12.9 million**, respectively, presented on an undiscounted basis.  

- **Acquisition of six liquid barges** carries principal obligations of **$4.4 million** and **$5.3 million**. These amounts do not include the expected interest of $0.3 million (≤1 year), $1.8 million (1‑3 years), $0.9 million (3‑5 years) and $0.1 million (>5 years) associated with the shipbuilding contract.  

- **Rent obligations** are minimal, at **$0.4 million** and **$0.1 million**, relating to lease agreements for operating port terminals and various offices. Following the August 30 2019 sale of the management division, Navios Holdings no longer has office‑lease commitments.  

- **Land‑lease agreements** amount to **$1.1 million** in both reporting lines.  

Summing all categories, the total contractual obligations are **$1,623.2 million** for the primary set and **$170.1 million** for the secondary set. These figures provide stakeholders with a clear view of the company’s upcoming payment commitments, exclusive of interest expenses, and highlight the financial structure underpinning its maritime operations.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
As of December 31 2019, Navios Logistics reported contractual payment obligations amounting to **$2.05 billion** for its primary operating entity and **$168.7 million** for a secondary segment. These obligations are categorized into long‑term debt, operating lease commitments for vessels, acquisition payments for six liquid barges, rent obligations, and land‑lease agreements.

**Key Obligation Categories**

| Obligation Type | Primary Entity (US$ million) | Secondary Segment (US$ million) |
|-----------------|------------------------------|---------------------------------|

\*Approximately 41 % of the time‑charter lease payments relate to operational costs for the vessels. The amounts shown are undiscounted lease payments (footnote 4).  
\**Represents principal payments for the future obligation to acquire six liquid barges; interest on these obligations is excluded (footnote 5).

**Additional Context**

* **Long‑term debt** figures exclude all interest costs associated with the outstanding credit facilities, which are tied to LIBOR plus a margin of 2.75 %–3.25 % per annum. Expected interest payments for 2019 total $298.8 million, distributed across various maturities (less than 1 year, 1‑3 years, 3‑5 years, and beyond 5 years).  
* **Rent obligations** pertain to lease agreements for Navios Logistics’ operating port terminals and offices. Following the August 30 2019 sale of the management division, Navios Holdings no longer carries office‑lease obligations.  
* All lease and acquisition figures are presented on an undiscounted basis; the associated interest components are disclosed separately in the footnotes.

**Interpretation**

Long‑term debt dominates Navios Logistics’ contractual commitments, representing roughly 77 % of the total $2.05 billion obligation for the primary entity. Operating lease obligations for vessels in operation are the next most significant category, accounting for about 18 % of total commitments. The acquisition of six liquid barges, while relatively modest in principal amount, adds a fixed‑rate financing component that will generate additional interest expenses not reflected in the principal totals.

Overall, the company’s contractual landscape is heavily weighted toward debt financing, with lease and acquisition obligations forming a smaller but material portion of its future cash‑flow commitments.

text.value: Indebtedness
The following table presents selected financial information on our indebtedness (in thousands):

As of December 27, 2019, we have various floating- and fixed-rate debt instruments with varying maturities for an aggregate principal amount of $392.1 million. See Note 9 “Debt Obligations” to our consolidated financial statements for a full description of our debt instruments.

On November 22, 2019, we issued $150.0 million aggregate principal amount of 1.875% Convertible Senior Notes (the “Senior Notes”). Approximately $43.2 million of the net proceeds were used to repay all outstanding borrowings then outstanding under our ABL and we intend to use the remainder for working capital and general corporate purposes, which may include future acquisitions.

On July 25, 2018, the holders of the $36.8 million principal amount of convertible subordinated notes that were issued in connection with our acquisition of Del Monte converted these notes and related accrued interest of $0.3 million into 1,246,272 shares of the Company’s common stock.

On June 29, 2018, we entered into an asset-based loan facility (“ABL”) that increased our borrowing capacity from $75.0 million to $150.0 million. Additionally, we reduced the fixed-rate portion of interest charged on our senior secured term loan (“Term Loan”) from 475 basis points to 350 basis points over Adjusted LIBOR as a result of repricings executed on December 14, 2017 and November 16, 2018.

A portion of the interest rate charged on our Term Loan is currently based on LIBOR and, at our option, a component of the interest charged on the borrowings outstanding on our ABL, if any, may bear interest rates based on LIBOR. LIBOR has been the subject of reform and is expected to phase out by the end of fiscal 2021. The consequences of the discontinuation of LIBOR cannot be entirely predicted but could impact the interest expense we incur on these debt instruments. We will negotiate alternatives to LIBOR with our lenders before LIBOR ceases to be a widely available reference rate.

text.value: NOTE 19—RESTRUCTURING

In 2019, we initiated projects to restructure and modify our supply chain strategy, functional responsibilities, methods, capabilities, processes and rationalize suppliers with the goal of reducing ongoing costs and increasing the efficiencies of our worldwide procurement organization. The majority of the costs associated with these restructuring activities are related to consultants that we have engaged in connection with these efforts, and such costs have been recognized by our corporate entity. The total costs of this restructuring project are expected to exceed amounts incurred to date by $0.9 million and these efforts are expected to be completed early in fiscal 2020. Also, in fiscal 2019 our CTS and CGD segments incurred restructuring charges, consisting primarily of employee severance costs related to headcount reductions initiated to optimize our cost positions. The total costs of each of these restructuring plans initiated thus far are not expected to be significantly greater than the charges incurred to date.

Our fiscal 2018 restructuring activities related primarily to expenses incurred by our corporate entity to establish a North American shared services center. Our fiscal 2017 restructuring activities included corporate efforts to increase the centralization and efficiency of our manufacturing processes, as well as restructuring charges incurred by our CGD businesses related to the elimination of a level of management in the CGD simulator business.

synth_text.title: Trends in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss (2017‑2019) for Two Entities
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The data summarize the evolution of accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOC loss) for two separate entities over the fiscal years ending January 31, 2017, 2018, and 2019.  The figures include the year‑end AOC balances, OCI before reclassifications, the portion reclassified to profit or loss, tax effects, and the net OCI for each period.

**Entity 1**  
- **AOC Balance:** ‑$33.8 million (2017) → ‑$29.3 million (2018) → ‑$16.3 million (2019).  
- **OCI before reclassifications:** $4.3 million (2017) → $14.7 million (2018).  
- **Reclassifications:** $0.9 million loss (2017) → $0.3 million gain (2018).  
- **Tax effects:** ‑$2.0 million (2017); none reported for 2018.  
- **Net OCI:** $4.5 million (2017) → $13.0 million (2018).  

The positive OCI each year reduced the accumulated loss, resulting in a steady improvement of the AOC balance.

**Entity 2**  
- **AOC Balance:** ‑$160.8 million (2017) → ‑$79.2 million (2018) → ‑$137.0 million (2019).  
- **OCI before reclassifications:** $86.3 million loss (2017) → ‑$58.3 million loss (2018).  
- **Reclassifications:** ‑$0.1 million loss (2017); none in 2018.  
- **Tax effects:** +$0.5 million (2017); none reported for 2018.  
- **Net OCI:** ‑$81.6 million loss (2017) → +$57.8 million gain (2018).  

Entity 2 experienced a large loss in 2017, a reversal to a gain in 2018, and a return to a higher loss in 2019, leading to a more volatile AOC balance.

**Contextual Insight**  
The accompanying notes explain that the accumulated other comprehensive loss is presented net of taxes.  Reclassifications related to gains and losses on available‑for‑sale debt securities, derivative instruments, and defined‑benefit pension components are recorded within “Interest and other expense, net,” which accounts for the relatively small reclassification amounts shown in the table.

**Key Takeaways**  
- Both entities show AOC loss balances that are gradually offset by positive OCI, though the magnitude and consistency differ.  
- Entity 1 demonstrates a clear, steady reduction in its accumulated loss, while Entity 2’s AOC balance fluctuates markedly due to a reversal of OCI in 2018.  
- The modest reclassification figures reflect that most adjustments for securities, derivatives, and pension components are captured elsewhere in the financial statements, as noted in the additional context.

synth_text.title: Summary of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss (2017‑2019)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOC loss) was tracked over three fiscal years, ending January 31, 2017, 2018, and 2019. The figures reflect both the underlying comprehensive loss before reclassifications and the net effect after accounting for reclassifications and related tax impacts.

**2017 (Year ending January 31, 2017)**  
- Opening balance: **$(178.5) million**.  
- Other comprehensive loss before reclassifications: **$65.5 million**.  
- Pre‑tax losses reclassified from accumulated OCI: **$(8.6) million**.  
- Tax effect on the reclassifications: **$(2.6) million**.  
- Net other comprehensive loss for the period: **$54.7 million**.  
- Closing balance: **$(123.8) million**.

**2018 (Year ending January 31, 2018)**  
- Opening balance: **$(123.8) million** (the 2017 closing balance).  
- Other comprehensive loss before reclassifications: **$(22.3) million**.  
- Pre‑tax gains reclassified to OCI: **$13.7 million**.  
- Tax effect on the reclassifications: not separately disclosed (implicitly included in the net figure).  
- Net other comprehensive loss for the period: **$(11.2) million**.  
- Closing balance: **$(135.0) million**.

**2019 (Year ending January 31, 2019)**  
- Opening balance: **$(135.0) million** (the 2018 closing balance).  
- No detailed breakdown is provided for 2019 in the table, but the balance remains negative, indicating a continued accumulated loss.

**Key Drivers and Context**  
- **Reclassifications**: Gains and losses on available‑for‑sale debt securities, derivative instruments, and defined‑benefit pension components are reclassified through “Interest and other expense, net,” as noted in the accompanying disclosures. These reclassifications directly affect the “Pre‑tax gains/losses reclassified” line items.  
- **Tax Effects**: The 2017 tax effect of $(2.6) million reduced the net loss for that year. Subsequent years do not list a separate tax effect, suggesting it is embedded within the net figures.  
- **Trend**: The accumulated loss narrowed from $(178.5) million at the start of 2017 to $(123.8) million by year‑end 2017, but increased again to $(135.0) million by the end of 2018, reflecting a net loss in 2018 despite the positive reclassification of $13.7 million.

**Conclusion**  
Across the 2017‑2019 period, the company’s accumulated other comprehensive loss remained negative, fluctuating due to both underlying comprehensive losses and the impact of reclassifications and tax adjustments. The disclosures indicate that reclassifications related to financial instruments and pension components are captured within “Interest and other expense, net,” providing further insight into the composition of the OCI figures.

synth_text.title: Summary of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (Loss) for 2017‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table presents accumulated other comprehensive income (OCI) – net of taxes – for two reporting entities over the three fiscal years ending January 31, 2017, 2018, and 2019. OCI includes unrealized gains and losses on available‑for‑sale debt securities, derivative instruments, and pension plan components, which are reclassified to “Interest and other expense, net” when realized (see the additional context).

**Entity 1**  
- **Balances**: $14.6 million (2017) → –$16.6 million (2018) → $15.0 million (2019).  
- **Net OCI for the period**: –$31.2 million in 2017, turning to a positive $31.6 million in 2019.  
- **Key drivers**:  
  - 2017 recorded a loss before reclassifications of $(24.5) million, with pre‑tax losses reclassified of $(9.9) million and a tax effect of $(1.1) million, resulting in the net loss.  
  - 2019 showed a gain before reclassifications of $20.6 million, with pre‑tax gains reclassified of $12.1 million, producing the net positive OCI.  

**Entity 2**  
- **Balances**: $1.5 million (2017) → $1.3 million (2018) → $3.3 million (2019).  
- **Net OCI for the period**: –$0.2 million in 2017, rising to $2.0 million in 2019.  
- **Key drivers**:  
  - 2017’s loss before reclassifications was $(0.6) million, partially offset by a $0.3 million pre‑tax gain reclassified, yielding a small net loss.  
  - 2019 recorded a gain before reclassifications of $0.7 million and a $1.3 million pre‑tax gain reclassified, resulting in a net OCI of $2.0 million.  

**Interpretation**  
Both entities experienced volatility in OCI, shifting from losses in 2017 to gains by 2019. The swings are largely attributable to reclassifications of unrealized gains/losses on available‑for‑sale securities, derivatives, and pension components, as noted in the accompanying disclosures. Tax effects modestly reduced the net OCI in 2017 for Entity 1, while no tax impact was reported for Entity 2.

Overall, the accumulated OCI balances moved from modest positive positions in 2017 to a mixed picture in 2018 (including a negative balance for Entity 1) and returned to stronger positive balances in 2019, reflecting the underlying market and actuarial changes captured in the OCI line items.

synth_text.title: Summary of Changes in Contract Assets and Deferred Revenue
synth_text.text:
The table compares key contract‑related balance‑sheet items for two consecutive reporting periods.

- **Contract assets (current)** fell from **$5,558** to **$3,711**, indicating a reduction in amounts earned but not yet billed to clients.  
- **Long‑term contract assets** decreased from **$5,420** to **$2,543**, showing a lower portion of contract assets expected to be realized beyond one year.  
- The combined figure for other current assets (the unnamed column) dropped from **$195,487** to **$190,489**.  

On the liability side:

- **Deferred revenue** declined from **$190,080** to **$185,145**, reflecting fewer billings received in advance of revenue recognition.  
- **Long‑term deferred revenue** showed a modest decline from **$5,407** to **$5,344**, indicating a slight reduction in advance payments that will be recognized after one year.  

**Contextual interpretation**  
Contract assets represent client‑committed amounts where revenue recognized exceeds the amount billed, and they are subject to performance‑obligation conditions. Deferred revenue consists of payments received before revenue can be recognized. The two items are netted at the contract level each period. The observed decrease in deferred revenue aligns with the explanation that the change in the year ended December 31, 2019 was mainly due to new billings in advance of revenue recognition, partially offset by revenue recognized during the period. The simultaneous decline in contract assets suggests that less revenue was recognized without corresponding billing, possibly because fewer performance obligations were completed or because billing cycles changed.

Overall, the data indicate a modest contraction in both the assets awaiting billing and the liabilities representing advance payments, consistent with the dynamics of billing and revenue recognition described in the additional context.

text.value: Significant components of our deferred tax assets and liabilities consist of the following:

The United States Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the “Tax Act”) was enacted on December 22, 2017 and introduced significant changes to the income tax law in the United States. Effective in 2018, the Tax Act reduced the United States statutory tax rate from 35% to 21% and created new taxes on certain foreign-sourced earnings and certain related-party payments, which are referred to as the global intangible low-taxed income tax and the base erosion tax, respectively.
In addition, in 2017 we were subject to a one-time transition tax on accumulated foreign subsidiary earnings not previously subject to income tax in the United States.

Due to the timing of the enactment and the complexity involved in applying the provisions of the Tax Act, we made reasonable estimates of the effects and recorded provisional expense of $15.3 million in our financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2017 in accordance with guidance in Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118 (“SAB 118”), which allows a measurement period of up to one year after the enactment date to finalize the recording of the related tax impacts.

This provisional expense included $10.1 million expense for the remeasurement of deferred tax balances to reflect the lower federal rate and expense of $5.2 million for the one-time transition tax on accumulated foreign subsidiary earnings not previously subject to income tax in the United States.

Adjustments to these provisional amounts that we recorded in 2018 did not have a significant impact on our consolidated financial statements. Our accounting for the effects of the enactment of U.S. Tax Reform is now complete. Due to our divestiture of our investment in Netsmart, the amounts noted above do not include the provisional amounts recorded by Netsmart in 2017.

We had federal net operating loss (“NOL”) carryforwards of $174 million and $164 million as of December 31, 2019, and 2018, respectively. The federal NOL carryforward includes US NOL carryovers of $8 million and Israeli NOL carryovers of $56 million that do not expire. As of December 31, 2019 and 2018, we had state NOL carryforwards of $1 million and $2 million, respectively.

The NOL carryforwards expire in various amounts starting in 2020 for both federal and state tax purposes. The utilization of the federal NOL carryforwards is subject to limitation under the rules regarding changes in stock ownership as determined by the Internal Revenue Code.
