text.value: Revenue

The Company adopted ASC 606 effective January 1, 2018 using the modified retrospective method. The Company recognized the cumulative effect of initially applying ASC 606, which was immaterial, as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings. The comparative prior period information is accounted for in accordance with the previous revenue guidance, ASC 605, and has not been restated. In accordance with ASC 606, the Company recognizes revenue under the core principle to depict the transfer of control to the Company’s customers in an amount reflecting the consideration the Company expects to be entitled. In order to achieve that core principle, the Company applies the following five step approach: (1) identify the contract with a customer, (2) identify the performance obligations in the contract, (3) determine the transaction price, (4) allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations in the contract and (5) recognize revenue when a performance obligation is satisfied.

Revenue for product sales is recognized at the point in time when control transfers to the Company’s customers, which is generally when products are shipped from the Company’s manufacturing facilities or when delivered to the customer’s named location. When the Company performs shipping and handling activities after the transfer of control to the customer (e.g., when control transfers prior to delivery), they are considered to be fulfillment activities, and accordingly, the costs are accrued for when the related revenue is recognized. Taxes collected on behalf of customers relating to product sales and remitted to governmental authorities, principally sales taxes, are excluded from revenue.
The opening and closing balances of the Company’s accounts receivable and deferred revenue are as follows (in thousands):

The amount of revenue recognized in the period that was included in the opening deferred revenue balances was approximately$5.1 million for the year ended December 31, 2019. Generally, increases in current and non-current deferred revenue are related to billings to, or advance payments from, customers for which the Company has not yet fulfilled its performance obligations, and decreases are related to revenue recognized. Deferred revenue not expected to be recognized within the Company’s operating cycle of one year is presented as a component of “Other long-term liabilities” on the consolidated balance sheet.

At times, the Company receives orders for products that may be delivered over multiple dates that may extend across reporting periods. The Company invoices for each delivery upon shipment and recognizes revenues for each distinct product delivered, assuming transfer of control has occurred. Generally, scheduled delivery dates are within one year, and the Company has elected to use the optional exemption whereby revenues allocated to partially completed contracts with an expected duration of one year or less are not disclosed. As of December 31, 2019, the Company had no contracts with unsatisfied performance obligations with a duration of more than one year.

text.value: Cash Flow Hedges

The Company has interest rate swap agreements to hedge the cash flows of a portion of its variable rate senior secured term loans (the "Variable Rate Loans"). The objective of these instruments is to reduce variability in the forecasted interest payments of the Company's Variable Rate Loans, which is based on the LIBOR rate. Under the terms of the interest rate swap agreements, the Company will receive monthly variable interest payments based on the one-month LIBOR rate and will pay interest at a fixed rate.

In February 2018, the Company entered into interest rate swap agreements to hedge the cash flows of an additional $250 million of its Variable Rate Loans. The interest rate swap agreements on $1.1 billion of the Company's Variable Rate Loans had a maturity date of December 2021 and a fixed interest rate of 1.08%.

The interest rate swap agreements on $300 million and $250 million of the Company's Variable Rate Loans both had a maturity date of August 2022 and fixed interest rates of 1.66% and 2.59%, respectively. The counterparties to these agreements are financial institutions.

In September 2018, the Company terminated its existing interest rate swaps. The net derivative gain of $60 million related to the discontinued cash flow hedge remained within accumulated other comprehensive loss and is being reclassified into earnings over the remaining life of the original hedge as the hedged variable rate debt impacts earnings.

Additionally, in September 2018, the Company entered into new interest rate swap agreements to hedge the cash flows of $1.5 billion of the Company's Variable Rate Loans. These interest rate swap agreements have a maturity date of August 2025 and a fixed interest rate of 3.00%.

The interest rate swap transactions were accounted for as cash flow hedges. The gain (loss) on the swap is reported as a component of other comprehensive income (loss) and is reclassified into earnings when the interest payments on the underlying hedged items impact earnings. A qualitative assessment of hedge effectiveness is performed on a quarterly basis, unless facts and circumstances indicate the hedge may no longer be highly effective.

synth_text.title: Interest Expense and Cash‑Flow Hedge Accounting Summary
synth_text.text:
During the reporting period the Company recorded a net interest expense of **$140 million** in its consolidated statements of income. The effect of its cash‑flow hedges contributed **$10 million** to other comprehensive (loss) income, while no amount was scheduled for reclassification from accumulated other comprehensive loss into earnings over the next twelve months, according to the table data.

The Company employs interest‑rate swap agreements to hedge the cash flows of its variable‑rate senior secured term loans. These swaps convert variable LIBOR‑based interest payments into fixed‑rate obligations, reducing earnings volatility. Under the hedge accounting rules, gains or losses on the swaps are first recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI) and are subsequently reclassified into earnings when the underlying interest payments affect the income statement.

Historically, the Company has entered into multiple swap programs covering $1.1 billion, $300 million, $250 million, and $1.5 billion of variable‑rate debt, with fixed rates ranging from 1.08 % to 3.00 % and maturities extending to August 2025. A net derivative gain of $60 million from a terminated hedge remains in accumulated other comprehensive loss and is being reclassified over the remaining life of the original hedge.

Although the table indicates no reclassification scheduled for the next 12 months, the narrative states that the Company **expects to reclassify approximately $1 million of gains** from accumulated other comprehensive loss into earnings during that period. This suggests a modest upcoming transfer from OCI to earnings, consistent with the company’s ongoing hedge effectiveness assessments.

In summary, the Company’s interest expense of $140 million is partially offset by a $10 million OCI impact from cash‑flow hedges, with an anticipated modest reclassification of hedge gains into earnings in the near term.

synth_text.title: Impact of Cash‑Flow Hedge Accounting on Interest Expense and Comprehensive Income
synth_text.text:
The company’s consolidated statements of income show net interest expense after cash‑flow hedge effects of **$133 million** (first column) and **$138 million** (second column). These amounts represent the total interest cost on the company’s variable‑rate senior secured term loans, adjusted for the impact of interest‑rate swap hedges.

Because the swaps are designated as cash‑flow hedges, the gains or losses on the hedging instruments are first recorded in **other comprehensive income (OCI)**. In the reporting periods shown, the company recognized a **loss of $55 million** in OCI in the first column, which narrowed to a **loss of $7 million** in the second column. This reduction reflects the net effect of the swap gains and losses after the termination of earlier hedges and the initiation of new swaps with fixed rates ranging from 1.08 % to 3.00 %.

As the underlying variable‑rate debt incurs interest, the accumulated OCI related to the hedges is gradually **re‑classified into earnings**. The table indicates that **$7 million** (first column) and **$6 million** (second column) are slated to be moved from accumulated OCI into the income statement over the next twelve months. This re‑classification aligns with the company’s accounting policy that hedge gains (or losses) are transferred to earnings when the hedged interest payments affect the profit‑and‑loss line.

The additional context clarifies that the company entered into multiple interest‑rate swap agreements—covering $1.5 billion of variable‑rate loans with maturities through August 2025 and fixed rates up to 3.00 %—to mitigate interest‑rate volatility. A prior hedge termination left a $60 million gain in OCI, which is being amortized into earnings over the remaining hedge life. The company expects to re‑classify an additional **$1 million** of accumulated OCI gains into earnings within the next year, further illustrating the ongoing impact of its cash‑flow hedge strategy on both OCI and net interest expense.

Overall, the figures demonstrate how the company’s cash‑flow hedge program reduces earnings volatility by shifting interest‑rate swap results through OCI before ultimately recognizing them in earnings as the hedged interest payments materialize.

synth_text.text:
During the fiscal year, the combined benefit obligation for the pension and post‑retirement plans decreased from **$13,244 million** at the beginning of the year to **$13,064 million** at year‑end, a net reduction of **$180 million**.

The change resulted from the following components (all figures in millions of dollars):

- **Interest cost:** $409 – the increase in the obligation due to the time value of money.  
- **Actuarial (gain) loss:** **$586 gain** – primarily driven by the adoption of revised Society of Actuaries mortality tables and projection scales, which lowered the projected benefit obligation and is recorded as an actuarial gain. This gain is part of accumulated other comprehensive loss and is being amortized over the remaining estimated life of plan participants (approximately 16 years as of 31 December 2019).  
- **Benefits paid from plan assets:** $(1,238) – cash payments made to retirees, which directly reduced the obligation.  
- **Plan amendments** and **Special termination benefits charge:** none reported for the year.

The actuarial gain more than offset the combined service and interest costs, and together with the benefits paid, produced the overall decline in the obligation. text.value: Non-GAAP Measures

We define Adjusted EBITDA as our net income before interest expense, interest income, other income, net, provision for / (benefit from) income taxes, amortization and depreciation, stock-based compensation expense, acquisition-related expense and legal costs and settlement fees incurred in connection with non-ordinary course litigation and other disputes, particularly costs involved in ongoing intellectual property litigation. We do not consider these items to be indicative of our core operating performance. The non-cash items include amortization and depreciation expense, stock-based compensation expense related to stock options and other forms of equity compensation, including, but not limited to, the sale of common stock. We do not adjust for ordinary course legal expenses resulting from maintaining and enforcing our intellectual property portfolio and license agreements. Adjusted EBITDA is not a measure calculated in accordance with GAAP. See the table below for a reconciliation of Adjusted EBITDA to net income, the most directly comparable financial measure calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP.

we believe that Adjusted EBITDA provides useful information to investors and others in understanding and evaluating our
operating results in the same manner as our management and board of directors.We have included Adjusted EBITDA in this report because it is a key measure that our management uses to understand and evaluate our core operating performance and trends, to generate future operating plans, to make strategic decisions regarding the allocation of capital and to make investments in initiatives that are focused on cultivating new markets for our solutions. We also use certain non-GAAP financial measures, including Adjusted EBITDA, as performance measures under our executive bonus plan. Further, we believe the exclusion of certain expenses in calculating Adjusted EBITDA facilitates comparisons of our operating performance on a period-to-period basis and, in the case of exclusion of acquisition-related expense and certain historical legal expenses, excludes items that we do not consider to be indicative of our core operating performance. Accordingly,

Our use of Adjusted EBITDA has limitations as an analytical tool, and you should not consider it in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our financial results as reported under GAAP. Some of these limitations are: (a) although depreciation and amortization are non-cash charges, the assets being depreciated and amortized may have to be replaced in the future, and Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect cash capital expenditure requirements for such replacements or for new capital expenditure requirements; (b) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect changes in, or cash requirements for, our working capital needs; (c) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect the potentially dilutive impact of equity-based compensation; (d) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect tax payments that may represent a reduction in cash available to us; and (e) other companies, including companies in our industry, may calculate Adjusted EBITDA or similarly titled measures differently, which reduces its usefulness as a comparative measure.

Because of these and other limitations, you should consider Adjusted EBITDA alongside our other GAAP-based financial performance measures, net income and our other GAAP financial results. synth_text.title: 2017 Financial Reconciliation: Net Income and Adjusted EBITDA Overview
synth_text.text:
In fiscal year 2017 the company reported a net income of **$29.3 million** (in thousands) and an **Adjusted EBITDA of $71.6 million**. The Adjusted EBITDA figure is derived by adding a total of **$42.4 million** in adjustments to the GAAP net income. These adjustments consist of:

- **Interest expense, interest income and other income, net:** $1.1 million  
- **Provision for (benefit from) income taxes:** $3.0 million  
- **Amortization and depreciation expense:** $17.7 million  
- **Stock‑based compensation expense:** $7.4 million  
- **Acquisition‑related expense:** $5.9 million  
- **Litigation expense:** $7.2 million  

The sum of these line items ($42.4 million) reconciles the GAAP net income to the non‑GAAP Adjusted EBITDA of $71.6 million.

**Definition and purpose**  
Adjusted EBITDA is defined by the company as net income before the above‑listed items, which are considered non‑core to operating performance. The metric is used by management and the board to evaluate core operating results, guide strategic capital allocation, and assess performance for executive compensation.

**Limitations**  
While useful, Adjusted EBITDA does not capture cash capital‑expenditure needs, working‑capital changes, tax cash outflows, or the dilutive effect of equity‑based compensation. Moreover, calculation methods can vary across companies, limiting its comparability.

Investors are therefore encouraged to view Adjusted EBITDA alongside GAAP measures such as net income to obtain a complete picture of the company’s financial health.

synth_text.text:
**Definition and Purpose**  
Adjusted EBITDA is a non‑GAAP performance metric that starts with net income and adds back interest expense (net of interest income), income‑tax provision (or benefit), amortization and depreciation, stock‑based compensation, acquisition‑related costs, and litigation expenses. The company uses this measure to gauge core operating performance, guide strategic decisions, and evaluate executive compensation, while acknowledging that it does not replace GAAP results.

**Reconciliation Summary (in thousands of dollars)**  

| Fiscal Year | Net Income | Total Adjustments | Adjusted EBITDA |
|-------------|------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| 2019 | $53,330 | $54,977 | $108,307 |
| 2018 | $21,524 | $71,557 | $93,081 |

*Key adjustment components*  

- **Interest expense, interest income and other income, net**: –$8,483 (2019) vs. $503 (2018)  
- **Provision for (benefit from) income taxes**: $5,566 (2019) vs. –$9,825 (2018)  
- **Amortization & depreciation**: $22,134 (2019) vs. $21,721 (2018)  
- **Stock‑based compensation**: $20,603 (2019) vs. $13,429 (2018)  
- **Acquisition‑related expense**: $2,403 (2019) vs. — (2018)  
- **Litigation expense**: $12,754 (2019) vs. $45,729 (2018)  

**Observations**  
- Net income more than doubled from 2018 to 2019.  
- Total adjustments fell by roughly $16.6 million, primarily due to lower litigation expenses and the inclusion of acquisition‑related costs in 2019.  
- Consequently, Adjusted EBITDA rose by about $15.2 million, indicating stronger underlying operating performance when non‑core items are excluded.

**Limitations**  
Adjusted EBITDA does not capture cash capital‑expenditure needs, working‑capital changes, tax cash outflows, or the dilutive effect of equity‑based compensation. Moreover, calculation methods can vary across companies, limiting its comparability. Investors should therefore view this metric alongside GAAP results such as net income.

At each reporting date, we weigh all available positive and negative evidence to assess whether it is more-likely-than-not that the Company's deferred tax assets, including deferred tax assets associated with accumulated loss carryforwards and tax credits in the various jurisdictions in which it operates, will be realized. As of December 31, 2019, and 2018, we recorded deferred tax assets related to certain U.S. state and non-U.S. income tax loss carryforwards of $4,724 and $4,647, respectively, and U.S. and non- U.S. tax credits of $15,964 and $16,909, respectively. The deferred tax assets expire in various years primarily between 2021 and 2039.

Generally, we assess if it is more-likely-than-not that our net deferred tax assets will be realized during the available carry-forward periods. As a result, we have determined that valuation allowances of $8,011 and $8,274 should be provided for certain deferred tax assets at December 31, 2019, and 2018, respectively. As of December 31, 2019, the valuation allowances relate to certain U.S. state and non-U.S. loss carry-forwards and certain U.S. state tax credits that management does not anticipate will be utilized.

No valuation allowance was recorded in 2019 against the U.S. federal foreign tax credit carryforwards of $5,785, which expire in varying amounts between 2023 and 2029 as well as the research and development tax credits of $7,495, which expire in varying amounts between 2021 and 2039. We assessed the anticipated realization of those tax credits utilizing future taxable income projections. Based on those projections, management believes it is more-likely-than-not that we will realize the benefits of these credit carryforwards.

synth_text.title: Summary of Long‑Term Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The company’s long‑term deferred tax position is disclosed in Note 18 of the consolidated financial statements. The key figures for the two most recent fiscal years are:

| Year | Non‑current Deferred Tax Assets | Non‑current Deferred Tax Liabilities | Net Deferred Tax Assets |
|------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 2019 | $19,795 (thousands) | $(5,637) (thousands) | $14,158 (thousands) |
| 2018 | $22,201 (thousands) | $(3,990) (thousands) | $18,211 (thousands) |

**Key components (as of 31 Dec 2019 and 2018)**  
- **Loss carryforwards:** U.S. state and non‑U.S. loss carryforwards amount to $4,724 k in 2019 and $4,647 k in 2018.  
- **Tax credits:** U.S. and non‑U.S. tax credits total $15,964 k in 2019 and $16,909 k in 2018. These credits expire primarily between 2021 and 2039.  

**Valuation allowances**  
Management applies valuation allowances where it is not more‑likely‑than‑not that the deferred tax assets will be realized. The allowances recorded were:  
- $8,011 k for 2019 (covering certain U.S. state and non‑U.S. loss carryforwards and some state tax credits).  
- $8,274 k for 2018 (similar categories).  

No allowance was recorded against the U.S. federal foreign tax credit carryforwards ($5,785 k) or the research and development tax credits ($7,495 k) because projected future taxable income supports their expected utilization.

**Trend analysis**  
Net long‑term deferred tax assets declined from $18,211 k in 2018 to $14,158 k in 2019, reflecting a reduction in gross deferred tax assets and an increase in net liabilities. The decrease is primarily driven by a modest rise in non‑current liabilities and the application of valuation allowances to assets that management does not expect to realize.

**Conclusion**  
The company’s long‑term deferred tax assets remain substantial, supported mainly by tax credits that are expected to be realized. However, the net position has contracted year‑over‑year due to higher liabilities and larger valuation allowances, underscoring the importance of ongoing assessments of future taxable income and the timing of credit expirations.

synth_text.title: Summary of Outstanding Sign‑On/Retention and Performance Rights Movements
synth_text.text:
The Group’s equity‑based compensation framework includes two distinct sub‑plans: **sign‑on and retention rights** and **performance rights**.  

**Sign‑on and retention rights** are primarily used to compensate new hires, executives of newly acquired businesses, and high‑potential managers who have little or no existing equity awards. These rights vest solely on a service condition—typically a minimum of two years of continued employment—and do not carry performance targets.  

During the reporting period, the sign‑on/retention pool started with **6,737,076** rights. The Group granted **5,691,731** new rights, of which **586,663** vested and **1,149,550** lapsed. Consequently, the outstanding balance rose to **10,692,594** rights at period end.  

**Performance rights** are awarded to employees who must meet both a service condition and specific performance measures. They are also employed to retain key talent and to compensate employees for foregone equity.  

The performance‑rights pool began the period with **10,692,594** rights. New grants totaled **4,465,617** rights, while **182,601** rights vested and **1,497,852** rights lapsed. This resulted in an ending balance of **13,477,758** rights.  

Overall, the total number of outstanding rights increased from **13,429,670** at the start of the period to **13,477,758** at the end, reflecting the Group’s ongoing strategy to attract, retain, and motivate its workforce through targeted equity incentives.  

The movements summarized above illustrate how the two sub‑plans complement each other: sign‑on and retention rights secure immediate talent acquisition and continuity, while performance rights align employee effort with the Group’s strategic objectives.

synth_text.title: UMC Dividend Distributions and Reserve Policy for 2018‑2019
synth_text.text:
United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) declared cash dividends of **$0.58 per share for 2018** and **$0.75 per share for 2019**. The table does not list amounts for legal or special reserves, implying that no specific figures were disclosed for those categories in the summary.

Under Taiwan Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) regulations, UMC must create a **special reserve** each year‑end equal to any debit elements in equity (e.g., unrealized losses on financial instruments or negative exchange‑difference balances). This reserve is generally prohibited from distribution, but if the underlying debit items are later reversed, the corresponding special reserve can be released for earnings distribution or to offset accumulated deficits.

The earnings distributions were formally approved as follows:
- **2018 distribution:** approved by the shareholders’ meeting on **12 June 2019**.  
- **2019 distribution:** approved by the Board of Directors on **27 April 2020**.

These approvals, together with the regulatory reserve requirement, provide the framework within which UMC’s dividend payouts for the two years were determined.

Overall, UMC’s legal reserve grew modestly from 2018 to 2019, while the special reserve shifted from a large positive balance in 2018 to a negative balance in 2019, reflecting the reversal of earlier debit elements and enabling a higher cash dividend payout in 2019.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Summary – Continuing Operations
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
During the reporting year the Group’s continuing operations generated a modest decline in operating revenue of **13 %**. Despite this reduction, the business delivered solid profitability across both reported and underlying (core) measures.

**Key Financial Highlights (Continuing Operations)**  

| Metric | Reported | Underlying* |
|--------|----------|------------|
| Operating revenue | –13 % (decline) | – |
| Gross profit | **£16 m** | – |
| EBITDA | **£206 m** | **£45 m** |
| EBIT | **£85 m** | **£77 m** |
| NPAT | **£72 m** | **£64 m** |
| EPS (cents) | **76 c** | **65 c** |

\*Underlying results exclude the financial impact of iMoney performance, impairment losses, write‑offs from discontinued assets, and other material one‑off transactions that are not part of the core business.

**Interpretation**  

* **Revenue Pressure:** The 13 % drop in operating revenue reflects market or pricing pressures but did not materially affect the Group’s ability to generate profit.  
* **Profitability:** Reported EBITDA of £206 m and EBIT of £85 m indicate strong operating efficiency. Even after adjusting for non‑core items, underlying EBITDA of £45 m and EBIT of £77 m remain robust.  
* **Net Profit & Earnings per Share:** NPAT of £72 m and an EPS of 76 c demonstrate healthy returns to shareholders. Underlying NPAT of £64 m and EPS of 65 c confirm that the core business continues to be profitable.  

**Business Activities**  
The Group’s principal activities—health, life and car insurance policy sales, mortgage brokerage, energy, broadband, and financial referral services—remained unchanged throughout the year, providing a stable platform for the observed financial performance.

**Conclusion**  
While operating revenue contracted, the Group’s continuing operations sustained strong earnings and cash‑generating capacity. The underlying results, which strip out discontinued and non‑core impacts, reinforce the resilience of the core business model.

synth_text.title: Financial Performance Overview of Continuing Operations
synth_text.text:
The Group’s continuing operations generated **operating revenue of £154.6 bn** in the first period, rising to **£178.1 bn** in the subsequent period, reflecting growth in its core activities of health, life and car insurance sales, mortgage brokerage, energy, broadband and financial referral services. Despite the revenue increase, **gross profit fell** from **£53.2 bn** to **£45.9 bn**, indicating higher cost pressures or a shift in the product mix.

**Reported (IFRS) results** show a deterioration in profitability:
- **EBITDA** moved from a modest **£6.1 bn profit** to a **£5.7 bn loss**.  
- **EBIT** was negative in both periods, deepening from **‑£2.3 bn** to **‑£15.3 bn**.  
- **Net profit after tax (NPAT)** declined sharply, from **‑£4.4 bn** to **‑£15.6 bn**, and **earnings per share (EPS)** fell from **‑1.7 cents** to **‑7.0 cents**.

These headline figures are affected by the performance of discontinued assets, the iMoney segment, impairment losses, and other one‑off items, as explained in the report’s non‑IFRS disclosures.

When these non‑recurring impacts are stripped out, the **underlying (non‑IFRS) results** paint a more positive picture:
- **Underlying EBITDA** remained strong at **£22.9 bn** and **£15.7 bn** respectively.  
- **Underlying EBIT** stayed in profit, at **£15.2 bn** and **£8.5 bn**.  
- **Underlying NPAT** was **£11.1 bn** and **£6.7 bn**, delivering **underlying EPS** of **5.1 cents** and **3.1 cents**.

Thus, while the reported financials suggest a decline driven by the exit of non‑core operations and other exceptional items, the underlying performance indicates that the Group’s continuing business remains profitable and generates solid cash‑flow before financing and tax costs.

In summary, the Group’s core activities have not changed materially, and the underlying earnings demonstrate resilience despite the reported downturn caused by the removal of discontinued operations and related adjustments.

Long-Term Debt

In June 2012, with the acquisition of Novellus, we assumed $700 million in aggregate principal amount of 2.625% Convertible Senior Notes due May 2041. We pay cash interest on the 2041 Notes at an annual rate of 2.625%, on a semi-annual basis. The 2041 Notes may be converted, under certain circumstances, into our Common Stock.

During the quarter-ended June 30, 2019, the market value of our Common Stock was greater than or equal to 130% of the 2041 Notes conversion prices for 20 or more trading days of the 30 consecutive trading days preceding the quarter end. As a result, the 2041 Notes are convertible at the option of the holder and are classified as current liabilities in our Consolidated Balance Sheets for fiscal year 2019.

On March 12, 2015, we completed a public offering of $500 million aggregate principal amount of Senior Notes due March 15, 2020 (the “2020 Notes”) and $500 million aggregate principal amount of Senior Notes due March 15, 2025 (the “2025 Notes”). We pay interest at an annual rate of 2.75% and 3.80%, respectively, on the 2020 Notes and 2025 Notes, on a semi-annual basis on March 15 and September 15 of each year.

On June 7, 2016, we completed a public offering of $800.0 million aggregate principal amount of Senior Notes due June 15, 2021, (the “2021 Notes”), together with the 2020 Notes, and 2021 Notes, the “Senior Notes”, and collectively with the Convertible Notes, the “Notes”). We pay interest at an annual rate of 2.80% on the 2021 Notes on a semi-annual basis on June 15 and December 15 of each year.

On March 4, 2019, we completed a public offering of $750 million aggregate principal amount of the Company’s Senior Notes due March 15, 2026 (the “2026 Notes”), $1 billion aggregate principal amount of the Company’s Senior Notes due March 15, 2029 (the “2029 Notes”), and $750 million aggregate principal amount of the Company’s Senior Notes due March 15, 2049 (the “2049 Notes”, collectively with the 2026 and 2029 Notes, the “Senior Notes issued in 2019”). We will pay interest at an annual rate of 3.75%, 4.00%, and 4.875%, respectively on the 2026, 2029 and 2049 Notes, on a semi-annual basis on March 15 and September 15 of each year, beginning September 15, 2019.

We may redeem the 2020, 2021, 2025, 2026, 2029 and 2049 Notes (collectively the “Senior Notes”) at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of such series (“par”), plus a “make whole” premium as described in the indenture in respect to the Senior Notes and accrued and unpaid interest before February 15, 2020, for the 2020 Notes, before May 15, 2021 for the 2021 Notes, before December 15, 2024 for the 2025 Notes, before January 15, 2026 for the 2026 Notes, before December 15, 2028 for the 2029 Notes, and before September 15, 2048 for the 2049 Notes. We may redeem the Senior Notes at par, plus accrued and unpaid interest at any time on or after February 15, 2020, for the 2020 Notes, on or after May 15, 2021 for the 2021 Notes, on or after December 24, 2024, for the 2025 Notes, on or after January 15, 2026 for the 2026 Notes, on or after December 15, 2028 for the 2029 Notes, and on or after September 15, 2048 for the 2049 Notes. synth_text.title: 2019 Summary of Long‑Term Obligations and Contractual Commitments
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
As of June 30 2019, the company reported total long‑term obligations of **$5.09 billion**. These obligations are grouped into operating leases, capital leases, purchase obligations, long‑term debt (including interest expense), a one‑time transition tax on unrepatriated foreign earnings, and other long‑term liabilities.

| Obligation Category | Amount (in $ millions) |
|---------------------|------------------------|
| Operating leases | $11.8 |
| Capital leases (excludes $26.5 M of build‑to‑sit leases) | $14.8 |
| Purchase obligations (minimum non‑cancelable portion) | $36.7 |
| Long‑term debt and interest expense* | $4,470.9 |
| One‑time transition tax on accumulated unrepatriated foreign earnings** | $390.8 |
| Other long‑term liabilities*** | $164.5 |
| **Total** | **$5,089.6** |

\* Long‑term debt comprises several series of senior and convertible notes issued between 2012 and 2019, including 2.625 % convertible senior notes due 2041, senior notes due 2020, 2021, 2025, 2026, 2029 and 2049, with varying interest rates (2.75 %–4.875 %). The 2041 convertible notes were classified as current liabilities because the conversion price was in‑the‑money for an extended period.

\** The transition tax reflects the one‑time U.S. tax on accumulated foreign earnings recognized under the 2017 tax reform; the final amount settled was $868.4 million, of which $390.8 million is shown for the reporting period.

\*** Includes tax‑related liabilities and post‑retirement benefit obligations whose timing is uncertain, as well as other non‑current liabilities.

**Key Points from the Context**

* **Operating Leases** – Primarily for administrative, R&D, manufacturing facilities, and equipment. Most are non‑cancelable; some provide options to extend or purchase the leased property. Residual‑value guarantees for certain California facilities total up to $250 million (not reflected in the table).

* **Capital Leases** – Represent lease obligations for buildings and office equipment; the amounts shown already include the interest component of the payments.

* **Purchase Obligations** – Contractual commitments for outsourcing, vendor‑consigned inventory, and other material services. The table reflects only the non‑cancelable portion or minimum cancellation fees; actual cash outflows will vary with transaction volume.

* **Exclusions** – The figures do **not** include $373 million of uncertain tax‑benefit liabilities nor $10 million of funding commitments for non‑marketable equity investments, as the company could not reasonably estimate settlement timing.

* **Debt Features** – The convertible 2041 notes may be converted into common stock, and the company retains redemption rights for all senior notes, typically at par plus accrued interest and, in some cases, a make‑whole premium.

**Conclusion**  
The company’s long‑term financial commitments are dominated by long‑term debt (approximately 88 % of total obligations). Off‑balance‑sheet items—operating leases, capital leases, and purchase obligations—represent a modest but material portion of the overall liability profile. Understanding the composition and terms of these obligations is essential for assessing the company’s future cash‑flow requirements and financial flexibility.

synth_text.title: 2019 Contractual Obligations and Long‑Term Liabilities – Summary by Category and Maturity
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
As of June 30 2019, the company reported contractual cash obligations totaling **$9.16 billion**, split between obligations due within the next five years and those extending beyond five years. These commitments encompass operating and capital leases, purchase obligations, long‑term debt (including interest), a one‑time transition tax on unrepatriated foreign earnings, and other long‑term liabilities.

**Breakdown by Maturity**

| Maturity | Operating Leases | Capital Leases* | Purchase Obligations | Long‑Term Debt & Interest | Transition Tax | Other Liabilities | Total |
|----------|------------------|-----------------|----------------------|---------------------------|----------------|-------------------|-------|
| **≤ 5 years** | $98.4 B | $50.0 B | $424.6 B | $6,468.5 B | $798.9 B | $190.8 B | **$8.03 B** |
| **> 5 years** | $37.4 B | $7.7 B | $345.5 B | $660.8 B | $69.5 B | $4.8 B | **$1.13 B** |

\*Capital lease figures exclude $26.5 million of build‑to‑suit lease arrangements that are recorded as capital leases on the balance sheet.

**Key Points**

* **Operating Leases** – Non‑cancelable leases for administrative, R&D, manufacturing facilities and equipment. Some leases (e.g., in Fremont, Livermore, and Tualatin) include options to extend or purchase the premises and may have rent escalations tied to inflation. Residual‑value guarantees for certain California facilities total up to $250 million.  
* **Capital Leases** – Primarily reflect lease‑financing of buildings and office equipment; the amounts shown already incorporate the interest component of the lease payments.  
* **Purchase Obligations** – Represent minimum contractual commitments for outsourcing, vendor‑consigned inventory, and other material services. For agreements with cancellation provisions, only the non‑cancelable portion or the minimum cancellation fee is included.  
* **Long‑Term Debt & Interest** – Includes principal balances of senior notes (2020, 2021, 2025, 2026, 2029, 2049) and 2.625 % convertible senior notes due 2041, together with the cash interest that will be paid over the life of these instruments. The 2041 convertible notes are classified as current liabilities because the conversion feature was exercisable at the reporting date.  
* **One‑Time Transition Tax** – A tax charge of $868.4 million (final amount) related to the 2017 U.S. tax reform on accumulated foreign earnings; the company may apply existing tax credits to reduce the cash outflow.  
* **Other Long‑Term Liabilities** – Capture tax‑related liabilities and post‑retirement benefit obligations whose timing is uncertain; they are reported in the “more than 5 years” bucket.  

**Exclusions**  
The totals above do **not** include $373 million of uncertain tax‑benefit liabilities nor $10 million of funding commitments for non‑marketable equity investments, as the company cannot reasonably estimate the timing or amount of settlement for these items.

**Conclusion**  
The company’s long‑term financial commitments are heavily weighted toward debt service and purchase obligations, with operating leases also representing a significant, though off‑balance‑sheet, liability. Understanding the composition and timing of these obligations is essential for assessing future cash‑flow requirements and the firm’s overall financial flexibility.

synth_text.title: Summary of Long‑Term and Off‑Balance‑Sheet Obligations as of June 30 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
As of June 30 2019 the company reported contractual payment obligations totaling **$1.82 billion** (in thousands). These obligations are split between commitments that mature **more than five years** from the reporting date and those that mature **within five years**.

| Maturity | Operating Leases | Capital Leases | Purchase Obligations | Long‑Term Debt & Interest | One‑Time Transition Tax | Other Long‑Term Liabilities | Total |

| **Combined** | **$49,137** | **$27,519** | **$42,388** | **$1,336,726** | **$338,661** | **$21,494** | **$1,815,925** |

*All figures are expressed in thousands of dollars.*

**Key Components**

- **Operating Leases ($49 M)** – Non‑cancelable leases for administrative, R&D, manufacturing facilities, sales offices, and equipment. Certain leases include options to extend or purchase the premises and may contain inflation‑linked rent escalations. Residual value guarantees for some California facilities total up to $250 M (not reflected in the table).

- **Capital Leases ($27.5 M)** – Lease obligations for buildings and office equipment that include an interest component. The table excludes $26.5 M related to build‑to‑suit lease arrangements classified as capital leases on the balance sheet.

- **Purchase Obligations ($42.4 M)** – Minimum contractual spend commitments for outsourcing activities, vendor‑consigned inventories, and other material contracts. For agreements with cancellation provisions, only the non‑cancelable portion or minimum cancellation fee is included.

- **Long‑Term Debt & Interest ($1.34 B)** – Principal and accrued interest on senior notes and convertible notes, including:
  * 2.625 % Convertible Senior Notes due May 2041 (originally $700 M, assumed in 2012);
  * Senior Notes issued in 2015, 2016, and 2019 with maturities ranging from 2020 to 2049;
  * Interest rates from 2.75 % to 4.875 % paid semi‑annually.
  The 2041 convertible notes were classified as current liabilities at the reporting date because the conversion price was in‑the‑money for a sustained period.

- **One‑Time Transition Tax ($339 M)** – Tax on accumulated unrepatriated foreign earnings arising from the 2017 U.S. tax reform. The final recognized amount was $868.4 M; the portion shown reflects the portion attributable to the reporting periods.

- **Other Long‑Term Liabilities ($21.5 M)** – Includes tax‑related liabilities and post‑retirement benefit obligations whose timing is uncertain, as well as other non‑current liabilities recorded on the balance sheet.

**Exclusions**  
The totals above **exclude**:
- $373 M of liabilities tied to uncertain tax benefits (valuation not reasonably estimable);
- $10 M of funding commitments for non‑marketable equity investments (timing of capital calls not estimable).

**Conclusion**  
The company’s long‑term financial commitments are dominated by long‑term debt, which accounts for roughly **73 %** of total obligations. Off‑balance‑sheet items—operating and capital leases—represent a modest share but are significant for facility and equipment usage. Understanding the composition and timing of these obligations is essential for assessing liquidity, debt service capacity, and future cash‑flow requirements.

header: Cost of license and subscription revenue

text.value: Cost of Revenue:

The $29.3 million increase in our cost of license and subscription revenue was primarily attributable to increases of $14.9 million in personnel expenses, $8.6 million in cloud infrastructure costs incurred in order to support the growth of our subscription offerings, $3.3 million in royalties, $1.8 million in professional services, and $0.9 million related to the amortization of internal-use software development and acquired intangible assets.

Cloud infrastructure costs include $9.5 million of hosting related costs that were recorded in cost of services revenue in fiscal year 2018. The treatment of these hosting related costs is consistent with the treatment of the related revenue in each fiscal year.

We anticipate higher cost of license and subscription revenue as we continue to invest in our cloud operations to increase operational efficiency and scale while growing our customer base. Cost of maintenance revenue increased by $1.7 million primarily due to the increase in personnel required to support our term and perpetual license customers.

Our cost of services revenue would have increased if cloud infrastructure costs totaling $9.5 million were not reclassified to cost of license and subscription revenue, consistent with the treatment of the related revenue. synth_text.title: Breakdown and Drivers of Cost of Revenue for FY 2019
synth_text.text:
For fiscal year 2019, the company reported total cost of revenue of **$324.35 million**, representing **45 %** of total revenue. The cost structure is divided among three primary streams:

| Cost Stream                | Dollar Amount | % of Revenue |
|----------------------------|---------------|--------------|
| License & Subscription     | $64.80 million| 9 % |
| Maintenance                | $16.50 million| 2 % |
| Services                   | $243.05 million| 34 % |
| **Total**                  | **$324.35 million**| **45 %** |

Embedded within these costs is stock‑based compensation totaling **$27.61 million**, allocated as follows:

* License & Subscription: **$3.01 million**  
* Maintenance: **$1.82 million**  
* Services: **$22.78 million**  

### Key Drivers of Cost Increases
- **License & Subscription** costs rose by **$29.3 million**, driven by:
  * **$14.9 million** in additional personnel expenses.  
  * **$8.6 million** for cloud infrastructure needed to scale subscription offerings.  
  * **$3.3 million** in royalties.  
  * **$1.8 million** for professional services.  
  * **$0.9 million** related to amortization of internal‑use software and acquired intangibles.  

- **Cloud infrastructure** costs of **$9.5 million** were reclassified from cost of services to cost of license & subscription, aligning expense recognition with the related revenue.

- **Maintenance** costs increased by **$1.7 million**, primarily due to added personnel supporting term and perpetual license customers.

- **Services** costs would have been higher without the reclassification; excluding that effect, third‑party consultant fees for InsuranceNow implementations grew by **$3.2 million**, and personnel expenses rose by **$2.8 million**.

### Workforce Changes
- Professional service employees grew from **838 (FY 2018)** to **781 (FY 2019)**.  
- Technical support and licensing operations staff increased from **121** to **198** over the same period.

### Outlook
The company expects continued growth in license & subscription costs as it invests further in cloud operations to improve efficiency, scale infrastructure, and expand its customer base.

synth_text.title: Cost of Revenue Growth: Drivers and Breakdown for License, Subscription, Maintenance, and Services (FY 2019)
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal year 2019, total cost of revenue rose to **$27.6 million**, up from **$9 million** in the prior year. The increase was driven primarily by higher expenses in the license and subscription segment, supported by growth in maintenance and a reallocation of cloud‑infrastructure costs.

**Key Cost Components (FY 2019 vs. FY 2018)**  

| Category                     | FY 2019 | FY 2018 |
|------------------------------|---------|---------|
| License & subscription       | $29.3 M | $83 k   |
| Maintenance                  | $1.7 M  | $12 k   |
| Services (net)               | $(3.5 M) | $(1 k) |
| **Total cost of revenue**    | $27.6 M | $9 k    |
| Stock‑based compensation – License & subscription | $2.0 M | – |
| Stock‑based compensation – Maintenance | $(0.07 M) | – |
| Stock‑based compensation – Services | $0.9 M | – |
| **Total stock‑based compensation** | $2.9 M | – |

**Drivers of the $29.3 million Increase in License & Subscription Costs**  

1. **Personnel expenses** – $14.9 M increase, reflecting the addition of professional‑service staff (781 vs. 838 in FY 2018) and technical support/licensing employees (198 vs. 121).  
2. **Cloud infrastructure** – $8.6 M rise, largely due to expanded hosting capacity needed for subscription growth. Of this, $9.5 M of hosting costs were re‑classified from “cost of services” to “cost of license and subscription,” aligning expense recognition with the related revenue.  
3. **Royalties** – $3.3 M higher payments.  
4. **Professional services** – $1.8 M increase, driven by more implementation engagements (e.g., InsuranceNow).  
5. **Amortization of internal‑use software and acquired intangibles** – $0.9 M.

**Maintenance Cost Growth**  
Maintenance expenses rose by $1.7 M, primarily from additional personnel required to support both term and perpetual license customers.

**Services Cost Impact**  
If the $9.5 M cloud‑hosting expense had remained classified under services, services costs would have been higher. Excluding this reclassification, third‑party consultant fees for implementation rose by $3.2 M and personnel costs for new and existing staff grew by $2.8 M.

**Stock‑Based Compensation**  
Stock‑based compensation contributed $2.9 M to total costs, with the majority ($2.0 M) linked to the license and subscription segment.

**Conclusion**  
The pronounced rise in cost of revenue for FY 2019 reflects strategic investments in cloud infrastructure, personnel, and service capabilities to scale the subscription business. While these expenditures increase short‑term costs, they are positioned to support operational efficiency, customer acquisition, and long‑term revenue growth.

synth_text.title: FY19 Hotel Segment Financial Highlights and Underlying Drivers
synth_text.text:
The hotel portfolio delivered modest overall growth in FY19, with headline sales increasing by **3.7%** (1.8% on a normalised basis). The uplift was largely powered by stronger Bars, Food and Accommodation revenues, a result of **49 venue refurbishments** completed during the year and the opening or acquisition of five new venues, bringing the total to **328 hotels** at year‑end. Gaming sales, however, remained subdued, especially in Victoria.

EBITDA rose by **3.5%** (2.5% normalised), reflecting the sales momentum, while depreciation and amortisation grew uniformly by **9.9%** in both reporting formats. EBIT showed a slight headline increase of **1.0%**, but fell **0.5%** on a normalised basis, indicating that the first half of the year weighed on profitability. Normalised EBIT rebounded in the second half, climbing **1.3%**.

Profitability metrics were pressured by a shift in business mix and higher food input costs. Gross margin contracted by **55 basis points** (54 bps normalised), and the cost of doing business (CODB) was trimmed modestly by **12 bps** (18 bps normalised), demonstrating effective cost control despite the margin squeeze.

Funds employed expanded by **3.7%**, driven by the extensive refurbishments and hotel acquisitions, which in turn reduced the return on funds employed (ROFE) by **20 bps** on a headline basis and **38 bps** on a normalised basis.

In summary, FY19 saw the hotel segment achieve modest sales and EBITDA growth, underpinned by venue upgrades and a stronger food‑and‑beverage offering, while margin compression and higher capital deployment moderated earnings and ROFE performance.

synth_text.title: Hotels Segment Financial and Operational Performance – FY19 Overview
synth_text.text:
**Financial Highlights**

- **Sales** grew to **$1,671 million**, up 3.7% year‑on‑year (1.8% on a normalised basis) from $1,612 million in the prior 52‑week period. The increase was driven primarily by stronger Bars, Food and Accommodation revenues, especially in the second half of the year after completing 49 venue refurbishments.
- **EBITDA** rose modestly to **$372 million** (up $11 million) while **EBIT** reached **$261 million**, a slight 0.5% normalised decline versus the previous year, reflecting a weaker first half but a 1.3% normalised rebound in the second half.
- **Depreciation & amortisation** expenses increased to **$(111) million** from $(102) million, reflecting higher capital spending on refurbishments and hotel acquisitions.
- **Gross margin** slipped to **83.6%** (down 0.6 percentage points) as the business mix shifted and food input costs rose, resulting in a 54‑basis‑point decline in normalised gross profit.
- **Cost of doing business (CODB)** remained well‑controlled, falling to **68.0%** of sales (down 0.1 pp), an 18‑basis‑point improvement on a normalised basis.
- **EBIT‑to‑sales** fell to **15.6%** (from 16.1%) due to the modest EBIT dip and higher depreciation.
- **Funds employed** increased to **$2,068 million** from $1,995 million, driven by the refurbishments and the acquisition of five new venues, bringing the total hotel portfolio to 328 properties at year‑end.
- **Return on Funds Employed (ROFE)** decreased to **12.9%** (down 0.2 pp), a 38‑basis‑point normalised decline linked to the higher capital base.

**Operational Drivers**

- The second‑half sales acceleration stemmed from the completion of 49 venue refurbishments, which boosted Bars, Food and Accommodation performance.
- Gaming revenue remained subdued, particularly in Victoria, offsetting some of the hospitality gains.
- Five new venues were opened or acquired during the year, expanding the hotel footprint and contributing to the rise in funds employed.

**Overall Assessment**

The hotels segment delivered modest top‑line growth and maintained strong profitability despite pressure from a less favourable product mix and higher food costs. Cost discipline kept CODB in check, while strategic refurbishments and acquisitions supported sales momentum but modestly diluted ROFE. The results indicate a resilient core business with continued upside potential as refurbishment programmes and portfolio expansion mature.

text.value: Goodwill

Goodwill consists of the excess of the consideration transferred over the fair value of net assets acquired in business combinations. Autodesk tests goodwill for impairment annually in its fourth fiscal quarter or more often if circumstances indicate a potential impairment may exist, or if events have affected the composition of reporting units.

When goodwill is assessed for impairment, Autodesk has the option to perform an assessment of qualitative factors of impairment (“optional assessment”) prior to necessitating a quantitative impairment test. Should the optional assessment be used for any given fiscal year, qualitative factors to consider include cost factors; financial performance; legal, regulatory, contractual, political, business, or other factors; entity specific factors; industry and market considerations, macroeconomic conditions, and other relevant events and factors affecting the reporting unit. If, after assessing the totality of events or circumstances, it is more likely than not that the fair value of the reporting unit is greater than its carrying value, then performing the quantitative impairment test is unnecessary.

The quantitative impairment test is necessary when either Autodesk does not use the optional assessment or, as a result of the optional assessment, it is not more likely than not that the fair value of the reporting unit is greater than its carrying value. In situations in which an entity's reporting unit is publicly traded, the fair value of the Company may be approximated by its market capitalization, in performing the quantitative impairment test.

Goodwill impairment exists when the estimated fair value of goodwill is less than its carrying value. If impairment exists, the carrying value of the goodwill is reduced to fair value through an impairment charge recorded in the Company's statements of operations. The process of evaluating the potential impairment of goodwill is subjective and requires significant judgment at many points during the analysis. The value of Autodesk’s goodwill could also be impacted by future adverse changes such as: (i) declines in Autodesk’s actual financial results, (ii) a sustained decline in Autodesk’s market capitalization, (iii) a significant slowdown in the worldwide economy or the industries Autodesk serves, or (iv) changes in Autodesk’s business strategy.

For the annual impairment test, Autodesk's market capitalization was substantially in excess of the carrying value of the Company as of January 31, 2019. Accordingly, Autodesk has determined there was no goodwill impairment during the fiscal year ended January 31, 2019. In addition, Autodesk did not recognize any goodwill impairment losses in fiscal 2018 or 2017.

synth_text.title: VMware Consolidated Revenue by Category – FY 2019 vs FY 2020
synth_text.text:
VMware reports all of its financial results in a single operating segment, so the figures below reflect the company’s total revenue. For the fiscal year ending **January 31 2020**, total revenue reached **$10.8 billion**, up from **$9.6 billion** in the prior year (February 1 2019), representing a **12.5 % increase**.

**License revenue** grew modestly, rising from **$3.0 billion** to **$3.2 billion** (+4.6 %). **Subscription and SaaS** revenue showed the strongest growth, climbing from **$1.3 billion** to **$1.9 billion** (+44 %). Combined, license and subscription revenues contributed **$5.1 billion** in 2020, compared with **$4.3 billion** in 2019.

On the services side, **Software Maintenance** increased from **$4.35 billion** to **$4.75 billion** (+9.3 %), while **Professional Services** rose from **$0.92 billion** to **$1.0 billion** (+9 %). Total services revenue therefore grew from **$5.27 billion** to **$5.75 billion** (+9.2 %).

Overall, the 2020 fiscal year demonstrated balanced growth across all revenue streams, with subscription‑based offerings driving the most significant year‑over‑year expansion.

* The combined license, subscription, and SaaS revenue represented **42.6 %** of the overall figure, underscoring the growing importance of recurring revenue streams alongside traditional licensing.

These figures illustrate VMware’s diversified revenue model, with a significant shift toward service‑based income even as the company continues to generate substantial licensing revenue.

synth_text.title: Microsoft FY 2019 Financial Highlights: Strong Revenue and Operating Growth Amid GAAP Net‑Income Decline
synth_text.text:
Microsoft reported robust year‑over‑year growth in FY 2019, with revenue increasing 14 % to add $15.5 billion, driven by all three major segments. Intelligent Cloud saw higher sales of server products and cloud services, Productivity and Business Processes grew on strong Office and LinkedIn performance, and More Personal Computing was boosted by Surface, Gaming and Windows.

Gross margin rose 16 % (up $10.9 billion), helped by a 5‑point improvement in commercial cloud margins and a favorable sales mix. Operating income climbed 21 % (up $7.9 billion), reflecting the same broad‑based segment growth.

GAAP net income and diluted earnings per share, however, fell sharply—down 35 % and 34 % respectively—due to a $2.6 billion net tax benefit from intangible‑property transfers and a $157 million charge related to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). The prior year had been negatively impacted by a larger TCJA charge, which magnified the apparent decline.

When tax and restructuring items are excluded, the non‑GAAP picture is more positive. Non‑GAAP operating income, net income, and diluted EPS all grew double‑digit, up 20 %, 18 % and 18 % respectively, underscoring the strength of the underlying business.

Key expense changes included a 12 % rise in cost of revenue (driven by commercial cloud, Surface and Gaming), a 15 % increase in research and development (focused on cloud, AI, Gaming, LinkedIn and GitHub), and a modest 4 % rise in sales and marketing (offset by a favorable foreign‑currency impact).

Overall, Microsoft’s FY 2019 results demonstrate solid top‑line growth and operating profitability across all segments, while GAAP net‑income volatility is largely attributable to one‑time tax effects rather than core operational weakness.

synth_text.title: Microsoft Fiscal Year 2019 Financial Highlights and Year‑over‑Year Growth Overview
synth_text.text:
**Financial Summary (FY 2019 vs. FY 2018)**  
- **Revenue:** $96.6 billion, up **14%** YoY. Growth was broad‑based across all three segments: Intelligent Cloud (driven by server products and cloud services), Productivity & Business Processes (Office and LinkedIn), and More Personal Computing (Surface, Gaming, Windows).  
- **Gross Margin:** $62.3 billion, up **15%** YoY, reflecting both higher sales and a modest improvement in margin percentages. A notable 5‑point contribution came from the commercial cloud (Azure) mix shift.  
- **Operating Income:** $29.0 billion, up **23%** YoY, supported by the same segment‑level revenue expansion.  
- **Net Income:** $25.5 billion, up **137%** YoY. The surge was largely due to a $2.6 billion net tax benefit from intangible‑property transfers and a $157 million charge related to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), which together added $2.4 billion to net income and $0.31 to diluted EPS.  
- **Diluted EPS:** $3.25, up **138%** YoY.

**Non‑GAAP Measures (excluding tax impacts of intangible transfers, the TCJA, and restructuring expenses)**  
- **Non‑GAAP Operating Income:** $29.3 billion, **23%** higher YoY.  
- **Non‑GAAP Net Income:** $25.7 billion, **22%** higher YoY.  
- **Non‑GAAP Diluted EPS:** $3.29, **22%** higher YoY.  

**Expense Highlights**  
- **Cost of Revenue:** +$4.6 billion (**12%**) driven by higher commercial‑cloud, Surface, and Gaming volumes.  
- **Research & Development:** +$2.2 billion (**15%**) reflecting continued investment in cloud, AI engineering, Gaming, LinkedIn, and GitHub.  
- **Sales & Marketing:** +$744 million (**4%**) mainly for expanding commercial sales capacity and LinkedIn/GitHub initiatives, partially offset by reduced marketing spend; also benefited from a 2% favorable foreign‑currency effect.  

**Key Takeaways**  
- Revenue growth was evenly distributed across Microsoft’s three core segments, with cloud services being a primary catalyst.  
- Gross margin improvements were driven by a more profitable commercial‑cloud mix and modest margin gains across all segments.  
- Net income and EPS showed exceptional growth due to a one‑time tax benefit, while underlying operating performance remained strong.  
- Non‑GAAP figures provide a clearer view of operating trends by stripping out the tax and restructuring items that affected GAAP results.  

Overall, FY 2019 demonstrated robust top‑line expansion, margin enhancement, and profitability, underscoring the effectiveness of Microsoft’s cloud strategy and continued investment in high‑growth areas.

synth_text.title: Microsoft FY 2019 Financial Highlights: Year‑over‑Year Performance and Key Drivers
synth_text.text:
Microsoft reported a strong fiscal 2019, delivering $125.8 billion in revenue—up $15.5 billion (14%) from the prior year’s $110.4 billion. Growth was broad‑based across all three segments: Intelligent Cloud benefited from higher server sales and accelerated Azure adoption; Productivity and Business Processes saw increased Office and LinkedIn revenue; and More Personal Computing was driven by higher sales of Surface devices, Gaming products, and Windows.

Gross margin expanded to $82.9 billion, a $10.9 billion (15%) increase, while the gross‑margin percentage improved modestly thanks to a better sales mix and a 5‑point uplift in commercial‑cloud profitability. Operating income rose 23% to $42.9 billion, and net income more than doubled, reaching $39.2 billion—an increase of $22.6 billion (136%). Diluted earnings per share climbed from $2.13 to $5.06.

Non‑GAAP results, which exclude the net tax impact of intangible‑property transfers, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), and restructuring expenses, mirrored the GAAP trend. Non‑GAAP operating income remained at $42.9 billion, non‑GAAP net income grew to $36.8 billion, and non‑GAAP diluted EPS increased to $4.75.

Expenses rose in line with revenue. Cost of revenue increased 12% ($4.6 billion) driven by cloud, Surface, and Gaming growth. Research and development rose 15% ($2.2 billion) reflecting continued investment in cloud, AI, Gaming, LinkedIn, and GitHub. Sales and marketing expenses grew modestly by 4% ($744 million), aided by a 2% favorable foreign‑currency effect.

Net income was positively impacted by a $2.6 billion tax benefit from intangible‑property transfers and a $157 million TCJA‑related charge, which together added $2.4 billion to net income and $0.31 to diluted EPS. In contrast, FY 2018 net income had been depressed by a $13.7 billion TCJA charge.

Overall, Microsoft’s FY 2019 performance demonstrates robust top‑line growth, improved profitability, and effective cost management, underpinned by strong cloud adoption, productivity‑software demand, and expanding hardware and gaming businesses.

synth_text.text:
The financial statements for the two most recent fiscal years show a mixed performance.  

**Operating profit (EBIT)** rose from €713 million to €828 million, indicating stronger core earnings. The **net financial result** improved, moving from a loss of €‑137 million to €‑119 million. This improvement stems mainly from a lower interest expense (‑€119 million versus ‑€136 million in the prior year) and a modest positive other‑financial result of €1 million, reflecting more favourable refinancing terms as noted in the accompanying commentary.  

Consequently, **earnings before tax (EBT)** increased from €576 million to €709 million. After accounting for higher income taxes (‑€216 million to ‑€298 million), **profit from continuing operations** grew from €359 million to €411 million.  

However, the overall result was heavily affected by discontinued operations. The loss from discontinued activities swung from a modest €‑22 million to a substantial €‑526 million, turning the **total profit for the period** from a positive €337 million in the first year to a net loss of €‑115 million in the second year.  

In summary, while operating performance and the net financial position improved year‑over‑year, the sharp loss from discontinued operations and higher tax charges led to an overall negative result in the most recent year.

synth_text.title: Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy – FY 2019 Financial Highlights and Market Outlook
synth_text.text:
**Financial performance (2018 vs 2019)**  
- **Orders:** €12.749 bn in 2019, up 7 % from €11.875 bn in 2018.  
- **Revenue:** €10.227 bn in 2019, a 12 % increase over €9.122 bn in 2018.  
- **Adjusted EBITA:** €482 m in 2019, essentially unchanged from €483 m the previous year.  
- **Adjusted EBITA margin:** fell to 4.7 % in 2019 from 5.3 % in 2018.

**Drivers of order growth**  
Order intake rose across all business lines, propelled by two large offshore‑wind contracts in Asia and Australia (including service in Taiwan) worth €2.3 bn, and several sizable on‑shore orders in the United States. Conversely, orders in Europe, the CIS, Africa and the Middle East dropped sharply after the previous year’s €1.3 bn offshore‑wind order in the United Kingdom.

**Revenue dynamics**  
Revenue growth was strongest in the offshore and service segments, with clear gains in the on‑shore business as well. Geographically, revenue increased markedly in Europe, the CIS, Africa and the Middle East, while it declined in the other two reporting regions.

**Adjusted EBITA explanation**  
Adjusted EBITA remained flat because productivity improvements and higher revenue were offset by lower prices, an unfavourable project mix, and higher integration and capacity‑adjustment costs. Severance charges amounted to €32 m in 2019, up from €77 m in 2018.

**Order backlog and outlook**  
At year‑end, SGRE’s order backlog stood at €26 bn, of which €9 bn is expected to be recognised as revenue in fiscal 2020.

**Market context**  
- **Offshore wind:** 2019 saw robust growth in the UK and China, offsetting a slight decline in Europe.  
- **On‑shore wind:** Growth was driven mainly by China (the world’s largest on‑shore market, still largely closed to foreign manufacturers) and the United States, while Germany experienced a notable downturn.  
- **2020 expectations:** Global on‑shore installations are projected to rise, led by the U.S. and India, while offshore capacity is expected to expand, primarily due to China’s momentum. Both segments will likely face adverse price development and currency effects.

Overall, SGRE delivered higher orders and revenue in 2019, maintained EBITA despite cost pressures, and entered 2020 with a strong backlog and a market environment that supports continued growth in both on‑shore and offshore wind sectors.

synth_text.title: SGRE FY2019 Financial Highlights: Orders, Revenue, and Adjusted EBITA in Context
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019 Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy (SGRE) delivered solid top‑line growth while maintaining profitability at the prior‑year level.  

**Key financial movements**  
- **Orders** increased by **7 %** year‑over‑year. The rise was broad‑based, driven by large offshore wind contracts in Asia and Australia (totaling €2.3 bn) and by several sizeable on‑shore orders in the United States. Europe, the CIS, Africa and the Middle East recorded lower order intake compared with the previous year, which had benefited from a €1.3 bn UK offshore order.  
- **Revenue** grew **12 %**, reflecting strong performance in the offshore and service businesses and clear growth in the on‑shore segment. Geographically, revenue rose markedly in Europe, the CIS, Africa and the Middle East, while it fell in the other two reporting regions.  
- **Adjusted EBITA** was essentially unchanged (**0 %** growth). Productivity improvements and higher revenue were offset by adverse price trends, a less favourable project mix, and higher integration and capacity‑adjustment costs. Severance charges fell to €32 million in 2019 from €77 million in 2018, partially cushioning the impact.  

**Market backdrop**  
The wind market expanded significantly in 2019, with both on‑shore and offshore installations increasing. On‑shore growth was led by China and the United States, whereas Germany saw a notable decline. Offshore expansion was driven by the United Kingdom and China, offsetting a modest downturn in Europe. Despite the volume growth, market prices in euros faced downward pressure, a trend expected to continue in 2020.  

**Outlook**  
SGRE entered 2020 with an order backlog of €26 billion, of which €9 billion is slated for conversion into revenue during the year. The company anticipates continued on‑shore growth in the United States and India, and offshore growth primarily from China, while remaining vigilant about price dynamics and regional market shifts.  

Overall, the 7 % rise in orders and 12 % increase in revenue underscore SGRE’s ability to capture expanding wind‑energy demand, even as profitability remains constrained by market pricing and cost‑structure challenges.

In summary, the sharp rise in acquisition‑related and restructuring expenses in fiscal 2019 played a pivotal role in weakening Transportation Solutions’ profitability, compounding the adverse effects of market‑driven volume and pricing pressures.

synth_text.title: Summary of Income‑Tax Calculations and Adjustments for the Years Ended 30 March 2019 and 2017/18
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table details the income‑tax computation for two financial periods – the year ended 30 March 2019 and the prior year 2017/18. Although the statutory corporation‑tax rate in the United Kingdom is 19 % for both periods, the final tax credit or charge differs because of several adjustments required by tax legislation and the company’s specific circumstances.

**2019 Period (Loss of £42.7 m)**  
* **Statutory tax credit:** Applying the 19 % rate to the loss yields a credit of £8.2 m.  
* **Adjustments reducing the credit:**  
  * Non‑deductible items: –£0.9 m  
  * Share‑based payment adjustment: –£0.4 m  
  * Deferred‑tax rate correction (17 %): –£0.8 m  
* **Adjustments increasing the credit:**  
  * Prior‑period adjustment (revised losses and capital allowances): +£1.7 m  
  * Current tax relating to overseas business: +£1.1 m  
* **Net result:** After all items, the company records an **income‑tax credit of £8.9 m** for the period.  
* **Loss movements:** No loss movements are recognised (nil), reflecting the policy that corporation‑tax losses are not recognised when future recoverability is uncertain.

**2017/18 Period (Profit of £20.9 m)**  
* **Statutory tax charge:** The 19 % rate on profit generates a charge of –£4.0 m.  
* **Adjustments increasing the charge:**  
  * Non‑deductible items: –£0.1 m  
  * Other disallowable items: –£0.4 m  
  * Impairment of goodwill: –£0.8 m  
  * Share‑based payment adjustment: –£0.6 m  
  * Deferred‑tax rate correction (17 %): +£0.7 m  
  * Movements in losses recognised: +£1.1 m  
  * Current tax relating to overseas business: +£0.8 m  
* **Adjustments decreasing the charge:**  
  * Prior‑period adjustment (revisions to earlier losses and capital allowances): –£8.1 m  
* **Net result:** The cumulative effect leads to an **income‑tax charge of £13.7 m** for the year.

**Why the Effective Tax Differs from 19 %**  
The headline 19 % corporation‑tax rate is only a starting point. The final tax credit/charge is adjusted for:

1. **Non‑deductible and other disallowable items** – expenses that tax law does not permit as deductions.  
2. **Impairment of goodwill** – written‑down goodwill is not tax‑deductible.  
3. **Share‑based payments** – tax treatment differs from accounting treatment, requiring adjustments.  
4. **Deferred‑tax rate corrections** – the company applies a 17 % rate for deferred tax, creating a further adjustment.  
5. **Prior‑period revisions** – after filing tax returns, the company revised losses and capital allowances, resulting in significant adjustments (+£1.7 m in 2019, –£8.1 m in 2017/18).  
6. **Overseas tax components** – current tax relating to overseas operations adds to the UK tax position.

**Key Take‑aways**  

* The 2019 loss generated a net tax credit despite the loss, mainly because of prior‑period adjustments and overseas tax recoveries.  
* The 2017/18 profit resulted in a substantial tax charge after accounting for multiple disallowable items and a large negative prior‑period adjustment.  
* Movements in losses are recognised only when future recoverability is reasonably certain; hence, they are nil for the 2019 period.  

These calculations provide a transparent view of how the company’s effective tax position is derived from the statutory rate, reflecting the impact of specific tax adjustments and policy considerations.

text.value: Deferred income taxes on the Consolidated Balance Sheets result from temporary differences between the amount of assets and liabilities recognized for financial reporting and tax purposes. The principal components of our current and non-current deferred taxes were as follows:

In December 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (“the Act”) was signed into law. As a result of the Act, we recognized an estimated expense of $11.9 million in the fourth quarter of 2017, of which $9.2 million related to the writedown of deferred tax assets and $2.7 million related to tax on unrepatriated foreign earnings. We calculated our best estimate of the impact of the Act in our 2017 year-end income tax provision in accordance with Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118, which was issued to address the application of U.S. GAAP in situations when a registrant does not have the necessary information available, prepared or analyzed to finalize the accounting for certain income tax effects of the Act. Additional work to complete a more detailed analysis of historical foreign earnings, as well as the full impact relating to the write-down of deferred tax assets, was completed in the third quarter of 2018 and resulted in a tax benefit of $4.0 million for the year ended December 31, 2018.

As of December 31, 2019 and 2018, non-current deferred taxes related to our investments and our defined benefit pension plan reflect deferred taxes on the net unrealized gains and losses on available-for-sale investments and deferred taxes on unrealized losses in our pension plan. The net change in non-current deferred taxes associated with these items, which resulted in a deferred tax benefit of $0.4 million and $2.8 million in 2019 and 2018, respectively, was recorded as an adjustment to other comprehensive income (loss), presented in the Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income (Loss).

The Company continually reviews the adequacy of our valuation allowance and recognizes the benefits of deferred tax assets only as the reassessment indicates that it is more likely than not that the deferred tax assets will be realized in accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes. Due to our recent decrease in revenue and profitability for 2019, and all other positive and negative objective evidence considered as part of our analysis, our ability to consider other subjective evidence such as projections for future growth is limited when evaluating whether our deferred tax assets will be realized. As such, the Company was no longer able to conclude that it was more likely than not that our domestic deferred tax assets would be realized and a valuation allowance against our domestic deferred tax assets was established in the third quarter of 2019. The amount of the deferred tax assets considered realizable may be adjusted in future periods in the event that sufficient evidence is present to support a conclusion that it is more likely than not that all or a portion of our domestic deferred tax assets will be realized.

As of December 31, 2019, the Company had gross deferred tax assets totaling $56.2 million offset by a valuation allowance totaling $48.6 million. Of the valuation allowance, $42.8 million was established in the current year primarily related to our domestic deferred tax assets. The remaining $5.8 million established in prior periods related to state research and development credit carryforwards and foreign net operating loss and research and development credit carryforwards where we lack sufficient activity to realize those deferred tax assets. The remaining $7.6 million in deferred tax assets that were not offset by a valuation allowance are located in various foreign jurisdictions where the Company believes it is more likely than not we will realize these deferred tax assets.
