synth_text.title: Singtel Group – Share of Associates’ Profits (Pre‑ and Post‑Tax) – FY 2018 vs FY 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Singapore Telecommunications (Singtel) Group’s share of its associates’ earnings increased markedly from FY 2018 to FY 2019. The figures below reflect the Group’s proportionate share of both pre‑tax and post‑tax results, after excluding the Group’s own exceptional items (as per footnote 3).

| Fiscal Year | Group share of associates’ pre‑tax profit (S$ m) | Group share of associates’ post‑tax profit (S$ m) |
|-------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| FY 2018 | 1,536 | 1,383 |
| FY 2019 | 2,461 | 1,823 |

**Key associate contributors**

| Associate (Equity interest) | FY 2018 contribution (S$ m) | FY 2019 contribution (S$ m) |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Telkomsel** (Singtel’s majority‑owned Indonesian mobile operator) | 843 | 1,031 |
| **AIS** (Thai mobile operator) | 286 | 292 |
| **Regional associates** (combined results of other regional entities) | 1,287 | 1,694 |
| **Intouch** (21 % Singtel equity; holds 40.5 % of AIS) – operating result | 101 | 106 |
| – Amortisation of acquired intangibles | (22) | (21) |
| **Airtel** (via BTL’s 50.1 % stake) | (131) | 101 |
| **BTL** (Bharti Telecom Ltd.) – loss mainly from interest expense | (40) | (18) |
| **NetLink NBN Trust / NetLink Trust** (24.8 % interest) | 48 | 72 |
| **Other associates** (includes Singapore Post Limited) | 47 | 57 |
| **Globe** (Philippines) – no profit share reported for either year | – | – |
| **Ordinary results** (non‑exceptional) | 251 | 180 |
| **Exceptional items** (excluded from the share) | – | 22 |

**Interpretation**

* The Group’s share of associate pre‑tax profit grew by **60 %** year‑on‑year, driven primarily by higher contributions from Telkomsel and the broader regional associate portfolio.  
* Post‑tax profit share rose by **32 %**, reflecting both the increase in operating results and the exclusion of exceptional items (which were present only in FY 2019 for the regional associates).  
* Negative contributions from Airtel and BTL in FY 2018 turned positive for Airtel in FY 2019, while BTL’s loss narrowed, indicating an improvement in the financial health of these entities.  
* The amortisation of acquired intangibles remains modest and consistent across the two years.  

**Contextual notes**

1. All figures are prepared under Singapore Financial Reporting Standards (International) and assume constant exchange rates for the regional currencies (Indian Rupee, Indonesian Rupiah, Philippine Peso, Thai Baht).  
2. The share of results excludes the Group’s one‑off exceptional items (footnote 3).  
3. Singtel’s 21 % stake in Intouch, which itself holds 40.5 % of AIS, influences the reported AIS share (footnote 4).  
4. BTL’s 50.1 % interest in Airtel means that Airtel’s performance is reflected in the Group’s share of associate results (footnote 5).  
5. The NetLink Trust interest includes an amortisation of a deferred gain of S$20 million (down from S$32 million in FY 2018) (footnote 6).  
6. “Other associates” also capture the share of Singapore Post Limited (footnote 7).  

Overall, the data demonstrate a solid upward trajectory in the profitability of Singtel’s associate portfolio, underpinned by strong performance in its core Southeast Asian mobile businesses.

synth_text.title: Singtel’s Associate Performance – Share of Pre‑Tax and Post‑Tax Profits (Two Recent Fiscal Years)
synth_text.text:
The table summarises Singtel’s share of results from its major associates for two consecutive fiscal periods. In both periods the group recorded a **negative share of associates’ pre‑tax profits**, amounting to **‑37.6 %** in the first year and **‑36.2 %** in the second year. The negative contribution is driven primarily by:

* **Telkomsel** – the largest negative contributor, with shares of **‑18.3 %** and **‑12.4 %** respectively.  
* **AIS** – also negative, at **‑1.7 %** and **‑3.9 %**.  

Conversely, **Bharti Telecom Limited (BTL)** delivered a **positive contribution**, reporting **S$127.8 million** and **S$140.9 million** in the two periods. BTL holds a 50.1 % equity interest in Airtel; its standalone loss is mainly due to interest charges on borrowings, which explains the positive net share after accounting for Airtel’s results.

Other associate groups posted negative shares:

* **Regional associates** – ‑24.0 % and ‑21.5 %  
* **NetLink NBN Trust/NetLink Trust** – ‑32.9 % (both periods)  
* **Other associates** (including Singapore Post) – ‑17.6 % (both periods)  

Accordingly, the **group’s share of associates’ post‑tax profits** was also negative, at **‑24.1 %** and **‑21.8 %** for the two periods.

The table contains several “nm” entries, which the accompanying notes define as **“not meaningful”** and therefore are excluded from the analysis. Additional context from the notes clarifies that:

* The share of results **excludes one‑off exceptional items** (see note 3).  
* Singtel holds a **21 % stake in Intouch**, which itself holds **40.5 % of AIS** (note 4).  
* BTL’s loss is largely **interest expense**, while its positive share reflects its 50.1 % holding in Airtel (note 5).  
* Singtel’s interest in **NetLink Trust** transitioned to NetLink NBN Trust in 2017, with a residual 24.8 % holding (note 6).  

Overall, the data indicate that Singtel’s associate portfolio generated **overall negative earnings**, with the exception of BTL’s contribution, and that the negative performance is concentrated in its telecom operating associates (Telkomsel, AIS, regional partners) and the NetLink entities.

The realized losses relate to amounts we actually realized for settlements related to these derivative instruments in normal course and amounts

During 2019 and 2018, we had interest rate swap agreements with aggregate average net outstanding notional amounts of approximately $1.1 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, with average fixed rates of approximately 3.0% and 2.9%, respectively. Short-term variable benchmark interest rates during these periods were generally less than 3.0% and, as such, we incurred realized losses of $8.3 million and $13.9 million during 2019 and 2018, respectively, under the interest rate swap agreements.

We did not incur any realized losses related to the termination of interest rate swaps in 2019, compared to realized losses of $13.7 million during 2018. Primarily as a result of significant changes in long-term benchmark interest rates during 2019 and 2018, we recognized unrealized losses of $7.9 million in 2019 compared to unrealized gains of $33.7 million in 2018 under the interest rate swap agreements.

During the year ended December 31, 2019, we recognized a reversal of previously unrealized losses of $26.9 million on all the warrants held by Teekay to purchase common units of Altera (or the Warrants) as a result of the sale of the Warrants to Brookfield, and we concurrently recognized a realized loss of $25.6 million during the same period. During the year ended December 31, 2018, we recognized unrealized losses of $21.1 million on the Warrants. Please read “Item 18 – Financial Statements: Note 12 – Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments.”

Foreign Exchange Loss. Foreign currency exchange losses were $13.6 million in 2019 compared to gains of $6.1 million in 2018. Our foreign currency exchange gains and losses, substantially all of which are unrealized, are primarily due to the relevant period-end revaluation of our Norwegian-Krone (or NOK)-denominated debt and our Euro-denominated term loans, finance leases and restricted cash for financial reporting purposes and the realized and unrealized (losses) gains on our cross currency swaps.

Gains on NOK-denominated and Euro-denominated monetary liabilities reflect a stronger U.S. Dollar against the NOK and Euro on the date of revaluation or settlement compared to the rate in effect at the beginning of the period. Losses on NOK-denominated and Euro-denominated monetary liabilities reflect a weaker U.S. Dollar against the NOK and Euro on the date of revaluation or settlement compared to the rate in effect at the beginning of the period.

For 2019, foreign currency exchange loss included realized losses of $5.1 million (2018 – $6.5 million) and unrealized losses of $13.2 million (2018 – gains of $21.2 million) on our cross currency swaps, realized losses on maturity and termination of cross currency swaps of $nil (2018 – $42.3 million) and unrealized gains of $5.8 million (2018 – gains of $19.2 million) on the revaluation of our NOK-denominated debt.

Other loss. Other loss was $14.5 million in 2019 compared to $2.0 million in 2018. synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The table compares several non‑core operating items for 2019 and 2018 (in thousands of U.S. dollars). Overall, most line‑items increased in 2019, driven by new financing activities, derivative market movements, and higher tax expenses.

| Item | 2019 | 2018 | Year‑over‑Year Change |

| **Interest expense** | $(279,059) | $(254,126) | ↑ $24.9 M |
| **Interest income** | $7,804 | $8,525 | ↓ $0.7 M |
| **Realized & unrealized losses on non‑designated derivatives** | $(13,719) | $(14,852) | ↓ $1.1 M |

| **Loss on deconsolidation of Altera** | — | $(7,070) | Eliminated in 2019 |
| **Other loss** | $(14,475) | $(2,013) | ↑ $12.5 M |
| **Income tax expense** | $(25,482) | $(19,724) | ↑ $5.8 M |

**Key Drivers**

* **Interest expense (+$24.9 M)** – Primarily caused by:  
  * $29.9 M increase from Teekay LNG’s finance‑lease obligations on the Myrina, Megara and Yamal Spirit LNG carriers and additional debt for the Bahrain Spirit and Sean Spirit newbuildings.  
  * $6.7 M extra interest from three Teekay Tankers sale‑lease‑back financings (Sept 2018, Nov 2018, May 2019).  
  * $6.3 M rise due to reduced capitalized interest as vessels were delivered in 2018‑19.  
  * A $4.1 M offset from lower interest on Teekay Parent’s revolving credit facilities.

* **Interest income (‑$0.7 M)** – Slight decline, reflecting modest changes in cash balances and investment yields.

* **Derivative losses (‑$13.7 M vs. ‑$14.9 M)** – Net losses fell by $1.1 M. Realized losses dropped because no interest‑rate‑swap terminations occurred in 2019 (versus $13.7 M realized losses in 2018). However, unrealized losses rose to $7.9 M in 2019 after a swing from a $33.7 M unrealized gain in 2018, driven by long‑term benchmark rate shifts.

* **Foreign‑exchange loss (‑$13.6 M vs. +$6.1 M gain)** – The loss resulted from:  
  * $5.1 M realized losses on cross‑currency swaps (vs. $6.5 M realized loss in 2018).  
  * $13.2 M unrealized losses on those swaps (versus a $21.2 M unrealized gain in 2018).  
  * Revaluation of NOK‑denominated debt produced a $5.8 M unrealized gain, but overall the weaker U.S. dollar against the NOK and Euro generated a net loss.

* **Loss on deconsolidation of Altera** – No loss recorded in 2019 after the Altera assets were sold; the 2018 loss of $7.1 M is therefore eliminated.

* **Other loss (↑ $12.5 M)** – Largely attributable to:

text.value: 2. Net Income (Loss) Per Share

Basic earnings per share, or EPS, is calculated by dividing net income (loss) by the weighted-average number of common shares outstanding for the period, without consideration for common stock equivalents. Diluted EPS is computed by dividing net income by the weighted-average number of common shares outstanding for the period and the weighted-average number of dilutive common stock equivalents outstanding for the period determined using the treasury-stock method.

For purposes of this calculation, common stock options, restricted stock units and restricted stock awards are considered to be common stock equivalents and are only included in the calculation of diluted EPS when their effect is dilutive. In periods in which the Company has a net loss, dilutive common stock equivalents are excluded from the calculation of diluted EPS.

Based on the current amortizing asset base, the company estimates an average annual amortization of **$58.3 million** over the next five years, peaking at $59.9 million in FY 2020 and tapering to $54.2 million by FY 2024.

NOTE 12 — Debt
Long-term debt was comprised of the following:

On February 12, 2019, we entered into an amended and restated five-year Credit Agreement with a group of banks (the "Credit Agreement") to extend the term of the facility. The Credit Agreement provides for a revolving credit facility of $300,000, which may be increased by $150,000 at the request of the Company, subject to the administrative agent's approval. This new unsecured credit facility replaces the prior $300,000 unsecured credit facility, which would have expired August 10, 2020. Borrowings of $50,000 under the prior credit agreement were refinanced into the Credit Agreement. The prior agreement was terminated as of February 12, 2019.

The Revolving Credit Facility includes a swing line sublimit of $15,000 and a letter of credit sublimit of $10,000. Borrowings under the Revolving Credit Facility bear interest at the base rate defined in the Credit Agreement. We also pay a quarterly commitment fee on the unused portion of the Revolving Credit Facility. The commitment fee ranges from 0.20% to 0.30% based on our total leverage ratio.

The Revolving Credit Facility requires, among other things, that we comply with a maximum total leverage ratio and a minimum fixed charge coverage ratio. Failure to comply with these covenants could reduce the borrowing availability under the Revolving Credit Facility. We were in compliance with all debt covenants at December 31, 2019. The Revolving Credit Facility requires that we deliver quarterly financial statements, annual financial statements, auditor certifications, and compliance certificates within a specified number of days after the end of a quarter and year. Additionally, the Revolving Credit Facility contains restrictions limiting our ability to: dispose of assets; incur certain additional debt; repay other debt or amend subordinated debt instruments; create liens on assets; make investments, loans or advances; make acquisitions or engage in mergers or consolidations; engage in certain transactions with our subsidiaries and affiliates; and make stock repurchases and dividend payments. Interest rates on the Revolving Credit Facility fluctuate based upon the LIBOR and the Company’s quarterly total leverage ratio.

We have debt issuance costs related to our long-term debt that are being amortized using the straight-line method over the life of the debt. Amortization expense for the twelve months ended December 31, 2019 was approximately $163 and $185 in 2018 and 2017. These costs are included in interest expense in our Consolidated Statement of Earnings.

We use interest rate swaps to convert the revolving credit facility's variable rate of interest into a fixed rate on a portion of the debt as described more fully in Note 13 "Derivatives." These swaps are treated as cash flow hedges and consequently, the changes in fair value were recorded in other comprehensive earnings.

synth_text.text:
The impairment test for goodwill requires the carrying amount of each cash‑generating unit (CGU) to be compared with its recoverable amount, which is derived from value‑in‑use calculations based on three‑year cash‑flow projections. The carrying amount of a CGU comprises goodwill, property, plant and equipment, and intangible assets.

The table below summarises the current carrying values (in £ million) for the relevant CGU components:

| Category | Digital | Webzone | Total |

| **Current** | 327.6 | 6.6 | 334.2 |

Key observations:

* **Overall increase:** The total CGU carrying amount has risen from **£334.2 m** to **£349.5 m**, an uplift of **£15.3 m**.
* **Digital assets:** The primary driver of this increase is the Digital segment, which grew by **£15.0 m** (from £327.6 m to £342.6 m).
* **Webzone assets:** The Webzone segment saw a modest rise of **£0.3 m** (from £6.6 m to £6.9 m).

These updated figures will be used in the forthcoming impairment analysis to determine whether the CGU’s recoverable amount exceeds its carrying value, thereby assessing the need for any goodwill write‑down.

text.value: Contractual Obligations

The following table summarizes our significant contractual obligations at March 31, 2019, and the effect such obligations are expected to have on our liquidity and cash flows in future periods (in millions):

(1) Operating lease obligations include $18.1 million of future lease payments which is recorded as a liability on the balance sheet as of March 31, 2019. This obligation is due under an operating lease from our acquisition of Atmel for a building in San Jose, California.

(2) Capital purchase obligations represent commitments for construction or purchases of property, plant and equipment. These obligations were not recorded as liabilities on our balance sheet as of March 31, 2019, as we have not yet received the related goods or taken title to the property.
(3) Other purchase obligations and commitments include payments due under various types of licenses and outstanding purchase commitments with our wafer foundries.
(4) The Term Loan Facility matures on May 29, 2025.

(5) For purposes of this table, we have assumed that the principal of our 2023 revolving loans outstanding at March 31, 2019 will be paid on May 18, 2023, which is the maturity date of such borrowings.
(6) For purposes of this table, we have assumed that the principal of our 2017 senior convertible debt will be paid on February 15, 2027, which is the maturity date of such debt.
(7) For purposes of this table, we have assumed that the principal of our 2015 Senior Convertible Debt will be paid on February 15, 2025, which is the maturity date of such debt.
(8) For purposes of this table, we have assumed that the principal of our 2017 Junior Convertible Debt will be paid on February 15, 2037, which is the maturity date of such debt.
(9) For purposes of this table, pension obligations due in more than 5 years represent the expected pension payments from 2025 through 2029. It excludes pension obligations subsequent to 2029.

(10) During fiscal 2018, we recognized a provisionary one-time transition tax on accumulated unrepatriated foreign earnings, estimated at $644.7 million, as a result of the recent U.S. tax reform. As of December 31, 2018, with the conclusion of the measurement period in accordance with SAB 118, we increased this amount by $13.1 million to $657.8 million, of which we expect cash payments of approximately $280.7 million after offsets by the utilization of various tax attribute carryforwards in the United States. Our first payment on this obligation of $35.0 million was made in the quarter ended September 30, 2018 and we expect future cash payments of approximately $245.7 million. This tax is to be paid over a period of eight years, with 8% of the transition tax paid each year for fiscal 2019 through fiscal 2023, and 15%, 20%, and 25%, respectively, to be paid during fiscal 2024, 2025, and 2026.
(11) The contractual obligations do not include amounts related to uncertain tax positions because reasonable estimates cannot be made.

Purchase orders or contracts for the purchase of raw materials and other goods and services, with the exception of commitments to our wafer foundries, are not included in the table above. We are not able to determine the aggregate amount of such purchase orders that represent contractual obligations, as purchase orders may represent authorizations to purchase rather than binding agreements. For the purpose of this table, contractual obligations for the purchase of goods or services are defined as agreements that are enforceable and legally binding on us and that specify all significant terms, including: fixed or minimum quantities to be purchased; fixed, minimum or variable price provisions; and the approximate timing of the transaction. Our purchase orders are based on our current manufacturing needs and are fulfilled by our vendors with short time horizons. We do not have significant agreements for the purchase of raw materials or other goods specifying minimum quantities or set prices that exceed our expected requirements for three months. We also enter into contracts for outsourced services; however, the obligations under these contracts were not significant and the contracts generally contain clauses allowing for cancellation without significant penalty.

The expected timing of payment of the obligations discussed above is estimated based on current information. Timing of payments and actual amounts paid may be different depending on the time of receipt of goods or services or changes to agreed-upon amounts for some obligations.

synth_text.text:
The company’s contractual obligations at March 31 2019 total **$6,985.3 million**. The most material components are:

| Obligation | Amount ( $ million) | Key Details |
|------------|--------------------|-------------|
| **Operating lease obligations** | 22.6 | Future lease payments for the Atmel‑acquired building in San Jose, California. |
| **Term Loan Facility** | 2,013.8 | Fixed‑rate loan maturing on **29 May 2025**. |
| **2017 Senior Convertible Debt** | 2,170.9 | Principal assumed to be repaid on **15 Feb 2027**. |
| **2015 Senior Convertible Debt** | 1,753.0 | Principal assumed to be repaid on **15 Feb 2025**. |
| **2017 Junior Convertible Debt** | 886.8 | Principal assumed to be repaid on **15 Feb 2037**. |
| **Pension obligations ( > 5 years)** | 11.9 | Expected cash payments for 2025‑2029; obligations after 2029 are excluded. |
| **Transition tax obligation** | 126.3 | One‑time tax on unrepatriated foreign earnings; paid over eight years (8 % annually 2019‑2023, then 15 %, 20 % and 25 % in 2024‑2026). |

All other categories—capital purchase obligations, other purchase commitments, revolving credit facility, 2023/2021 senior notes—are reported as “—”, indicating no recorded liability at the reporting date.

**Key observations**

* The **Term Loan Facility** and the two **senior convertible debts** together represent roughly **78 %** of total obligations, underscoring the company’s reliance on long‑term borrowing.
* The **junior convertible debt** extends the debt profile to 2037, adding a long‑dated liability.
* **Pension** and **transition tax** obligations are relatively modest but are scheduled over multiple future years, affecting cash‑flow planning.
* The figures exclude uncertain tax positions and non‑binding purchase orders, as the company could not reliably estimate those amounts.

Overall, the $6.99 billion obligation portfolio is dominated by long‑term debt instruments, with smaller, defined‑purpose liabilities for leases, pensions, and transition tax. These commitments shape the company’s liquidity outlook and will be serviced according to the maturity dates and payment schedules described above.

**Overview**  
As of March 31 2019 the company reported total contractual obligations of **$14,461.6 million**, of which **$652.9 million** (approximately 4.5 %) is due within the next twelve months. These obligations encompass lease payments, purchase commitments, debt facilities, pension liabilities, and a transition‑tax charge.

| Category | Total ( $ million ) | Due < 1 yr ( $ million ) | Key Notes |

**Additional Context**

- The operating lease figure reflects a specific lease tied to the Atmel acquisition.  
- Capital purchase commitments are forward‑looking and therefore not capitalized on the balance sheet.

synth_text.title: Key Assumptions and Financial Parameters for Post‑Employment Benefit Obligations (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
The organization’s post‑employment benefit (PEB) obligations for the fiscal years ended December 31, 2018 and 2019 were measured using a consistent set of long‑term actuarial assumptions, reflecting the nature of defined‑benefit (DB) pension and other post‑employment benefit (OPEB) plans.

**Core actuarial assumptions**

| Year | Discount rate | Compensation increase | Cost‑of‑living indexation* | Life expectancy at age 65 |
|------|---------------|-----------------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| 2019 | 3.1 % | 2.25 % | 1.6 % | 23.2 years |
| 2018 | 3.8 % | 2.25 % | 1.6 % | 23.1 years |

\*The cost‑of‑living indexation rate applies only to DB pension plans.

**Supporting assumptions**

- The weighted average duration of the PEB obligation is 14 years, indicating the average time over which benefits are expected to be paid.
- Healthcare cost trends were incorporated to reflect the expected growth in OPEB plan expenses:
  - Medication costs: 6.5 % annual increase in 2019, tapering to 4 % over the next 20 years.
  - Dental benefits: 4 % annual increase.
  - Hospital benefits: 3.7 % annual increase.
  - Other covered healthcare benefits: 4 % annual increase.
- These healthcare cost trend rates have a significant effect on the amounts reported for the organization’s healthcare plans.

Together, these assumptions provide the basis for calculating the net benefit cost of the DB pension and OPEB plans, ensuring that the valuation reflects both financial market conditions (through the discount rate) and expected future benefit growth (through compensation, inflation, and healthcare cost trends).

text.value: Market and Market Prices of Common Stock

During 2016 fiscal year and through February 22, 2017, our common stock was traded on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol “ACUR”. On February 23, 2017, our common stock was delisted from the Nasdaq Capital Market due to our failure to comply with Nasdaq’s Listing Rule 5550(b)(1), which requires that we maintain $2.5 million in stockholders’ equity for continued listing (or meet the alternatives of market value of listed securities of $35 million or net income from continuing operations). NASDAQ had granted us a grace period through February 10, 2017, to regain compliance with Listing Rule 5550(b)(1), but we were unable to regain compliance within such period.

Commencing on February 23, 2017, our common stock was quoted on the OTCQB under the symbol “ACUR”, however commencing June 4, 2018 and lasting until July 2, 2018 it was quoted on the OTC Markets OTC Pink tier. The downgrade was a result of the late filing of our 2017 Annual Report on Form 10-K beyond any applicable grace periods. However, commencing May 20, 2019 as a result of late filing of our 2018 Annual Report on Form 10-K our common stock was again relegated to the OTC Markets OTC Pink tier. synth_text.title: Cash Flow and Unlevered Free Cash Flow – Current Period vs Prior Period
synth_text.text:
The company generated $167.9 million of Cash EBITDA in the current period, down from $199.2 million a year earlier. Adjusted operating profit improved to $109.0 million from $58.3 million, reflecting higher revenue deferrals ($49.7 million versus $129.6 million) and lower expense deferrals (‑$0.9 million versus ‑$8.4 million). Exceptional items fell sharply to $3.1 million from $13.0 million, while foreign‑exchange effects moved from a $8.1 million gain to a $1.5 million loss.

Working‑capital efficiency also improved, with a smaller cash outflow of $5.2 million (versus $12.2 million previously). However, higher overheads—particularly in sales and marketing—partially offset these gains. As a result, net cash flow from operating activities decreased modestly by $4.8 million to $142.9 million from $147.7 million in the prior period. The reduction in cash outflow on exceptional items ($9.9 million) and the better use of working capital ($7.0 million) were the primary positive contributors, while the increase in overheads drove the net decline.

Net capital expenditure remained broadly unchanged, at a cash outflow of $22.2 million versus $21.1 million previously. After accounting for the cash impact of exceptional items, unlevered free cash flow fell by $15.8 million to $123.8 million from $139.6 million, underscoring the sensitivity of free cash generation to both operating performance and one‑off items.

Overall, the company’s cash‑generation capability remains strong, with positive operating cash flow and a solid unlevered free cash flow base, despite the modest declines driven by higher overhead costs and the transition in exceptional items.

text.value: Key Metrics

In addition to our results determined in accordance with GAAP, we believe the following operating metrics are useful as supplements in evaluating our ongoing operational performance and help provide an enhanced understanding of our business:

Total bookings. Total bookings represents cash receipts from the sale of products to customers in a given period adjusted for products where we recognize revenue on a net basis and without giving effect to certain adjustments, primarily net refunds granted in the period. Total bookings provides valuable insight into the sales of our products and the performance of our business since we typically collect payment at the time of sale and recognize revenue ratably over the term of our customer contracts. We report total bookings without giving effect to refunds granted in the period because refunds often occur in periods different from the period of sale for reasons unrelated to the marketing efforts leading to the initial sale. Accordingly, by excluding net refunds, we believe total bookings reflects the effectiveness of our sales efforts in a given period.

Total customers. We define a customer as an individual or entity, as of the end of a period, having an account with one or more paid product subscriptions. A single user may be counted asacustomer more than once if the user maintains paid subscriptions in multiple accounts. Total customers is one way we measure the scale of our business and is an important part of our ability to increase our revenue base

Average revenue per user (ARPU). We calculate ARPU as total revenue during the preceding 12 month period divided by the average of the number of total customers at the beginning and end of the period. ARPU provides insight into our ability to sell additional products to customers, though the impact to date has been muted due to our continued growth in total customers.

**Metric definitions**

- **Total customers** count all individual or entity accounts with at least one paid subscription at period end. A single user may be counted multiple times if they hold subscriptions in multiple accounts, making this metric a measure of the business’s scale.  
- **ARPU** is calculated as total revenue over the preceding 12‑month period divided by the average number of customers at the beginning and end of the period. It reflects the company’s ability to generate more revenue per customer.

text.value: We have included Adjusted EBITDA in this report because it is a key measure that our management uses to understand and evaluate our core operating performance and trends, to generate future operating plans, to make strategic decisions regarding the allocation of capital and to make investments in initiatives that are focused on cultivating new markets for our solutions. We also use certain non-GAAP financial measures, including Adjusted EBITDA, as performance measures under our executive bonus plan. Further, we believe the exclusion of certain expenses in calculating Adjusted EBITDA facilitates comparisons of our operating performance on a period-to-period basis and, in the case of exclusion of acquisition-related expense and certain historical legal expenses, excludes items that we do not consider to be indicative of our core operating performance. Accordingly, we believe that Adjusted EBITDA provides useful information to investors and others in understanding and evaluating our operating results in the same manner as our management and board of directors.

Our use of Adjusted EBITDA has limitations as an analytical tool, and you should not consider it in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our financial results as reported under GAAP. Some of these limitations are: (a) although depreciation and amortization are non-cash charges, the assets being depreciated and amortized may have to be replaced in the future, and Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect cash capital expenditure requirements for such replacements or for new capital expenditure requirements; (b) Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect changes in, or cash requirements for, our working capital needs; (c) Adjusted EBITDA does  may represent a reduction in cash available to us; and (e) other companies, including companies in our industry, may calculate Adjusted EBITDA or similarly titled measures differently, which reduces its usefulness as a comparative measure.

Because of these and other limitations, you should consider Adjusted EBITDA alongside our other GAAP-based financial performance measures, our net income and our other GAAP financial results. - Litigation expenses fell sharply in 2017, offsetting part of the increase from other adjustments.  

**Why Adjusted EBITDA is reported**  
Management uses Adjusted EBITDA to gauge core operating performance, guide strategic capital allocation, and assess progress toward new market initiatives. It also serves as a performance metric under the executive bonus plan. By excluding items such as acquisition‑related costs and historical legal expenses, the measure aims to provide a clearer view of recurring operating results.

**Limitations**  
Adjusted EBITDA is a non‑GAAP metric and should not be viewed in isolation. It does not reflect cash needed for capital replacements, working‑capital changes, or future cash outflows, and different companies may calculate it differently, limiting comparability. Investors should therefore consider Adjusted EBITDA alongside GAAP measures such as net income and cash flow.

**Key observations**

* Adjusted EBITDA rose from **$93.1 million in 2018** to **$108.3 million in 2019**, reflecting higher net income and lower litigation expense in 2019.
* The largest single adjustment in 2018 was litigation expense ($45.7 million), whereas in 2019 it dropped to $12.8 million, contributing to the EBITDA increase.
* Stock‑based compensation and amortization/depreciation remain significant, together accounting for roughly one‑third of total adjustments each year.
* Acquisition‑related expense appeared only in 2019 ($2.4 million), indicating a modest acquisition activity that year.

**Management’s rationale for reporting Adjusted EBITDA**

* It isolates core operating performance by excluding items that are not indicative of ongoing operations (e.g., acquisition costs, certain legal expenses).
* The metric supports internal planning, capital‑allocation decisions, and executive compensation assessments.
* Adjusted EBITDA facilitates period‑to‑period comparisons of operating results.

**Limitations**

* Adjusted EBITDA omits cash‑intensive items such as capital expenditures required to replace depreciated assets.
* It does not reflect changes in working‑capital needs or cash requirements for future investments.
* Because other companies may calculate similarly titled measures differently, direct comparisons across the industry can be misleading.

**Conclusion**

While Adjusted EBITDA provides valuable insight into the company’s underlying operating performance, investors should evaluate it alongside GAAP measures—particularly net income—and consider the noted limitations when assessing overall financial health.

For the fiscal year ended 2015, the company reported a GAAP net income of **$11.8 million**. To provide a clearer view of core operating performance, management presented an Adjusted EBITDA of **$34.4 million**, derived by adding a series of non‑GAAP adjustments totaling **$22.6 million**.

**Why Adjusted EBITDA is Reported**  
Management uses Adjusted EBITDA as a key performance indicator to:

* Evaluate core operating trends and develop future operating plans.  
* Guide strategic capital allocation and investment decisions, especially for new market initiatives.  
* Align executive compensation with performance, as the metric is incorporated into the bonus plan.  

By excluding items such as acquisition‑related costs and historical legal expenses—expenses that management does not view as reflective of ongoing operations—the metric aims to facilitate period‑to‑period comparisons of operating performance.

**Limitations of Adjusted EBITDA**  
The company cautions that Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered in isolation:

1. **Capital Replacement Needs** – Depreciation and amortization are non‑cash charges, yet the underlying assets may require future capital outlays that Adjusted EBITDA does not capture.  
2. **Working‑Capital Requirements** – The metric ignores changes in working capital and associated cash needs.  
3. **Cash Availability** – Adjusted EBITDA may overstate cash available for the business.  
4. **Comparability** – Other firms may calculate similarly named metrics differently, limiting cross‑company comparability.

**Conclusion**  
The 2015 reconciliation demonstrates that after adding $22.6 million of adjustments to the GAAP net income of $11.8 million, the company’s Adjusted EBITDA stands at $34.4 million. While this non‑GAAP measure offers valuable insight into core operating performance and informs strategic decisions, investors should evaluate it alongside GAAP results and consider its inherent limitations.

synth_text.title: Shift in Other Income (Expense), Net: 2018 vs. 2019
synth_text.text:
The “Other Income (Expense), Net” line experienced a dramatic reversal between 2018 and 2019.  

- **2018**: The total other income (expense) was **$2.364 billion**, driven by modest interest income ($94 million), a net benefit credit of $3.068 billion, early debt extinguishment costs of $725 million, and a small other net expense of $73 million.  
- **2019**: The total turned **negative $2.900 billion**. While interest income rose slightly to $121 million, the other components shifted sharply: net periodic benefit costs became a $627 million charge, early debt extinguishment costs surged to **$(3.604 billion)**, and other net expenses were $(44 million).  

The change is primarily explained by two items highlighted in the supplemental notes:  

1. **Early debt redemption costs** increased dramatically, from $725 million in 2018 to $3.6 billion in 2019.  
2. **Pension and benefit items** moved from a $2.1 billion credit in 2018 to a $126 million charge in 2019.  

Together, these factors reversed the net other income from a positive $2.364 billion to a negative $2.900 billion, reflecting the significant impact of debt‑related expenses and pension adjustments on the company’s financial results for 2019.

synth_text.text:

- **Early debt extinguishment costs:** **‑$2,879**

The negative total is driven primarily by two large items:

1. **Early debt extinguishment costs** – $2,879 million, reflecting the redemption of debt. The additional context notes that early debt redemption costs rose sharply to **$3.6 billion** in 2019 (up from $725 million in 2018), a key factor behind the sizable outflow.

2. **Net periodic benefit cost** – a shift from a $2.1 billion pension/benefit credit in 2018 to a $126 million charge in 2019, turning this line into a $2.4 billion expense.

When comparing 2019 to 2018, the percentage changes for the individual components were:

- **Other components of net periodic benefit cost:** **‑79.6 %** (from a credit to a charge)  
- **Other, net:** **+39.7 %**  

Early debt extinguishment costs and the overall total are marked “nm” (not meaningful) for the percentage column because the absolute dollar changes are dominated by large, non‑recurring items rather than normal operating fluctuations.

In summary, the 2019 net other income (expense) was heavily impacted by a substantial increase in debt redemption costs and a reversal of pension/benefit credits, resulting in a net loss of **$5.3 billion** for the period.

text.value: Stock-Based Compensation Expense

All share-based awards are measured based on the grant date fair value of the awards and recognized in the Consolidated Statements of Operations and Comprehensive Loss over the period during which the employee is required to perform services in exchange for the award (generally the vesting period of the award).

The Company estimates the fair value of stock options granted using the Black-Scholes option valuation model, which requires assumptions, including the fair value of the Company's underlying common stock, expected term, expected volatility, risk-free interest rate and dividend yield of the Company's common stock. These estimates involve inherent uncertainties and the application of management’s judgment. If factors change and different assumptions are used, share-based compensation expense could be materially different in the future.
These assumptions are estimated as follows:
• Fair Value of Common Stock. The Company uses the five-day volume weighted average price for its common stock as reported on the New York Stock Exchange.

• #Expected Term. The Company determines the expected term based on the average period the stock options are expected to remain outstanding. The Company bases the expected term assumptions on its historical behavior combined with estimates of the post-vesting holding period.
• Expected Volatility. The Company determines the price volatility factor based on the Company's historical volatility over the expected life of the stock options.

• Risk-Free Interest Rate. The Company bases the risk-free interest rate used in the Black-Scholes valuation model on the yield available on U.S. Treasury zero-coupon issues with an equivalent remaining term of the stock options for each stock option group.

• Expected Dividend. The Company has not paid and does not anticipate paying any cash dividends in the foreseeable future and, therefore, uses an expected dividend yield of zero in the option pricing model.

synth_text.title: Key Assumptions Used in Stock Option Valuation – Comparison of 2018 and 2019
synth_text.text:
The Company’s share‑based compensation expense is calculated using the Black‑Scholes option‑pricing model, which requires several market‑based assumptions. For the fiscal years ending December 31, 2018 and December 31, 2019, the weighted‑average inputs were as follows:

| Fiscal Year‑End | Expected Volatility | Risk‑Free Interest Rate | Dividend Yield | Average Expected Life (years) |
|-----------------|---------------------|------------------------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **December 31, 2019** | 50.7 % | 2.25 % | Nil | 4.77 |
| **December 31, 2018** | 54.2 % | 2.72 % | Nil | 5.31 |

**Key observations**

* **Volatility** – The price‑volatility factor fell from 54.2 % in 2018 to 50.7 % in 2019, reflecting a modest reduction in the Company’s historical stock‑price fluctuations over the expected option life.
* **Risk‑free rate** – The rate used in the model decreased from 2.72 % to 2.25 %, mirroring lower yields on U.S. Treasury zero‑coupon securities with comparable maturities.
* **Dividend yield** – Consistent with the Company’s policy of not paying cash dividends, the expected dividend yield remained zero for both periods.
* **Average expected life** – The estimated term of the options shortened from 5.31 years in 2018 to 4.77 years in 2019, based on the Company’s historical option‑exercise behavior and post‑vesting holding period assumptions.

These assumptions are integral to estimating the fair value of stock options granted to employees. Changes in any of the inputs—particularly volatility, risk‑free rate, or expected term—can materially affect the recognized share‑based compensation expense in future periods.

synth_text.title: Summary of Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities – FY 2018
synth_text.text:
The company’s deferred tax position for the year ended 31 March 2018 shows a significant turnaround in deferred tax assets. The opening balance on 1 April 2017 was a negative S$ 285.3 million, reflecting a net tax liability. After applying the effects of adopting Singapore Financial Reporting Standard (SFRS) (I) 15 (a reduction of S$ 1.0 million) and restating the opening balance, the asset position improved to a positive S$ 2.1 million. During the year, a credit of S$ 9.2 million was recognised in the income statement, further strengthening the asset base to a closing balance of S$ 11.3 million as at 31 March 2018.

On the liability side, the adoption of SFRS (I) 1 contributed an increase of S$ 10.2 million to deferred tax liabilities (reported in S$ million). 

According to the provided notes, deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only when a legally enforceable right to set‑off exists and when both relate to the same fiscal authority. Consequently, the reported figures represent the net positions after applying the applicable offsetting rules.

Overall, the company moved from a net deferred tax deficit at the start of the year to a net deferred tax asset of S$ 11.3 million by year‑end, driven by accounting standard adoptions and income‑statement credits.

| **Deferred tax assets – main component** | (285.3) | (1.0) | 1.8 | 9.0 | 10.8 |
| **Deferred tax liabilities** | – | – | – | – | 10.2* |

\*The increase of S$ 10.2 million in deferred tax liabilities stems from the adoption of **SFRS(I) 1**, primarily related to accelerated depreciation.

**Key points**

1. **Asset side** – The company moved from a large negative balance (‑285.3 million) on 1 April 2017 to a positive balance of **S$ 10.8 million** at year‑end. The reversal was driven by a **S$ 9.0 million credit** to the income statement during the year, after accounting for a modest S$ 0.2 million credit to a smaller asset component.

2. **Liability side** – Adoption of **SFRS(I) 1** introduced an additional **S$ 10.2 million** of deferred tax liability, reflecting the tax effect of accelerated depreciation recognised in the financial statements.

3. **Offsetting rule** – Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only when a legally enforceable right to set‑off exists and both relate to the same fiscal authority, as noted in the accompanying remarks.

**Conclusion**  
The net effect of the year’s accounting changes and operational results was a substantial improvement in the company’s deferred tax asset position, turning a prior net liability into a modest net asset of **S$ 10.8 million**. Simultaneously, the adoption of new SFRS standards added **S$ 10.2 million** to deferred tax liabilities, primarily due to accelerated tax depreciation.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal 2019 the company adopted ASC Topic 606, the new revenue‑recognition standard, using the modified retrospective approach. A comprehensive review determined that the new guidance did not create material differences in revenue contracts or require major changes to business processes, systems, or controls. The adoption generated a cumulative effect adjustment of $0.5 million (net of tax) to opening retained earnings and produced modest adjustments to several balance‑sheet line items.

**Pre‑adjustment balances (as of May 26 2019)**

- Other accrued liabilities: **$691.6 million**

(Current liabilities were not disclosed in the excerpt.)

| Line Item | Adjustment (million $) |

| Prepaid expenses and other current assets | **‑ $16.6** |
| Other accrued liabilities | **‑ $1.1** |

These adjustments reflect timing changes in the recognition of certain customer charges, trade promotional expenditures, and volume discounts. While the net effect on retained earnings was modest ($0.5 million), the line‑item movements illustrate the specific areas where the new revenue‑recognition rules altered the presentation of assets and liabilities.

**Key take‑aways**  
- The adoption of Topic 606 did not produce material differences to revenue contracts.  
- Adjustments were relatively small, with the largest absolute change occurring in inventories (a $3.1 million decrease).  
- The overall impact on the consolidated balance sheet was limited, confirming that the company’s existing accounting policies and controls were largely compatible with the new guidance.

text.value: 16. INCOME TAXES (Continued)

The reconciliation of the income tax expense at the U.S. Federal statutory rate (21.0% in fiscal 2019, 24.5% in fiscal 2018 and 35.0% in fiscal 2017) to actual income tax expense is as follows (in thousands):

On December 22, 2017, the Tax Act was enacted. The Tax Act contains significant changes to U.S. tax law, including lowering the U.S. corporate income tax rate to 21.0%, implementing a territorial tax system with a one-time transition tax assessment on previously tax-deferred foreign earnings and imposing new taxes on certain foreign-sourced income. We elected to pay the one-time transition tax over a period of up to eight years.

In conjunction with the Tax Act, the SEC issued guidance under Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118 (‘‘SAB 118’’) directing taxpayers to record the impact of the Tax Act as ‘‘provisional’’ when they do not have all the necessary information to complete the accounting under ASC 740. The guidance allowed for a measurement period of up to one year after the enactment date of the Tax Act to finalize the recording of the related tax impact. In accordance with SAB 118, we recorded provisional estimates to our consolidated financial statements in fiscal 2018 based on the Tax Act. During the first quarter of fiscal 2019, we further analyzed the income tax effects of the Tax Act and determined there were no material changes to the provisional amounts disclosed in our fiscal 2018 financial statements. Although our accounting for the effects of the Tax Act is complete under SAB 118, there may be future adjustments based on interpretations by the U.S. federal and state governments and regulatory organizations, legislative updates or new regulations, or changes in accounting standards for income taxes.

The Tax Act also includes provisions for Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (‘‘GILTI’’) wherein taxes on foreign income are imposed in excess of a deemed return on tangible assets of foreign corporations. In general, this income will effectively be taxed at a 10.5% tax rate reduced by any available current year foreign tax credits. This provision became effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017, which was our fiscal 2019. We have elected to treat tax generated by the GILTI provisions as a period expense.

The effective tax rate on income from continuing operations before income taxes for fiscal 2019 of 10.4% was lower than the U.S. federal tax rate of 21.0% primarily due to the tax benefit from losses of our German subsidiaries, which are subject to higher tax rates than U.S. tax rates, adjustments related to the Tax Act’s transition tax, the net excess tax benefits from restricted stock unit vesting, the benefit of federal research and development tax credits and our Singapore and South Korea tax exemptions. These amounts are partially offset by an accrual for foreign withholding taxes on certain current year foreign earnings not considered permanently reinvested, stock-based compensation not deductible for tax purposes and limitations on the deductibility of compensation under Internal Revenue Code Section 162(m).

synth_text.title: Income Tax Provision Summary for Fiscal Years 2018 and 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The reconciliation of the U.S. federal statutory tax expense to the actual provision for income taxes shows a sharp decline from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2019.  In FY 2018 the company recorded a provision of **$114.2 million** with an **effective tax rate of 31.6 %**.  In FY 2019 the provision fell to **$6.2 million**, yielding an **effective tax rate of 10.4 %**.

**Key Drivers of the FY 2019 Reduction**

| Item (FY 2019) | Impact (in $ thousands) |
|----------------|--------------------------|
| Federal statutory tax expense | $12,610 |
| Valuation allowance (increase) | $7,925 |
| Foreign taxes at rates greater than U.S. rates (net) | –$8,210 |
| Stock‑based compensation (non‑deductible) | $556 |
| State income taxes (net) | $1,131 |
| Research & development credit | –$3,665 |
| Deferred compensation | –$206 |
| Release of unrecognized tax benefits | –$6,688 |
| Release of interest on unrecognized tax benefits | –$205 |
| Deferred taxes on foreign earnings | $1,215 |
| Write‑off of withholding tax credits | $1,134 |
| Other, net | $626 |
| **Provision for income taxes** | **$6,223** |

Compared with FY 2018, several line items moved in the opposite direction (e.g., a $8.5 M credit for foreign taxes turned into a $8.2 M charge, and a $8.5 M stock‑based compensation expense became a $0.6 M charge).  The net effect of these reversals, together with a larger valuation allowance, drove the provision down dramatically.

**Impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act)**  

* Enacted 22 December 2017, the Tax Act lowered the U.S. corporate rate to **21 %** (from 35 % in 2017) and introduced a **one‑time transition tax** on previously deferred foreign earnings.  
* The company elected to amortize the transition tax over up to eight years and recorded provisional estimates in FY 2018 under SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin 118. No material adjustments were required in FY 2019.  
* New GILTI provisions, effective for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2017 (FY 2019 for the company), are taxed at an effective **10.5 %** after foreign tax credits and are treated as a period expense.  

**Other Influencing Factors**  

* Loss carryforwards from German subsidiaries, which are subject to higher foreign rates, provided a tax benefit that lowered the effective rate.  
* Tax exemptions in Singapore and South Korea further reduced the overall tax burden.  
* Federal research and development credits, releases of previously unrecognized tax benefits, and the treatment of restricted‑stock‑unit vesting contributed additional tax savings.  
* Offsetting items included non‑deductible stock‑based compensation, limitations on compensation deductions under IRC §162(m), and accruals for foreign withholding taxes on earnings not permanently reinvested.

**Conclusion**  
The combination of the Tax Act’s lower statutory rate, the amortization of the transition tax, GILTI treatment, and a series of favorable foreign‑tax and credit items resulted in a **substantially lower income tax provision and effective tax rate in FY 2019** compared with FY 2018.  While the provision is expected to remain modest, future adjustments could arise from changes in tax legislation, regulatory guidance, or accounting standards.

synth_text.title: 2017 Income Tax Reconciliation and Impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
In fiscal year 2017 the company recorded a federal statutory tax expense of **$105.7 million** based on the pre‑Tax Act corporate rate of **35 %**. After applying a series of adjustments, the provision for income taxes reported on the consolidated financial statements was **$93.4 million**, yielding an **effective tax rate of 30.9 %**.

**Key Adjustments to the Statutory Tax Expense**  

| Adjustment | Amount (in $ thousands) |
|------------|--------------------------|
| Valuation allowance | 4,454 |
| Foreign taxes at rates greater (less) than U.S. rates, net | (12,346) |
| Stock‑based compensation (non‑deductible) | 3,969 |
| State income taxes, net of federal benefit | 398 |
| Research & development credit | (7,884) |
| Deferred compensation | (1,022) |
| Release of unrecognized tax benefits | (538) |
| Release of interest accrued for unrecognized tax benefits | (78) |
| Other, net | 739 |
| **Total adjustments** | **(12,306)** |

These adjustments collectively reduced the statutory expense by **$12.3 million**, bringing the final provision to $93.4 million.

**Context – The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act)**  

- The Tax Act was enacted on **December 22, 2017**, after the close of the 2017 fiscal year. Consequently, the 2017 tax figures were calculated under the **35 % federal rate** that applied before the Act’s reduction to **21 %** for subsequent years.  
- The Act introduced a **one‑time transition tax** on previously tax‑deferred foreign earnings and a shift to a **territorial tax system**. The company elected to pay the transition tax over up to eight years.  
- In line with **SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118 (SAB 118)**, provisional estimates of the Tax Act’s impact were recorded in fiscal 2018, with final adjustments completed in early 2019. No material changes were identified after the provisional amounts were refined.  
- The Act also created the **Global Intangible Low‑Taxed Income (GILTI)** regime, which taxes certain foreign earnings at an effective rate of **10.5 %** (subject to foreign tax credits). GILTI became effective for taxable years beginning after **December 31, 2017** and is treated as a period expense.

**Implications**  

The 2017 effective tax rate of **30.9 %** reflects the higher statutory rate and the net effect of the adjustments listed above. The subsequent reduction in the U.S. corporate tax rate and the introduction of the transition tax, GILTI, and related provisions explain why the company’s effective tax rate declined in fiscal 2018 and 2019. While the 2017 numbers are not directly impacted by the Tax Act, the context clarifies the timing of the legislative changes and sets the stage for the lower rates observed in later periods.

**Conclusion**  

The 2017 tax reconciliation demonstrates how statutory tax obligations are modified by valuation allowances, foreign tax differentials, non‑deductible compensation, and tax credits, resulting in an effective tax rate of **30.9 %**. The enactment of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act at the end of 2017 introduced significant future tax considerations—transition tax, SAB 118 provisional accounting, and GILTI—that would shape the company’s tax position in the years that followed.

synth_text.title: 2018 Full‑Year Financial Highlights – Comparison with 2017
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
For the year ended December 31, 2018, the company delivered solid financial performance, with consolidated revenue increasing 5% year‑over‑year to **$15.1 billion**. This growth was driven primarily by the Wireless segment, which posted a 7% increase, while Cable and Media each grew 1%.

**Segment Revenue**  
- **Wireless:** $4.09 billion (up 7%), reflecting a higher mix of subscribers on premium plans and stronger sales of higher‑value devices.  
- **Cable:** $1.874 billion (up 1%), supported by customers moving to higher‑speed Internet tiers, partially offset by a decline in legacy television subscribers and phone‑package pricing impacts.  
- **Media:** $196 million (up 1%), boosted by higher revenue from the Toronto Blue Jays, MLB distribution, and increased Sportsnet and other network subscriptions, despite lower advertising revenue.

After accounting for corporate items and intercompany eliminations, **total service revenue** reached **$12.974 billion** in 2018, compared with $12.550 billion in 2017.

**Adjusted EBITDA**  
Adjusted EBITDA rose to **$5.983 billion**, a 9% increase, delivering an adjusted EBITDA margin of **39.6%** (up from 38.3% in 2017).  
- Wireless adjusted EBITDA grew 10% due to strong revenue flow‑through, offset by higher subscriber‑related costs and device expenses.  
- Cable adjusted EBITDA increased 3%, driven by robust Internet revenue, a shift toward higher‑margin services, and cost‑efficiency initiatives.  
- Media adjusted EBITDA surged 54%, reflecting the modest revenue uplift and significant reductions in operating expenses.

**Net Income**  
Net income improved to **$2.059 billion** in 2018 from $1.845 billion in 2017, while **adjusted net income** rose to **$2.241 billion** from $1.902 billion. The increases stem mainly from higher adjusted EBITDA, partially offset by greater depreciation and amortization.

**Additional Notes**  
- Effective January 1, 2019, the company adopted IFRS 16; the 2018 and 2017 results have not been restated for this change.  
- Adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin, and adjusted net income are non‑GAAP measures and should not be considered substitutes for GAAP metrics.

Overall, the 2018 results demonstrate continued growth across all business lines, improved profitability, and effective cost‑management initiatives.

Basic EPS is calculated by dividing net income by the weighted‑average number of common shares outstanding. In 2018, the basic share count was **266,085 thousand**, while in 2019 it was **268,784 thousand**. Diluted EPS incorporates the effect of dilutive securities—primarily stock options—using the treasury‑stock method. The dilutive effect added **1,407 thousand** shares in 2018 and **1,124 thousand** shares in 2019, resulting in diluted share totals of **267,492 thousand** and **269,908 thousand**, respectively.

Both years show a small number of options excluded as anti‑dilutive (2,770 thousand in 2018 and 2,759 thousand in 2019) because their exercise prices were at or above the average market price during the periods. These exclusions do not affect the diluted EPS figures.

Overall, the data indicate that OpenText’s profitability improved in 2019, with higher net income and EPS, while the share base remained relatively stable, and the impact of dilutive securities was modest.

synth_text.title: OpenText 2017 Net Income and Earnings‑Per‑Share Overview
synth_text.text:

In assessing the realizability of deferred tax assets, the Company considers whether it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. The ultimate realization of deferred tax assets is dependent upon the generation of future taxable income during the periods in which those temporary differences become deductible. The Company considers projected future taxable income, carryback opportunities, and tax planning strategies in making this assessment. Based upon the level of historical taxable income and projections for future taxable income over the periods which the deferred tax assets are deductible, the Company believes it is more likely than not that it will realize the benefits of these deductible differences, net of the valuation allowances recorded. During the year ended December 31, 2019, the Company decreased its valuation allowance by $12.8 million which relates to a reduction in the valuation allowance on U.S. foreign tax credits offset by an increase in valuation allowance on foreign net operating losses.

At December 31, 2019, the Company had domestic federal tax net operating losses (“NOLs”) of $65.9 million, which will begin to expire in 2020. The Company had deferred tax assets equal to $1.4 million related to domestic state tax NOLs which will begin to expire in 2020. The Company does not have any valuation allowance against the federal tax NOLs but has provided a $1.2 million valuation allowance against the deferred tax asset associated with the state NOLs. The Company had foreign tax NOLs of $30.4 million, of which $28.1 million may be utilized over an indefinite life, with the remainder expiring over the next 17 years. The Company has provided a $0.7 million valuation allowance against the deferred tax asset associated with the foreign NOLs.

The Company had U.S. foreign tax credit carryforwards at December 31, 2019, of $40.7 million, for which an $1.2 million valuation allowance has been provided. The U.S. foreign tax credits will begin to expire in 2022. The Company had foreign tax credit carryforwards in other foreign jurisdictions at December 31, 2019, of $1.9 million, of which $1.3 million may be utilized over an indefinite life, with the remainder expiring over the next seven years. The Company has provided a $1.2 million valuation allowance against the tax benefit associated with these foreign credits. The Company also has domestic federal and state general business tax credit carryforwards at December 31, 2019, of $15.7 million and $0.8 million, respectively, which will begin to expire in 2020 and 2022, respectively.

synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The Company’s balance sheet reflects significant deferred tax items that arise from timing differences between tax and financial reporting. For 2019, gross deferred income tax assets totaled **$124.4 million**, compared with **$131.1 million** in 2018. After applying valuation allowances, net deferred tax assets increased to **$116.7 million** in 2019 from **$110.7 million** in 2018.

**Key Components of Deferred Tax Assets**  

| Component (in $ thousands) | 2019 | 2018 |
|-----------------------------|------|------|
| Net operating loss (NOL) carryforwards | 23,030 | 25,745 |
| Tax credits | 52,902 | 43,838 |
| Compensation | 18,791 | 15,934 |

| **Gross assets** | 124,387 | 131,128 |

The valuation allowance fell sharply by **$12.8 million** in 2019, primarily due to a reduction on U.S. foreign tax credits, offset by a modest increase on foreign NOLs. This reduction reflects the Company’s confidence that a larger portion of its deferred tax assets will be realized.

**Deferred Tax Liabilities**  

| Component (in $ thousands) | 2019 | 2018 |
|-----------------------------|------|------|
| Depreciation & amortization | (52,978) | (60,872) |
| **Total liabilities** | (97,176) | (115,380) |
| **Net deferred taxes** | **19,558** | **(4,667)** |

Net deferred tax assets turned positive in 2019, moving from a net liability position in 2018.

**Balance‑Sheet Presentation**  
- Non‑current deferred tax asset: **$51.6 million** (2019) vs **$27.0 million** (2018)  
- Non‑current deferred tax liability: **$(32.1 million)** (2019) vs **$(31.7 million)** (2018)

**Realizability Assessment**  
The Company evaluates the likelihood of realizing deferred tax assets by considering projected future taxable income, carryback opportunities, and tax‑planning strategies. Based on historical earnings and forward‑looking forecasts, management concluded that it is “more likely than not” that the net deferred tax assets, net of valuation allowances, will be realized.

**Carryforwards and Related Valuation Allowances (as of 12/31/2019)**  

- **Domestic federal NOLs:** $65.9 million (no allowance) – expiring 2020  
- **Domestic state NOLs:** $1.4 million (allowance $1.2 million) – expiring 2020  
- **Foreign NOLs:** $30.4 million (allowance $0.7 million); $28.1 million indefinite, remainder over 17 years  
- **U.S. foreign tax credit carryforwards:** $40.7 million (allowance $1.2 million) – expiring 2022  
- **Other foreign tax credits:** $1.9 million (allowance $1.2 million) – partial indefinite life, remainder over 7 years  
- **Domestic federal and state general business tax credits:** $15.7 million and $0.8 million, expiring 2020 and 2022 respectively  

These details underscore the composition of the deferred tax assets and the specific allowances applied to portions deemed less certain to be realized.

**Conclusion**  
The Company’s deferred tax position improved markedly in 2019, driven by a reduction in valuation allowances and a shift from a net deferred tax liability to a net deferred tax asset. Ongoing assessments of future taxable income and strategic tax planning support the Company’s view that the majority of these assets will be realized in the coming periods.

synth_text.title: General and Administrative Expenses: 2019 Amount, Revenue Share, and 66.5 % YoY Increase
synth_text.text:
In 2019, Shopify’s General and Administrative (G&A) expenses totaled **$67.7 million**, representing **10.1 % of the company’s total revenues**. Compared with 2018, G&A costs rose sharply by **66.5 %**.

The increase was driven by several factors:

* **Employee‑related costs** grew by $28.7 million, including $12.2 million of stock‑based compensation and related payroll taxes.  
* **Finance costs** rose $14.9 million, reflecting an $8.1 million non‑recurring HST liability to the Government of Canada, plus higher taxes, insurance, and bank fees.  
* **Shopify Payments losses** increased by $9.0 million due to higher gross merchandise volume processed through the platform.  
* **Shopify Capital losses and insurance** climbed $8.6 million as the company expanded its capital‑offering programs.  
* **Professional services** (legal and tax) rose $6.9 million, supporting international expansion and overall business growth.  
* **Computer and software costs** grew $1.8 million, and **general bad‑debt expense** increased $1.6 million.

These components together explain the substantial 66.5 % year‑over‑year rise in G&A expenses while the expense level remained a modest 10.1 % of total revenue.

synth_text.title: Growth and Composition of General & Administrative Expenses (2018‑2019)
synth_text.text:
In 2018, Shopify’s General and Administrative (G&A) expenses accounted for **58.7 % of total revenues**, reflecting a **$39.7 million (58.7 %) increase** over the prior year. The surge was primarily driven by a **$30.3 million rise in employee‑related costs**, supplemented by higher professional services fees ($4.5 million), finance costs ($4.0 million) and computer/software expenses ($1.7 million).

The upward trajectory continued in 2019, when G&A expenses grew **$71.5 million (66.5 %)** compared with 2018. Key contributors to this larger increase included:

* **Employee‑related costs:** +$28.7 million (of which $12.2 million stemmed from stock‑based compensation and related payroll taxes)  
* **Finance costs:** +$14.9 million, featuring an $8.1 million non‑recurring HST liability to the Canadian government, plus insurance, sales/use taxes and bank fees  
* **Shopify Payments losses:** +$9.0 million, driven by higher gross merchandise volume processed through the platform  
* **Shopify Capital losses & insurance:** +$8.6 million, reflecting expanded capital‑offering programs  
* **Professional services (legal & tax):** +$6.9 million, linked to international expansion and overall business growth  
* **Computer and software costs:** +$1.8 million  
* **General bad‑debt expense:** +$1.6 million  

Overall, the data illustrate a consistent rise in G&A spending, with employee compensation and finance-related items being the dominant cost drivers, while the share of G&A expenses relative to revenue remained substantial at **58.7 % in 2018** and likely increased further in 2019.

synth_text.title: Growth in General and Administrative Expenses: 2018‑2019 Overview
synth_text.text:
In fiscal 2019, Shopify’s General and Administrative (G&A) expenses reached **$178.9 million**, representing **11.3 % of total revenue**. This marks a substantial rise from fiscal 2018, when G&A costs were **$107.4 million**, or **10.0 % of revenue**.  

The increase of **$71.5 million (66.5 %)** in 2019 was driven by several key factors:

* **Employee‑related costs** grew by $28.7 million, including $12.2 million for stock‑based compensation and related payroll taxes.  
* **Finance costs** rose $14.9 million, reflecting a non‑recurring HST liability of $8.1 million, plus higher taxes, insurance, and bank fees.  
* **Shopify Payments losses** increased by $9.0 million due to higher gross merchandise volume processed through the service.  
* **Shopify Capital losses and insurance** climbed $8.6 million as the capital‑offering program expanded.  
* **Professional services** (legal and tax) rose $6.9 million, supporting international expansion and overall business growth.  
* **Computer and software costs** and **general bad‑debt expense** added $1.8 million and $1.6 million respectively.

In 2018, G&A expenses had already risen by $39.7 million (58.7 %) compared with 2017, primarily because of $30.3 million in additional employee‑related costs, higher professional‑services fees, modest finance cost increases, and greater computer/software spending.  

Overall, the data illustrate a clear upward trend in Shopify’s administrative overhead, reflecting both the company’s rapid scaling and the associated investments in personnel, financial infrastructure, and service expansion.

synth_text.title: Group Financial Position Summary – Assets, Liabilities and Equity (S$ million)
synth_text.text:
**Financial Position Overview**

The Group’s balance sheet shows a stable financial position across the two reporting periods. Total assets remained around **S$ 48.9 billion**, with a modest decline from **S$ 48,915 million** to **S$ 48,496 million**. This stability reflects the addition of Videology assets and the equity interest in Airtel Africa, which were largely offset by currency‑translation effects.

* **Current assets** decreased slightly from **S$ 7,078 million** to **S$ 6,759 million**, while **non‑current assets** were virtually unchanged (≈ S$ 41.8 billion).  
* **Total liabilities** rose modestly, moving from **S$ 19,105 million** to **S$ 18,784 million**. The increase is attributed to higher trade payables linked to handset‑leasing programmes and ongoing network investments.  
* **Net assets** (equity) stayed steady at roughly **S$ 29.8 billion**. Share capital remained constant at **S$ 4,127 million**, and retained earnings grew marginally from **S$ 27,513 million** to **S$ 27,269 million**.  

**Currency‑Translation Impact**

The **currency‑translation reserve** widened from **–S$ 1,768 million** to **–S$ 1,284 million**, reflecting translation losses primarily due to a weaker Australian Dollar and Indian Rupee against the Singapore Dollar. These losses stem from translating the net assets of foreign subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures denominated in Australian Dollar, Indian Rupee, Indonesian Rupiah, Philippine Peso, Thai Baht and US Dollar.

Overall, despite minor fluctuations in asset composition and a slight rise in liabilities, the Group’s financial health remains robust, underpinned by stable equity and manageable translation effects.

text.value: (8) LONG-TERM DEBT

On September 23, 2016, Roper entered into a five-year $2.5 billion unsecured credit facility, as amended December 2, 2016, (the “2016 Facility”) with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., as administrative agent, and a syndicate of lenders, which replaced its previous $1.85 billion unsecured credit facility dated as of July 27, 2012, as amended as of October 28, 2015 (the “2012 Facility”). The 2016 Facility comprises a five year $2.5 billion revolving credit facility, which includes availability of up to $150.0 for letters of credit. Roper may also, subject to compliance with specified conditions, request term loans or additional revolving credit commitments in an aggregate amount not to exceed $500.0. At December 31, 2019, there were $0.0 of outstanding borrowings under the 2016 Facility.

The 2016 Facility contains affirmative and negative covenants which, among other things, limit Roper’s ability to incur new debt, enter into certain mergers and acquisitions, sell assets and grant liens, make restricted payments (including the payment of dividends on our common stock) and capital expenditures, or change its line of business. Roper is also subject to financial covenants which require the Company to limit its consolidated total leverage ratio and to maintain a consolidated interest coverage ratio. The most restrictive covenant is the consolidated total leverage ratio which is limited to 3.50 to 1.

The 2016 Facility provides that the consolidated total leverage ratio may be increased, no more than twice during the term of the 2016 Facility, to 4.00 to 1 for a consecutive four quarter fiscal period per increase (or, for any portion of such four quarter fiscal period in which the maximum would be 4.25 to 1). In conjunction with the Deltek acquisition in December of 2016, we increased the maximum consolidated total leverage ratio covenant to 4.25 to 1 through June 30, 2017 and 4.00 to 1 through December 31, 2017.
The Company was in compliance with its debt covenants throughout the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2018.

On August 26, 2019, the Company completed a public offering of $500.0 aggregate principal amount of 2.35% senior unsecured notes due September 15, 2024 and $700.0 aggregate principal amount of 2.95% senior unsecured notes due September 15, 2029 (the “2019 Offering”). The notes bear interest at a fixed rate and are payable semi-annually in arrears on March 15 and September 15 of each year, beginning March 15, 2020. The net proceeds were used to fund a portion of the purchase of iPipeline Holdings, Inc.

On August 28, 2018, the Company completed a public offering of $700.0 aggregate principal amount of 3.65% senior unsecured notes due September 15, 2023 and $800.0 aggregate principal amount of 4.20% senior unsecured notes due September 15, 2028 (the “2018 Offering”). The notes bear interest at a fixed rate and are payable semi-annually in arrears on March 15 and September 15 of each year, beginning March 15, 2019.

On December 19, 2016, the Company completed a public offering of $500.0 aggregate principal amount of 2.80% senior unsecured notes due December 15, 2021 and $700.0 aggregate principal amount of 3.80% senior unsecured notes due December 15, 2026. The notes bear interest at a fixed rate and are payable semi-annually in arrears on June 15 and December 15 of each year, beginning June 15, 2017.

On December 7, 2015, the Company completed a public offering of $600.0 aggregate principal amount of 3.00% senior unsecured notes due December 15, 2020 and $300.0 aggregate principal amount of 3.85% senior unsecured notes due December 15, 2025. The notes bear interest at a fixed rate and are payable semi-annually in arrears on June 15 and December 15 of each year, beginning June 15, 2016.

On November 21, 2012, the Company completed a public offering of $500.0 aggregate principal amount of 3.125% senior unsecured notes due November 15, 2022. The notes bear interest at a fixed rate and are payable semi-annually in arrears on May 15 and November 15 of each year, beginning May 15, 2013.

During 2018 a portion of the net proceeds of the 2018 Offering were used to redeem all of the $500.0 of outstanding 2019 Notes. The Company incurred a debt extinguishment charge in connection with the redemption of the 2019 Notes of $15.9, which represents the make-whole premium and unamortized deferred financing costs.
